Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Fully Self-Enlightened One.

Saṃyuttanikāye

In the Connected Discourses

Sagāthāvagga-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary to the Section with Verses

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ[V 1.0001][P 1.0001][M 1.0001], paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ;

Sanarāmaralokagaruṃ, vande sugataṃ gativimuttaṃ.

I pay homage to the Well-Gone One—freed from the destinations, whose heart is cooled by compassion, who has dispelled the utter darkness of ignorance with the lamp of wisdom, the teacher of the world with its humans and devas.

Buddhopi buddhabhāvaṃ, bhāvetvā ceva sacchikatvā ca;

Yaṃ upagato gatamalaṃ, vande tamanuttaraṃ dhammaṃ.

I pay homage to that supreme and stainless Dhamma, by developing and realizing which even the Buddha attained Buddhahood.

Sugatassa orasānaṃ, puttānaṃ mārasenamathanānaṃ;

Aṭṭhannampi samūhaṃ, sirasā vande ariyasaṅghaṃ.

I bow my head to the Noble Sangha, the assembly of the eight, who are the true sons of the Sugata and who crush Māra's army.

Iti [V 1.0002] me pasannamatino, ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ;

Yaṃ suvihatantarāyo, hutvā tassānubhāvena.

Thus, by the power of this merit, which I, with a devoted mind, have acquired through this homage to the Triple Gem, may I, having become one for whom obstacles are well dispelled,

Saṃyuttavaggapaṭimaṇḍitassa, saṃyuttaāgamavarassa;

Buddhānubuddhasaṃvaṇṇitassa, ñāṇappabhedajananassa.

Of the excellent Saṃyutta Āgama, which is adorned with the connected sections, praised by the Buddhas and the enlightened disciples, and which generates varieties of knowledge;

Atthappakāsanatthaṃ, aṭṭhakathā ādito vasisatehi;

Pañcahi yā saṅgītā, anusaṅgītā ca pacchāpi.

For the purpose of explaining the meaning, the commentary which was recited in the beginning by five hundred masters, and was subsequently recited again.

Sīhaḷadīpaṃ pana ābhatātha, vasinā mahāmahindena;

Ṭhapitā sīhaḷabhāsāya, dīpavāsīnamatthāya.

Then, it was brought to the island of Sīhaḷa by the master Mahāmahinda and established in the Sīhaḷa language for the benefit of the island's inhabitants.

Apanetvāna [M 1.0002] tatohaṃ, sīhaḷabhāsaṃ manoramaṃ bhāsaṃ;

Tantinayānucchavikaṃ, āropento vigatadosaṃ.

Therefore, I, having removed the Sīhaḷa language from it, am rendering it into the delightful language of Māgadha, which is free from faults and suitable to the method of the Canon.

Samayaṃ avilomento, therānaṃ theravaṃsadīpānaṃ;

Sunipuṇavinicchayānaṃ, mahāvihāre nivāsīnaṃ.

Not contradicting the doctrine of the Elders who dwell in the Mahāvihāra—they who are lamps of the Elders' lineage and possess keen discernment—

Hitvā [P 1.0002] punappunāgata-matthaṃ, atthaṃ pakāsayissāmi;

Sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ, ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassa.

Having omitted the repeated matter, I will explain the meaning for the delight of good people and for the long-lasting stability of the Dhamma.

Sāvatthipabhūtīnaṃ, nagarānaṃ vaṇṇanā katā heṭṭhā;

Saṅgītīnaṃ dvinnaṃ, yā me atthaṃ vadantena.

The description of cities beginning with Sāvatthī, which I made while explaining the meaning of the two Collections, has already been done in the previous commentaries.

Vitthāravasena sudaṃ, vatthūni ca yāni tattha vuttāni;

Tesampi na idha bhiyyo, vitthārakathaṃ karissāmi.

And whatever subjects were explained there in detail, I will not provide a further detailed explanation of them here.

Suttānaṃ [V 1.0003] pana atthā, na vinā vatthūhi ye pakāsanti;

Tesaṃ pakāsanatthaṃ, vatthūnipi dassayissāmi.

However, for the meanings of those suttas that are not clear without their background stories, I will also present those stories for the sake of clarification.

Sīlakathā dhutadhammā, kammaṭṭhānāni ceva sabbāni;

Cariyāvidhānasahito, jhānasamāpattivitthāro.

The discourse on virtue, the ascetic practices, and all the meditation subjects; the explanation of temperaments, together with the detailed exposition of jhāna and attainments.

Sabbā ca abhiññāyo, paññāsaṅkalananicchayo ceva;

Khandhādhātāyatanindriyāni, ariyāni ceva cattāri.

All the higher knowledges, the ascertainment of the enumeration of wisdom, the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, and the four noble truths.

Saccāni paccayākāradesanā, suparisuddhanipuṇanayā;

Avimuttatantimaggā, vipassanābhāvanā ceva.

The exposition of dependent origination by means of the perfectly pure and subtle method, the path of the unbroken textual lineage, and the development of insight.

Iti pana sabbaṃ yasmā, visuddhimagge mayā suparisuddhaṃ;

Vuttaṃ tasmā bhiyyo, na taṃ idha vicārayissāmi.

And thus, since all this has been set forth by me with perfect purity in the Visuddhimagga, therefore I will not discuss it further here.

“Majjhe visuddhimaggo, esa catunnampi āgamānañhi;

Ṭhatvā pakāsayissati, tattha yathābhāsitamatthaṃ”.

This Path of Purification is indeed in the middle of all four Āgamas; standing, it will reveal the meaning as spoken there.

Icceva kato tasmā, tampi gahetvāna saddhimetāya;

Aṭṭhakathāya vijānatha, saṃyuttavinissitaṃ atthanti.

Thus it was composed; therefore, having taken that also, together with this commentary, understand the meaning that is based on the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

1. Devatāsaṃyuttaṃ

1. Connected Discourses with Devas

1. Naḷavaggo

1. The Chapter on Reeds

1. Oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on Crossing the Flood

Tattha [V 1.0004][M 1.0003] saṃyuttāgamo nāma sagāthāvaggo, nidānavaggo, khandhakavaggo, saḷāyatanavaggo, mahāvaggoti pañcavaggo hoti. Suttato –

Therein, the collection known as the Saṃyutta Āgama consists of five divisions: the Sagāthāvagga, the Nidānavagga, the Khandhakavagga, the Saḷāyatanavagga, and the Mahāvagga. In terms of suttas:

“Satta suttasahassāni, satta suttasatāni ca;

Dvāsaṭṭhi ceva suttāni, eso saṃyuttasaṅgaho”.

Seven thousand suttas, seven hundred suttas, and sixty-two suttas: this is the Saṃyutta Collection.

Bhāṇavārato [P 1.0003] bhāṇavārasataṃ hoti. Tassa vaggesu sagāthāvaggo ādi, suttesu oghataraṇasuttaṃ. Tassāpi “evaṃ me suta”ntiādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānamādi. Sā panesā paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya ādimhi vitthāritā, tasmā sā tattha vitthāritanayeneva veditabbā.

In terms of recitation units, there are one hundred recitation units. Among its divisions, the Sagāthāvagga is the first; among its suttas, the Oghataraṇa Sutta is the first. Of that sutta too, the introduction beginning with 'Thus have I heard,' spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the beginning. Now, this First Great Council has been explained in detail at the beginning of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya; therefore, it should be understood there according to the way it has been elaborated.

1. Yaṃ [P 1.0004] panetaṃ “evaṃ me suta”ntiādikaṃ nidānaṃ, tattha evanti nipātapadaṃ. Metiādīni nāmapadāni. Sāvatthiyaṃ viharatīti ettha vīti upasaggapadaṃ, haratīti ākhyātapadanti iminā tāva nayena padavibhāgo veditabbo.

1. Now, as for this introduction beginning with ‘Thus have I heard,’ therein, ‘evaṃ’ is a particle. The words beginning with ‘me’ are nominals. In the phrase ‘Sāvatthiyaṃ viharati,’ ‘vi’ is a prefix and ‘harati’ is a verb. In this manner, the analysis of the words should first be understood.

Atthato pana evaṃsaddo tāva upamūpadesa-sampahaṃsana-garahaṇa-vacanasampaṭiggahākāranidassanāvadhāraṇādi-anekatthappabhedo. Tathā hesa – “evaṃ jātena maccena, kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti (dha. pa. 53) evamādīsu upamāyaṃ āgato. “Evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ[V 1.0005], evaṃ te paṭikkamitabba”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.122) upadese. “Evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) sampahaṃsane. “Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.187) garahaṇe. “Evaṃ, bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosu”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.1) vacanasampaṭiggahe. “Evaṃ byā kho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.398) ākāre[M 1.0004]. “Ehi tvaṃ māṇavaka, yena samaṇo ānando tenupasaṅkama; upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha – ‘subho māṇavo todeyyaputto bhavantaṃ ānandaṃ appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti. Evañca vadehi – ‘sādhu kira bhavaṃ ānando yena subhassa māṇavassa [P 1.0005] todeyyaputtassa nivesanaṃ, tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā’ti”ādīsu (dī. ni. 1.445) nidassane. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha kālāmā, ime dhammā kusalā vā akusalā vāti? Akusalā, bhante. Sāvajjā vā anavajjā vāti? Sāvajjā, bhante. Viññugarahitā vā viññuppasatthā vāti? Viññugarahitā, bhante. Samattā samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti vā no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotīti? Samattā, bhante, samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti, evaṃ no ettha hotī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) avadhāraṇe. Svāyamidha ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇesu daṭṭhabbo.

But as to its meaning, the word `evaṃ` first of all has many different meanings, such as simile, instruction, approval, censure, acceptance of words, manner, illustration, determination, and so on. For example: "Thus, by a mortal being born, much merit should be done" (Dhp. 53)—here it occurs in the sense of simile. "In this way, you should advance; in this way, you should retreat" (AN 4.122)—here it is used for instruction. "Thus it is, O Blessed One; thus it is, O Well-gone One" (AN 3.66)—here it is used for approval. "Even so, this wretch praises that shaven-headed ascetic on any pretext whatsoever" (SN 1.187)—here it is used for censure. "Yes, venerable sir"—thus those monks responded to the Blessed One (MN 1.1)—here it is used for acceptance of words. "Thus indeed, venerable sir, do I understand the Dhamma as taught by the Blessed One" (MN 1.398)—here it is used to indicate manner. "Go, young man, to the ascetic Ānanda. Having gone, greet the ascetic Ānanda in my name, inquiring whether he is free from illness, free from disease, light in body, strong, and dwelling at ease, saying, ‘The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, inquires about your health.’ And speak thus: ‘It would be good if the venerable Ānanda would approach the residence of the young man Subha, son of Todeyya, out of compassion’" (DN 1.445)—here it is used for illustration. "What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these qualities wholesome or unwholesome?"—"Unwholesome, venerable sir."—"Blameworthy or blameless?"—"Blameworthy, venerable sir."—"Condemned or praised by the wise?"—"Condemned by the wise, venerable sir."—"When undertaken and practiced, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? How does it seem to you in this matter?"—"When undertaken and practiced, venerable sir, they lead to harm and suffering. Thus it seems to us in this matter" (AN 3.66)—here it is used for determination. This word, here, should be understood in the senses of manner, illustration, and determination.

Tattha ākāratthena evaṃsaddena etamatthaṃ dīpeti – nānānayanipuṇaṃ anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ atthabyañjanasampannaṃ vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ dhammatthadesanā paṭivedhagambhīraṃ sabbasattānaṃ sakasakabhāsānurūpato sotapathamāgacchantaṃ tassa bhagavato vacanaṃ sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātuṃ? Sabbathāmena pana sotukāmataṃ janetvāpi evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi ekenākārena sutanti.

Therein, by the word `evaṃ` in the sense of manner, this meaning is revealed: Who is capable of fully understanding the word of that Blessed One—which is subtle with various methods, arisen from manifold intentions, endowed with meaning and expression, causing diverse marvels, profound in the teaching of cause and effect and in its realization, and reaching the ear-path of all beings according to their own language? However, even after generating the desire to listen with all one's efforts, [the meaning is expressed as]: 'Thus have I heard,' that is, 'I too have heard it in one manner.'

Nidassanatthena – “nāhaṃ sayambhū, na mayā idaṃ sacchikata”nti attānaṃ parimocento – “evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi evaṃ suta”nti idāni vattabbaṃ sakalasuttaṃ nidasseti.

In the sense of illustration, by freeing himself from the thought, ‘I am not self-originated, nor have I realized this myself,’ he illustrates the entire sutta that is now to be recited with the words, ‘Thus have I heard; I too have thus heard.’

Avadhāraṇatthena – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando, gatimantānaṃ, satimantānaṃ, dhitimantānaṃ, upaṭṭhākānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando”ti (a. ni. 1.220-223) evaṃ [V 1.0006] bhagavatā – “āyasmā ānando atthakusalo dhammakusalo byañjanakusalo niruttikusalo pubbāparakusalo”ti (a. ni. 5.169) evaṃ dhammasenāpatinā ca pasatthabhāvānurūpaṃ attano dhāraṇabalaṃ dassento sattānaṃ sotukāmataṃ janeti – “evaṃ me sutaṃ, tañca kho atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnamanadhikaṃ, evameva na aññathā daṭṭhabba”nti.

In the sense of determination: showing his own power of retention, in accordance with his being praised thus by the Blessed One—‘This, monks, is the foremost among my monk disciples who are learned, namely Ānanda; among those who are wise, who are mindful, who are resolute, who are attendants, namely Ānanda’ (AN 1.220-223)—and thus by the General of the Dhamma—‘Venerable Ānanda is skilled in meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in expression, skilled in language, skilled in what precedes and what follows’ (AN 5.169)—he generates in beings the desire to listen, [saying]: ‘Exactly thus have I heard, and that [hearing] is neither deficient nor excessive in meaning or in expression; it should be regarded in this very way and not otherwise.’

Mesaddo [M 1.0005] tīsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hissa – “gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyya”ntiādīsu (su. ni. 81) mayāti attho. “Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū [P 1.0006]” tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.88) mayhanti attho. “Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavathā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.29) mamāti attho. Idha pana “mayā suta”nti ca “mama suta”nti ca atthadvaye yujjati.

The word 'me' is seen in three meanings. For example, in 'Verses sung by me are not to be eaten' (Sn. 81), it means 'by me.' In 'Good, venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma briefly' (SN 4.88), it means 'to me.' In 'Be my heirs in the Dhamma, monks' (MN 1.29), it means 'my.' Here, however, the word 'me' is applicable in two senses: as 'heard by me' (mayā sutaṃ) and as 'my hearing' (mama sutaṃ).

Sutanti ayaṃ sutasaddo saupasaggo anupasaggo ca gamana-vissuta-kilinnaupacitānuyoga-sotaviññeyya-sotadvārānusāraviññātādianekatthappabhedo. Tathā hissa – “senāya pasuto”tiādīsu gacchantoti attho. “Sutadhammassa passato”tiādīsu (udā. 11) vissutadhammassāti attho. “Avassutā avassutassā”tiādīsu (pāci. 657) kilinnākilinnassāti attho. “Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappaka”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 7.12) upacitanti attho. “Ye jhānapasutā dhīrā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 181) jhānānuyuttāti attho. “Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.241) sotaviññeyyanti attho. “Sutadharo sutasannicayo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.339) sotadvārānusāraviññātadharoti attho. Idha panassa sotadvārānusārena upadhāritanti vā upadhāraṇanti vā attho. Me-saddassa hi mayāti atthe sati – “evaṃ mayā sutaṃ, sotadvārānusārena upadhārita”nti yujjati. Mamāti atthe sati – “evaṃ mama sutaṃ, sotadvārānusārena upadhāraṇa”nti yujjati.

The word 'suta', whether with or without a prefix, has various meanings, such as: going, well-known, stained, accumulated, devoted, knowable through ear-consciousness, and known by recollecting what has come through the ear-door. Thus, in passages such as 'senāya pasuto', it means 'going'. In passages such as 'sutadhammassa passato', it means 'of one with well-known Dhamma'. In passages such as 'avassutā avassutassā', it means 'stained, for the stained'. In passages such as 'tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ', it means 'accumulated'. In passages such as 'ye jhānapasutā dhīrā', it means 'devoted to jhāna'. In passages such as 'diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ', it means 'knowable through ear-consciousness'. In passages such as 'sutadharo sutasannicayo', it means 'one who retains what is known by recollecting what has come through the ear-door'. Here, however, it means 'ascertained' or 'ascertainment' by recollecting what has come through the ear-door. For, when the word 'me' means 'by me', it is suitable as: 'Thus by me it was heard, ascertained by recollecting what has come through the ear-door.' When it means 'of me', it is suitable as: 'Thus is my hearing, an ascertainment by recollecting what has come through the ear-door.'

Evametesu tīsu padesu evanti sotaviññāṇādiviññāṇakiccanidassanaṃ. Meti vuttaviññāṇasamaṅgipuggalanidassanaṃ. Sutanti assavanabhāvapaṭikkhepato anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassanaṃ. Tathā evanti tassa sotadvārānusārena pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā nānappakārena ārammaṇe [V 1.0007] pavattibhāvappakāsanaṃ. Meti attappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti dhammappakāsanaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepo – “nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā mayā na aññaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ pana kataṃ, ayaṃ dhammo suto”ti.

Thus, in these three terms, 'evaṃ' is an indication of the function of consciousness, beginning with ear-consciousness. 'Me' is an indication of the individual endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. 'Sutaṃ', by way of rejecting the state of non-hearing, is an indication of apprehension that is not deficient, not excessive, and not perverted. Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is a disclosure of the occurrence of that stream of consciousness—which arises by following the ear-door—in various ways with respect to the object. 'Me' is a disclosure of the self. 'Sutaṃ' is a disclosure of the Dhamma. Herein, this is the summary: 'By me, with the stream of consciousness proceeding in various ways with respect to the object, nothing else was done; but this was done: this Dhamma was heard.'

Tathā [M 1.0006] evanti niddisitabbappakāsanaṃ. Meti puggalappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti puggalakiccappakāsanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yaṃ suttaṃ niddisissāmi, taṃ mayā evaṃ suta”nti.

Likewise, 'evaṃ' is a disclosure of that which is to be indicated. 'Me' is a disclosure of the individual. 'Sutaṃ' is a disclosure of the individual's function. This is what is meant: 'Whatever discourse I shall indicate, that was heard by me thus.'

Tathā evanti yassa cittasantānassa nānākārappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanagahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa nānākāraniddeso[P 1.0007]. Evanti hi ayaṃ ākārapaññatti. Meti kattuniddeso. Sutanti visayaniddeso. Ettāvatā nānākārappavattena cittasantānena taṃsamaṅgino kattuvisaye gahaṇasanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ hoti.

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is a designation of the various modes of that mental continuum, through whose functioning in various modes the grasping of various meanings and expressions occurs. For this 'evaṃ' is a designation of mode. 'Me' is a designation of the agent. 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of the object. By this much, through the mental continuum functioning in various modes, the determination of grasping in the agent's object-field is accomplished for one endowed with that continuum.

Atha vā evanti puggalakiccaniddeso. Sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso. Meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – “mayā savanakiccaviññāṇasamaṅginā puggalena viññāṇavasena laddhasavanakiccavohārena suta”nti.

Alternatively, 'evaṃ' is a designation of the individual's function. 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of consciousness's function. 'Me' is a designation of the individual endowed with both functions. Herein, this is the summary: 'It was heard by me, an individual endowed with the consciousness that has the function of hearing, who, by way of consciousness, has acquired the designation of the function of hearing.'

Tattha evanti ca meti ca saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññatti. Kiñhettha taṃ paramatthato atthi, yaṃ evanti vā meti vā niddesaṃ labhetha. Sutanti vijjamānapaññatti. Yañhi taṃ ettha sotena upaladdhaṃ, taṃ paramatthato vijjamānanti. Tathā evanti ca meti ca taṃ taṃ upādāya vattabbato upādāpaññatti. Sutanti diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato upanidhāpaññatti.

Therein, both 'evaṃ' and 'me' are non-existent designations by way of ultimate reality in its true sense. For what is there herein that exists in an ultimate sense, which could obtain the designation 'evaṃ' or 'me'? 'Sutaṃ' is an existent designation. For whatever phenomenon is apprehended herein by the ear, that phenomenon exists in an ultimate sense. Furthermore, both 'evaṃ' and 'me', because they are spoken of in dependence on this or that, are dependent designations. 'Sutaṃ', because it is spoken of in comparison with things seen, etc., is a comparative designation.

Ettha ca evanti vacanena asammohaṃ dīpeti. Na hi sammūḷho nānappakārapaṭivedhasamattho hoti. Sutanti vacanena sutassa asammosaṃ dīpeti. Yassa hi sutaṃ sammuṭṭhaṃ hoti, na so kālantarena mayā sutanti paṭijānāti. Iccassa asammohena paññāsiddhi, asammosena pana satisiddhi. Tattha paññāpubbaṅgamāya satiyā byañjanāvadhāraṇasamatthatā, satipubbaṅgamāya paññāya atthapaṭivedhasamatthatā[V 1.0008]. Tadubhayasamatthatāyogena atthabyañjanasampannassa dhammakosassa anupālanasamatthato dhammabhaṇḍāgārikattasiddhi.

And here, by the word 'evaṃ', he indicates non-bewilderment. For one who is bewildered is not capable of penetrating the various aspects. By the word 'sutaṃ', he indicates non-forgetfulness of what was heard. For one for whom what was heard has been forgotten does not, after a long time, acknowledge, 'It was heard by me.' Thus, for him, by non-bewilderment, the accomplishment of wisdom occurs, and by non-forgetfulness, the accomplishment of mindfulness occurs. Therein, by mindfulness which has wisdom as its forerunner, the capacity for retaining the phrasing is accomplished; by wisdom which has mindfulness as its forerunner, the capacity for penetrating the meaning is accomplished. Through the union of the capacity for both, due to the ability to maintain the treasury of the Dhamma, complete with meaning and phrasing, the accomplishment of the state of being a treasurer of the Dhamma occurs.

Aparo nayo – evanti vacanena yoniso manasikāraṃ dīpeti, ayoniso manasikaroto hi nānappakārapaṭivedhābhāvato. Sutanti vacanena avikkhepaṃ dīpeti vikkhittacittassa savanābhāvato. Tathā hi vikkhittacitto puggalo sabbasampattiyā vuccamānopi “na mayā sutaṃ, puna [M 1.0007] bhaṇathā”ti bhaṇati. Yoniso manasikārena cettha attasammāpaṇidhiṃ pubbe ca katapuññataṃ sādheti, sammā appaṇihitattassa pubbe akatapuññassa vā tadabhāvato. Avikkhepena [P 1.0008] saddhammassavanaṃ sappurisūpanissayañca sādheti. Na hi vikkhittacitto sotuṃ sakkoti, na ca sappurise anupanissayamānassa savanaṃ atthīti.

Another method: By the word 'evaṃ', he indicates appropriate attention, for in one who applies the mind inappropriately, there is an absence of penetrating the various aspects. By the word 'sutaṃ', he indicates non-distraction, for there is an absence of hearing for one with a distracted mind. Indeed, a person with a distracted mind, even when spoken to with all completeness, says, 'It was not heard by me; speak again.' And here, by appropriate attention, one accomplishes the right directing of oneself and the state of having previously done meritorious deeds, because of its absence in one who has not rightly directed oneself or has not previously done meritorious deeds. By non-distraction, one accomplishes the hearing of the good Dhamma and reliance on noble persons. For one with a distracted mind is not able to hear, and for one who does not rely on noble persons, there is no hearing.

Aparo nayo – yasmā “evanti yassa cittasantānassa nānākārappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa nānākāraniddeso”ti vuttaṃ, so ca evaṃ bhaddako ākāro na sammā appaṇihitattano pubbe akatapuññassa vā hoti, tasmā evanti iminā bhaddakena ākārena pacchimacakkadvayasampattimattano dīpeti. Sutanti savanayogena purimacakkadvayasampattiṃ. Na hi appatirūpadese vasato sappurisūpanissayavirahitassa vā savanaṃ atthi. Iccassa pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyā āsayasuddhi siddhā hoti, purimacakkadvayasiddhiyā payogasuddhi, tāya ca āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhi, payogasuddhiyā āgamabyattisiddhi. Iti payogāsayasuddhassa āgamādhigamasampannassa vacanaṃ aruṇuggaṃ viya sūriyassa udayato, yoniso manasikāro viya ca kusalakammassa, arahati bhagavato vacanassa pubbaṅgamaṃ bhavitunti ṭhāne nidānaṃ ṭhapento evaṃ me sutantiādimāha.

Another method: Because it was said, “'Evaṃ' is the designation of the various modes of a mind-continuum whose functioning in various ways is the grasping of diverse meanings and expressions,” and that excellent mode does not belong to one whose self is not rightly directed or who has not previously made merit; therefore, by this word 'evaṃ', with this excellent mode, he indicates his own attainment of the two later wheels. By 'sutaṃ', through the connection with hearing, he indicates the attainment of the two former wheels. For there is no hearing for one dwelling in an unsuitable place or for one devoid of reliance on true persons. Thus, for him, by the accomplishment of the two later wheels, purity of aspiration is accomplished; by the accomplishment of the two former wheels, purity of effort is accomplished. And by that purity of aspiration, the accomplishment of skill in attainment is achieved; by the purity of effort, the accomplishment of skill in the scriptures is achieved. Thus, the word of one who possesses purity of effort and aspiration, who is accomplished in the scriptures and attainment, is worthy to be the forerunner of the Blessed One’s word, just as the break of dawn is worthy to be the forerunner of the rising sun, and just as wise attention is worthy to be the forerunner of wholesome kamma. Thus, wishing to establish the introduction in its proper place, Ānanda said the words beginning with, 'Thus have I heard.'

Aparo nayo – evanti iminā nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakena vacanena attano atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Sutanti iminā sotabbabhedapaṭivedhadīpakena dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ. Evanti ca idaṃ yoniso manasikāradīpakavacanaṃ bhāsamāno – “ete mayā dhammā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā”ti dīpeti. Sutanti idaṃ savanayogadīpakavacanaṃ bhāsamāno – “bahū mayā dhammā sutā dhātā vacasā paricitā”ti dīpeti. Tadubhayenapi atthabyañjanapāripūriṃ dīpento savane ādaraṃ janeti. Atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇañhi [V 1.0009] dhammaṃ ādarena assuṇanto mahatā [P 1.0009] hitā paribāhiro hotīti ādaraṃ janetvā sakkaccaṃ dhammo sotabboti.

Another method: By this word 'Thus,' a statement indicating the penetration of various kinds, he indicates the manifest existence of his own accomplishment in the analytical knowledges of meaning and spontaneous exposition. By this word 'Heard,' a statement indicating the penetration of the divisions of what is to be heard, he indicates the manifest existence of his own accomplishment in the analytical knowledges of the Dhamma and of language. And speaking this word 'Thus,' a statement indicating wise attention, he indicates: “These Dhammas have been repeatedly reflected upon by me with the mind and well penetrated by wisdom.” Speaking this word 'Heard,' a statement indicating the connection with hearing, he indicates: “Many Dhammas have been heard by me, borne in mind, and familiarized by recitation.” By both, while indicating the completeness in meaning and expression, he generates reverence in hearing. For one who does not listen with reverence to the Dhamma that is complete in meaning and expression is excluded from great benefit. Therefore, having generated reverence, the Dhamma should be listened to respectfully.

Evaṃ [M 1.0008] me sutanti iminā pana sakalena vacanena āyasmā ānando tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammaṃ attano adahanto asappurisabhūmiṃ atikkamati, sāvakattaṃ paṭijānanto sappurisabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asaddhammā cittaṃ vuṭṭhāpeti, saddhamme cittaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. “Kevalaṃ sutamevetaṃ mayā, tasseva pana bhagavato vacana”nti dīpento attānaṃ parimoceti, satthāraṃ apadisati, jinavacanaṃ appeti, dhammanettiṃ patiṭṭhāpeti.

With this entire statement, 'Thus have I heard,' the Venerable Ānanda, not placing the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the domain of the ignoble. Acknowledging the state of being a disciple, he enters the domain of the noble. Thus, he causes the mind to rise from the false Dhamma and establishes the mind in the true Dhamma. By showing, 'This is merely what has been heard by me; it is the word of that Blessed One alone,' he frees himself, refers to the Teacher, presents the word of the Conqueror, and establishes the guideline of the Dhamma.

Apica “evaṃ me suta”nti attanā uppāditabhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto purimavacanaṃ vivaranto – “sammukhā paṭiggahitamidaṃ mayā tassa bhagavato catuvesārajjavisāradassa dasabaladharassa āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyino sīhanādanādino sabbasattuttamassa dhammissarassa dhammarājassa dhammādhipatino dhammadīpassa dhammasaraṇassa saddhammavaracakkavattino sammāsambuddhassa vacanaṃ, na ettha atthe vā dhamme vā pade vā byañjane vā kaṅkhā vā vimati vā kattabbā”ti sabbadevamanussānaṃ imasmiṃ dhamme assaddhiyaṃ vināseti, saddhāsampadaṃ uppādetīti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Furthermore, by the statement, ‘Thus have I heard,’ not acknowledging the state of having produced it himself but clarifying the previous statement, he declares: 'This word was received by me in the presence of that Blessed One—who is skilled in the four kinds of fearlessness, the bearer of the ten powers, who stands in the place of the bull, who utters the lion’s roar, the most excellent of all beings, the lord of the Dhamma, the king of the Dhamma, the sovereign of the Dhamma, the lamp of the Dhamma, the refuge of the Dhamma, the supreme wheel-turning monarch of the true Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, no strong doubt or weak wavering should be made regarding the meaning, or the text, or the word, or the letter.' Thus, he destroys the disbelief of all devas and humans in this Dhamma and causes the accomplishment of faith to arise. Therefore, it is said:

“Vināsayati assaddhaṃ, saddhaṃ vaḍḍheti sāsane;

Evaṃ me sutamiccevaṃ, vadaṃ gotamasāvako”ti.

The disciple of Gotama, by saying, 'Thus have I heard,' destroys disbelief and increases faith in the Dispensation.

Ekanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Samayanti paricchinnaniddeso. Ekaṃ samayanti aniyamitaparidīpanaṃ. Tattha samayasaddo –

'Ekaṃ' is an indication of numerical demarcation. 'Samayaṃ' is an indication of what is delimited. 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ' is an illustration of the indefinite. Therein, the word 'samaya'—

“Samavāye khaṇe kāle, samūhe hetudiṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati”.

It is seen in concurrence of causes, opportunity, time, assembly, cause, view, attainment, abandonment, and penetration.

Tathā hissa “appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.447) samavāyo attho. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo [V 1.0010] ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) khaṇo. “Uṇhasamayo pariḷāhasamayo”tiādīsu (pāci. 358) kālo. “Mahāsamayo [P 1.0010] pavanasmi”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.332) samūho. “Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi, bhagavā kho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, bhagavāpi maṃ jānissati – ‘bhaddāli, nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya aparipūrakārī’ti. Ayampi kho te[M 1.0009], bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.135) hetu. “Tena kho pana samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.260) diṭṭhi.

Thus, for this word, in such passages as, 'Perhaps we might approach even tomorrow, having considered the time and the occasion,' the meaning is 'concurrence of causes.' In such passages as, 'Monks, there is but one opportunity and one opportune moment for living the holy life,' the meaning is 'opportunity.' In such passages as, 'the hot season, the scorching season,' the meaning is 'time.' In such passages as, 'A great assembly in the forest,' the meaning is 'assembly.' In such passages as, 'You, Bhaddāli, also did not penetrate the cause; the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, and the Blessed One would know of me: “The monk named Bhaddāli is one who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.” This too, Bhaddāli, was a cause you did not penetrate,' the meaning is 'cause.' In such passages as, 'Now at that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, an exponent of views, was dwelling at Ekasālaka in Mallikā's park at Tindukācīra,' the meaning is 'view.'

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. –

Whatever benefit there is in this present life, and whatever benefit pertains to the future life; through the attainment of this twofold benefit, the wise one is called 'learned'.

Ādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.129) paṭilābho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.28) pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 2.8) paṭivedho. Idha panassa kālo attho. Tena saṃvacchara-utu-māsaḍḍhamāsa-ratti-diva-pubbaṇha-majjhanhika-sāyanha-paṭhamamajjhimapacchimayāma-muhuttādīsu kālappabhedabhūtesu samayesu ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti.

In such passages, its meaning is 'attainment.' In such passages as, 'By the complete abandonment of conceit, he made an end of suffering,' its meaning is 'abandonment.' In such passages as, 'Of suffering, the meaning is oppression, the meaning is being conditioned, the meaning is torment, the meaning is change, and the meaning is to be penetrated,' its meaning is 'penetration.' Here, however, its meaning is 'time.' By this, it indicates 'one time' among the divisions of time, such as year, season, month, half-month, night, day, forenoon, midday, afternoon, the first, middle, and last watches of the night, moment, and so on.

Tattha kiñcāpi etesu saṃvaccharādīsu samayesu yaṃ yaṃ suttaṃ yasmiṃ yasmiṃ saṃvacchare utumhi māse pakkhe rattibhāge divasabhāge vā vuttaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ therassa suviditaṃ suvavatthāpitaṃ paññāya. Yasmā pana “evaṃ me sutaṃ asukasaṃvacchare asukautumhi asukamāse asukapakkhe asukarattibhāge asukadivasabhāge vā”ti evaṃ vutte na sakkā sukhena dhāretuṃ vā uddisituṃ vā uddisāpetuṃ vā, bahu ca vattabbaṃ hoti, tasmā ekeneva padena tamatthaṃ samodhānetvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha.

In this regard, although it was well known and well established for the Elder through wisdom in which year, season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day each and every sutta was spoken among those times beginning with the year, yet because, were it said, 'Thus have I heard: in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight, in such-and-such a part of the night, or in such-and-such a part of the day,' it would not be possible to easily bear in mind, recite, or cause to be recited, and much would have to be said; therefore, having combined that meaning into a single term, he said, 'at one time.'

Ye vā ime gabbhokkantisamayo jātisamayo saṃvegasamayo abhinikkhamanasamayo dukkarakārikasamayo māravijayasamayo abhisambodhisamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo desanāsamayo parinibbānasamayoti evamādayo bhagavato devamanussesu ativiya suppakāsā [P 1.0011] anekakālappabhedā [V 1.0011] eva samayā. Tesu samayesu desanāsamayasaṅkhātaṃ ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti. Yo cāyaṃ ñāṇakaruṇākiccasamayesu karuṇākiccasamayo, attahitaparahitapaṭipattisamayesu parahitapaṭipattisamayo[M 1.0010], sannipatitānaṃ karaṇīyadvayasamayesu dhammikathāsamayo, desanāpaṭipattisamayesu desanāsamayo, tesupi samayesu aññataraṃ sandhāya “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha.

Or, there are these times of the Blessed One—such as the time of conception, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency, the time of renunciation, the time of practicing austerities, the time of conquering Māra, the time of perfect enlightenment, the time of dwelling in bliss in the present life, the time of teaching, and the time of Parinibbāna—which are indeed times with many distinctions, exceedingly well-known among gods and humans. Among these times, he indicates 'one time' as that which is designated the time of teaching. Furthermore, referring to any one of these times—that which, among the times for the tasks of wisdom and compassion, is the time for the task of compassion; that which, among the times for practicing for one's own welfare and for the welfare of others, is the time for practicing for the welfare of others; that which, among the times for the two duties for those assembled, is the time for righteous discourse; and that which, among the times for teaching and practice, is the time for teaching—he said 'at one time'.

Kasmā panettha yathā abhidhamme “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacara”nti ca ito aññesu suttapadesu “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehī”ti ca bhummavacanena niddeso kato, vinaye ca “tena samayena buddho bhagavā”ti karaṇavacanena, tathā akatvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti upayogavacanena niddeso katoti. Tattha tathā, idha ca aññathā atthasambhavato. Tattha hi abhidhamme ito aññesu suttapadesu ca adhikaraṇattho bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattho ca sambhavati. Adhikaraṇañhi kālattho samūhattho ca samayo, tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa ca samayassa bhāvena tesaṃ bhāvo lakkhīyati. Tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha bhummavacananiddeso kato.

Why here is the indication made with 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' using the accusative case, and not as it is done in the Abhidhamma with 'at the time when [consciousness is] of the sense-sphere,' and in other Sutta passages other than this one with 'at the time when, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures,' where the indication is made with the locative case; nor as it is done in the Vinaya with 'at that time the Buddha, the Blessed One,' where it is with the instrumental case? Because there the meaning is possible in that way, whereas here it is possible in another way. For there, in the Abhidhamma and in other Sutta passages other than this one, the meaning of a basis (adhikaraṇa) and the meaning of a characteristic by means of an occurrence (bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇa) are possible. Indeed, the word 'samaya', functioning as a basis (adhikaraṇa), has the meaning of time and the meaning of a collection. Therein, by the occurrence of the 'samaya'—which is designated as the momentary, concomitant cause—the occurrence of those phenomena such as contact, which are mentioned therein, is marked. Therefore, to illuminate those meanings, the indication there is made with the locative case.

Vinaye ca hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Yo hi so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo sāriputtādīhipi dubbiññeyyo, tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtena ca sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsi. Tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha karaṇavacanena niddeso kato.

And in the Vinaya, the meaning of cause (hetu) and the meaning of instrument (karaṇa) are possible. For that occasion for the promulgation of the training rule was difficult to be known even by Sāriputta and others. By means of that occasion, which served as a cause and an instrument, the Blessed One, while promulgating the training rules and considering the cause for their promulgation, dwelt in various places. Therefore, to illuminate those meanings, the indication there is made with the instrumental case.

Idha pana aññasmiṃ ca evaṃjātike accantasaṃyogattho sambhavati. Yañhi samayaṃ bhagavā imaṃ aññaṃ vā suttantaṃ desesi, accantameva taṃ samayaṃ karuṇāvihārena vihāsi. Tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ idha upayogavacananiddeso katoti.

Here, however, and in other similar instances, the meaning of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga) is possible. For during the entire time the Blessed One taught this or another discourse, he dwelt continuously with the abiding in compassion. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication here is made with the accusative case.

Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Therefore, this is said:

“Taṃ taṃ atthamapekkhitvā, bhummena karaṇena ca;

Aññatra samayo vutto, upayogena so idhā”ti.

“Having considered each respective meaning, elsewhere the word ‘samaya’ is stated by means of the locative and instrumental cases; here, that word is stated by means of the accusative.”

Porāṇā [V 1.0012][P 1.0012] pana vaṇṇayanti – “tasmiṃ samaye”ti vā “tena samayenā”ti vā “ekaṃ samaya”nti vā abhilāpamattabhedo esa, sabbattha bhummameva [M 1.0011] atthoti. Tasmā “ekaṃ samaya”nti vuttepi “ekasmiṃ samaye”ti attho veditabbo.

The ancient commentators, however, explain: Whether it is 'tasmiṃ samaye' or 'tena samayena' or 'ekaṃ samayaṃ', this is a difference merely in expression; in all cases, the meaning is indeed that of the locative case. Therefore, even when 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' is said, the meaning should be understood as 'ekasmiṃ samaye'.

Bhagavāti garu. Garuṃ hi loke “bhagavā”ti vadanti. Ayañca sabbaguṇavisiṭṭhatāya sabbasattānaṃ garu, tasmā “bhagavā”ti veditabbo. Porāṇehipi vuttaṃ –

Bhagavā means 'the venerable one'. For in the world, they call a venerable one 'bhagavā'. And this one, due to being distinguished by all virtues, is venerable to all beings; therefore, he should be understood as 'Bhagavā'. It has also been said by the ancients:

“Bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garu gāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti. (visuddhi. 1.142);

“The word 'Bhagavā' is excellent, the word 'Bhagavā' is supreme; He is venerable and endowed with reverence, for that reason he is called 'Bhagavā'.”

Apica –

Moreover:

“Bhagyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti. –

“Possessing fortune (bhagyavā), having broken (bhaggavā) defilements, and endowed (yutto) with the special qualities (bhagehi); having analyzed (vibhattavā) the dhammas, having frequented (bhattavā) noble states, and having given up travel (vantagamano) in the states of existence (bhavesu); for these reasons (tato) he is Bhagavā.”

Imissā gāthāya vasenassa padassa vitthārato attho veditabbo. So ca visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.144) buddhānussatiniddese vuttoyeva.

By means of this verse, the meaning of this term should be understood in detail. And that has indeed been stated in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of the Recollection of the Buddha.

Ettāvatā cettha evaṃ me sutanti vacanena yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ dassento bhagavato dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karoti. Tena “nayidaṃ atikkantasatthukaṃ pāvacanaṃ, ayaṃ vo satthā”ti satthu adassanena ukkaṇṭhitaṃ janaṃ samassāseti. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavāti vacanena tasmiṃ samaye bhagavato avijjamānabhāvaṃ dassento rūpakāyaparinibbānaṃ sādheti. Tena “evaṃvidhassa nāma ariyadhammassa desako dasabaladharo vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyo sopi bhagavā parinibbuto, kena aññena jīvite āsā janetabbā”ti jīvitamadamattaṃ janaṃ saṃvejeti, saddhamme cassa ussāhaṃ janeti. Evanti ca bhaṇanto desanāsampattiṃ niddisati. Me sutanti sāvakasampattiṃ. Ekaṃ samayanti kālasampattiṃ. Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ.

Herein, by this much, with the words 'Thus have I heard', he who presents the Dhamma as it was heard makes the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One manifest. Thereby, he comforts the people distressed by not seeing the Teacher, saying, 'This teaching is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this is your Teacher.' With the words 'At one time, the Blessed One', by showing the non-existence of the Blessed One at that time, he establishes the Parinibbāna of the form-body. Thereby, he stirs with spiritual urgency the people intoxicated with the pride of life, saying, 'Even that Blessed One—the teacher of such a noble Dhamma, the possessor of the ten powers, with a body like a solid diamond—has attained Parinibbāna. By what other person should hope in life be generated?' And he generates enthusiasm in them for the good Dhamma. And by saying 'Thus', he indicates the perfection of the teaching. By 'have I heard', the perfection of the disciple. By 'At one time', the perfection of the time. By 'The Blessed One', the perfection of the teacher.

Sāvatthiyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Samīpatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Viharatīti [P 1.0013] avisesena iriyāpathadibbabrahmaariyavihāresu [V 1.0013] aññataravihārasamaṅgīparidīpanametaṃ. Idha pana ṭhānagamananisajjāsayanappabhedesu iriyāpathesu aññatarairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ[M 1.0012], tena ṭhitopi gacchantopi nisinnopi sayānopi bhagavā viharaticceva veditabbo. So hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavatteti, tasmā “viharatī”ti vuccati.

Sāvatthiyaṃ means: in the city so named. And this is a term in the locative case in the sense of proximity. The word 'viharati' (dwells) is a term that indicates, without distinction, being endowed with any one of the abidings: the abiding of posture, the divine abiding, the sublime abiding, or the noble abiding. Here, however, it indicates being well-associated with any one of the postures, which are divided into standing, walking, sitting, and lying down. Therefore, it should be understood thus: whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, the Blessed One 'dwells'. Indeed, having cut off the affliction of one posture with another posture, he carries on and causes his existence to proceed without collapsing; therefore, it is said, 'he dwells'.

Jetavaneti jetassa rājakumārassa vane. Tañhi tena ropitaṃ saṃvaḍḍhitaṃ paripālitaṃ ahosi, tasmā “jetavana”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Tasmiṃ jetavane. Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmeti anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā catupaññāsahiraññakoṭipariccāgena buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa niyyātitattā “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo”ti saṅkhaṃ gate ārāme. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana papañcasūdaniyā majjhimaṭṭhakathāya sabbāsavasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.14) vutto.

Jetavane means: in the park of Prince Jeta. Indeed, it was planted, nurtured, and protected by him; therefore, it came to be reckoned as 'Jetavana.' In that Jetavana. Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme means: in the monastery that came to be reckoned as 'Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery' because it was dedicated by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha through the relinquishment of fifty-four crores of gold. This is the summary here; the detailed account, however, has been stated in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya, in the explanation of the Sabbāsava Sutta.

Tattha siyā – yadi tāva bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, “jetavane”ti na vattabbaṃ. Atha tattha viharati, “sāvatthiya”nti na vattabbaṃ. Na hi sakkā ubhayattha ekaṃ samayaṃ viharitunti. Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, an objection might be raised: If, in the first place, the Blessed One dwells in Sāvatthī, 'in Jetavana' should not be said. Or, if he dwells there, 'in Sāvatthī' should not be said. For it is not possible to dwell in both places at one time. But this should not be regarded in such a way.

Nanu avocumha “samīpatthe bhummavacana”nti. Tasmā yathā gaṅgāyamunādīnaṃ samīpe goyūthāni carantāni “gaṅgāyaṃ caranti, yamunāyaṃ carantī”ti vuccati, evamidhāpi yadidaṃ sāvatthiyā samīpe jetavanaṃ, tattha viharanto vuccati “sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane”ti. Gocaragāmanidassanatthaṃ hissa sāvatthivacanaṃ, pabbajitānurūpanivāsaṭṭhānanidassanatthaṃ sesavacanaṃ.

Did we not say, 'The locative case is used in the sense of proximity'? Therefore, just as herds of cattle grazing near the Ganges and Yamuna rivers are said to be 'grazing in the Ganges, grazing in the Yamuna,' so too here, since this Jetavana is near Sāvatthī, one dwelling there is said to be 'dwelling in Sāvatthī, in Jetavana.' Indeed, the mention of Sāvatthī is for the purpose of indicating his alms-resort village, while the remaining words are for the purpose of indicating the dwelling place suitable for renunciants.

Aññatarā devatāti nāmagottavasena apākaṭā ekā devatāti attho. “Abhijānāti no, bhante, bhagavā ahu ñātaññatarassa mahesakkhassa yakkhassa saṃkhittena taṇhāsaṅkhayavimuttiṃ bhāsitā”ti ettha pana abhiññāto sakkopi devarājā “aññataro”ti vutto. “Devatā”ti [P 1.0014] ca idaṃ devānampi devadhītānampi sādhāraṇavacanaṃ. Imasmiṃ panatthe devo adhippeto, so ca kho rūpāvacarānaṃ devānaṃ aññataro.

‘A certain deity’ means a particular deity who is not well-known by way of name and clan. However, in another passage, even the well-known Sakka, king of the devas, is referred to as ‘a certain one.’ And this word ‘deity’ is a common term for both male devas and female devas. In this present context, however, a male deva is intended. And he, indeed, is one of the devas of the form realm.

Abhikkantāya rattiyāti ettha abhikkanta-saddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhānumodanādīsu dissati[V 1.0014]. Tattha “abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo[M 1.0013], ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho, uddisatu, bhante, bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ pātimokkha”nti evamādīsu (a. ni. 8.20; cūḷava. 383) khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

In the phrase 'abhikkantāya rattiyā,' the term 'abhikkanta' is found in contexts meaning passing away, beauty, lovely form, and approval. Therein, in instances such as, 'Venerable sir, the night has passed, the first watch is over, the community of monks has been seated for a long time. May the Blessed One, venerable sir, recite the Pātimokkha for the monks,' it is seen in the sense of passing away. In statements such as, 'This one is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons,' it is seen in the sense of beauty.

“Ko me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. –

‘Who is it that worships my feet, blazing with psychic power and glory, with a surpassing complexion, illuminating all directions?’

Evamādīsu (vi. va. 857) abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ bho gotamā”ti evamādīsu (pārā. 15) abbhānumodane. Idha pana khaye. Tena abhikkantāya rattiyā, parikkhīṇāya rattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatthāyaṃ devaputto majjhimayāmasamanantare āgatoti veditabbo. Niyāmo hi kiresa devatānaṃ yadidaṃ buddhānaṃ vā buddhasāvakānaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ āgacchantā majjhimayāmasamanantareyeva āgacchanti.

In such verses, it is seen in the sense of lovely form. In passages such as, ‘Excellent, venerable Gotama, excellent, venerable Gotama,’ it is seen in the sense of approval. Here, however, it is in the sense of passing away. Therefore, ‘with the night far advanced’ means ‘with the night waning.’ In this context, this devaputta should be understood as having arrived immediately after the middle watch. For this, it is said, is the fixed rule for deities: when coming to attend upon the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddha, they arrive only immediately after the middle watch.

Abhikkantavaṇṇāti idha abhikkanta-saddo abhirūpe, vaṇṇa-saddo pana chavithuti-kulavagga-kāraṇa-saṇṭhānappamāṇa-rūpāyatanādīsu dissati. Tattha “suvaṇṇavaṇṇosi bhagavā”ti evamādīsu (su. ni. 553) chaviyā. “Kadā saññūḷhā pana te, gahapati, ime samaṇassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 2.77) thutiyaṃ. “Cattārome, bho gotama, vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 3.115) kulavagge. “Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhathenoti vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.234) kāraṇe. “Mahantaṃ hatthirājavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.138) saṇṭhāne. “Tayo pattassa vaṇṇā”ti evamādīsu (pārā. 602) pamāṇe. “Vaṇṇo gandho raso ojā”ti evamādīsu rūpāyatane. So idha chaviyā daṭṭhabbo. Tena abhikkantavaṇṇā abhirūpacchavi, iṭṭhavaṇṇā manāpavaṇṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Devatā hi manussalokaṃ āgacchamānā pakativaṇṇaṃ pakatiiddhiṃ jahitvā oḷārikaṃ attabhāvaṃ katvā [P 1.0015] atirekavaṇṇaṃ atirekaiddhiṃ māpetvā naṭasamajjādīni gacchantā manussā viya abhisaṅkhatena kāyena āgacchanti. Tattha kāmāvacarā anabhisaṅkhatenapi āgantuṃ sakkonti, rūpāvacarā pana na [M 1.0014] sakkonti. Tesañhi atisukhumo attabhāvo, na tena [V 1.0015] iriyāpathakappanaṃ hoti. Tasmā ayaṃ devaputto abhisaṅkhateneva āgato. Tena vuttaṃ “abhikkantavaṇṇā”ti.

Abhikkantavaṇṇā: Here the word abhikkanta is seen in the sense of ‘beautiful,’ while the word vaṇṇa is seen in such senses as complexion, praise, class, cause, shape, measure, and the sense-sphere of form. Among these: in passages such as, “The Blessed One is of golden complexion,” it is in the sense of complexion. In passages such as, “When, householder, did you learn by heart these praises of the ascetic Gotama?” it is in the sense of praise. In passages such as, “There are, Master Gotama, these four classes,” it is in the sense of class. In passages such as, “Then for what reason is one called ‘a thief of scents’?” it is in the sense of cause. In passages such as, “Having created a great elephant-king’s form,” it is in the sense of shape. In passages such as, “There are three measures of a bowl,” it is in the sense of measure. In passages such as, “Color, scent, taste, and nutritive essence,” it is in the sense of the sense-sphere of form. Here, it should be understood in the sense of complexion. Therefore, by abhikkantavaṇṇā is meant having a beautiful complexion, a desirable complexion, and a pleasing complexion. For when deities come to the human world, they abandon their natural complexion and natural psychic power, assume a gross physical form, and manifest an extraordinary complexion and extraordinary psychic power; they come with a fabricated body, like humans going to theatrical performances and the like. Among them, deities of the sense-sphere realm are able to come even without a fabricated body, but deities of the form-sphere realm are not. For their physical existence is extremely subtle, and with it, the assuming of postures is not possible. Therefore, this devaputta has come only with a fabricated body. For that reason, it was said, “of surpassing complexion.”

Kevalakappanti ettha kevala-saddo anavasesa-yebhuyyābyāmissānatirekadaḷhatthavisaṃyogādianekattho. Tathā hissa “kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariya”nti evamādīsu (pārā. 1) anavasesatthamattho. “Kevalakappā ca aṅgamagadhā pahūtaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ ādāya upasaṅkamissantī”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 43) yebhuyyatā. “Kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hotī”ti evamādīsu (vibha. 225) abyāmissatā. “Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ nūna ayamāyasmā”ti evamādīsu (mahāva. 244) anatirekatā. “Āyasmato, bhante, anuruddhassa bāhiyo nāma saddhivihāriko kevalakappaṃ saṅghabhedāya ṭhito”ti evamādīsu (a. ni. 4.243) daḷhatthatā. “Kevalī vusitavā uttamapurisoti vuccatī”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.57) visaṃyogo attho. Idha panassa anavasesattho adhippeto.

Herein, in the phrase `kevalakappaṃ`, the word `kevala` has many meanings, such as: without remainder (anavasesa), for the most part (yebhuyyatā), unmixed (abyāmissatā), not going beyond (anatirekatā), firmness (daḷhatthatā), and disjoined (visaṃyoga). Thus, for this word, in passages such as, “the holy life, entirely complete and pure” (Pārā. 1), its meaning is ‘without remainder’. In passages such as, “For the most part, the people of Aṅga and Magadha will come bringing abundant hard and soft food” (Mahāva. 43), it means ‘for the most part’. In passages such as, “There is an arising of the unmixed mass of suffering” (Vibha. 225), it means ‘unmixed’. In passages such as, “Surely, this venerable one has merely faith” (Mahāva. 244), it means ‘not going beyond’. In passages such as, “Venerable sir, the Venerable Anuruddha’s co-resident pupil named Bāhiya is firmly resolved on causing a schism in the Saṅgha” (A.N. 4.243), it means ‘firmness’. In passages such as, “One who is complete, who has lived the holy life, is called the supreme person” (S.N. 3.57), its meaning is ‘disjoined’. Here, however, its intended meaning is ‘without remainder’.

Kappa-saddo panāyaṃ abhisaddahana-vohāra-kāla-paññatti-chedana-vikappa-lesasamantabhāvādianekattho. Tathā hissa “okappaniyametaṃ bhoto gotamassa, yathā taṃ arahato sammāsambuddhassā”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) abhisaddahanamattho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañcahi samaṇakappehi phalaṃ paribhuñjitu”nti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 250) vohāro. “Yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”ti evamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) kālo. “Iccāyasmā kappo”ti evamādīsu paññatti. “Alaṅkato kappitakesamassū”ti evamādīsu (vi. va. 1094, 1101) chedanaṃ. “Kappati dvaṅgulakappo”ti evamādīsu (cūḷava. 446) vikappo. “Ātthi kappo nipajjitu”nti [P 1.0016] evamādīsu (a. ni. 8.80) leso. “Kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā”ti evamādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.94) samantabhāvo. Idha panassa samantabhāvattho adhippeto. Tasmā kevalakappaṃ jetavananti ettha “anavasesaṃ samantato jetavana”nti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

The word `kappa` has many meanings, such as: belief (abhisaddahana), usage (vohāra), time (kāla), designation (paññatti), cutting (chedana), alternative (vikappa), opportunity (lesa), all-encompassing (samantabhāva), and so forth. Thus, for this word, in passages such as, “This is to be believed of the venerable Gotama, as it is of an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One” (ma. ni. 1.387), its meaning is ‘belief’. In passages such as, “I allow, bhikkhus, the partaking of fruit according to five monastic usages” (cūḷava. 250), it means ‘usage’. In passages such as, “by which I dwell perpetually” (ma. ni. 1.387), it means ‘time’. In passages such as, “thus the Venerable Kappa,” it means ‘designation’. In passages such as, “adorned, with hair and beard trimmed” (vi. va. 1094, 1101), it means ‘cutting’. In passages such as, “The two-finger-breadth allowance is permissible” (cūḷava. 446), it means ‘alternative’. In passages such as, “Is there an opportunity to lie down?” (a. ni. 8.80), it means ‘opportunity’. In passages such as, “illuminating the entire Veḷuvana” (saṃ. ni. 1.94), it means ‘all-encompassing’. Here, however, its meaning of ‘all-encompassing’ is intended. Therefore, in the phrase `kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ`, the meaning should be understood as “the Jeta’s Grove entirely and on all sides, without remainder”.

Obhāsetvāti [M 1.0015] vatthālaṅkārasarīrasamuṭṭhitāya ābhāya pharitvā, candimā viya sūriyo viya ca ekobhāsaṃ ekapajjotaṃ karitvāti attho.

‘Illuminating’ (obhāsetvā) means having pervaded it with the radiance arising from garments, ornaments, and the body, making it a single lustre, a single illumination, like the moon and the sun.

Yenāti [V 1.0016] bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti tasmā “yattha bhagavā, tattha upasaṅkamī”ti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yena vā kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena, sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya. Upasaṅkamīti ca gatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ gatā tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavato samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvātipi vuttaṃ hoti.

The word `yena` is an instrumental case in the sense of location. Therefore, in the phrase `yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami`, the meaning should be understood thus: “Where the Blessed One was, there he approached.” Alternatively, the meaning should be understood thus: “For the reason that the Blessed One is to be approached by devas and humans, for that reason he approached.” And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached? With the intention of attaining various special qualities, just as a great, ever-fruitful tree is to be approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying its sweet fruits. `Upasaṅkami` means “he went near.” `Upasaṅkamitvā` indicates the completion of the act of approaching. Or, it is also said that having gone thus, from that place he went to a much closer place, designated as the presence of the Blessed One.

Idāni yenatthena loke aggapuggalassa upaṭṭhānaṃ āgatā, taṃ pucchitukāmā dasanakhasamodhānasamujjalaṃ añjuliṃ sirasi patiṭṭhapetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso – “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Tasmā yathā ṭhitā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā hoti, tathā aṭṭhāsīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Aṭṭhāsīti ṭhānaṃ kappesi. Paṇḍitā hi devamanussā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ tiṭṭhanti, ayañca devo tesaṃ aññataro, tasmā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

Now, desiring to ask about the purpose for which she had come to attend upon the foremost person in the world, she placed her joined hands, radiant with the collection of her ten fingernails, upon her head and stood to one side. ‘To one side’ (ekamantaṃ) is an adverbial neuter expression—as in passages such as “the sun and moon revolve irregularly.” Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: ‘She stood just as one stands to one side.’ Alternatively, this is an accusative case in the sense of location. ‘Stood’ (aṭṭhāsi) means she took up her position. For wise devas and humans, when approaching one worthy of reverence, stand to one side out of skill in comportment; and as this deva was one of them, she stood to one side.

Kathaṃ ṭhito pana ekamantaṃ ṭhito hotīti? Cha ṭhānadose vajjetvā. Seyyathidaṃ – atidūraṃ, accāsannaṃ, uparivātaṃ[P 1.0017], unnatappadesaṃ, atisammukhaṃ, atipacchāti. Atidūre ṭhito hi sace kathetukāmo hoti, uccāsaddena kathetabbaṃ hoti. Accāsanne ṭhito saṅghaṭṭanaṃ karoti. Uparivāte ṭhito sarīragandhena bādhati. Unnatappadese ṭhito agāravaṃ pakāseti. Atisammukhā ṭhito sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Atipacchā ṭhito sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā ayampi ete cha ṭhānadose vajjetvā aṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsī”ti.

How then does one stand to one side? By avoiding the six faults of place. What are they? Too far, too near, upwind, on higher ground, too directly in front, and too far behind. For if one stands too far and wishes to speak, one must speak with a loud voice. If one stands too near, one makes contact. If one stands upwind, one causes annoyance with body odor. If one stands on higher ground, one displays disrespect. If one stands too directly in front and wishes to look, one must look eye to eye. If one stands too far behind and wishes to look, one must crane one’s neck. Therefore, this devatā also stood avoiding these six faults of place. Hence it is said, “stood to one side.”

Etadavocāti [M 1.0016] etaṃ avoca. Kathaṃ nūti kāraṇapucchā. Bhagavato hi tiṇṇoghabhāvo dasasahassilokadhātuyā pākaṭo, tenimissā devatāya tattha kaṅkhā natthi, iminā pana kāraṇena “tiṇṇo”ti na jānāti, tena sā taṃ kāraṇaṃ pucchamānā evamāha.

‘Etadavoca’ means: she spoke this statement. The question ‘Kathaṃ nu’ is a question asking for the reason. For the Blessed One’s state of having crossed the flood is manifest in the ten-thousandfold world-system; therefore, this devatā has no doubt about that. But she does not know the reason by which ‘He has crossed’. Therefore, she, inquiring about that reason, spoke thus.

Mārisāti [V 1.0017] devatānaṃ piyasamudācāravacanametaṃ. Niddukkhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yadi evaṃ “yadā kho te, mārisa, saṅkunā saṅku hadaye samāgaccheyya, atha naṃ tvaṃ jāneyyāsi ‘vassasahassaṃ me niraye paccamānassā’”ti (ma. ni. 1.512) idaṃ virujjhati. Na hi nerayikasatto niddukkho nāma hoti. Kiñcāpi na niddukkho, ruḷhīsaddena pana evaṃ vuccati. Pubbe kira paṭhamakappikānaṃ niddukkhānaṃ sukhasamappitānaṃ esa vohāro, aparabhāge dukkhaṃ hotu vā mā vā, ruḷhīsaddena ayaṃ vohāro vuccateva nippadumāpi nirudakāpi vā pokkharaṇī pokkharaṇī viya.

‘Mārisa’ is a term of affectionate address for devas. It is said to mean ‘one free from suffering’. If that were so, then this statement would be contradicted: ‘When, Mārisa, a spike should meet a spike in your heart, then you would know of it: “For a thousand years I have been cooking in hell”’. For a hell-being is not called ‘one free from suffering’. Although one may not be free from suffering, it is, however, spoken thus by conventional usage. It is said that formerly this was the term of address for the first beings of the eon, who were free from suffering and endowed with happiness. In a later period, whether there was suffering or not, this term of address was spoken by conventional usage—just as a pond is called a lotus pond even when it has no lotuses or water.

Oghamatarīti ettha cattāro oghā, kāmogho bhavogho diṭṭhogho avijjoghoti. Tattha pañcasu kāmaguṇesu chandarāgo kāmogho nāma. Rūpārūpabhavesu chandarāgo jhānanikanti ca bhavogho nāma. Dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo diṭṭhogho nāma. Catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ avijjogho nāma. Tattha kāmogho aṭṭhasu lobhasahagatesu cittuppādesu uppajjati, bhavogho catūsu diṭṭhigatavippayuttalobhasahagatesu cittuppādesu uppajjati, diṭṭhogho catūsu diṭṭhigatasampayuttesu cittuppādesu uppajjati, avijjogho sabbākusalesu uppajjati.

Here, in the phrase 'one who has crossed over the flood', there are four floods: the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. Therein, desire and passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure are called the flood of sensuality. In the form and formless existences, desire and passion and delight in jhāna are called the flood of existence. The sixty-two views are called the flood of views. Ignorance concerning the four truths is called the flood of ignorance. Therein, the flood of sensuality arises in the eight states of consciousness accompanied by greed; the flood of existence arises in the four states of consciousness accompanied by greed but dissociated from views; the flood of views arises in the four states of consciousness associated with views; and the flood of ignorance arises in all unwholesome states of consciousness.

Sabbopi cesa avahananaṭṭhena rāsaṭṭhena ca oghoti veditabbo. Avahananaṭṭhenāti [P 1.0018] adhogamanaṭṭhena. Ayañhi attano vasaṃ gate satte adho gameti, nirayādibhedāya duggatiyaṃyeva nibbatteti, uparibhāvaṃ vā nibbānaṃ gantuṃ adento adho tīsu bhavesu catūsu yonīsu pañcasu gatīsu sattasu viññāṇaṭṭhitīsu navasu sattāvāsesu ca gametītipi attho. Rāsaṭṭhenāti mahantaṭṭhena. Mahā heso kilesarāsi avīcito paṭṭhāya yāva bhavaggā patthaṭo, yadidaṃ pañcasu kāmaguṇesu chandarāgo nāma. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Evamayaṃ rāsaṭṭhenāpi oghoti [M 1.0017] veditabbo. Atarīti imaṃ catubbidhampi oghaṃ kena nu tvaṃ, mārisa, kāraṇena tiṇṇoti pucchati.

Furthermore, all this should be understood as a 'flood' in the sense of carrying downwards and in the sense of a mass. 'In the sense of carrying downwards' means in the sense of causing to go downwards. For this carries downwards beings who have come under its control, causing them to be reborn only in woeful states such as hell; or, by not allowing them to go to the higher state, Nibbāna, it leads them downwards into the three existences, four modes of generation, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and nine abodes of beings. 'In the sense of a mass' means in the sense of magnitude. For this great mass of defilements is spread out from Avīci up to the summit of existence—namely, that which is called desire and passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure. This same method applies to the remaining floods as well. Thus, this should be understood as a 'flood' also in the sense of a mass. 'You have crossed over': this means he asks, 'Venerable Sir, by what cause have you crossed over this fourfold flood?'

Athassā bhagavā pañhaṃ vissajjento appatiṭṭhaṃ khvāhantiādimāha. Tattha appatiṭṭhanti appatiṭṭhahanto. Anāyūhanti anāyūhanto, avāyamantoti attho. Iti bhagavā gūḷhaṃ paṭicchannaṃ katvā pañhaṃ kathesi. Devatāpi naṃ sutvā “bāhirakaṃ tāva oghaṃ tarantā nāma ṭhātabbaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhantā taritabbaṭṭhāne āyūhantā taranti, ayaṃ pana avīcito yāva bhavaggā patthaṭaṃ [V 1.0018] kilesoghaṃ kilesarāsiṃ appatiṭṭhahanto anāyūhanto atarinti āha. Kiṃ nu kho etaṃ? Kathaṃ nu kho eta”nti? Vimatiṃ pakkhantā pañhassa atthaṃ na aññāsi.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer the question, spoke the verse beginning with 'Without standing...'. Herein, 'without standing' means not standing still. 'Without striving' means not making an effort, not exerting oneself—this is the meaning. Thus, the Blessed One answered the question in a concealed and hidden manner. The devatā, upon hearing this, thought: 'Those who cross an external flood do so by standing where one should stand and striving where one should strive. But this one says, “I have crossed the flood of defilements, this mass of defilements that spreads from Avīci up to the summit of existence, without standing and without striving.” What indeed is this? How indeed is this?' Falling into doubt, the devatā did not understand the meaning of the answer.

Kiṃ pana bhagavatā yathā sattā na jānanti, evaṃ kathanatthāya pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutā paṭividdhāti? Na etadatthāya paṭividdhā. Dve pana bhagavato desanā niggahamukhena ca anuggahamukhena ca. Tattha ye paṇḍitamānino honti aññātepi ñātasaññino pañcasatā brāhmaṇapabbajitā viya, tesaṃ mānaniggahatthaṃ yathā na jānanti, evaṃ mūlapariyāyādisadisaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Ayaṃ niggahamukhena desanā. Vuttampi cetaṃ “niggayha niggayhāhaṃ, ānanda, vakkhāmi, pavayha pavayha, ānanda, vakkhāmi, yo sāro, so ṭhassatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.196). Ye [P 1.0019] pana ujukā sikkhākāmā, tesaṃ suviññeyyaṃ katvā ākaṅkheyyasuttādisadisaṃ dhammaṃ deseti, “abhirama, tissa, abhirama, tissa, ahamovādena ahamanuggahena ahamanusāsaniyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.84) ca ne samassāseti. Ayaṃ anuggahamukhena desanā.

But did the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections, penetrate to omniscience in order to teach in such a way that beings would not understand? He did not penetrate to it for that purpose. Rather, the Blessed One's teachings are twofold: by way of subduing and by way of favoring. Herein, for those who are conceited about their wisdom, who perceive as known what is not known—like the five hundred brahmin wanderers—for the purpose of subduing their conceit, he teaches the Dhamma in a way that they do not understand, similar to the Mūlapariyāya Sutta and others. This is teaching by way of subduing. And it has been said: 'Having subdued, having subdued, Ānanda, I will speak; having favored, having favored, Ānanda, I will speak. What is essential will remain.' But for those who are upright and desirous of the training, he teaches the Dhamma, having made it easy to understand, like the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta and others, and he encourages them, saying: 'Delight, Tissa, delight! By my exhortation, by my favor, and by my instruction.' This is teaching by way of favoring.

Ayaṃ pana devaputto mānatthaddho paṇḍitamānī, evaṃ kirassa ahosi – ahaṃ oghaṃ jānāmi, tathāgatassa oghatiṇṇabhāvaṃ jānāmi, “iminā pana kāraṇena tiṇṇo”ti ettakamattaṃ na jānāmi. Iti mayhaṃ ñātameva bahu, appaṃ aññātaṃ, tamahaṃ kathitamattameva jānissāmi. Kiñhi nāma taṃ bhagavā vadeyya, yassāhaṃ atthaṃ na jāneyyanti. Atha satthā “ayaṃ kiliṭṭhavatthaṃ viya [M 1.0018] raṅgajātaṃ abhabbo imaṃ mānaṃ appahāya desanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ, mānaniggahaṃ tāvassa katvā puna nīcacittena pucchantassa pakāsessāmī”ti paṭicchannaṃ katvā pañhaṃ kathesi. Sopi nihatamāno ahosi, sā cassa nihatamānatā uttaripañhapucchaneneva veditabbā. Tassa pana pañhapucchanassa ayamattho – kathaṃ pana tvaṃ, mārisa, appatiṭṭhaṃ anāyūhaṃ oghamatari, yathāhaṃ jānāmi, evaṃ me kathehīti.

This devaputta, however, was stiff with conceit and conceited about his wisdom. It is said that he thought thus: 'I know the flood, and I know that the Tathāgata has crossed the flood; but I do not know just this much—the reason by which he crossed. Thus, what is known to me is much, and what is unknown is little; that I will know merely upon it being spoken. For what indeed could the Blessed One say, the meaning of which I would not know?' Then the Teacher, thinking, 'This one, like a stained cloth unfit to receive dye, is incapable of receiving the teaching without abandoning this conceit. First, I will subdue his conceit, and then, when he asks again with a humble mind, I will explain,' answered the question in a concealed manner. And his conceit was crushed. That his conceit was crushed is to be understood from his subsequent questioning. The meaning of his questioning is this: 'How, venerable sir, did you cross the flood without standing, without striving? Explain it to me so that I may know.'

Athassa bhagavā kathento yadāsvāhantiādimāha. Tattha yadā svāhanti yasmiṃ kāle ahaṃ. Sukāro nipātamattaṃ. Yathā ca ettha, evaṃ sabbapadesu. Saṃsīdāmīti paṭicchannaṃ katvā ataranto tattheva osīdāmi. Nibbuyhāmīti ṭhātuṃ asakkonto ativattāmi. Iti ṭhāne ca vāyāme ca dosaṃ disvā atiṭṭhanto avāyamanto oghamatarinti evaṃ bhagavatā pañho kathito. Devatāyapi paṭividdho, na pana pākaṭo, tassa pākaṭīkaraṇatthaṃ satta dukā dassitā. Kilesavasena [V 1.0019] hi santiṭṭhanto saṃsīdati nāma, abhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanto nibbuyhati nāma. Taṇhādiṭṭhīhi vā santiṭṭhanto saṃsīdati nāma, avasesakilesānañceva abhisaṅkhārānañca vasena āyūhanto nibbuyhati nāma. Taṇhāvasena vā santiṭṭhanto saṃsīdati nāma, diṭṭhivasena āyūhanto nibbuyhati nāma. Sassatadiṭṭhiyā vā santiṭṭhanto saṃsīdati nāma, ucchedadiṭṭhiyā āyūhanto nibbuyhati nāma. Olīyanābhinivesā hi bhavadiṭṭhi, atidhāvanābhinivesā vibhavadiṭṭhi[P 1.0020]. Līnavasena vā santiṭṭhanto saṃsīdati nāma, uddhaccavasena āyūhanto nibbuyhati nāma. Tathā kāmasukhallikānuyogavasena santiṭṭhanto saṃsīdati nāma, attakilamathānuyogavasena āyūhanto nibbuyhati nāma. Sabbākusalābhisaṅkhāravasena santiṭṭhanto saṃsīdati nāma, sabbalokiyakusalābhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanto nibbuyhati nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “seyyathāpi, cunda, ye keci akusalā dhammā, sabbe te adhobhāgaṅgamanīyā, ye keci kusalā dhammā, sabbe te uparibhāgaṅgamanīyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.86).

Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer that devatā, spoke the words beginning with 'yadāsvāhaṃ'. Therein, 'yadāsvāhaṃ' means: at which time, I. The sound 'su' is merely a particle without meaning. 'Saṃsīdāmi' means: not making an effort to cross, I sink right there in that very flood. 'Nibbuyhāmi' means: being unable to stand, I am carried past. Thus, having seen the fault in both standing still and in striving, by not standing still and not striving, I crossed the flood. In this way, the question was answered by the Blessed One. It was also penetrated by the devatā, but it was not manifest. For the purpose of making it manifest, seven pairs were shown. Indeed, standing still by way of defilements is called sinking; striving by way of formations is called being carried away. Alternatively, standing still by way of craving and views is called sinking; striving by way of the remaining defilements and formations is called being carried away. Alternatively, standing still by way of craving is called sinking; striving by way of views is called being carried away. Alternatively, standing still by way of the eternalist view is called sinking; striving by way of the annihilationist view is called being carried away. For the view of existence has the adherence of sinking back, and the view of non-existence has the adherence of over-running. Alternatively, standing still by way of sluggishness is called sinking; striving by way of restlessness is called being carried away. Likewise, standing still by way of devotion to indulgence in sensual pleasures is called sinking; striving by way of devotion to self-mortification is called being carried away. Standing still by way of all unwholesome formations is called sinking; striving by way of all worldly wholesome formations is called being carried away. And this has been said: 'Just as, Cunda, whatever unwholesome states there are, all tend downwards; whatever wholesome states there are, all tend upwards.' (MN 1.86)

Imaṃ pañhavissajjanaṃ sutvāva devatā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya tuṭṭhā pasannā attano tuṭṭhiñca pasādañca pakāsayantī cirassaṃ vatāti gāthamāha. Tattha cirassanti cirassa kālassa accayenāti attho. Ayaṃ [M 1.0019] kira devatā kassapasammāsambuddhaṃ disvā tassa parinibbānato paṭṭhāya antarā aññaṃ buddhaṃ na diṭṭhapubbā, tasmā ajja bhagavantaṃ disvā evamāha. Kiṃ panimāya devatāya ito pubbe satthā na diṭṭhapubboti. Diṭṭhapubbo vā hotu adiṭṭhapubbo vā, dassanaṃ upādāya evaṃ vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Brāhmaṇanti bāhitapāpaṃ khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇaṃ. Parinibbutanti kilesanibbānena nibbutaṃ. Loketi sattaloke. Visattikanti rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu āsattavisattatādīhi kāraṇehi visattikā vuccati taṇhā, taṃ visattikaṃ appatiṭṭhamānaṃ anāyūhamānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ nittiṇṇaṃ uttiṇṇaṃ cirassaṃ vata khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇaṃ passāmīti attho.

Having heard this answer to the question, the devatā, established in the fruit of stream-entry, was delighted and pleased. Expressing its joy and faith, the devatā spoke the verse beginning, 'After a long time indeed...'. Therein, 'after a long time' means 'after the passing of a long time'. It is said that this devatā had seen the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, but from the time of his final Nibbāna onwards, in the interim, had not seen another Buddha. Therefore, having seen the Blessed One today, the devatā spoke thus. But had this devatā not seen the Teacher before this? Whether the devatā had seen him before or not, it is fitting to speak thus in reference to this seeing. 'Brahmin' means a brahmin who has excluded evil, a taint-destroyed brahmin. 'Fully extinguished' means extinguished by the extinguishing of the defilements. 'In the world' means in the world of beings. 'Clinging' (visattikā) refers to craving, which is so called for reasons such as attachment and entanglement in objects like forms, etc. The meaning is: 'After a long time indeed I see a taint-destroyed brahmin who, not standing still and not striving, has crossed, completely crossed, and utterly crossed over that clinging.'

Samanuñño satthā ahosīti tassā devatāya vacanaṃ citteneva samanumodi, ekajjhāsayo ahosi. Antaradhāyīti abhisaṅkhatakāyaṃ jahitvā attano pakatiupādiṇṇakakāyasmiṃyeva ṭhatvā laddhāsā laddhapatiṭṭhā hutvā dasabalaṃ gandhehi ca mālehi ca pūjetvā attano bhavanaṃyeva agamāsīti.

The Teacher was pleased: He mentally rejoiced in the words of that devatā; He was of the same intention. 'Disappeared' means: having abandoned the specially fashioned body and remaining in its own natural, appropriated body, having its wish fulfilled and its footing gained, the devatā honored the One with Ten Powers with perfumes and garlands and went to its own abode.

Oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on Crossing the Flood is concluded.

2. Nimokkhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Nimokkha Sutta

2. Idāni [V 1.0020] dutiyasuttato paṭṭhāya paṭhamamāgatañca uttānatthañca pahāya yaṃ yaṃ anuttānaṃ, taṃ tadeva vaṇṇayissāma. Jānāsi noti jānāsi nu. Nimokkhantiādīni maggādīnaṃ nāmāni[P 1.0021]. Maggena hi sattā kilesabandhanato nimuccanti, tasmā maggo sattānaṃ nimokkhoti vutto. Phalakkhaṇe pana te kilesabandhanato pamuttā, tasmā phalaṃ sattānaṃ pamokkhoti vuttaṃ. Nibbānaṃ patvā sattānaṃ sabbadukkhaṃ viviccati, tasmā nibbānaṃ vivekoti vuttaṃ. Sabbāni vā etāni nibbānasseva nāmāni. Nibbānañhi patvā sattā sabbadukkhato nimuccanti pamuccanti viviccanti, tasmā tadeva “nimokkho pamokkho viveko”ti vuttaṃ. Jānāmi khvāhanti jānāmi kho ahaṃ. Avadhāraṇattho khokāro[M 1.0020]. Ahaṃ jānāmiyeva. Sattānaṃ nimokkhādijānanatthameva hi mayā samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭividdhanti sīhanādaṃ nadati. Buddhasīhanādaṃ nāma kira etaṃ suttaṃ.

2. Now, starting from the second sutta, having set aside what came first and what has a manifest meaning, we shall explain only that which has a meaning that is not manifest. The phrase `jānāsi no` means `jānāsi nu`, 'Do you not know?'. ‘Nimokkha’ and the like are names for the path and so on. For by the path, beings are released from the bondage of defilements; therefore, the path is called the release of beings. But at the moment of fruition, they are utterly freed from the bondage of defilements; therefore, the fruit is called the liberation of beings. Having attained Nibbāna, all suffering of beings is removed; therefore, Nibbāna is called seclusion. Or, all these are names for Nibbāna itself. For having attained Nibbāna, beings are released, liberated, and secluded from all suffering; therefore, that very Nibbāna is called 'release', 'liberation', and 'seclusion'. The phrase `Jānāmi khvāhaṃ` is to be parsed as `jānāmi kho ahaṃ`. The particle `kho` has the meaning of emphasis, meaning, 'I indeed know'.
