For it was precisely for the sake of knowing the release, and so on, of beings that by me, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, the knowledge of omniscience was penetrated. Thus, he utters a lion's roar. This sutta, it is said, is named the Buddha's Lion's Roar.

Nandībhavaparikkhayāti nandīmūlakassa kammabhavassa parikkhayena. Nandiyā ca bhavassa cātipi vaṭṭati. Tattha hi purimanaye nandībhavena tividhakammābhisaṅkhāravasena saṅkhārakkhandho gahito, saññāviññāṇehi taṃsampayuttā ca dve khandhā. Tehi pana tīhi khandhehi sampayuttā vedanā tesaṃ gahaṇena gahitāvāti anupādiṇṇakānaṃ catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ appavattivasena saupādisesaṃ nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ hoti. Vedanānaṃ nirodhā upasamāti upādiṇṇakavedanānaṃ nirodhena ca upasamena ca. Tattha vedanāgahaṇena taṃsampayuttā tayo khandhā gahitāva honti, tesaṃ vatthārammaṇavasena rūpakkhandhopi. Evaṃ imesaṃ upādiṇṇakānaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ appavattivasena anupādisesaṃ nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ hoti. Dutiyanaye pana nandiggahaṇena saṅkhārakkhandho gahito, bhavaggahaṇena upapattibhavasaṅkhāto rūpakkhandho, saññādīhi sarūpeneva tayo khandhā. Evaṃ imesaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ appavattivasena nibbānaṃ kathitaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Imameva ca nayaṃ catunikāyikabhaṇḍikatthero roceti. Iti nibbānavaseneva bhagavā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesīti.

As for 'with the destruction of delight and existence,' this means by the destruction of kamma-existence which is rooted in delight. Or, 'by the destruction of delight and of existence' is also suitable. To elaborate, therein, in the first method, by the term 'delight-existence,' by way of the threefold kamma-formations, the aggregate of formations is taken; by 'perception' and 'consciousness,' the two aggregates associated with it are taken. Furthermore, by the taking of those three aggregates, the aggregate of feeling associated with them is indeed taken. Thus, by way of the non-occurrence of the four non-material aggregates that are not clung to, Nibbāna with residue is taught. As for 'with the cessation and pacification of feelings,' this means by the cessation and pacification of feelings that are clung to. Therein, by the term 'feeling,' the three aggregates associated with it are indeed taken; by way of their basis and object, the aggregate of form is also taken. Thus, by way of the non-occurrence of these five aggregates that are clung to, Nibbāna without residue is taught. But in the second method, by the term 'delight,' the aggregate of formations is taken; by the term 'existence,' the aggregate of form, designated as rebirth-existence, is taken; by 'perception' and so on, the three aggregates are taken by their own nature. Thus, by way of the non-occurrence of these five aggregates, Nibbāna is taught; it should be understood thus. And this very method is what the Elder Bhaṇḍika, who is versed in the four Nikāyas, prefers. Thus, the Blessed One concluded the discourse by way of Nibbāna.

Nimokkhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nimokkha Sutta is completed.

3. Upanīyasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Upanīya Sutta

3. Tatiye [V 1.0021][P 1.0022] upanīyatīti parikkhīyati nirujjhati, upagacchati vā, anupubbena maraṇaṃ upetīti attho. Yathā vā gopālena gogaṇo nīyati, evaṃ jarāya maraṇasantikaṃ upanīyatīti attho. Jīvitanti jīvitindriyaṃ. Appanti parittaṃ thokaṃ. Tassa dvīhākārehi parittatā veditabbā sarasaparittatāya ca khaṇaparittatāya ca. Sarasaparittatāyapi hi “yo, bhikkhave, ciraṃ jīvati, so vassasataṃ appaṃ vā bhiyyo”ti (dī. ni. 2.7; saṃ. ni. 2.143) vacanato parittaṃ. Khaṇaparittatāyapi. Paramatthato hi atiparitto sattānaṃ jīvitakkhaṇo ekacittappavattimattoyeva[M 1.0021]. Yathā nāma rathacakkaṃ pavattamānampi ekeneva nemippadesena pavattati, tiṭṭhamānampi ekeneva tiṭṭhati, evamevaṃ ekacittakkhaṇikaṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ, tasmiṃ citte niruddhamatte satto niruddhoti vuccati. Yathāha – atīte cittakkhaṇe jīvittha na jīvati na jīvissati, anāgate cittakkhaṇe jīvissati na jīvati na jīvittha, paccuppanne cittakkhaṇe jīvati na jīvittha na jīvissati.

3. In the third sutta, 'is led on' means it is exhausted, it ceases, or it approaches; the meaning is that one gradually approaches death. Or, just as a herd of cattle is led by a cowherd, so too is one led on by aging to the proximity of death—this is the meaning. 'Life' means the life faculty. 'Brief' means limited, little. Its brevity should be understood in two ways: by the brevity of its continuity and by the brevity of the moment. For, regarding the brevity of its continuity, it is said: 'Monks, one who lives long lives for a hundred years, or a little more'; thus it is brief. And also regarding the brevity of the moment. For, in the ultimate sense, the life-moment of beings is extremely brief, lasting only for the duration of the occurrence of a single mind-moment. Just as a chariot wheel, when rolling, rolls on only a single point of its rim, and when standing, stands on only a single point, so too is the life of beings for the duration of a single mind-moment. When that mind-moment has just ceased, the being is said to have ceased. As the Elder, the General of the Dhamma, said: 'In a past mind-moment, one lived, one does not live, one will not live. In a future mind-moment, one will live, one does not live, one did not live. In the present mind-moment, one lives, one did not live, one will not live.'

“Jīvitaṃ attabhāvo ca, sukhadukkhā ca kevalā;

Ekacittasamāyuttā, lahuso vattate khaṇo.

“Life, individuality, and pleasure and pain exclusively, are all associated with a single mind-moment; swiftly the moment passes.

“Ye niruddhā marantassa, tiṭṭhamānassa vā idha;

Sabbepi sadisā khandhā, gatā appaṭisandhikā.

“Those aggregates that have ceased, whether for one who is dying or for one who is living here, are all similar: they are gone, without relinking.

“Anibbattena na jāto, paccuppannena jīvati;

Cittabhaṅgā mato loko, paññatti paramatthiyā”ti. (mahāni. 10);

“One does not live by that which has not yet arisen; one lives by the present. With the dissolution of the mind, the world is dead. The designation is a matter of ultimate reality.”

Jarūpanītassāti jaraṃ upagatassa, jarāya vā maraṇasantikaṃ upanītassa. Na santi tāṇāti tāṇaṃ leṇaṃ saraṇaṃ bhavituṃ samatthā nāma keci natthi. Etaṃ bhayanti etaṃ jīvitindriyassa maraṇūpagamanaṃ, āyuparittatā, jarūpanītassa tāṇābhāvoti tividhaṃ bhayaṃ bhayavatthu bhayakāraṇanti [P 1.0023] attho. Puññāni kayirātha sukhāvahānīti viññū puriso sukhāvahāni sukhadāyakāni puññāni kareyya. Iti devatā rūpāvacarajjhānaṃ sandhāya pubbacetanaṃ aparacetanaṃ muñcacetanañca gahetvā bahuvacanavasena [V 1.0022] “puññānī”ti āha. Jhānassādaṃ jhānanikantiṃ jhānasukhañca gahetvā “sukhāvahānī”ti āha. Tassā kira devatāya sayaṃ dīghāyukaṭṭhāne brahmaloke nibbattattā heṭṭhā kāmāvacaradevesu parittāyukaṭṭhāne cavamāne upapajjamāne ca thullaphusitake vuṭṭhipātasadise satte disvā etadahosi “ahovatime sattā jhānaṃ bhāvetvā aparihīnajjhānā kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke ekakappa-dvekappa-catukappa-aṭṭhakappa-soḷasakappa-dvattiṃsakappa-catusaṭṭhikappappamāṇaṃ addhānaṃ tiṭṭheyyu”nti. Tasmā evamāha.

“For one overcome by old age” means: for one who has reached old age, or for one who has been brought near to death by old age. “There are no shelters” means: there is no shelter, hiding place, or refuge; that is, there are none capable of being so. “This fear” refers to this threefold fear: the approach of death to the life-faculty, the shortness of life, and the absence of a protector for one overcome by old age—this is the meaning of fear, the basis of fear, and the cause of fear. “One should do meritorious deeds that bring happiness” means a wise person should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness. Thus, the devatā, referring to the form-sphere jhāna, and taking into account the preliminary volition, the subsequent volition, and the volition at the moment of release, spoke in the plural as “meritorious deeds.” Considering the enjoyment of jhāna, the craving for jhāna, and the bliss of jhāna, he said “that bring happiness.” It is said that this devatā, having himself been reborn in the Brahma world, a place of long life, saw beings in the lower sense-sphere realms, places of short life, passing away and being reborn like a heavy shower of rain, and thought, “Oh, if only these beings would develop jhāna and, not falling away from it, at death be reborn and remain in the Brahma world for one, two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four aeons!” Therefore, he spoke thus.

Atha bhagavā – “ayaṃ devatā aniyyānikaṃ vaṭṭakathaṃ kathetī”ti vivaṭṭamassā dassento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha lokāmisanti dve lokāmisā [M 1.0022] pariyāyena ca nippariyāyena ca. Pariyāyena tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ lokāmisaṃ, nippariyāyena cattāro paccayā. Idha pariyāyalokāmisaṃ adhippetaṃ. Nippariyāyalokāmisampi vaṭṭatiyeva. Santipekkhoti nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ accantasantiṃ pekkhanto icchanto patthayantoti.

Then the Blessed One, thinking, “This devatā speaks a talk about the round of existence, which does not lead to liberation,” and wishing to show him that which is free from the round, uttered the second verse. Therein, “worldly bait” is of two kinds: figurative and literal. Figuratively, “worldly bait” is the round of existence in the three planes; literally, it is the four requisites. Here, the figurative “worldly bait” is intended, though the literal is also applicable. “One who looks for peace” means one who beholds, desires, and aspires to the ultimate peace called Nibbāna.

Upanīyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Upanīya Sutta is completed.

4. Accentisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Accenti Sutta

4. Catutthe accentīti atikkamanti. Kālāti purebhattādayo kālā. Tarayanti rattiyoti rattiyo atikkamamānā puggalaṃ maraṇūpagamanāya tarayanti sīghaṃ sīghaṃ gamayanti. Vayoguṇāti paṭhamamajjhimapacchimavayānaṃ guṇā, rāsayoti attho. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ahatānaṃ vatthānaṃ diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti (mahāva. 348) ettha hi paṭalaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Sataguṇā dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā”ti (ma. ni. 3.379) ettha ānisaṃsaṭṭho. “Antaṃ antaguṇa”nti ettha koṭṭhāsaṭṭho. “Kayirā mālāguṇe bahū”ti (dha. pa. 53) ettha rāsaṭṭho. “Pañca kāmaguṇā”ti ettha bandhanaṭṭho. Idha pana rāsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. Tasmā vayoguṇāti vayorāsayo veditabbā. Anupubbaṃ [P 1.0024] jahantīti anupaṭipāṭiyā puggalaṃ jahanti. Majjhimavaye ṭhitaṃ hi paṭhamavayo jahati, pacchimavaye ṭhitaṃ dve paṭhamamajjhimā jahanti, maraṇakkhaṇe pana tayopi vayā jahanteva. Etaṃ bhayanti etaṃ kālānaṃ atikkamanaṃ, rattidivānaṃ taritabhāvo, vayoguṇānaṃ jahanabhāvoti tividhaṃ bhayaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

4. In the fourth sutta, 'accenti' means 'they pass beyond.' 'Kālā' means times, such as the time before the meal and so on. 'Tarayanti rattiyo' means: the nights, as they pass, cause a person to hasten toward death, making them go very quickly. 'Vayoguṇā' means the collections of the first, middle, and last ages; the meaning is 'masses.' For in the passage, “I allow, O monks, a double-layered outer robe of new cloths,” the meaning of 'guṇa' is 'layer.' In, “A hundredfold benefit from the offering is to be expected,” it means 'benefit.' In, 'the intestine, the intestinal coil,' it means 'portion.' In, 'One should make many garlands,' it means 'collection.' In, 'The five strands of sensual pleasure,' it means 'bond.' Here, however, the meaning of 'guṇa' is 'collection.' Therefore, 'vayoguṇā' should be understood as 'the collections of age.' 'Anupubbaṃ jahanti' means they abandon a person in sequence. Indeed, the first age abandons one who is established in the middle age; the first two—the first and middle ages—abandon one who is established in the last age. At the moment of death, however, all three ages indeed abandon them. 'Etaṃ bhayaṃ' means this threefold fear: the passing of the times, the state of being hastened by nights and days, and the state of being abandoned by the collections of age. The rest is just the same as the preceding sutta.

Accentisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Accenti Sutta is finished.

5. Katichindasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Katichinda Sutta

5. Pañcame [V 1.0023][M 1.0023] kati chindeti chindanto kati chindeyya. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca “chinde jahe”ti atthato ekaṃ. Gāthābandhassa pana maṭṭhabhāvatthaṃ ayaṃ devatā saddapunaruttiṃ vajjayantī evamāha. Kati saṅgātigoti kati saṅge atigato, atikkantoti attho. Saṅgātikotipi pāṭho, ayameva attho. Pañca chindeti chindanto pañca orambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni chindeyya. Pañca jaheti jahanto pañcuddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni jaheyya. Idhāpi chindanañca jahanañca atthato ekameva, bhagavā pana devatāya āropitavacanānurūpeneva evamāha. Atha vā pādesu baddhapāsasakuṇo viya pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni heṭṭhā ākaḍḍhamānākārāni honti, tāni anāgāmimaggena chindeyyāti vadati. Hatthehi gahitarukkhasākhā viya pañcuddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni upari ākaḍḍhamānākārāni honti, tāni arahattamaggena jaheyyāti vadati. Pañca cuttari bhāvayeti etesaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ chindanatthāya ceva pahānatthāya ca uttari atirekaṃ visesaṃ bhāvento saddhāpañcamāni indriyāni bhāveyyāti attho. Pañca saṅgātigoti rāgasaṅgo dosasaṅgo mohasaṅgo mānasaṅgo diṭṭhisaṅgoti ime pañca saṅge atikkanto. Oghatiṇṇoti vuccatīti caturoghatiṇṇoti kathīyati. Imāya pana gāthāya pañcindriyāni lokiyalokuttarāni kathitānīti.

5. In the fifth sutta, 'how many should one cut off?' means 'when cutting off, how many should one cut off?' The same method applies to the remaining phrases. Here, 'cut off' and 'abandon' are one in meaning. However, for the sake of the verse's clarity, this devatā, avoiding the repetition of the word, spoke thus. 'One who has gone beyond how many attachments?' means 'how many attachments has one gone beyond, has one transcended?'—this is the meaning. There is also the reading 'one who has crossed the attachments,' which has the very same meaning. 'One should cut off five' means that when cutting off, one should cut off the five lower fetters. 'One should abandon five' means that when abandoning, one should abandon the five higher fetters. Here too, cutting off and abandoning are one and the same in meaning, but the Blessed One spoke thus in accordance with the words presented by the devatā. Alternatively, like a bird with its feet bound by a snare, the five lower fetters have the nature of pulling one downward; He says that one should cut them off with the path of the non-returner. Like a tree branch grasped by the hands, the five higher fetters have the nature of pulling one upward; He says that one should abandon them with the path of arahantship. 'One should further develop five' means that for the sake of cutting off and abandoning these fetters, by developing a further, surpassing quality, one should develop the five faculties which have faith as the fifth—this is the meaning. 'One who has gone beyond the five attachments' means one who has transcended these five attachments: the attachment of lust, the attachment of hatred, the attachment of delusion, the attachment of conceit, and the attachment of views. 'Is called "one who has crossed the flood"' means one is said to be 'one who has crossed the four floods.' By this verse, the five faculties, both mundane and supramundane, are spoken of.

Katichindasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Katichinda Sutta is finished.

6. Jāgarasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Jāgara Sutta

6. Chaṭṭhe [P 1.0025] jāgaratanti jāgarantānaṃ. Pañca jāgaratanti vissajjanagāthāyaṃ pana saddhādīsu pañcasu indriyesu jāgarantesu pañca nīvaraṇā suttā nāma. Kasmā? Yasmā taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo yattha katthaci nisinno vā ṭhito vā aruṇaṃ uṭṭhapentopi pamādatāya akusalasamaṅgitāya sutto nāma hoti. Evaṃ suttesu pañcasu nīvaraṇesu pañcindriyāni jāgarāni nāma. Kasmā[M 1.0024]? Yasmā taṃsamaṅgīpuggalo yattha katthaci nipajjitvā niddāyantopi appamādatāya kusalasamaṅgitāya jāgaro nāma hoti. Pañcahi pana nīvaraṇeheva kilesarajaṃ ādiyati gaṇhāti parāmasati. Purimā [V 1.0024] hi kāmacchandādayo pacchimānaṃ paccayā hontīti pañcahi indriyehi parisujjhatīti ayamattho veditabbo. Idhāpi pañcindriyāni lokiyalokuttarāneva kathitānīti.

6. In the sixth, 'they are awake' refers to those who are awake. In the explanatory verse, however, when the five faculties—faith and so on—are awake, the five hindrances are called 'asleep'. Why? Because a person endowed with them, wherever they may be sitting or standing, even while staying up until dawn, is called 'asleep' due to negligence and being endowed with the unwholesome. Similarly, when the five hindrances are asleep, the five faculties are called 'awake'. Why? Because a person endowed with them, wherever they may lie down and fall asleep, is called 'awake' due to non-negligence and being endowed with the wholesome. Furthermore, it is by the five hindrances that one acquires, grasps, and misapprehends the dust of defilements. And since the former—sensual desire and so on—become conditions for the latter, it should be understood that one is purified by the five faculties. Here too, the five faculties are spoken of as both mundane and supramundane.

Jāgarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Jāgara Sutta is finished.

7. Appaṭividitasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Appaṭividita Sutta

7. Sattame dhammāti catusaccadhammā. Appaṭividitāti ñāṇena appaṭividdhā. Paravādesūti dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhigatavādesu. Te hi ito paresaṃ titthiyānaṃ vādattā paravādā nāma. Nīyareti attano dhammatāyapi gacchanti, parenapi nīyanti. Tattha sayameva sassatādīni gaṇhantā gacchanti nāma, parassa vacanena tāni gaṇhantā nīyanti nāma. Kālo tesaṃ pabujjhitunti tesaṃ puggalānaṃ pabujjhituṃ ayaṃ kālo. Lokasmiñhi buddho uppanno, dhammo desiyati, saṅgho suppaṭipanno, paṭipadā bhaddikā, ime ca pana mahājanā vaṭṭe suttā nappabujjhantīti devatā āha. Sambuddhāti sammā hetunā kāraṇena buddhā. Cattāro hi buddhā – sabbaññubuddho, paccekabuddho, catusaccabuddho, sutabuddhoti. Tattha samatiṃsapāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ patto sabbaññubuddho nāma. Kappasatasahassādhikāni dve asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūretvā sayambhutaṃ patto paccekabuddho nāma. Avasesā khīṇāsavā catusaccabuddhā nāma. Bahussuto sutabuddho nāma. Imasmiṃ atthe tayopi purimā vaṭṭanti. Sammadaññāti sammā hetunā [P 1.0026] kāraṇena jānitvā. Caranti visame samanti visame vā lokasannivāse visame vā sattanikāye visame vā kilesajāte samaṃ carantīti.

7. In the seventh, 'Dhamma' means the Dhamma of the Four Truths. 'Not penetrated' means not penetrated by knowledge. 'In others' doctrines' means in the sixty-two wrong views. For these are called 'others' doctrines' because they are the doctrines of other sectarians. 'They are led' means they proceed by their own nature and are also led by another. Therein, those who grasp views such as eternalism by themselves are said to 'proceed'; those who grasp them through the word of another are said to be 'led'. 'It is time for them to awaken' means this is the time for those persons to awaken. For in the world a Buddha has arisen, the Dhamma is taught, the Saṅgha is of good practice, the path is excellent, yet these great masses of people, asleep in the cycle of rebirth, do not awaken—thus said the devatā. 'Fully enlightened' means enlightened rightly, by a suitable cause and reason. For there are four types of Buddhas: the Omniscient Buddha, the Paccekabuddha, the Four-Truths Buddha, and the Learned Buddha. Therein, the one who, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, has attained perfect self-enlightenment is called the Omniscient Buddha. The one who, having fulfilled the perfections for two incalculable aeons and one hundred thousand more aeons, has attained the state of being self-become is called the Paccekabuddha. The remaining Arahants are called Four-Truths Buddhas. One of great learning is called a Learned Buddha. In this context, the first three are applicable. 'Having known rightly' means having known rightly, by a suitable cause and reason. 'They fare evenly in the uneven' means they fare evenly in the uneven world of beings, or in the uneven group of beings, or in the uneven collection of defilements.

Appaṭividitasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Appaṭividita Sutta is finished.

8. Susammuṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Susammuṭṭha Sutta

8. Aṭṭhame [M 1.0025] susammuṭṭhāti paññāya appaṭividdhabhāveneva sunaṭṭhā. Yathā hi dve khettāni kasitvā, ekaṃ vapitvā, bahudhaññaṃ adhigatassa avāpitakhettato aladdhaṃ sandhāya “bahuṃ me dhaññaṃ naṭṭha”nti vadanto aladdhameva “naṭṭha”nti vadati, evamidhāpi appaṭividitāva susammuṭṭhā nāma. Asammuṭṭhāti paññāya paṭividdhabhāveneva anaṭṭhā. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

8. In the eighth, 'thoroughly forgotten' means utterly lost precisely because of the state of not being penetrated by wisdom. Just as someone who, having plowed two fields and sown one, has obtained much grain, might say with reference to what was not obtained from the unsown field, 'Much grain has been lost to me,' thus speaking of what was never obtained as 'lost'; so too here, it is precisely the state of not being penetrated that is called 'thoroughly forgotten.' 'Not forgotten' means not lost precisely because of the state of being penetrated by wisdom. The rest is just the same as the preceding.

Susammuṭṭhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Susammuṭṭha Sutta is completed.

9. Mānakāmasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Mānakāma Sutta

9. Navame [V 1.0025] mānakāmassāti mānaṃ kāmentassa icchantassa. Damoti evarūpassa puggalassa samādhipakkhiko damo natthīti vadati. “Saccena danto damasā upeto, vedantagū vusitabrahmacariyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.195) ettha hi indriyasaṃvaro damoti vutto. “Yadi saccā damā cāgā, khantyā bhiyyodha vijjatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 191) ettha paññā. “Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena atthi puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.365) ettha uposathakammaṃ. “Sakkhissasi kho tvaṃ, puṇṇa, iminā damūpasamena samannāgato sunāparantasmiṃ janapade viharitu”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.88; ma. ni. 3.396) ettha adhivāsanakhanti. Imasmiṃ pana sutte damoti samādhipakkhikadhammānaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Tenevāha – “na monamatthi asamāhitassā”ti. Tattha monanti catumaggañāṇaṃ, tañhi munātīti monaṃ, catusaccadhamme jānātīti attho. Maccudheyyassāti tebhūmakavaṭṭassa. Tañhi maccuno patiṭṭhānaṭṭhena maccudheyyanti vuccati. Pāranti [P 1.0027] tasseva pāraṃ nibbānaṃ. Tareyyāti paṭivijjheyya pāpuṇeyya vā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – eko araññe viharanto pamatto puggalo maccudheyyassa pāraṃ na tareyya na paṭivijjheyya na pāpuṇeyyāti.

9. In the ninth, 'one desiring conceit' (mānakāmassa) means one who craves and seeks conceit. 'Taming' (dama)—he says there is no taming pertaining to concentration for such a person. For in the verse, 'Restrained by truth, endowed with taming, a master of knowledge, having lived the holy life' (SN 1.195), restraint of the senses is called 'taming.' In 'If there are truth, taming, generosity, and patience is found here in abundance' (SN 1.246; Sn 191), it refers to wisdom. In 'By giving, taming, restraint, and truthful speech, there is merit, there is the accumulation of merit' (SN 4.365), it refers to the Uposatha observance. In 'Will you be able, Puṇṇa, endowed with this taming and pacification, to dwell in the Sunāparanta country?' (SN 4.88; MN 3.396), it refers to patient endurance. But in this discourse, 'taming' (dama) is a name for qualities pertaining to concentration. Therefore, he says: 'There is no sage-wisdom for one who is uncomposed.' Here, 'sage-wisdom' (mona) refers to the knowledge of the four paths, for it 'knows' (munāti), thus it is sage-wisdom—the meaning is that it knows the Dhamma of the Four Truths. 'The realm of Death' (maccudheyya) refers to the threefold-plane round of existence, for it is called 'the realm of Death' in the sense of being the foundation of Death. 'The far shore' (pāra) is Nibbāna, the further shore of that. 'Cross over' (tareyya) means to penetrate or attain it. This is what is said: 'A person dwelling alone in the forest, heedless, would not cross over, penetrate, or attain the far shore of the realm of Death.'

Mānaṃ pahāyāti arahattamaggena navavidhamānaṃ pajahitvā. Susamāhitattoti upacārappanāsamādhīhi suṭṭhu samāhitatto. Sucetasoti ñāṇasampayuttatāya [M 1.0026] sundaracitto. Ñāṇavippayuttacittena hi sucetasoti na vuccati, tasmā ñāṇasampayuttena sucetaso hutvāti attho. Sabbadhi vippamuttoti sabbesu khandhāyatanādīsu vippamutto hutvā. Tareyyāti ettha tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ samatikkamanto nibbānaṃ paṭivijjhanto taratīti paṭivedhataraṇaṃ nāma vuttaṃ. Iti imāya gāthāya tisso sikkhā kathitā honti. Kathaṃ – māno nāmāyaṃ sīlabhedano, tasmā “mānaṃ pahāyā”ti iminā adhisīlasikkhā kathitā hoti. “Susamāhitatto”ti iminā adhicittasikkhā. “Sucetaso”ti ettha cittena paññā dassitā, tasmā iminā adhipaññāsikkhā kathitā. Adhisīlañca nāma sīle sati hoti, adhicittaṃ citte sati, adhipaññā paññāya sati. Tasmā sīlaṃ nāma pañcapi dasapi sīlāni, pātimokkhasaṃvaro adhisīlaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo cittaṃ, vipassanāpādakajjhānaṃ adhicittaṃ. Kammassakatañāṇaṃ paññā, vipassanā adhipaññā. Anuppannepi hi buddhuppāde pavattatīti pañcasīlaṃ [V 1.0026] dasasīlaṃ sīlameva, pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ buddhuppādeyeva pavattatīti adhisīlaṃ. Cittapaññāsupi eseva nayo. Apica nibbānaṃ patthayantena samādinnaṃ pañcasīlampi dasasīlampi adhisīlameva. Samāpannā aṭṭha samāpattiyopi adhicittameva. Sabbampi vā lokiyasīlaṃ sīlameva, lokuttaraṃ adhisīlaṃ. Cittapaññāsupi eseva nayoti. Iti imāya gāthāya samodhānetvā tisso sikkhā sakalasāsanaṃ kathitaṃ hotīti.

‘Having abandoned conceit’ means having abandoned the ninefold conceit by means of the path of Arahantship. ‘Well-composed’ means being thoroughly composed by means of access and absorption concentrations. ‘Of excellent mind’ means having a beautiful mind due to its association with knowledge. For one with a mind dissociated from knowledge is not called ‘of excellent mind’; therefore, the meaning is ‘having become of excellent mind through association with knowledge.’ ‘Liberated in every respect’ means having become liberated in all aggregates, sense bases, and so forth. Regarding ‘one should cross over,’ here, one crosses over by transcending the round of the three planes and by penetrating Nibbāna; this is called ‘penetrative crossing.’ Thus, by this verse, the three trainings are explained. How so? This which is called conceit is a breaker of virtue; therefore, by ‘having abandoned conceit,’ the training in higher virtue is explained. By ‘well-composed,’ the training in higher mind is explained. Here, in ‘of excellent mind,’ wisdom is shown by means of the mind; therefore, by this, the training in higher wisdom is explained. And higher virtue exists when there is virtue; higher mind exists when there is mind; higher wisdom exists when there is wisdom. Therefore, it should be understood that what is called virtue are the five precepts and the ten precepts; restraint by the Pātimokkha is called higher virtue. The eight attainments are called mind; the jhāna that is the basis for insight is called higher mind. The knowledge of kamma as one's own property is called wisdom; insight is called higher wisdom. For the five precepts and the ten precepts exist even when a Buddha has not arisen; therefore, they are merely virtue. The virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha, however, exists only with the appearance of a Buddha; therefore, it is higher virtue. This same method applies also to mind and wisdom. Furthermore, for one aspiring to Nibbāna, the five and ten precepts that have been undertaken are indeed higher virtue, and the eight attainments that have been entered upon are indeed higher mind. Alternatively, all mundane virtue is merely virtue, while supramundane virtue is higher virtue. This same method applies also to mind and wisdom. Thus, by this verse, the entire teaching is explained by bringing together the three trainings.

Mānakāmasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mānakāma Sutta is finished.

10. Araññasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Arañña Sutta

10. Dasame santānanti santakilesānaṃ, paṇḍitānaṃ vā. “Santo have sabbhi pavedayanti (jā. 2.21.413), dūre santo pakāsantī”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 304) hi paṇḍitāpi [P 1.0028] santoti vuttā. Brahmacārinanti seṭṭhacārīnaṃ maggabrahmacariyavāsaṃ vasantānaṃ. Kena vaṇṇo pasīdatīti kena kāraṇena chavivaṇṇo pasīdatīti pucchati. Kasmā panesā evaṃ pucchati? Esā kira vanasaṇḍavāsikā bhummadevatā āraññake bhikkhū pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkante araññaṃ pavisitvā [M 1.0027] rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nisinne passati. Tesañca evaṃ nisinnānaṃ balavacittekaggatā uppajjati. Tato visabhāgasantati vūpasammati, sabhāgasantati okkamati, cittaṃ pasīdati. Citte pasanne lohitaṃ pasīdati, cittasamuṭṭhānāni upādārūpāni parisuddhāni honti, vaṇṭā pamuttatālaphalassa viya mukhassa vaṇṇo hoti. Taṃ disvā devatā cintesi – “sarīravaṇṇo nāmāyaṃ paṇītāni rasasampannāni bhojanāni sukhasamphassāni nivāsanapāpuraṇasayanāni utusukhe tebhūmikādibhede ca pāsāde mālāgandhavilepanādīni ca labhantānaṃ pasīdati, ime pana bhikkhū piṇḍāya caritvā missakabhattaṃ bhuñjanti, viraḷamañcake vā phalake vā silāya vā sayanāni kappenti, rukkhamūlādīsu vā abbhokāse vā vasanti, kena nu kho kāraṇena etesaṃ vaṇṇo pasīdatī”ti. Tasmā pucchi.

10. In the tenth sutta, ‘of the peaceful’ means of those whose defilements are pacified, or of the wise. For in passages such as, “Indeed, the good make the peaceful known,” and “The peaceful shine from afar,” the wise are also called ‘peaceful.’ ‘Of the holy life practitioners’ means of those who practice the supreme conduct, living the holy life of the path. ‘By what does the complexion become clear?’ means by what reason does the skin's complexion become clear?—thus she asks. But why does she ask in this way? It is said that this earth-deity, dwelling in a forest grove, sees the forest-dwelling monks who, after the meal, having returned from their alms-round, enter the forest and sit in their night-time and day-time places, having taken up their root meditation subject. And for those sitting thus, strong one-pointedness of mind arises. Then, the dissimilar mental continuum subsides, the similar mental continuum proceeds, and the mind becomes serene. When the mind is serene, the blood becomes clear, the mind-originated derived material forms become purified, and the complexion of the face becomes like that of a palm fruit freed from its stalk. Seeing this, the deity thought: “This bodily complexion becomes clear for those who obtain excellent foods rich in flavor; pleasant-to-touch garments, coverings, and beds; and garlands, perfumes, and ointments in mansions of various kinds, such as those with three stories, providing seasonal comfort. But these monks, having wandered for alms, eat mixed food; they prepare their beds on a sparse couch, or a plank, or a stone slab; and they dwell at the foot of trees or in the open air. For what reason, indeed, does their complexion become clear?” Therefore, she asked.

Athassā bhagavā kāraṇaṃ kathento dutiyaṃ gāthaṃ āha. Tattha atītanti atīte asuko nāma rājā dhammiko ahosi, so amhākaṃ paṇīte paccaye adāsi. Ācariyupajjhāyā lābhino ahesuṃ. Atha mayaṃ evarūpāni bhojanāni bhuñjimhā, cīvarāni pārupimhāti evaṃ ekacce [V 1.0027] paccayabāhullikā viya ime bhikkhū atītaṃ nānusocanti. Nappajappanti nāgatanti anāgate dhammiko rājā bhavissati, phītā janapadā bhavissanti, bahūni sappinavanītādīni uppajjissanti, “khādatha bhuñjathā”ti tattha tattha vattāro bhavissanti, tadā mayaṃ evarūpāni bhojanāni bhuñjissāma, cīvarāni pārupissāmāti evaṃ anāgataṃ na patthenti. Paccuppannenāti yena kenaci taṅkhaṇe laddhena yāpenti. Tenāti tena tividhenāpi kāraṇena.

Then, explaining the reason to her, the Blessed One spoke the second verse. Therein, ‘the past’ means: ‘In the past, a certain king of such-and-such a name was righteous. He gave us excellent requisites. Our teachers and preceptors were recipients of gain. Then we ate such foods and wore such robes.’ Thus, unlike certain monks who dwell on the abundance of requisites, these monks do not grieve over the past. ‘They do not yearn for what has not yet come’ means: they do not long for the future, thinking: ‘In the future, a righteous king will arise, the districts will be prosperous, much ghee, fresh butter, and so on will be produced. In various places, there will be those who say, “Eat, partake!” Then we will eat such foods and we will wear such robes.’ Thus, they do not long for what has not yet come. ‘With the present’ means: they maintain themselves with whatever is received at that moment. ‘By that’ means: by that threefold reason.

Evaṃ vaṇṇasampattiṃ dassetvā idāni tasseva vaṇṇassa vināsaṃ dassento anantaraṃ gāthamāha. Tattha [P 1.0029] anāgatappajappāyāti anāgatassa patthanāya. Etenāti etena kāraṇadvayena. Naḷova harito lutoti yathā harito naḷo lāyitvā uṇhapāsāṇe pakkhitto sussati, evaṃ sussantīti.

Having thus shown the perfection of complexion, now, showing the destruction of that very complexion, He spoke the next verse. Therein, ‘by yearning for what has not yet come’ means: by longing for what has not yet come. ‘By this’ means: by this combination of two reasons. ‘Like a green reed cut down’ means: just as a green reed, when cut and thrown upon a hot stone slab, withers, so do fools wither.

Araññasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā. Naḷavaggo paṭhamo.

The commentary on the Arañña Sutta is finished. The Naḷa Vagga, the first.

2. Nandanavaggo

2. The Nandana Vagga

1. Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Nandana Sutta

11. Nandanavaggassa [M 1.0028] paṭhame tatrāti tasmiṃ ārāme. Khoti byañjanasiliṭṭhatāvasena nipātamattaṃ. Bhikkhū āmantesīti parisajeṭṭhake bhikkhū jānāpesi. Bhikkhavoti tesaṃ āmantanākāradīpanaṃ. Bhadanteti pativacanadānaṃ. Te bhikkhūti ye tattha sammukhībhūtā dhammapaṭiggāhakā bhikkhū. Bhagavato paccassosunti bhagavato vacanaṃ patiassosuṃ, abhimukhā hutvā suṇiṃsu sampaṭicchiṃsūti attho. Etadavocāti etaṃ idāni vattabbaṃ “bhūtapubba”ntiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha tāvatiṃsakāyikāti tāvatiṃsakāye nibbattā. Tāvatiṃsakāyo nāma dutiyadevaloko vuccati. Maghena māṇavena saddhiṃ macalagāme kālaṃ katvā tattha uppanne tettiṃsa devaputte upādāya kira tassa devalokassa ayaṃ paṇṇatti jātāti vadanti. Yasmā pana sesacakkavāḷesupi cha kāmāvacaradevalokā atthi. Vuttampi cetaṃ “sahassaṃ [V 1.0028] cātumahārājikānaṃ sahassaṃ tāvatiṃsāna”nti (a. ni. 10.29), tasmā nāmapaṇṇattiyevesā tassa devalokassāti veditabbā. Evañhi niddosaṃ padaṃ hoti.

11. In the first sutta of the Nandana Vagga, 'there' refers to that park. 'Kho' is merely a particle serving for stylistic fluency. 'He addressed the monks' means he informed the senior monks in the assembly. 'Monks' serves to clarify the manner of address. 'Venerable sir' is a term of response. 'Those monks' refers to those monks present who were receivers of the Dhamma. 'They responded to the Blessed One' means they listened attentively to the Blessed One’s words; having become attentive, they listened and accepted them—this is the meaning. 'He said this' refers to the words now to be spoken, beginning with 'Once upon a time.' Here, 'belonging to the Tāvatiṃsa realm' means born in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. The Tāvatiṃsa heaven is called the second deva world. It is said that this designation for that deva world arose on account of the thirty-three devaputtas who, after passing away in the village of Macala with the young man Magha, were born there. However, since there are six sense-sphere deva worlds in other world-systems as well—and this has been stated: 'A thousand of the Cātumahārājikas, a thousand of the Tāvatiṃsas'—it should be understood that this is merely a name-designation for that deva world. For in this way, the term is faultless.

Nandane vaneti ettha taṃ vanaṃ paviṭṭhe paviṭṭhe nandayati tosetīti nandanaṃ. Pañcasu hi maraṇanimittesu uppannesu “sampattiṃ pahāya cavissāmā”ti paridevamānā devatā sakko devānamindo “mā paridevittha, abhijjanadhammā nāma saṅkhārā natthī”ti ovaditvā tattha pavesāpeti. Tāsaṃ aññāhi devatāhi bāhāsu gahetvā pavesitānampi [P 1.0030] tassa sampattiṃ disvāva maraṇasoko vūpasammati, pītipāmojjameva uppajjati. Atha tasmiṃ kīḷamānā eva uṇhasantatto himapiṇḍo viya vilīyanti, vātāpahatadīpasikhā viya vijjhāyantīti evaṃ yaṃkiñci anto paviṭṭhaṃ nandayati tosetiyevāti nandanaṃ, tasmiṃ nandane. Accharāsaṅghaparivutāti accharāti devadhītānaṃ nāmaṃ, tāsaṃ samūhena parivutā.

Herein, regarding the phrase 'in the Nandana grove': Because it delights (nandayati) and satisfies (toseti) those who repeatedly enter that grove, it is called Nandana. Indeed, when the five signs of death have arisen, and deities are lamenting, 'Having abandoned our prosperity, we shall pass away,' Sakka, the lord of the devas, advises them, saying, 'Do not grieve; there are no conditioned things that are of an imperishable nature,' and then causes them to enter that grove. Even for those who are made to enter, having been taken by the arms by other deities, the sorrow of death is pacified just upon seeing the splendor of that grove; only joy and delight arise. Then, while they are playing therein, they melt away like a lump of snow thoroughly heated by the sun's warmth, and they are extinguished like the flame of a lamp struck by the wind. Thus, because it delights and indeed satisfies whosoever has entered within, it is called Nandana. In that Nandana grove. Regarding the phrase 'surrounded by a host of nymphs': 'accharā' is a name for celestial maidens, and the meaning is 'surrounded by their multitude'.

Dibbehīti devaloke nibbattehi. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehīti manāpiyarūpasaddagandharasaphoṭṭhabbasaṅkhātehi pañcahi kāmabandhanehi kāmakoṭṭhāsehi vā[M 1.0029]. Samappitāti upetā. Itaraṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Paricārayamānāti ramamānā, tesu tesu vā rūpādīsu indriyāni sañcārayamānā. Tāyaṃ velāyanti tasmiṃ paricāraṇakāle. So panassa devaputtassa adhunā abhinibbattakālo veditabbo. Tassa hi paṭisandhikkhaṇeyeva rattasuvaṇṇakkhandho viya virocayamāno tigāvutappamāṇo attabhāvo nibbatti. So dibbavatthanivattho dibbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito dibbamālāvilepanadharo dibbehi candanacuṇṇehi samaṃ vikiriyamāno dibbehi pañcahi kāmaguṇehi ovuto nivuto pariyonaddho lobhābhibhūto hutvā lobhanissaraṇaṃ nibbānaṃ apassanto āsabhiṃ vācaṃ bhāsanto viya mahāsaddena “na te sukhaṃ pajānantī”ti imaṃ gāthaṃ gāyamāno nandanavane vicari. Tena vuttaṃ – “tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsī”ti.

By 'divine' is meant arisen in the realm of the gods. 'By the five strands of sensual pleasure' refers to the five sensual bonds, or the five portions of sensual pleasure, known as pleasing sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. 'Endowed' means possessed of. The other word is a synonym of that very one. 'Being ministered to' means delighting, or engaging their senses in those various sights and so on. 'At that time' refers to that moment of being ministered to. Now, the time of that devaputta’s recent arising should be understood. For at the very moment of his relinking, his existence, shining like a heap of red gold, manifested with a size of three gāvutas. Clad in divine garments, adorned with divine ornaments, wearing divine garlands and perfumes, and sprinkled with divine sandalwood powder, he was enveloped, enclosed, and enmeshed by the five divine strands of sensual pleasure. Overpowered by greed, and failing to see Nibbāna, the escape from greed, he wandered in the Nandana Grove, speaking as if with a bull-like voice and singing this verse with a loud voice: "They do not know happiness." Thus it is said: "At that time, he spoke this verse."

Ye na passanti nandananti ye tatra pañcakāmaguṇānubhavanavasena nandanavanaṃ na passanti. Naradevānanti devanarānaṃ, devapurisānanti attho. Tidasānanti tikkhattuṃ dasannaṃ. Yasassinanti parivārasaṅkhātena yasena sampannānaṃ.

'Those who do not see Nandana' means those who, on account of their experience of the five sensual pleasures there, do not see the Nandana grove. 'Of divine men' means of god-men, that is, of male gods. 'Of the Thirty' means of three times ten. 'Of the glorious' means of those endowed with glory in the sense of an entourage.

Aññatarā devatāti ekā ariyasāvikā devatā. Paccabhāsīti “ayaṃ bāladevatā imaṃ sampattiṃ [V 1.0029] niccaṃ acalaṃ maññati, nāssā chedanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammataṃ jānātī”ti adhippāyaṃ vivaṭṭetvā dassentī “na tvaṃ bāle”ti imāya gāthāya patiabhāsi. Yathā arahataṃ vacoti yathā arahantānaṃ vacanaṃ, tathā tvaṃ na jānāsīti. Evaṃ tassā adhippāyaṃ paṭikkhipitvā [P 1.0031] idāni arahantānaṃ vacanaṃ dassentī aniccātiādimāha. Tattha aniccā vata saṅkhārāti sabbe tebhūmakasaṅkhārā hutvā abhāvatthena aniccā. Uppādavayadhamminoti uppādavayasabhāvā. Uppajjitvā nirujjhantīti idaṃ purimasseva vevacanaṃ. Yasmā vā uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tasmā uppādavayadhamminoti. Uppādavayaggahaṇena cettha tadanantarā vemajjhaṭṭhānaṃ gahitameva hoti. Tesaṃ vūpasamo sukhoti tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vūpasamasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānameva sukhaṃ. Idaṃ arahataṃ vacoti.

‘A certain deity’ means a certain female deity who is a noble disciple. ‘She replied’ means: countering his intention—‘This foolish male deity thinks this fortune is permanent and unmoving, not knowing its nature of being subject to cutting, breaking, and destruction’—and demonstrating this, she spoke in response with the verse beginning, ‘Na tvaṃ bāle...’. ‘As is the word of the arahants’ means: just as the word of the arahants is, so you do not know. Thus, having refuted his intention, now showing the word of the arahants, she spoke the words beginning with ‘Impermanent,’ and so on. Therein, ‘Impermanent, alas, are formations’ means: all formations of the three realms, having come to be, are impermanent in the sense of their subsequent non-existence. ‘Of the nature to arise and pass away’ means: they have the nature of arising and passing away. ‘Having arisen, they cease’: this is just a synonym for the former. Or, because they arise and then cease, they are therefore of the nature to arise and pass away. And herein, by the taking up of ‘arising and passing away,’ the moment of duration in between them is also taken. ‘Their stilling is bliss’ means: the stilling of those formations, which is reckoned as Nibbāna, is itself bliss. This is the word of the arahants.

Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Nandana Sutta is concluded.

2. Nandatisuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Nandati Sutta

12. Dutiye [M 1.0030] nandatīti tussati attamano hoti. Puttimāti bahuputto. Tassa hi ekacce puttā kasikammaṃ katvā dhaññassa koṭṭhe pūrenti, ekacce vaṇijjaṃ katvā hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ āharanti, ekacce rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahitvā yānavāhanagāmanigamādīni labhanti. Atha tesaṃ ānubhāvasaṅkhātaṃ siriṃ anubhavamānā mātā vā pitā vā nandati. Chaṇadivasādīsu vā maṇḍitapasādhite putte sampattiṃ anubhavamāne disvā nandatīti, “nandati puttehi puttimā”ti āha. Gohi tathevāti yathā puttimā puttehi, tathā gosāmikopi sampannaṃ gomaṇḍalaṃ disvā gāvo nissāya gorasasampattiṃ anubhavamāno gohi nandati. Upadhī hi narassa nandanāti, ettha upadhīti cattāro upadhī – kāmūpadhi, khandhūpadhi, kilesūpadhi, abhisaṅkhārūpadhīti. Kāmāpi hi “yaṃ pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ kāmānaṃ assādo”ti (ma. ni. 1.166) evaṃ vuttassa sukhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato “upadhiyati ettha sukha”nti iminā vacanatthena upadhīti vuccati. Khandhāpi khandhamūlakassa dukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, kilesāpi apāyadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvato, abhisaṅkhārāpi bhavadukkhassa adhiṭṭhānabhāvatoti. Idha pana kāmūpadhi adhippeto. Pañca hi kāmaguṇā tebhūmikādipāsāda-uḷārasayana-vatthālaṅkāra-nāṭakaparivārādivasena [P 1.0032] paccupaṭṭhitā pītisomanassaṃ upasaṃharamānā naraṃ nandayanti. Tasmā yathā puttā ca gāvo ca, evaṃ imepi upadhī hi narassa nandanāti veditabbā. Na hi so nandati yo nirūpadhīti yo kāmaguṇasampattirahito daliddo dullabhaghāsacchādano[V 1.0030], na hi so nandati. Evarūpo manussapeto ca manussanerayiko ca kiṃ nandissati bhagavāti āha.

12. In the second verse, 'he delights' means he is pleased and glad-minded. 'One with sons' means having many sons. For some of his sons, having done agricultural work, fill the granaries with grain; some, having done trading, bring gold and silver; some, having attended upon the king, obtain vehicles, conveyances, villages, towns, and so on. Then the mother or father, experiencing the glory known as their influence, delights. Or, on festival days and the like, seeing their sons, adorned and decorated, experiencing success, they delight. Thus it was said: 'One with sons delights in sons.' 'With cattle, it is just so' means: just as one with sons delights in sons, so too the owner of cattle, seeing a prosperous herd of cattle and, depending on the cows, experiencing the good fortune of dairy products, delights in his cattle. 'For attachments are a man's delight': here, 'attachments' refers to the four attachments—the attachment to sensual pleasures, the attachment to the aggregates, the attachment to the defilements, and the attachment to volitional formations. For sensual pleasures, too, are called 'attachments' because they are the basis for the happiness spoken of thus: 'Whatever pleasure and gladness arise in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure, this is the gratification of sensual pleasures' (MN 1.166), and it is called 'attachment' (upadhi) with the verbal meaning 'happiness is founded on this.' The aggregates, too, are called attachments because they are the basis for suffering rooted in the aggregates; the defilements, too, because they are the basis for suffering in the lower realms; and the volitional formations, too, because they are the basis for the suffering of existence. Here, however, the attachment to sensual pleasures is intended. For the five strands of sensual pleasure—presented in the form of three-storied palaces, excellent beds, clothing, ornaments, entertainments, retinues, and so on—bring joy and gladness, making a person delight. Therefore, it should be understood that just as sons and cattle, so too these attachments are a man's delight. 'He who is without attachments does not delight' means: one who is poor, devoid of the good fortune of sensual pleasures, for whom food and clothing are hard to get—he does not delight. He said: 'O Blessed One, how could such a human ghost or a human hell-being delight?'

Idaṃ sutvā satthā cintesi – “ayaṃ devatā sokavatthumeva nandavatthuṃ karoti, sokavatthubhāvamassā dīpessāmī”ti phalena phalaṃ pātento viya tāyeva upamāya tassā vādaṃ bhindanto tameva gāthaṃ parivattetvā socatīti āha. Tattha socati puttehīti videsagamanādivasena puttesu naṭṭhesupi nassantesupi idāni nassissantīti nāsasaṅkīpi [M 1.0031] socati, tathā matesupi marantesupi corehi rājapurisehi gahitesu vā paccatthikānaṃ hatthaṃ upagatesu vā maraṇasaṅkīpi hutvā socati. Rukkhapabbatādīhi patitvā hatthapādādīnaṃ bhedavasena bhinnesupi bhijjantesupi bhedasaṅkīpi hutvā socati. Yathā ca puttehi puttimā, gosāmikopi tatheva navahākārehi gohi socati. Upadhī hi narassa socanāti yathā ca puttagāvo, evaṃ pañca kāmaguṇopadhīpi –

Having heard this, the Teacher thought: 'This devatā makes a basis for sorrow into a basis for delight. I shall reveal to him its nature as a basis for sorrow.' Like one knocking down a fruit with another fruit, using that very same simile to break his view, he reversed that very verse and said, 'One sorrows.' Therein, as to 'one sorrows because of sons': by way of going to another country and so forth, when sons have perished, are perishing, or being apprehensive of their destruction, thinking, 'Now they will perish,' one sorrows. Similarly, when they have died, are dying, have been seized by thieves or royal officers, or have fallen into the hands of enemies, being apprehensive of their death, one sorrows. Having fallen from a tree, a mountain, or the like, by way of the breaking of hands, feet, and so on, when they are broken or are being broken, being apprehensive of their breaking, one sorrows. And just as one with sons sorrows because of his sons, so too a cattle-owner sorrows because of his cattle in the very same way for nine reasons. As to 'For attachments are a man's sorrow': just as sons and cattle cause sorrow, so too do the five strands of sensual pleasure, which are attachments—

“Tassa ce kāmayānassa, chandajātassa jantuno;

Te kāmā parihāyanti, sallaviddhova ruppatī”ti. (su. ni. 773) –

For that being who is desiring, for whom craving has arisen, if those sensual pleasures should diminish, he is tormented, just as one pierced by an arrow.

Vuttanayena naraṃ socanti. Tasmā narassa socanā sokavatthukamevāti veditabbā. Na hi so socati, yo nirūpadhīti yassa pana catubbidhāpete upadhiyo natthi, so nirupadhi mahākhīṇāsavo kiṃ socissati, na socati devateti.

In the manner stated, they [the attachments] cause a man to sorrow. Therefore, it should be known that the causes of a man's sorrow are indeed a basis for sorrow. As to 'For he does not sorrow, who is without attachments': for whom these fourfold attachments do not exist, he, being without attachments, the great one whose cankers are destroyed—for what would he sorrow? He does not sorrow, O devatā.

Nandatisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Nandati Sutta is concluded.

3. Natthiputtasamasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Natthiputtasama Sutta

13. Tatiye natthi puttasamaṃ pemanti virūpepi hi attano puttake suvaṇṇabimbakaṃ viya maññanti, mālāguḷe viya sīsādīsu katvā pariharamānā tehi ohaditāpi omuttikāpi gandhavilepanapatitā viya somanassaṃ āpajjanti. Tenāha – “natthi puttasamaṃ pema”nti[P 1.0033]. Puttapemasamaṃ pemaṃ nāma natthīti vuttaṃ hoti. Gosamitaṃ dhananti gohi samaṃ godhanasamaṃ godhanasadisaṃ [V 1.0031] aññaṃ dhanaṃ nāma natthi bhagavāti āha. Sūriyasamā ābhāti sūriyābhāya samā aññā ābhā nāma natthīti dasseti. Samuddaparamāti ye keci aññe sarā nāma, sabbe te samuddaparamā, samuddo tesaṃ uttamo, samuddasadisaṃ aññaṃ udakanidhānaṃ nāma natthi, bhagavāti.

13. In the third sutta, regarding 'There is no love equal to that for a son': for even if their own children are unattractive, they regard them as if they were a golden image, carry them on their heads and so forth like balls of flowers, and though soiled by their excrement and urine, they attain gladness as if fragrant paste had fallen upon them. Therefore, He said: 'There is no love equal to that for a son.' This means it is said that there is no so-called love that is equal to the love for a son. Regarding 'Wealth equal to cattle': he said, 'O Blessed One, there is no other so-called wealth that is equal to cattle, equal to cattle-wealth, or like cattle-wealth.' Regarding 'Light equal to the sun': this shows that 'There is no other so-called light that is equal to the sun's radiance.' Regarding 'The ocean is supreme': whatever other rivers so-called there may be, all of them have the ocean as supreme—the ocean is the highest of them; there is no other so-called repository of water like the ocean, O Blessed One.

Yasmā pana attapemena samaṃ pemaṃ nāma natthi. Mātāpitādayo hi chaḍḍetvāpi puttadhītādayo ca aposetvāpi sattā attānameva [M 1.0032] posenti. Dhaññena ca samaṃ dhanaṃ nāma natthi. (Yadā hi sattā dubbhikkhā honti), tathārūpe hi kāle hiraññasuvaṇṇādīni gomahiṃsādīnipi dhaññaggahaṇatthaṃ dhaññasāmikānameva santikaṃ gahetvā gacchanti. Paññāya ca samā ābhā nāma natthi. Sūriyādayo hi ekadesaṃyeva obhāsanti, paccuppannameva ca tamaṃ vinodenti. Paññā pana dasasahassimpi lokadhātuṃ ekappajjotaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, atītaṃsādipaṭicchādakañca tamaṃ vidhamati. Meghavuṭṭhiyā ca samo saro nāma natthi. Nadīvāpi hotu talākādīni vā, vuṭṭhisamo saro nāma natthi. Meghavuṭṭhiyā hi pacchinnāya mahāsamuddo aṅgulipabbatemanamattampi udakaṃ na hoti, vuṭṭhiyā pana pavattamānāya yāva ābhassarabhavanāpi ekodakaṃ hoti. Tasmā bhagavā devatāya paṭigāthaṃ vadanto natthi attasamaṃ pemantiādimāhāti.

Moreover, because there is no love so-called that is equal to love for oneself. Indeed, beings, even abandoning their mothers, fathers, and so on, and not nourishing their sons, daughters, and so on, nourish only themselves. And there is no wealth so-called that is equal to grain. For in such a time of famine, people take even gold, silver, cattle, and buffaloes, and go to the presence of the owners of grain in order to obtain grain. And there is no light so-called that is equal to wisdom. For the sun and other luminaries illuminate only one region and dispel only the present darkness. But wisdom is able to make the entire ten-thousandfold world-system into a single radiance, and it dispels the darkness that conceals the past and so on. And there is no stream so-called that is equal to rainfall. Whether it be a river, or a lake, and so on, there is no stream so-called that is equal to rainfall. For when the rain has ceased, in the great ocean there is not even water to the measure of a finger-joint, but when the rain is falling, it becomes a single body of water even up to the Ābhassara realm. Therefore, the Blessed One, giving the verse in response to the deity, spoke the words beginning with, 'There is no love equal to self-love,' and so on.

Natthiputtasamasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Natthiputtasama Sutta is concluded.

4. Khattiyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta

14. Catutthe khattiyo dvipadanti dvipadānaṃ rājā seṭṭho. Komārīti kumārikāle gahitā. Ayaṃ sesabhariyānaṃ seṭṭhāti vadati. Pubbajoti paṭhamaṃ jāto kāṇo vāpi hotu kuṇiādīnaṃ vā aññataro, yo paṭhamaṃ jāto, ayameva putto imissā devatāya vāde seṭṭho nāma hoti. Yasmā pana dvipadādīnaṃ buddhādayo seṭṭhā, tasmā bhagavā paṭigāthaṃ āha. Tattha kiñcāpi bhagavā sabbesaṃyeva apadādibhedānaṃ sattānaṃ seṭṭho, uppajjamāno panesa sabbasattaseṭṭho dvipadesuyeva uppajjati, tasmā sambuddho dvipadaṃ seṭṭhoti āha. Dvipadesu uppannassa cassa sabbasattaseṭṭhabhāvo [P 1.0034] appaṭihatova hoti. Ājānīyoti hatthī vā hotu assādīsu aññataro vā, yo kāraṇaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ ājānīyova catuppadānaṃ seṭṭhoti attho. Kūṭakaṇṇarañño guḷavaṇṇaasso viya. Rājā kira pācīnadvārena nikkhamitvā cetiyapabbataṃ gamissāmīti kalambanadītīraṃ sampatto, asso tīre ṭhatvā udakaṃ otarituṃ na icchati[V 1.0032], rājā assācariyaṃ āmantetvā, “aho [M 1.0033] vata tayā asso sikkhāpito udakaṃ otarituṃ na icchatī”ti āha. Ācariyo “susikkhāpito deva asso, etassa hi cittaṃ – ‘sacāhaṃ udakaṃ otarissāmi, vālaṃ temissati, vāle tinte rañño aṅge udakaṃ pāteyyā’ti, evaṃ tumhākaṃ sarīre udakapātanabhayena na otarati, vālaṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti āha. Rājā tathā kāresi. Asso vegena otaritvā pāraṃ gato. Sussūsāti sussūsamānā. Kumārikāle vā gahitā hotu pacchā vā, surūpā vā virūpā vā, yā sāmikaṃ sussūsati paricarati toseti, sā bhariyānaṃ seṭṭhā. Assavoti āsuṇamāno. Jeṭṭho vā hi hotu kaniṭṭho vā, yo mātāpitūnaṃ vacanaṃ suṇāti, sampaṭicchati, ovādapaṭikaro hoti, ayaṃ puttānaṃ seṭṭho, aññehi sandhicchedakādicorehi puttehi ko attho devateti.

14. In the fourth, 'khattiyo dvipadanti' means: among two-footed beings, the king is supreme. 'Komārīti' refers to a wife taken in her maidenly youth. This one, it is said, is supreme among other wives. 'Pubbajo' means the first-born; whether he be blind, or one among the crippled and so on, whichever son is born first, this very son, in the view of this deity, is called supreme. However, since among two-footed beings and so on, the Buddhas and others are supreme, the Blessed One spoke the reply-verse. Therein, although the Blessed One is supreme among all beings with their various divisions, such as the footless and so on, nevertheless this one, being supreme among all beings, when he arises, arises only among two-footed beings. Therefore, he said, 'The Perfectly Enlightened One is the supreme among the two-footed.' And for him who is born among the two-footed, his state of being supreme among all beings is indeed unopposed. 'Ājānīyoti' means: whether it be an elephant or one among horses and so on, whichever one knows the proper reason, this very one is a thoroughbred and is supreme among quadrupeds; this is the meaning. Like the horse named Guḷavaṇṇa of King Kūṭakaṇṇa. It is said that the king, having set out from the eastern gate with the intention of going to Cetiyapabbata, reached the bank of the Kalamba river. The horse, standing on the bank, did not wish to enter the water. The king, summoning the horse trainer, said, 'Alas, this horse trained by you does not wish to enter the water!' The trainer said, 'The horse is well-trained, Your Majesty. Indeed, its thought is this: "If I enter the water, my tail will get wet; when the tail is wet, water might fall upon the king's person." Thus, out of fear of water falling upon your body, it does not enter. Have its tail held up.' The king had it done so. The horse swiftly entered the water and went to the other side. 'Sussūsāti' means one who listens well. Whether she is taken in her maidenly youth or later, whether beautiful or ugly, whichever wife listens to her husband, serves him, and pleases him, she is supreme among wives. 'Assavoti' means one who is obedient. Whether he be the eldest or the youngest, whichever son listens to his parents' words, accepts them, and acts in accordance with their instruction, he is supreme among sons. O deity, what is the use of other sons who are thieves, such as housebreakers and so on?

Khattiyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Khattiya Sutta is concluded.

5. Saṇamānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Saṇamāna Sutta

15. Pañcame ṭhite majjhanhiketi ṭhitamajjhanhike. Sannisīvesūti yathā phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ upagantvā sannisinnesu vissamamānesu. Ṭhitamajjhanhikakālo nāmesa sabbasattānaṃ iriyāpathadubbalyakālo. Idha pana pakkhīnaṃyeva vasena dassito. Saṇatevāti saṇati viya mahāviravaṃ viya muccati. Saṇamānameva cettha “saṇatevā”ti vuttaṃ. Tappaṭibhāgaṃ nāmetaṃ. Nidāghasamayasmiñhi ṭhitamajjhanhikakāle catuppadagaṇesu ceva pakkhīgaṇesu ca sannisinnesu vātapūritānaṃ susirarukkhānañceva chiddaveṇupabbānañca khandhena khandhaṃ sākhāya sākhaṃ saṅghaṭṭayantānaṃ pādapānañca araññamajjhe mahāsaddo uppajjati[P 1.0035]. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Taṃ bhayaṃ paṭibhāti manti taṃ evarūpe kāle mahāaraññassa saṇamānaṃ mayhaṃ bhayaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti. Dandhapaññā kiresā devatā tasmiṃ khaṇe attano nisajjaphāsukaṃ kathāphāsukaṃ dutiyakaṃ alabhantī evamāha. Yasmā pana tādise kāle piṇḍapātapaṭikkantassa vivitte araññāyatane kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nisinnassa bhikkhuno anappakaṃ sukhaṃ uppajjati, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

15. In the fifth sutta, `ṭhite majjhanhike` means at high noon. `Sannisīvesu` means when they have approached a comfortable place and are settled and resting. The time of high noon is indeed a time of weakness in posture for all beings. Here, however, it is shown only in the case of birds. `Saṇatevā` means it is released like a resounding, like a great clamor. What is merely resounding is here called `saṇatevā`. This is its counterpart. For in the hot season, at the time of high noon, when the groups of four-footed animals and flocks of birds have settled down, a great sound arises in the middle of the forest from hollow trees filled with wind, from hollow bamboo joints, and from trees striking trunk against trunk and branch against branch. This is said in reference to that. `Taṃ bhayaṃ paṭibhāti maṃ` means: at such a time, that resounding of the great forest presents itself to me as a danger. This devatā, it seems, is of slow wisdom; not finding at that moment a second companion for comfortable sitting and pleasant conversation, they speak thus. But because at such a time, for a bhikkhu who has returned from the alms-round and is sitting in a secluded forest abode, having taken up a meditation subject, much happiness arises, in reference to which it was said—

“Suññāgāraṃ [M 1.0034] paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī ratī hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato”ti. (dha. pa. 373) ca,

For a bhikkhu who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is stilled, there is a non-human delight when he rightly sees the Dhamma.

“Purato [V 1.0033] pacchato vāpi, aparo ce na vijjati;

Atīva phāsu bhavati, ekassa vasato vane”ti. (theragā. 537) ca;

Whether before or behind, if no other is found, it is exceedingly pleasant for one living alone in the forest.

Tasmā bhagavā dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha sā rati paṭibhāti manti yā evarūpe kāle ekakassa nisajjā nāma, sā rati mayhaṃ upaṭṭhātīti attho. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Therefore, the Blessed One spoke the second verse. Therein, `sā rati paṭibhāti maṃ` means: that delight which is called 'sitting alone' at such a time, that delight presents itself to me—this is the meaning. The rest is just the same.

Saṇamānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saṇamāna Sutta is concluded.

6. Niddātandīsuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Niddātandī Sutta

16. Chaṭṭhe niddāti, “abhijānāmahaṃ, aggivessana, gimhānaṃ pacchime māse niddaṃ okkamitā”ti (ma. ni. 1.387) evarūpāya abyākataniddāya pubbabhāgāparabhāgesu sekhaputhujjanānaṃ sasaṅkhārikaakusale citte uppannaṃ thinamiddhaṃ. Tandīti aticchātātisītādikālesu uppannaṃ āgantukaṃ ālasiyaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “tattha katamā tandī? Yā tandī tandiyanā tandimanatā ālasyaṃ ālasyāyanā ālasyāyitattaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati tandī”ti (vibha. 857). Vijambhitāti kāyavijambhanā. Aratīti akusalapakkhā ukkaṇṭhitatā. Bhattasammadoti bhattamucchā bhattakilamatho. Vitthāro pana tesaṃ – “tattha katamā [P 1.0036] vijambhitā? Yā kāyassa jambhanā vijambhanā”tiādinā nayena abhidhamme āgatova. Etenāti etena niddādinā upakkilesena upakkiliṭṭho nivāritapātubhāvo. Nappakāsatīti na jotati, na pātubhavatīti attho. Ariyamaggoti lokuttaramaggo. Idhāti imasmiṃ loke. Pāṇinanti sattānaṃ. Vīriyenāti maggasahajātavīriyena. Naṃ paṇāmetvāti etaṃ kilesajātaṃ nīharitvā. Ariyamaggoti lokiyalokuttaramaggo. Iti maggeneva upakkilese nīharitvā maggassa visuddhi vuttāti.

16. In the sixth, 'sleepiness' means: 'I know, Aggivessana, of having fallen asleep in the last month of the hot season' (MN 1.387). In the preliminary and subsequent stages of such indeterminate sleep, for trainees and ordinary people, it is the sloth and torpor that has arisen in a prompted unwholesome consciousness. 'Lethargy' means the adventitious laziness that arises at times of excessive hunger, extreme cold, and so on. And this was said: 'Therein, what is lethargy? That which is lethargy, the manner of being lethargic, the state of mind of being lethargic, laziness, the manner of being lazy, the state of being lazy—this is called lethargy' (Vibh. 857). 'Yawning' means the stretching of the body. 'Discontent' means dissatisfaction on the unwholesome side. 'Drowsiness after a meal' means intoxication from a meal or fatigue from a meal. The detailed explanation of these, however, has come in the Abhidhamma in this way: 'Therein, what is yawning? That which is the body's yawning, stretching,' and so on. 'By this' means: defiled by this defilement of sleepiness and so on, his manifestation is obstructed. 'It does not shine' means it does not glow, it does not become manifest—this is the meaning. 'The noble path' means the supramundane path. 'Here' means in this world. 'Of beings' means of living beings. 'With energy' means with the energy concomitant with the path. 'Having dispelled it' means having removed this mass of defilements. 'The noble path' means the mundane and supramundane path. Thus, it is said that the purity of the supramundane path is achieved by removing the defilements with the mundane and supramundane path itself.

Niddātandīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Niddātandī Sutta is concluded.

7. Dukkarasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse on Difficult Deeds

17. Sattame [M 1.0035] duttitikkhanti dukkhamaṃ duadhivāsiyaṃ. Abyattenāti bālena. Sāmaññanti samaṇadhammo. Iminā devatā idaṃ dasseti – yaṃ paṇḍitā kulaputtā dasapi vassāni vīsatipi saṭṭhipi [V 1.0034] vassāni dante abhidantamādhāya jivhāya tāluṃ āhaccapi cetasā cittaṃ abhiniggaṇhitvāpi ekāsanaṃ ekabhattaṃ paṭisevamānā āpāṇakoṭikaṃ brahmacariyaṃ carantā sāmaññaṃ karonti. Taṃ bhagavā bālo abyatto kātuṃ na sakkotīti. Bahū hi tattha sambādhāti tasmiṃ sāmaññasaṅkhāte ariyamagge bahū sambādhā maggādhigamāya paṭipannassa pubbabhāge bahū parissayāti dasseti.

17. In the seventh discourse, 'duttitikkhaṃ' means 'hard to endure,' 'difficult to bear.' 'Abyattenā' means 'by a fool.' 'Sāmaññaṃ' means 'the practice of a recluse.' By this, the devatā shows this meaning: That which wise clansmen undertake as the practice of a recluse—practicing for ten, twenty, or even sixty years, having placed the lower teeth on the upper teeth, having struck the palate with the tongue, having subdued the unwholesome mind with the wholesome mind, observing the practice of one session and one meal, and living the noble life until its very end—the Bhagavā cannot call that person a fool or an unskilled one. 'Bahū hi tattha sambādhā' means: in that noble path known as the practice of a recluse, there are many hindrances. It shows that for one practicing for the attainment of the path, there are many dangers in the preliminary stage.

Cittañce na nivārayeti yadi ayoniso uppannaṃ cittaṃ na nivāreyya, kati ahāni sāmaññaṃ careyya? Ekadivasampi na careyya. Cittavasiko hi samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Pade padeti ārammaṇe ārammaṇe. Ārammaṇañhi idha padanti adhippetaṃ. Yasmiṃ yasmiṃ hi ārammaṇe kileso uppajjati, tattha tattha bālo visīdati nāma. Iriyāpathapadampi vaṭṭati. Gamanādīsu hi yattha yattha kileso uppajjati, tattha tattheva visīdati nāma. Saṅkappānanti kāmasaṅkappādīnaṃ.

'Cittaṃ ce na nivāraye' means: if one were not to restrain a mind that has arisen improperly, for how many days could one practice the state of a recluse? One could not practice for even a single day. Indeed, one who is under the sway of the mind is not able to practice the dhamma of a recluse. 'Pade pade' means: in every object. For here, by 'pada' is meant 'object' (ārammaṇa). Indeed, in whatever object a defilement arises, in that very object the fool is said to sink. The word 'pada' also applies to posture (iriyāpatha). Indeed, in whatever posture, such as walking, etc., a defilement arises, in that very posture one is said to sink. 'Saṅkappānaṃ' means: of thoughts such as sensual thought, etc.

Kummo vāti kacchapo viya. Aṅgānīti gīvapañcamāni aṅgāni. Samodahanti samodahanto, samodahitvā vā. Manovitakketi manamhi uppannavitakke. Ettāvatā idaṃ dasseti – yathā kummo soṇḍipañcamāni aṅgāni sake kapāle samodahanto siṅgālassa otāraṃ na deti, samodahitvā cassa [P 1.0037] appasayhataṃ āpajjati, evamevaṃ bhikkhu manamhi uppannavitakke sake ārammaṇakapāle samodahaṃ mārassa otāraṃ na deti, samodahitvā cassa appasayhataṃ āpajjatīti. Anissitoti taṇhādiṭṭhinissayehi anissito hutvā. Aheṭhayānoti avihiṃsamāno. Parinibbutoti kilesanibbānena parinibbuto. Nūpavadeyya kañcīti yaṃkiñci puggalaṃ ācāravipattiādīsu yāya kāyaci maṅkuṃ kātukāmo hutvā na vadeyya, “kālena vakkhāmi no akālenā”tiādayo pana pañca dhamme ajjhattaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhitena cittena kāruññataṃ paṭicca vadeyyāti.

“Like a tortoise” means like a turtle. “Aṅgāni” refers to the limbs, with the neck as the fifth. “Samodahanti” means drawing in well, or having drawn in well. “Manovitakke” refers to thoughts that have arisen in the mind. By this, it is shown: Just as a tortoise, drawing its limbs, with the snout-like neck as the fifth, into its own shell, does not give an opening to the jackal, and having drawn them in, becomes unassailable by it; in the very same way, a bhikkhu, drawing in the thoughts that have arisen in the mind into the shell that is his own meditation object, does not give an opening to Māra, and having drawn them in, becomes unassailable by him. “Anissito” means having become unreliant on the supports of craving and wrong views. “Aheṭhayāno” means not harming. “Parinibbuto” means fully extinguished through the extinction of defilements. “Nūpavadeyya kañci” means that, desiring to make someone ashamed, one should not reprove any person whatsoever regarding any kind of failure, such as a failure in conduct. However, having established the five factors within oneself, such as, “I will speak at the right time, not at the wrong time,” one should speak based on compassion, with a mind well-established in the nature of uplifting.

Dukkarasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on Difficult Deeds is concluded.

8. Hirīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Discourse on Moral Shame

18. Aṭṭhame [M 1.0036] hirīnisedhoti hiriyā akusale dhamme nisedhetīti hirīnisedho. Koci lokasmiṃ [V 1.0035] vijjatīti koci evarūpo vijjatīti pucchati. Yo nindaṃ apabodhatīti yo garahaṃ apaharanto bujjhati. Asso bhadro kasāmivāti yathā bhadro assājānīyo kasaṃ apaharanto bujjhati, patodacchāyaṃ disvā saṃvijjhanto viya kasāya attani nipātaṃ na deti, evameva yo bhikkhu bhūtassa dasaakkosavatthuno attani nipātaṃ adadanto nindaṃ apabodhati apaharanto bujjhati, evarūpo koci khīṇāsavo vijjatīti pucchati. Abhūtakkosena pana parimutto nāma natthi. Tanuyāti tanukā, hiriyā akusale dhamme nisedhetvā carantā khīṇāsavā nāma appakāti attho. Sadā satāti niccakālaṃ sativepullena samannāgatā. Antaṃ dukkhassa pappuyyāti vaṭṭadukkhassa koṭiṃ antabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ pāpuṇitvā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

18. In the eighth discourse, 'hirīnisedho' (restrained by moral shame) means: by moral shame, he restrains unwholesome states; for this reason, he is called 'hirīnisedho'. 'Is there anyone in the world?' means: 'Does any such person exist?' Thus he asks. 'Who awakens to reproach' means: he who, warding off blame, understands. 'Like a fine horse under the whip' means: just as a fine thoroughbred horse, warding off the whip, understands—seeing the shadow of the goad, as if being prodded, it does not allow the whip to fall upon itself—even so, that monk who, not allowing the ten true grounds for abuse to fall upon himself, awakens to reproach, warding it off and understanding. 'Does any such taint-free one exist?' Thus he asks. However, there is no one, indeed, who is free from false accusation. 'Tanu' (few) means: they are few. The meaning is: those taint-free ones who live restraining unwholesome states through moral shame are few. 'Ever mindful' means: always endowed with an abundance of mindfulness. 'They would reach the end of suffering' means: having reached Nibbāna, the end and final state of the suffering of the round of rebirths. The rest is just as has been stated.

Hirīsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on Moral Shame is concluded.

9. Kuṭikāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discourse on Huts

19. Navame kacci te kuṭikāti ayaṃ devatā dasa māse antovasanaṭṭhānaṭṭhena mātaraṃ kuṭikaṃ katvā, yathā sakuṇā divasaṃ gocarapasutā rattiṃ kulāvakaṃ allīyanti, evamevaṃ sattā [P 1.0038] tattha tattha gantvāpi mātugāmassa santikaṃ āgacchanti, ālayavasena bhariyaṃ kulāvakaṃ katvā. Kulapaveṇiṃ santānakaṭṭhena putte santānake katvā, taṇhaṃ bandhanaṃ katvā, gāthābandhanena ime pañhe samodhānetvā bhagavantaṃ pucchi, bhagavāpissā vissajjento tagghātiādimāha. Tattha tagghāti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Natthīti pahāya pabbajitattā vaṭṭasmiṃ vā puna mātukucchivāsassa dārabharaṇassa puttanibbattiyā vā abhāvato natthi.

19. In the ninth discourse, regarding 'Do you have a hut?': this devatā, having made his mother a hut by way of having dwelt inside her for ten months; just as birds, intent on foraging by day, cling to their nest at night, even so do beings, though having gone here and there, come to the presence of a woman, making a wife a nest by way of clinging. Having made sons a continuation by way of continuing the family lineage, and having made craving a bond, he combined these questions by means of composing a verse and asked the Blessed One. The Blessed One, replying to him, said 'Indeed,' and so on. Therein, 'Indeed' is a particle in the sense of affirmation. 'There is not' means: because of having renounced and gone forth, there is no dwelling again in a mother's womb in the round of rebirths, nor the maintaining of a wife, nor the production of sons; due to the absence of these, 'there is not'.

Devatā “mayā sannāhaṃ bandhitvā guḷhā pañhā pucchitā, ayañca samaṇo pucchitamatteyeva vissajjesi, jānaṃ nu kho me ajjhāsayaṃ kathesi, udāhu [M 1.0037] ajānaṃ yaṃ vā taṃ vā mukhāruḷhaṃ kathesī”ti cintetvā puna kintāhantiādimāha. Tattha kintāhanti kiṃ te ahaṃ. Athassā bhagavā ācikkhanto mātarantiādimāha. Sāhu teti gāthāya anumoditvā sampahaṃsitvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā attano devaṭṭhānameva gatāti.

The devatā thought: 'By me, a hidden question was asked, having been firmly formulated. And this ascetic answered just as soon as he was asked. Did he speak knowing my intention, or did he speak without knowing, saying whatever came to his mouth?' Having thought thus, he again said, 'Kiṃ tāhaṃ,' and so on. Therein, 'kiṃ tāhaṃ' should be parsed as 'kiṃ te ahaṃ' (What am I to you?). Then, the Blessed One, explaining to him, said, 'Mātaraṃ,' and so on. That devatā, having rejoiced with the verse beginning 'Sāhu te,' and being greatly delighted, paid homage to the Blessed One, honored him with perfumes, garlands, and so on, and went to his own divine abode.

Kuṭikāsuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kuṭikā Sutta is concluded.

10. Samiddhisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta

20. Dasame [V 1.0036] tapodārāmeti tapodassa tattodakassa rahadassa vasena evaṃ laddhanāme ārāme. Vebhārapabbatassa kira heṭṭhā bhummaṭṭhakanāgānaṃ pañcayojanasatikaṃ nāgabhavanaṃ devalokasadisaṃ maṇimayena talena ārāmuyyānehi ca samannāgataṃ. Tattha nāgānaṃ kīḷanaṭṭhāne mahāudakarahado, tato tapodā nāma nadī sandati kuthitā uṇhodakā. Kasmā panesā edisā? Rājagahaṃ kira parivāretvā mahāpetaloko tiṭṭhati, tattha dvinnaṃ mahālohakumbhinirayānaṃ antarena ayaṃ tapodā āgacchati, tasmā kuthitā sandati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

20. In the tenth sutta, 'at Tapodārāma' means: in the monastery that received its name on account of the hot-water lake named Tapoda. It is said that below Mount Vebhāra, there is a nāga abode of the earth-dwelling nāgas, five hundred yojanas in extent, like a deva world, endowed with a jeweled floor and with parks and gardens. There, in the nāgas' pleasure ground, is a great water lake. From it, the river named Tapodā flows, boiling and with hot water. But why is it like this? It is said that surrounding Rājagaha there is a great peta-world. There, this Tapodā comes through the space between two great Lohakumbhī hells; therefore, it flows boiling. And this has been said:

“Yatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, tapodā sandati, so daho acchodako sītodako sātodako setodako suppatittho ramaṇīyo pahūtamacchakacchapo, cakkamattāni ca padumāni pupphanti. Apicāyaṃ, bhikkhave, tapodā dvinnaṃ mahānirayānaṃ antarikāya āgacchati, tenāyaṃ tapodā kuthitā sandatī”ti (pārā. 231).

'Monks, the lake from which this Tapodā flows has clear water, cool water, pleasant-tasting water, and pure water; it has good bathing places, is delightful, and has abundant fish and turtles; and lotuses the size of chariot wheels bloom. And yet, monks, this Tapodā comes from the space between two great hells. For that reason, this Tapodā flows boiling.'

Imassa pana ārāmassa [P 1.0039] abhimukhaṭṭhāne tato mahāudakarahado jāto, tassa vasenāyaṃ vihāro “tapodārāmo”ti vuccati.

Furthermore, in a place facing this monastery, a great water lake was formed from that river. On account of it, this monastery is called 'Tapodārāma'.

Samiddhīti tassa kira therassa attabhāvo samiddho abhirūpo pāsādiko, tasmā “samiddhī”tveva saṅkhaṃ gato. Gattāni parisiñcitunti padhānikatthero esa, balavapaccūse uṭṭhāyāsanā sarīraṃ utuṃ gāhāpetvā bahi [M 1.0038] saṭṭhihatthamatte mahācaṅkame aparāparaṃ caṅkamitvā “sedagahitehi gattehi paribhuñjamānaṃ senāsanaṃ kilissatī”ti maññamāno gattāni parisiñcanatthaṃ sarīradhovanatthaṃ upasaṅkami. Ekacīvaro aṭṭhāsīti nivāsanaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ hatthena gahetvā aṭṭhāsi.

Samiddhi—it is said that this elder's being was flourishing, beautiful, and pleasing; therefore, he came to be known as 'Samiddhi.' As for the words, 'to sprinkle his limbs': this elder was one engaged in striving. Having risen from his seat early at dawn and having had his body warmed, he went outside to a great walking path sixty cubits in measure. After walking back and forth, thinking, 'The lodging, being used with limbs soaked in sweat, will become soiled,' he approached for the purpose of sprinkling his limbs and washing his body. As for the words, 'he stood with a single robe': having put on his lower robe, fastened his waistband, and taking his upper robe in his hand, he stood.

Gattāni pubbāpayamānoti gattāni pubbasadisāni vodakāni kurumāno. Allasarīre pārutaṃ hi cīvaraṃ kilissati duggandhaṃ hoti, na cetaṃ vattaṃ. Thero pana vattasampanno, tasmā vatte ṭhitova nhāyitvā paccuttaritvā aṭṭhāsi. Tattha idaṃ nhānavattaṃ – udakatitthaṃ gantvā yattha katthaci cīvarāni nikkhipitvā vegena ṭhitakeneva na otaritabbaṃ, sabbadisā pana oloketvā [V 1.0037] vivittabhāvaṃ ñatvā khāṇugumbalatādīni vavatthapetvā tikkhattuṃ ukkāsitvā avakujja ṭhitena uttarāsaṅgacīvaraṃ apanetvā pasāretabbaṃ, kāyabandhanaṃ mocetvā cīvarapiṭṭheyeva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sace udakasāṭikā natthi, udakante ukkuṭikaṃ nisīditvā nivāsanaṃ mocetvā sace sinnaṭṭhānaṃ atthi, pasāretabbaṃ. No ce atthi, saṃharitvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Udakaṃ otarantena saṇikaṃ nābhippamāṇamattaṃ otaritvā vīciṃ anuṭṭhāpentena saddaṃ akarontena nivattitvā āgatadisābhimukhena nimujjitabbaṃ, evaṃ cīvaraṃ rakkhitaṃ hoti. Ummujjantenapi saddaṃ akarontena saṇikaṃ ummujjitvā nhānapariyosāne udakante ukkuṭikena nisīditvā nivāsanaṃ parikkhipitvā uṭṭhāya suparimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ apārupitvāva ṭhātabbanti.

Drying the limbs means making the limbs free of water, as they were before. For a robe wrapped around a wet body becomes soiled and foul-smelling, and this is not proper conduct. The elder, however, being endowed with proper conduct, therefore, established in that conduct, bathed, and having emerged from the water, stood. Herein, this is the proper conduct for bathing: Having gone to the bathing place, one should not, having cast down one's robes just anywhere, enter hastily while still standing. Rather, one should look in all directions, ascertain the seclusion of the place, take note of any stumps, bushes, vines, and so on, clear one's throat three times, and then, while standing bent over, remove the upper robe and spread it out. The waistband should be loosened and placed upon the robe itself. If there is no bathing cloth, one should sit squatting at the water's edge, loosen the lower garment, and if there is a sweat-soaked part, it should be spread out. If there is not, it should be folded and set aside. When entering the water, one should enter slowly, only up to the measure of the navel, without causing waves or making a sound. One should then turn to face the direction from which one came and submerge. In this way, the robe is protected. When emerging, too, one should do so slowly without making a sound. At the end of the bath, one should sit squatting at the water's edge, wrap the lower garment around oneself, rise, put it on neatly all around, fasten the waistband, and only after having draped the robe over oneself, should one stand.

Theropi tathā nhāyitvā paccuttaritvā vigacchamānaudakaṃ kāyaṃ olokayamāno aṭṭhāsi. Tassa pakatiyāpi pāsādikassa [P 1.0040] paccūsasamaye sammā pariṇatāhārassa uṇhodakena nhātassa ativiya mukhavaṇṇo viroci, bandhanā pavuttatālaphalaṃ viya pabhāsampanno puṇṇacando viya taṅkhaṇavikasitapadumaṃ viya mukhaṃ sassirikaṃ ahosi, sarīravaṇṇopi vippasīdi. Tasmiṃ samaye vanasaṇḍe adhivatthā bhummadevatā pāsādikaṃ bhikkhuṃ olokayamānā samanaṃ niggahetuṃ asakkontī kāmapariḷāhābhibhūtā hutvā, “theraṃ palobhessāmī”ti attabhāvaṃ uḷārena [M 1.0039] alaṅkārena alaṅkaritvā sahassavaṭṭipadīpaṃ pajjalamānā viya candaṃ uṭṭhāpayamānā viya sakalārāmaṃ ekobhāsaṃ katvā theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā avanditvāva vehāse ṭhitā gāthaṃ abhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “atha kho aññatarā devatā…pe… ajjhabhāsī”ti.

The Elder also, having bathed in that manner and emerged from the water, stood observing his body from which the water was departing.
