Even by nature, the Elder's appearance was pleasing, but at dawn, having well-digested his food and bathed in warm water, the complexion of his face shone exceedingly. Like a ripe palm fruit freed from its stalk, like the radiant full moon, like a lotus just bloomed at that moment, his face was glorious, and the complexion of his body was also especially clear. At that time, a terrestrial deity dwelling in the forest thicket, unable to restrain her mind upon seeing the pleasing monk, became overwhelmed by the burning of sensual desire. Thinking, 'I will entice the Elder,' she adorned her form with splendid ornaments and, making the entire monastery a single radiance as if a thousand-wick lamp were blazing or as if causing the moon to rise, she approached the Elder. Standing in the air without saluting, she spoke a verse. Therefore, it was said: 'Then a certain deity... addressed him.'

Abhutvāti pañca kāmaguṇe aparibhuñjitvā. Bhikkhasīti piṇḍāya carasi. Mā taṃ kālo upaccagāti ettha kālo nāma pañcakāmaguṇapaṭisevanakkhamo daharayobbanakālo. Jarājiṇṇena hi obhaggena daṇḍaparāyaṇena pavedhamānena kāsasāsābhibhūtena na sakkā kāme paribhuñjituṃ. Iti imaṃ kālaṃ sandhāya devatā “mā taṃ kālo upaccagā”ti āha. Tattha mā upaccagāti mā atikkami.

'Not having enjoyed' means not having indulged in the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'You beg' means you wander for alms. In 'Let not that time pass you by,' 'time' here means the time of youth, which is suitable for indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure. Indeed, for one who is old and decrepit, bent, whose resort is a staff, who is trembling, and who is overwhelmed by coughs and panting, it is not possible to enjoy sensual pleasures. Thus, referring to this time, the deity said, 'Let not that time pass you by.' Therein, 'let not pass by' means 'do not let it pass'.

Kālaṃ vohaṃ na jānāmīti ettha voti nipātamattaṃ. Kālaṃ na jānāmīti maraṇakālaṃ sandhāya vadati. Sattānañhi –

In 'I do not know the time,' the word 'vo' is merely a particle. 'I do not know the time' is said referring to the time of death. For beings, indeed—

“Jīvitaṃ [V 1.0038] byādhi kālo ca, dehanikkhepanaṃ gati;

Pañcete jīvalokasmiṃ, animittā na nāyare”.

'Life, sickness, and time, the casting down of the body, the destination—these five in the world of the living are without signs; they are not known.'

Tattha jīvitaṃ tāva “ettakameva, na ito para”nti vavatthānābhāvato animittaṃ. Kalalakālepi hi sattā maranti, abbuda-pesi-ghana-aḍḍhamāsa-ekamāsa-dvemāsa-temāsa-catumāsapañcamāsa…pe… dasamāsakālepi, kucchito nikkhantasamayepi, tato paraṃ vassasatassa antopi bahipi marantiyeva. Byādhipi “imināva byādhinā sattā maranti, na aññenā”ti vavatthānābhāvato animitto. Cakkhurogenapi hi sattā maranti sotarogādīnaṃ aññatarenapi. Kālopi, “imasmiṃ yeva kāle maritabbaṃ, na aññasmi”nti evaṃ [P 1.0041] vavatthānābhāvato animitto. Pubbaṇhepi hi sattā maranti majjhanhikādīnaṃ aññatarasmimpi. Dehanikkhepanampi, “idheva mīyamānānaṃ dehena patitabbaṃ, na aññatthā”ti evaṃ vavatthānābhāvato animittaṃ. Antogāme jātānañhi bahigāmepi attabhāvo patati, bahigāmepi jātānaṃ antogāmepi. Tathā thalajānaṃ jale, jalajānaṃ thaleti anekappakārato vitthāretabbaṃ. Gatipi, “ito cutena idha nibbattitabba”nti evaṃ vavatthānābhāvato animittā. Devalokato hi cutā manussesupi nibbattanti[M 1.0040], manussalokato cutā devalokādīnaṃ yattha katthaci nibbattantīti evaṃ yante yuttagoṇo viya gatipañcake loko samparivattati. Tassevaṃ samparivattato “imasmiṃ nāma kāle maraṇaṃ bhavissatī”ti imaṃ maraṇassa kālaṃ vohaṃ na jānāmi.

Here, firstly, life is indeterminate, because it cannot be determined: 'Only this much, no more.' For beings die even at the kalala stage, the abbudā stage, the pesi stage, the ghana stage, half a month, one month, two months, three months, four months, five months... even at ten months, at the time of emerging from the womb, and even after that; they die within or beyond a hundred years. Sickness, too, is indeterminate, because it cannot be determined: 'Beings die only from this sickness, not from another.' For beings die even from eye disease or from any other disease, such as ear disease. Time, too, is indeterminate, because it cannot be determined: 'One must die only at this time, not at another.' For beings die even in the morning or at any other time, such as midday. The casting down of the body, too, is indeterminate, because it cannot be determined: 'The body of those who are dying must fall only here, not elsewhere.' For those born inside a village may have their body fall outside, and those born outside may have their body fall inside. Similarly, the bodies of land-born beings may fall in water, and those of water-born beings on land—this should be elaborated in many ways. Rebirth, too, is indeterminate, because it cannot be determined: 'Having passed away from here, one must be reborn here.' For those who pass away from the heavenly realm are reborn among humans, and those who pass away from the human realm are reborn in the heavenly realm or elsewhere. Thus the world revolves in the five courses of rebirth, like an ox yoked to a machine. As it thus revolves, I do not know this time of death: 'Death will occur at this particular time.'

Channo kālo na dissatīti ayaṃ kālo mayhaṃ paṭicchanno avibhūto na paññāyati. Tasmāti yasmā ayaṃ kālo paṭicchanno na paññāyati, tasmā pañca kāmaguṇe abhutvāva bhikkhāmi. Mā maṃ kālo upaccagāti ettha samaṇadhammakaraṇakālaṃ sandhāya “kālo”ti āha. Ayañhi samaṇadhammo nāma pacchime kāle tisso vayosīmā atikkantena obhaggena daṇḍaparāyaṇena pavedhamānena kāsasāsābhibhūtena na sakkā kātuṃ. Tadā hi na sakkā hoti icchiticchitaṃ buddhavacanaṃ vā gaṇhituṃ, dhutaṅgaṃ vā paribhuñjituṃ, araññavāsaṃ vā vasituṃ, icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpattiṃ vā samāpajjituṃ, padabhāṇa-sarabhaññadhammakathā-anumodanādīni vā kātuṃ, taruṇayobbanakāle panetaṃ sabbaṃ sakkā kātunti ayaṃ samaṇadhammakaraṇassa kālo mā maṃ upaccagā, yāva maṃ nātikkamati, tāva kāme abhutvāva samaṇadhammaṃ karomīti āha.

“The time is concealed, it is not seen” means: this time of death is concealed from me, unmanifest, not apparent. “Therefore” means: since this time of death is concealed and not apparent, therefore I live as a mendicant without having enjoyed the five strands of sensual pleasure. In the phrase “May time not pass me by,” he said “time” referring to the time for undertaking the recluse's practice. For this recluse's practice cannot be undertaken in the last stage of life by one who has surpassed the three limits of age, who is stooped, supported by a staff, trembling, and overcome by coughing and asthma. For at that time, it is not possible to learn the desired words of the Buddha, or to undertake the ascetic practices, or to dwell in the forest, or to enter a meditative attainment at any desired moment, or to perform recitations, melodious chanting, Dhamma talks, expressions of appreciation, and so on. But in the prime of youth, all this can be done. Therefore, he said: “May this time for undertaking the recluse's practice not pass me by. As long as it does not pass me by, I will undertake the recluse's practice without having enjoyed sensual pleasures.”

Pathaviyaṃ [V 1.0039] patiṭṭhahitvāti sā kira devatā – “ayaṃ bhikkhu samaṇadhammakaraṇassa kālaṃ nāma katheti, akālaṃ nāma katheti, sahetukaṃ katheti sānisaṃsa”nti ettāvatāva there lajjaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā mahābrahmaṃ viya aggikkhandhaṃ viya [P 1.0042] ca naṃ maññamānā gāravajātā ākāsā oruyha pathaviyaṃ aṭṭhāsi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi pathaviyaṃ ṭhitā, yena panatthena āgatā, punapi tameva gahetvā daharo tvantiādimāha. Tattha susūti taruṇo. Kāḷakesoti suṭṭhu kāḷakeso. Bhadrenāti bhaddakena. Ekacco hi daharopi samāno kāṇo vā hoti kuṇiādīnaṃ vā aññataro, so bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato nāma na hoti. Yo pana abhirūpo hoti dassanīyo pāsādiko sabbasampattisampanno, yaṃ yadeva alaṅkāraparihāraṃ icchati, tena tena alaṅkato devaputto viya carati, ayaṃ bhadrena yobbanena samannāgato nāma hoti. Thero ca uttamarūpasampanno, tena naṃ evamāha.

Having stood on the ground: It is said that the deity thought, 'This monk speaks of a time for practicing the ascetic's life, he speaks of an untimely moment, he speaks with reason, he speaks with benefit.' By just this much, having caused a sense of shame to arise in the Elder, yet regarding him as like a great Brahmā or a mass of fire, she became filled with reverence, descended from the sky, and stood on the ground. With reference to that, this was said. Although she stood on the ground, taking up again the very purpose for which she had come, she said the words beginning with, 'You are very young...' Therein, 'very young' means youthful. 'With black hair' means with very black hair. By 'with auspicious' means with excellent. For a certain person, though young, might be blind or have a crooked limb or some other such defect; he is not called one endowed with auspicious youth. But one who is handsome, pleasant to see, inspiring, endowed with all accomplishments, who goes about like a son of a deva, adorned with whatever adornment and attire he desires—this one is called endowed with auspicious youth. And the Elder was endowed with supreme beauty; therefore, she spoke to him thus.

Anikkīḷitāvī [M 1.0041] kāmesūti kāmesu akīḷitakīḷo abhuttāvī, akatakāmakīḷoti attho. Mā sandiṭṭhikaṃ hitvāti yebhuyyena hi tā adiṭṭhasaccā avītarāgā aparacittavidūniyo devatā bhikkhū dasapi vassāni vīsatimpi…pe… saṭṭhimpi vassāni parisuddhaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caramāne disvā – “ime bhikkhū mānusake pañca kāmaguṇe pahāya dibbe kāme patthayantā samaṇadhammaṃ karontī”ti saññaṃ uppādenti, ayampi tattheva uppādesi. Tasmā mānusake kāme sandiṭṭhike, dibbe ca kālike katvā evamāha.

Not having played in sensual pleasures means not having played the play in sensual pleasures, not having enjoyed them; that is, not having engaged in sensual play. Do not, having abandoned what is visible here and now: For the most part, those deities who have not seen the truth, are not free from passion, and do not know the minds of others, upon seeing monks who have practiced the pure, unbroken noble life for ten, twenty, or even sixty years, give rise to the perception: 'These monks, having abandoned the five strands of human sensual pleasure, undertake the ascetic's practice while aspiring to divine sensual pleasures.' This deity, too, gave rise to such a perception in the very same way. Therefore, considering human sensual pleasures as visible here and now, and divine ones as belonging to a future time, she spoke thus.

Na kho ahaṃ, āvusoti, āvuso, ahaṃ sandiṭṭhike kāme hitvā kālike kāme na anudhāvāmi na patthemi na pihemi. Kalikañca kho ahaṃ, āvusoti ahaṃ kho, āvuso, kālikaṃ kāmaṃ hitvā sandiṭṭhikaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ anudhāvāmi. Iti thero cittānantaraṃ aladdhabbatāya dibbepi mānusakepi pañca kāmaguṇe kālikāti akāsi, cittānantaraṃ laddhabbatāya lokuttaradhammaṃ sandiṭṭhikanti. Pañcakāmaguṇesu samohitesupi sampannakāmassāpi kāmino cittānantaraṃ icchiticchitārammaṇānubhavanaṃ na sampajjati. Cakkhudvāre iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ anubhavitukāmena hi cittakārapotthakārarūpakārādayo pakkosāpetvā, “idaṃ nāma sajjethā”ti vattabbaṃ hoti. Etthantare anekakoṭisatasahassāni cittāni uppajjitvā nirujjhanti. Atha pacchā taṃ ārammaṇaṃ sampāpuṇāti[P 1.0043]. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo. Sotāpattimaggānantaraṃ pana sotāpattiphalameva [V 1.0040] uppajjati, antarā aññassa cittassa vāro natthi. Sesaphalesupi eseva nayoti.

'Indeed not I, friend. Having abandoned sensual pleasures visible here and now, I do not pursue, long for, or hanker after temporal sensual pleasures. But I, friend, having abandoned temporal sensual pleasures, do pursue the supramundane Dhamma that is visible here and now.' Thus, the elder, because they are not attainable immediately after a thought, considered even the fivefold sensual pleasures, both divine and human, as temporal. And because it is attainable immediately after a thought, he considered the supramundane Dhamma as visible here and now. Even when the fivefold sensual pleasures are fully provided and available to a sensualist, the immediate enjoyment of a desired object does not occur. For one who wishes to experience a pleasing object through the eye-door, one must summon painters, plasterers, sculptors, and so on, saying, 'Let this be prepared.' In the meantime, countless millions of thoughts arise and cease. Only afterward does one reach that object. The same applies to the other sense doors. However, immediately after the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry arises without any intervening thought. The same applies to the other fruits.

So tamevatthaṃ gahetvā kālikā hi, āvusotiādimāha. Tattha kālikāti vuttanayena samohitasampattināpi kālantare pattabbā. Bahudukkhāti pañca kāmaguṇe nissāya pattabbadukkhassa bahutāya bahudukkhā. Taṃvatthukasseva upāyāsassa bahutāya bahupāyāsā. Ādīnavo ettha bhiyyoti pañca kāmaguṇe nissāya laddhabbasukhato ādīnavo bhiyyo, dukkhameva bahutaranti attho. Sandiṭṭhiko ayaṃ dhammoti ayaṃ lokuttaradhammo yena yena adhigato hoti, tena tena parasaddhāya gantabbataṃ hitvā paccavekkhaṇañāṇena sayaṃ daṭṭhabboti [M 1.0042] sandiṭṭhiko. Attano phaladānaṃ sandhāya nāssa kāloti akālo, akāloyeva akāliko. Yo ettha ariyamaggadhammo, so attano pavattisamanantarameva phalaṃ detīti attho. “Ehi passa imaṃ dhamma”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ ehipassavidhiṃ arahatīti ehipassiko. Ādittaṃ celaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā ajjhupekkhitvāpi bhāvanāvasena attano citte upanayaṃ arahatīti opaneyyiko. Sabbehi ugghaṭitaññūādīhi viññūhi “bhāvito me maggo, adhigataṃ phalaṃ, sacchikato nirodho”ti attani attani veditabboti paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhīti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.146 ādayo) dhammānussativaṇṇanāyaṃ vutto.

Grasping that very meaning, he said, 'They are temporal, friend,' and so on. Therein, 'temporal' means that which, according to the method already stated, is to be attained at another time, even with the full complement of accumulated resources. 'Of much suffering' means they are of much suffering because of the abundance of suffering to be experienced—by way of guarding them—in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Of much distress' means they are of much distress because of the abundance of distress that has that very suffering as its cause. 'The drawback here is greater' means that the drawback in dependence on the five strands of sensual pleasure is greater than the happiness to be obtained; suffering itself is much more—this is the meaning. 'This Dhamma is to be seen for oneself' means that this supramundane Dhamma, by whichever noble disciple it is realized, is to be seen for oneself by that very noble disciple with the knowledge of reflection, having abandoned the state of having to be known through the faith of another; therefore, it is called 'to be seen for oneself' (sandiṭṭhika). With reference to its own giving of fruit, there is no time for it, thus it is 'timeless' (akāla); 'timeless' itself becomes 'akālika'. The meaning is that whichever noble path-Dhamma there is here, it gives its fruit immediately after its own arising. It is called 'inviting one to come and see' (ehipassika) because it is worthy of the exhortation 'Come and see,' which proceeds thus: 'Come, see this Dhamma.' It is called 'to be brought inwards' (opaneyyika) because, even having disregarded a burning cloth or a burning head, it is worthy of being brought to bear in one's own mind by the power of meditation. It is called 'to be known personally by the wise' (paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi) because it is to be known and experienced by all wise persons, beginning with those of swift understanding, each in their own mind, thus: 'The path has been developed by me, the fruit has been attained, cessation has been realized.' This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is given in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition on the recollection of the Dhamma.

Idāni sā devatā andho viya rūpavisesaṃ therena kathitassa atthe ajānantī kathañca bhikkhūtiādimāha. Tattha kathañcātipadassa “kathañca bhikkhu kālikā kāmā vuttā bhagavatā, kathaṃ bahudukkhā, kathaṃ bahupāyāsā”ti? Evaṃ sabbapadehi sambandho veditabbo.

Now that deity, not knowing the meaning of what was said by the elder—like a blind person not knowing the distinction of forms—said, 'But how, O monk?' and so on. Therein, regarding the phrase 'But how,' the connection should be understood with all the terms in this way: 'How, O monk, were sensual pleasures said by the Blessed One to be temporal? How are they of much suffering? How are they of much distress?' Thus, the connection with all the terms should be understood.

Navoti aparipuṇṇapañcavasso hi bhikkhu navo nāma hoti, pañcavassato paṭṭhāya majjhimo, dasavassato paṭṭhāya thero. Aparo nayo – aparipuṇṇadasavasso navo, dasavassato paṭṭhāya majjhimo, vīsativassato paṭṭhāya thero. Tesaṃ ahaṃ navoti vadati.

'New'—a bhikkhu with less than five rains is called 'new.' From five rains onward, he is a middle bhikkhu, and from ten rains onward, an elder. Another method: a bhikkhu with less than ten rains is 'new'; from ten rains onward, a middle bhikkhu; and from twenty rains onward, an elder. He says, 'I am new among them.'

Navopi ekacco sattaṭṭhavassakāle pabbajitvā dvādasaterasavassāni [P 1.0044] sāmaṇerabhāveneva atikkanto cirapabbajito hoti, ahaṃ pana acirapabbajitoti vadati. Imaṃ dhammavinayanti imaṃ dhammañca vinayañca. Ubhayampetaṃ sāsanasseva nāmaṃ. Dhammena hettha dve piṭakāni vuttāni, vinayena [V 1.0041] vinayapiṭakaṃ, iti tīhi piṭakehi pakāsitaṃ paṭipattiṃ adhunā āgatomhīti vadati.

A certain new bhikkhu, having gone forth at the age of seven or eight and having passed twelve or thirteen years only as a novice, is one who has been gone forth for a long time. But he says, 'I, however, have not been gone forth for long.' 'This Dhamma-Vinaya' means this Dhamma and this Vinaya. Both of these are a name for the Dispensation. Here, by 'Dhamma' the two Piṭakas are meant, and by 'Vinaya' the Vinaya Piṭaka is meant. Thus, he says, 'I have now come to the practice revealed by the three Piṭakas.'

Mahesakkhāhīti mahāparivārāhi. Ekekassa hi devarañño koṭisatampi koṭisahassampi parivāro hoti, te attānaṃ mahante ṭhāne ṭhapetvā tathāgataṃ passanti. Tattha amhādisānaṃ appesakkhānaṃ mātugāmajātikānaṃ kuto okāsoti dasseti.

'Of great power' means with large retinues. Indeed, each king of the devas has a retinue of a hundred koṭis or even a thousand koṭis; they, having placed themselves in a high position, see the Tathāgata. This shows the meaning: 'There, what opportunity is there for those like us, of little power and of female birth?'

Mayampi [M 1.0043] āgaccheyyāmāti idaṃ sā devatā “sacepi cakkavāḷaṃ pūretvā parisā nisinnā hoti, mahatiyā buddhavīthiyā satthu santikaṃ gantuṃ labhatī”ti ñatvā āha. Puccha bhikkhu, puccha bhikkhūti thirakaraṇavasena āmeḍitaṃ kataṃ.

'May we too come'—that devatā said this, knowing: 'Even if an assembly were seated, filling the world-system, one is able to go to the Teacher's presence by the great Buddha-avenue.' 'Ask, bhikkhu, ask, bhikkhu'—the repetition was made for the sake of emphasis.

Akkheyyasaññinoti ettha “devo, manusso, gahaṭṭho, pabbajito, satto, puggalo, tisso, phusso”tiādinā nayena akkheyyato sabbesaṃ akkhānānaṃ sabbāsaṃ kathānaṃ vatthubhūtato pañcakkhandhā “akkheyyā”ti vuccanti. “Satto naro poso puggalo itthī puriso”ti evaṃ saññā etesaṃ atthīti saññino, akkheyyesveva saññinoti akkheyyasaññino, pañcasu khandhesu sattapuggalādisaññinoti attho. Akkheyyasmiṃ patiṭṭhitāti pañcasu khandhesu aṭṭhahākārehi patiṭṭhitā. Ratto hi rāgavasena patiṭṭhito hoti, duṭṭho dosavasena, mūḷho mohavasena, parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhivasena, thāmagato anusayavasena, vinibaddho mānavasena, aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchāvasena, vikkhepagato uddhaccavasena patiṭṭhito hoti. Akkheyyaṃ apariññāyāti pañcakkhandhe tīhi pariññāhi aparijānitvā. Yogamāyanti maccunoti maccuno yogaṃ payogaṃ pakkhepaṃ upakkhepaṃ upakkamaṃ abbhantaraṃ āgacchanti, maraṇavasaṃ gacchantīti attho. Evamimāya gāthāya kālikā kāmā kathitā.

Here, in the phrase 'Akkheyyasaññino': the five aggregates are called 'akkheyya' (the expressible) because, in the manner of 'a deva, a human, a householder, a renunciant, a being, a person, Tissa, Phussa,' and so on, they are expressible and are the basis for all expressions and all discussions. They are 'saññino' (perceivers) because they have such perceptions as 'a being, a man, a person, a woman, a man'; thus, 'akkheyyasaññino' means those who perceive in regard to the expressible. The meaning is: those who have perceptions of a being, a person, and so on, in the five aggregates. 'Established in the expressible' means established in the five aggregates in eight ways. Indeed, one who is lustful is established by way of lust; one who is hateful, by way of hatred; one who is deluded, by way of delusion; one who misapprehends, by way of views; one who is obstinate, by way of latent tendencies; one who is bound, by way of conceit; one who is undecided, by way of doubt; and one who is distracted is established by way of restlessness. 'Not fully understanding the expressible' means not having fully known the five aggregates through the three kinds of full understanding. 'They come to the yoke of Death' means they come into the yoke of Death, his application, his casting down, his successive casting down, his undertaking, and his inner domain; that is, they come under the sway of Death. Thus, by this verse, temporal sensual pleasures are spoken of.

Pariññāyāti ñātapariññā, tīraṇapariññā, pahānapariññāti imāhi tīhi pariññāhi parijānitvā. Tattha katamā ñātapariññā? Pañcakkhandhe [P 1.0045] parijānāti – “ayaṃ rūpakkhandho, ayaṃ vedanākkhandho, ayaṃ saññākkhandho, ayaṃ saṅkhārakkhandho, ayaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, imāni tesaṃ lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānī”ti, ayaṃ ñātapariññā. Katamā tīraṇapariññā? Evaṃ ñātaṃ katvā pañcakkhandhe tīreti aniccato dukkhato rogatoti dvācattālīsāya ākārehi. Ayaṃ [V 1.0042] tīraṇapariññā. Katamā pahānapariññā? Evaṃ tīrayitvā aggamaggena pañcasu khandhesu chandarāgaṃ pajahati. Ayaṃ pahānapariññā.

'By full understanding' means having fully understood by these three kinds of full understanding: full understanding through knowledge, full understanding through scrutiny, and full understanding through abandoning. Among these, what is full understanding through knowledge? One fully knows the five aggregates: 'This is the form aggregate, this is the feeling aggregate, this is the perception aggregate, this is the formations aggregate, this is the consciousness aggregate; these are their characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause.' This is full understanding through knowledge. What is full understanding through scrutiny? Having thus known, one scrutinizes the five aggregates in forty-two ways, such as: as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease. This is full understanding through scrutiny. What is full understanding through abandoning? Having thus scrutinized, one abandons desire and lust for the five aggregates by means of the supreme path. This is full understanding through abandoning.

Akkhātāraṃ na maññatīti evaṃ tīhi pariññāhi pañcakkhandhe parijānitvā khīṇāsavo bhikkhu akkhātāraṃ puggalaṃ na maññati. Akkhātāranti kammavasena kāraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ, akkhātabbaṃ kathetabbaṃ puggalaṃ na maññati, na passatīti attho[M 1.0044]. Kinti akkhātabbanti? “Tisso”ti vā “phusso”ti vā evaṃ yena kenaci nāmena vā gottena vā pakāsetabbaṃ. Tañhi tassa na hotīti taṃ tassa khīṇāsavassa na hoti. Yena naṃ vajjāti yena naṃ “rāgena ratto”ti vā “dosena duṭṭho”ti vā “mohena mūḷho”ti vāti koci vadeyya, taṃ kāraṇaṃ tassa khīṇāsavassa natthi.

‘He does not conceive of a speaker,’ thus: having fully understood the five aggregates by means of the three kinds of full understanding, the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed does not conceive of a person who is a speaker. ‘A speaker’ should be understood as the agent in relation to action; he does not conceive of, does not see, a person to be proclaimed or spoken of—this is the meaning. How is one to be proclaimed? As ‘Tissa’ or ‘Phussa,’ thus by any name or clan is one to be designated. ‘For that does not exist for him’—thus, that does not exist for that one whose taints are destroyed. ‘By which one might speak of him’—by which cause someone might say of him, ‘He is attached by lust,’ or ‘He is corrupted by aversion,’ or ‘He is deluded by ignorance’—that cause does not exist for that one whose taints are destroyed.

Sace vijānāsi vadehīti sace evarūpaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ jānāsi, “jānāmī”ti vadehi. No ce jānāsi, atha “na jānāmī”ti vadehi. Yakkhāti devataṃ ālapanto āha. Iti imāya gāthāya sandiṭṭhiko navavidho lokuttaradhammo kathito. Sādhūti āyācanatthe nipāto.

‘If you know, speak,’ means: if you know such a one whose taints are destroyed, say, ‘I know.’ If you do not know, then say, ‘I do not know.’ ‘O Yakkha’—he spoke, addressing the deity. Thus, by this verse, the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, which is directly visible, is taught. ‘Sādhu’ is a particle in the sense of entreaty.

Yo maññatīti yo attānaṃ “ahaṃ samo”ti vā “visesī”ti vā “nihīno”ti vā maññati. Etena “seyyohamasmī”tiādayo tayo mānā gahitāva. Tesu gahitesu nava mānā gahitāva honti. So vivadetha tenāti so puggalo teneva mānena yena kenaci puggalena saddhiṃ – “kena maṃ tvaṃ pāpuṇāsi, kiṃ jātiyā pāpuṇāsi, udāhu gottena, kulapadesena, vaṇṇapokkharatāya, bāhusaccena, dhutaguṇenā”ti evaṃ vivadeyya. Iti imāyapi upaḍḍhagāthāya kālikā kāmā kathitā.

‘One who conceives’—one who conceives of oneself as ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am inferior.’ By this, the three conceits—‘I am better,’ etc.—are included. When these are included, the nine conceits are included. ‘He would dispute with that’—that person, with that very conceit, might dispute with some other person, saying: ‘By what do you match me? Do you match me by birth? Or by lineage? By family designation? By beauty of complexion? By great learning? By the ascetic qualities?’ Thus, by this half-verse also, temporal sensual pleasures are spoken of.

Tīsu vidhāsūti tīsu mānesu. “Ekavidhena rūpasaṅgaho”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 584) hi koṭṭhāso “vidho”ti vutto. “Kathaṃvidhaṃ sīlavantaṃ vadanti, kathaṃvidhaṃ paññavantaṃ vadantī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.95) ākāro. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vidhā. Katamā tisso[P 1.0046]? Seyyohamasmīti vidhā, sadisohamasmīti vidhā, hīnohamasmīti vidhā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.162) māno “vidhā”ti vutto. Idhāpi mānova. Tena vuttaṃ “tīsu vidhāsūti tīsu mānesū”ti. Avikampamānoti so puggalo etesu saṅkhepato tīsu[V 1.0043], vitthārato navasu mānesu na kampati, na calati. Samo visesīti na tassa hotīti tassa pahīnamānassa khīṇāsavassa “ahaṃ sadiso”ti vā “seyyo”ti vā “hīno”ti vā na hotīti dasseti. Pacchimapadaṃ vuttanayameva. Iti imāyapi upaḍḍhagāthāya navavidho sandiṭṭhiko lokuttaradhammo kathito.

'Among the three kinds' (tīsu vidhāsu) means among the three conceits (tīsu mānesu). For in passages such as, 'The aggregate of form is of one kind,' the term 'kind' (vidho) is used for a division (koṭṭhāso). In passages such as, 'What kind of person do they call virtuous? What kind of person do they call wise?,' it refers to a mode (ākāro). In passages such as, 'Monks, there are these three kinds (vidhā). What three? The kind "I am superior," the kind "I am equal," the kind "I am inferior,"' conceit (māno) is called a 'kind' (vidhā). Here too, conceit is intended. Therefore, it is said, 'Among the three kinds means among the three conceits.' 'Not trembling' (avikampamāno) means that person does not tremble or shake on account of these conceits—three in brief, or nine in detail. 'For him there is no equal or superior' (Samo visesīti na tassa hoti) shows that for that one whose conceit is abandoned, for the one whose taints are destroyed, there is no 'I am equal,' or 'I am superior,' or 'I am inferior.' The last phrase is just as has been explained. Thus, by this half-verse too, the ninefold, directly visible (sandiṭṭhiko), supramundane Dhamma is declared.

Pahāsi [M 1.0045] saṅkhanti, “paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāretī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.120, 239) paññā “saṅkhā”ti āgatā. “Atthi te koci gaṇako vā muddiko vā saṅkhāyako vā, yo pahoti gaṅgāya vālukaṃ gaṇetu”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.410) ettha gaṇanā. “Saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 880) koṭṭhāso. “Yā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā”ti (dha. sa. 1313-1315) ettha paṇṇatti “saṅkhā”ti āgatā. Idhāpi ayameva adhippetā. Pahāsi saṅkhanti padassa hi ayamevattho – ratto duṭṭho mūḷho iti imaṃ paṇṇattiṃ khīṇāsavo pahāsi jahi pajahīti.

He abandoned designation (Pahāsi saṅkhaṃ). In passages such as, 'one partakes of food after wise reflection,' 'saṅkhā' is used for wisdom (paññā). In, 'Is there any accountant, calculator, or reckoner who can count the sands of the Ganges?,' it is used for calculation (gaṇanā). In passages such as, 'For classifications of proliferation have perception as their source,' it is used for a portion (koṭṭhāso). In, 'Whatever is the reckoning (saṅkhā), the designation (samaññā) of those various phenomena,' 'saṅkhā' is used for designation (paṇṇatti). Here too, this very meaning is intended. For the phrase 'He abandoned designation' means this: the one whose taints are destroyed has abandoned, relinquished, and cast off such designations as 'lustful,' 'hateful,' or 'deluded.'

Na vimānamajjhagāti navabhedaṃ tividhamānaṃ na upagato. Nivāsaṭṭhena vā mātukucchi “vimāna”nti vuccati, taṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhivasena na upagacchītipi attho. Anāgatatthe atītavacanaṃ. Acchecchīti chindi. Chinnaganthanti cattāro ganthe chinditvā ṭhitaṃ. Anīghanti niddukkhaṃ. Nirāsanti nittaṇhaṃ. Pariyesamānāti olokayamānā. Nājjhagamunti na adhigacchanti na vindanti na passanti. Vattamānatthe atītavacanaṃ. Idha vā huraṃ vāti idhaloke vā paraloke vā. Sabbanivesanesūti tayo bhavā, catasso yoniyo, pañca gatiyo, satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo, nava sattāvāsā, iti imesupi sabbesu sattanivesanesu evarūpaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ kāyassa bhedā uppajjamānaṃ vā uppannaṃ [P 1.0047] vā na passantīti attho. Imāya gāthāya sandiṭṭhikaṃ lokuttaradhammameva kathesi.

"He did not enter a mansion" means: he did not approach the ninefold conceit, which is threefold in its essential nature. Alternatively, because it is a dwelling place, the mother's womb is called a "mansion," and the meaning is also that he will not approach it in the future by way of rebirth-linking. The past tense is used for the future meaning. "He cut off" means: he severed. "With ties cut" means: he stands, having severed the four ties. "Free from anguish" means: without suffering. "Free from craving" means: without craving. "Seeking" means: looking. "They did not find" means: they do not attain, do not find, or do not see. The past tense is used for the present meaning. "Here or beyond" means: in this world or in the next world. "In all abodes" means: in all these abodes of beings—the three existences, four modes of generation, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and nine abodes of beings—they do not see such a one whose taints are destroyed, whether arising or already arisen after the breakup of the body. This is the meaning. With this verse, he taught only the supramundane Dhamma that is visible here and now.

Imañca gāthaṃ sutvā sāpi devatā atthaṃ sallakkhesi, teneva kāraṇena imassa khvāhaṃ, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha pāpaṃ na kayirāti gāthāya dasakusalakammapathavasenapi kathetuṃ vaṭṭati aṭṭhaṅgikamaggavasenapi. Dasakusalakammapathavasena tāva vacasāti catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritaṃ gahitaṃ. Manasāti tividhaṃ manosucaritaṃ gahitaṃ. Kāyena vā kiñcana sabbaloketi tividhaṃ kāyasucaritaṃ gahitaṃ. Ime tāva dasakusalakammapathadhammā honti. Kāme pahāyāti iminā pana kāmasukhallikānuyogo [V 1.0044] paṭikkhitto. Satimā sampajānoti iminā dasakusalakammapathakāraṇaṃ satisampajaññaṃ gahitaṃ. Dukkhaṃ na sevetha anatthasaṃhitanti iminā attakilamathānuyogo paṭisiddho. Iti devatā “ubho ante vivajjetvā [M 1.0046] kāraṇehi satisampajaññehi saddhiṃ dasakusalakammapathadhamme tumhehi kathite ājānāmi bhagavā”ti vadati.

Having heard this verse, that deity also discerned its meaning, and for that very reason, she said, 'Indeed, venerable sir, I...' In that context, the meaning of the verse 'One should not do evil' can be explained by way of the ten wholesome courses of action, and also by way of the Noble Eightfold Path. Firstly, by way of the ten wholesome courses of action: by 'by speech,' the fourfold wholesome verbal conduct is taken. By 'by mind,' the threefold wholesome mental conduct is taken. By 'by body or anything in all the world,' the threefold wholesome bodily conduct is taken. These, firstly, are the ten wholesome courses of action. Furthermore, by 'having abandoned sensual pleasures,' indulgence in sensual pleasure is rejected. By 'mindful and clearly comprehending,' mindfulness and clear comprehension, the cause for the ten wholesome courses of action, is taken. By 'one should not pursue what is painful and unbeneficial,' the practice of self-mortification is prohibited. Thus, the deity says, 'Having avoided both extremes, I understand the ten wholesome courses of action, together with their causes—mindfulness and clear comprehension—as taught by you, O Blessed One.'

Aṭṭhaṅgikamaggavasena pana ayaṃ nayo – tasmiṃ kira ṭhāne mahatī dhammadesanā ahosi. Desanāpariyosāne devatā yathāṭhāne ṭhitāva desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya attanā adhigataṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ dassentī evamāha. Tattha vacasāti sammāvācā gahitā, mano pana aṅgaṃ na hotīti manasāti maggasampayuttakaṃ cittaṃ gahitaṃ. Kāyena vā kiñcana sabbaloketi sammākammanto gahito, ājīvo pana vācākammantapakkhikattā gahitova hoti. Satimāti iminā vāyāmasatisamādhayo gahitā. Sampajānotipadena sammādiṭṭhisammāsaṅkappā. Kāme pahāya, dukkhaṃ na sevethātipadadvayena antadvayavajjanaṃ. Iti ime dve ante anupagamma majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ tumhehi kathitaṃ, ājānāmi bhagavāti vatvā tathāgataṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti.

By means of the Eightfold Path, this is the method: In that place, it is said, a great teaching of the Dhamma occurred. At the conclusion of the teaching, the deity, remaining in her own place, sent forth knowledge in accordance with the teaching, and having become established in the fruit of stream-entry, demonstrating the Eightfold Path she herself had attained, spoke thus. Therein, by 'with speech' (vacasā), Right Speech is taken. But since the mind is not a factor of the path, by 'with mind' (manasā), the mind associated with the path is taken. By 'by body or anything in all the world,' Right Action is taken. And Right Livelihood, being included on the side of speech and action, is indeed taken. By this word 'mindful' (satimā), Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration are taken. By the word 'clearly comprehending' (sampajāno), Right View and Right Intention are taken. By the two phrases 'having abandoned sensual pleasures' and 'one should not cultivate suffering,' the avoidance of the two extremes is taken. Thus, having said, 'Not approaching these two extremes, I understand, O Blessed One, the Middle Path taught by you,' she honored the Tathāgata with perfumes, garlands, and so on, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

Samiddhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta is concluded.

Nandanavaggo dutiyo.

The Nandana Vagga, the Second.

3. Sattivaggo

3. The Satti Vagga

1. Sattisuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Satti Sutta

21. Sattivaggassa paṭhame [P 1.0048] sattiyāti desanāsīsametaṃ. Ekatokhārādinā satthenāti attho. Omaṭṭhoti pahato. Cattāro hi pahārā omaṭṭho ummaṭṭho maṭṭho vimaṭṭhoti. Tattha upari ṭhatvā adhomukhaṃ dinnapahāro omaṭṭho nāma; heṭṭhā ṭhatvā uddhaṃmukhaṃ dinno ummaṭṭho nāma; aggaḷasūci viya vinivijjhitvā gato maṭṭho nāma; seso sabbopi vimaṭṭho nāma. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne omaṭṭho gahito. So hi sabbadāruṇo duruddharasallo duttikiccho antodoso antopubbalohitova hoti[V 1.0045], pubbalohitaṃ anikkhamitvā vaṇamukhaṃ pariyonandhitvā tiṭṭhati. Pubbalohitaṃ [M 1.0047] niharitukāmehi mañcena saddhiṃ bandhitvā adhosiro kātabbo hoti, maraṇaṃ vā maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Paribbajeti vihareyya.

21. In the first sutta of the Satti Vagga, 'by a spear' (sattiyā) is the heading of the discourse. The meaning is: with a weapon such as one with a single edge. 'Struck down' (omaṭṭho) means struck. Indeed, there are four kinds of strikes: struck down (omaṭṭha), struck up (ummaṭṭha), struck through (maṭṭha), and struck around (vimaṭṭha). Among these, a blow given from above downwards is called 'struck down'; a blow given from below upwards is called 'struck up'; a blow that pierces through like a door-bolt is called 'struck through'; and all the rest are called 'struck around.' In this context, however, 'struck down' is taken. For it is the most terrible of all, a dart difficult to extract, hard to treat, with an internal defect, and with internal pus and blood. The pus and blood, without exiting, cover the mouth of the wound and remain. Those wishing to remove the pus and blood must bind him to a bed and make him head-downwards; he reaches death or suffering equal to death. 'One should wander' (paribbaje) means 'one should dwell' (vihareyya).

Imāya gāthāya kiṃ katheti? Yathā sattiyā omaṭṭho puriso sallubbahana-vaṇatikicchanānaṃ atthāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati, payogaṃ karoti parakkamati. Yathā ca ḍayhamāno matthake ādittasīso tassa nibbāpanatthāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati, payogaṃ karoti parakkamati, evameva bhikkhu kāmarāgaṃ pahānāya sato appamatto hutvā vihareyya bhagavāti kathesi.

What is explained by this verse? Just as a man struck downwards by a spear arouses energy, makes an effort, and strives for the sake of extracting the embedded dart and treating the wound; and just as a person with a blazing head arouses energy, makes an effort, and strives for the sake of extinguishing it, even so, a bhikkhu, being mindful and heedful, should dwell in order to abandon sensual desire. Thus the Blessed One spoke.

Atha bhagavā cintesi – imāya devatāya upamā tāva daḷhaṃ katvā ānītā, atthaṃ pana parittakaṃ gahetvā ṭhitā, punappunaṃ kathentīpi hesā kāmarāgassa vikkhambhanapahānameva katheyya. Yāva ca kāmarāgo maggena na samugghāṭiyati, tāva anubaddhova hoti. Iti tameva opammaṃ gahetvā paṭhamamaggavasena desanaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā desento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tassattho purimānusāreneva veditabboti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Then the Blessed One thought: "This deity has indeed brought a strong simile, but she stands having grasped only a little of the meaning. Even if she were to speak repeatedly, she would only speak of the abandonment by suppression of sensual desire. And as long as sensual desire is not uprooted by the path, it remains persistent." Thus, taking up that same simile of the wound, he turned the teaching towards the first path and, while teaching, spoke the second verse. Its meaning should be understood in accordance with the previous one. The first (sutta).

2. Phusatisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Phusati Sutta

22. Dutiye nāphusantaṃ phusatīti kammaṃ aphusantaṃ vipāko na phusati, kammameva vā aphusantaṃ kammaṃ na phusati. Kammañhi nākaroto kariyati. Phusantañca tato [P 1.0049] phuseti kammaṃ phusantaṃ vipāko phusati, kammameva vā phusati. Kammañhi karoto kariyati. Tasmā phusantaṃ phusati, appaduṭṭhapadosinanti yasmā na aphusantaṃ phusati, phusantañca phusati, ayaṃ kammavipākānaṃ dhammatā, tasmā yo “appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati, suddhassa posassa anaṅgaṇassā”ti evaṃ vutto appaduṭṭhapadosī puggalo, taṃ puggalaṃ kammaṃ phusantameva kammaṃ phusati, vipāko vā phusati. So hi parassa upaghātaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti vā mā vā, attā panānena catūsu apāyesu ṭhapito nāma hoti. Tenāha bhagavā – “tameva bālaṃ pacceti pāpaṃ, sukhumo rajo paṭivātaṃva khitto”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

2. In the second sutta, as for the phrase 'it does not touch one who does not touch': the result does not touch one who does not perform an action, or the action itself does not touch one who does not perform it. Indeed, an action is not done by one who does not do it. And it touches one who touches: the result touches one who performs an action, or the action itself touches. Indeed, an action is done by one who does it. Therefore, 'it touches one who touches, one who wrongs the untainted': because an action does not touch one who does not act, but it does touch one who acts—this is the nature of kamma and its results—therefore, regarding the person who wrongs an uncorrupted one, as stated, 'He who wrongs an uncorrupted man, a pure person without blemish,' the action touches that person, who is indeed one who performs the action, or the result touches him. For whether or not he is able to cause harm to another, by this act he has indeed placed himself in the four states of misery. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Evil recoils on that very fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.' The second (sutta).

3. Jaṭāsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Jaṭā Sutta

23. Tatiye [V 1.0046][M 1.0048] antojaṭāti gāthāyaṃ jaṭāti taṇhāya jāliniyā adhivacanaṃ. Sā hi rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu heṭṭhupariyavasena punappunaṃ uppajjanato saṃsibbanaṭṭhena veḷugumbādīnaṃ sākhājālasaṅkhātā jaṭā viyāti jaṭā. Sā panesā sakaparikkhāraparaparikkhāresu sakaattabhāva-paraattabhāvesu ajjhattikāyatana-bāhirāyatanesu ca uppajjanato antojaṭā bahijaṭāti vuccati. Tāya evaṃ uppajjamānāya jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā. Yathā nāma veḷujaṭādīhi veḷuādayo, evaṃ tāya taṇhājaṭāya sabbāpi ayaṃ sattanikāyasaṅkhātā pajā jaṭitā vinaddhā, saṃsibbitāti attho. Yasmā ca evaṃ jaṭitā, taṃ taṃ gotama pucchāmīti tasmā taṃ pucchāmi. Gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Ko imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti imaṃ evaṃ tedhātukaṃ jaṭetvā ṭhitaṃ jaṭaṃ ko vijaṭeyya, vijaṭetuṃ ko samatthoti pucchati.

22. In the third sutta, in the verse beginning 'Antojaṭā', 'jaṭā' (tangle) is a designation for craving, which is net-like. For that craving arises repeatedly in objects such as forms, stitching them together in a crisscrossing manner, like the tangle known as the net of branches of a bamboo thicket; hence, it is called a 'tangle'. This craving, moreover, is called the 'internal tangle' and the 'external tangle' because it arises in one’s own and others’ requisites, in one’s own and others’ beings, and in the internal and external sense bases. By this tangle thus arising, beings are entangled. Just as bamboos and so on are entangled by the tangles of bamboo, so too are all these beings, this host of creatures, entangled, intertwined, and stitched together by this tangle of craving—this is the meaning. And because they are thus entangled, 'taṃ taṃ gotama pucchāmi' means: 'Therefore, I ask you, Gotama'. 'Gotama' is addressing the Blessed One by his clan name. 'Ko imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ' ('Who can disentangle this tangle?') means: 'Who could disentangle this tangle that stands having thus entangled the three realms? Who is capable of disentangling it?'—thus he asks.

Athassa bhagavā tamatthaṃ vissajjento sīle patiṭṭhāyātiādimāha. Tattha sīle patiṭṭhāyāti catupārisuddhisīle ṭhatvā. Ettha ca bhagavā jaṭāvijaṭanaṃ pucchito sīlaṃ ārabhanto na “aññaṃ puṭṭho aññaṃ kathetī”ti veditabbo. Jaṭāvijaṭakassa hi patiṭṭhādassanatthamettha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ.

3. Then the Blessed One, elucidating that meaning for him, began by saying, "Established in virtue..." and so on. Here, "established in virtue" means standing firm in the fourfold purified virtue. In this context, although the Blessed One was asked about disentangling the tangle, he begins by discussing virtue; this should not be understood as "answering one question with another." For here, virtue is taught to show the foundation for one who disentangles the tangle.

Naroti [P 1.0050] satto. Sapaññoti kammajatihetukapaṭisandhipaññāya paññavā. Cittaṃ paññañca bhāvayanti samādhiñceva vipassanañca bhāvayamāno. Cittasīsena hettha aṭṭha samāpattiyo kathitā, paññānāmena vipassanā. Ātāpīti vīriyavā. Vīriyañhi kilesānaṃ ātāpanaparitāpanaṭṭhena “ātāpo”ti vuccati, tadassa atthīti ātāpī. Nipakoti nepakkaṃ vuccati paññā, tāya samannāgatoti attho. Iminā padena pārihāriyapaññaṃ dasseti. Pārihāriyapaññā nāma “ayaṃ kālo uddesassa, ayaṃ kālo paripucchāyā”tiādinā nayena sabbattha kārāpitā pariharitabbapaññā. Imasmiñhi pañhābyākaraṇe tikkhattuṃ paññā āgatā. Tattha paṭhamā jātipaññā, dutiyā vipassanāpaññā, tatiyā sabbakiccapariṇāyikā pārihāriyapaññā.

23. 'A person' (nara) means a being. 'Wise' (sapañña) means endowed with the wisdom of a triple-rooted rebirth-linking that is the result of kamma. 'Develops mind and wisdom' means one who develops both concentration and insight. Here, under the heading of 'mind,' the eight attainments are taught, and by the name 'wisdom,' insight is taught. 'Ardent' (ātāpī) means energetic. Indeed, energy is called 'ardor' (ātāpo) because it thoroughly burns and torments the defilements; one who possesses it is 'ardent' (ātāpī). 'Discerning' (nipaka): wisdom is called 'prudence' (nepakka), and the meaning is one endowed with that. By this term, he shows administrative wisdom. Administrative wisdom (pārihāriyapaññā) is the wisdom that knows, 'This is the time for recitation, this is the time for questioning,' and so on, guiding all actions appropriately. Indeed, in this explanation of the question, wisdom is mentioned three times. The first is wisdom-at-birth, the second is insight-wisdom, and the third is the administrative wisdom that directs all activities.

So [M 1.0049] imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭanti so imehi sīlādīhi samannāgato bhikkhu. Yathā nāma puriso pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya sunisitaṃ satthaṃ ukkhipitvā mahantaṃ veḷugumbaṃ vijaṭeyya, evamevaṃ sīle [V 1.0047] patiṭṭhāya samādhisilāyaṃ sunisitaṃ vipassanāpaññāsatthaṃ vīriyabalapaggahitena pārihāriyapaññāhatthena ukkhipitvā sabbampi taṃ attano santāne patitaṃ taṇhājaṭaṃ vijaṭeyya sañchindeyya sampadāleyyāti.

'He should disentangle this tangle' means that monk endowed with these virtues and so on. Just as a man, standing firmly on the ground, lifts a well-sharpened knife and unravels a large clump of bamboo, so too, being established in virtue, he lifts the well-sharpened knife of insight-wisdom, sharpened on the whetstone of concentration, raised by the power of energy and wielded by the hand of administrative wisdom, and should disentangle, cut through, and completely destroy all that tangle of craving that has arisen in his own continuity.

Ettāvatā sekhabhūmiṃ kathetvā idāni jaṭaṃ vijaṭetvā ṭhitaṃ mahākhīṇāsavaṃ dassento yesantiādimāha. Evaṃ jaṭaṃ vijaṭetvā ṭhitaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ dassetvā puna jaṭāya vijaṭanokāsaṃ dassento yattha nāmañcātiādimāha. Tattha nāmanti cattāro arūpino khandhā. Paṭighaṃ rūpasaññā cāti ettha paṭighasaññāvasena kāmabhavo gahito, rūpasaññāvasena rūpabhavo. Tesu dvīsu gahitesu arūpabhavo gahitova hoti bhavasaṅkhepenāti. Etthesā chijjate jaṭāti ettha tebhūmakavaṭṭassa pariyādiyanaṭṭhāne esā jaṭā chijjati, nibbānaṃ āgamma chijjati nirujjhatīti ayaṃ attho dassito hoti. Tatiyaṃ.

Having thus spoken about the stage of a trainee, now, wishing to show the great one with taints destroyed who stands having disentangled the tangle, he says, 'Of whom...' (yesaṃ) and so on. Having thus shown the one with taints destroyed who stands having disentangled the tangle, then, wishing to show the occasion for disentangling the tangle, he says, 'Where name...' (yattha nāmañca) and so on. Therein, 'name' means the four immaterial aggregates. In the phrase 'resistance and perception of form' (paṭighaṃ rūpasaññā ca), the realm of sensual existence is taken by way of perception of resistance, and the realm of form by way of perception of form. When these two are taken, the formless realm is also taken, due to the summarization of existence. In the phrase 'Here this tangle is cut' (etthesā chijjate jaṭā), it means that here, in the place of the complete exhaustion of the round of the three planes, this tangle is cut; having reached Nibbāna, it is cut, it ceases—this is the meaning that is shown. The Third Sutta.

4. Manonivāraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Discourse on Restraining the Mind

24. Catutthe yato yatoti pāpato vā kalyāṇato vā. Ayaṃ kira devatā “yaṃkiñci kusalādibhedaṃ lokiyaṃ vā lokuttaraṃ vā mano, taṃ nivāretabbameva, na uppādetabba”nti evaṃladdhikā[P 1.0051]. Sa sabbatoti so sabbato. Atha bhagavā – “ayaṃ devatā aniyyānikakathaṃ katheti, mano nāma nivāretabbampi atthi bhāvetabbampi, vibhajitvā namassā dassessāmī”ti cintetvā dutiyagāthaṃ āha. Tattha na mano saṃyatattamāgatanti, yaṃ vuttaṃ “na sabbato mano nivāraye”ti, kataraṃ taṃ mano, yaṃ taṃ sabbato na nivāretabbanti ce. Mano saṃyatattaṃ āgataṃ, yaṃ mano yattha saṃyatabhāvaṃ āgataṃ, “dānaṃ dassāmi, sīlaṃ rakkhissāmī”tiādinā nayena uppannaṃ, etaṃ mano na nivāretabbaṃ, aññadatthu brūhetabbaṃ vaḍḍhetabbaṃ. Yato yato ca pāpakanti yato yato akusalaṃ uppajjati, tato tato ca taṃ nivāretabbanti. Catutthaṃ.

4. In the fourth sutta, 'from whatever' (yato yato) means from evil or from good. This devatā, it seems, held the view: 'Whatever mind there is—whether worldly or supramundane, of the nature of wholesome, etc.—that should just be restrained, it should not be allowed to arise.' The phrase `sa sabbato` is to be understood as `so sabbato` (he from all). Then the Blessed One, thinking, 'This devatā speaks words that do not lead to deliverance. The mind is something that should be restrained and also something that should be developed. I will give a teaching to her after analyzing it,' spoke the second verse. Therein, regarding what was said, 'One should not restrain the mind from everything,' if it is asked, 'Which mind is that, which should not be restrained from everything?' The answer is: The mind that has come to a state of restraint. The mind that has reached a state of being well-guarded, arisen in the manner of, 'I will give alms,' 'I will observe virtue,' and so on—this mind should not be restrained. Indeed, it should be cultivated and developed. And as for 'from whatever is evil' (yato yato ca pāpakaṃ): from whatever unwholesome state arises, from that the mind should be restrained. The Fourth Sutta.

5. Arahantasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Arahant Sutta

25. Pañcame [M 1.0050] katāvīti catūhi maggehi katakicco. Ahaṃ vadāmīti ayaṃ devatā vanasaṇḍavāsinī, sā āraññakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ “ahaṃ bhuñjāmi, ahaṃ nisīdāmi, mama patto, mama [V 1.0048] cīvara”ntiādikathāvohāraṃ sutvā cintesi – “ahaṃ ime bhikkhū ‘khīṇāsavā’ti maññāmi, khīṇāsavānañca nāma evarūpā attupaladdhinissitakathā hoti, na hoti nu kho”ti jānanatthaṃ evaṃ pucchati.

24. In the fifth sutta, as for `katāvī` (one who has done), it means one who has completed the task by means of the four paths. With the words beginning 'I say,' this deity, who was a forest-grove dweller, having heard the spoken usage of the forest-dwelling monks, such as 'I eat,' 'I sit,' 'my bowl,' 'my robe,' thought: 'I consider these monks to be Arahants. But for those who are Arahants, does such speech based on the view of a self arise, or does it not?' For the purpose of knowing this, he asks thus.

Sāmaññanti lokaniruttiṃ lokavohāraṃ. Kusaloti khandhādīsu kusalo. Vohāramattenāti upaladdhinissitakathaṃ hitvā vohārabhedaṃ akaronto “ahaṃ, mamā”ti vadeyya. “Khandhā bhuñjanti, khandhā nisīdanti, khandhānaṃ patto, khandhānaṃ cīvara”nti hi vutte vohārabhedo hoti, na koci jānāti. Tasmā evaṃ avatvā lokavohārena voharatīti.

5. As for `sāmaññaṃ` (common parlance), it means worldly language, worldly usage. As for `kusalo` (skillful), it means skilled in the aggregates and so on. As for `vohāramattena` (by way of convention only), it means that having abandoned speech based on the view of a self, not breaking conventional usage, one may say 'I' and 'mine.' For indeed, if it were said, 'The aggregates eat, the aggregates sit, the bowl of the aggregates, the robe of the aggregates,' there would be a breaking of conventional usage, and no one would understand. Therefore, not speaking thus, one speaks according to worldly usage.

Atha devatā – “yadi diṭṭhiyā vasena na vadati, mānavasena nu kho vadatī”ti cintetvā puna yo hotīti pucchi. Tattha mānaṃ nu khoti so bhikkhu mānaṃ upagantvā mānavasena vadeyya nu khoti. Atha bhagavā – “ayaṃ devatā khīṇāsavaṃ samānaṃ viya karotī”ti cintetvā, “khīṇāsavassa navavidhopi māno pahīno”ti dassento paṭigāthaṃ āha. Tattha vidhūpitāti vidhamitā. Mānaganthassāti mānā ca [P 1.0052] ganthā ca assa. Maññatanti maññanaṃ. Tividhampi taṇhā-diṭṭhi-māna-maññanaṃ so vītivatto, atikkantoti attho. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti. Pañcamaṃ.

25. Then the deity, thinking, 'If he does not speak by way of views, does he perhaps speak by way of conceit?' again asked with the words, 'He who is...' Therein, as for 'Is it conceit?': 'Might that monk, having given way to conceit, speak through the influence of conceit?' Then the Blessed One, thinking, 'This deity is treating an Arahant as if he had conceit,' and in order to show that 'For an Arahant, the ninefold conceit is abandoned,' spoke the reply verse. Therein, `vidhūpitā` means destroyed. As for `mānaganthassa`, it means 'for him, conceit and fetters.' As for `maññataṃ`, it means conceiving. He has overcome and gone beyond all three kinds of conceiving: that of craving, that of views, and that of conceit. The rest has an obvious meaning. The Fifth Sutta.

6. Pajjotasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Pajjota Sutta

26. Chaṭṭhe puṭṭhunti pucchituṃ. Kathaṃ jānemūti kathaṃ jāneyyāma. Divārattinti divā ca rattiñca. Tattha tatthāti yattha yattheva pajjalito hoti, tattha tattha. Esā ābhāti esā buddhābhā. Katamā pana sāti? Ñāṇāloko vā hotu pītiāloko vā pasādāloko vā dhammakathāāloko vā, sabbopi buddhānaṃ pātubhāvā uppanno āloko buddhābhā nāma. Ayaṃ anuttarā sabbaseṭṭhā asadisāti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

In the sixth sutta, `puṭṭhuṃ` means 'to ask.' `Kathaṃ jānemu` means 'How should we know?' `Divārattiṃ` means 'in the day and in the night.' `Tattha tattha` means 'wherever it is blazing, there, there.' `Esā ābhā` means 'this is the light of the Buddha.' But what is that? Whether it is the light of knowledge, the light of joy, the light of serenity, or the light of the Dhamma teaching—all the light that arises from the appearance of Buddhas is called the light of the Buddha. This is unsurpassed, supreme, and matchless. The Sixth Sutta.

7. Sarasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sara Sutta

27. Sattame [M 1.0051] kuto sarā nivattantīti ime saṃsārasarā kuto nivattanti, kiṃ āgamma nappavattantīti [V 1.0049] attho. Na gādhatīti na patiṭṭhāti. Atoti ato nibbānato. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti. Sattamaṃ.

In the seventh sutta, 'From where do the streams turn back?' means: from where do these streams of saṃsāra turn back? Having come to what, do they not flow on? 'Does not gain a footing' (na gādhati) means 'does not become established.' 'From that' (ato) means 'from that, from Nibbāna.' The rest has an obvious meaning. The Seventh Sutta.

8. Mahaddhanasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Mahaddhana Sutta

28. Aṭṭhame nidhānagataṃ muttasārādi mahantaṃ dhanametesanti mahaddhanā. Suvaṇṇarajatabhājanādi mahābhogo etesanti mahābhogā. Aññamaññābhigijjhantīti aññamaññaṃ abhigijjhanti patthenti pihenti. Analaṅkatāti atittā apariyattajātā. Ussukkajātesūti nānākiccajātesu anuppannānaṃ rūpādīnaṃ uppādanatthāya uppannānaṃ anubhavanatthāya ussukkesu. Bhavasotānusārīsūti vaṭṭasotaṃ anusarantesu. Anussukāti avāvaṭā. Agāranti mātugāmena saddhiṃ gehaṃ. Virājiyāti virājetvā. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

28. In the eighth (sutta), 'of great wealth' (mahaddhanā) means they possess great wealth such as stored treasures, pearls, and gems. 'Of great possessions' (mahābhogā) means they have great possessions such as gold and silver vessels. 'They covet one another' (aññamaññābhigijjhanti) means they intensely crave one another's possessions; they desire and long for them. 'Unsatisfied' (analaṅkatā) means not content, of an endless nature. 'Eager in pursuits' (ussukkajātesu) means eager in various kinds of tasks, for the purpose of producing forms and so on that have not yet arisen, and for experiencing those that have arisen. 'Following the stream of existence' (bhavasotānusārīsu) means following the stream of the round of existence. 'Unconcerned' (anussukā) means not engaged. 'A house' (agāraṃ) means a home with a woman. 'Having become dispassionate' (virājiya) means having become dispassionate. The rest is clear. The eighth.

9. Catucakkasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Catucakka Sutta

29. Navame [P 1.0053] catucakkanti catuiriyāpathaṃ. Iriyāpatho hi idha cakkanti adhippeto. Navadvāranti navahi vaṇamukhehi navadvāraṃ. Puṇṇanti asucipūraṃ. Lobhena saṃyutanti taṇhāya saṃyuttaṃ. Kathaṃ yātrā bhavissatīti etassa evarūpassa sarīrassa kathaṃ niggamanaṃ bhavissati, kathaṃ mutti parimutti samatikkamo bhavissatīti pucchati. Naddhinti upanāhaṃ, pubbakāle kodho, aparakāle upanāhoti evaṃ pavattaṃ balavakodhanti attho. Varattanti “chetvā naddhi varattañca, sandānaṃ sahanukkama”nti gāthāya (dha. pa. 398; su. ni. 627) taṇhā varattā, diṭṭhi sandānaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Idha pana pāḷiniddiṭṭhe kilese ṭhapetvā avasesā “varattā”ti veditabbā, iti kilesavarattañca chetvāti attho. Icchā lobhanti ekoyeva dhammo icchanaṭṭhena icchā, lubbhanaṭṭhena lobhoti vutto. Paṭhamuppattikā vā dubbalā icchā, aparāparuppattiko balavā lobho. Aladdhapatthanā vā icchā, paṭiladdhavatthumhi lobho. Samūlaṃ taṇhanti avijjāmūlena samūlakaṃ taṇhaṃ. Abbuyhāti aggamaggena uppāṭetvā. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Navamaṃ.

29. In the ninth (sutta), 'four wheels' (catucakkaṃ) refers to the four postures. Here, 'wheel' (cakkaṃ) is intended to mean posture. 'Nine doors' (navadvāraṃ) means having nine doors by way of the nine bodily orifices. 'Full' (puṇṇaṃ) means filled with impurities. 'Bound by greed' (lobhena saṃyuttaṃ) means bound by craving. 'How will the journey be?' (kathaṃ yātrā bhavissati) asks: For such a body, how will there be an escape? How will there be release, complete release, and transcendence? 'Thong' (naddhi) refers to a grudge (upanāhaṃ); what was anger (kodho) in a former time becomes a grudge (upanāho) in a later time. Thus, the meaning is strong anger that has so arisen. 'Strap' (varattaṃ): As in the verse, “Having cut the thong and the strap, the rope with its underlying tendency…” (Dhp. 398; Snp. 627), craving (taṇhā) has become the strap (varattā), and wrong view (diṭṭhi) has become the rope (sandānaṃ). But here, setting aside the defilements indicated in the Pāḷi text, the remaining defilements should be known as 'straps' (varattā). Thus, the meaning is 'having cut the strap of defilements.' 'Desire and greed' (icchā lobhaṃ): It is one and the same state, called 'desire' (icchā) in the sense of wanting, and 'greed' (lobho) in the sense of coveting. Or, weak greed that arises first is 'desire' (icchā), while strong greed that arises repeatedly is 'greed' (lobho). Or, longing for what has not been obtained is 'desire' (icchā), and greed for what has been obtained is 'greed' (lobho). 'Craving with its root' (samūlaṃ taṇhaṃ) means craving rooted in ignorance. 'Uprooting' (abbuyha) means uprooting by the highest path. The rest is clear. The ninth.

10. Eṇijaṅghasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Eṇijaṅgha Sutta

30. Dasame [V 1.0050][M 1.0052] eṇijaṅghanti eṇimigassa viya suvaṭṭitajaṅghaṃ. Kisanti athūlaṃ samasarīraṃ. Atha vā ātapena milātaṃ mālāgandhavilepanehi anupabrūhitasarīrantipi attho. Vīranti vīriyavantaṃ. Appāhāranti bhojane mattaññutāya mitāhāraṃ, vikālabhojanapaṭikkhepavasena vā parittāhāraṃ. Alolupanti [P 1.0054] catūsu paccayesu loluppavirahitaṃ. Rasataṇhāpaṭikkhepo vā esa. Sīhaṃvekacaraṃ nāganti ekacaraṃ sīhaṃ viya, ekacaraṃ nāgaṃ viya. Gaṇavāsino hi pamattā honti, ekacarā appamattā, tasmā ekacarāva gahitāti. Paveditāti pakāsitā kathitā. Etthāti etasmiṃ nāmarūpe. Pañcakāmaguṇavasena hi rūpaṃ gahitaṃ, manena nāmaṃ, ubhayehi pana avinibhuttadhamme gahetvā pañcakkhandhādivasenapettha bhummaṃ yojetabbanti. Dasamaṃ.

30. In the tenth (sutta), 'antelope-shanked' means having well-rounded shanks like those of an eṇi deer. 'Lean' means not stout, of a balanced body. Alternatively, this meaning should also be understood: a body withered by ascetic practice, not enhanced by means of garlands, perfumes, and ointments. 'Heroic' means possessing great energy. 'Of little food' means eating moderately by knowing the measure in food, or eating sparingly by way of rejecting untimely meals. 'Not greedy' means free from greed in regard to the four requisites. This is indeed the rejection of craving for tastes. 'A lion, a solitary-faring elephant' means like a lion that wanders alone, and like an elephant that wanders alone. For those who live in groups are heedless, while those who wander alone are heedful; therefore, only wandering alone is taken up. 'Proclaimed' means made known, spoken. 'Herein' means in this name-and-form. Indeed, form is taken by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure, and name is taken by the mind. Furthermore, having taken both as inseparable phenomena, the locative case should be applied here also by way of the five aggregates, and so on. The tenth.

Sattivaggo tatiyo.

The Satti Vagga, the Third.

4. Satullapakāyikavaggo

4. The Satullapakāyika Vagga

1. Sabbhisuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Sabbhi Sutta

31. Satullapakāyikavaggassa paṭhame satullapakāyikāti sataṃ dhammaṃ samādānavasena ullapetvā sagge nibbattāti satullapakāyikā. Tatridaṃ vatthu – sambahulā kira samuddavāṇijā nāvāya samuddaṃ pakkhandiṃsu. Tesaṃ khittasaravegena gacchantiyā nāvāya sattame divase samuddamajjhe mahantaṃ uppātikaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, mahāūmiyo uṭṭhahitvā nāvaṃ udakassa pūrenti. Nāvāya nimujjamānāya mahājano attano attano devatānaṃ nāmāni gahetvā āyācanādīni karonto paridevi. Tesaṃ majjhe eko puriso – “atthi nu kho me evarūpe bhaye patiṭṭhā”ti āvajjento attano parisuddhāni saraṇāni ceva sīlāni ca disvā yogī viya pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi. Tamenaṃ itare sabhayakāraṇaṃ pucchiṃsu. So tesaṃ [M 1.0053] kathesi – “ambho ahaṃ nāvaṃ abhirūhanadivase bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ datvā saraṇāni ceva sīlāni ca aggahesiṃ, tena me bhayaṃ natthī”ti. Kiṃ pana sāmi etāni aññesampi vattantīti? Āma vattantīti [P 1.0055] tena hi [V 1.0051] amhākampi dethāti. So te manusse sataṃ sataṃ katvā satta koṭṭhāse akāsi, tato pañcasīlāni adāsi. Tesu paṭhamaṃ jaṅghasataṃ gopphakamatte udake ṭhitaṃ aggahesi, dutiyaṃ jāṇumatte, tatiyaṃ kaṭimatte, catutthaṃ nābhimatte, pañcamaṃ thanamatte, chaṭṭhaṃ galappamāṇe, sattamaṃ mukhena loṇodake pavisante aggahesi. So tesaṃ sīlāni datvā – “aññaṃ tumhākaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, sīlameva āvajjethā”ti ugghosesi. Tāni sattapi jaṅghasatāni tattha kālaṃ katvā āsannakāle gahitasīlaṃ nissāya tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbattiṃsu, tesaṃ ghaṭāvaseneva vimānāni nibbattiṃsu. Sabbesaṃ majjhe ācariyassa yojanasatikaṃ suvaṇṇavimānaṃ nibbatti, avasenāni tassa parivārāni hutvā sabbaheṭṭhimaṃ dvādasayojanikaṃ ahosi. Te nibbattakkhaṇeyeva kammaṃ āvajjentā ācariyaṃ nissāya sampattilābhaṃ ñatvā, “gacchāma tāva, dasabalassa santike amhākaṃ ācariyassa vaṇṇaṃ katheyyāmā”ti majjhimayāmasamanantare bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamiṃsu, tā devatā ācariyassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ ekekaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsiṃsu.

31. In the first sutta of the Satullapakāyika Vagga, 'Satullapakāyikā' are those who, having extolled the Dhamma of the good by undertaking it, are reborn in heaven. Here is the story: A large group of sea merchants set sail on a ship. On the seventh day of their voyage, as the ship was moving with the speed of a shot arrow, a great disaster arose in the middle of the ocean. Massive waves surged up, filling the ship with water. As the ship began to sink, the great multitude of people cried out, calling upon the names of their various deities and lamenting. Among them, one man reflected, 'Is there any refuge for me in such danger?' Seeing his own pure refuges and precepts, he sat cross-legged like a yogī. The others asked him the reason for his fearlessness. He explained, 'Friends, on the day I boarded this ship, I gave alms to the Sangha of monks and undertook the refuges and precepts. Therefore, I have no fear.' 'But, sir, are these available to others as well?' 'Yes, they are.' 'Then please give them to us too.' So he divided the people into seven groups of one hundred each and gave them the five precepts. The first group of one hundred took the precepts while standing in water up to their ankles, the second up to their knees, the third up to their waists, the fourth up to their navels, the fifth up to their chests, the sixth up to their necks, and the seventh as the salty water entered their mouths. After giving them the precepts, he proclaimed, 'You have no other refuge—reflect only on the precepts!' All seven hundred people died there, and relying on the precepts they had taken near the time of death, they were reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. By the power of their group, mansions arose for them. In the midst of them all, the teacher’s golden mansion of one hundred yojanas arose, while the others became his retinue, of which the very smallest was twelve yojanas. As soon as they were reborn, reflecting on their kamma and knowing their attainment was due to their teacher, they thought, 'Let us go at once to the presence of the Ten-Powered One and speak the praises of our teacher.' Immediately after the middle watch of the night, they approached the Blessed One, and each of those deities spoke a verse in praise of their teacher.

Tattha sabbhirevāti paṇḍitehi, sappurisehi eva. Ra-kāro padasandhikaro. Samāsethāti saha nisīdeyya. Desanāsīsameva cetaṃ, sabbairiyāpathe sabbhireva saha kubbeyyāti attho. Kubbethāti kareyya. Santhavanti mittasanthavaṃ. Taṇhāsanthavo pana na kenaci saddhiṃ kātabbo, mittasanthavo buddha-paccekabuddha-buddhasāvakehi saha kātabbo. Idaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Satanti buddhādīnaṃ sappurisānaṃ. Saddhammanti pañcasīladasasīlacatusatipaṭṭhānādibhedaṃ saddhammaṃ, idha pana pañcasīlaṃ adhippetaṃ. Seyyo hotīti vaḍḍhi hoti. Na pāpiyoti lāmakaṃ kiñci na hoti. Nāññatoti vālikādīhi telādīni viya aññato andhabālato paññā nāma na labbhati, tilādīhi pana telādīni viya sataṃ dhammaṃ ñatvā paṇḍitameva sevanto bhajanto labhatīti. Sokamajjheti [P 1.0056] sokavatthūnaṃ sokānugatānaṃ vā sattānaṃ majjhagato na socati bandhulamallasenāpatissa [M 1.0054] upāsikā viya, pañcannaṃ corasatānaṃ majjhe dhammasenāpatissa saddhivihāriko saṃkiccasāmaṇero viya ca.

Therein, 'sabbhireva' means: with the wise, only with the virtuous. The letter 'ra' serves as a connective. 'Samāsetha' means one should sit together. And this is merely the head of the discourse; the meaning is that in all postures, one should act only with the virtuous. 'Kubbetha' means one should do. 'Santhavaṃ' means friendly association. However, association based on craving should not be made with anyone; friendly association should be made with the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha. It was with reference to this that this was said. 'Sataṃ' means: of the virtuous ones, such as the Buddha and others. 'Saddhammaṃ' means the good Dhamma, which has divisions such as the five precepts, the ten precepts, the four foundations of mindfulness, and so on; but here, the five precepts are intended. 'Seyyo hoti' means there is growth. 'Na pāpiyo' means nothing base arises. 'Nāññato' means: just as oil and the like are not obtained from sand and the like, so wisdom is not obtained from another, from a blind fool; but just as oil and the like are obtained from sesame seeds and the like, so too, by knowing the Dhamma of the virtuous and associating with and frequenting the wise, one obtains wisdom. 'Sokamajjhe' means: being in the midst of things that are a cause for sorrow, or of beings afflicted by sorrow, one does not grieve, like the female lay disciple of the general Bandhula the Malla, and like the novice Saṅkicca, the co-resident pupil of the General of the Dhamma, in the midst of five hundred thieves.

Ñātimajjhe virocatīti ñātigaṇamajjhe saṃkiccatherassa saddhivihāriko adhimuttakasāmaṇero viya sobhati. So kira therassa bhāgineyyo hoti, atha naṃ thero āha – “sāmaṇera, mahallakosi jāto, gaccha, vassāni pucchitvā ehi, upasampādessāmi ta”nti. So “sādhū”ti theraṃ vanditvā pattacīvaramādāya coraaṭaviyā orabhāge bhaginigāmaṃ gantvā piṇḍāya [V 1.0052] cari, taṃ bhaginī disvā vanditvā gehe nisīdāpetvā bhojesi. So katabhattakicco vassāni pucchi. Sā “ahaṃ na jānāmi, mātā me jānātī”ti āha. Atha so “tiṭṭhatha tumhe, ahaṃ mātusantikaṃ gamissāmī”ti aṭaviṃ otiṇṇo. Tamenaṃ dūratova corapuriso disvā corānaṃ ārocesi. Corā “sāmaṇero kireko aṭaviṃ otiṇṇo, gacchatha naṃ ānethā”ti āṇāpetvā ekacce “mārema na”nti āhaṃsu, ekacce vissajjemāti. Sāmaṇero cintesi – “ahaṃ sekho sakaraṇīyo, imehi saddhiṃ mantetvā sotthimattānaṃ karissāmī”ti corajeṭṭhakaṃ āmantetvā, “upamaṃ te, āvuso, karissāmī”ti imā gāthā abhāsi –

“Shining in the midst of relatives” means he shines like the novice Adhimuttaka, the co-resident disciple of the Elder Saṃkicca, in the midst of a group of relatives. It is said that he was the Elder's nephew. Then the Elder said to him: 'Novice, you have grown old. Go, ask your age and come back; I will give you the higher ordination.' Saying, 'Very well,' he paid homage to the Elder, took his bowl and robe, and having gone to his sister's village on this side of the forest of thieves, he wandered for alms. His sister, seeing him, paid homage, had him sit in the house, and served him a meal. Having finished his meal, he asked his age. She said, 'I do not know; my mother knows.' Then he said, 'You stay here, I will go to my mother's presence,' and entered the forest. A robber's spy, seeing him from afar, informed the robbers. The robbers commanded, 'It is said a lone novice has entered the forest; go and bring him.' Some said, 'Let us kill him,' while others said, 'Let us release him.' The novice thought: 'I am a learner with a task yet to be done. Having conferred with these men, I will make myself safe.' Addressing the chief of the robbers, he said, 'Friend, I will make a comparison for you,' and spoke these verses:

“Ahu atītamaddhānaṃ, araññasmiṃ brahāvane;

Ceto kūṭāni oḍḍetvā, sasakaṃ avadhī tadā.

“In a time long past, in a great forest, a wilderness, there was a hunter. Having set treacherous snares, he then killed a hare.”

“Sasakañca mataṃ disvā, ubbiggā migapakkhino;

Ekarattiṃ apakkāmuṃ, ‘akiccaṃ vattate idha’.

“And seeing the dead hare, the beasts and birds were alarmed. Thinking, ‘An improper deed occurs here,’ they departed after only one night.”

“Tatheva samaṇaṃ hantvā, adhimuttaṃ akiñcanaṃ;

Addhikā nāgamissanti, dhanajāni bhavissatī”ti.

“In that same way, having killed the recluse Adhimutta, who is without possessions, travelers will not come, and there will be a loss of wealth.”

“Saccaṃ kho samaṇo āha, adhimutto akiñcano;

Addhikā nāgamissanti, dhanajāni bhavissati.

“Indeed, the recluse speaks the truth. Adhimutta is without possessions; travelers will not come, and there will be a loss of wealth.”

“Sace paṭipathe disvā, nārocessasi kassaci;

Tava saccamanurakkhanto, gaccha bhante yathāsukha”nti.

“If, having seen anyone on the path ahead, you will not inform them, then, honoring your truthful speech, go, Venerable Sir, as you please.”

So [V 1.0053][P 1.0057][M 1.0055] tehi corehi vissajjito gacchanto ñātayopi disvā tesampi na ārocesi. Atha te anuppatte corā gahetvā viheṭhayiṃsu, uraṃ paharitvā paridevamānañcassa mātaraṃ corā etadavocuṃ –

That novice, having been released by those thieves, while going, saw even his relatives but did not inform them. Then, the thieves seized those relatives who had arrived and harassed them. And to his mother, who was striking her chest and lamenting, the thieves said this:

“Kiṃ te hoti adhimutto, udare vasiko asi;

Puṭṭhā me amma akkhāhi, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ maya”nti.

“Mother, what is Adhimutta to you? Is he one who dwelt in your womb? Being asked, O mother, please tell me. How else shall we know this?”

“Adhimuttassa ahaṃ mātā, ayañca janako pitā;

Bhaginī bhātaro cāpi, sabbeva idha ñātayo.

“I am the mother of Adhimutta, and this is his birth father. These also are his sisters and brothers; indeed, all here are his relatives.”

“Akiccakārī adhimutto, yaṃ disvā na nivāraye;

Etaṃ kho vattaṃ samaṇānaṃ, ariyānaṃ dhammajīvinaṃ.

“Adhimutta is not one who engages in the affairs of relatives; whom, having seen, he did not prevent. This, indeed, is the practice of recluses, of the noble ones who live righteously.”

“Saccavādī adhimutto, yaṃ disvā na nivāraye;

Adhimuttassa suciṇṇena, saccavādissa bhikkhuno;

Sabbeva abhayaṃ pattā, sotthiṃ gacchantu ñātayo”ti.

“Adhimutta is a speaker of truth; whom, having seen, he did not prevent. Through the well-practiced conduct of Adhimutta, the truth-speaking monk, all have attained fearlessness. May the relatives go in safety!”

Evaṃ te corehi vissajjitā gantvā adhimuttaṃ āhaṃsu –

Thus, having been released by the thieves, they went and said to Adhimutta:

“Tava tāta suciṇṇena, saccavādissa bhikkhuno;

Sabbeva abhayaṃ pattā, sotthiṃ paccāgamamhase”ti.

“Dear son, through your well-practiced conduct, that of a truth-speaking monk, all of us, having attained fearlessness, have returned in safety.”

Tepi pañcasatā corā pasādaṃ āpajjitvā adhimuttassa sāmaṇerassa santike pabbajiṃsu. So te ādāya upajjhāyassa santikaṃ gantvā paṭhamaṃ attanā upasampanno pacchā te pañcasate attano antevāsike katvā upasampādesi. Te adhimuttatherassa ovāde ṭhitā sabbe aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Imamatthaṃ gahetvā devatā “sataṃ saddhammamaññāya ñātimajjhe virocatī”ti āha.

Those five hundred thieves, having gained faith, went forth in the presence of the novice Adhimutta. Taking them, he went to his preceptor. First, he himself received the higher ordination; afterwards, having made those five hundred his own resident pupils, he gave them the higher ordination. Established in the instruction of the Elder Adhimutta, all of them attained the supreme fruit, Arahantship. Taking up this meaning, a devatā said: “Having understood the True Dhamma of the good, one shines in the midst of relatives.”

Sātatanti satataṃ sukhaṃ vā ciraṃ tiṭṭhantīti vadati. Sabbāsaṃ voti sabbāsaṃ tumhākaṃ. Pariyāyenāti kāraṇena. Sabbadukkhā pamuccatīti, na kevalaṃ seyyova hoti, na ca kevalaṃ paññaṃ labhati, sokamajjhe na socati, ñātimajjhe virocati, sugatiyaṃ nibbattati, ciraṃ sukhaṃ tiṭṭhati, sakalasmā pana vaṭṭadukkhāpi muccatīti. Paṭhamaṃ.

‘Sātataṃ’ means they abide ‘constantly’ or ‘happily for a long time,’ so it is said. ‘Sabbāsaṃ vo’ means ‘of all of you.’ ‘Pariyāyena’ means ‘by reason of.’ ‘Sabbadukkhā pamuccati’ (one is freed from all suffering) means: it is not merely that one becomes better, nor merely that one obtains wisdom, nor merely that one does not grieve in the midst of sorrow, nor merely that one shines in the midst of relatives, nor merely that one is reborn in a good destination, nor merely that one abides happily for a long time; but rather, one is freed even from all the suffering of the round of existence. The First Sutta.

2. Maccharisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on Miserliness

32. Dutiye [V 1.0054][P 1.0058][M 1.0056] maccherā ca pamādā cāti attasampattinigūhanalakkhaṇena maccherena ceva sativippavāsalakkhaṇena pamādena ca. Ekacco hi ‘idaṃ me dentassa parikkhayaṃ gamissati, mayhaṃ vā gharamānusakānaṃ vā na bhavissatī”ti macchariyena dānaṃ na deti. Ekacco khiḍḍādipasutattā ‘dānaṃ dātabba”nti cittampi na uppādeti. Evaṃ dānaṃ na dīyatīti evametaṃ yasadāyakaṃ sirīdāyakaṃ sampattidāyakaṃ sukhadāyakaṃ dānaṃ nāma na dīyatītiādinā kāraṇaṃ kathesi. Puññaṃ ākaṅkhamānenāti pubbacetanādibhedaṃ puññaṃ icchamānena. Deyyaṃ hoti vijānatāti atthi dānassa phalanti jānantena dātabbamevāti vadati.

2. In the second, ‘from stinginess and from heedlessness’ means: through stinginess, which has the characteristic of concealing one's own wealth, and through heedlessness, which has the characteristic of the absence of mindfulness. For a certain person, thinking, ‘If I give this, it will lead to my depletion; it will not be for me or for the people of my house,’ does not give a gift out of stinginess. Another, being engrossed in play and the like, does not even give rise to the thought, ‘A gift should be given.’ ‘Thus, a gift is not given’: in this way, he stated the reason that this, which is called a gift—which gives fame, glory, wealth, and happiness—is not given. ‘By one desiring merit’ means: by one who desires merit of various kinds, such as prior volition. ‘It should be given by one who knows’ means: by one who knows that ‘there is a fruit of giving,’ he says, ‘it should certainly be given.’

Tameva bālaṃ phusatīti taṃyeva bālaṃ idhalokaparalokesu jighacchā ca pipāsā ca phusati anubandhati na vijahati. Tasmāti yasmā tameva phusati, tasmā. Vineyya maccheranti maccheramalaṃ vinetvā. Dajjā dānaṃ malābhibhūti malābhibhū hutvā taṃ maccheramalaṃ abhibhavitvā dānaṃ dadeyya.

32. ‘It touches that very fool’ means: that very fool is touched by hunger and thirst, which follow him and do not abandon him. ‘Therefore’ means: because it touches that very one, therefore. ‘Having removed stinginess’ means: having removed the stain of stinginess. ‘Having overcome the stain, one should give a gift’ means: having become one who has overcome the stain, having overcome that stain of stinginess, one should give a gift.

Te matesu na mīyantīti adānasīlatāya maraṇena matesu na mīyanti. Yathā hi mato samparivāretvā ṭhapite bahumhipi annapānādimhi “idaṃ imassa hotu, idaṃ imassā”ti uṭṭhahitvā saṃvibhāgaṃ na karoti, evaṃ adānasīlopīti matakassa ca adānasīlassa ca bhogā samasamā nāma honti. Tena dānasīlā evarūpesu matesu na mīyantīti attho. Panthānaṃva saha vajaṃ, appasmiṃ ye pavecchantīti yathā addhānaṃ kantāramaggaṃ saha vajantā pathikā saha vajantānaṃ pathikānaṃ appasmiṃ pātheyye saṃvibhāgaṃ katvā pavecchanti dadantiyeva, evamevaṃ ye pana anamataggaṃ saṃsārakantāraṃ saha vajantā saha vajantānaṃ appasmimpi deyyadhamme saṃvibhāgaṃ katvā dadantiyeva, te matesu na mīyanti.

“They do not die among the dead” means: they are not counted among those who are as good as dead because of their habit of not giving. For just as a dead person, though much food and drink is placed surrounding them, does not rise and make a division, saying, “Let this be for this one, let this be for that one,” so too one who has the habit of not giving does not make a division. Thus, the possessions of a dead person and of one who has the habit of not giving are said to be exactly the same. Therefore, those who have the habit of giving do not die among such dead ones; this is the meaning. As for “Like travelers going together, those who share from a little”: Just as travelers going together on a long journey, a desert road, having made a division of their little provision for the journey, give to the travelers going with them; just so, those who, journeying together through the desert of saṃsāra which has no discernible beginning, having made a division of even a small gift-object, give to those journeying with them—they do not die among the dead.

Esa dhammo sanantanoti esa porāṇako dhammo, sanantanānaṃ [P 1.0059] vā paṇḍitānaṃ esa dhammoti. Appasmeketi appasmiṃ deyyadhamme eke. Pavecchantīti [M 1.0057] dadanti. Bahuneke na dicchareti bahunāpi bhogena samannāgatā ekacce na dadanti. Sahassena samaṃ mitāti sahassena saddhiṃ mitā, sahassa dānasadisā hoti.

“This is the eternal Dhamma” means: this is the ancient Dhamma; or alternatively, this is the Dhamma of the eternal wise ones. “Some from a little” means: some, from a small gift-object. “Give” means: they give. “From much, some do not wish to give” means: some, though endowed with much wealth, do not give. “Measured equal to a thousand” means: measured together with a thousand, it is like a gift of a thousand.

Duranvayoti [V 1.0055] duranugamano, duppūroti attho. Dhammaṃ careti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ carati. Yopi samuñjakañcareti yo api khalamaṇḍalādisodhanapalālapoṭhanādivasena samuñjakañcarati. Dārañca posanti dārañca posanto. Dadaṃ appakasminti appakasmiṃ paṇṇasākamattasmimpi saṃvibhāgaṃ katvā dadantova so dhammaṃ carati.
