Sataṃ sahassānanti sahassaṃ sahassaṃ katvā gaṇitānaṃ purisānaṃ sataṃ, satasahassanti attho. Sahassayāginanti bhikkhusahassassa vā yāgo kahāpaṇasahassena vā nibbattito yāgopi sahassayāgo. So etesaṃ atthīti sahassayāgino, tesaṃ sahassayāginaṃ. Etena dasannaṃ vā bhikkhukoṭīnaṃ dasannaṃ vā kahāpaṇakoṭīnaṃ piṇḍapāto dassito hoti. Ye ettakaṃ dadanti, te kalampi nagghanti tathāvidhassāti āha. Yvāyaṃ samuñjakaṃ carantopi dhammaṃ carati, dāraṃ posentopi, appakasmiṃ dadantopi, tathāvidhassa ete sahassayāgino kalampi nagghanti. Yaṃ tena daliddena ekapaṭivīsakamattampi salākabhattamattampi vā dinnaṃ, tassa dānassa sabbesampi tesaṃ dānaṃ kalaṃ nagghatīti. Kalaṃ nāma soḷasabhāgopi satabhāgopi sahassabhāgopi. Idha satabhāgo gahito. Yaṃ tena dānaṃ dinnaṃ, tasmiṃ satadhā vibhatte itaresaṃ dasakoṭisahassadānaṃ tato ekakoṭṭhāsampi nagghatīti āha.

“Duranvayo” means difficult to follow; “duppūro” means difficult to fulfill. “To practice the Dhamma” means to practice the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action. As for “even one who practices gleaning,” it refers to one who, by means such as cleaning the threshing floor and beating straw, practices gleaning. “And supporting a family” means while supporting one's family. As for “giving from what is little,” even when giving from what is little, such as a mere leaf-vegetable, by sharing it, one practices the Dhamma. “A hundred of thousands” means a hundred men counted by thousands; that is, one hundred thousand. As for “of those who make a thousand-offerings,” an offering to a thousand bhikkhus, or an offering accomplished with a thousand kahāpaṇas, is a “thousand-offering.” Because this exists for them, they are called “sahassayāgino” (those who make a thousand-offering); it refers to those “sahassayāgino.” By this is shown the almsfood given to ten crores of bhikkhus or almsfood procured with ten crores of kahāpaṇas. He said: “Those who give that much are not worth even a fraction of one of such a nature.” This person who practices the Dhamma while practicing gleaning, while supporting his family, and while giving from what is little—of such a person, these givers of a thousand-offering are not worth even a fraction. Whatever is given by that poor person, even a single portion or a mere ticket-meal, the gift of all those others is not worth a fraction of that gift. “A fraction” (kalā) can mean a sixteenth part, a hundredth part, or a thousandth part. Here, a hundredth part is taken. He said: “The gift that was given by that person, when it is divided a hundredfold, the ten-crore thousand-offering of the others is not worth even one of those parts.”

Evaṃ tathāgate dānassa agghaṃ karonte samīpe ṭhitā devatā cintesi – “evaṃ bhagavā mahantaṃ dānaṃ pādena pavaṭṭetvā ratanasatike viya narake pakkhipanto idaṃ evaṃ parittakaṃ [P 1.0060] dānaṃ candamaṇḍale paharanto viya ukkhipati, kathaṃ nu kho etaṃ mahapphalatara”nti jānanatthaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi. Tattha kenāti kena kāraṇena. Mahaggatoti mahattaṃ gato, vipulassetaṃ vevacanaṃ. Samena dinnassāti samena dinnassa dānassa. Athassā bhagavā dānaṃ vibhajitvā dassento dadanti heketiādimāha. Tattha visame niviṭṭhāti visame kāyavacīmanokamme patiṭṭhitā hutvā. Chetvāti pothetvā. Vadhitvāti māretvā. Socayitvāti paraṃ [M 1.0058] sokasamappitaṃ katvā. Assumukhāti assumukhasammissā. Paraṃ rodāpetvā dinnadānañhi assumukhadānanti vuccati. Sadaṇḍāti daṇḍena tajjetvā paharitvā dinnadakkhiṇā sadaṇḍāti vuccati. Evanti nāhaṃ sammāsambuddhatāya mahādānaṃ gahetvā appaphalaṃ nāma kātuṃ sakkomi parittakadānaṃ vā mahapphalaṃ nāma. Idaṃ pana mahādānaṃ attano uppattiyā aparisuddhatāya evaṃ appaphalaṃ nāma hoti, itaraṃ parittadānaṃ attano uppattiyā parisuddhatāya evaṃ mahapphalaṃ nāmāti imamatthaṃ dassento evantiādimāhāti. Dutiyaṃ.

Thus, when the Tathāgata was assessing the value of the gift, a deity standing nearby thought: ‘The Blessed One, having rolled forth a great gift with his foot as if casting it into a hell one hundred cubits deep, elevates this small gift as if spreading it upon the disk of the moon. How, indeed, can this be of greater fruit?’ In order to know this, he addressed him in a verse. Therein, ‘by what’ means by what reason. ‘Greatly’ means gone to greatness; this is a synonym for ‘vast.’ ‘Given appropriately’ means of a gift given appropriately. Then the Blessed One, wishing to explain by analyzing the gift, said, ‘Some give,’ and so on. Therein, ‘established in wrong’ means being established in unrighteous bodily, verbal, and mental action. ‘Having struck’ means having beaten. ‘Having killed’ means having slain. ‘Having caused sorrow’ means having inflicted sorrow upon another. ‘With tearful faces’ means mixed with tears. For a gift given after making others weep is called a gift with tearful faces. ‘With violence’ means a gift given after threatening or striking with a rod is called a gift with violence. ‘Thus’ means: ‘I, in my capacity as a Perfectly Enlightened One, cannot take a great gift and cause it to be of little fruit, nor a small gift and cause it to be of great fruit. Rather, this great gift, due to the impurity of its origin, is of little fruit, while that other small gift, due to the purity of its origin, is of great fruit.’ Explaining this meaning, he said, ‘Thus,’ and so on. The second.

3. Sādhusuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Sādhu Sutta

33. Tatiye [V 1.0056] udānaṃ udānesīti udāhāraṃ udāhari. Yathā hi yaṃ telaṃ mānaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti vissanditvā gacchati, taṃ avasesakoti vuccati. Yañca jalaṃ taḷākaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, ajjhottharitvā gacchati, taṃ oghoti vuccati, evamevaṃ yaṃ pītivacanaṃ hadayaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkoti, adhikaṃ hutvā anto asaṇṭhahitvā bahi nikkhamati, taṃ udānanti vuccati. Evarūpaṃ pītimayaṃ vacanaṃ nicchāresīti attho. Saddhāyapi sāhu dānanti kammañca kammaphalañca saddahitvāpi dinnadānaṃ sāhu laddhakaṃ bhaddakameva. Āhūti [P 1.0061] kathenti. Kathaṃ panetaṃ ubhayaṃ samaṃ nāma hotīti? Jīvitabhīruko hi yujjhituṃ na sakkoti, khayabhīruko dātuṃ na sakkoti. “Jīvitañca rakkhissāmi yujjhissāmi cā”ti hi vadanto na yujjhati. Jīvite pana ālayaṃ vissajjetvā, “chejjaṃ vā hotu maraṇaṃ vā, gaṇhissāmetaṃ issariya”nti ussahantova yujjhati. “Bhoge ca rakkhissāmi, dānañca dassāmī”ti vadanto na dadāti. Bhogesu pana ālayaṃ vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ dassāmīti ussahantova deti. Evaṃ dānañca yuddhañca samaṃ hoti. Kiñca bhiyyo? Appāpi santā bahuke jinantīti yathā ca yuddhe appakāpi vīrapurisā bahuke bhīrupurise jinanti, evaṃ saddhādisampanno appakampi dānaṃ dadanto bahumaccheraṃ maddati, bahuñca dānavipākaṃ adhigacchati. Evampi dānañca yuddhañca samānaṃ. Tenevāha –

33. In the third sutta, ‘he uttered an udāna’ means he brought forth a joyful utterance. For just as oil that cannot be held in a measure spills over and goes forth, and is called ‘residue,’ and just as water that cannot be held in a pond overflows and goes forth, and is called a ‘flood,’ so too a joyful utterance that cannot be contained in the heart, being excessive, not remaining inside, goes out—this is called an ‘udāna’ (inspired utterance). He uttered such a speech filled with joy—this is the meaning. ‘Even with faith, a gift is good’ means that a gift given, having believed in kamma and its result, is good, a gain, and indeed excellent. They say this. But how are these two indeed equal? One who is afraid of death cannot fight, and one who is afraid of loss cannot give. For one who says, ‘I will protect my life and I will fight,’ does not fight. But only one who, having abandoned attachment to life, strives, thinking, ‘Let there be dismemberment or let there be death, I will seize this dominion,’ is able to fight. One who says, ‘I will protect my wealth and I will give a gift,’ does not give. But only one who, having abandoned attachment to wealth, strives, thinking, ‘I will give a great gift,’ gives. Thus, giving and fighting are equal. What is more? As for ‘Though few, they conquer many’: just as in battle, even a few brave men conquer many cowardly men, so too one endowed with faith and other virtues, while giving even a small gift, crushes much stinginess and obtains the great result of giving. In this way also, giving and fighting are the same. Therefore, He said:

“Appampi ce saddahāno dadāti,

Teneva so hoti sukhī paratthā”ti.

“Even if one gives a little with faith, by that very act one is happy hereafter.”

Imassa [M 1.0059] ca panatthassa pakāsanatthaṃ ekasāṭakabrāhmaṇavatthu ca aṅkuravatthu ca vitthāretabbaṃ.

And for the purpose of clarifying this meaning, the story of the brahmin with a single cloak and the story of Aṅkura should be elaborated.

Dhammaladdhassāti dhammena samena laddhassa bhogassa dhammaladdhassa ca puggalassa. Ettha puggalo laddhadhammo nāma adhigatadhammo ariyapuggalo. Iti yaṃ dhammaladdhassa bhogassa dānaṃ dhammaladdhassa ariyapuggalassa dīyati, tampi sādhūti attho. Yo dhammaladdhassāti imasmimpi gāthāpade ayameva attho. Uṭṭhānavīriyādhigatassāti uṭṭhānena ca vīriyena ca adhigatassa bhogassa. Vetaraṇinti [V 1.0057] desanāsīsamattametaṃ. Yamassa pana vetaraṇimpi sañjīvakāḷasuttādayopi ekatiṃsamahānirayepi sabbasova atikkamitvāti attho.

The phrase 'of/to the righteously gained' means of wealth acquired righteously and equitably, and to a person who has attained the Dhamma. Here, a person called 'one who has attained the Dhamma' is a noble person who has realized the Dhamma. Thus, the meaning is that the gift of righteously gained wealth given to a noble person who has attained the Dhamma is also good. In this line of the verse, 'Who to the righteously gained,' this very same meaning should be understood. The phrase 'of that acquired through exertion and energy' means of wealth obtained through exertion and energy. 'Vetaraṇī' is merely the chief point of the teaching. But the meaning is that one transcends even the Vetaraṇī of Yama, as well as the Sañjīva, Kāḷasutta, and so on—all thirty-one great hells—altogether.

Viceyya dānanti vicinitvā dinnadānaṃ. Tattha dve vicinanā dakkhiṇāvicinanaṃ dakkhiṇeyyavicinanañca. Tesu lāmakalāmake paccaye apanetvā paṇītapaṇīte vicinitvā tesaṃ dānaṃ dakkhiṇāvicinanaṃ nāma. Vipannasīle [P 1.0062] ito bahiddhā pañcanavutipāsaṇḍabhede vā dakkhiṇeyye pahāya sīlādiguṇasampannānaṃ sāsane pabbajitānaṃ dānaṃ dakkhiṇeyyavicinanaṃ nāma. Evaṃ dvīhākārehi viceyya dānaṃ. Sugatappasatthanti sugatena vaṇṇitaṃ. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyavicinanaṃ dassento ye dakkhiṇeyyātiādimāha. Bījāni vuttāni yathāti iminā pana dakkhiṇāvicinanaṃ āha. Avipannabījasadisā hi vicinitvā gahitā paṇītapaṇītā deyyadhammāti.

The phrase 'giving after discerning' means a gift given after discriminating. Herein, there are two kinds of discrimination: discrimination of the gift and discrimination of the worthy recipient. Among these, removing inferior and paltry requisites, discerning the exquisite and excellent ones, and giving them is called 'discrimination of the gift.' Avoiding recipients with flawed morality, or those of the ninety-five heretical sects outside this Dispensation, and giving to those who have gone forth in the Dispensation, endowed with virtues such as morality, is called 'discrimination of the worthy recipient.' Thus, a gift given after discriminating in these two ways is 'praised by the Sugata,' which means praised by the Well-Gone One. Therein, to show the discrimination of the worthy recipient, he said, 'those who are worthy recipients,' and so on. But with the phrase, 'just as seeds are sown,' he indicates discrimination of the gift. For excellent and exquisite things to be given, chosen after careful discernment, are like seeds that are not spoiled.

Pāṇesupi sādhu saṃyamoti pāṇesu saṃyatabhāvopi bhaddako. Ayaṃ devatā itarāhi kathitaṃ dānānisaṃsaṃ atikkamitvā sīlānisaṃsaṃ kathetumāraddhā. Aheṭhayaṃ caranti avihiṃsanto caramāno. Parūpavādāti parassa upavādabhayena. Bhayāti upavādabhayā. Dānā ca kho dhammapadaṃva seyyoti dānato nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ dhammapadameva seyyo. Pubbe ca hi pubbatare ca santoti pubbe ca kassapabuddhādikāle pubbatare ca koṇāgamanabuddhādikāle, sabbepi vā ete pubbe ca pubbatare ca santo nāmāti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Restraint towards living beings is good” means restraint towards living beings is indeed excellent. This deity, surpassing the benefits of giving spoken of by others, began to speak of the benefits of virtue. “They live without harming” means living without causing injury. “From the criticism of others” means through fear of the criticism of others. “From fear” means from fear of criticism. “But the Dhamma-path is better than giving” means the Dhamma-path, which is called Nibbāna, is better than giving. “For the good in the past and in more distant times” means in the past, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, and in more distant times, during the time of Koṇāgamana Buddha; or, all these are called 'the good' of the past and more distant times. The third.

4. Nasantisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Nasantisutta

34. Catutthe [M 1.0060] kamanīyānīti rūpādīni iṭṭhārammaṇāni. Apunāgamanaṃ anāgantā puriso maccudheyyāti tebhūmakavaṭṭasaṅkhātā maccudheyyā apunāgamanasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ anāgantā. Nibbānañhi sattā na punāgacchanti, tasmā taṃ apunāgamananti vuccati. Taṃ kāmesu baddho ca pamatto ca anāgantā nāma hoti, so taṃ pāpuṇituṃ na sakkoti, tasmā evamāha. Chandajanti taṇhāchandato jātaṃ. Aghanti pañcakkhandhadukkhaṃ. Dutiyapadaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Chandavinayā aghavinayoti taṇhāvinayena pañcakkhandhavinayo[P 1.0063]. Aghavinayā dukkhavinayoti pañcakkhandhavinayena vaṭṭadukkhaṃ vinītameva hoti. Citrānīti ārammaṇacittāni. Saṅkapparāgoti saṅkappitarāgo. Evamettha vatthukāmaṃ paṭikkhipitvā kilesakāmo kāmoti vutto. Ayaṃ panattho pasūrasuttena [V 1.0058] (su. ni. 830 ādayo) vibhāvetabbo. Pasūraparibbājako hi therena “saṅkapparāgo purisassa kāmo”ti vutte –

34. In the fourth (sutta), 'pleasant things' (kamanīyāni) refers to agreeable objects such as forms. Regarding 'A person does not reach the state of non-returning from the realm of death,' this means: from the realm of death, which is the cycle of existence in the three realms, one does not reach Nibbāna, which is called 'non-returning'. For beings, having reached Nibbāna, do not come back again; therefore, it is called 'non-returning'. One who is bound and heedless in sensual pleasures is called 'one who does not attain it' (anāgantā), for he cannot attain it; thus it is said. 'Born of desire' (chandajaṃ) means born from craving-desire. 'Misery' (aghaṃ) refers to the suffering of the five aggregates. The second phrase is a synonym for this. 'The removal of desire is the removal of misery' means the removal of the five aggregates through the removal of craving. 'The removal of misery is the removal of suffering' means the suffering of the cycle of existence is removed by the removal of the five aggregates. 'Diverse' (citrāni) refers to diverse objects. 'Lust of intentions' (saṅkapparāga) means lust that is intentionally conceived. Thus, here, rejecting sensuality of objects, defilement-sensuality is called 'sensual pleasure.' This meaning should be elucidated by the Pasūra Sutta (Sn. 830, etc.). For when the Elder said to the wanderer Pasūra, 'Lust of intentions is a person’s sensual pleasure,'—

“Na te kāmā yāni citrāni loke,

Saṅkapparāgañca vadesi kāmaṃ;

Saṅkappayaṃ akusale vitakke,

Bhikkhūpi te hehinti kāmabhogī”ti. –

“Those diverse things in the world are not sensual pleasures. You call lust of intentions sensual pleasure. Thinking unwholesome thoughts, even monks will become enjoyers of sensual pleasures.”

Āha. Atha naṃ thero avoca –

He said. Then the Elder said to him:

“Te ce kāmā yāni citrāni loke,

Saṅkapparāgaṃ na vadesi kāmaṃ;

Passanto rūpāni manoramāni,

Satthāpi te hehiti kāmabhogī.

“If those diverse things in the world are sensual pleasures, and you do not declare lust of intentions to be a sensual pleasure, then seeing delightful forms, even your Teacher will become an enjoyer of sensual pleasures.

Suṇanto saddāni, ghāyanto gandhāni;

Sāyanto rasāni, phusanto phassāni manoramāni;

Satthāpi te hehiti kāmabhogī”ti.

Hearing sounds, smelling scents, tasting flavors, touching pleasant contacts, even your Teacher will become an enjoyer of sensual pleasures.”

Athettha dhīrāti atha etesu ārammaṇesu paṇḍitā chandarāgaṃ vinayanti. Saṃyojanaṃ sabbanti dasavidhampi saṃyojanaṃ. Akiñcananti rāgakiñcanādivirahitaṃ. Nānupatanti dukkhāti vaṭṭadukkhā pana tassa upari na patanti. Iccāyasmā [M 1.0061] mogharājāti, “pahāsi saṅkha”nti gāthaṃ sutvā tassaṃ [P 1.0064] parisati anusandhikusalo mogharājā nāma thero “imissā gāthāya attho na yathānusandhiṃ gato”ti cintetvā yathānusandhiṃ ghaṭento evamāha. Tattha idha vā huraṃ vāti idhaloke vā paraloke vā. Naruttamaṃ atthacaraṃ narānanti kiñcāpi sabbe khīṇāsavā naruttamā ceva atthacarā ca narānaṃ, thero pana dasabalaṃ sandhāyevamāha. Ye taṃ namassanti pasaṃsiyā teti yadi tathāvimuttaṃ devamanussā namassanti, atha ye taṃ bhagavantaṃ kāyena vā vācāya vā anupaṭipattiyā vā namassanti, te kiṃ pasaṃsiyā, udāhu apasaṃsiyāti. Bhikkhūti mogharājattheraṃ [V 1.0059] ālapati. Aññāya dhammanti catusaccadhammaṃ jānitvā. Saṅgātigā tepi bhavantīti ye taṃ kāyena vā vācāya vā anupaṭipattiyā vā namassanti. Te catusaccadhammaṃ aññāya vicikicchaṃ pahāya saṅgātigāpi honti, pasaṃsiyāpi hontīti. Catutthaṃ.

Here, “the wise” (dhīrā) means the wise who remove desire and lust in these objects. “All fetters” (saṃyojanaṃ sabbaṃ) means all ten fetters. “Owning nothing” (akiñcanaṃ) means being free from the impediments of lust, etc. “Suffering does not pursue” (nānupatanti dukkhā) means the suffering of the cycle does not fall upon him. “Thus, venerable Mogharāja” (iccāyasmā mogharājā)—having heard the verse “he abandoned conceit” (pahāsi saṅkhaṃ), the elder Mogharāja, skilled in connecting meanings in that assembly, thought, “The meaning of this verse has not been properly connected,” and thus spoke, striving to connect it properly. Here, “here or hereafter” (idha vā huraṃ vā) means in this world or the next. “The best of men, the benefactor of men” (naruttamaṃ atthacaraṃ narānaṃ)—though all arahants are the best of men and benefactors of men, the elder said this referring to the Blessed One with ten powers. “Those who revere him, are they praiseworthy?” (ye taṃ namassanti pasaṃsiyā te)—if devas and humans revere one thus liberated, then those who revere the Blessed One by body, speech, or by corresponding practice—are they praiseworthy, or are they not praiseworthy? “Monk” (bhikkhu)—he addresses the elder Mogharāja. “Having known the Dhamma” (aññāya dhammaṃ) means having known the Four Noble Truths. “They too have gone beyond attachment” (saṅgātigā tepi bhavanti) means those who revere him by body, speech, or by corresponding practice, having known the Four Noble Truths and abandoned doubt, have also gone beyond attachment and are also praiseworthy. The fourth.

5. Ujjhānasaññisuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ujjhānasaññisutta

35. Pañcame ujjhānasaññikāti ujjhānasaññī devaloko nāma pāṭiyekko natthi, imā pana devatā tathāgatassa catupaccayaparibhogaṃ nissāya ujjhāyamānā āgatā. Tāsaṃ kira evaṃ ahosi – “samaṇo gotamo bhikkhūnaṃ paṃsukūlacīvara-piṇḍiyālopa-rukkhamūlasenāsanapūtimuttabhesajjehi santosasseva pariyantakāritaṃ vaṇṇeti, sayaṃ pana pattuṇṇadukūla khomādīni paṇītacīvarāni dhāreti, rājārahaṃ uttamaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjati, devavimānakappāya gandhakuṭiyā varasayane sayati, sappinavanītādīni bhesajjāni paṭisevati, divasaṃ mahājanassa dhammaṃ deseti, vacanamassa aññato gacchati, kiriyā aññato”ti ujjhāyamānā āgamiṃsu. Tena tāsaṃ dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi “ujjhānasaññikā”ti nāmaṃ gahitaṃ.

35. In the fifth, regarding “those with a perception for finding fault”: there is no separate celestial realm called “the world of fault-finding devas,” but these devas came because, based on the Tathāgata’s use of the four requisites, they were inclined to find fault. It seems they thought thus: “The ascetic Gotama praises for the bhikkhus the defined completion of contentment with rag-robes, almsfood, dwelling at the foot of a tree, and medicine of putrid urine. Yet he himself wears fine robes of wool, fine cloth, linen, and so forth; eats the most excellent food fit for a king; sleeps on an excellent bed in a fragrant chamber like a celestial palace; uses medicines like ghee, fresh butter, and so on; and teaches the Dhamma to the masses all day. His words go one way, and his actions another.” Thus, being inclined to find fault, they came. Therefore, the elder compilers of the Dhamma gave them the name “those with a perception for finding fault.”

Aññathā santanti aññenākārena bhūtaṃ. Nikaccāti nikatiyā vañcanāya, vañcetvāti attho. Kitavassevāti kitavo vuccati sākuṇiko. So [M 1.0062] hi agumbova samāno sākhapaṇṇādipaṭicchādanena gumbavaṇṇaṃ dassetvā upagate moratittirādayo [P 1.0065] sakuṇe māretvā dārabharaṇaṃ karoti. Iti tassa kitavassa imāya vañcanāya evaṃ vañcetvā sakuṇamaṃsabhojanaṃ viya kuhakassāpi paṃsukūlena attānaṃ paṭicchādetvā kathāchekatāya mahājanaṃ vañcetvā khādamānassa vicarato. Bhuttaṃ theyyena tassa tanti sabbopi tassa catupaccayaparibhogo theyyena paribhutto nāma hotīti devatā bhagavantaṃ sandhāya vadati. Parijānanti paṇḍitāti ayaṃ kārako vā akārako vāti paṇḍitā jānanti. Iti tā devatā “tathāgatāpi mayameva paṇḍitā”ti maññamānā evamāhaṃsu.

“Otherwise, he is” means being so in another way. “Deceitfully” means by deceit, by trickery; the meaning is “having deceived.” “Like a fowler”: a fowler is called a ‘kitava.’ For he, though not a bush, shows the appearance of a bush by covering himself with branches, leaves, and so forth, and when birds like peacocks and partridges approach, he kills them and supports his family. Just as that fowler eats the flesh of birds, having tricked them thus with this deceit, so too does a hypocrite who wanders about consuming, having concealed himself with a rag-robe and deceived the populace with clever talk. “What he consumes is stolen from him” means all his use of the four requisites is indeed consumed by theft. Thus the devas spoke with reference to the Blessed One. “The wise fully understand” means the wise know whether this one is a doer or a non-doer. Thus, those devas, thinking, “We ourselves are wiser even than the Tathāgata,” spoke thus.

Atha bhagavā nayidantiādimāha. Tattha yāyaṃ paṭipadā daḷhāti ayaṃ dhammānudhammapaṭipadā daḷhā thirā. Yāya paṭipadāya dhīrā paṇḍitā ārammaṇūpanijjhānena lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena cāti dvīhi jhānehi jhāyino mārabandhanā pamuccanti, taṃ paṭipadaṃ bhāsitamattena vā savanamattena vā okkamituṃ [V 1.0060] paṭipajjituṃ na sakkāti attho. Na ve dhīrā pakubbantīti dhīrā paṇḍitā viditvā lokapariyāyaṃ saṅkhāralokassa udayabbayaṃ ñatvā catusaccadhammañca aññāya kilesanibbānena nibbutā loke visattikaṃ tiṇṇā evaṃ na kubbanti, mayaṃ evarūpāni na kathemāti attho.

Then the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with “This is not...” Herein, as for “this path is firm,” this practice in accordance with the Dhamma is firm and steady. By which practice the steadfast and wise ones, being those who burn away defilements through two kinds of meditation—namely, meditation by closely examining the object and meditation by closely examining the characteristics—are liberated from the bondage of Māra. It is not possible to enter upon or to practice that path merely by what is spoken or by what is heard; this is the meaning. As for “the wise do not make a display,” the wise ones, having known the course of the world, having known the arising and passing away of the conditioned world, and having understood the Four Noble Truths, are extinguished by the Nibbāna of defilements; they have crossed over the craving called ‘visattikā’ in the world. They do not act thus, meaning they do not declare, “We are of such a nature.”

Pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvāti “ayuttaṃ amhehi kataṃ, akārakameva mayaṃ kārakavādena samudācarimhā”ti lajjamānā mahābrahmani viya bhagavati gāravaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā aggikkhandhaṃ viya bhagavantaṃ durāsadaṃ katvā passamānā ākāsato otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhatvāti attho. Accayoti aparādho. No, bhante, accāgamāti amhe atikkamma abhibhavitvā pavatto. Āsādetabbanti ghaṭṭayitabbaṃ. Tā kira devatā bhagavantaṃ kāyena vācāyāti dvīhipi ghaṭṭayiṃsu. Tathāgataṃ avanditvā ākāse patiṭṭhamānā kāyena ghaṭṭayiṃsu, kitavopamaṃ āharitvā nānappakārakaṃ asabbhivādaṃ vadamānā vācāya ghaṭṭayiṃsu. Tasmā āsādetabbaṃ amaññimhāti āhaṃsu. Paṭiggaṇhātūti khamatu. Āyatiṃ saṃvarāyāti [M 1.0063] anāgate saṃvaraṇatthāya, puna evarūpassa aparādhassa dosassa akaraṇatthāya.

“Having stood on the ground” means: being ashamed, thinking, “An improper deed was done by us; though he is not a doer of wrong, we have addressed him with words befitting a doer of wrong,” and having established reverence for the Blessed One as for a Great Brahmā, and having made the Blessed One difficult to approach like a great mass of fire, while seeing him, they descended from the sky and stood on the ground. This is the meaning. “Transgression” means offense. “It has overcome us, venerable sir” means it has occurred, having overcome and overwhelmed us. “To be assailed” means to be offended. It is said that those devas assailed the Blessed One by both means: by body and by speech. Not having paid homage to the Tathāgata, while standing in the sky, they assailed him with their bodies. Bringing forth the simile of the fowler and speaking various kinds of ignoble speech, they assailed him with their speech. Therefore, they said, “We considered him as one to be assailed.” “May you accept” means “May he forbear.” “For restraint in the future” means for the sake of restraint in the future; for the purpose of not committing such an offense, such a fault, again.

Sitaṃ [P 1.0066] pātvākāsīti aggadante dassento pahaṭṭhākāraṃ dassesi. Kasmā? Tā kira devatā na sabhāvena khamāpenti, lokiyamahājanañca sadevake loke aggapuggalaṃ tathāgatañca ekasadisaṃ karonti. Atha bhagavā “parato kathāya uppannāya buddhabalaṃ dīpetvā pacchā khamissāmī”ti sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Bhiyyoso mattāyāti atirekappamāṇena. Imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsīti kupito esa amhākanti maññamānā abhāsi.

“He made a smile appear” means he revealed the tips of his teeth, showing a delighted demeanor. Why? It is said that those devas do not ask for forgiveness sincerely, and they treat the worldly multitude and the Tathāgata, the supreme individual in the world with its devas, as one and the same. Then the Blessed One, thinking, “When a discussion arises later, I will display the Buddha's power and then forgive,” made a smile appear. “In excessive measure” means in an exceeding amount. “They spoke this verse” means they spoke thinking, “This one is angry with us.”

Na paṭigaṇhatīti na khamati nādhivāseti. Kopantaroti abbhantare uppannakopo. Dosagarūti dosaṃ garuṃ katvā ādāya viharanto. Sa veraṃ paṭimuñcatīti so evarūpo gaṇṭhikaṃ paṭimuñcanto viya taṃ veraṃ attani paṭimuñcati ṭhapeti, na paṭinissajjatīti attho. Accayo ce na vijjethāti sace accāyikakammaṃ na bhaveyya. No cidhāpagataṃ siyāti yadi aparādho nāma na bhāveyya. Kenīdha kusalo siyāti yadi verāni na sammeyyuṃ, kena kāraṇena kusalo bhaveyya.

“He does not accept” means he does not approve, he does not tolerate. “One with anger within” means one in whom anger has arisen internally. “One who regards hatred as weighty” means one who dwells having taken up and given weight to hatred. “He binds on enmity” means such a person binds that enmity to himself, like one putting on a knot; he establishes it and does not relinquish it—this is the meaning. “If there were no transgression” means if a transgressive act were not to occur. “There would be no fault here” means if there were no offense. “How could one be faultless here” means if enmities were not calmed, for what reason would one be faultless?

Kassaccayāti [V 1.0061] gāthāya kassa atikkamo natthi? Kassa aparādho natthi? Ko sammohaṃ nāpajjati? Ko niccameva paṇḍito nāmāti attho? Imaṃ kira gāthaṃ bhaṇāpanatthaṃ bhagavato sitapātukammaṃ. Tasmā idāni devatānaṃ buddhabalaṃ dīpetvā khamissāmīti tathāgatassa buddhassātiādimāha. Tattha tathāgatassāti tathā āgatoti evamādīhi kāraṇehi tathāgatassa. Buddhassāti catunnaṃ saccānaṃ buddhattādīhi kāraṇehi vimokkhantikapaṇṇattivasena evaṃ laddhanāmassa. Accayaṃ desayantīnanti yaṃ vuttaṃ tumhehi “accayaṃ desayantīnaṃ…pe… sa veraṃ paṭimuñcatī”ti, taṃ sādhu vuttaṃ, ahaṃ pana taṃ veraṃ nābhinandāmi na patthayāmīti attho. Paṭiggaṇhāmi voccayanti tumhākaṃ aparādhaṃ khamāmīti. Pañcamaṃ.

In the verse beginning 'Kassaccayā': Whose transgression is there not? Whose offense is there not? Who does not fall into delusion? Who is always named 'wise'? This is the meaning. It is said that the Blessed One's manifestation of a smile was for the purpose of having this verse recited. Therefore, thinking, 'Now, having displayed the Buddha's power to the devas, I will forgive,' he spoke the verse beginning with 'Of the Tathāgata, the Buddha.' Therein, 'of the Tathāgata' means of the one who is a Tathāgata for such reasons as 'He has thus gone.' 'Of the Buddha' means of him who has obtained this name by way of the designation that occurs at the culmination of liberation, for such reasons as his having understood the four truths. As for 'for those confessing a transgression': that which was said by you, 'For those confessing a transgression… (etc.)… is released from enmity,' that was well said. I, however, do not delight in that enmity, nor do I long for it—this is the meaning. 'I accept your transgression' means I forgive your offense. The Fifth.

6. Saddhāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sutta on Faith

36. Chaṭṭhe [M 1.0064] saddhā dutiyā purisassa hotīti purisassa devaloke manussaloke ceva nibbānañca gacchantassa saddhā dutiyā hoti, sahāyakiccaṃ sādheti. No ce assaddhiyaṃ avatiṭṭhatīti yadi [P 1.0067] assaddhiyaṃ na tiṭṭhati. Yasoti parivāro. Kittīti vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ. Tatvassa hotīti tato assa hoti. Nānupatanti saṅgāti rāgasaṅgādayo pañca saṅgā na anupatanti. Pamādamanuyuñjantīti ye pamādaṃ karonti nibbattenti, te taṃ anuyuñjanti nāma. Dhanaṃ seṭṭhaṃva rakkhatīti muttāmaṇisārādiuttamadhanaṃ viya rakkhati. Jhāyantoti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena ca ārammaṇūpanijjhānena ca jhāyanto. Tattha lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ nāma vipassanāmaggaphalāni. Vipassanā hi tīṇi lakkhaṇāni upanijjhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. Maggo vipassanāya āgatakiccaṃ sādhetīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. Phalaṃ tathalakkhaṇaṃ nirodhasaccaṃ upanijjhāyatīti lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ. Aṭṭha samāpattiyo pana kasiṇārammaṇassa upanijjhāyanato ārammaṇūpanijjhānanti veditabbā. Paramaṃ nāma arahattasukhaṃ adhippetanti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

36. In the sixth: 'Faith is a man's second companion'—for a man going to the deva-world, the human world, and also Nibbāna, faith is his second companion; it accomplishes the duty of a helper. 'He does not dwell in faithlessness'—if he does not abide in faithlessness. 'Fame' is retinue. 'Reputation' is praise. 'That becomes his'—from that, it becomes his. 'Attachments do not follow'—the five attachments, such as the attachment of lust, do not follow. 'Those who indulge in heedlessness'—those who perform and produce heedlessness, they are said to indulge in it. 'He guards his wealth like the finest'—he guards it like the finest wealth of pearls, gems, essence, and so on. 'Meditating'—meditating by both contemplation of characteristics and contemplation of an object. Therein, 'contemplation of characteristics' is insight, path, and fruition. Indeed, insight contemplates the three characteristics, hence it is called 'contemplation of characteristics.' The path accomplishes the task brought about by insight, hence it is called 'contemplation of characteristics.' The fruition contemplates the truth of cessation, which has an unfailing characteristic, hence it is called 'contemplation of characteristics.' The eight attainments, however, should be known as 'contemplation of an object' because they contemplate the object of the kasiṇa. 'The highest' is intended as the bliss of Arahantship. The Sixth.

7. Samayasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Sutta on the Occasion

37. Sattame sakkesūti “sakyā vata, bho kumārā”ti (dī. ni. 1.267) udānaṃ paṭicca sakkāti laddhanāmānaṃ rājakumārānaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado rūḷhīsaddena sakkāti vuccati[V 1.0062]. Tasmiṃ sakkesu janapade. Mahāvaneti sayaṃjāte aropime himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhe mahati vane. Sabbeheva arahantehīti imaṃ suttaṃ kathitadivaseyeva pattaarahantehi.

37. In the seventh: 'Among the Sakyans'—on account of the inspired utterance 'Indeed, sirs, the princes are capable (sakyā)!', the royal princes acquired the name 'Sakyans.' Even a single district, the residence of those princes, is also called 'Sakyans' by common usage. In that Sakyan district. 'In the Great Wood'—in a great, naturally grown, unplanted forest, contiguous with the Himālaya. 'With all the Arahants'—with those who had attained Arahantship on the very day this sutta was spoken.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – sākiyakoliyā hi kira kapilavatthunagarassa ca koliyanagarassa ca antare rohiṇiṃ nāma nadiṃ ekeneva āvaraṇena bandhāpetvā sassāni kārenti. Atha jeṭṭhamūlamāse sassesu milāyantesu ubhayanagaravāsīnampi kammakārā sannipatiṃsu. Tattha koliyanagaravāsino āhaṃsu – “idaṃ udakaṃ ubhayato āhariyamānaṃ na tumhākaṃ, na amhākaṃ pahossati[P 1.0068], amhākaṃ pana sassaṃ ekena udakeneva nipphajjissati, idaṃ udakaṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti. Kapilavatthuvāsino āhaṃsu – “tumhesu koṭṭhe pūretvā ṭhitesu mayaṃ rattasuvaṇṇanīlamaṇikāḷakahāpaṇe [M 1.0065] ca gahetvā pacchipasibbakādihatthā na sakkhissāma tumhākaṃ gharadvāre vicarituṃ, amhākampi sassaṃ ekeneva udakena nipphajjissati, idaṃ udakaṃ amhākaṃ dethā”ti. “Na mayaṃ dassāmā”ti. “Mayampi na dassāmā”ti. Evaṃ kathaṃ vaḍḍhetvā eko uṭṭhāya ekassa pahāraṃ adāsi, sopi aññassāti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ paharitvā rājakulānaṃ jātiṃ ghaṭṭetvā kalahaṃ vaḍḍhayiṃsu.

Herein is the sequential narrative: It is said that the Sākiyas and the Koliyas built a single dam across the Rohiṇī River between the city of Kapilavatthu and the city of Koliyanagara to cultivate their crops. Then, in the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, when the crops were withering, the laborers from both cities gathered. There, the residents of Koliyanagara said, 'This water, being drawn from both sides, will be sufficient neither for you nor for us. Our crops, however, will ripen with just one watering. Give this water to us.' The residents of Kapilavatthu replied, 'When you have filled your granaries, we, taking red gold, blue gems, and black coins, with baskets, sacks, and so forth in hand, will not be able to go about at your doors. Our crops, too, will ripen with just one watering. Give this water to us.' 'We will not give it.' 'We also will not give it.' Thus escalating the talk, one rose up and struck another, and that one in turn struck another. In this way, striking one another and disparaging the lineage of the royal families, they intensified the quarrel.

Koliyakammakārā vadanti – “tumhe kapilavatthuvāsike gahetvā gajjatha, ye soṇasiṅgālādayo viya attano bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvasiṃsu, etesaṃ hatthino ca assā ca phalakāvudhāni ca amhākaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? Sākiyakammakārā vadanti – “tumhe dāni kuṭṭhino dārake gahetvā gajjatha, ye anāthā niggatikā tiracchānā viya kolarukkhe vasiṃsu, etesaṃ hatthino ca assā ca phalakāvudhāni ca amhākaṃ kiṃ karissantī”ti? Te gantvā tasmiṃ kamme niyuttaamaccānaṃ kathesuṃ, amaccā rājakulānaṃ kathesuṃ. Tato sākiyā – “bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvasitakānaṃ thāmañca balañca dassessāmā”ti yuddhasajjā nikkhamiṃsu. Koliyāpi – “kolarukkhavāsīnaṃ thāmañca balañca dassessāmā”ti yuddhasajjā nikkhamiṃsu.

The Koliya laborers said: 'You boast, relying on the residents of Kapilavatthu, who cohabited with their own sisters like dogs and jackals. What will their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do to us?' The Sākiya laborers said: 'Do you now boast, relying on the children of lepers, who, being without refuge and expelled, lived in a Kola tree like animals? What will their elephants, horses, shields, and weapons do to us?' They went and reported this to the ministers appointed to that task, and the ministers reported it to the royal families. Then the Sākiyas, having prepared for battle, marched out, saying, 'We will show the strength and the forces of those who cohabited with their sisters.' The Koliyas also, having prepared for battle, marched out, saying, 'We will show the strength and the forces of those who lived in the Kola tree.'

Bhagavāpi rattiyā paccūsasamayeva mahākaruṇāsamāpattito uṭṭhāya lokaṃ volokento ime evaṃ yuddhasajje nikkhamante addasa. Disvā – “mayi gate ayaṃ kalaho vūpasammissati nu kho udāhu no”ti upadhārento – “ahamettha gantvā kalahavūpasamanatthaṃ tīṇi jātakāni kathessāmi, tato kalaho vūpasammissati. Atha sāmaggidīpanatthāya dve jātakāni kathetvā attadaṇḍasuttaṃ [V 1.0063] desessāmi. Desanaṃ sutvā [P 1.0069] ubhayanagaravāsinopi aḍḍhatiyāni aḍḍhatiyāni kumārasatāni dassanti, ahaṃ te pabbājessāmi, tadā mahāsamāgamo bhavissatī”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ akāsi. Tasmā imesu yuddhasajjesu nikkhamantesu kassaci anārocetvā sayameva pattacīvaramādāya gantvā dvinnaṃ senānaṃ antare ākāse pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajjetvā nisīdi.

The Blessed One, rising from the attainment of great compassion at the very time of dawn, while surveying the world, saw them marching out thus prepared for battle. Having seen them, and reflecting, "If I go, will this conflict cease or will it not?" He made this resolution: "I will go there and, for the purpose of pacifying the conflict, I will relate three Jātakas. Then that conflict will cease. Then, for the purpose of demonstrating harmony, having related two Jātakas, I will teach the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Having heard the teaching, the residents of both cities will each give two hundred and fifty princes. I will give them the going forth, and then there will be a great assembly." Therefore, while they were marching out prepared for battle, without informing anyone, He Himself alone, taking His bowl and robe, went and sat cross-legged in the sky between the two armies, emitting the six-colored rays.

Kapilavatthuvāsino bhagavantaṃ disvāva, “amhākaṃ ñātiseṭṭho satthā āgato. Diṭṭho nu kho tena amhākaṃ kalahakaraṇabhāvo”ti cintetvā, “na kho pana sakkā bhagavati āgate amhehi parassa sarīre satthaṃ [M 1.0066] pātetuṃ. Koliyanagaravāsino amhe hanantu vā bajjhantu vā”ti. Āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā, bhagavantaṃ vanditvā, nisīdiṃsu. Koliyanagaravāsinopi tatheva cintetvā āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā, bhagavantaṃ vanditvā, nisīdiṃsu.

Just upon seeing the Blessed One, the inhabitants of Kapilavatthu thought, 'Our noble kinsman, the Teacher, has come. Has he perhaps seen our state of quarreling?' Having thought thus, they considered, 'Indeed, with the Blessed One having come, it is not possible for us to strike another's body with a weapon. Let the inhabitants of Koliyanagara kill us or bind us.' Having discarded their weapons, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down. The inhabitants of Koliyanagara also, having thought in that very same way, discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down.

Bhagavā jānantova, “kasmā āgatattha, mahārājā”ti pucchi? “Na, bhagavā, titthakīḷāya na pabbatakīḷāya, na nadīkīḷāya, na giridassanatthaṃ, imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne saṅgāmaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā āgatamhā”ti. “Kiṃ nissāya vo kalaho, mahārājāti? Udakaṃ, bhanteti. Udakaṃ kiṃ agghati, mahārājāti? Appaṃ, bhanteti. Pathavī nāma kiṃ agghati, mahārājāti? Anagghā, bhanteti. Khattiyā kiṃ agghantīti? Khattiyā nāma anagghā, bhanteti. Appamūlaṃ udakaṃ nissāya kimatthaṃ anagghe khattiye nāsetha, mahārāja, kalahe assādo nāma natthi, kalahavasena, mahārāja, aṭṭhāne veraṃ katvā ekāya rukkhadevatāya kāḷasīhena saddhiṃ baddhāghāto sakalampi imaṃ kappaṃ anuppattoyevāti vatvā phandanajātakaṃ (jā. 1.13.14 ādayo) kathesi”. Tato “parapattiyena nāma, mahārāja, na bhavitabbaṃ. Parapattiyā hutvā hi ekassa sasakassa kathāya tiyojanasahassavitthate himavante catuppadagaṇā mahāsamuddaṃ pakkhandino [P 1.0070] ahesuṃ. Tasmā parapattiyena na bhavitabba”nti vatvā, pathavīundriyajātakaṃ kathesi. Tato “kadāci, mahārāja, dubbalopi mahābalassa randhaṃ vivaraṃ passati, kadāci mahābalo dubbalassa. Laṭukikāpi hi sakuṇikā hatthināgaṃ ghātesī”ti laṭukikajātakaṃ (jā. 1.5.39 ādayo) kathesi. Evaṃ kalahavūpasamanatthāya tīṇi jātakāni kathetvā sāmaggiparidīpanatthāya dve jātakāni kathesi. Kathaṃ? “Samaggānañhi, mahārāja, koci otāraṃ nāma passituṃ na sakkotīti vatvā, rukkhadhammajātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.74) kathesi[V 1.0064]. Tato “samaggānaṃ, mahārāja, koci vivaraṃ dassituṃ na sakkhi. Yadā pana aññamaññaṃ vivādamakaṃsu, atha te nesādaputto jīvitā voropetvā ādāya gatoti vivāde assādo nāma natthī”ti vatvā, vaṭṭakajātakaṃ (jā. 1.1.118) kathesi. Evaṃ imāni pañca jātakāni kathetvā avasāne attadaṇḍasuttaṃ (su. ni. 941 ādayo) kathesi.

The Blessed One, knowing full well, asked, “For what reason have you come, great kings?” “Not, O Blessed One, for sport at the fords, not for mountain-sport, not for river-sport, nor for the purpose of seeing the mountains; but rather, having prepared for battle in this place, we have come.” “On what account is your quarrel, great kings?” “Over water, venerable sir.” “What is water worth, great kings?” “Little, venerable sir.” “What is the earth worth, great kings?” “It is priceless, venerable sir.” “What are khattiyas worth?” “Khattiyas are priceless, venerable sir.” “For what reason, great kings, do you destroy the priceless khattiyas on account of water of little value? There is no satisfaction in a quarrel. Through quarreling, great kings, having made enmity without cause, the enmity that a certain tree-deity formed with a black bear has persisted for this entire aeon.” Having said this, he told the Phandana Jātaka. Then he said, “One should not, great kings, rely on another's report. For by relying on another's report, on the word of a single hare, the herds of four-footed creatures in the Himalayas, three thousand yojanas in extent, plunged into the great ocean. Therefore, one should not rely on another's report.” Having said this, he told the Pathavīundriya Jātaka. Then he said, “Sometimes, great kings, even the weak sees an opening in the strong, and sometimes the strong sees one in the weak. For even a small quail-hen killed a great elephant.” He told the Laṭukika Jātaka. Thus, to pacify the quarrel, he told three Jātakas. Then, to illustrate harmony, he told two Jātakas. How? “For, great kings, no one is able to find an opportunity among those who are united,” he said, and told the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka. Then he said, “Among those who are united, great kings, no one was able to see a breach. But when they quarreled with one another, a hunter's son deprived them of life, took them, and went away. Thus, there is no satisfaction in strife.” Having said this, he told the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. Thus, having told these five Jātakas, at the end he taught the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

Rājāno pasannā – “sace satthā nāgamissa, mayaṃ sahatthā aññamaññaṃ vadhitvā lohitanadiṃ pavattayissāma. Amhākaṃ puttabhātaro ca gehadvāre [M 1.0067] na passeyyāma, sāsanapaṭisāsanampi no āharaṇako nābhavissa. Satthāraṃ nissāya no jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ. Sace pana satthā āgāraṃ ajjhāvasissa dīpasahassadvayaparivāraṃ catumahādīparajjamassa hatthagataṃ abhavissa, atirekasahassaṃ kho panassa puttā abhavissaṃsu, tato khattiyaparivāro avicarissa. Taṃ kho panesa sampattiṃ pahāya nikkhamitvā sambodhiṃ patto. Idānipi khattiyaparivāroyeva vicaratū”ti ubhayanagaravāsino aḍḍhatiyāni aḍḍhatiyāni kumārasatāni adaṃsu. Bhagavāpi te pabbājetvā mahāvanaṃ agamāsi. Tesaṃ garugāravena na attano ruciyā pabbajitānaṃ anabhirati uppajji. Purāṇadutiyikāyopi tesaṃ – “ayyaputtā ukkaṇṭhantu, gharāvāso na saṇṭhātī”tiādīni vatvā sāsanaṃ pesenti. Te ca atirekataraṃ ukkaṇṭhiṃsu.

The kings were pleased, thinking: “If the Teacher had not come, we would have killed one another with our own hands and caused a river of blood to flow. We would not have seen our sons and brothers at the doors of our homes, nor would there have been a messenger for us. It is by relying on the Teacher that our lives have been obtained. Furthermore, if the Teacher had remained living in a house, the kingship of the four great continents, surrounded by two thousand islands, would have come into his hand, and he would have had more than a thousand sons; then he would have gone about surrounded by a retinue of nobles. But abandoning that prosperity, he went forth and attained perfect enlightenment. Even now, let him go about only with a retinue of nobles.” Thus, the inhabitants of both cities each gave two hundred and fifty princes. The Blessed One also ordained them and went to the Great Forest. In those who had gone forth out of deep reverence and not of their own inclination, discontent arose. Their former wives also sent messages, saying such things as: “Let the noble sons become discontent; household life is not stable.” And they became exceedingly discontent.

Bhagavā āvajjento tesaṃ anabhiratibhāvaṃ ñatvā – “ime bhikkhū mādisena buddhena saddhiṃ ekato vasantā ukkaṇṭhanti, handa nesaṃ [P 1.0071] kuṇāladahassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā tattha netvā anabhiratiṃ vinodemī”ti kuṇāladahassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi. Te taṃ daṭṭhukāmā ahesuṃ. Daṭṭhukāmattha, bhikkhave, kuṇāladahanti? Āma bhagavāti. Yadi evaṃ etha gacchāmāti. Iddhimantānaṃ bhagavā gamanaṭṭhānaṃ mayaṃ kathaṃ gamissāmāti. Tumhe gantukāmā hotha, ahaṃ mamānubhāvena gahetvā gamissāmīti. Sādhu, bhanteti. Bhagavā pañca bhikkhusatāni gahetvā ākāse uppatitvā kuṇāladahe patiṭṭhāya te bhikkhū āha – “bhikkhave, imasmiṃ kuṇāladahe yesaṃ macchānaṃ nāmaṃ na jānātha mamaṃ pucchathā”ti.

The Blessed One, reflecting and knowing their state of discontent, thought: “These monks, while living together with a Buddha such as myself, are becoming discontent. Well now, let me speak of the qualities of Lake Kuṇāla to them, and taking them there, I shall dispel their discontent.” He then spoke of the qualities of Lake Kuṇāla. They became desirous of seeing it. “Monks, are you desirous of seeing Lake Kuṇāla?” “Yes, Blessed One.” “If so, come, let us go.” “Blessed One, it is a place for those with psychic power to go; how shall we go?” “If you are desirous of going, I will take you by my power and go.” “Very well, venerable sir.” The Blessed One, taking the five hundred monks, rose up into the sky, and having established himself at Lake Kuṇāla, said to those monks: “Monks, in this Lake Kuṇāla, of whatever fish you do not know the name, you may ask me.”

Te pucchiṃsu. Bhagavā pucchitaṃ pucchitaṃ kathesi. Na kevalañca, macchānaṃyeva, tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe rukkhānampi pabbatapāde dvipadacatuppadasakuṇānampi nāmāni pucchāpetvā kathesi. Atha dvīhi [V 1.0065] sakuṇehi mukhatuṇḍakena ḍaṃsitvā gahitadaṇḍake nisinno kuṇālasakuṇarājā purato pacchato ubhosu ca passesu sakuṇasaṅghaparivuto āgacchati. Bhikkhū taṃ disvā – “esa, bhante, imesaṃ sakuṇānaṃ rājā bhavissati, parivārā ete etassā”ti maññāmāti. Evametaṃ, bhikkhave, ayampi mameva vaṃso mama paveṇīti. Idāni tāva mayaṃ, bhante, ete sakuṇe passāma. Yaṃ pana bhagavā [M 1.0068] “ayampi mameva vaṃso mama paveṇī”ti āha, taṃ sotukāmamhāti. Sotukāmattha, bhikkhaveti? Āma bhagavāti. Tena hi suṇāthāti tīhi gāthāsatehi maṇḍetvā kuṇālajātakaṃ (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) kathento anabhiratiṃ vinodesi. Desanāpariyosāne sabbepi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu, maggeneva ca nesaṃ iddhipi āgatā. Bhagavā “hotu tāva ettakaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūna”nti ākāse uppatitvā mahāvanameva agamāsi. Tepi bhikkhū gamanakāle dasabalassa ānubhāvena gantvā āgamanakāle attano ānubhāvena bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā mahāvane otariṃsu.

They asked. The Blessed One answered each question as it was asked. And it was not only the names of the fish that he spoke; having had them ask, he also spoke the names of the trees in that forest grove, and of the two-footed and four-footed creatures and birds at the foot of the mountain. Then, Kuṇāla, the cuckoo king, seated on a staff gripped by two birds with their beaks, surrounded by flocks of birds in front, behind, and on both sides, approached. The monks, seeing him, said, “Venerable sir, we think that this will be the king of these birds, and these his attendants.” “It is so, monks. This one is also of my own lineage, my own tradition.” “Now, venerable sir, we see these birds. But as for what the Blessed One has said, ‘This one is also of my own lineage, my own tradition,’ we wish to hear that.” “Do you wish to hear, monks?” “Yes, Blessed One.” “Then listen.” Teaching the Kuṇāla Jātaka, which he adorned with three hundred verses, he dispelled their discontent. At the conclusion of the discourse, all of them were established in the fruit of stream-entry, and psychic power also came to them by means of the path. The Blessed One, thinking, “Let this much suffice for these monks for now,” rose up into the sky and went to the Great Forest. Those monks too, having gone at the time of departure by the power of the Ten-Powered One, at the time of return, by their own power, surrounding the Blessed One, descended into the Great Forest.

Bhagavā paññattāsane nisīditvā te bhikkhū āmantetvā – “etha, bhikkhave, nisīdatha. Uparimaggattayavajjhānaṃ vo kilesānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathessāmī”ti kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Bhikkhū cintayiṃsu – “bhagavā amhākaṃ anabhiratabhāvaṃ ñatvā kuṇāladahaṃ netvā anabhiratiṃ [P 1.0072] vinodesi, tattha sotāpattiphalaṃ pattānaṃ no idāni idha tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi, na kho pana amhehi ‘sotāpannā maya’nti vītināmetuṃ vaṭṭati, purisapurisehi no bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti te dasabalassa pāde vanditvā uṭṭhāya nisīdanaṃ papphoṭetvā visuṃ visuṃ pabbhārarukkhamūlesu nisīdiṃsu.

The Blessed One, having sat down on the prepared seat, addressed those monks, saying: “Come, monks, sit down. I will teach you the meditation subject concerning the defilements to be destroyed by the three higher paths.” And he taught the meditation subject. The monks reflected: “The Blessed One, knowing our state of discontent, led us to Lake Kuṇāla and dispelled our discontent. To us, who attained the fruit of stream-entry there, he has now, here, given the meditation subject for the three higher paths. Indeed, it is not proper for us to pass the time thinking, ‘We are stream-enterers’; it is proper for us to become true men.” Having paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, they rose, shook out their sitting mats, and sat down separately at the foot of trees in the ravines.

Bhagavā cintesi – “ime bhikkhū pakatiyāpi avissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhānā, laddhupāyassa pana bhikkhuno kilamanakāraṇaṃ nāma natthi. Gacchantā gacchantā ca vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ patvā ‘attanā paṭividdhaguṇaṃ ārocessāmā’ti mama santikaṃ āgamissanti. Etesu āgatesu dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā ekacakkavāḷe sannipatissanti, mahāsamayo bhavissati, vivitte okāse mayā nisīdituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tato vivitte okāse buddhāsanaṃ paññāpetvā nisīdi.

The Blessed One thought: “These monks are by nature diligent in their meditation subject, and for a monk who has found the way, there is no cause for weariness. As they go about, they will develop insight, attain Arahantship, and come to my presence, intending to announce, ‘We have penetrated the quality by ourselves.’ When they have arrived, the deities of ten thousand world-systems will gather in a single world-system; there will be a great assembly. It is fitting for me to sit in a secluded place.” Then, having had the Buddha-seat prepared in a secluded place, he sat down.

Sabbapaṭhamaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gatatthero saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tato aparo tato aparoti pañcasatāpi paduminiyaṃ padumāni viya vikasiṃsu. Sabbapaṭhamaṃ arahattaṃ pattabhikkhu [V 1.0066] “bhagavato ārocessāmī”ti pallaṅkaṃ vinibbhujitvā nisīdanaṃ papphoṭetvā uṭṭhāya dasabalābhimukho ahosi. Evaṃ aparopi aparopīti pañcasatā bhattasālaṃ pavisantā [M 1.0069] viya paṭipāṭiyāva āgamiṃsu. Paṭhamaṃ āgato vanditvā nisīdanaṃ paññāpetvā, ekamantaṃ nisīditvā, paṭividdhaguṇaṃ ārocetukāmo “atthi nu kho añño koci? Natthī”ti nivattitvā āgatamaggaṃ olokento aparampi addasa aparampi addasayevāti sabbepi te āgantvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā, ayaṃ imassa harāyamāno na kathesi, ayaṃ imassa harāyamāno na kathesi. Khīṇāsavānaṃ kira dve ākārā honti – “aho vata mayā paṭividdhaguṇaṃ sadevako loko khippameva paṭivijjheyyā”ti cittaṃ uppajjati. Paṭividdhabhāvaṃ pana nidhiladdhapuriso viya na aññassa ārocetukāmā honti.

First of all, the elder who had taken up the meditation subject and gone forth attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Then another, and then another; in this way, all five hundred blossomed like lotuses in a lotus pond. The monk who first attained Arahantship thought, ‘I will inform the Blessed One.’ He undid his cross-legged posture, shook out his sitting cloth, arose, and faced the One of Ten Powers. Thus, another and yet another, the five hundred came in succession, as if entering a refectory. The first to arrive paid homage, prepared his sitting cloth, and sat to one side. Desiring to announce the quality he had penetrated, he thought, ‘Is there anyone else? No.’ Turning back and looking at the path by which he had come, he saw another, and then another. Thus, all of them came and sat to one side. This one, feeling shy before that one, did not speak; that one, feeling shy before this one, did not speak. It is said that for those whose cankers are destroyed, there are two characteristics. The thought arises: ‘Oh, that the world with its devas might quickly penetrate the quality I have penetrated!’ Yet, regarding the state of having penetrated it, they are not desirous of announcing it to another, like a man who has found a treasure.

Evaṃ osaṭamatte pana tasmiṃ ariyamaṇḍale pācīnayugandharaparikkhepato abbhā [P 1.0073] mahikā dhūmo rajo rāhūti, imehi upakkilesehi vippamuttaṃ buddhuppādapaṭimaṇḍitassa lokassa rāmaṇeyyakadassanatthaṃ pācīnadisāya ukkhittarajatamayamahāādāsamaṇḍalaṃ viya, nemivaṭṭiyaṃ gahetvā, parivattiyamānarajatacakkasassirikaṃ puṇṇacandamaṇḍalaṃ ullaṅghitvā, anilapathaṃ paṭipajjittha. Iti evarūpe khaṇe laye muhutte bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ mahāvane mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi sabbeheva arahantehi.

Then, just as that noble assembly had gathered, the full moon disc ascended and reached the path of the wind, appearing from the eastern circumference of Yugandhara. It was freed from these defilements: clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu; it was like a great mirror-disc made of silver, lifted up from the eastern direction to reveal the delightfulness of the world adorned by the arising of a Buddha; and it possessed the splendor of a silver wheel being turned on its rim. Thus, at such a moment, at such an instant, at such a point in time, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in Kapilavatthu, in the Great Wood, together with a great Saṅgha of monks, with five hundred monks, all of whom were indeed Arahants.

Tattha bhagavāpi mahāsammatassa vaṃse uppanno, tepi pañcasatā bhikkhū mahāsammatassa kule uppannā. Bhagavāpi khattiyagabbhe jāto, tepi khattiyagabbhe jātā. Bhagavāpi rājapabbajito, tepi rājapabbajitā. Bhagavāpi setacchattaṃ pahāya hatthagataṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ nissajjitvā pabbajito, tepi setacchattaṃ pahāya hatthagatāni rajjāni vissajjitvā pabbajitā. Iti bhagavā parisuddhe okāse, parisuddhe rattibhāge, sayaṃ parisuddho parisuddhaparivāro, vītarāgo vītarāgaparivāro, vītadoso vītadosaparivāro, vītamoho vītamohaparivāro, nittaṇho nittaṇhaparivāro, nikkileso nikkilesaparivāro, santo santaparivāro, danto dantaparivāro, mutto muttaparivāro, ativiya virocatīti. Vaṇṇabhūmi nāmesā, yattakaṃ sakkoti, tattakaṃ vattabbaṃ. Iti ime bhikkhū sandhāya vuttaṃ, “pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi sabbeheva arahantehī”ti.

Therein, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of Mahāsammata, and those five hundred monks were born in the family of Mahāsammata. The Blessed One was born in the womb of a noble, and they too were born in the wombs of nobles. The Blessed One went forth from kingship, and they too went forth from kingship. The Blessed One, having abandoned the white parasol, having relinquished the universal sovereignty that had come into his hand, went forth; they too, having abandoned the white parasol, having relinquished the kingships that had come into their hands, went forth. Thus the Blessed One—in a perfectly pure place, in a perfectly pure part of the night, himself perfectly pure with a perfectly pure retinue, free from lust with a retinue free from lust, free from hatred with a retinue free from hatred, free from delusion with a retinue free from delusion, free from craving with a retinue free from craving, free from defilements with a retinue free from defilements, serene with a serene retinue, tamed with a tamed retinue, liberated with a liberated retinue—shines forth exceedingly. This is called the ground for praise; as much as one is able, so much should be spoken. Thus, with reference to these monks it was said: 'with five hundred monks, all of them arahants.'

Yebhuyyenāti [V 1.0067][M 1.0070] bahutarā sannipatitā, mandā na sannipatitā asaññī arūpāvacaradevatā samāpannadevatāyo ca. Tatrāyaṃ sannipātakkamo – mahāvanassa kira sāmantā devatā caliṃsu, “āyāma bho! Buddhadassanaṃ nāma bahūpakāraṃ, dhammassavanaṃ bahūpakāraṃ, bhikkhusaṅghadassanaṃ bahūpakāraṃ. Āyāma āyāmā”ti! Mahāsaddaṃ [P 1.0074] kurumānā āgantvā bhagavantañca taṃmuhuttaṃ arahattappattakhīṇāsave ca vanditvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Eteneva upāyena tāsaṃ tāsaṃ saddaṃ sutvā saddantaraaḍḍhagāvutagāvutaaḍḍhayojanayojanādivasena tiyojanasahassavitthate himavante, tikkhattuṃ tesaṭṭhiyā nagarasahassesu, navanavutiyā doṇamukhasatasahassesu, chanavutiyā paṭṭanakoṭisatasahassesu, chapaṇṇāsāya ratanākaresūti sakalajambudīpe, pubbavidehe, aparagoyāne, uttarakurumhi, dvīsu parittadīpasahassesūti sakalacakkavāḷe, tato dutiyatatiyacakkavāḷeti evaṃ dasasahassacakkavāḷesu devatā sannipatitāti veditabbā. Dasasahassacakkavāḷañhi idha dasalokadhātuyoti adhippetaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “dasahi ca lokadhātūhi devatā yebhuyyena sannipatitā hontī”ti.

'For the most part' means that the greater number had gathered. Few had not gathered: only the non-percipient deities and the formless-realm deities. Here is the sequence of their gathering: It is said that the deities around the Great Forest stirred, saying, 'Come, friends! Seeing the Buddha is greatly beneficial, hearing the Dhamma is greatly beneficial, seeing the Saṅgha of monks is greatly beneficial. Come, come!' Making a great noise, they arrived, paid homage to the Blessed One and the destroyers of the taints who had attained Arahantship at that moment, and then stood to one side. In this way, hearing the sounds from one another, the deities gathered from distances of half a gāvuta, a gāvuta, half a yojana, a yojana, and so forth, across the three-thousand-yojana expanse of the Himālaya; in one hundred and eighty-nine thousand cities, ninety-nine hundred-thousand doṇamukha towns, ninety-six hundred-thousand port cities, and fifty-six jewel-mines—thus throughout all of Jambudīpa, Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and two thousand small islands—thus throughout the entire world-system. Then, from the second and third world-systems, and so forth, up to ten-thousand world-systems, the deities had gathered. For here, the ten-thousand world-systems are what is meant by 'the ten world-spheres'. Therefore, it is said: 'Deities from ten world-spheres had for the most part gathered.'

Evaṃ sannipatitāhi devatāhi sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ yāva brahmalokā sūcighare nirantaraṃ pakkhittasūcīhi viya paripuṇṇaṃ hoti. Tattha brahmalokassa evaṃ uccattanaṃ veditabbaṃ – lohapāsāde kira sattakūṭāgārasamo pāsāṇo brahmaloke ṭhatvā adho khitto catūhi māsehi pathaviṃ pāpuṇāti. Evaṃ mahante okāse yathā heṭṭhā ṭhatvā khittāni pupphāni vā dhūmo vā upari gantuṃ, upari vā ṭhatvā khittasāsapā heṭṭhā otarituṃ antaraṃ na labhanti, evaṃ nirantarā devatā ahesuṃ. Yathā kho pana cakkavattirañño nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ asambādhaṃ hoti, āgatāgatā mahesakkhā khattiyā okāsaṃ labhantiyeva, parato parato pana atisambādhaṃ hoti. Evameva bhagavato nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ asambādhaṃ, āgatāgatā mahesakkhā devā ca brahmāno ca okāsaṃ labhantiyeva. Api sudaṃ bhagavato āsannāsannaṭṭhāne vālagganittudanamatte padese dasapi vīsatipi devā sukhume attabhāve māpetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Sabbaparato saṭṭhi saṭṭhi devatā aṭṭhaṃsu.

With the deities thus assembled, the entire interior of the world-system, up to the Brahma-world, becomes completely full, like a needle case completely filled with needles inserted without any interval. Therein, the height of the Brahma-world should be understood thus: it is said that a stone, equal to the finial on the seventh storey of the Lohapāsāda, being positioned in the lowest Brahma-world and thrown downwards, reaches the earth in four months. In such a vast space, just as flowers scattered or smoke, from one standing below, do not find an interval to go upwards, or a mustard seed thrown from one standing above does not find an interval to descend below, so too were the deities without any interval between them. Indeed, it is just as the seating place of a wheel-turning king is unconstricted; the warrior-nobles of great power who come one after another certainly find their space. However, further and further away, it becomes extremely constricted. In this very same way, the seating place of the Blessed One is unconstricted; the deities and brahmās of great power who come one after another certainly find their space. Furthermore, in the very nearest place to the Blessed One, in a space the measure of a horse-hair's tip, ten or even twenty deities stood, having manifested subtle forms of individual existence. Furthest behind of all, deities stood sixty by sixty.

Suddhāvāsakāyikānanti [M 1.0071][P 1.0075] suddhāvāsavāsīnaṃ. Suddhāvāsā nāma suddhānaṃ anāgāmikhīṇāsavānaṃ āvāsā pañca brahmalokā. Etadahosīti kasmā ahosi? Te kira brahmāno samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā yathā paricchedena vuṭṭhitā brahmabhavanaṃ olokentā pacchābhatte bhattagehaṃ viya suññataṃ addasaṃsu. Tato “kuhiṃ brahmāno gatā”ti āvajjantā mahāsamāgamaṃ ñatvā [V 1.0068] – “ayaṃ samāgamo mahā, mayaṃ ohīnā, ohīnakānaṃ pana okāso dullabho hoti, tasmā gacchantā atucchahatthā hutvā ekekaṃ gāthaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā gacchāma. Tāya mahāsamāgame ca attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpessāma, dasabalassa ca vaṇṇaṃ bhāsissāmā”ti. Iti tesaṃ samāpattito uṭṭhāya āvajjitattā etadahosi.

`Suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ` means 'of those dwelling in the Pure Abodes.' The Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsā) are the five Brahmā realms, the dwelling places of the pure, the non-returners (anāgāmins) and those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavas). As for `Etadahosi`—why did this thought occur? It is said that those Brahmās, having entered meditative absorption (samāpatti) and having arisen from it according to the determined period, looked at their Brahmā abode and saw it was empty, like a dining hall after the meal. Then, reflecting, 'Where have the Brahmās gone?' they came to know of the great assembly and thought: 'This assembly is great, and we have been left behind. For those who have been left behind, an opportunity is rare. Therefore, let us go, not with empty hands, but having each composed a verse. In that great assembly, we will make known the fact of our arrival and also speak of the praise of the Ten-Powered One.' Thus, because they reflected in this way upon rising from their absorption, this thought occurred.

Bhagavato purato pāturahesunti pāḷiyaṃ bhagavato santike abhimukhaṭṭhāneyeva otiṇṇā viya katvā vuttā, na kho panettha evaṃ attho veditabbo. Te pana brahmaloke ṭhitāyeva gāthā abhisaṅkharitvā eko puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otari, eko dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ, eko pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ, eko uttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otari. Tato puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otiṇṇabrahmā nīlakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā nīlarasmiyo vissajjetvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ maṇivammaṃ paṭimuñcanto viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā buddhavīthi nāma kenaci uttarituṃ na sakkā, tasmā mahatiyā buddhavīthiyāva āgantvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Ekamantaṃ ṭhito kho attanā abhisaṅkhataṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

They appeared before the Blessed One: in the Pāḷi, this is stated as if they had descended right in the presence of the Blessed One, in a place directly facing him; however, the meaning here should not be understood thus. Rather, those Brahmās, while still remaining in the Brahmā world, composed their verses. One descended at the rim of the eastern world-system, one at the rim of the southern world-system, one at the rim of the western world-system, and one descended at the rim of the northern world-system. Then, the Brahmā who had descended at the rim of the eastern world-system, having entered the blue kasiṇa, emitted blue rays and made known the fact of his arrival to the devas of the ten-thousandfold world-system as if clothing them in sapphire armor. The path of the Buddhas, it is called, cannot be obstructed by anyone; therefore, having come by the great path of the Buddhas itself, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, he recited the verse he himself had composed.

Dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otiṇṇabrahmā pītakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā suvaṇṇapabhaṃ muñcitvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭaṃ pārupanto viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā tatheva akāsi. Pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otiṇṇabrahmā lohitakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā lohitakarasmiyo muñcitvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ rattavarakambalena parikkhipanto viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā tatheva akāsi. Uttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ otiṇṇabrahmā odātakasiṇaṃ [P 1.0076] samāpajjitvā [M 1.0072] odātarasmiyo vissajjetvā dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānaṃ sumanakusumapaṭaṃ pārupanto viya attano āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpetvā tatheva akāsi.

The Brahmā who had descended at the rim of the southern world-system entered the yellow kasiṇa and released a golden effulgence, as if clothing the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system in a golden robe, thus making known his arrival, and he did likewise. The Brahmā who had descended at the rim of the western world-system entered the red kasiṇa and released crimson rays, as if enveloping the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system with an excellent red blanket, thus making known his arrival, and he did likewise. The Brahmā who had descended at the rim of the northern world-system entered the white kasiṇa and released white rays, as if clothing the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-system in a jasmine-flower robe, thus making known his arrival, and he did likewise.

Pāḷiyaṃ pana bhagavato purato pāturahesuṃ. Atha kho tā devatā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsūti evaṃ ekakkhaṇe viya purato pātubhāvo ca abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitabhāvo ca vutto, so iminā anukkamena ahosi, ekato katvā pana dassito. Gāthābhāsanaṃ pana pāḷiyampi visuṃ visuṃyeva vuttaṃ.

In the Pāḷi, however, it is said: 'They appeared before the Blessed One. Then those deities, having paid homage to the Blessed One, stood to one side.' Thus, their appearance before him, their paying homage, and their standing to one side are described as if in a single moment, but it occurred in this sequence; however, it is presented as a single event. The speaking of the verses, however, is stated separately even in the Pāḷi.

Tattha [V 1.0069] mahāsamayoti mahāsamūho. Pavanaṃ vuccati vanasaṇḍo. Ubhayenapi bhagavā “imasmiṃ pana vanasaṇḍe ajja mahāsamūho sannipāto”ti āha. Tato yesaṃ so sannipāto, te dassetuṃ devakāyā samāgatāti āha. Tattha devakāyāti devaghaṭā. Āgatamha imaṃ dhammasamayanti evaṃ samāgate devakāye disvā mayampi imaṃ dhammasamūhaṃ āgatā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Dakkhitāye aparājitasaṅghanti kenaci aparājitaṃ ajjeva tayo māre madditvā vijitasaṅgāmaṃ imaṃ aparājitasaṅghaṃ dassanatthāya āgatamhāti attho. So pana, brahmā, imaṃ gāthaṃ bhāsitvā, bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā, puratthimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Herein, 'mahāsamayo' means a great gathering. 'Pavana' is said to be a grove. By both terms, the Blessed One said: “In this grove, there is today a great gathering assembled.” Then, to show whose assembly it was, he said, “The hosts of devas have come.” Herein, 'hosts of devas' means a multitude of devas. The meaning of 'We have come to this Dhamma assembly to see the unconquered Saṅgha' is: “We have come for the purpose of seeing this unconquered Saṅgha, who is unconquered by anyone, who, just today, having crushed the three Māras, has won the battle.” Then that Brahmā, having spoken this verse and paid homage to the Blessed One, stood right at the rim of the eastern world-system.

Atha dutiyo vuttanayeneva āgantvā abhāsi. Tattha tatra bhikkhavoti tasmiṃ sannipātaṭṭhāne bhikkhū. Samādahaṃsūti samādhinā yojesuṃ. Cittamattano ujukaṃ akaṃsūti attano citte sabbe vaṅkakuṭilajimhabhāve haritvā ujukaṃ akariṃsu. Sārathīva nettāni gahetvāti yathā samappavattesu sindhavesu odhastapatodo sārathī sabbayottāni gahetvā acodento avārento tiṭṭhati, evaṃ chaḷaṅgupekkhāya samannāgatā guttadvārā sabbepete pañcasatā bhikkhū indriyāni rakkhanti paṇḍitā, ete daṭṭhuṃ idhāgatamhā bhagavāti, sopi gantvā yathāṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Then the second Brahmā came in the same way as stated and spoke. Therein, 'tatra bhikkhavo' means the monks at that place of assembly. 'Samādahaṃsu' means they composed their minds with supramundane concentration. 'Cittamattano ujukaṃ akaṃsu' means having removed all crookedness, deceit, and dishonesty from their own minds, they made them straight. 'Sārathīva nettāni gahetvā' means: just as a charioteer with well-trained thoroughbred horses, his goad laid aside, stands holding all the reins without urging or restraining, so too these five hundred monks, endowed with six-factored equanimity and with guarded doors, being wise, guard their sense faculties. 'O Blessed One, we have come here to see these wise ones.' That Brahmā also, having gone, stood in his very own place.

Atha tatiyo vuttanayeneva āgantvā abhāsi. Tattha chetvā khīlanti rāgadosamohakhīlaṃ chinditvā. Palighanti rāgadosamohapalighameva. Indakhīlanti rāgadosamohaindakhīlameva[P 1.0077]. Ūhacca manejāti ete taṇhāejāya anejā bhikkhū indakhīlaṃ ūhacca samūhanitvā catūsu disāsu appaṭihatacārikaṃ [M 1.0073] caranti. Suddhāti nirupakkilesā. Vimalāti nimmalā. Idaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ. Cakkhumatāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumantena. Sudantāti cakkhutopi dantā sotatopi ghānatopi jivhātopi kāyatopi manatopi dantā. Susunāgāti taruṇanāgā. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – chandādīhi na gacchantīti nāgā, tena tena maggena pahīne kilese na āgacchantīti nāgā, nānappakāraṃ āguṃ na karontīti nāgā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana mahāniddese (mahāni. 80) vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Then the third Brahmā came in the same way as stated and spoke. Therein, 'chetvā khīlaṃ' means having cut the stake of greed, hatred, and delusion. 'Palighaṃ' means the very cross-bar of greed, hatred, and delusion. 'Indakhīlaṃ' means the very threshold-post of greed, hatred, and delusion. 'Ūhacca manejā' means: these monks, being unagitated by the agitation of craving, having uprooted and removed the threshold-post, wander with unimpeded travel in the four directions. 'Suddhā' means they are without defilements. 'Vimalā' means they are stainless; this is a synonym for the former term. 'Cakkhumatā' means by the one possessing the five eyes. 'Sudantā' means they are tamed in terms of the eye, tamed in terms of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the mind. 'Susunāgā' means young nāgas. Therein, this is the etymological explanation: they do not go (na gacchanti) by way of desire, etc., thus they are nāgas; they do not come back (na āgacchanti) to the defilements abandoned by this or that path, thus they are nāgas; they do not commit any offense (āguṃ na karonti), thus they are nāgas. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood in the way stated in the Mahāniddesa.

Apica –

Moreover:

“Āguṃ na karoti kiñci loke,

Sabbasaṃyoga visajja bandhanāni;

Sabbattha [V 1.0070] na sajjatī vimutto,

Nāgo tādi pavuccate tathattā”ti. –

“He who commits no wrongdoing whatsoever in the world, having cast off all fetters and bonds; unattached everywhere, liberated—such a one, because of being thus, is called a Nāga.”

Evamettha attho veditabbo. Susunāgāti susū nāgā, susunāgabhāvasampattiṃ pattāti attho. Te evarūpe anuttarena yoggācariyena damite taruṇanāge dassanāya āgatamha bhagavāti. Sopi gantvā yathāṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsi.

Thus, the meaning here should be understood. 'Susunāgā' means young nāgas; the meaning is that they have attained the accomplishment of the state of a young Arahant. 'We have come, O Blessed One, to see those young Arahants of such a kind, who have been tamed by the incomparable trainer.' He too, having gone, stood in his very own place.

Atha catuttho vuttanayeneva āgantvā abhāsi. Tattha gatāseti nibbematikasaraṇagamanena gatā. Sopi gantvā yathāṭhāneyeva aṭṭhāsīti. Sattamaṃ.

Then the fourth Brahmā came in the very manner described and spoke. Herein, 'gatāse' means they have gone for refuge by means of the supramundane going for refuge that is free from doubt. He too, having gone, stood in his very own place. The Seventh.

8. Sakalikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Splinter Sutta

38. Aṭṭhame maddakucchisminti evaṃnāmake uyyāne. Tañhi ajātasattumhi kucchigate tassa mātarā – “ayaṃ mayhaṃ kucchigato gabbho rañño sattu bhavissati. Kiṃ me iminā”ti? Gabbhapātanatthaṃ kucchi maddāpitā. Tasmā “maddakucchī”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Migānaṃ pana abhayavāsatthāya dinnattā migadāyoti vuccati.

38. In the eighth sutta, maddakucchismiṃ means in the garden of that name. For when Ajātasattu was in the womb, his mother thought: 'This embryo in my womb will be an enemy to the king. What use is he to me?' To cause an abortion, she had her womb pressed. Therefore, it came to be called 'Maddakucchi.' But because it was given as a dwelling place of safety for deer, it is called Migadāya.

Tena kho pana samayenāti ettha ayaṃ anupubbikathā – devadatto hi ajātasattuṃ nissāya dhanuggahe ca dhanapālakañca [P 1.0078] payojetvāpi tathāgatassa [M 1.0074] jīvitantarāyaṃ kātuṃ asakkonto “sahattheneva māressāmī”ti gijjhakūṭapabbataṃ abhiruhitvā mahantaṃ kūṭāgārappamāṇaṃ silaṃ ukkhipitvā, “samaṇo gotamo cuṇṇavicuṇṇo hotū”ti pavijjhi. Mahāthāmavā kiresa pañcannaṃ hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāreti. Aṭṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, yaṃ buddhānaṃ parūpakkamena jīvitantarāyo bhaveyyāti taṃ tathāgatassa sarīrābhimukhaṃ āgacchantaṃ ākāse aññā silā uṭṭhahitvā sampaṭicchi. Dvinnaṃ silānaṃ sampahārena mahanto pāsāṇassa sakalikā uṭṭhahitvā bhagavato piṭṭhipādapariyantaṃ abhihani, pādo mahāpharasunā pahato viya samuggatalohitena lākhārasamakkhito viya ahosi. Bhagavā uddhaṃ ulloketvā devadattaṃ etadavoca – “bahu tayā moghapurisa, apuññaṃ pasutaṃ, yo tvaṃ paduṭṭhacitto vadhakacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādesī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya bhagavato aphāsu jātaṃ. Bhikkhū cintayiṃsu – “ayaṃ vihāro ujjaṅgalo [V 1.0071] visamo, bahūnaṃ khattiyādīnañceva pabbajitānañca anokāso”ti. Te tathāgataṃ mañcasivikāya ādāya maddakucchiṃ nayiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavato pādo sakalikāya khato hotī”ti.

Here, concerning 'At that time,' this is the sequential story: Devadatta, relying on Ajātasattu, employed archers and the elephant Dhanapālaka, but being unable to cause danger to the life of the Tathāgata, he thought, 'I will kill him with my own hand.' Climbing Mount Gijjhakūṭa, he lifted a great rock the size of a pinnacled hall and rolled it down, thinking, 'Let the ascetic Gotama be crushed to dust!' It is said that he possessed great strength, the strength of five elephants. But it is an impossibility that a danger to a Buddha’s life should occur through another’s exertion. As that rock was coming towards the Tathāgata, other rocks rose up in the sky and received it. From the forceful collision of the two rocks, a large splinter of rock arose and struck the Blessed One’s instep; the foot, with welling-up blood, became as if struck by a great axe, as if smeared with lac-dye. The Blessed One looked up and said this to Devadatta: 'Worthless man, much demerit has been generated by you, in that you, with a corrupt mind, with a murderous mind, caused the blood of the Tathāgata to be shed.' From then on, discomfort arose for the Blessed One. The monks thought, 'This dwelling is desolate and uneven, unsuitable for many nobles and renunciants.' So they carried the Tathāgata on a litter to Maddakucchi. Therefore it is said: 'At that time, the Blessed One’s foot was injured by a splinter.'

Bhusāti balavatiyo. Sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Dukkhanti sukhapaṭikkhepo. Tibbāti bahalā. Kharāti pharusā. Kaṭukāti tikhiṇā. Asātāti amadhurā. Na tāsu mano appeti, na tā manaṃ appāyanti vaḍḍhentīti amanāpā. Sato sampajānoti vedanādhivāsanasatisampajaññena samannāgato hutvā. Avihaññamānoti apīḷiyamāno, samparivattasāyitāya vedanānaṃ vasaṃ agacchanto.

Bhusā means forceful. Sudaṃ is merely a particle. Dukkha means the opposite of happiness. Tibbā means intense. Kharā means harsh. Kaṭukā means sharp. Asātā means unpleasant. The mind does not engage with them, nor do they cause the mind to increase—thus, they are disagreeable. Sato sampajāno means being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension for enduring feelings. Avihaññamāno means not being afflicted; not coming under the sway of feelings by rolling over and over.

Sīhaseyyanti ettha kāmabhogiseyyā, petaseyyā, sīhaseyyā, tathāgataseyyāti catasso seyyā. Tattha “yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, kāmabhogī sattā vāmena passena sentī”ti ayaṃ kāmabhogiseyyā. Tesu hi yebhuyyena dakkhiṇapassena [P 1.0079] sayāno nāma natthi. “Yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, petā uttānā sentī”ti ayaṃ petaseyyā. Appamaṃsalohitattā hi aṭṭhisaṅghāṭajaṭitā ekena passena sayituṃ na sakkonti, uttānāva senti. “Yebhuyyena, bhikkhave, sīho migarājā naṅguṭṭhaṃ antarasatthimhi anupakkhipitvā dakkhiṇena passena setī”ti ayaṃ sīhaseyyā. Tejussadattā [M 1.0075] hi sīho migarājā dve purimapāde ekasmiṃ, ‘pacchimapāde ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā naṅguṭṭhaṃ antarasatthimhi pakkhipitvā purimapādapacchimapādanaṅguṭṭhānaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā dvinnaṃ purimapādānaṃ matthake sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā sayati, divasampi sayitvā pabujjhamāno na utrasanto pabujjhati, sīsaṃ pana ukkhipitvā purimapādādīnaṃ ṭhitokāsaṃ sallakkheti’. Sace kiñci ṭhānaṃ vijahitvā ṭhitaṃ hoti, “nayidaṃ tuyhaṃ jātiyā, na sūrabhāvassa anurūpa”nti anattamano hutvā tattheva sayati, na gocarāya pakkamati. Avijahitvā ṭhite pana “tuyhaṃ jātiyā ca sūrabhāvassa ca anurūpamida”nti haṭṭhatuṭṭho uṭṭhāya sīhavijambhitaṃ vijambhitvā kesarabhāraṃ vidhunitvā tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā gocarāya pakkamati. Catutthajjhānaseyyā pana “tathāgataseyyā”ti vuccati. Tāsu idha sīhaseyyā āgatā. Ayañhi tejussadairiyāpathattā uttamaseyyā nāma.

Here, concerning 'the lion's posture,' there are four postures: the posture of one who indulges in sensual pleasures, the posture of a peta, the lion's posture, and the Tathāgata's posture. Among these, "For the most part, monks, beings who indulge in sensual pleasures lie on their left side"—this is the posture of one who indulges in sensual pleasures. Indeed, among them, there is for the most part no one who lies on the right side. "For the most part, monks, petas lie on their backs"—this is the posture of a peta. Indeed, due to having little flesh and blood, being entangled with a mass of bones, they are not able to lie on one side; they lie only on their backs. "For the most part, monks, the lion, the king of beasts, having placed its tail between its thighs, lies on its right side"—this is the lion's posture. Indeed, due to its majestic power, the lion, the king of beasts, having placed its two forepaws together in one place and its hind paws together in one place, having inserted its tail between its thighs, having noted the position of its forepaws, hind paws, and tail, and having placed its head on top of its two forepaws, lies down. Even having slept for a whole day, when awakening, it awakens without being startled. But, having lifted its head, it notes the position of its forepaws and so on.
