If it has shifted even a little from its position, thinking, "This is not suitable for your birth, nor for your heroic nature," it becomes displeased, lies down right there, and does not go out for its feeding ground. But if it is situated without having shifted, thinking, "This is suitable for your birth and for your heroic nature," it becomes joyful and delighted, rises, stretches a lion's stretch, shakes the mass of its mane, roars a lion's roar three times, and goes out for its feeding ground. The posture of the fourth jhāna, however, is called "the Tathāgata's posture." Among these, the lion's posture is mentioned here. Indeed, this is called the supreme posture because it is a deportment of majestic power.

Pāde pādanti dakkhiṇapāde vāmapādaṃ. Accādhāyāti atiādhāya, īsakaṃ atikkamma ṭhapetvā[V 1.0072]. Gopphakena hi gopphake jāṇunā vā jāṇumhi saṅghaṭṭiyamāne abhiṇhaṃ vedanā uppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na hoti, seyyā aphāsukā hoti. Yathā na saṅghaṭṭeti, evaṃ atikkamma ṭhapite vedanā nuppajjati, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, seyyā phāsu hoti. Tasmā evaṃ nipajji. Sato sampajānoti sayanapariggāhakasatisampajaññena samannāgato. “Uṭṭhānasañña”nti panettha na vuttaṃ, gilānaseyyā hesā tathāgatassa.

'Foot upon foot' means the left foot upon the right foot. 'Placing slightly over' means placing it slightly beyond. For if the ankle rubs against the ankle or the knee against the knee, constant pain arises, the mind does not become unified, and lying down becomes uncomfortable. When placed slightly beyond so they do not rub, no pain arises, the mind becomes unified, and lying down is comfortable. Therefore, he lay down thus. 'Mindful and fully aware' means endowed with the mindfulness and clear comprehension that encompasses the act of lying down. Here, 'perception of rising' is not mentioned, for this is the Tathāgata's sickbed posture.

Sattasatāti [P 1.0080] imasmiṃ sutte sabbāpi tā devatā gilānaseyyaṭṭhānaṃ āgatā. Udānaṃ udānesīti gilānaseyyaṃ āgatānaṃ domanassena bhavitabbaṃ siyā. Imāsaṃ pana tathāgatassa vedanādhivāsanaṃ disvā, “aho buddhānaṃ mahānubhāvatā! Evarūpāsu nāma vedanāsu vattamānāsu vikāramattampi natthi, sirīsayane alaṅkaritvā ṭhapitasuvaṇṇarūpakaṃ viya aniñjamānena kāyena nipanno, idānissa adhikataraṃ mukhavaṇṇo virocati, ābhāsampanno puṇṇacando viya sampati vikasitaṃ viya ca aravindaṃ assa mukhaṃ sobhati, kāyepi vaṇṇāyatanaṃ idāni susammaṭṭhakañcanaṃ viya vippasīdatī”ti udānaṃ udapādi.

'Seven hundred' means that in this discourse, all those deities had come to the place of the sickbed. Regarding 'uttered an inspired utterance': it would have been fitting for those who came to the sickbed to feel sorrow. However, for these deities, upon seeing the Tathāgata's endurance of painful feeling, this inspired utterance arose: "Oh, the great power of the Buddhas! Even while such painful feelings are occurring, there is not the slightest alteration. Like a golden statue placed on a glorious, adorned couch, he lies with an unmoving body. Now his facial complexion shines even more, like the full moon endowed with splendor, and his face is as beautiful as a newly blossomed lotus. The complexion of his body, too, is now exceptionally clear, like well-burnished gold."

Nāgo [M 1.0076] vata bhoti, ettha bhoti dhammālapanaṃ. Balavantaṭṭhena nāgo. Nāgavatāti nāgabhāvena. Sīho vatātiādīsu asantāsanaṭṭhena sīho. Byattaparicayaṭṭhena kāraṇākāraṇajānanena vā ājānīyo. Appaṭisamaṭṭhena nisabho. Gavasatajeṭṭhako hi usabho, gavasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho, gavasatasahassajeṭṭhako nisabhoti vuccati. Bhagavā pana appaṭisamaṭṭhena āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti. Tenevatthena idha “nisabho”ti vutto. Dhuravāhaṭṭhena dhorayho. Nibbisevanaṭṭhena danto.

In 'Indeed, a nāga, venerable sir,' the word 'venerable sir' is a term of address in Dhamma discourse. A 'nāga' in the sense of being powerful. 'Like a nāga' means by way of being like a great elephant. In phrases like 'Indeed, a lion,' a 'lion' in the sense of being unafraid. An 'ājānīya' in the sense of being skilled and experienced, or by knowing cause and non-cause. A 'nisabha' in the sense of being without equal. For the chief of a hundred cattle is called an 'usabha'; the chief of a thousand cattle, a 'vasabha'; and the chief of a hundred thousand cattle is called a 'nisabha'. But the Blessed One, in the sense of being without equal, claims the supreme position. For that very reason, he is called 'nisabha' here. A 'dhorayha' in the sense of carrying the burden. A 'danta' in the sense of being free from poison.

Passāti aniyamitāṇatti. Samādhinti arahattaphalasamādhiṃ. Suvimuttanti phalavimuttiyā suvimuttaṃ. Rāgānugataṃ pana cittaṃ abhinataṃ nāma hoti, dosānugataṃ apanataṃ. Tadubhayapaṭikkhepena na cābhinataṃ na cāpanatanti āha. Na ca sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagatanti na sasaṅkhārena sappayogena kilese niggahetvā vāritavataṃ, kilesānaṃ pana chinnattā vataṃ phalasamādhinā samāhitanti attho. Atikkamitabbanti viheṭhetabbaṃ ghaṭṭetabbaṃ. Adassanāti aññāṇā. Aññāṇī hi andhabālova evarūpe satthari aparajjheyyāti devadattaṃ ghaṭṭayamānā vadanti.

'See!' means an unspecified command. 'Concentration' means the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship. 'Well-liberated' means well-liberated by the liberation of the fruit. A mind that follows after lust is called 'inclined towards,' and a mind that follows after aversion is called 'inclined away from.' Rejecting both, he said, 'neither inclined towards nor inclined away from.' And 'not one whose conduct is restrained by exertion' means: his conduct is not restrained by suppressing the defilements with effort and application; rather, because the defilements have been cut off, his conduct is composed by the concentration of the fruit. This is the meaning. 'To be transgressed' means to be afflicted, to be harassed. 'Not seeing' means through ignorance. For an ignorant one, like a blind fool, would offend such a Teacher. Thus they speak, harassing Devadatta.

Pañcavedāti [P 1.0081] itihāsapañcamānaṃ vedānaṃ dhārakā. Sataṃ samanti vassasataṃ. Tapassīti tapanissitakā [V 1.0073] hutvā. Caranti carantā. Na sammāvimuttanti sacepi evarūpā brāhmaṇā vassasataṃ caranti, cittañca nesaṃ sammā vimuttaṃ na hoti. Hīnattarūpā na pāraṃ gamā teti hīnattasabhāvā te nibbānaṅgamā na honti. “Hīnattharūpā”tipi pāṭho, hīnatthajātikā parihīnatthāti attho. Taṇhādhipannāti taṇhāya ajjhotthaṭā. Vatasīlabaddhāti ajavatakukkuravatādīhi ca vatehi tādiseheva ca sīlehi baddhā. Lūkhaṃ tapanti pañcātapatāpanaṃ kaṇṭakaseyyādikaṃ tapaṃ. Idāni sā devatā sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ kathentī na mānakāmassātiādimāha. Taṃ vuttatthamevāti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

'The five Vedas' means bearers of the Vedas with the Itihāsas as the fifth. 'A hundred years' means for a hundred years. 'Practicing asceticism' means having resorted to austerity. 'They wander' means wandering. 'Not rightly liberated' means: even if such brahmins practice for a hundred years, their mind is not rightly liberated. 'Of inferior nature, they do not go to the beyond' means: they, being of an inferior nature, do not go to Nibbāna. There is also the reading 'of inferior purpose' (hīnattharūpā), which means of a low nature and deprived of the goal. 'Overcome by craving' means overwhelmed by craving. 'Bound by vows and precepts' means bound by vows such as the goat-vow and the dog-vow, and by similar precepts. 'They practice harsh austerity' means austerities such as the five-fires penance and lying on thorns. Now that devatā, speaking of the liberating nature of the Teaching, said, 'Not for one who desires pride,' and so on. That has the meaning already stated. The eighth.

9. Paṭhamapajjunnadhītusuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Sutta on Pajjunna's Daughter

39. Navame pajjunnassa dhītāti pajjunnassa nāma vassavalāhakadevarañño cātumahārājikassa dhītā. Abhivandeti bhagavā tumhākaṃ pāde [M 1.0077] vandāmi. Cakkhumatāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumantena tathāgatena. Dhammo anubuddhoti, “idaṃ mayā pubbe paresaṃ santike kevalaṃ sutaṃyeva āsī”ti vadati. Sāhaṃ dānīti, sā ahaṃ idāni. Sakkhi jānāmīti, paṭivedhavasena paccakkhameva jānāmi. Vigarahantāti, “hīnakkharapadabyañjano”ti vā “aniyyāniko”ti vā evaṃ garahantā. Roruvanti, dve roruvā – dhūmaroruvo ca jālaroruvo ca. Tattha dhūmaroruvo visuṃ hoti, jālaroruvoti pana avīcimahānirayassevetaṃ nāmaṃ. Tattha hi sattā aggimhi jalante jalante punappunaṃ ravaṃ ravanti, tasmā so “roruvo”ti vuccati. Ghoranti dāruṇaṃ. Khantiyā upasamena upetāti ruccitvā khamāpetvā gahaṇakhantiyā ca rāgādiupasamena ca upetāti. Navamaṃ.

39. In the ninth sutta, ‘Pajjunna’s daughter’ means the daughter of the cloud-deva king named Pajjunna, belonging to the Cātumahārājika devas. ‘She pays homage’: ‘Blessed One, I worship your feet.’ ‘By the one possessing vision’: by the Tathāgata, who possesses vision through the five eyes. ‘The Dhamma is fully understood’: she says, ‘This was previously only heard by me in the presence of others.’ ‘Now I’: that is, ‘I now.’ ‘I know as a witness’: I know directly through the power of penetration. ‘Those who criticize’: those who criticize thus, saying, ‘It has inferior letters, words, and phrases,’ or ‘It does not lead to deliverance.’ ‘Roruva’: there are two Roruva hells—the Smoke-Roruva and the Flame-Roruva. Among them, the Smoke-Roruva is a separate hell, but ‘Flame-Roruva’ is another name for the Avīci Great Hell. For there, while the fire is blazing intensely, beings scream again and again; therefore, it is called ‘Roruva.’ ‘Terrible’: dreadful. ‘Endowed with patience and tranquility’ means endowed with the patience of acceptance—having approved and induced forbearance—and with tranquility, which is the stilling of lust and so on. The ninth.

10. Dutiyapajjunnadhītusuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Pajjunna's Daughter

40. Dasame dhammañcāti ca saddena saṅghañca, iti tīṇi ratanāni namassamānā idhāgatāti vadati. Atthavatīti, atthavatiyo. Bahunāpi kho tanti yaṃ dhammaṃ sā abhāsi, taṃ [P 1.0082] dhammaṃ bahunāpi pariyāyena ahaṃ vibhajeyyaṃ. Tādiso dhammoti, tādiso hi ayaṃ bhagavā dhammo, taṃsaṇṭhito tappaṭibhāgo bahūhi pariyāyehi vibhajitabbayuttakoti dasseti. Lapayissāmīti, kathayissāmi. Yāvatā me manasā pariyattanti yattakaṃ mayā manasā pariyāpuṭaṃ, tassatthaṃ [V 1.0074] divasaṃ avatvā madhupaṭalaṃ pīḷentī viya muhutteneva saṃkhittena kathessāmi. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Dasamaṃ.

40. In the tenth sutta, regarding ‘and the Dhamma’: by the word ‘ca’ (and), the Sangha is also included. Thus, she says that wishing to pay homage to the three jewels, she has come here. ‘Possessed of meaning’: that is, ‘possessed of meanings.’ ‘Even with many methods’: ‘I would analyze that Dhamma which she spoke even with many methods.’ ‘Such is the Dhamma’: this shows that ‘such indeed is this Dhamma of the Blessed One—it is established in that nature, has a portion corresponding to it, and is fit to be analyzed through many methods.’ ‘I will speak’: I will relate. ‘As much as has been mastered by my mind’: Of that which I have learned with my mind, I will speak its meaning concisely in just a moment, without speaking for a whole day, like one squeezing a honeycomb. The rest is clear indeed. The tenth.

Satullapakāyikavaggo catuttho.

The Satullapakāyika Chapter, the fourth.

5. Ādittavaggo

5. The Chapter on Burning

1. Ādittasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sutta on Burning

41. Ādittavaggassa paṭhame jarāya maraṇena cāti desanāsīsametaṃ, rāgādīhi pana ekādasahi aggīhi loko ādittova. Dānenāti dānacetanāya. Dinnaṃ hoti sunīhatanti dānapuññacetanāhi dāyakasseva hoti gharasāmikassa viya nīhatabhaṇḍakaṃ, tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Corā harantīti [M 1.0078] adinne bhoge corāpi haranti rājānopi, aggipi ḍahati, ṭhapitaṭṭhānepi nassanti. Antenāti maraṇena. Sarīraṃ sapariggahanti sarīrañceva corādīnaṃ vasena avinaṭṭhabhoge ca. Saggamupetīti vessantaramahārājādayo viya sagge nibbattatīti. Paṭhamaṃ.

41. In the first sutta of the Chapter on Burning, ‘By aging and by death’ (jarāya maraṇena ca): this is the heading of the discourse. Indeed, the world is truly burning with the eleven fires beginning with lust. ‘By giving’ (dānena): by the volition of giving. ‘What is given is well-removed’ (dinnaṃ hoti sunīhataṃ): the wholesome volition of giving is for the benefit of the giver alone, just as goods removed from a burning house are for the benefit of the householder; therefore, this was said. ‘Thieves steal’ (corā haranti): thieves steal wealth that has not been given, kings also take it, fire also burns it, and it also perishes even in the place where it was put. ‘By the end’ (antena): by death. ‘The body together with its possessions’ (sarīraṃ sapariggahaṃ): refers to both the body and the wealth not destroyed by the power of thieves and so on. ‘He goes to heaven’ (saggaṃ upeti): he is reborn in heaven, like the great king Vessantara and others. The first sutta.

2. Kiṃdadasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Kiṃdada Sutta.

42. Dutiye annadoti yasmā atibalavāpi dve tīṇi bhattāni abhutvā uṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, bhutvā pana dubbalopi hutvā balasampanno hoti, tasmā “annado balado”ti āha. Vatthadoti yasmā surūpopi duccoḷo vā acoḷo vā virūpo hoti ohīḷito duddasiko, vatthacchanno devaputto viya sobhati[P 1.0083], tasmā “vatthado hoti vaṇṇado”ti āha. Yānadoti hatthiyānādīnaṃ dāyako. Tesu pana –

42. In the second sutta, ‘Giver of food’ (annado): because even a very strong person is unable to get up without having eaten two or three meals, but having eaten, even a weak person becomes possessed of strength; therefore, it is said, ‘the giver of food gives strength.’ ‘Giver of cloth’ (vatthado): because even a handsome person who is poorly clothed or unclothed looks ugly, despised, and unpleasant to see, but covered with cloth, he shines like a son of a deva; therefore, it is said, ‘the giver of cloth gives beauty.’ ‘Giver of vehicles’ (yānado): the giver of vehicles such as elephant-vehicles and so on. But among these—

“Na hatthiyānaṃ samaṇassa kappati,

Na assayānaṃ, na rathena yātuṃ;

Idañca yānaṃ samaṇassa kappati,

Upāhanā rakkhato sīlakhandha”nti.

“An elephant vehicle is not proper for a recluse,

Nor a horse vehicle, nor traveling by chariot;

But this vehicle is proper for a recluse:

Sandals, while protecting the aggregate of virtue.”

Tasmā [V 1.0075] chattupāhanakattarayaṭṭhimañcapīṭhānaṃ dāyako, yo ca maggaṃ sodheti, nisseṇiṃ karoti, setuṃ karoti, nāvaṃ paṭiyādeti, sabbopi yānadova hoti. Sukhado hotīti yānassa sukhāvahanato sukhado nāma hoti. Cakkhudoti andhakāre cakkhumantānampi rūpadassanābhāvato dīpado cakkhudo nāma hoti, anuruddhatthero viya dibbacakkhu sampadampi labhati.

Therefore, the giver of umbrellas, sandals, walking sticks, beds, and benches, and whoever clears a path, builds a ladder, constructs a bridge, or prepares a boat—all are indeed givers of vehicles. ‘He is a giver of happiness’ (sukhado hoti): because a vehicle is a conveyor of comfort, he is called a giver of happiness. ‘Giver of sight’ (cakkhudo): because in darkness even those with eyes cannot see forms, the giver of a lamp is called a giver of sight; and one also obtains the accomplishment of the divine eye, like the Elder Anuruddha.

Sabbadado hotīti sabbesaṃyeva balādīnaṃ dāyako hoti. Dve tayo gāme piṇḍāya caritvā kiñci aladdhā āgatassāpi sītalāya pokkharaṇiyā nhāyitvā patissayaṃ pavisitvā muhuttaṃ mañce nipajjitvā uṭṭhāya nisinnassa hi kāye balaṃ āharitvā pakkhittaṃ viya hoti. Bahi vicarantassa ca kāye vaṇṇāyatanaṃ vātātapehi jhāyati, patissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya muhuttaṃ nipannassa ca visabhāgasantati vūpasammati, sabhāgasantati okkamati, vaṇṇāyatanaṃ āharitvā pakkhittaṃ [M 1.0079] viya hoti. Bahi vicarantassa pāde kaṇṭako vijjhati, khāṇu paharati, sarīsapādiparissayo ceva corabhayañca uppajjati, patissayaṃ pavisitvā dvāraṃ pidhāya nipannassa sabbete parissayā na honti, dhammaṃ sajjhāyantassa dhammapītisukhaṃ, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontassa upasamasukhaṃ uppajjati. Tathā bahi vicarantassa ca sedā muccanti, akkhīni phandanti, senāsanaṃ pavisanakkhaṇe kūpe otiṇṇo viya hoti, mañcapīṭhādīni na paññāyanti. Muhuttaṃ nisinnassa pana akkhipasādo āharitvā pakkhitto viya hoti, dvārakavāṭavātapānamañcapīṭhādīni [P 1.0084] paññāyanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “so ca sabbadado hoti, yo dadāti upassaya”nti.

‘He is a giver of all’ (sabbadado hoti): he is a giver of all things such as strength. For one who has wandered for alms in two or three villages and returned having received nothing, upon bathing in a cool pond, entering his dwelling, lying down on the bed for a moment, and then rising and sitting, strength is restored to his body as if brought and placed there. And while wandering outside, the complexion of his body is scorched by wind and sun, but upon entering the dwelling, closing the door, and lying down for a moment, the discordant continuity subsides, and a concordant continuity arises—his complexion is restored as if brought and placed there. While wandering outside, a thorn pierces his foot, he strikes a stump, dangers from snakes and other creatures arise, as well as fear of thieves. But upon entering the dwelling, closing the door, and lying down, all these dangers cease. For one reciting the Dhamma, joy and happiness in the Dhamma arise; for one contemplating a meditation subject, the happiness of tranquility arises. Similarly, while wandering outside, sweat pours out, his eyes flicker, and at the moment of entering the dwelling, he feels as if he has fallen into a pit—the bed, chair, and other things are not discernible. But after sitting for a moment, the clarity of his eyes is restored as if brought and placed there, and the door-leaf, window, bed, chair, and other things become discernible. Therefore, it is said: ‘He is a giver of all, who gives a dwelling.’

Amataṃdado ca so hotīti paṇītabhojanassa pattaṃ pūrento viya amaraṇadānaṃ nāma deti. Yo dhammamanusāsatīti yo dhammaṃ anusāsati, aṭṭhakathaṃ katheti, pāḷiṃ vāceti, pucchitapañhaṃ vissajjeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhati, dhammassavanaṃ karoti, sabbopesa dhammaṃ anusāsati nāma. Sabbadānānañca idaṃ dhammadānameva agganti veditabbaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

‘And he is a giver of the deathless’ (amataṃdado ca so hoti): just as one might fill a bowl with excellent food, so does he give the gift called the gift of deathlessness. ‘Whoever instructs in the Dhamma’ (yo dhammaṃ anusāsati): whoever instructs in the Dhamma, explains the commentary, teaches the Pāli, answers a question that is asked, explains a meditation subject, or brings about the hearing of the Dhamma—all this is called instructing in the Dhamma. And it should be understood that among all gifts, this gift of the Dhamma is indeed the highest. This, too, has been said:

“Sabbadānaṃ dhammadānaṃ jināti,

Sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jināti;

Sabbaratiṃ [V 1.0076] dhammarati jināti,

Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jinātī”ti. (dha. pa. 354); Dutiyaṃ;

“The gift of the Dhamma excels all gifts;

The taste of the Dhamma excels all tastes;

The delight in the Dhamma excels all delights;

The destruction of craving conquers all suffering.” (Dhp. 354)

The second sutta.

3. Annasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Anna Sutta.

43. Tatiye abhinandantīti patthenti. Bhajatīti upagacchati, cittagahapatisīvalittherādike viya pacchato anubandhati. Tasmāti yasmā idhaloke paraloke ca annadāyakameva anugacchati, tasmā. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Tatiyaṃ.

43. In the third sutta, ‘they rejoice in’ (abhinandanti) means they long for. ‘He partakes of’ (bhajati) means he approaches; it follows him from behind, as in the case of the householder Citta, the Elder Sīvali, and so forth. ‘Therefore’ (tasmā) means: because it follows only the giver of food in this world and the next, therefore... The rest is clear. The third sutta.

4. Ekamūlasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Ekamūla Sutta.

44. Catutthe ekamūlanti avijjā taṇhāya mūlaṃ, taṇhā avijjāya. Idha pana taṇhā adhippetā. Dvīhi sassatucchedadiṭṭhīhi āvaṭṭatīti dvirāvaṭṭā. Sā ca rāgādīhi tīhi malehi timalā. Tatrāssā moho sahajātakoṭiyā [M 1.0080] malaṃ hoti, rāgadosā upanissayakoṭiyā. Pañca pana kāmaguṇā assā pattharaṇaṭṭhānā, tesu sā pattharatīti pañcapattharā. Sā ca apūraṇīyaṭṭhena samuddo. Ajjhattikabāhiresu panesā dvādasāyatanesu [P 1.0085] āvaṭṭati parivaṭṭatīti dvādasāvaṭṭā. Apatiṭṭhaṭṭhena pana pātāloti vuccatīti. Ekamūlaṃ…pe… pātālaṃ, atari isi, uttari samatikkamīti attho. Catutthaṃ.

44. In the fourth sutta, ‘single-rooted’ (ekamūlaṃ) means that ignorance is the root of craving, and craving is the root of ignorance. Here, however, craving is intended. It revolves between the two views of eternalism and annihilationism, thus it is called ‘twofold-revolving’ (dvirāvaṭṭā). It is also defiled by three stains, lust and so on, hence ‘threefold-stained’ (timalā). Therein, delusion is its stain by way of the co-nascent condition, while lust and hatred are stains by way of the decisive support condition. Moreover, the five strands of sensual pleasure are its grounds for spreading; thus it is called ‘fivefold-spreading’ (pañcapattharā). And it is the ocean in the sense of being insatiable. Furthermore, it revolves and turns around in the twelve sense bases, internal and external, hence ‘twelvefold-revolving’ (dvādasāvaṭṭā). And because it is ungrounded, it is called ‘the abyss’ (pātāla). ‘Single-rooted’... and so on up to ‘the abyss’—the sage has crossed, gone beyond, and transcended it: this is the meaning. The fourth sutta.

5. Anomasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Anoma Sutta.

45. Pañcame anomanāmanti sabbaguṇasamannāgatattā avekallanāmaṃ, paripūranāmanti attho. Nipuṇatthadassinti bhagavā saṇhasukhume khandhantarādayo atthe passatīti nipuṇatthadassī. Paññādadanti anvayapaññādhigamāya paṭipadaṃ kathanavasena paññāya dāyakaṃ. Kāmālaye asattanti pañcakāmaguṇālaye alaggaṃ. Kamamānanti bhagavā mahābodhimaṇḍeyeva ariyamaggena gato, na idāni gacchati, atītaṃ pana upādāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahesinti mahantānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ esitāraṃ pariyesitāranti. Pañcamaṃ.

45. In the fifth discourse: ‘Of peerless name’ (anomanāma) means, on account of being endowed with all virtues, having a name that is not deficient (avekallanāma), a complete name (paripūranāma); this is the meaning. ‘One who sees the subtle meaning’ (nipuṇatthadassī) means that because the Blessed One sees subtle and refined meanings, such as the distinctions among the aggregates, he is called ‘nipuṇatthadassī’. ‘Giver of wisdom’ (paññādada) means the giver of wisdom by way of explaining the path for the attainment of supramundane wisdom. ‘Unattached in the abode of sensuality’ (kāmālaye asatta) means unattached in the abode of the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Going’ (kamamāna) means that the Blessed One went by the noble path only at the seat of great awakening; he is not going now, but this is said with reference to the past. ‘Great Seeker’ (mahesi) means one who seeks for great things such as the aggregate of virtue. The fifth.

6. Accharāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Accharā Sutta

46. Chaṭṭhe [V 1.0077] accharāgaṇasaṅghuṭṭhanti ayaṃ kira devaputto satthusāsane pabbajitvā vattapaṭipattiṃ pūrayamāno pañcavassakāle pavāretvā dvemātikaṃ paguṇaṃ katvā kammākammaṃ uggahetvā cittarucitaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhitvā sallahukavuttiko araññaṃ pavisitvā yo bhagavatā majjhimayāmo sayanassa koṭṭhāsoti anuññāto. Tasmimpi sampatte “pamādassa bhāyāmī”ti mañcakaṃ ukkhipitvā rattiñca divā ca nirāhāro kammaṭṭhānameva manasākāsi.

46. In the sixth sutta, as for the phrase 'resounding with a host of nymphs': It is heard that this devaputta, having gone forth in the Teacher's Dispensation and fulfilling the practice of duties, after the period of five vassas, having studied orally, having learned the distinction between what is and is not a formal act, having learned a meditation subject that was pleasing to his mind, and having a light livelihood, entered the forest. That middle watch which was permitted by the Blessed One as the portion for sleeping—even when that arrived, thinking, “I fear heedlessness,” he lifted up his small couch and, being without food, applied his mind only to the meditation subject both by night and by day.

Athassa abbhantare satthakavātā uppajjitvā jīvitaṃ pariyādiyiṃsu. So dhurasmiṃyeva kālamakāsi. Yo hi koci bhikkhu caṅkame caṅkamamāno vā ālambanatthambhaṃ nissāya ṭhito vā caṅkamakoṭiyaṃ cīvaraṃ [P 1.0086] sīse ṭhapetvā nisinno vā nipanno vā parisamajjhe alaṅkatadhammāsane dhammaṃ desento vā kālaṃ karoti, sabbo so dhurasmiṃ kālaṃ [M 1.0081] karoti nāma. Iti ayaṃ caṅkamane kālaṃ katvā upanissayamandatāya āsavakkhayaṃ appatto tāvatiṃsabhavane mahāvimānadvāre niddāyitvā pabujjhanto viya paṭisandhiṃ aggahesi. Tāvadevassa suvaṇṇatoraṇaṃ viya tigāvuto attabhāvo nibbatti.

Then, cutting winds arose within him and took his life. He passed away right in the midst of the struggle. Indeed, any bhikkhu who passes away while walking on a walking path, or standing leaning on a support post, or sitting at the end of the walking path with his robe placed on his head, or lying down, or teaching the Dhamma in the midst of an assembly on a decorated Dhamma-seat—all such are said to pass away in the midst of the struggle. Thus this monk, having passed away on the walking path, not having reached the destruction of the cankers due to the weakness of the supporting condition for Arahantship, took rebirth-linking in the Tāvatiṃsa celestial realm at the gate of a great celestial mansion, as if awakening from sleep. At that very moment, a body of three gāvutas, like a golden archway, came into being for him.

Antovimāne sahassamattā accharā taṃ disvā, “vimānasāmiko devaputto āgato, ramayissāma na”nti tūriyāni gahetvā parivārayiṃsu. Devaputto na tāva cutabhāvaṃ jānāti, pabbajitasaññīyeva accharā oloketvā vihāracārikaṃ āgataṃ mātugāmaṃ disvā lajjī. Paṃsukūliko viya upari ṭhitaṃ ghanadukūlaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karonto aṃsakūṭaṃ paṭicchādetvā indriyāni okkhipitvā adhomukho aṭṭhāsi. Tassa kāyavikāreneva tā devatā “samaṇadevaputto aya”nti ñatvā evamāhaṃsu – “ayya, devaputta, devaloko nāmāyaṃ, na samaṇadhammassa karaṇokāso, sampattiṃ anubhavanokāso”ti. So tatheva aṭṭhāsi. Devatā “na tāvāyaṃ sallakkhetī”ti tūriyāni paggaṇhiṃsu. So tathāpi anolokentova aṭṭhāsi.

Inside the mansion, about a thousand nymphs saw him and, thinking, “The devaputta, the lord of the mansion, has arrived; we shall delight him,” they took musical instruments and surrounded him. The devaputta did not yet realize he had passed away; having only the perception of being a renunciant, he was ashamed upon seeing the nymphs, as if he had seen women who had come to tour the monasteries. Like a rag-robed bhikkhu, he arranged the heavy fine cloth that was on him over one shoulder, covering his shoulder-tip, lowered his gaze, and stood with downcast face. Just by his bodily posture, those deities, recognizing, “This is a renunciant devaputta,” said thus: “Venerable devaputta, this is the world of the devas, not a place for practicing the renunciant's life, but a place for experiencing prosperity.” He remained standing thus. The deities, thinking, “He has not yet taken note,” raised their instruments. Still, he stood without looking.

Athassa sabbakāyikaṃ ādāsaṃ purato ṭhapayiṃsu. So chāyaṃ disvā cutabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “na mayā imaṃ ṭhānaṃ patthetvā samaṇadhammo kato, uttamatthaṃ arahattaṃ patthetvā kato”ti sampattiyā vippaṭisārī ahosi, “suvaṇṇapaṭaṃ paṭilabhissāmī”ti takkayitvā yuddhaṭṭhānaṃ otiṇṇamallo [V 1.0078] mūlakamuṭṭhiṃ labhitvā viya. So – “ayaṃ saggasampatti nāma sulabhā, buddhānaṃ pātubhāvo dullabho”ti cintetvā vimānaṃ apavisitvāva asambhinneneva sīlena accharāsaṅghaparivuto dasabalassa santikaṃ āgamma abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

Then they placed a full-length mirror before him. Seeing his reflection and realizing his passing away, he thought, “I did not practice the renunciant's life aspiring to this state; I practiced it aspiring to the highest goal, arahantship.” He was filled with remorse over his attainment, as if a champion who had entered the battlefield, thinking, “I will obtain a golden plate,” had gained only a handful of raw rice. Reflecting, “This heavenly bliss is easily obtained, but the appearance of Buddhas is rare,” he did not even enter the celestial mansion. Surrounded by a host of nymphs, with his virtue unbroken, he approached the Ten-Powered One, paid homage, stood to one side, and spoke this verse:

Tattha accharāgaṇasaṅghuṭṭhanti accharāgaṇena gītavāditasaddehi saṅghositaṃ. Pisācagaṇasevitanti tameva accharāgaṇaṃ pisācagaṇaṃ katvā vadati. Vananti nandanavanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Ayañhi niyāmacittatāya attano garubhāvena devagaṇaṃ “devagaṇo”ti vattuṃ na roceti. “Pisācagaṇo”ti vadati. Nandanavanañca “nandana”nti avatvā “mohana”nti vadati[M 1.0082]. Kathaṃ yātrā bhavissatīti [P 1.0087] kathaṃ niggamanaṃ bhavissati, kathaṃ atikkamo bhavissati, arahattassa me padaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ vipassanaṃ ācikkhatha bhagavāti vadati.

Herein, ‘resounding with a host of nymphs’ means resounded with the sounds of singing and music from the host of nymphs. ‘Frequented by a host of demons’ means he speaks of that very host of nymphs, referring to them as a host of demons. By ‘grove,’ he speaks with reference to the Nandana Grove. Indeed, because his mind is inclined towards the fixed course and because of his own gravity, he does not like to call the host of devas a ‘host of devas.’ He says, ‘a host of demons.’ And not wishing to say ‘Nandana’ for the Nandana Grove, he says ‘Mohana’ (delusion). ‘How will the journey be?’ means: ‘How will there be a departure? How will there be a transcending? O Blessed One, please declare to me the insight that is the proximate cause of Arahantship,’ thus he speaks.

Atha bhagavā “atisallikhateva ayaṃ devaputto, kiṃ nu kho ida”nti? Āvajjento attano sāsane pabbajitabhāvaṃ ñatvā – “ayaṃ accāraddhavīriyatāya kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatto, ajjāpissa caṅkamanasmiṃyeva attabhāvo asambhinnena sīlena āgato”ti cintesi. Buddhā ca akatābhinivesassa ādikammikassa akataparikammassa antevāsino cittakāro bhittiparikammaṃ viya – “sīlaṃ tāva sodhehi, samādhiṃ bhāvehi, kammassakatapaññaṃ ujuṃ karohī”ti paṭhamaṃ pubbabhāgappaṭipadaṃ ācikkhanti, kārakassa pana yuttapayuttassa arahattamaggapadaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ saṇhasukhumaṃ suññatāvipassanaṃyeva ācikkhanti, ayañca devaputto kārako abhinnasīlo, eko maggo assa anāgatoti suññatāvipassanaṃ ācikkhanto ujuko nāmātiādimāha.

Then the Blessed One reflected, “This devaputta is exceedingly austere. What can this be?” Understanding that he had gone forth in His dispensation, He thought: “Due to excessive exertion of energy, this one passed away and was reborn in the deva world; even today his physical body is still on the walking path, and he has come with unbroken virtue.” And Buddhas, to a disciple who is a beginner, who has not made a firm resolve, who has not done the preliminary work—like a painter who instructs on the preparation of a wall—first teach the preliminary part of the practice, saying: “First, purify your virtue, develop concentration, make straight the wisdom of ownership of kamma.” But to one who is a practitioner, yoked and striving, they teach only the subtle and refined insight into emptiness, which is the proximate cause for the path to Arahantship. And this devaputta is a practitioner with unbroken virtue; for him, one path remains. Thus, teaching him insight into emptiness, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning, “Straight is it named.”

Tattha ujukoti kāyavaṅkādīnaṃ abhāvato aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo ujuko nāma. Abhayā nāma sā disāti nibbānaṃ sandhāyāha. Tasmiṃ hi kiñci bhayaṃ natthi, taṃ vā pattassa bhayaṃ natthīti “abhayā nāma sā disā”ti vuttaṃ. Ratho akūjanoti aṭṭhaṅgiko maggova adhippeto. Yathā hi pākatikaratho akkhe vā anabbhañjite atirekesu vā manussesu abhiruḷhesu kūjati viravati, na evaṃ ariyamaggo. So hi ekappahārena caturāsītiyāpi pāṇasahassesu abhiruhantesu [V 1.0079] na kūjati na viravati. Tasmā “akūjano”ti vutto. Dhammacakkehi saṃyutoti kāyikacetasikavīriyasaṅkhātehi dhammacakkehi saṃyutto.

Herein, ‘ujuko’ (straight) means the Eightfold Path is called straight due to the absence of bodily crookedness and so forth. ‘Abhayā nāma sā disā’ (That direction is called fearless) was said in reference to Nibbāna. For in that Nibbāna, there is no fear whatsoever; or, for one who has reached it, there is no fear. Therefore, it is said, “That direction is called fearless.” By ‘Ratho akūjano’ (a non-creaking chariot), the Eightfold Path itself is intended. For just as an ordinary chariot creaks and rattles when its axle is not greased or when it is overloaded with people, the Noble Path is not so. Indeed, even when eighty-four thousand beings mount it at once, it does not creak, it does not rattle. Therefore, it is called ‘akūjano’ (non-creaking). ‘Dhammacakkehi saṃyutto’ (yoked with the wheels of Dhamma) means yoked with the wheels of Dhamma, which are designated as physical and mental effort.

Hirīti ettha hiriggahaṇena ottappampi gahitameva hoti. Tassa apālamboti yathā bāhirakarathassa rathe ṭhitānaṃ yodhānaṃ apatanatthāya dārumayaṃ apālambanaṃ hoti, evaṃ imassa maggarathassa ajjhattabahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ hirottappaṃ apālambanaṃ. Satyassa [P 1.0088] parivāraṇanti rathassa sīhacammādiparivāro viya imassāpi maggarathassa sampayuttā sati parivāraṇaṃ. Dhammanti lokuttaramaggaṃ[M 1.0083]. Sammādiṭṭhipurejavanti vipassanāsammādiṭṭhipurejavā assa pubbayāyikāti sammādiṭṭhipurejavo, taṃ sammādiṭṭhipurejavaṃ. Yathā hi paṭhamataraṃ rājapurisehi kāṇakuṇiādīnaṃnīharaṇena magge sodhite pacchā rājā nikkhamati, evamevaṃ vipassanā sammādiṭṭhiyā aniccādivasena khandhādīsu sodhitesu pacchā bhūmiladdhavaṭṭaṃ parijānamānā maggasammādiṭṭhi uppajjati. Tena vuttaṃ “dhammāhaṃ sārathiṃ brūmi, sammādiṭṭhipurejava”nti.

Herein, by the taking of ‘hirī’ (moral shame), ‘ottappa’ (moral dread) is also included. Its support is like the wooden railing on an external chariot, which prevents the warriors standing on it from falling. Similarly, for this chariot of the path, the support is moral shame and dread, which arise from internal and external causes. The surrounding of mindfulness is like the surrounding of a chariot with lion’s skin and so forth. For this chariot of the path, associated mindfulness is its surrounding. ‘Dhammaṃ’ refers to the supramundane path. ‘Sammādiṭṭhipurejavaṃ’ (having right view as its forerunner) means that insight-right-view is its forerunner; thus, it is called ‘sammādiṭṭhipurejavo’. For just as a king proceeds only after the path has first been cleared by royal attendants through the removal of the blind, the crooked-limbed, and so on, in the very same way, when the aggregates and so forth have been cleansed by insight-right-view by way of impermanence, etc., afterwards path-right-view arises, fully comprehending the round of existence that has become its ground. Therefore, it was said: “I say Dhamma is the charioteer, with right view as its forerunner.”

Iti bhagavā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā avasāne cattāri saccāni dīpesi. Desanāpariyosāne devaputto sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Yathā hi rañño bhojanakāle attano mukhappamāṇe kabaḷe ukkhitte aṅke nisinno putto attano mukhappamāṇeneva tato kabaḷaṃ karoti, evamevaṃ bhagavati arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ desentepi sattā attano upanissayānurūpena sotāpattiphalādīni pāpuṇanti. Ayampi devaputto sotāpattiphalaṃ patvā bhagavantaṃ gandhādīhi pūjetvā pakkāmīti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Thus, the Blessed One, having completed the teaching, at the end revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse, the devaputta was established in the fruit of stream-entry. For just as when a king is eating, from a morsel the size of his own mouth that has been lifted up, a child sitting on his lap takes a portion only the size of his own mouth, in the same way, even while the Blessed One teaches with the summit of Arahantship, beings attain the fruits of stream-entry and so on, according to their own supporting conditions. This devaputta too, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, honored the Blessed One with perfumes and other offerings, and departed. The sixth.

7. Vanaropasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Vanaropa Sutta

47. Sattame dhammaṭṭhā sīlasampannāti ke dhammaṭṭhā, ke sīlasampannāti pucchati. Bhagavā imaṃ pañhaṃ thāvaravatthunā dīpento ārāmaropātiādimāha. Tattha ārāmaropāti pupphārāmaphalārāmaropakā. Vanaropāti sayaṃjāte aropimavane sīmaṃ parikkhipitvā cetiyabodhicaṅkamanamaṇḍapakuṭileṇarattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānānaṃ kārakā chāyūpage rukkhe ropetvā dadamānāpi vanaropāyeva nāma. Setukārakāti visame setuṃ karonti, udake nāvaṃ paṭiyādenti[V 1.0080]. Papanti pānīyadānasālaṃ. Udapānanti yaṃkiñci pokkharaṇītaḷākādiṃ. Upassayanti vāsāgāraṃ. “Upāsaya”ntipi pāṭho.

47. In the seventh sutta, regarding 'dhammaṭṭhā sīlasampannā', one asks: 'Who are established in Dhamma? Who are accomplished in virtue?' The Blessed One, illuminating this question with a steadfast basis, spoke the verse beginning with 'ārāmaropā'. Therein, 'ārāmaropā' refers to those who plant flower gardens and fruit orchards. 'Vanaropā' means those who, having enclosed a boundary in a naturally grown, unplanted forest, are makers of cetiyas, Bodhi trees, walkways, pavilions, huts, caves, and places for the night and day; even those who, having planted shade-giving trees, give them, are indeed called 'vanaropā'. 'Setukārakā' means they build bridges in uneven places and prepare boats on the water. 'Papā' means a hall for giving drinking water. 'Udapāna' means any kind of pond, reservoir, and so on. 'Upassaya' means a dwelling place. There is also a reading, 'upāsaya'.

Sadā puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatīti na akusalavitakkaṃ [P 1.0089] vā vitakkentassa niddāyantassa vā pavaḍḍhati. Yadā yadā pana anussarati, tadā tadā tassa vaḍḍhati. Imamatthaṃ sandhāya “sadā puññaṃ pavaḍḍhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Dhammaṭṭhā sīlasampannāti tasmiṃ dhamme ṭhitattā tenapi sīlena sampannattā dhammaṭṭhā sīlasampannā. Atha vā [M 1.0084] evarūpāni puññāni karontānaṃ dasa kusalā dhammā pūrenti, tesu ṭhitattā dhammaṭṭhā. Teneva ca sīlena sampannattā sīlasampannāti. Sattamaṃ.

Regarding 'Merit always increases': it does not increase for one who is thinking an unwholesome thought or for one who is sleeping. But whenever one recollects, then it increases for them. It is with reference to this meaning that 'Merit always increases' was said. Regarding 'Established in Dhamma, accomplished in virtue': because they are established in that Dhamma and because they are also accomplished in that virtue, they are called 'established in Dhamma, accomplished in virtue'. Alternatively, for those who perform such meritorious deeds, the ten wholesome states are fulfilled. Because they are established in those, they are 'established in Dhamma'. And because they are accomplished in that very virtue, they are 'accomplished in virtue'. The seventh.

8. Jetavanasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Jetavana Sutta

48. Aṭṭhame idaṃ hi taṃ jetavananti anāthapiṇḍiko devaputto jetavanassa ceva buddhādīnañca vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ āgato evamāha. Isisaṅghanisevitanti bhikkhusaṅghanisevitaṃ.

48. In the eighth sutta, regarding 'This is indeed that Jetavana,' the devaputta Anāthapiṇḍika, having come to praise the virtues of the Jetavana and of the Buddha and others, spoke thus. 'Frequented by the community of sages' means 'frequented by the community of monks.'

Evaṃ paṭhamagāthāya jetavanassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā idāni ariyamaggassa kathento kammaṃ vijjātiādimāha. Tattha kammanti maggacetanā. Vijjāti maggapaññā. Dhammoti samādhipakkhikā dhammā. Sīlaṃ jīvitamuttamanti sīle patiṭṭhitassa jīvitaṃ uttamanti dasseti. Atha vā vijjāti diṭṭhisaṅkappā. Dhammoti vāyāmasatisamādhayo. Sīlanti vācākammantājīvā. Jīvitamuttamanti etasmiṃ sīle ṭhitassa jīvitaṃ nāma uttamaṃ. Etena maccā sujjhantīti etena aṭṭhaṅgikamaggena sattā visujjhanti.

Having thus described the excellence of Jetavana in the first verse, now, wishing to speak of the excellence of the Noble Path, he speaks of 'action, knowledge,' and so forth. Therein, 'action' means path-volition. 'Knowledge' means path-wisdom. 'Dhamma' refers to the qualities pertaining to concentration. The phrase 'Virtue is the supreme life' shows that for one established in virtue, life is supreme. Alternatively, 'knowledge' means right view and right thought. 'Dhamma' refers to right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. 'Virtue' means right speech, right action, and right livelihood. The phrase 'the supreme life' means that for one established in this virtue, life is indeed supreme. The phrase 'By this, mortals are purified' means that by this Eightfold Path, beings are purified.

Tasmāti yasmā maggena sujjhanti, na gottadhanehi, tasmā. Yoniso vicine dhammanti upāyena samādhipakkhiyadhammaṃ vicineyya. Evaṃ tattha visujjhatīti evaṃ tasmiṃ ariyamagge visujjhati. Atha vā yoniso vicine dhammanti upāyena pañcakkhandhadhammaṃ vicineyya. Evaṃ tattha visujjhatīti evaṃ tesu catūsu saccesu visujjhati.

The word 'Therefore' is used because they are purified by the path, not by lineage or wealth. The phrase 'One should wisely investigate the Dhamma' means one should investigate, by proper means, the Dhamma pertaining to concentration. The phrase 'Thus one is purified therein' means thus one is purified in that Noble Path. Alternatively, the phrase 'one should wisely investigate the Dhamma' means one should investigate, by proper means, the Dhamma of the five aggregates. The phrase 'Thus one is purified therein' means thus one is purified in those four truths.

Idāni sāriputtattherassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento sāriputtovātiādimāha. Tattha sāriputtovāti avadhāraṇavacanaṃ, etehi paññādīhi sāriputtova seyyoti vadati. Upasamenāti kilesaupasamena[V 1.0081]. Pāraṃ gatoti nibbānaṃ gato. Yo koci nibbānaṃ patto bhikkhu, so etāvaparamo siyā, na therena uttaritaro nāma atthīti vadati. Sesaṃ uttānamevāti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Now, wishing to speak in praise of the Elder Sāriputta, he says, 'Sāriputta alone,' and so forth. Therein, 'Sāriputtova' (Sāriputta alone) is a word of determination, stating that with these qualities beginning with wisdom, Sāriputta alone is best. 'By peace' means by the calming of the defilements. 'Gone to the far shore' means gone to Nibbāna. Whatever monk has reached Nibbāna, he could only be of this measure at most; there is no one, it is said, who is superior to the Elder. The rest is self-evident. The eighth.

9. Maccharisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Macchari Sutta

49. Navame [P 1.0090] maccharinoti maccherena samannāgatā. Ekacco hi attano vasanaṭṭhāne bhikkhuṃ hatthaṃ pasāretvāpi na vandati, aññattha gato vihāraṃ [M 1.0085] pavisitvā sakkaccaṃ vanditvā madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ karoti – “bhante, amhākaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ nāgacchatha, sampanno padeso, paṭibalā mayaṃ ayyānaṃ yāgubhattādīhi upaṭṭhānaṃ kātu”nti. Bhikkhū “saddho ayaṃ upāsako”ti yāgubhattādīhi saṅgaṇhanti. Atheko thero tassa gāmaṃ gantvā piṇḍāya carati. So taṃ disvā aññena vā gacchati, gharaṃ vā pavisati. Sacepi sammukhībhāvaṃ āgacchati, hatthena vanditvā – “ayyassa bhikkhaṃ detha, ahaṃ ekena kammena gacchāmī”ti pakkamati. Thero sakalagāmaṃ caritvā tucchapattova nikkhamati. Idaṃ tāva mudumacchariyaṃ nāma, yena samannāgato adāyakopi dāyako viya paññāyati. Idha pana thaddhamacchariyaṃ adhippetaṃ, yena samannāgato bhikkhūsu piṇḍāya paviṭṭhesu, “therā ṭhitā”ti vutte, “kiṃ mayhaṃ pādā rujjantī”tiādīni vatvā silāthambho viya khāṇuko viya ca thaddho hutvā tiṭṭhati, sāmīcimpi na karoti. Kadariyāti idaṃ maccharinoti padasseva vevacanaṃ. Mudukampi hi macchariyaṃ “macchariya”nteva vuccati, thaddhaṃ pana kadariyaṃ nāma. Paribhāsakāti bhikkhū gharadvāre ṭhite disvā, “kiṃ tumhe kasitvā āgatā, vapitvā, lāyitvā? Mayaṃ attanopi na labhāma, kuto tumhākaṃ, sīghaṃ nikkhamathā”tiādīhi saṃtajjakā. Antarāyakarāti [P 1.0091] dāyakassa saggantarāyo, paṭiggāhakānaṃ lābhantarāyo, attano upaghātoti imesaṃ antarāyānaṃ kārakā.

49. In the ninth, 'maccharino' means those endowed with stinginess. For instance, a certain person in their own dwelling place does not pay homage to a monk even by extending a hand. But when they go elsewhere and enter a monastery, they respectfully pay homage and offer a sweet welcome, saying, 'Venerable sirs, you do not come to our dwelling place; the area is prosperous, and we are able to serve the venerable ones with rice-gruel, meals, and so on.' The monks, thinking, 'This lay follower is faithful,' expect to be supported by him with rice-gruel, meals, and so on. Then, a certain elder goes to that person's village for alms. Upon seeing him, that person either goes another way or enters a house. Even if they happen to meet, they pay respects with their hand and say, 'Give alms to the venerable one. I have some business to attend to,' and then leave. The elder walks through the entire village and comes out with an empty bowl. This, in the first place, is called 'mild stinginess,' by which even a non-giver appears as a giver. Here, however, 'harsh stinginess' is intended. Endowed with this, when monks have entered for alms, upon being told, 'The elders are standing,' one says, 'What, do my feet ache?' and the like, and stands stiff like a stone pillar or a stump, not even performing a respectful gesture. The word 'kadariyā' is a synonym for the word 'maccharino.' For even mild stinginess is called 'stinginess,' but harsh stinginess is called 'kadariya' (miserliness). 'Paribhāsakā' (abusive ones) are those who, seeing monks standing at the door, threaten them with words like, 'What, have you come here after plowing, sowing, or reaping? We do not even get enough for ourselves, so how could we give to you? Get out quickly!' 'Antarāyakarā' (creators of obstacles) are those who create an obstacle to heaven for the donor, an obstacle to gain for the recipients, and harm to oneself—they are the makers of these obstacles.

Samparāyoti paraloko. Ratīti pañcakāmaguṇarati. Khiḍḍāti kāyikakhiḍḍādikā tividhā khiḍḍā. Diṭṭhe dhammesa vipākoti tasmiṃ nibbattabhavane diṭṭhe dhamme esa vipāko. Samparāye ca duggatīti “yamalokaṃ upapajjare”ti vutte samparāye ca duggati.

'Samparāya' means the next world. 'Rati' means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Khiḍḍā' means the three kinds of play, such as bodily play. 'Diṭṭhe dhamme...vipāko' means this is the result in the visible here-and-now, in the state of existence where one is reborn. 'Samparāye ca duggati' means, as was said, 'They are reborn in the realm of Yama,' thus a bad destination in the future state.

Vadaññūti bhikkhū gharadvāre ṭhitā kiñcāpi tuṇhīva honti, atthato pana – “bhikkhaṃ dethā”ti vadanti nāma. Tatra ye “mayaṃ pacāma, ime pana na pacanti, pacamāne patvā alabhantā [V 1.0082] kuhiṃ labhissantī”ti? Deyyadhammaṃ saṃvibhajanti, te vadaññū nāma. Pakāsantīti vimānappabhāya jotanti. Parasambhatesūti parehi sampiṇḍitesu. Samparāye ca suggatīti, “ete saggā”ti [M 1.0086] evaṃ vuttasamparāye sugati. Ubhinnampi vā etesaṃ tato cavitvā puna samparāyepi duggatisugatiyeva hotīti. Navamaṃ.

'Vadaññū' means that although the monks standing at the house door are indeed silent, in essence, they are said to be speaking, 'Give alms.' Therein, those who think, 'We cook, but these do not cook. Having come to those who are cooking, if they do not receive, where will they receive?' and share a gift to be given, they are called 'vadaññū' (those who understand the request). 'Pakāsanti' means they shine with the splendor of celestial mansions. 'Parasambhatesu' means on what is gathered together by others. 'Samparāye ca suggati' means: in the future state thus described as 'these are heavens,' there is a good destination. Or, for both of these, having passed away from there, again in a future state, there is only a bad or a good destination. The ninth.

10. Ghaṭīkārasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Ghaṭīkāra Sutta

50. Dasame upapannāseti nibbattivasena upagatā. Vimuttāti avihābrahmalokasmiṃ upapattisamanantarameva arahattaphalavimuttiyā vimuttā. Mānusaṃ dehanti idha pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni eva vuttāni. Dibbayoganti pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni. Upaccagunti atikkamiṃsu. Upakotiādīni tesaṃ therānaṃ nāmāni. Kusalī bhāsasī tesanti, “kusala”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ imassa atthīti kusalī, tesaṃ therānaṃ tvaṃ kusalaṃ anavajjaṃ bhāsasi, thomesi pasaṃsasi[P 1.0092], paṇḍitosi devaputtāti vadati. Taṃ te dhammaṃ idhaññāyāti te therā taṃ dhammaṃ idha tumhākaṃ sāsane jānitvā. Gambhīranti gambhīratthaṃ. Brahmacārī nirāmisoti nirāmisabrahmacārī nāma anāgāmī, anāgāmī ahosinti attho. Ahuvāti ahosi. Sagāmeyyoti ekagāmavāsī. Pariyosānagāthā saṅgītikārehi ṭhapitāti. Dasamaṃ.

50. In the tenth: 'Upapannāse' means they have arrived by way of rebirth. 'Vimuttā' means they were liberated by the liberation of the fruit of arahantship immediately upon their rebirth in the Avihā Brahma world. 'Mānusaṃ dehaṃ' refers here only to the five lower fetters. 'Dibbayogaṃ' refers to the five higher fetters. 'Upaccaguṃ' means they transcended. 'Upako,' and so on, are the names of those elders. 'Kusalī bhāsasi tesaṃ' means: because this word 'kusala' (skillful) applies to him, he is 'kusalī' (a skillful one); you, O devaputta, speak of the skillful, blameless state of those elders, you praise and commend them; you are wise, he says. 'Taṃ te dhammaṃ idha ñāya' means: those elders, having known that Dhamma here in your dispensation. 'Gambhīraṃ' means profound in meaning. 'Brahmacārī nirāmiso' means a non-returner, one who practices the holy life without material concerns; the meaning is 'I became a non-returner.' 'Ahuva' means he became. 'Sagāmeyyo' means a resident of the same village. The concluding verse was placed by the compilers of the canon. The tenth.

Ādittavaggo pañcamo.

The Āditta Chapter, the fifth.

6. Jarāvaggo

6. The Chapter on Aging

1. Jarāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Jarā Sutta

51. Jarāvaggassa paṭhame sādhūti laddhakaṃ bhaddakaṃ. Sīlaṃ yāva jarāti iminā idaṃ dasseti – yathā muttāmaṇirattavatthādīni ābharaṇāni taruṇakāleyeva sobhanti, jarājiṇṇakāle tāni dhārento “ayaṃ ajjāpi bālabhāvaṃ pattheti, ummattako maññe”ti vattabbataṃ āpajjati[V 1.0083], na evaṃ sīlaṃ. Sīlañhi niccakālaṃ sobhati. Bālakālepi hi sīlaṃ rakkhantaṃ “kiṃ imassa sīlenā”ti? Vattāro natthi. Majjhimakālepi mahallakakālepīti.

51. In the first sutta of the Jarā Chapter, 'sādhu' means good, excellent. By the phrase 'Virtue is good even unto old age,' this is shown: just as ornaments such as pearls, gems, and fine garments are beautiful only in youth—for when wearing them in old age one becomes liable to be called, 'This person still desires youth; I think they are mad'—it is not so with virtue. Virtue, indeed, is always beautiful. For even in youth, regarding one who protects virtue, there is no one who would say, 'What is the use of virtue to this person?' The same applies in middle age and also in old age.

Saddhā [M 1.0087] sādhu patiṭṭhitāti hatthāḷavakacittagahapatiādīnaṃ viya maggena āgatā patiṭṭhitasaddhā nāma sādhu. Paññā narānaṃ ratananti ettha cittīkataṭṭhādīhi ratanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'Faith well-established is good' means that faith which has arisen through the path, like that of Hatthāḷavaka, Citta the householder, and others, is called established faith, and it is good. In the phrase 'Wisdom is a jewel for humans,' a jewel is to be understood by way of its being esteemed, and so forth. For this was said:

“Yadi cittīkatanti ratanaṃ, nanu bhagavā cittīkato purisasīho, ye ca loke cittīkatā, tesaṃ cittīkato bhagavā. Yadi ratikaranti ratanaṃ, nanu bhagavā ratikaro purisasīho, tassa vacanena carantā jhānaratisukhena abhiramanti. Yadi atulyanti ratanaṃ, nanu bhagavā atulo purisasīho. Na hi [P 1.0093] sakkā tuletuṃ guṇehi guṇapāramiṃ gato. Yadi dullabhanti ratanaṃ, nanu bhagavā dullabho purisasīho. Yadi anomasattaparibhoganti ratanaṃ, nanu bhagavā anomo sīlena samādhinā paññāya vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanenā”ti.

‘If “esteemed” is a jewel, then is not the Blessed One the esteemed lion among men? And among those esteemed in the world, the Blessed One is esteemed. If “source of joy” is a jewel, then is not the Blessed One the source of joy, the lion among men? Those who live according to his words revel in the joy and happiness of meditative absorption. If “unequalled” is a jewel, then is not the Blessed One the unequalled lion among men? For it is not possible to compare him by his virtues, as he has reached the perfection of qualities. If “hard to find” is a jewel, then is not the Blessed One the hard-to-find lion among men? If “for the use of a superior being” is a jewel, then is not the Blessed One superior in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation?’

Idha pana dullabhapātubhāvaṭṭhena paññā “ratana”nti vuttaṃ. Puññanti puññacetanā, sā hi arūpattā pariharituṃ na sakkāti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Here, however, wisdom is called a ‘jewel’ because of the difficulty of its arising. ‘Merit’ refers to meritorious volition; since it is formless, it cannot be carried. The first.

2. Ajarasāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ajarasā Sutta

52. Dutiye ajarasāti ajīraṇena, avipattiyāti attho. Sīlañhi avipannameva sādhu hoti, vipannasīlaṃ ācariyupajjhāyādayopi na saṅgaṇhanti, gatagataṭṭhāne niddhamitabbova hotīti. Dutiyaṃ.

52. In the second sutta, ajarasā means 'by not decaying,' that is, 'by not being destroyed.' For virtue is indeed good only when unimpaired. One with impaired virtue is not supported even by teachers and preceptors; wherever they go, they are to be expelled. The second.

3. Mittasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Mitta Sutta

53. Tatiye satthoti saddhiṃcaro, jaṅghasattho vā sakaṭasattho vā. Mittanti roge uppanne pāṭaṅkiyā vā aññena vā yānena haritvā khemantasampāpanena mittaṃ. Sake ghareti attano gehe[V 1.0084]. Tathārūpe roge jāte puttabhariyādayo jigucchanti, mātā pana asucimpi candanaṃ viya maññati. Tasmā sā sake ghare mittaṃ. Sahāyo atthajātassāti uppannakiccassa yo taṃ kiccaṃ vahati nittharati, so kiccesu saha ayanabhāvena sahāyo mittaṃ, surāpānādisahāyā pana na mittā. Samparāyikanti samparāyahitaṃ. Tatiyaṃ.

53. In the third sutta, 'sattha' means a fellow traveler, either a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan. 'Mitta' means a friend by bringing one to a place of safety, having carried one on a stretcher or by some other vehicle when illness arises. 'Sake ghare' means in one's own house. When such an illness arises, sons, wives, and others are disgusted, but a mother regards even impurity as sandalwood. Therefore, she is a friend in one's own home. 'Sahāyo atthajātassa' means one who undertakes and completes the task for one for whom a task has arisen; such a one is a companion in tasks, a friend by way of being together. However, companions in drinking liquor and so on are not friends. 'Samparāyikaṃ' means beneficial for the next world. The third.

4. Vatthusuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vatthu Sutta

54. Catutthe [M 1.0088] puttā vatthūti mahallakakāle paṭijagganaṭṭhena puttā patiṭṭhā. Paramoti aññesaṃ akathetabbassapi guyhassa kathetabbayuttatāya bhariyā paramo sakhā nāma. Catutthaṃ.

54. In the fourth sutta, 'puttā vatthu' means that in old age, sons are a support by way of tending to one. 'Paramo' means that by being fit to be told even of a secret that should not be told to others, a wife is called the supreme friend. The fourth.

5-7. Paṭhamajanasuttādivaṇṇanā

5-7. Commentary on the First Jana Sutta and others

55. Pañcame vidhāvatīti parasamuddādigamanavasena ito cito ca vidhāvati. Pañcamaṃ.

55. In the fifth sutta, 'vidhāvati' means it runs here and there by way of going to the other side of the ocean and so on. The fifth.

56. Chaṭṭhe [P 1.0094] dukkhāti vaṭṭadukkhato. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

56. In the sixth sutta, 'dukkhā' means from the suffering of the round of existence. The sixth.

57. Sattame parāyaṇanti nipphatti avassayo. Sattamaṃ.

57. In the seventh sutta, 'parāyaṇaṃ' means fulfillment, a reliance. The seventh.

8. Uppathasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Uppatha Sutta

58. Aṭṭhame rāgo uppathoti sugatiñca nibbānañca gacchantassa amaggo. Rattindivakkhayoti rattidivehi, rattidivesu vā khīyati. Itthī malanti sesaṃ bāhiramalaṃ bhasmakhārādīhi dhovitvā sakkā sodhetuṃ, mātugāmamalena duṭṭho pana na sakkā suddho nāma kātunti itthī “mala”nti vuttā. Etthāti ettha itthiyaṃ pajā sajjati. Tapoti indriyasaṃvaradhutaṅgaguṇavīriyadukkarakārikānaṃ nāmaṃ, idha pana ṭhapetvā dukkarakārikaṃ sabbāpi kilesasantāpikā paṭipadā vaṭṭati. Brahmacariyanti methunavirati. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

58. In the eighth sutta, 'rāgo uppatho' means it is not the path for one going to a good destination and to Nibbāna. 'Rattindivakkhayo' means it is consumed by days and nights, or in days and nights. 'Itthī malaṃ' means that because other external stains can be cleansed by washing with ashes, alkali, and so on, but one corrupted by the stain of a woman cannot be made pure, a woman is therefore called a 'stain.' 'Etthā' means: herein, in a woman, beings are ensnared. 'Tapo' is the name for restraint of the senses, the qualities of the ascetic practices, effort, and difficult practices; here, however, setting aside difficult practices, any practice that torments the defilements is suitable. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' means abstention from sexual intercourse. The eighth.

9. Dutiyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Dutiya Sutta

59. Navame [V 1.0085] kissa cābhiratoti kismiṃ abhirato. Dutiyāti sugatiñceva nibbānañca gacchantassa dutiyikā. Paññā cenaṃ pasāsatīti paññā etaṃ purisaṃ “idaṃ karohi, idaṃ mākarī”ti anusāsati. Navamaṃ.

59. In the ninth sutta, 'kissa cābhirato' means delighting in what. 'Dutiyā' refers to a companion for one going to a good destination and to Nibbāna. 'Paññā cenaṃ pasāsati' means wisdom instructs this person, saying, 'Do this, do not do that.' The ninth.

10. Kavisuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Kavi Sutta

60. Dasame chando nidānanti gāyattiādiko chando gāthānaṃ nidānaṃ. Pubbapaṭṭhāpanagāthā ārabhanto hi “kataracchandena hotū”ti ārabhati[M 1.0089]. Viyañjananti jananaṃ. Akkharaṃ hi padaṃ janeti, padaṃ gāthaṃ janeti, gāthā atthaṃ pakāsetīti. Nāmasannissitāti samuddādipaṇṇattinissitā. Gāthā [P 1.0095] ārabhanto hi samuddaṃ vā pathaviṃ vā yaṃ kiñci nāmaṃ nissayitvāva ārabhati. Āsayoti patiṭṭhā. Kavito hi gāthā pavattanti. So tāsaṃ patiṭṭhā hotīti. Dasamaṃ.

60. In the tenth sutta, 'chando nidānanti' means that meter, such as gāyatrī and so forth, is the foundation of verses. For when beginning an introductory verse, one begins by considering, 'In what meter should it be?' 'Viyañjananti' means generation. For a letter generates a word, a word generates a verse, and a verse illuminates the meaning. 'Nāmasannissitāti' means it is dependent on a designation, such as 'ocean'. For when beginning a verse, one begins only after relying on some name, whether it be 'ocean' or 'earth' or anything else. 'Āsayoti' means basis. For verses proceed from a poet. He is their basis. The tenth.

Jarāvaggo chaṭṭho.

The Sixth Chapter on Old Age.

7. Addhavaggo

7. The Addhabhū Chapter

1. Nāmasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Nāma Sutta

61. Addhavaggassa paṭhame nāmaṃ sabbaṃ addhabhavīti nāmaṃ sabbaṃ abhibhavati anupatati. Opapātikena vā hi kittimena vā nāmena mutto satto vā saṅkhāro vā natthi. Yassapi hi rukkhassa vā pāsāṇassa vā “idaṃ nāma nāma”nti na jānanti, anāmakotveva tassa nāmaṃ hoti. Paṭhamaṃ.

61. In the first sutta of the Addhabhū Chapter, 'nāmaṃ sabbaṃ addhabhavīti' means that name governs and applies to everything. For there is no being or conditioned thing that is free from a spontaneously arisen or conventionally designated name. Even for a tree or a rock, for which one does not know 'this is its name,' its name is simply 'nameless.' The first.

2-3. Cittasuttādivaṇṇanā

2–3. Commentary on the Citta Sutta, etc.

62. Dutiye [V 1.0086] sabbeva vasamanvagūti ye cittassa vasaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃyeva anavasesapariyādānametaṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

62. In the second sutta, 'sabbeva vasamanvagūti' means this is the complete encompassing of just those things that come under the power of the mind. The second.

63. Tatiyepi eseva nayo. Tatiyaṃ.

63. In the third sutta as well, this is the same method. The third.

4-5. Saṃyojanasuttādivaṇṇanā

4–5. Commentary on the Saṃyojana Sutta, etc.

64. Catutthe kiṃ su saṃyojanoti kiṃ saṃyojano kiṃ bandhano? Vicāraṇanti vicaraṇā pādāni. Bahuvacane ekavacanaṃ kataṃ. Vitakkassa vicāraṇanti vitakko tassa pādā. Catutthaṃ.

64. In the fourth sutta, 'kiṃ su saṃyojanoti' means what is the fetter, what is the bond? 'Vicāraṇanti' means the supports for investigation; the singular is used for the plural. 'Vitakkassa vicāraṇanti' means thought is its support. The fourth.

65. Pañcamepi eseva nayo. Pañcamaṃ.

65. In the fifth sutta as well, this is the same method. The fifth.

6. Attahatasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Attahata Sutta

66. Chaṭṭhe kenassubbhāhatoti kena abbhāhato. Su-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Icchādhūpāyitoti icchāya āditto. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

66. In the sixth sutta, 'kenassubbhāhatoti' means by what is one struck. The particle 'su' is merely an expletive. 'Icchādhūpāyitoti' means ignited by desire. The sixth.

7-9. Uḍḍitasuttādivaṇṇanā

7–9. Commentary on the Uḍḍita Sutta, etc.

67. Sattame [M 1.0090][P 1.0096] taṇhāya uḍḍitoti taṇhāya ullaṅghito. Cakkhuñhi taṇhārajjunā āvunitvā rūpanāgadante uḍḍitaṃ, sotādīni saddādīsūti taṇhāya uḍḍito loko. Maccunā pihitoti anantare attabhāve kataṃ kammaṃ na dūraṃ ekacittantaraṃ, balavatiyā pana māraṇantikavedanāya pabbatena viya otthaṭattā sattā taṃ na bujjhantīti “maccunā pihito loko”ti vuttaṃ. Sattamaṃ.

67. In the seventh discourse, 'snared by craving' means snared by craving. Indeed, the eye, having been bound by the rope of craving, is snared on the wooden peg of form; the ear and so on are snared by the rope of craving on the wooden pegs of sound and so on. For this reason, the world is snared by craving. 'Covered by death' means that the kamma done in the immediately following existence is not far; it is one thought-moment away. However, because beings, as if overwhelmed by a great mountain, are overwhelmed by the powerful, painful feeling that has death as its end, they do not understand that kamma. For that reason, it is said, 'the world is covered by death.' The seventh.

68. Aṭṭhame sveva pañho devatāya heṭṭhupariyāyavasena pucchito. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

68. In the eighth discourse, that very same question was asked by a certain deva by way of inversion. The eighth.

69. Navame [V 1.0087] sabbaṃ uttānameva. Navamaṃ.

69. In the ninth discourse, everything is just self-evident. The ninth.

10. Lokasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the World

70. Dasame kismiṃ loko samuppannoti kismiṃ uppanne loko uppannoti pucchati. Chasūti chasu ajjhattikesu āyatanesu uppannesu uppannoti vuccati. Chasu kubbatīti tesuyeva chasu santhavaṃ karoti. Upādāyāti tāniyeva ca upādāya āgamma paṭicca pavattati. Vihaññatīti tesuyeva chasu vihaññati pīḷiyati. Iti ajjhattikāyatanavasena ayaṃ pañho āgato, ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ pana vasena āharituṃ vaṭṭati. Chasu hi ajjhattikāyatanesu uppannesu ayaṃ uppanno nāma hoti, chasu bāhiresu santhavaṃ karoti, channaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ upādāya chasu bāhiresu vihaññatīti. Dasamaṃ.

10. In the tenth discourse, 'In what has the world arisen?' asks: 'When what has arisen has the world arisen?' 'In the six' means: it is said to have arisen when the six internal sense bases have arisen. 'Makes association with the six' means: it makes association with those very six. 'Clinging' means: it proceeds by clinging to, resorting to, and depending on those very same bases. 'Is vexed' means: on account of those very six, the world is vexed and oppressed. Thus this question has come by way of the internal sense bases, but it is proper to apply it by way of the internal and external bases. For when the six internal sense bases have arisen, this world of beings is said to have arisen; it makes association with the six external bases; and by clinging to the six internal bases, it is vexed on account of the six external bases. The tenth.

Addhavaggo sattamo.

70. The Addha Chapter is the seventh.

8. Chetvāvaggo

The Chetvā Chapter

1. Chetvāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on Cutting

71. Chetvāvaggassa [P 1.0097] paṭhame chetvāti vadhitvā. Sukhaṃ setīti kodhapariḷāhena aparidayhamānattā sukhaṃ sayati. Na socatīti kodhavināsena vinaṭṭhadomanassattā na socati. Visamūlassāti dukkhavipākassa[M 1.0091]. Madhuraggassāti kuddhassa paṭikujjhitvā, akkuṭṭhassa paccakkositvā, pahaṭassa ca paṭipaharitvā sukhaṃ uppajjati, taṃ sandhāya madhuraggoti vutto. Imasmiṃ hi ṭhāne pariyosānaṃ agganti vuttaṃ. Ariyāti buddhādayo. Paṭhamaṃ.

8. In the first discourse of the Chetvā Chapter, 'having cut' means having slain. 'Sleeps happily' means: because of not being burned by the fever of anger, one sleeps happily. 'Does not grieve' means: because displeasure is destroyed through the destruction of anger, one does not grieve. 'Of the poison-root' means: of that which has a painful result. 'Of the sweet tip' means: happiness arises for one who gets angry back at the angry, who reviles back at the reviler, and who strikes back at the striker; referring to that, it is called 'sweet-tipped.' For in this context, 'tip' (agga) is said to mean the conclusion. 'The noble ones' means: the noble ones, such as the Buddha and others, praise it. The first.

2. Rathasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Chariot

72. Dutiye paññāyati etenāti paññāṇaṃ. Dhajo rathassāti mahantasmiṃ hi saṅgāmasīse dūratova [V 1.0088] dhajaṃ disvā “asukarañño nāma ayaṃ ratho”ti ratho pākaṭo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “dhajo rathassa paññāṇa”nti. Aggipi dūratova dhūmena paññāyati. Coḷaraṭṭhaṃ paṇḍuraṭṭhanti evaṃ raṭṭhampi raññā paññāyati. Cakkavattirañño dhītāpi pana itthī “asukassa nāma bhariyā”ti bhattāraṃ patvāva paññāyati. Tasmā dhūmo paññāṇamagginotiādi vuttaṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

1. In the second discourse: It is a sign (paññāṇaṃ) because one knows by it. Regarding 'The banner of a chariot': for at the head of a great battle, seeing the banner from afar, the chariot becomes evident as 'This is the chariot of such-and-such a king.' Therefore it is said, 'The banner is the sign of the chariot.' Fire, too, is known from afar by its smoke. A kingdom, such as the Coḷa kingdom or the Paṇḍu kingdom, is thus known by its king. Furthermore, even the daughter of a wheel-turning monarch, a woman, becomes known only upon reaching her husband, as 'She is the wife of so-and-so.' Therefore, it is said, 'Smoke is the sign of fire,' and so on. The second.

3. Vittasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Vitta Sutta

73. Tatiye saddhīdha vittanti yasmā saddho saddhāya muttamaṇiādīnipi vittāni labhati, tissopi kulasampadā, cha kāmasaggāni, nava brahmaloke patvā pariyosāne amatamahānibbānadassanampi labhati, tasmā maṇimuttādīhi vittehi saddhāvittameva seṭṭhaṃ. Dhammoti dasakusalakammapatho. Sukhamāvahatīti sabbampi sāsavānāsavaṃ asaṃkiliṭṭhasukhaṃ āvahati. Sādutaranti [P 1.0098] lokasmiṃ loṇambilādīnaṃ sabbarasānaṃ saccameva madhurataraṃ. Saccasmiṃ hi ṭhitā sīghavegaṃ nadimpi nivattenti, visampi nimmaddenti, aggimpi paṭibāhanti, devampi vassāpenti, tasmā taṃ sabbarasānaṃ madhurataranti vuttaṃ. Paññājīviṃ jīvitamāhu seṭṭhanti yo paññājīvī gahaṭṭho samāno pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāya salākabhattādīni paṭṭhapetvā paññāya jīvati, pabbajito vā pana dhammena uppanne paccaye “idamattha”nti paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanto kammaṭṭhānaṃ ādāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ariyaphalādhigamavasena paññāya jīvati, taṃ paññājīviṃ puggalaṃ seṭṭhaṃ jīvitaṃ jīvatīti āhu. Tatiyaṃ.

71. In the third discourse, regarding 'Here, faith is a treasure': because a faithful person, through faith, obtains treasures such as pearls and gems, the threefold family accomplishments, and having reached the six kāma-heavens and the nine brahma-realms, in the end obtains even the vision of the deathless, great Nibbāna. Therefore, among treasures such as pearls and gems, the treasure of faith is indeed the best. 'Dhamma' means the ten wholesome courses of action. 'Brings happiness' means it brings all unstained happiness, both with taints and without taints. 'Sweeter' means that in the world, among all tastes such as salty and sour, truth is indeed the sweetest. For those established in truth can make even a swift-flowing river turn back, neutralize even poison, ward off even fire, and make the heavens rain. Therefore, it is said to be sweeter than all tastes. Regarding 'They say the best life is one lived with wisdom': this refers to one who lives by wisdom. Whether a householder who, established in the five precepts and having established the giving of ticket-food and so on, lives by wisdom; or one who has gone forth who, reflecting 'This is for this purpose' while using requisites that have arisen in accordance with the Dhamma, and having undertaken a meditation subject and established insight, lives by wisdom by means of attaining the noble fruits—of that person who lives by wisdom, they say that they live the best life. The third.

4. Vuṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vuṭṭhi Sutta

74. Catutthe [M 1.0092] bījanti uppatantānaṃ sattavidhaṃ dhaññabījaṃ seṭṭhaṃ. Tasmiñhi uggate janapado khemo hoti subhikkho. Nipatatanti nipatantānaṃ meghavuṭṭhi seṭṭhā. Meghavuṭṭhiyañhi sati vividhāni sassāni uppajjanti, janapadā phītā honti khemā subhikkhā. Pavajamānānanti jaṅgamānaṃ padasā caramānānaṃ gāvo seṭṭhā. Tā nissāya hi sattā pañca gorase paribhuñjamānā sukhaṃ viharanti. Pavadatanti rājakulamajjhādīsu vadantānaṃ putto varo. So hi mātāpitūnaṃ anatthāvahaṃ na vadati.

2. In the fourth discourse, as for 'seeds': among things that sprout upwards, the seven kinds of grain-seed are best. For when it has sprouted, the country becomes safe and has abundant food. As for 'falling': among things that fall downwards, rain from clouds is best. For when there is rain, various crops arise, and countries become prosperous, safe, and have abundant food. As for 'moving about': among beings that move about on foot, cows are best. For relying on them, beings live happily, enjoying the five products of the cow. As for 'speaking': among those who speak in royal courts and so on, a son is excellent. For he does not speak what is detrimental to his parents.

Vijjā [V 1.0089] uppatataṃ seṭṭhāti purimapañhe kira sutvā samīpe ṭhitā ekā devatā “devate, kasmā tvaṃ etaṃ pañhaṃ dasabalaṃ pucchasi? Ahaṃ te kathessāmī”ti attano khantiyā laddhiyā pañhaṃ kathesi. Atha naṃ itarā devatā āha – “yāva padhaṃsī vadesi devate yāva pagabbhā mukharā, ahaṃ buddhaṃ bhagavantaṃ pucchāmi. Tvaṃ mayhaṃ kasmā kathesī”ti? Nivattetvā tadeva pañhaṃ dasabalaṃ pucchi. Athassā satthā vissajjento vijjā uppatatantiādimāha. Tattha vijjāti catumaggavijjā. Sā hi uppatamānā sabbākusaladhamme samugghāteti. Tasmā “uppatataṃ seṭṭhā”ti vuttā. Avijjāti vaṭṭamūlakamahāavijjā. Sā hi nipatantānaṃ osīdantānaṃ varā. Pavajamānānanti padasā caramānānaṃ jaṅgamānaṃ [P 1.0099] anomapuññakkhettabhūto saṅgho varo. Tañhi tattha tattha disvā pasannacittā sattā sotthiṃ pāpuṇanti. Buddhoti yādiso putto vā hotu añño vā, yesaṃ kesañci vadamānānaṃ buddho varo. Tassa hi dhammadesanaṃ āgamma anekasatasahassānaṃ pāṇānaṃ bandhanamokkho hotīti. Catutthaṃ.

Regarding 'Knowledge is the best of things that arise': having heard this in connection with the previous question, a certain deity standing nearby, it seems, explained the question based on her own acceptance and view, saying: 'O deity, why do you ask this question of the Ten-Powered One? I will explain it to you.' Then the other deity said to her: 'How aggressively you speak, O deity, how bold and garrulous! I am asking the Blessed Buddha. Why do you explain it to me?' Turning away, she asked the same question of the Ten-Powered One. Then the Teacher, in answering her, spoke the verse beginning 'Knowledge is the best of things that arise.' Therein, 'knowledge' is the knowledge of the four paths. For it, arising, uproots all unwholesome states. Therefore, it is said to be 'the best of things that arise.' 'Ignorance' is the great ignorance that is the root of the cycle of existence. For among things that sink and fall down, it is foremost. As for 'moving about': among moving beings who walk on foot, the Sangha—the faultless field of merit—is excellent. For having seen them here and there, beings with confident minds attain well-being. As for 'the Buddha': among any who speak whatsoever, be it a son or another, the Buddha is excellent. For on account of his teaching of the Dhamma, release from bondage occurs for many hundreds of thousands of living beings. The fourth.

5. Bhītāsuttavaṇṇanā

5. The commentary on the Bhīta Sutta.

75. Pañcame kiṃsūdha bhītāti kiṃ bhītā? Maggo canekāyatanappavuttoti aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇavasena anekehi kāraṇehi kathito. Evaṃ sante kissa bhītā hutvā ayaṃ janatā dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo aggahesīti vadati. Bhūripaññāti bahupañña ussannapañña. Paralokaṃ na bhāyeti imasmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ gacchanto na bhāyeyya. Paṇidhāyāti ṭhapetvā. Bahvannapānaṃ [M 1.0093] gharamāvasantoti anāthapiṇḍikādayo viya bahvannapāne ghare vasanto. Saṃvibhāgīti accharāya gahitampi nakhena phāletvā parassa datvāva bhuñjanasīlo. Vadaññūti vuttatthameva.

75. In the fifth sutta, regarding 'Why are they afraid?': Why are they afraid? Regarding 'The path is taught from many bases': it is taught by means of the thirty-eight objects and by many reasons. This being so, why does this multitude of beings, having become afraid, grasp the sixty-two wrong views? Thus it is said. 'One of great wisdom' means one of much wisdom, one of abundant wisdom. 'Does not fear the next world' means one going from this world to the next world should not be afraid. 'Having established' means having placed. 'Dwelling in a house with much food and drink' means dwelling in a house with much food and drink like Anāthapiṇḍika and others. 'One who shares' means one who is of the habit of eating only after having given to another, splitting with a fingernail even what has been taken as a morsel. 'Generous' has the meaning already stated.

Idāni gāthāya aṅgāni uddharitvā dassetabbāni – “vāca”nti hi iminā cattāri vacīsucaritāni gahitāni, “manenā”tipadena tīṇi manosucaritāni, “kāyenā”ti padena tīṇi kāyasucaritāni. Iti ime dasa kusalakammapathā pubbasuddhiaṅgaṃ nāma. Bahvannapānaṃ gharamāvasantoti iminā yaññaupakkharo gahito. Saddhoti ekamaṅgaṃ, mudūti ekaṃ, saṃvibhāgīti ekaṃ, vadaññūti ekaṃ. Iti imāni cattāri aṅgāni sandhāya “etesu dhammesu ṭhito catūsū”ti āha.

Now, the factors of the verse should be extracted and shown. By 'speech', the four kinds of good verbal conduct are taken; by the word 'with the mind', the three kinds of good mental conduct; by the word 'with the body', the three kinds of good bodily conduct. Thus, these ten wholesome courses of action are called the factor of preliminary purity. By 'dwelling in a house with much food and drink', the requisite for sacrifice is taken. 'Faithful' is one factor, 'gentle' is one, 'one who shares' is one, 'generous' is one. Thus, referring to these four factors, he said, 'established in these four dhammas'.

Aparopi [V 1.0090] pariyāyo – vācantiādīni tīṇi aṅgāni, bahvannapānanti iminā yaññaupakkharova gahito, saddho mudū saṃvibhāgī vadaññūti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ. Aparo dukanayo nāma hoti. “Vācaṃ manañcā”ti idamekaṃ aṅgaṃ, “kāyena pāpāni akubbamāno, bahvannapānaṃ gharamāvasanto”ti ekaṃ, “saddho mudū”ti ekaṃ, “saṃvibhāgī vadaññū”ti ekaṃ. Etesu catūsu dhammesu ṭhito dhamme ṭhito nāma hoti. So ito paralokaṃ gacchanto na bhāyati. Pañcamaṃ.

There is also another method: 'speech' and so on are three factors; by 'much food and drink', the requisite for sacrifice itself is taken; 'faithful, gentle, one who shares, generous' is one factor. Another is called the method of pairs. 'Speech and mind' is one factor; 'not doing evil deeds with the body, dwelling in a house with much food and drink' is one; 'faithful, gentle' is one; 'one who shares, generous' is one. One established in these four dhammas is called one established in the Dhamma. Such a one, going from here to the next world, does not fear. The fifth.

6. Najīratisuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Najīrati Sutta.

76. Chaṭṭhe [P 1.0100] nāmagottaṃ na jīratīti atītabuddhānaṃ yāvajjadivasā nāmagottaṃ kathiyati, tasmā na jīratīti vuccati. Porāṇā pana “addhāne gacchante na paññāyissati, jīraṇasabhāvo pana na hotiyevā”ti vadanti. Ālasyanti ālasiyaṃ, yena ṭhitaṭṭhāne ṭhitova, nisinnaṭṭhāne nisinnova hoti, telepi uttarante ṭhitiṃ na karoti. Pamādoti niddāya vā kilesavasena vā pamādo. Anuṭṭhānanti kammasamaye kammakaraṇavīriyābhāvo. Asaṃyamoti sīlasaññamābhāvo vissaṭṭhācāratā. Niddāti soppabahulatā. Tāya gacchantopi ṭhitopi nisinnopi niddāyati, pageva nipanno. Tandīti aticchātādivasena āgantukālasiyaṃ. Te chiddeti tāni cha chiddāni vivarāni. Sabbasoti [M 1.0094] sabbākārena. Tanti nipātamattaṃ. Vivajjayeti vajjeyya jaheyya. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

76. In the sixth sutta, regarding 'The name and clan do not decay': This means that the names and clans of past Buddhas are spoken of even up to the present day; hence, it is said they do not decay. The ancients, however, say, 'Though time passes, it will not be evident; but the nature of decay is simply not present.' Sloth—this is laziness, by which one remains standing while standing, and sitting while sitting, and does not take action even when oil is overflowing. Heedlessness—this is negligence due to sleep or by the power of defilements. Inactivity—this is the absence of energy to perform duties at the time of work. Lack of restraint—this is the absence of moral restraint, unrestrained conduct. Sleep—this is excessive sleepiness. By it, one dozes off even while walking, standing, or sitting—how much more so when lying down. Drowsiness—this is adventitious laziness arising from excessive hunger, etc. These six—these six openings or holes. Completely—in every way. 'Taṃ' is merely a particle. 'Vivajjaye' means one should shun, one should abandon. The sixth.

7. Issariyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Explanation of the Issariya Sutta.

77. Sattame satthamalanti malaggahitasatthaṃ. Kiṃ su harantaṃ vārentīti kaṃ harantaṃ nisedhenti. Vasoti āṇāpavattanaṃ. Itthīti avissajjanīyabhaṇḍattā “itthī bhaṇḍānamuttamaṃ, varabhaṇḍa”nti āha. Atha vā sabbepi bodhisattā ca cakkavattino ca mātukucchiyaṃyeva nibbattantīti “itthī bhaṇḍānamuttama”nti āha. Kodho satthamalanti kodho malaggahitasatthasadiso, paññāsatthassa vā malanti satthamalaṃ. Abbudanti vināsakāraṇaṃ, corā lokasmiṃ vināsakāti attho. Harantoti salākabhattādīni gahetvā gacchanto. Salākabhattādīni hi paṭṭhapitakāleyeva manussehi pariccattāni. Tesaṃ tāni haranto samaṇo piyo hoti, anāharante puññahāniṃ nissāya vippaṭisārino honti. Sattamaṃ.

77. In the seventh sutta, 'the stain of a weapon' means a rust-covered weapon. 'Who stops one taking what?' means: whom do they prevent from taking? 'Power' means the exercise of command. 'A woman'—because she is property that cannot be dispensed with, it was said, "A woman is the highest of treasures, the excellent treasure." Alternatively, since all Bodhisattas and wheel-turning monarchs are born only in a mother’s womb, it was said, "A woman is the highest of treasures." Regarding 'Anger is the stain of a weapon': anger is like a rust-covered weapon, or it is the stain of the weapon of wisdom, therefore it is called 'the stain of a weapon'. 'A cause of destruction' means a cause of ruin; the meaning is that thieves in the world are destructive. 'Taking' means going after taking ticket-food, etc. For ticket-food and so on are relinquished by people at the very time they are established. A monk who takes these is pleasing; when he does not take them, people become remorseful on account of the loss of merit. The seventh.

8. Kāmasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Explanation of the Kāma Sutta.

78. Aṭṭhame [V 1.0091][P 1.0101] attānaṃ na dadeti parassa dāsaṃ katvā attānaṃ na dadeyya ṭhapetvā sabbabodhisatteti vuttaṃ. Na pariccajeti sīhabyagghādīnaṃ na pariccajeyya sabbabodhisatte ṭhapetvāyevāti vuttaṃ. Kalyāṇanti saṇhaṃ mudukaṃ. Pāpikanti pharusaṃ vācaṃ. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

78. In the eighth sutta, 'one should not give oneself' means: one should not give oneself to another as a slave; it is said that this is with the exception of all Bodhisattas.
