'One should not relinquish' means: one should not relinquish oneself to lions, tigers, and so on; here too, it is said that this is with the exception of all Bodhisattas indeed. 'Good' means gentle and soft. 'Evil' means harsh speech. The eighth.

9. Pātheyyasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Pātheyya Sutta.

79. Navame saddhā bandhati pātheyyanti saddhaṃ uppādetvā dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ rakkhati, uposathakammaṃ karoti, tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sirīti issariyaṃ. Āsayoti vasanaṭṭhānaṃ. Issariye hi abhimukhībhūte thalatopi jalatopi bhogā āgacchantiyeva. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Parikassatīti parikaḍḍhati. Navamaṃ.

79. In the ninth sutta, "faith binds provisions" (saddhā bandhati pātheyyaṃ) means: having generated faith, one gives gifts, observes precepts, and performs Uposatha duties; therefore, this was said. "Splendor" (sirī) means sovereignty. "Abode" (āsayo) means a dwelling place. Indeed, when sovereignty is manifest, wealth comes from both land and water; therefore, this was said. "Attracts" (parikassati) means it pulls. The ninth.

10. Pajjotasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Pajjota Sutta

80. Dasame pajjototi padīpo viya hoti. Jāgaroti jāgarabrāhmaṇo viya hoti. Gāvo kamme sajīvānanti kammena saha jīvantānaṃ [M 1.0095] gāvova kamme kammasahāyā kammadutiyakā nāma honti. Gomaṇḍalehi saddhiṃ kasikammādīni nipphajjanti. Sītassa iriyāpathoti sītaṃ assa sattakāyassa iriyāpatho jīvitavutti. Sītanti naṅgalaṃ. Yassa hi naṅgalehi khettaṃ appamattakampi kaṭṭhaṃ na hoti, so kathaṃ jīvissatīti vadati. Dasamaṃ.

80. In the tenth sutta, "light" (pajjoto) is like a lamp. "Wakeful" (jāgaro) is like an ever-wakeful Arahant. "Cows are for those who live by work" (gāvo kammesajīvānaṃ) means: for those who make a living by work, cows are indeed companions in work, called the second partner in work. Farming and other tasks are accomplished together with herds of cattle. "The plow is the mode of living" (sītassa iriyāpatho) means: the plow is the mode of living, the livelihood, for this group of beings. "Plow" (sītaṃ) is a plow. Indeed, it is said: 'For whom a field is not tilled even a little by plows, how will that person live?' The tenth.

11. Araṇasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Araṇa Sutta

81. Ekādasame araṇāti nikkilesā. Vusitanti vusitavāso. Bhojissiyanti adāsabhāvo. Samaṇāti khīṇāsavasamaṇā. Te hi ekantena araṇā nāma. Vusitaṃ na nassatīti tesaṃ ariyamaggavāso [P 1.0102] na nassati. Parijānantīti puthujjanakalyāṇakato paṭṭhāya sekhā lokiyalokuttarāya pariññāya parijānanti. Bhojissiyanti khīṇāsavasamaṇānaṃyeva niccaṃ bhujissabhāvo nāma. Vandantīti pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya vandanti. Patiṭṭhitanti sīle patiṭṭhitaṃ[V 1.0092]. Samaṇīdhāti samaṇaṃ idha. Jātihīnanti api caṇḍālakulā pabbajitaṃ. Khattiyāti na kevalaṃ khattiyāva, devāpi sīlasampannaṃ samaṇaṃ vandantiyevāti. Ekādasamaṃ.

81. In the eleventh sutta, 'non-conflict' (araṇā) means free from defilements. 'Dwelt' (vusitaṃ) means having lived the life. 'To be a master' (bhojissiyaṃ) means not being a slave. 'Ascetics' (samaṇā) refers to ascetics who have destroyed the cankers. They are indeed entirely free from conflict. 'The lived life does not perish' means their dwelling in the noble path does not perish. 'They fully understand' (parijānanti) means, starting from the time of being a virtuous worldling, trainees fully understand through mundane and supramundane full understanding. 'To be a master' (bhojissiyaṃ) refers specifically to ascetics whose cankers are destroyed, who are always in a state of mastery. 'They venerate' (vandanti) means they pay respects from the day of going forth. 'Established' (patiṭṭhitaṃ) means established in morality. 'Here is an ascetic' (samaṇīdha) means an ascetic in this world. 'Of low birth' (jātihīnaṃ) means one who has gone forth even from a caṇḍāla family. 'Khattiyas' (khattiyā) means not only khattiyas, but even devas venerate an ascetic endowed with virtue. The eleventh.

Chetvāvaggo aṭṭhamo.

The 'Having Cut Off' Chapter, the Eighth.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Devatāsaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the Commentary on the Devatā Saṃyutta is concluded.

2. Devaputtasaṃyuttaṃ

2. The Connected Discourses with the Sons of the Devas

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Paṭhamakassapasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the First Kassapa Sutta

82. Devaputtasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0093][P 1.0103][M 1.0096] paṭhame devaputtoti devānañhi aṅke nibbattā purisā devaputtā nāma, itthiyo devadhītaro nāma honti. Nāmavasena apākaṭāva “aññatarā devatā”ti vuccati, pākaṭo “itthannāmo devaputto”ti. Tasmā heṭṭhā “aññatarā devatā”ti vatvā idha “devaputto”ti vuttaṃ. Anusāsanti anusiṭṭhiṃ. Ayaṃ kira devaputto bhagavatā sambodhito sattame vasse yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā tidasapure vassaṃ upagamma abhidhammaṃ desentena jhānavibhaṅge – “bhikkhūti samaññāya bhikkhu, paṭiññāya bhikkhū”ti (vibha. 510). Evaṃ bhikkhuniddesaṃ kathiyamānaṃ assosi. “Evaṃ vitakketha, mā evaṃ vitakkayittha, evaṃ manasikarotha, mā evaṃ manasākattha. Idaṃ pajahatha, idaṃ upasampajja viharathā”ti (pārā. 19). Evarūpaṃ pana bhikkhuovādaṃ bhikkhuanusāsanaṃ na assosi. So taṃ sandhāya – “bhikkhuṃ bhagavā pakāsesi, no ca bhikkhuno anusāsa”nti āha.

82. In the first sutta of the Devaputtasaṃyutta, the term 'devaputta' should be understood thus: Indeed, men born in the lap of the devas are called 'devaputtas,' and women are called 'devadhītaras.' By name, an obscure one is called 'a certain devatā,' while a well-known one is called 'a devaputta of such-and-such a name.' Therefore, having said 'a certain devatā' in the preceding Devatāsaṃyutta, here 'devaputta' is said. 'Anusāsanti' means instruction. It is said that this devaputta, in the seventh year after the Blessed One's full enlightenment, while the Blessed One—having performed the Twin Miracle and entered the rains-retreat in the city of the Tidasas—was teaching the Abhidhamma, heard the exposition of 'bhikkhu' being taught in the Jhānavibhaṅga thus: 'A bhikkhu by designation is a bhikkhu; a bhikkhu by admission is a bhikkhu.' However, he had not heard such an exhortation to a bhikkhu, an instruction to a bhikkhu, as: 'Think thus, do not think thus; apply your mind thus, do not apply your mind thus. Abandon this; having attained this, dwell therein.' Referring to that, he said, 'The Blessed One made known the bhikkhu, but not the instruction for the bhikkhu.'

Tena hīti yasmā mayā bhikkhuno anusiṭṭhi na pakāsitāti vadasi, tasmā. Taññevettha paṭibhātūti tuyhevesā anusiṭṭhipakāsanā upaṭṭhātūti. Yo hi pañhaṃ kathetukāmo hoti, na ca sakkoti sabbaññutaññāṇena saddhiṃ saṃsanditvā kathetuṃ. Yo vā na kathetukāmo hoti, sakkoti pana kathetuṃ. Yo vā [P 1.0104] neva kathetukāmo hoti, kathetuṃ na ca sakkoti. Sabbesampi tesaṃ bhagavā pañhaṃ bhāraṃ na karoti. Ayaṃ pana devaputto kathetukāmo ceva, sakkoti ca kathetuṃ. Tasmā tasseva bhāraṃ karonto bhagavā evamāha. Sopi pañhaṃ kathesi.

'Tena hi' means: 'Since you say that instruction for a bhikkhu was not made known by me, therefore...' 'Let it occur to you alone in this matter' means: 'Let this making known of the instruction be present for you alone.' Indeed, there is one who wishes to answer a question but is unable to answer after correlating with the knowledge of omniscience. There is another who does not wish to answer but is able to answer. And there is one who neither wishes to answer nor is able to answer. For all of them, the Blessed One does not make the question a burden. This devaputta, however, both wishes to answer and is able to answer. Therefore, the Blessed One, placing the burden on him alone, spoke thus. And so he answered the question.

Tattha [V 1.0094] subhāsitassa sikkhethāti subhāsitaṃ sikkheyya, catusaccanissitaṃ dasakathāvatthunissitaṃ sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyanissitaṃ catubbidhaṃ vacīsucaritameva sikkheyya. Samaṇūpāsanassa cāti samaṇehi upāsitabbaṃ samaṇūpāsanaṃ [M 1.0097] nāma aṭṭhatiṃsabhedaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ, tampi sikkheyya bhāveyyāti attho. Bahussutānaṃ vā bhikkhūnaṃ upāsanampi samaṇūpāsanaṃ. Tampi ‘kiṃ, bhante, kusala”ntiādinā pañhapucchanena paññāvuddhatthaṃ sikkheyya. Cittavūpasamassa cāti aṭṭhasamāpattivasena cittavūpasamaṃ sikkheyya. Iti devaputtena tisso sikkhā kathitā honti. Purimapadena hi adhisīlasikkhā kathitā, dutiyapadena adhipaññāsikkhā, cittavūpasamena adhicittasikkhāti evaṃ imāya gāthāya sakalampi sāsanaṃ pakāsitameva hoti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Herein, as to 'one should train in what is well-spoken': one should train in what is well-spoken, that is, based on the four truths, based on the ten topics of discussion, based on the thirty-seven requisites of enlightenment. One should train solely in the fourfold good conduct of speech. And as to 'association with ascetics': that which is to be cultivated by ascetics is called 'association with ascetics' (samaṇūpāsanaṃ), namely, the thirty-eight kinds of meditation subjects; one should train in and develop that as well—this is the meaning. Alternatively, associating with monks of great learning is also 'association with ascetics.' One should train in that as well, for the growth of wisdom, by asking questions such as, 'Venerable sir, what is wholesome?' And as to 'the calming of the mind': one should train in the calming of the mind by means of the eight attainments. Thus, the devaputta has spoken of the three trainings. For by the first phrase, the training in higher virtue is spoken of; by the second phrase, the training in higher wisdom is spoken of; and by the calming of the mind, the training in higher mind is spoken of. In this way, by this stanza, the entire teaching is indeed revealed. The first.

2. Dutiyakassapasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Second Kassapa Sutta

83. Dutiye jhāyīti dvīhi jhānehi jhāyī. Vimuttacittoti kammaṭṭhānavimuttiyā vimuttacitto. Hadayassānupattinti arahattaṃ. Lokassāti saṅkhāralokassa. Anissitoti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi anissito, taṇhādiṭṭhiyo vā anissito. Tadānisaṃsoti arahattānisaṃso. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – arahattānisaṃso bhikkhu arahattaṃ patthento jhāyī bhaveyya, suvimuttacitto bhaveyya, lokassa udayabbayaṃ ñatvā anissito bhaveyya. Tantidhammo pana imasmiṃ sāsane pubbabhāgoti. Dutiyaṃ.

83. In the second sutta, as for 'jhāyī' (a meditator): one who contemplates by means of two contemplations is a 'jhāyī'. As for 'with a liberated mind' (vimuttacitto): one has a mind liberated by the liberation of the meditation subject. As for 'attaining the heart' (hadayassānupattiṃ): this means arahantship. As for 'of the world' (lokassa): this means of the world of formations. As for 'not relying' (anissito): not relying on craving and views, or not being relied upon by craving and views. As for 'having that benefit' (tadānisaṃso): this means having the benefit of arahantship. This is what is said: A monk with the benefit of arahantship, aspiring to arahantship, should be a meditator; he should have a well-liberated mind; having known the arising and passing away of the world, he should be one who does not rely. The scriptural teaching, however, is the preliminary part in this dispensation. The second.

3-4. Māghasuttādivaṇṇanā

3-4. Commentary on the Māgha Sutta and others

84. Tatiye māghoti sakkassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sveva vattena aññe abhibhavitvā devissariyaṃ pattoti vatrabhū, vatranāmakaṃ vā asuraṃ abhibhavatīti vatrabhū. Tatiyaṃ.

84. In the third sutta, 'Māgha' is a name for Sakka. He, having overcome others by his observance and attained sovereignty over the devas, is thus called Vatrabhū. Alternatively, because he overcomes the asura named Vatra, he is called Vatrabhū. The third.

85. Catutthaṃ [P 1.0105] vuttatthameva. Catutthaṃ.

85. The fourth has the meaning already explained. The fourth.

5. Dāmalisuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Dāmali Sutta

86. Pañcame na tenāsīsate bhavanti tena kāraṇena yaṃ kiñci bhavaṃ na pattheti. Āyatapaggaho nāmesa devaputto, khīṇāsavassa kiccavosānaṃ natthi. Khīṇāsavena hi ādito arahattappattiyā [V 1.0095] vīriyaṃ kataṃ[M 1.0098], aparabhāge mayā arahattaṃ pattanti mā tuṇhī bhavatu, tatheva vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ karotu parakkamatūti cintetvā evamāha.

86. In the fifth sutta, regarding 'He does not long for existence thereby': for that reason, he does not long for any existence. This devaputta is named Āyatapaggaha. For one whose cankers are destroyed, there is no completion of the task. Indeed, by one whose cankers are destroyed, effort was made from the beginning for the attainment of Arahantship. In the later period, let him not be silent, thinking, 'Arahantship has been attained by me,' but let him make his effort firm and strive on. Having thought thus, he spoke thus.

Atha bhagavā “ayaṃ devaputto khīṇāsavassa kiccavosānaṃ akathento mama sāsanaṃ aniyyānikaṃ katheti, kiccavosānamassa kathessāmī”ti cintetvā natthi kiccantiādimāha. Tīsu kira piṭakesu ayaṃ gāthā asaṃkiṇṇā. Bhagavatā hi aññattha vīriyassa doso nāma dassito natthi. Idha pana imaṃ devaputtaṃ paṭibāhitvā “khīṇāsavena pubbabhāge āsavakkhayatthāya araññe vasantena kammaṭṭhānaṃ ādāya vīriyaṃ kataṃ, aparabhāge sace icchati, karotu, no ce icchati, yathāsukhaṃ viharatū”ti khīṇāsavassa kiccavosānadassanatthaṃ evamāha. Tattha gādhanti patiṭṭhaṃ. Pañcamaṃ.

Then the Blessed One, thinking, 'This devaputta, by not speaking of the completion of the task for one whose cankers are destroyed, declares my dispensation to be one that does not lead to deliverance. I will teach him the completion of the task,' spoke the verse beginning, 'There is no task….' It is said that this verse is unique in the three Piṭakas. Indeed, nowhere else has the Blessed One shown any fault in effort. But here, having rebuked this devaputta, he spoke thus to show the completion of the task for one whose cankers are destroyed: 'In the former period, one whose cankers are destroyed, dwelling in the forest for the destruction of the cankers, having undertaken a meditation subject, made effort. In the later period, if he wishes, let him do so; if he does not wish, let him dwell at ease.' Therein, 'gādha' means a foundation. The fifth.

6. Kāmadasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Kāmada Sutta

87. Chaṭṭhe dukkaranti ayaṃ kira devaputto pubbayogāvacaro bahalakilesatāya sappayogena kilese vikkhambhento samaṇadhammaṃ katvā pubbūpanissayamandatāya ariyabhūmiṃ appatvāva kālaṃ katvā devaloke nibbatto. So “tathāgatassa santikaṃ gantvā dukkarabhāvaṃ ārocessāmī”ti āgantvā evamāha. Tattha dukkaranti dasapi vassāni…pe… saṭṭhipi yadetaṃ ekantaparisuddhassa samaṇadhammassa karaṇaṃ nāma, taṃ dukkaraṃ. Sekhāti satta sekhā. Sīlasamāhitāti sīlena samāhitā samupetā. Ṭhitattāti patiṭṭhitasabhāvā. Evaṃ pucchitapañhaṃ vissajjetvā idāni uparipañhasamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ anagāriyupetassātiādimāha. Tattha [P 1.0106] anagāriyupetassāti anagāriyaṃ niggehabhāvaṃ upetassa. Sattabhūmikepi hi pāsāde vasanto bhikkhu vuḍḍhatarena āgantvā “mayhaṃ idaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti vutte pattacīvaraṃ ādāya nikkhamateva. Tasmā “anagāriyupeto”ti vuccati. Tuṭṭhīti catupaccayasantoso. Bhāvanāyāti cittavūpasamabhāvanāya.

87. In the sixth sutta, regarding 'difficult to do': It seems this devaputta had previously been a practitioner, but due to the abundance of defilements, though he suppressed defilements with effort and performed the ascetic's practice, because his earlier supporting conditions were weak, he passed away without reaching the noble state and was reborn in the deva realm. Thinking, 'I will go to the presence of the Tathāgata and declare the difficulty,' he came and spoke thus. Therein, 'difficult to do' refers to ten years... even sixty years—indeed, the practice of the perfectly pure ascetic discipline is called difficult. 'Trainees' refers to the seven trainees. 'Composed in virtue' means those who are composed by means of virtue and well-endowed. 'Established' means those whose nature is firmly grounded. Having answered the question thus, now, to introduce the next question, he spoke the words beginning, 'for one who has entered homelessness….' Herein, 'for one who has entered homelessness' means for one who has taken up the state of being without a home. For even a monk living in a seven-story mansion, when an elder arrives and says, 'This belongs to me,' takes his bowl and robe and simply leaves. Therefore, he is called 'one who has entered homelessness.' 'Contentment' means satisfaction with the four requisites. 'By meditation' means by the cultivation of mental tranquility.

Te chetvā maccuno jālanti ye rattindivaṃ indriyūpasame ratā, te dussamādahaṃ cittaṃ samādahanti. Ye ca samāhitacittā, te catupaccayasantosaṃ pūrentā na kilamanti. Ye santuṭṭhā, te sīlaṃ pūrentā na kilamanti[M 1.0099]. Ye sīle patiṭṭhitā satta sekhā, te ariyā maccuno jālasaṅkhātaṃ kilesajālaṃ chinditvā gacchanti. Duggamoti “saccametaṃ, bhante, ye indriyūpasame [V 1.0096] ratā, te dussamādahaṃ samādahanti…pe… ye sīle patiṭṭhitā, te maccuno jālaṃ chinditvā gacchanti”. Kiṃ na gacchissanti? Ayaṃ pana duggamo bhagavā visamo maggoti āha. Tattha kiñcāpi ariyamaggo neva duggamo na visamo, pubbabhāgapaṭipadāya panassa bahū parissayā honti. Tasmā evaṃ vutto. Avaṃsirāti ñāṇasirena adhosirā hutvā papatanti. Ariyamaggaṃ ārohituṃ asamatthatāyeva ca te anariyamagge papatantīti ca vuccanti. Ariyānaṃ samo maggoti sveva maggo ariyānaṃ samo hoti. Visame samāti visamepi sattakāye samāyeva. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

As for 'They, having cut the net of death': Those who delight in the calming of the faculties well compose the mind that is difficult to compose. And those with well-composed minds, while fulfilling contentment with the four requisites, do not become weary. Those who are content, while fulfilling virtue, do not become weary. The seven trainees, the noble ones established in virtue, cut the net of defilements known as the net of death, and go. As for 'Difficult to traverse': 'This is true, venerable sir. Those who delight in the calming of the faculties well compose the mind that is difficult to compose… those who are established in virtue, having cut the net of death, go.' Why would they not go? But he said, 'Blessed One, this path is difficult to traverse, uneven.' Therein, although the noble path is in fact neither difficult to traverse nor uneven, for its preliminary stage of practice there are many dangers. Therefore, it was spoken thus. As for 'Head-downward': having become head-downward with the head of wisdom, they fall. And it is also said that because of being unable to ascend the noble path, they fall onto the ignoble path. As for 'The path is even for the noble ones': that very path is even for the noble ones. As for 'Even in the uneven': even among the host of beings who are uneven, they are even indeed. The sixth.

7. Pañcālacaṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Pañcālacaṇḍa Sutta

88. Sattame sambādheti nīvaraṇasambādhaṃ kāmaguṇasambādhanti dve sambādhā. Tesu idha nīvaraṇasambādhaṃ adhippetaṃ. Okāsanti jhānassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Paṭilīnanisabhoti paṭilīnaseṭṭho. Paṭilīno nāma pahīnamāno vuccati. Yathāha – “kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭilīno hoti[P 1.0107]. Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno asmimāno pahīno hoti ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo”ti (a. ni. 4.38; mahāni. 87). Paccalatthaṃsūti paṭilabhiṃsu. Sammā teti ye nibbānapattiyā satiṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, te lokuttarasamādhināpi susamāhitāti missakajjhānaṃ kathitaṃ. Sattamaṃ.

88. In the seventh sutta, as for 'constriction', there are two constrictions: the constriction of the hindrances and the constriction of sensual pleasures. Among them, the constriction of the hindrances is intended here. 'Opportunity' is a name for jhāna. As for 'the noble one who is withdrawn', it means the foremost of the withdrawn. One who has abandoned conceit is called 'withdrawn'. As it is said: 'And how, monks, is a monk withdrawn? Here, monks, for a monk the conceit "I am" is abandoned, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, brought to a state of non-becoming, having the nature of not arising in the future.' As for 'they have received', it means they have obtained. As for 'they are rightly...': those who have obtained mindfulness for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, they are also well-composed through supramundane concentration. Thus, mixed jhāna is spoken of. The seventh.

8. Tāyanasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Tāyana Sutta

89. Aṭṭhame purāṇatitthakaroti pubbe titthakaro. Ettha ca titthaṃ nāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo, titthakaro nāma tāsaṃ uppādako satthā. Seyyathidaṃ nando, vaccho, kiso, saṃkicco. Purāṇādayo pana titthiyā nāma. Ayaṃ pana diṭṭhiṃ uppādetvā kathaṃ sagge nibbattoti? Kammavāditāya. Esa kira uposathabhattādīni adāsi, anāthānaṃ vattaṃ paṭṭhapesi, patissaye akāsi, pokkharaṇiyo khaṇāpesi, aññampi bahuṃ kalyāṇaṃ akāsi. So tassa nissandena sagge nibbatto, sāsanassa [M 1.0100] pana niyyānikabhāvaṃ jānāti. So tathāgatassa santikaṃ gantvā sāsanānucchavikā vīriyappaṭisaṃyuttā gāthā vakkhāmīti āgantvā chinda sotantiādimāha.

89. In the eighth sutta, 'the ancient sect-maker' (purāṇatitthakaro) means a former sect-maker. Here, 'sect' (tittha) means the sixty-two wrong views, and 'sect-maker' (titthakaro) means the teacher who originated them, such as Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, and Saṅkicca. Pūraṇa and others, however, are called sectarians. But how, having originated a wrong view, was this one reborn in the heavenly world? Because of being a proponent of kamma. It is said that this one gave offerings such as the Uposatha meal, established provisions for the helpless, made shelters, had lotus ponds dug, and performed many other meritorious deeds. As a consequence of that, he was reborn in the heavenly world, but he knows the liberating nature of the Teaching. Approaching the Tathāgata, thinking, 'I will recite verses suitable for the Teaching and connected with energy,' he came and said the verse beginning with, 'Cut the stream...'

Tattha [V 1.0097] chindāti aniyamitaāṇatti. Sotanti taṇhāsotaṃ. Parakkammāti parakkamitvā vīriyaṃ katvā. Kāmeti kilesakāmepi vatthukāmepi. Panudāti nīhara. Ekattanti jhānaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kāme ajahitvā muni jhānaṃ na upapajjati, na paṭilabhatīti attho. Kayirā ce kayirāthenanti yadi vīriyaṃ kareyya, kareyyātha, taṃ vīriyaṃ na osakkeyya. Daḷhamenaṃ parakkameti daḷhaṃ enaṃ kareyya. Sithilo hi paribbājoti sithilagahitā pabbajjā. Bhiyyo ākirate rajanti atirekaṃ [P 1.0108] upari kilesarajaṃ ākirati. Akataṃ dukkaṭaṃ seyyoti dukkaṭaṃ akatameva seyyo. Yaṃ kiñcīti na kevalaṃ dukkaṭaṃ katvā katasāmaññameva, aññampi yaṃ kiñci sithilaṃ kataṃ evarūpameva hoti. Saṃkiliṭṭhanti dukkarakārikavataṃ. Imasmiṃ hi sāsane paccayahetu samādinnadhutaṅgavataṃ saṃkiliṭṭhameva. Saṅkassaranti saṅkāya saritaṃ, “idampi iminā kataṃ bhavissati, idampi iminā”ti evaṃ āsaṅkitaparisaṅkitaṃ. Ādibrahmacariyikāti maggabrahmacariyassa ādibhūtā pubbapadhānabhūtā. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Here, 'cut' (chinda) is an unrestricted command. 'The stream' (sotaṃ) is the stream of craving. 'Striving' (parakkamma) means having striven, having made an effort. 'Desires' (kāme) refers both to defilement-desires and object-desires. 'Dispel' (panuda) means remove. 'Unification' (ekattaṃ) refers to jhāna. This is what is said: 'Without abandoning desires, a sage does not attain jhāna, does not achieve it'—this is the meaning. 'If one should do, one should do it' (kayirā ce kayirāthenaṃ) means that if one should make an effort, one should indeed make it, and that effort should not be slackened. 'Let him strive at it firmly' (daḷhamenaṃ parakkame) means he should do it firmly. 'For a slack wanderer' (sithilo hi paribbājo) means the going forth has been loosely undertaken. 'He scatters more dust' (bhiyyo ākirate rajaṃ) means he scatters an excess of the dust of defilements upon himself. 'Better undone is a wrong deed' (akataṃ dukkaṭaṃ seyyo) means a wrong deed is better left undone. 'Whatever' (yaṃ kiñci) means it is not only the state of a recluse undertaken after having done a wrong deed, but also any other thing whatsoever done loosely is of this very nature. 'Corrupted' (saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ) refers to vows of self-mortification. For in this Dispensation, dhutaṅga vows undertaken for the sake of requisites are indeed corrupted. 'A cause for suspicion' (saṅkassaraṃ) means recalled with doubt, 'This too will have been done by him, and this too by him'—thus a state of being suspected and doubted by others. 'The basis of the holy life' (ādibrahmacariyikā) means the initial and primary basis of the holy life of the path. The eighth.

9. Candimasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Candima Sutta

90. Navame candimāti candavimānavāsī devaputto. Sabbadhīti sabbesu khandhaāyatanādīsu. Lokānukampakāti tuyhampi etassapi tādisā eva. Santaramānovāti turito viya. Pamuñcasīti atītatthe vattamānavacanaṃ. Navamaṃ.

90. In the ninth sutta, 'Candimā' refers to the devaputta dwelling in the moon mansion. 'In every way' (sabbadhi) means in all aggregates, sense bases, and so forth. 'Compassionate for the world' (lokānukampaka): it is the same for you as it is for him. 'Hurrying' (santaramāno) means as if hurried. 'You release' (pamuñcasi) is a present-tense verb used with a past meaning. The ninth.

10. Sūriyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Sūriya Sutta

91. Dasame sūriyoti sūriyavimānavāsī devaputto. Andhakāreti cakkhuviññāṇuppattinivāraṇena andhabhāvakaraṇe. Virocatīti verocano. Maṇḍalīti maṇḍalasaṇṭhāno. Mā, rāhu, gilī caramantalikkheti antalikkhe caraṃ sūriyaṃ, rāhu, mā gilīti vadati. Kiṃ panesa taṃ gilatīti[M 1.0101]? Āma, gilati. Rāhussa hi attabhāvo mahā, uccattanena aṭṭhayojanasatādhikāni cattāri yojanasahassāni, bāhantaramassa dvādasayojanasatāni, bahalattena cha yojanasatāni, sīsaṃ nava yojanasataṃ, nalāṭaṃ tiyojanasataṃ, bhamukantaraṃ paṇṇāsayojanaṃ, mukhaṃ dviyojanasataṃ, ghānaṃ tiyojanasataṃ, mukhādhānaṃ tiyojanasatagambhīraṃ hatthatalapādatalāni puthulato dviyojanasatāni[P 1.0109]. Aṅgulipabbāni paṇṇāsa yojanāni. So candimasūriye virocamāne disvā issāpakato [V 1.0098] tesaṃ gamanavīthiṃ otaritvā mukhaṃ vivaritvā tiṭṭhati. Candavimānaṃ sūriyavimānaṃ vā tiyojanasatike mahānarake pakkhittaṃ viya hoti. Vimāne adhivatthā devatā maraṇabhayatajjitā ekappahāreneva viravanti. So pana vimānaṃ kadāci hatthena chādeti, kadāci hanukassa heṭṭhā pakkhipati, kadāci jivhāya parimajjati, kadāci avagaṇḍakārakaṃ bhuñjanto viya kapolantare ṭhapeti. Vegaṃ pana vāretuṃ na sakkoti. Sace vāressāmīti gaṇḍakaṃ katvā tiṭṭheyya, matthakaṃ tassa bhinditvā nikkhameyya, ākaḍḍhitvā vā naṃ onameyya. Tasmā vimānena saheva gacchati. Pajaṃ mamanti candimasūriyā kira dvepi devaputtā mahāsamayasuttakathanadivase sotāpattiphalaṃ pattā. Tena bhagavā “pajaṃ mama”nti āha, putto mama esoti attho. Dasamaṃ.

91. In the tenth, 'the sun' (sūriyo) refers to the devaputta dwelling in the sun-mansion. 'In darkness' (andhakāre) means in the making of a state of blindness by preventing the arising of eye-consciousness. 'He shines' (virocati), hence he is 'the Radiant One' (verocano). 'The orb' (maṇḍalī) means having a circular form. 'Do not, Rāhu, swallow the one moving in the sky' (mā, rāhu, gilī caramantalikkhe)—thus he speaks, saying, 'Rāhu, do not swallow the sun moving in the sky.' But does he swallow it? Yes, he swallows. For Rāhu’s body is immense: in height, four thousand eight hundred yojanas; the span between his arms is twelve hundred yojanas; in thickness, six hundred yojanas; his head is nine hundred yojanas; his forehead is three hundred yojanas; the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas; his mouth is two hundred yojanas; his nose is three hundred yojanas; and his mouth cavity is three hundred yojanas deep. The palms of his hands and soles of his feet are two hundred yojanas broad, and his finger joints are fifty yojanas long. When he sees the moon and sun shining, moved by envy, he descends into their path, opens his mouth, and stands there. The moon-mansion or sun-mansion appears as if cast into a great hell-chasm three hundred yojanas deep. The deities dwelling in the mansion, terrified by the fear of death, cry out all at once. Sometimes he covers the mansion with his hand, sometimes places it under his chin, sometimes licks it with his tongue, and sometimes holds it in his cheek like someone eating a mouthful. But he cannot stop its motion. If he were to try to stop it by holding it in his cheek, it would break through the top of his head and escape, or it would drag him down. Therefore, he moves along with the mansion. 'My offspring' (pajaṃ mama)—it is said that both the moon and sun devaputtas attained the fruit of stream-entry on the day the Mahāsamaya Sutta was taught. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'my offspring,' meaning 'this is my son.' The tenth.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Anāthapiṇḍikavaggo

2. The Anāthapiṇḍika Chapter

1. Candimasasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Candimasa Sutta

92. Dutiyavaggassa paṭhame kacchevāti kacche viya. Kaccheti pabbatakacchepi nadīkacchepi. Ekodi nipakāti ekaggacittā ceva paññānepakkena ca samannāgatā. Satāti satimanto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye jhānāni labhitvā [M 1.0102] ekodī nipakā satā viharanti, te amakase pabbatakacche vā nadīkacche vā magā viya sotthiṃ gamissantīti. Pāranti nibbānaṃ. Ambujoti maccho. Raṇañjahāti kilesañjahā. Yepi jhānāni labhitvā appamattā kilese jahanti, te suttajālaṃ bhinditvā macchā viya nibbānaṃ gamissantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṭhamaṃ.

92. In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'in a thicket' (kacche) means as in a thicket. 'Thicket' refers to both a mountain thicket and a river thicket. 'Concentrated, discerning' (ekodi nipakā) means endowed with a one-pointed mind and with discerning wisdom. 'Mindful' (satā) means possessing mindfulness. This is what is said: those who, having attained the jhānas, dwell concentrated, discerning, and mindful, will go to safety, like deer in a mountain thicket or a river thicket free from gadflies. 'The far shore' (pāraṃ) means Nibbāna. 'Water-born' (ambujo) means a fish. 'Having abandoned conflict' (raṇañjahā) means having abandoned defilements. And those who, having attained the jhānas, heedfully abandon the defilements, will, having broken through the net of craving, go to Nibbāna like fish—this is what is said. The first.

2. Veṇḍusuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Veṇḍu Sutta

93. Dutiye [P 1.0110] veṇḍūti tassa devaputtassa nāmaṃ. Payirupāsiyāti parirupāsitvā. Anusikkhareti [V 1.0099] sikkhanti. Siṭṭhipadeti anusiṭṭhipade. Kāle te appamajjantāti kāle te appamādaṃ karontā. Dutiyaṃ.

93. In the second sutta, 'Veṇḍu' is the name of that devaputta. 'One should attend upon' (payirupāsiya) means having attended upon. 'One should train accordingly' (anusikkhare) means they train. 'In the teaching' (siṭṭhipade) means in the repeated instruction. 'They, being heedful at the proper time' (kāle te appamajjantā) means they practice heedfulness at the proper time. The second.

3. Dīghalaṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Dīghalaṭṭhi Sutta

94. Tatiye dīghalaṭṭhīti devaloke sabbe samappamāṇā tigāvutikāva honti, manussaloke panassa dīghattabhāvatāya evaṃnāmaṃ ahosi. So puññāni katvā devaloke nibbattopi tatheva paññāyi. Tatiyaṃ.

94. In the third sutta, regarding 'Dīghalaṭṭhi'—in the deva world all are of equal measure, being three gāvutas tall, but in the human world, because of his tall stature, this name came to be. Having done meritorious deeds, even when reborn in the deva world, he was known by that same name. The third.

4. Nandanasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Nandana Sutta

95. Catutthe gotamāti bhagavantaṃ gottena ālapati. Anāvaṭanti tathāgatassa hi sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pesentassa rukkho vā pabbato vā āvarituṃ samattho nāma natthi. Tenāha “anāvaṭa”nti. Iti tathāgataṃ thometvā devaloke abhisaṅkhatapañhaṃ pucchanto kathaṃvidhantiādimāha. Tattha dukkhamaticca iriyatīti dukkhaṃ atikkamitvā viharati. Sīlavāti lokiyalokuttarena sīlena samannāgato khīṇāsavo. Paññādayopi missakāyeva veditabbā. Pūjayantīti gandhapupphādīhi pūjenti. Catutthaṃ.

95. In the fourth sutta, 'Gotama' addresses the Blessed One by his clan name. 'Unobstructed'—for there is nothing, whether a tree or a mountain, capable of obstructing the omniscient knowledge of the Tathāgata when he directs it. Therefore, he said, 'unobstructed.' Having praised the Tathāgata in this way, wishing to ask a question prepared in the deva world, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Of what kind?' Therein, 'one fares having transcended suffering' means one dwells having overcome suffering. 'Virtuous' means an Arahant endowed with mundane and supramundane virtue. Wisdom and the others should also be understood as mixed. 'They honor' means they honor with perfumes, flowers, and so on. The fourth.

5-6. Candanasuttādivaṇṇanā

5–6. The Commentary on the Candana Sutta and Others

96. Pañcame appatiṭṭhe anālambeti heṭṭhā apatiṭṭhe upari anālambane. Susamāhitoti appanāyapi upacārenapi suṭṭhu samāhito[M 1.0103]. Pahitattoti pesitatto. Nandīrāgaparikkhīṇoti parikkhīṇanandīrāgo. Nandīrāgo nāma tayo kammābhisaṅkhārā. Iti imāya gāthāya kāmasaññāgahaṇena pañcorambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni, rūpasaṃyojanagahaṇena pañca uddhambhāgiyasaṃyojanāni, nandīrāgena tayo kammābhisaṅkhārā [P 1.0111] gahitā. Evaṃ yassa dasa saṃyojanāni tayo ca kammābhisaṅkhārā pahīnā, so gambhīre mahoghe na sīdatīti. Kāmasaññāya vā kāmabhavo, rūpasaṃyojanena rūpabhavo gahito, tesaṃ gahaṇena arūpabhavo gahitova[V 1.0100], nandīrāgena tayo kammābhisaṅkhārā gahitāti evaṃ yassa tīsu bhavesu tayo saṅkhārā natthi, so gambhīre na sīdatītipi dasseti. Pañcamaṃ.

96. In the fifth sutta, 'without a foothold, without a support' means without a foothold below in the sensual existence and without a support above in the form and formless existences. 'Well-concentrated' means well-established in both absorption and access concentration. 'With mind directed' means with mind sent forth to Nibbāna. 'With delight and lust destroyed' means with delight and lust exhausted. 'Delight and lust' refers to the three kamma-formations. Thus, in this verse, by taking up sensual perception, the five lower fetters are taken; by taking up the fetter of form, the five higher fetters are taken; and by delight and lust, the three kamma-formations are taken. In this way, for one whose ten fetters and three kamma-formations are abandoned, he does not sink in the deep, vast flood. Alternatively, by sensual perception, the sensual existence is taken; by the fetter of form, the form existence is taken; and by the taking of these, the formless existence is also taken. By delight and lust, the three kamma-formations are taken. Thus, for one for whom the three formations do not exist in the three existences, it is also shown that he does not sink in the deep. The fifth.

97. Chaṭṭhaṃ vuttatthameva. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

97. The sixth sutta has the meaning already stated. The sixth.

7. Subrahmasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Subrahma Sutta.

98. Sattame subrahmāti so kira devaputto accharāsaṅghaparivuto nandanakīḷikaṃ gantvā pāricchattakamūle paññattāsane nisīdi. Taṃ pañcasatā devadhītaro parivāretvā nisinnā, pañcasatā rukkhaṃ abhiruḷhā. Nanu ca devatānaṃ cittavasena yojanasatikopi rukkho onamitvā hatthaṃ āgacchati, kasmā tā abhiruḷhāti. Khiḍḍāpasutatāya. Abhiruyha pana madhurassarena gāyitvā gāyitvā pupphāni pātenti, tāni gahetvā itarā ekatovaṇṭikamālādivasena ganthenti. Atha rukkhaṃ abhiruḷhā upacchedakakammavasena ekappahāreneva kālaṃ katvā avīcimhi nibbattā mahādukkhaṃ anubhavanti.

98. In the seventh sutta, 'Subrahma'—it is said that this devaputta, surrounded by a host of nymphs, went to the Nandana Grove for amusement and sat on a prepared seat at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree. Five hundred goddesses sat around him, while five hundred others climbed the tree. Now, for devas, even a tree a hundred yojanas high bends down at their will and comes within reach—so why did they climb it? For the sake of playfulness. Having climbed, singing in sweet voices, they scattered flowers, which the others gathered and strung into garlands with single stalks, and so on. Then, those who had climbed the tree, by the power of a life-interrupting kamma, died all at once and were reborn in Avīci, experiencing great suffering.

Atha kāle gacchante devaputto “imāsaṃ neva saddo suyyati, na pupphāni pātenti. Kahaṃ nu kho gatā”ti? Āvajjento niraye nibbattabhāvaṃ disvā piyavatthukasokena ruppamāno cintesi – “etā tāva yathākammena gatā, mayhaṃ āyusaṅkhāro kittako”ti. So – “sattame divase mayāpi avasesāhi pañcasatāhi saddhiṃ kālaṃ katvā tattheva nibbattitabba”nti disvā balavatarena sokena ruppi. So – “imaṃ mayhaṃ sokaṃ sadevake loke aññatra tathāgatā niddhamituṃ samattho nāma natthī”ti cintetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā niccaṃ utrastanti gāthamāha.

Then, as time was passing, the devaputta thought, “The sound of their singing is not heard, nor do they cause flowers to fall. Where, indeed, have they gone?” Reflecting, he saw their state of having been reborn in hell and, being tormented by sorrow for his beloved ones, he considered: “For their part, they have gone according to their kamma, but how much of my life-span remains?” He, seeing that “On the seventh human day, I too, together with the remaining five hundred celestial nymphs, must die and be reborn in that very place,” was afflicted by a very strong sorrow. He thought, “In this world with its devas, there is no one capable of dispelling this sorrow of mine other than the Tathāgata.” Having thought thus, he went to the Teacher's presence and spoke the verse beginning with 'Niccaṃ utrastaṃ'.

Tattha [M 1.0104] idanti attano cittaṃ dasseti. Dutiyapadaṃ purimasseva [P 1.0112] vevacanaṃ. Niccanti ca padassa devaloke nibbattakālato paṭṭhāyāti attho na gahetabbo, sokuppattikālato pana paṭṭhāya niccanti veditabbaṃ. Anuppannesu kicchesūti ito sattāhaccayena yāni dukkhāni uppajjissanti, tesu. Atho uppatitesu cāti yāni pañcasatānaṃ accharānaṃ niraye nibbattānaṃ diṭṭhāni, tesu cāti evaṃ imesu uppannānuppannesu dukkhesu niccaṃ mama utrastaṃ cittaṃ, abbhantare ḍayhamāno viya homi bhagavāti dasseti.

Therein, by 'this' (idaṃ), he indicates his own mind. The second phrase is merely a synonym for the first. And the meaning of the word 'niccaṃ' (constantly) should not be taken as 'beginning from the time of rebirth in the deva world'; rather, it should be understood as 'constantly' beginning from the time of the arising of sorrow. 'Anuppannesu kicchesu' (Regarding things that have not yet arisen) means: on account of those sufferings that will arise after the passing of seven days from here. 'Atho uppatitesu ca' (And also regarding those that have arisen) means: and also on account of those sufferings that were seen in the case of the five hundred celestial nymphs who were reborn in hell. Thus, he indicates: “On account of these sufferings, both arisen and unarisen, my mind is constantly terrified; I am as if burning inside, O Blessed One.”

Nāññatra [V 1.0101] bojjhā tapasāti bojjhaṅgabhāvanañca tapoguṇañca aññatra muñcitvā sotthiṃ na passāmīti attho. Sabbanissaggāti nibbānato. Ettha kiñcāpi bojjhaṅgabhāvanā paṭhamaṃ gahitā, indriyasaṃvaro pacchā, atthato pana indriyasaṃvarova paṭhamaṃ veditabbo. Indiyasaṃvare hi gahite catupārisuddhisīlaṃ gahitaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ patiṭṭhito bhikkhu nissayamuttako dhutaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ tapoguṇaṃ samādāya araññaṃ pavisitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvento saha vipassanāya bojjhaṅge bhāveti. Tassa ariyamaggo yaṃ nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjati, so “sabbanissaggo”ti bhagavā catusaccavasena desanaṃ vinivattesi. Devaputto desanāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahīti. Sattamaṃ.

‘Not elsewhere than from awakening and austerity’ means: apart from the cultivation of the enlightenment factors and the quality of austerity, I see no safety. ‘Total relinquishment’ refers to Nibbāna. Here, although the cultivation of the enlightenment factors is taken up first and sense restraint afterwards, in terms of meaning, sense restraint itself should be understood as primary. For when sense restraint is taken up, the fourfold purity of virtue is taken up. A monk established in that, being free from dependence, having undertaken the quality of austerity known as the ascetic practices, having entered the forest and developing a meditation subject, cultivates the enlightenment factors together with insight. For him, the noble path arises having taken Nibbāna as its object. That Nibbāna is ‘total relinquishment.’ Thus the Blessed One concluded the discourse by way of the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse, the devaputta was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The seventh.

8-10. Kakudhasuttādivaṇṇanā

8–10. The Commentary on the Kakudha Sutta and Others.

99. Aṭṭhame kakudho devaputtoti ayaṃ kira kolanagare mahāmoggallānattherassa upaṭṭhākaputto daharakāleyeva therassa santike vasanto jhānaṃ nibbattetvā kālaṅkato, brahmaloke uppajji. Tatrāpi naṃ kakudho brahmātveva sañjānanti. Nandasīti tussasi. Kiṃ laddhāti tuṭṭhi nāma kiñci manāpaṃ labhitvā hoti, tasmā evamāha. Kiṃ jīyitthāti yassa hi kiñci manāpaṃ cīvarādivatthu jiṇṇaṃ hoti, so socati, tasmā evamāha. Aratī nābhikīratīti ukkaṇṭhitā nābhibhavati. Aghajātassāti dukkhajātassa, vaṭṭadukkhe ṭhitassāti attho. Nandījātassāti jātataṇhassa. Aghanti evarūpassa [P 1.0113] hi vaṭṭadukkhaṃ āgatameva hoti[M 1.0105]. “Dukkhī sukhaṃ patthayatī”ti hi vuttaṃ. Iti aghajātassa nandī hoti, sukhavipariṇāmena dukkhaṃ āgatamevāti nandījātassa aghaṃ hoti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

99. In the eighth, regarding ‘Kakudha the devaputta’: it is said that this one was the son of an attendant of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the country of Kosala. While still young, living in the presence of the elder, he produced jhāna, passed away, and arose in the Brahmā world. There too, they know him as Kakudha Brahmā. ‘You delight’ means you are pleased. ‘What have you gained?’: joy arises from obtaining something pleasing, therefore he said this. ‘What has worn out?’: because when for someone a pleasing object such as a robe wears out, he grieves, therefore he said this. ‘Discontent does not overwhelm you’ means restlessness does not overcome. ‘For one born of misery’ means for one born of suffering, that is, for one established in the suffering of the cycle. ‘For one in whom delight has arisen’ means for one in whom craving has arisen. ‘Misery’: for such a one, the suffering of the cycle has indeed come. For it is said, “One who suffers desires happiness.” Thus, for one born of misery, delight arises. Through the changing of pleasure, suffering indeed comes; thus, for one in whom delight has arisen, misery arises. The eighth.

100. Navamaṃ vuttatthameva. Navamaṃ.

100. The ninth has the meaning already stated. The ninth.

101. Dasame ānandattherassa anumānabuddhiyā ānubhāvappakāsanatthaṃ aññataroti āha. Dasamaṃ.

101. In the tenth, the phrase “a certain one” is stated in order to show the power of the Elder Ānanda’s wisdom of inference. The tenth.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Nānātitthiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter.

1-2. Sivasuttādivaṇṇanā

1–2. Commentary on the Siva Sutta, and so forth.

102. Tatiyavaggassa [V 1.0102] paṭhamaṃ vuttatthameva. Paṭhamaṃ.

102. The first of the third chapter has the meaning already stated. The first.

103. Dutiye paṭikaccevāti paṭhamaṃyeva. Akkhacchinnovajhāyatīti akkhacchinno avajhāyati, balavacintanaṃ cinteti. Dutiyagāthāya akkhacchinnovāti akkhacchinno viya. Dutiyaṃ.

103. In the second, `paṭikacceva` means `paṭhamaṃyeva`, beforehand. `Akkhacchinno avajhāyati` means: `akkhacchinno`, having a broken axle, he `avajhāyati`, broods; he thinks a powerful thought. In the second verse, `akkhacchinno` means `akkhacchinno viya`, like one with a broken axle. The second.

3-4. Serīsuttādivaṇṇanā

3–4. Commentary on the Serīsa Sutta, and so forth.

104. Tatiye dāyakoti dānasīlo. Dānapatīti yaṃ dānaṃ demi, tassa pati hutvā demi, na dāso na sahāyo. Yo hi attanā madhuraṃ bhuñjati, paresaṃ amadhuraṃ deti, so dānasaṅkhātassa deyyadhammassa dāso hutvā deti. Yo yaṃ attanā bhuñjati, tadeva deti, so sahāyo hutvā deti. Yo pana attanā yena tena yāpeti, paresaṃ madhuraṃ deti, so pati jeṭṭhako sāmi hutvā deti. Ahaṃ “tādiso ahosi”nti [P 1.0114] vadati.

104. In the third: `dāyako` means one who is habitually generous. `Dānapati` means: 'When I give a gift, I give as its master, not as a slave, not as a friend.' For one who eats sweet food himself but gives others what is not sweet, he gives as a slave to the gift-object called 'giving'. One who gives the same as what he himself eats, gives as a friend. But one who sustains himself with whatever is available yet gives others sweet food, gives as a lord, a senior, a master. He says, 'I was such a one,' that is, one with the nature of a lord of giving.

Catūsu dvāresuti tassa kira rañño sindhavaraṭṭhaṃ sodhivākaraṭṭhanti dve raṭṭhāni ahesuṃ, nagaraṃ roruvaṃ nāma. Tassa ekekasmiṃ dvāre devasikaṃ satasahassaṃ uppajjati, antonagare vinicchayaṭṭhāne satasahassaṃ. So bahuhiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ rāsibhūtaṃ disvā kammassakatañāṇaṃ uppādetvā catūsu dvāresu [M 1.0106] dānasālāyo kāretvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ dvāre uṭṭhitaāyena dānaṃ dethāti amacce ṭhapesi. Tenāha – “catūsu dvāresu dānaṃ dīyitthā”ti.

“At the four gates”—it is said that this king had two kingdoms, the Sindhu country and the Sodhivāka country; his capital was named Roruva. At each gate, a hundred thousand in revenue arose daily, and another hundred thousand arose in the judgment hall within the city. Seeing vast heaps of gold and silver, he generated the knowledge that deeds are one’s own property, and had alms halls built at the four gates, appointing ministers and instructing them: “At each respective gate, give alms with the revenue that arises there.” Therefore, it is said: “Alms were given at the four gates.”

Samaṇabrāhmaṇakapaṇaddhikavanibbakayācakānanti ettha samaṇāti pabbajjūpagatā. Brāhmaṇāti bhovādino. Samitapāpabāhitapāpe pana samaṇabrāhmaṇe esa nālattha. Kapaṇāti duggatā daliddamanussā kāṇakuṇiādayo. Addhikāti pathāvino. Vanibbakāti ye “iṭṭhaṃ, dinnaṃ, kantaṃ, manāpaṃ, kālena, anavajjaṃ dinnaṃ, dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādeyya, gacchatu bhavaṃ brahmaloka”ntiādinā nayena [V 1.0103] dānassa vaṇṇaṃ thomayamānā vicaranti. Yācakāti ye “pasatamattaṃ detha, sarāvamattaṃ dethā”tiādīni ca vatvā yācamānā vicaranti. Itthāgārassa dānaṃ dīyitthāti paṭhamadvārassa laddhattā tattha uppajjanakasatasahasse aññampi dhanaṃ pakkhipitvā rañño amacce hāretvā attano amacce ṭhapetvā raññā dinnadānato rājitthiyo mahantataraṃ dānaṃ adaṃsu. Taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Mama dānaṃ paṭikkamīti yaṃ mama dānaṃ tattha dīyittha, taṃ paṭinivatti. Sesadvāresupi eseva nayo. Kocīti katthaci. Dīgharattanti asītivassasahassāni. Ettakaṃ kira kālaṃ tassa rañño dānaṃ dīyittha. Tatiyaṃ.

“To ascetics, brahmins, the poor, travelers, mendicants, and beggars”—here, “ascetics” means those who have gone forth into the ascetic life. “Brahmins” means those who use the term “bho.” However, that king did not find ascetics and brahmins who had pacified and dispelled evil. “The poor” means wretched, destitute people, such as the blind and the crippled. “Travelers” means wayfarers. “Mendicants” means those who wander about praising the virtue of giving, saying, “Given is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; given in due time, given faultlessly. May the giver’s mind be serene; may you, sir, go to the Brahmā-world,” and so forth. “Beggars” means those who wander about asking, saying, “Give a handful, give a small bowlful,” and so forth. “The alms of the women’s quarters were given”—because the first gate was obtained by them, and having added other wealth to the one hundred thousand of revenue arising there, and having dismissed the king’s ministers and appointed their own, the royal women gave a much greater gift than the gift given by the king. Referring to this, it was said. “My alms declined”—meaning, the alms that were given there by me diminished. The same principle applies to the other gates as well. “Somewhere”—in some place. “For a long time”—for eighty thousand years. It is said that the king’s alms were given for such a long time. The third.

105. Catutthaṃ vuttatthameva. Catutthaṃ.

105. The fourth has the meaning already stated. The fourth.

5. Jantusuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Jantu Sutta

106. Pañcame [P 1.0115] kosalesu viharantīti bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā tattha gantvā viharanti. Uddhatāti akappiye kappiyasaññitāya ca kappiye akappiyasaññitāya ca anavajje sāvajjasaññitāya ca sāvajje anavajjasaññitāya ca uddhaccapakatikā hutvā. Unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā, uṭṭhitatucchamānāti vuttaṃ hoti. Capalāti pattacīvaramaṇḍanādinā cāpallena yuttā. Mukharāti mukhakharā, kharavacanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vikiṇṇavācāti asaṃyatavacanā, divasampi niratthakavacanapalāpino. Muṭṭhassatinoti naṭṭhassatino sativirahitā, idha kataṃ ettha pamussanti. Asampajānāti nippaññā. Asamāhitāti appanāupacārasamādhirahitā, caṇḍasote [M 1.0107] baddhanāvāsadisā. Vibbhantacittāti anavaṭṭhitacittā, panthāruḷhabālamigasadisā. Pākatindriyāti saṃvarābhāvena gihikāle viya vivaṭaindriyā.

106. In the fifth. "Living among the Kosalans" (kosalesu viharanti) means: they took a meditation subject from the Blessed One and went there to dwell. "Restless" (uddhatā) means being of a restless nature, perceiving the improper as proper and the proper as improper, and perceiving the blameless as blameworthy and the blameworthy as blameless. "Haughty" (unnaḷā) means having a raised reed; it is said to mean "with inflated, empty conceit." "Fickle" (capalā) means endowed with fickleness through adorning bowls and robes, etc. "Loose-tongued" (mukharā) means harsh-mouthed; it is said to mean "uttering harsh words." "Scattered in speech" (vikiṇṇavācā) means with unrestrained speech, indulging in meaningless chatter all day. "Unmindful" (muṭṭhassatino) means with lost mindfulness, devoid of mindfulness; what was done here, they forget there. "Uncomprehending" (asampajānā) means lacking wisdom. "Unconcentrated" (asamāhitā) means devoid of attainment and access concentration, like a boat moored in a strong current. "Distracted in mind" (vibbhantacittā) means with unfixed minds, like a foolish deer led onto a path. "With unrestrained senses" (pākatindriyā) means with senses unguarded due to a lack of restraint, like householders.

Jantūti evaṃnāmako devaputto. Tadahuposatheti tasmiṃ ahu uposathe, uposathadivaseti attho. Pannaraseti cātuddasikādipaṭikkhepo. Upasaṅkamīti codanatthāya upagato. So kira cintesi – “ime bhikkhū satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nikkhantā, idāni pamattā viharanti, na kho panete pāṭiyekkaṃ nisinnaṭṭhāne codiyamānā kathaṃ gaṇhissanti, samāgamanakāle codissāmī”ti uposathadivase tesaṃ sannipatitabhāvaṃ ñatvā upasaṅkami. Gāthāhi ajjhabhāsīti sabbesaṃ majjhe ṭhatvā gāthā abhāsi.

"Jantu" is a devaputta so named. "On that observance day" means on that observance, that is, on the uposatha day. "The fifteenth" is the exclusion of the fourteenth and so on. "Approached" means he went near for the purpose of admonition. It is said that he thought: "These bhikkhus took a meditation subject from the Teacher and departed, but now they dwell heedlessly. Indeed, if they are admonished individually in their seated places, they will not accept the admonition. I will admonish them at the time of their assembly." Thus, knowing they had assembled on the observance day, he approached. "He addressed them with verses" means, standing in the midst of them all, he spoke the verses.

Tattha [V 1.0104] yasmā guṇakathāya saddhiṃ nigguṇassa aguṇo pākaṭo hoti, tasmā guṇaṃ tāva kathento sukhajīvino pure āsuntiādimāha. Tattha sukhajīvino pure āsunti pubbe bhikkhū supposā subharā [P 1.0116] ahesuṃ, uccanīcakulesu sapadānaṃ caritvā laddhena missakapiṇḍena yāpesunti adhippāyena evamāha. Anicchāti nittaṇhā hutvā.

Herein, because when a talk on virtue is being given, the lack of virtue of one without virtue becomes apparent, therefore, speaking first of virtue, he said the words beginning with, "In the past, they lived happily." Therein, as to "In the past, they lived happily": formerly, the bhikkhus were easy to support and easy to be maintained; they sustained themselves with whatever mixed alms-food was obtained by going on alms round from house to house among high and low families. With this intention, he spoke thus. As to "without desire": it means having become free from craving.

Evaṃ porāṇakabhikkhūnaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kathetvā idāni tesaṃ avaṇṇaṃ kathento dupposantiādimāha. Tattha gāme gāmaṇikā viyāti yathā gāme gāmakuṭā nānappakārena janaṃ pīḷetvā khīradadhitaṇḍulādīni āharāpetvā bhuñjanti, evaṃ tumhepi anesanāya ṭhitā tumhākaṃ jīvikaṃ kappethāti adhippāyena vadati. Nipajjantīti uddesaparipucchāmanasikārehi anatthikā hutvā sayanamhi hatthapāde vissajjetvā nipajjanti. Parāgāresūti paragehesu, kulasuṇhādīsūti attho. Mucchitāti kilesamucchāya mucchitā.

Thus, having spoken of the praise of the ancient bhikkhus, now, speaking of their dispraise, he said the words beginning with, "Difficult to support." Therein, as to "like village headmen in a village": just as in a village, corrupt headmen, having oppressed the people in various ways and caused milk, curd, rice, and so on to be brought, consume them, in the same way, you too, being established in improper seeking, maintain your livelihood. With this intention, he speaks. As to "they lie down": having become without need for learning the sacred text, questioning on its meaning, and contemplation, they lie down on their beds, having cast aside their hands and feet. As to "in others' homes": it means in others' houses; the meaning is among the clan's daughters-in-law and so on. As to "infatuated": it means infatuated with the intoxication of defilement.

Ekacceti vattabbayuttakeyeva. Apaviddhāti chaḍḍitakā. Anāthāti apatiṭṭhā. Petāti susāne chaḍḍitā kālaṅkatamanussā. Yathā hi susāne chaḍḍitā nānāsakuṇādīhi khajjanti, ñātakāpi nesaṃ nāthakiccaṃ na [M 1.0108] karonti, na rakkhanti, na gopayanti, evamevaṃ evarūpāpi ācariyupajjhāyādīnaṃ santikā ovādānusāsaniṃ na labhantīti apaviddhā anāthā, yathā petā, tatheva honti. Pañcamaṃ.

As to "some": it means only those who are fit to be admonished. As to "cast out": it means abandoned. As to "without protector": it means without support. As to "the departed": it means like dead human bodies abandoned in a charnel ground. For just as those abandoned in a charnel ground are eaten by various birds and so on, and their relatives do not perform the duty of a protector for them, do not protect them, do not guard them, in the very same way, these bhikkhus of such a kind, not receiving admonition and instruction from their teachers, preceptors, and so on, are abandoned and without protector; they are just like the departed. The fifth.

6. Rohitassasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Rohitassa Sutta

107. Chaṭṭhe yatthāti cakkavāḷalokassa ekokāse bhummaṃ. Na cavati na upapajjatīti idaṃ aparāparaṃ cutipaṭisandhivasena gahitaṃ. Gamanenāti padagamanena. Nāhaṃ taṃ lokassa antanti satthā saṅkhāralokassa antaṃ sandhāya vadati. Ñāteyyantiādīsu ñātabbaṃ, daṭṭhabbaṃ, pattabbanti attho.

107. In the sixth sutta, as to "where": it is a term in the locative case referring to one region of the world-sphere. This phrase "one does not pass away, one is not reborn" is taken to mean again and again by way of death and rebirth-linking. As to "by going": it means by going on foot. As for the words, "I... the end of the world," the Teacher speaks with reference to the end of the world of formations. In the words beginning with "to be known," the meaning is "to be known, to be seen, to be attained."

Iti devaputtena cakkavāḷalokassa anto pucchito, satthārā saṅkhāralokassa kathito. So pana attano pañhena saddhiṃ satthu byākaraṇaṃ sametīti saññāya pasaṃsanto acchariyantiādimāha.

Thus, the end of the world-sphere was asked by the devaputta; the end of the world of formations was explained by the Teacher. And that devaputta, perceiving that the Teacher’s explanation was in accord with his own question, wishing to praise, said, "Wonderful!" and so on.

Daḷhadhammoti [V 1.0105] daḷhadhanu, uttamappamāṇena dhanunā samannāgato. Dhanuggahoti dhanuācariyo. Susikkhitoti [P 1.0117] dasa dvādasa vassāni dhanusippaṃ sikkhito. Katahatthoti usabhappamāṇepi vālaggaṃ vijjhituṃ samatthabhāvena katahattho. Katūpāsanoti katasarakkhepo dassitasippo. Asanenāti kaṇḍena. Atipāteyyāti atikkameyya. Yāvatā so tālacchāyaṃ atikkameyya, tāvatā kālena ekacakkavāḷaṃ atikkamāmīti attano javasampattiṃ dasseti.

“Daḷhadhamma” means “firm-bowed,” endowed with a bow of the highest measure. “An archer” means a teacher of archery. “Well-trained” means having been trained in the art of archery for ten or twelve years. “Skilled-handed” means having a practiced hand from being capable of piercing a hair-tip even at the distance of an usabha. “Accomplished in practice” means one who has perfected the casting of arrows and displayed his art. “With an arrow” means with a shaft. “Could shoot beyond” means could pass beyond. “In the time that that arrow could pass beyond the shadow of a palm tree, in that much time I can pass beyond one world-sphere”—thus he displays his accomplishment in speed.

Puratthimā samuddā pacchimoti yathā puratthimasamuddā pacchimasamuddo dūre, evaṃ me dūre padavītihāro ahosīti vadati. So kira pācīnacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhito pādaṃ pasāretvā pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ akkamati, puna dutiyaṃ pādaṃ pasāretvā paracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ akkamati. Icchāgatanti icchā eva. Aññatrevāti nippapañcataṃ dasseti. Bhikkhācārakāle kiresa nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā anotatte mukhaṃ dhovitvā kāle sampatte uttarakurumhi piṇḍāya caritvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ nisinno bhattakiccaṃ karoti, tattha muhuttaṃ vissamitvā puna javati. Vassasatāyukoti tadā dīghāyukakālo hoti, ayaṃ pana vassasatāvasiṭṭhe [M 1.0109] āyumhi gamanaṃ ārabhi. Vassasatajīvīti taṃ vassasataṃ anantarāyena jīvanto. Antarāva kālaṅkatoti cakkavāḷalokassa antaṃ appatvā antarāva mato. So pana tattha kālaṃ katvāpi āgantvā imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe nibbatti. Appatvāti saṅkhāralokassa antaṃ appatvā. Dukkhassāti vaṭṭadukkhassa. Antakiriyanti pariyantakaraṇaṃ. Kaḷevareti attabhāve. Sasaññimhi samanaketi sasaññe sacitte. Lokanti dukkhasaccaṃ. Lokasamudayanti samudayasaccaṃ. Lokanirodhanti nirodhasaccaṃ. Paṭipadanti maggasaccaṃ. Iti – “nāhaṃ, āvuso, imāni cattāri saccāni tiṇakaṭṭhādīsu paññapemi[P 1.0118], imasmiṃ pana cātumahābhūtike kāyasmiṃ yeva paññapemī”ti dasseti. Samitāvīti samitapāpo. Nāsīsatīti na pattheti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“From the eastern ocean to the western” means: just as the western ocean is far from the eastern ocean, so too was my stride far, he says. It is said that he, standing at the edge of the eastern world-sphere, would stretch out his foot to step onto the edge of the western world-sphere; then, stretching out his second foot, he would step onto the edge of another world-sphere. “Gone by wish” means simply by wish. “Except for” shows the state of not being complacent. It is said that at the time for the alms-round, having chewed a tooth-stick of nāga-creeper wood and washed his mouth in Lake Anotatta, when the time came, he would go for alms in Uttarakuru, then sit at the edge of the world-sphere to perform the act of eating his meal. After resting there for a moment, he would speed on again. “With a lifespan of a hundred years” means: at that time, it was an era of long life, but this one began his journey when only a hundred years of his life remained. “Living a hundred years” means living for that hundred years without danger. “He passed away in between” means he died in between, without having reached the end of the world of world-spheres. But he, even having passed away there, came and was reborn in this very world-sphere. “Without having reached” means without having reached the end of the world of formations. “Of suffering” means of the suffering of the round of rebirth. “Making an end” means making a limit. “In this body” means in this existence. “With perception and with mind” means with perception and with consciousness. “The world” means the truth of suffering. “The origin of the world” means the truth of origin. “The cessation of the world” means the truth of cessation. “The path” means the truth of the path. Thus, it is shown: “Friend, I do not declare these four truths in things like grass and wood; rather, I declare them only in this body composed of the four great elements.” “One who is pacified” means one whose evil is pacified. “Does not long for” means does not desire. The sixth.

108-109. Sattamaṭṭhamāni vuttatthāneva. Sattamaṃ, aṭṭhamaṃ.

108-109. The seventh and eighth suttas have the meaning already stated. The seventh, the eighth.

9. Susimasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Susima Sutta

110. Navame tuyhampi no, ānanda, sāriputto ruccatīti satthā therassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetukāmo, vaṇṇo ca nāmesa visabhāgapuggalassa santike kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tassa santike kathito [V 1.0106] hi matthakaṃ na pāpuṇāti. So hi “asuko nāma bhikkhu sīlavā”ti vutte. “Kiṃ tassa sīlaṃ? Gorūpasīlo so. Kiṃ tayā añño sīlavā na diṭṭhapubbo”ti vā? “Paññavā”ti vutte, “kiṃ pañño so? Kiṃ tayā añño paññavā na diṭṭhapubbo”ti? Vā, ādīni vatvā vaṇṇakathāya antarāyaṃ karoti. Ānandatthero pana sāriputtattherassa sabhāgo, paṇītāni labhitvā therassa deti, attano upaṭṭhākadārake pabbājetvā therassa santike upajjhaṃ gaṇhāpeti, upasampādeti. Sāriputtattheropi ānandattherassa tatheva karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Aññamaññassa guṇesu pasīditvā. Ānandatthero hi – “amhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātiko ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ satasahassañca kappe pāramiyo pūretvā soḷasavidhaṃ paññaṃ paṭivijjhitvā dhammasenāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhito”ti therassa guṇesu pasīditvāva theraṃ mamāyati. Sāriputtattheropi – “sammāsambuddhassa mayā kattabbaṃ mukhodakadānādikiccaṃ sabbaṃ ānando karoti. Ānandaṃ nissāya ahaṃ icchiticchitaṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjituṃ labhāmī”ti āyasmato ānandassa guṇesu [M 1.0110] pasīditvāva taṃ mamāyati. Tasmā bhagavā sāriputtattherassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetukāmo ānandattherassa santike kathetuṃ āraddho.

110. In the ninth sutta, the Teacher, wishing to speak in praise of the Elder, was about to say: 'Ānanda, does Sāriputta please you?' Furthermore, this speaking of praise is not appropriate in the presence of a person of dissimilar nature. For if spoken in his presence, it does not reach its culmination. Indeed, when it is said, 'A monk of such-and-such a name is virtuous,' he might say, 'What is his virtue? He has the virtue of a cow. Have you not seen another virtuous person before?' Or, when it is said, 'He is wise,' he might say, 'What wisdom does he have? Have you not seen another wise person before?' and so on, thus creating an obstacle to the words of praise. The Elder Ānanda, however, is of the same nature as the Elder Sāriputta. Having received excellent requisites, he gives them to the Elder. Having caused the young sons of his own attendant lay-supporters to go forth, he has them take the Elder as their preceptor and receive the higher ordination from him. The Elder Sāriputta also does likewise for the Elder Ānanda. For what reason? Because they have faith in each other's virtues. Indeed, the Elder Ānanda, having faith in the Elder's virtues, cherishes him, thinking: 'Our elder brother, having fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons and having penetrated the sixteen-fold wisdom, is established in the position of General of the Dhamma.' The Elder Sāriputta also, having faith in the virtues of the Venerable Ānanda, cherishes him, thinking: 'Ānanda performs all the duties, such as offering water for washing the face, that should be performed by me for the Perfectly Enlightened One. Relying on Ānanda, I am able to enter into any meditative attainment I wish.' Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to speak in praise of the Elder Sāriputta, began to speak in the presence of the Elder Ānanda.

Tattha tuyhampīti sampiṇḍanattho pi-kāro. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “ānanda, sāriputtassa ācāro gocaro vihāro abhikkamo [P 1.0119] paṭikkamo ālokitavilokitaṃ samiñjitapasāraṇaṃ mayhaṃ ruccati, asītimahātherānaṃ ruccati, sadevakassa lokassa ruccati. Tuyhampi ruccatī”ti?

Therein, in the word 'tuyhampi,' the particle 'pi' has the meaning of gathering together. This is what is meant: 'Ānanda, Sāriputta’s conduct, his resort, his abiding, his going forward and returning, his looking straight ahead and looking from side to side, his bending and stretching—these are pleasing to me, pleasing to the eighty great elders, and pleasing to the world with its devas. Are they pleasing to you also?'

Tato thero sāṭakantare laddhokāso balavamallo viya tuṭṭhamānaso hutvā – “satthā mayhaṃ piyasahāyassa vaṇṇaṃ kathāpetukāmo. Labhissāmi no ajja, dīpadhajabhūtaṃ mahājambuṃ vidhunanto viya valāhakantarato candaṃ nīharitvā dassento viya sāriputtattherassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetu”nti cintetvā paṭhamataraṃ tāva catūhi padehi puggalapalāpe haranto kassa hi nāma, bhante, abālassātiādimāha. Bālo hi bālatāya, duṭṭho dosatāya, mūḷho mohena, vipallatthacitto ummattako cittavipallāsena vaṇṇaṃ “vaṇṇo”ti vā avaṇṇaṃ “avaṇṇe”ti vā, “ayaṃ buddho, ayaṃ sāvako”ti vā na jānāti. Abālādayo pana jānanti, tasmā abālassātiādimāha. Na rucceyyāti bālādīnaṃyeva hi so na rucceyya, na aññassa kassaci na rucceyya.

Then the Elder, having obtained an opportunity within the screen of his robe, like a mighty wrestler with a delighted mind, thought: 'The Teacher wishes to have the praise of my dear companion spoken. Today I shall surely have the opportunity to speak the praise of the Elder Sāriputta, as if shaking the great Jambu tree that is like a banner for the island, or as if drawing forth the moon from amidst the clouds and showing it.' Having thought thus, first clearing away the chaff-like individuals with four phrases, he spoke, beginning with, 'To whom indeed, venerable sir, who is not a fool...' For a fool, due to foolishness; a corrupt person, due to corruptness; a deluded person, due to delusion; and an insane person with a distorted mind, due to mental derangement, does not know praise as 'praise' or dispraise as 'dispraise,' nor 'This is the Buddha, this is a disciple.' But those who are not fools and so on do know; therefore, he spoke beginning with 'for one who is not a fool...' As for 'he would not be pleasing': indeed, he would not be pleasing only to fools and so on; to whom else would he not be pleasing?

Evaṃ [V 1.0107] puggalapalāpe haritvā idāni soḷasahi padehi yathābhūtaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kathento paṇḍito, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha paṇḍitoti paṇḍiccena samannāgato, catūsu kosallesu ṭhitassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu dhātukusalo ca hoti āyatanakusalo ca paṭiccasamuppādakusalo ca ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalo ca, ettāvatā kho, ānanda, ‘paṇḍito bhikkhū’ti alaṃ vacanāyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.124). Mahāpaññotiādīsu mahāpaññādīhi samannāgatoti attho. Tatridaṃ mahāpaññādīnaṃ nānattaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.4) – katamā mahāpaññā? Mahante sīlakkhandhe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā, mahante samādhikkhandhe, paññākkhandhe, vimuttikkhandhe, vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhe pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā. Mahantāni ṭhānāṭṭhānāni, mahāvihārasamāpattiyo, mahantāni ariyasaccāni, mahante satipaṭṭhāne, sammappadhāne, iddhipāde, mahantāni indriyāni, balāni, bojjhaṅgāni, mahante [M 1.0111] ariyamagge[P 1.0120], mahantāni sāmaññaphalāni, mahāabhiññāyo, mahantaṃ paramatthaṃ nibbānaṃ pariggaṇhātīti mahāpaññā.

Having thus removed the persons who are like chaff, now, speaking the praise truthfully by means of sixteen terms, he began with 'Wise, venerable sir,' and so on. Herein, 'wise' means one endowed with wisdom; this is the name for one established in the four kinds of expertise. For this was said: 'When, Ānanda, a monk is skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible, to that extent, Ānanda, he is fit to be called a wise monk.' In the phrases like 'of great wisdom,' the meaning is 'endowed with great wisdom' and so on. Herein is the distinction of great wisdom and the rest: What is great wisdom? Because it comprehends the great aggregate of virtue, it is great wisdom; because it comprehends the great aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, it is great wisdom. Because it comprehends the great possibilities and impossibilities, the great meditative attainments of abiding, the great Noble Truths, the great foundations of mindfulness, the right strivings, the bases of psychic power, the great faculties, powers, and enlightenment factors, the great Noble Path, the great fruits of recluseship, the great direct knowledges, and the great ultimate reality, Nibbāna, it is great wisdom.

Sā pana therassa devorohanaṃ katvā saṅkassanagaradvāre ṭhitena satthārā puthujjanapañcake pañhe pucchite taṃ vissajjentassa pākaṭā jātā.

That great wisdom of the Elder, however, became manifest when the Teacher, having descended from the deva realm and standing at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa, asked a question concerning the five kinds of worldlings, and the Elder answered it.

Katamā puthupaññā? Puthu nānākhandhesu, (ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti puthupaññā.) Puthu nānādhātūsu, puthu nānāāyatanesu, puthu nānāpaṭiccasamuppādesu, puthu nānāsuññatamanupalabbhesu, puthu nānāatthesu, dhammesu niruttīsu paṭibhānesu, puthu nānāsīlakkhandhesu, puthu nānāsamādhi-paññāvimutti-vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhesu, puthu nānāṭhānāṭṭhānesu, puthu nānāvihārasamāpattīsu, puthu nānāariyasaccesu, puthu nānāsatipaṭṭhānesu, sammappadhānesu, iddhipādesu, indriyesu, balesu, bojjhaṅgesu, puthu nānāariyamaggesu, sāmaññaphalesu, abhiññāsu, puthu nānājanasādhāraṇe dhamme samatikkamma paramatthe nibbāne ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti puthupaññā.

What is extensive wisdom? Knowledge operates in the various diverse aggregates, thus it is extensive wisdom. Knowledge operates in the various diverse elements, in the various diverse sense bases, in the various diverse dependent originations, in the various diverse unapprehended emptinesses, in the various diverse results, causes, expressions, and analytical knowledges; in the various diverse aggregates of virtue; in the various diverse aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation; in the various diverse possible and impossible situations; in the various diverse abidings and attainments; in the various diverse Noble Truths; in the various diverse foundations of mindfulness, right exertions, bases of psychic power, faculties, powers, and enlightenment factors; in the various diverse Noble Paths, fruits of recluseship, and higher knowledges. Having transcended the various states common to ordinary people, the knowledge that operates in the ultimate reality, Nibbāna, is extensive wisdom.

Katamā hāsapaññā? Idhekacco hāsabahulo vedabahulo tuṭṭhibahulo pāmojjabahulo sīlaṃ paripūreti, indriyasaṃvaraṃ paripūreti, bhojane mattaññutaṃ, jāgariyānuyogaṃ, sīlakkhandhaṃ, samādhikkhandhaṃ, paññākkhandhaṃ, vimuttikkhandhaṃ, vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhaṃ paripūretīti, hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo pāmojjabahulo ṭhānāṭṭhānaṃ paṭivijjhatīti hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo vihārasamāpattiyo paripūretīti hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati. Satipaṭṭhāne[V 1.0108], sammappadhāne, iddhipāde, indriyāni, balāni[P 1.0121], bojjhaṅgāni, ariyamaggaṃ bhāvetīti hāsapaññā. Hāsabahulo sāmaññaphalāni sacchikaroti, abhiññāyo paṭivijjhatīti hāsapaññā, hāsabahulo vedatuṭṭhipāmojjabahulo paramatthaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarotīti hāsapaññā.

What is joyful wisdom? Here, a certain person who is often joyful, often full of delight, often full of satisfaction, and often full of gladness, fulfills virtue, fulfills sense restraint, moderation in eating, and devotion to wakefulness; he fulfills the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—this is joyful wisdom. Being often joyful and full of gladness, one penetrates what is possible and impossible—this is joyful wisdom. Being often joyful, one fulfills the abidings and attainments—this is joyful wisdom. Being often joyful, one penetrates the Noble Truths. One develops the foundations of mindfulness, the right exertions, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Path—this is joyful wisdom. Being often joyful, one realizes the fruits of recluseship and penetrates the higher knowledges—this is joyful wisdom. Being often joyful, full of delight, satisfaction, and gladness, one realizes the ultimate reality, Nibbāna—this is joyful wisdom.

Thero ca sarado nāma tāpaso hutvā anomadassissa bhagavato pādamūle aggasāvakapatthanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Taṃkālato paṭṭhāya hāsabahulo sīlaparipūraṇādīni akāsīti hāsapañño.

The elder named Sarada, having become an ascetic, made the aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Anomadassi for the position of chief disciple. From that time onward, being full of joy, he fulfilled virtue and so on; thus, he was one of joyful wisdom.

Katamā [M 1.0112] javanapaññā? Yaṃkiñci rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Dukkhato khippaṃ, anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Yā kāci vedanā…pe… yā kāci saññā… ye keci saṅkhārā… yaṃkiñci viññāṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… sabbaṃ viññāṇaṃ aniccato, dukkhato, anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Cakkhu…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccato, dukkhato, anattato khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena, dukkhaṃ bhayaṭṭhena, anattā asārakaṭṭhenāti tulayitvā tīrayitvā vibhāvayitvā vibhūtaṃ katvā rūpanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Vedanā… saññā… saṅkhārā… viññāṇaṃ… cakkhu…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ aniccaṃ khayaṭṭhena…pe… vibhūtaṃ katvā jarāmaraṇanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā. Rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ. Cakkhu…pe… jarāmaraṇaṃ aniccaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammanti [P 1.0122] tulayitvā tīrayitvā vibhāvayitvā vibhūtaṃ katvā jarāmaraṇanirodhe nibbāne khippaṃ javatīti javanapaññā.

What is swift wisdom? Whatever form is past, future, or present… whether it is far or near, one swiftly penetrates and knows all that form as impermanent; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. One swiftly penetrates and knows it as suffering and as non-self; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever formations… whatever consciousness is past, future, or present… one swiftly penetrates and knows all that consciousness as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. The eye… up to… aging-and-death, being past, future, or present, one swiftly penetrates and knows it as impermanent, as suffering, and as non-self; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Having weighed, investigated, made manifest, and made evident thus: 'Form that is past, future, or present is impermanent in the sense of perishing, suffering in the sense of fear, and non-self in the sense of being without substance,' one swiftly penetrates and knows Nibbāna, the cessation of form; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Feeling… perception… formations… consciousness… the eye… up to… aging-and-death, being past, future, or present, is impermanent in the sense of perishing… up to… having made it evident, one swiftly penetrates and knows Nibbāna, the cessation of aging-and-death; therefore, it is called swift wisdom. Form that is past, future, or present… up to… consciousness; the eye… up to… aging-and-death. Having weighed, investigated, made manifest, and made evident thus: 'It is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, of a nature to perish, of a nature to vanish, of a nature to fade away, and of a nature to cease,' one swiftly penetrates and knows Nibbāna, the cessation of aging-and-death; therefore, it is called swift wisdom.

Katamā tikkhapaññā? Khippaṃ kilese chindatīti tikkhapaññā. Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti, uppannaṃ byāpādavitakkaṃ… uppannaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ… uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme… uppannaṃ rāgaṃ… dosaṃ… mohaṃ… kodhaṃ… upanāhaṃ… makkhaṃ… paḷāsaṃ… issaṃ… macchariyaṃ… māyaṃ… sāṭheyyaṃ… thambhaṃ… sārambhaṃ… mānaṃ… atimānaṃ… madaṃ… pamādaṃ… sabbe kilese… sabbe duccarite… sabbe abhisaṅkhāre… sabbe bhavagāmikamme nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti, byantīkaroti, anabhāvaṃ gametīti tikkhapaññā. Ekasmiṃ āsane [V 1.0109] cattāro ca ariyamaggā, cattāri ca sāmaññaphalāni, catasso ca paṭisambhidāyo, cha ca abhiññāyo adhigatā honti sacchikatā phassitā paññāyāti tikkhapaññā.

What is sharp wisdom? It is called sharp wisdom because it quickly cuts off the defilements. One does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensuality, an arisen thought of ill will, an arisen thought of harm, or other arisen evil, unwholesome states; nor arisen lust, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, rivalry, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, stubbornness, contention, conceit, arrogance, vanity, or heedlessness. One does not tolerate any defilements, any misconduct, any volitional formations, or any kamma leading to states of becoming; one abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings them to non-existence—therefore, it is called sharp wisdom. In a single sitting, the four noble paths, the four fruits of recluseship, the four analytical knowledges, and the six super-knowledges are attained, realized, and experienced by wisdom—therefore, it is called sharp wisdom.

Thero ca bhāgineyyassa dīghanakhaparibbājakassa vedanāpariggahasutte desiyamāne ṭhitakova sabbakilese chinditvā sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ paṭividdhakālato paṭṭhāya tikkhapañño nāma jāto. Tenāha – “tikkhapañño, bhante, āyasmā sāriputto”ti.

And the Elder, while standing as the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being taught to his nephew, the wanderer Dīghanakha, cut off all defilements. From the time he penetrated the knowledge of a disciple's perfection, he became one of sharp wisdom. Therefore, it was said: 'Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is of sharp wisdom.'

Katamā [M 1.0113] nibbedhikapaññā? Idhekacco sabbasaṅkhāresu ubbegabahulo hoti uttāsabahulo ukkaṇṭhanabahulo aratibahulo anabhiratibahulo bahimukho na ramati sabbasaṅkhāresu, anibbiddhapubbaṃ appadālitapubbaṃ lobhakkhandhaṃ nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikapaññā. Anibbiddhapubbaṃ appadālitapubbaṃ dosakkhandhaṃ… mohakkhandhaṃ… kodhaṃ… upanāhaṃ…pe… sabbe bhavagāmikamme nibbijjhati padāletīti nibbedhikapaññā.

What is penetrating wisdom? Here, a certain one has much agitation towards all conditioned phenomena, much dread, much aversion, much displeasure, and much disinclination. With his mind turned outwards, he does not delight in any conditioned phenomena. The aggregate of greed, not previously pierced, not previously split, he pierces and splits—therefore, it is called penetrating wisdom. The aggregate of hatred, not previously pierced, not previously split… the aggregate of delusion… anger… resentment… all kamma leading to states of becoming, he pierces and splits—therefore, it is called penetrating wisdom.

Appicchoti santaguṇaniguhanatā, paccayapaṭiggahaṇe ca mattaññutā, etaṃ appicchalakkhaṇanti iminā lakkhaṇena samannāgato. Santuṭṭhoti catūsu paccayesu yathālābhasantoso yathābalasantoso yathāsāruppasantosoti, imehi tīhi santosehi samannāgato. Pavivittoti kāyaviveko ca [P 1.0123] vivekaṭṭhakāyānaṃ nekkhammābhiratānaṃ, cittaviveko ca parisuddhacittānaṃ paramavodānappattānaṃ, upadhiviveko ca nirupadhīnaṃ puggalānaṃ visaṅkhāragatānanti, imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ lābhī. Asaṃsaṭṭhoti dassanasaṃsaggo savanasaṃsaggo samullapanasaṃsaggo paribhogasaṃsaggo kāyasaṃsaggoti, imehi pañcahi saṃsaggehi virahito. Ayañca pañcavidho saṃsaggo rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi upāsakehi upasikāhi bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhīti aṭṭhahi puggalehi saddhiṃ jāyati, so sabbopi therassa natthīti asaṃsaṭṭho.

Being of few wishes means concealing one's existing good qualities and knowing the measure in accepting requisites—he is endowed with this characteristic.
