Being satisfied means he is endowed with these three kinds of contentment regarding the four requisites: contentment with whatever is obtained, contentment according to one's strength, and contentment with what is suitable. Being secluded means he is a gainer of these three kinds of seclusion: bodily seclusion, for those whose bodies are secluded and who delight in renunciation; mental seclusion, for those with purified minds who have attained supreme purity; and seclusion from the substrata of existence, for individuals without substrata who have reached the unconditioned. Being unassociated means being devoid of these five kinds of association: by seeing, by hearing, by conversation, by shared use, and by bodily contact. This fivefold association arises with eight types of people: kings, royal ministers, heretics, their disciples, male and female lay followers, monks, and nuns. The Elder has none of these at all; thus, he is unassociated.

Āraddhavīriyoti paggahitavīriyo paripuṇṇavīriyo. Tattha āraddhavīriyo bhikkhu gamane uppannakilesassa ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na deti, ṭhāne uppannassa nisajjaṃ, nisajjāya uppannassa seyyaṃ pāpuṇituṃ na deti, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ iriyāpathe uppannaṃ tattha tattheva niggaṇhāti. Thero pana catucattālīsa vassāni mañce piṭṭhiṃ na pasāreti. Taṃ sandhāya “āraddhavīriyo”ti āha. Vattāti [V 1.0110] odhunanavattā. Bhikkhūnaṃ ajjhācāraṃ disvā “ajja kathessāmi, sve kathessāmī”ti kathāvavatthānaṃ na karoti, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ yeva ṭhāne ovadati anusāsatīti attho.

Being energetic means one whose energy is exerted and perfected. In this regard, an energetic monk does not allow an arisen defilement to reach a standing position while walking; nor to reach a sitting position while standing; nor to reach a lying down position while sitting. He suppresses it right then and there, in that very posture in which it arose. Furthermore, the Elder for forty-four years did not stretch his back on a couch. It is with reference to this that it was said, 'energetic'. Being an admonisher means one who speaks for the sake of dispelling faults. Seeing a transgression by the monks, he does not postpone the admonishment, thinking, 'I will speak today,' or 'I will speak tomorrow.' Rather, in that very place, he admonishes and instructs; this is the meaning.

Vacanakkhamoti vacanaṃ khamati. Eko hi parassa ovādaṃ deti, sayaṃ pana aññena ovadiyamāno kujjhati. Thero pana parassapi ovādaṃ deti, sayaṃ [M 1.0114] ovadiyamānopi sirasā sampaṭicchati. Ekadivasaṃ kira sāriputtattheraṃ sattavassiko sāmaṇero – “bhante, sāriputta, tumhākaṃ nivāsanakaṇṇo olambatī”ti āha. Thero kiñci avatvāva ekamantaṃ gantvā parimaṇḍalaṃ nivāsetvā āgamma “ettakaṃ vaṭṭati ācariyā”ti añjaliṃ paggayha aṭṭhāsi.

Patient in speech means he is patient with words. For a certain person gives instruction to another, but when he himself is instructed by another, he becomes angry. The Elder, however, both gives instruction to others and, when he himself is instructed, accepts it with his head. Indeed, one day, a seven-year-old novice said to the Elder Sāriputta, "Venerable Sāriputta, the corner of your lower robe is hanging down." The Elder, without saying anything, went to one side, arranged his lower robe to be even all around, came back, and raising his joined hands in reverence, stood and said, "Teacher, is this much appropriate?"

“Tadahu pabbajito santo, jātiyā sattavassiko;

Sopi maṃ anusāseyya, sampaṭicchāmi matthake”ti. (mi. pa. 6.4.8) –

"Though ordained on this very day, and but seven years of age by birth; even he may instruct me—I accept it upon my head."

Āha.

He said.

Codakoti [P 1.0124] vatthusmiṃ otiṇṇe vā anotiṇṇe vā vītikkamaṃ disvā – “āvuso, bhikkhunā nāma evaṃ nivāsetabbaṃ, evaṃ pārupitabbaṃ, evaṃ gantabbaṃ, evaṃ ṭhātabbaṃ, evaṃ nisīditabbaṃ, evaṃ khāditabbaṃ, evaṃ bhuñjitabba”nti tantivasena anusiṭṭhiṃ deti.

"One who reproves" means that, having seen a transgression—whether the matter has been brought up or not—he gives instruction by means of the scripture, saying: "Friend, a monk should wear his lower robe thus, should wear his upper robe thus, should walk thus, should eat hard food thus, should eat soft food thus."

Pāpagarahīti pāpapuggale na passe, na tesaṃ vacanaṃ suṇe, tehi saddhiṃ ekacakkavāḷepi na vaseyyaṃ.

"One who censures evil" is one who thinks: "May I not see evil persons; may I not hear their words; may I not live together with them even in a single world-system."

“Mā me kadāci pāpiccho, kusīto hīnavīriyo;

Appassuto anādaro, sameto ahu katthacī”ti. –

"May I never, anywhere, be associated with one who has evil desires, is lazy, of deficient energy, has little learning, or is disrespectful."

Evaṃ pāpapuggalepi garahati, “samaṇena nāma rāgavasikena dosamohavasikena na hotabbaṃ, uppanno rāgo doso moho pahātabbo”ti evaṃ pāpadhammepi garahatīti dvīhi kāraṇehi “pāpagarahī, bhante, āyasmā sāriputto”ti vadati.

Thus, he censures evil persons. And saying, "A monk should not be under the sway of lust, hatred, and delusion; arisen lust, hatred, and delusion should be abandoned," he thus also censures evil states. For these two reasons, it is said: "Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is a censurer of evil."

Evaṃ [V 1.0111] āyasmatā ānandena soḷasahi padehi therassa yathābhūtavaṇṇappakāsane kate – “kiṃ ānando attano piyasahāyassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetuṃ na labhati, kathetu kiṃ pana tena kathitaṃ tatheva hoti, kiṃ so sabbaññū”ti? Koci pāpapuggalo vattuṃ mā labhatūti satthā taṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ akuppaṃ sabbaññubhāsitaṃ karonto jinamuddikāya lañchanto evametantiādimāha.

Thus, when the Venerable Ānanda had made a declaration of the Elder's true qualities with sixteen terms, the Teacher—lest any wicked person should say: “Does Ānanda not get to praise his dear friend? Let him speak, but how could what is said by him be just so? Is he omniscient?”—making that utterance of praise unassailable, as something spoken by the Omniscient One, and sealing it with the Victor's seal, spoke the words beginning with, 'So it is...'

Evaṃ [M 1.0115] tathāgatena ca ānandattherena ca mahātherassa vaṇṇe kathiyamāne bhumaṭṭhakā devatā uṭṭhahitvā eteheva soḷasahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Tato ākāsaṭṭhakadevatā sītavalāhakā uṇhavalāhakā cātumahārājikāti yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā devatā uṭṭhahitvā eteheva soḷasahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Etenupāyena ekacakkavāḷaṃ ādiṃ katvā dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu devatā uṭṭhahitvā kathayiṃsu. Athāyasmato sāriputtassa saddhivihāriko susīmo devaputto cintesi – “imā devatā attano attano nakkhattakīḷaṃ pahāya [P 1.0125] tattha tattha gantvā mayhaṃ upajjhāyasseva vaṇṇaṃ kathenti, gacchāmi tathāgatassa santikaṃ, gantvā etadeva vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ devatābhāsitaṃ karomī”ti, so tathā akāsi. Taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho susīmotiādi vuttaṃ.

Thus, while the Tathāgata and the Elder Ānanda were speaking in praise of the great Elder, the earth-dwelling deities rose up and spoke praise with these very same sixteen terms. Then the sky-dwelling deities, the cool-cloud deities, the hot-cloud deities, the deities of the Four Great Kings, and so on up to the deities of the Akaniṭṭha Brahmā world rose up and spoke praise with these very same sixteen terms. In this way, beginning with one world-system, deities in ten thousand world-systems rose up and spoke praise. Then the devaputta Susīma, a co-resident of the Venerable Sāriputta, thought: “These deities, abandoning their own celestial amusements, have gone to those places and are speaking in praise of my preceptor only. I shall go to the presence of the Tathāgata and, having gone, I will make this very same utterance of praise that was spoken by the deities.” And so he did. To show this, the passage beginning “Then the devaputta Susīma...” was spoken.

Uccāvacāti aññesu ṭhānesu paṇītaṃ uccaṃ vuccati, hīnaṃ avacaṃ. Idha pana uccāvacāti nānāvidhā vaṇṇanibhā. Tassā kira devaparisāya nīlaṭṭhānaṃ atinīlaṃ, pītakaṭṭhānaṃ atipītakaṃ, lohitaṭṭhānaṃ atilohitaṃ, odātaṭṭhānaṃ accodātanti, catubbidhā vaṇṇanibhā pātubhavi. Teneva seyyathāpi nāmāti catasso upamā āgatā. Tattha subhoti sundaro. Jātimāti jātisampanno. Suparikammakatoti dhovanādiparikammena suṭṭhu parikammakato. Paṇḍukambale nikkhittoti rattakambale ṭhapito. Evamevanti rattakambale nikkhittamaṇi viya sabbā ekappahāreneva virocituṃ āraddhā. Nikkhanti atirekapañcasuvaṇṇena katapiḷandhanaṃ. Tañhi ghaṭṭanamajjanakkhamaṃ hoti. Jambonadanti mahājambusākhāya pavattanadiyaṃ nibbattaṃ, mahājambuphalarase vā pathaviyaṃ paviṭṭhe suvaṇṇaṅkurā uṭṭhahanti, tena suvaṇṇena katapiḷandhanantipi attho. Dakkhakammāraputtaukkāmukhasukusalasampahaṭṭhanti sukusalena kammāraputtena ukkāmukhe pacitvā sampahaṭṭhaṃ. Dhātuvibhaṅge (ma. ni. 3.357 ādayo) akatabhaṇḍaṃ gahitaṃ, idha pana katabhaṇḍaṃ.

High and low: In other places, the excellent is called 'high', and the inferior 'low'. Here, however, 'high and low' refers to various kinds of radiance. In that divine assembly, it is said that the blue areas were extremely blue, the yellow areas extremely yellow, the red areas extremely red, and the white areas exceedingly white—thus, four kinds of radiance appeared. Therefore, four similes are given, introduced by the phrase 'just as.' Therein, 'subho' means beautiful. 'Jātimā' means endowed with good qualities. 'Suparikammakato' means well-prepared through processes like washing and polishing. 'Paṇḍukambale nikkhitto' means placed on a red blanket. Similarly—like a gem placed on a red blanket, all at once began to shine brilliantly. 'Nikkha' refers to an ornament made with an excess of five suvaṇṇas of gold. For it can withstand rubbing and polishing. 'Jambonada' means produced in the river that flows from the great Jambu tree branch, or when the juice of the great Jambu fruit enters the ground, golden sprouts arise; the meaning is also an ornament made with that gold. 'Dakkhakammāraputtaukkāmukhasukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ' means smelted in a furnace and well-wrought by a very skilled smith's son. In the Dhātuvibhaṅga (MN 3.357, etc.), unworked material is taken, but here worked material is meant.

Viddheti dūrībhūte. Deveti ākāse. Nabhaṃ abbhussakkamānoti ākāsaṃ abhilaṅghanto. Iminā [V 1.0112] taruṇasūriyabhāvo dassito. Soratoti [M 1.0116] soraccena samannāgato. Dantoti nibbisevano. Satthuvaṇṇābhatoti [P 1.0126] satthārā ābhatavaṇṇo. Satthā hi aṭṭhaparisamajjhe nisīditvā “sevatha, bhikkhave, sāriputtamoggallāne”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.371) nayena therassa vaṇṇaṃ āharīti thero ābhatavaṇṇo nāma hoti. Kālaṃ kaṅkhatīti parinibbānakālaṃ pattheti. Khīṇāsavo hi neva maraṇaṃ abhinandati, na jīvitaṃ pattheti, divasasaṅkhepaṃ vetanaṃ gahetvā ṭhitapuriso viya kālaṃ pana pattheti, olokento tiṭṭhatīti attho. Tenevāha –

'Viddhe' means having gone far away. 'Deve' means in the sky. 'Nabhaṃ abbhussakkamāno' means soaring into the sky. By this, the state of the newly risen sun is shown. 'Sorato' means endowed with meekness. 'Danto' means without venom. 'Satthuvaṇṇābhato' means one whose virtue has been brought forth by the Teacher. For the Teacher, seated amidst the eight assemblies, brought forth the elder's virtue by the method beginning with, "Monks, associate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna" (MN 3.371). Thus, the elder is called 'one whose virtue has been brought forth'. 'Kālaṃ kaṅkhati' means he longs for the time of final Nibbāna. For one whose taints are destroyed neither rejoices in death nor longs for life; but like a hired worker who has received his wages for the day, he longs for the time, looking on. This is the meaning. Therefore, he said:

“Nābhinandāmi maraṇaṃ, nābhinandāmi jīvitaṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, nibbisaṃ bhatako yathā”ti. (theragā. 1001-1002); Navamaṃ;

“I do not welcome death, I do not welcome life; I await the time, like a hired worker who has received his wages.” (Thag. 1001-1002). The ninth.

10. Nānātitthiyasāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Discourse on Disciples of Various Sects

111. Dasame nānātitthiyasāvakāti te kira kammavādino ahesuṃ, tasmā dānādīni puññāni katvā sagge nibbattā, te “attano attano satthari pasādena nibbattamhā”ti saññino hutvā “gacchāma dasabalassa santike ṭhatvā amhākaṃ satthārānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kathessāmā”ti āgantvā paccekagāthāhi kathayiṃsu. Tattha chinditamāriteti chindite ca mārite ca. Hatajānīsūti pothane ca dhanajānīsu ca. Puññaṃ vā panāti attano puññampi na samanupassati, saṅkhepato puññāpuññānaṃ vipāko natthīti vadati. Sa ve vissāsamācikkhīti so – “evaṃ katapāpānampi katapuññānampi vipāko natthī”ti vadanto sattānaṃ vissāsaṃ avassayaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ ācikkhati, tasmā mānanaṃ vandanaṃ pūjanaṃ arahatīti vadati.

111. In the tenth discourse, regarding the “disciples of various sects”—it is said that they were proponents of kamma. Therefore, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, they were reborn in heaven. Thinking, “We were reborn through faith in our own teachers,” they came intending to stand before the One with Ten Powers and proclaim the virtues of their teachers, and they spoke in individual verses. Therein, 'chinditamārite' means in cutting and in killing. 'Hatajānīsu' means in beating and in loss of wealth. 'Puññaṃ vā pana'—he does not even see his own merit; in short, he says there is no result of merit or demerit. 'Sa ve vissāsamācikkhī'—he, saying, “Thus, there is no result for evil deeds done nor for meritorious deeds done,” declares to beings confidence, a refuge, and a foundation. Therefore, he says that such a person is worthy of honor, veneration, and reverence.

Tapojigucchāyāti kāyakilamathatapena pāpajigucchanena. Susaṃvutattoti samannāgato pihito vā. Jegucchīti tapena pāpajigucchako. Nipakoti paṇḍito. Cātuyāmasusaṃvutoti cātuyāmena susaṃvuto. Cātuyāmo [P 1.0127] nāma sabbavārivārito ca hoti sabbavāriyutto ca sabbavāridhuto ca sabbavāriphuṭo cāti ime cattāro koṭṭhāsā. Tattha sabbavārivāritoti vāritasabbaudako, paṭikkhittasabbasītodakoti attho. So kira sītodake sattasaññī hoti[M 1.0117], tasmā taṃ na valañjeti. Sabbavāriyuttoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena yuto. Sabbavāridhutoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena dhutapāpo[V 1.0113]. Sabbavāriphuṭoti sabbena pāpavāraṇena phuṭṭho. Diṭṭhaṃ sutañca ācikkhanti diṭṭhaṃ “diṭṭhaṃ me”ti sutaṃ “sutaṃ me”ti ācikkhanto, na niguhanto. Na hi nūna kibbisīti evarūpo satthā kibbisakārako nāma na hoti.

“By austerity and disgust” means by the ascetic practice of bodily mortification and by disgust for evil. “Well-restrained” means endowed with, or guarded. “Disgusted” means one who is disgusted with evil through ascetic practice. “Wise” means intelligent. “Well-restrained in the fourfold restraint” means well-restrained by the fourfold restraint. The fourfold restraint is so called: he is restrained from all water, he is endowed with restraint from all evil, he is one whose evil is shaken off by restraint from all evil, and he is touched by restraint from all evil—these are the four divisions. Herein, “restrained from all water” means one who has refrained from all water, who has rejected all cool water; this is the meaning. It is said that he perceives beings in cool water; therefore, he does not use it. “Endowed with restraint from all evil” means endowed with restraint from all evil. “One whose evil is shaken off by restraint from all evil” means one whose evil is shaken off by restraint from all evil. “Touched by restraint from all evil” means touched by restraint from all evil. “They declare what is seen and heard” means declaring what is seen as “this is seen by me” and what is heard as “this is heard by me,” not concealing. Surely, such a teacher is not an evildoer.

Nānātitthiyeti so kira nānātitthiyānaṃyeva upaṭṭhāko, tasmā te ārabbha vadati. Pakudhako kātiyānoti pakudho kaccāyano. Nigaṇṭhoti nāṭaputto. Makkhalipūraṇāseti makkhali ca pūraṇo ca. Sāmaññappattāti samaṇadhamme koṭippattā. Na hi nūna teti sappurisehi na dūre, teyeva loke sappurisāti vadati. Paccabhāsīti “ayaṃ ākoṭako imesaṃ nagganissirikānaṃ dasabalassa santike ṭhatvā vaṇṇaṃ kathetīti tesaṃ avaṇṇaṃ kathessāmī”ti patiabhāsīti.

“Of various sects” means he was, it is said, an attendant of various sectarians; therefore, he speaks concerning them. “Pakudha Kātiyāna” means Pakudha Kaccāyana. “Nigaṇṭha” means Nāṭaputta. “Makkhalī and Pūraṇa” means Makkhalī and Pūraṇa. “Attained to asceticism” means having reached the peak of the ascetic life. “Surely not far from them” means not far from those good people; they alone are the good people in the world—so he says. “He replied” means thinking, “This Ākoṭaka, standing in the presence of the One with Ten Powers, speaks in praise of these inglorious naked sectarians; therefore, I will speak disparagingly of them,” he recited in response.

Tattha sahācaritenāti saha caritamattena. Chavo sigāloti lāmako kālasigālo. Kotthukoti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Saṅkassarācāroti āsaṅkitasamācāro. Na sataṃ sarikkhoti paṇḍitānaṃ sappurisānaṃ sadiso na hoti, kiṃ tvaṃ kālasigālasadise titthiye sīhe karosīti?

Herein, “by a lion's bearing” means merely by making a sound like a lion's. “A wretched jackal” means a lowly black jackal. “Kotthuka” is a synonym for the same. “Of suspect conduct” means one whose conduct is suspect. “Not like the good” means he is not like the wise, good people. Why do you make lions of these sectarians, who are like black jackals?

Anvāvisitvāti “ayaṃ evarūpānaṃ satthārānaṃ avaṇṇaṃ katheti, teneva naṃ mukhena vaṇṇaṃ kathāpessāmī”ti cintetvā tassa sarīre anuāvisi adhimucci, evaṃ anvāvisitvā. Āyuttāti tapojigucchane yuttapayuttā. Pālayaṃ pavivekiyanti pavivekaṃ pālayantā. Te kira “nhāpitapavivekaṃ pālessāmā”ti [P 1.0128] sayaṃ kese luñcanti. “Cīvarapavivekaṃ pātessāmā”ti naggā vicaranti. “Piṇḍapātapavivekaṃ pālessāmā”ti sunakhā viya bhūmiyaṃ vā bhuñjanti hatthesu vā. “Senāsanapavivekaṃ pālessāmā”ti kaṇṭakaseyyādīni kappenti. Rūpe niviṭṭhāti taṇhādiṭṭhīhi rūpe patiṭṭhitā. Devalokābhinandinoti devalokapatthanakāmā. Mātiyāti maccā, te ve maccā paralokatthāya sammā anusāsantīti vadati.

“Having entered” means: thinking, “This one speaks dispraise of such teachers; I will make him speak praise through that very mouth,” he stayed as if having entered his body and took control of him. Thus, “having entered.” “Devoted” means they are thoroughly engaged in austerity and aversion to evil. “Guarding seclusion” means they are guarding seclusion. It is said that thinking, “We will guard the seclusion from razors,” they pluck out their own hair. Thinking, “We will guard the seclusion from robes,” they wander naked. Thinking, “We will guard the seclusion from almsfood,” they eat on the ground or in their hands like dogs. Thinking, “We will guard the seclusion from lodging,” they prepare beds of thorns and so on. “Established in form” means they are established in form through craving and wrong views. “Delighting in the heavenly world” means they desire to aspire for the heavenly world. `Mātiyā` means mortals; indeed, they are mortals who rightly instruct for the sake of the next world—so he says.

Iti [M 1.0118] viditvāti “ayaṃ paṭhamaṃ etesaṃ avaṇṇaṃ kathetvā idāni vaṇṇaṃ katheti, ko nu kho eso”ti āvajjento jānitvāva. Ye cantalikkhasmiṃ pabhāsavaṇṇāti ye antalikkhe candobhāsasūriyobhāsasañjhārāgaindadhanutārakarūpānaṃ pabhāsavaṇṇā. Sabbeva te teti sabbeva te tayā. Namucīti māraṃ ālapati. Āmisaṃva macchānaṃ vadhāya khittāti yathā macchānaṃ vadhatthāya baḷisalaggaṃ [V 1.0114] āmisaṃ khipati, evaṃ tayā pasaṃsamānena ete rūpā sattānaṃ vadhāya khittāti vadati.

“Having known thus” means: reflecting, “This one first spoke dispraise of them, and now speaks praise; how can this be?” he knew indeed. “Those who are of radiant appearance in the sky” means: those in the sky whose appearance is like the radiance of the moon, the sun, the twilight glow, the rainbow, and the forms of stars. “`Sabbeva te te`” means: all of them by you. “Namuci” means: he addresses Māra. “Like bait thrown for the killing of fish” means: just as one throws bait attached to a hook for the purpose of killing fish, so too, these forms, being praised by you, are thrown for the killing of beings—so he says.

Māṇavagāmiyoti ayaṃ kira devaputto buddhupaṭṭhāko. Rājagahīyānanti rājagahapabbatānaṃ. Setoti kelāso. Aghagāminanti ākāsagāmīnaṃ. Udadhinanti udakanidhānānaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā rājagahīyānaṃ pabbatānaṃ vipulo seṭṭho, himavantapabbatānaṃ kelāso, ākāsagāmīnaṃ ādicco, udakanidhānānaṃ samuddo, nakkhattānaṃ cando, evaṃ sadevakassa lokassa buddho seṭṭhoti. Dasamaṃ.

“Māṇavagāmiya”: it is said this devaputta is an attendant of the Buddha. “Of the Rājagahans” (`Rājagahīyānaṃ`) means of the mountains of Rājagaha. “White” (`Seto`) means Mount Kelāsa. “Of those who go to woe” (`Aghagāminaṃ`) means of those who go in the sky. “Of the ocean” (`Udadhinaṃ`) means of the receptacles of water. This is what is said: just as among the mountains of Rājagaha, Mount Vipula is the best; among the mountains of Himavant, Mount Kelāsa is the best; among those that go in the sky, the sun is the best; among the receptacles of water, the ocean is the best; among the constellations, the moon is the best; so too, in the world with its devas, the Buddha is the best. The tenth.

Nānātitthiyavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter on Various Sectarians, the Third.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Devaputtasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Devaputta Saṃyutta is concluded.

3. Kosalasaṃyuttaṃ

The Kosala Saṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

The First Chapter

1. Daharasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Dahara Sutta

112. Kosalasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0115][M 1.0119] paṭhame [P 1.0129] bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodīti yathā khamanīyādīni pucchanto bhagavā tena, evaṃ sopi bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosi. Sītodakaṃ viya uṇhodakena sammoditaṃ ekībhāvaṃ agamāsi. Yāya ca – “kacci, bho gotama, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci bhoto ca gotamassa sāvakānañca appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāro”tiādikāya kathāya sammodi, taṃ pītipāmojjasaṅkhātasammodajananato sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato ca sammodanīyaṃ, atthabyañjanamadhuratāya cirampi kālaṃ sāretuṃ nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ araharūpato saritabbabhāvato ca sāraṇīyaṃ. Suyyamānasukhato ca sammodanīyaṃ, anussariyamānasukhato sāraṇīyaṃ. Tathā byañjanaparisuddhatāya sammodanīyaṃ, atthaparisuddhatāya sāraṇīyanti evaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā pariyosāpetvā niṭṭhapetvā ito pubbe tathāgatassa adiṭṭhattā guṇāguṇavasena gambhīrabhāvaṃ vā uttānabhāvaṃ vā ajānanto ekamantaṃ nisīdi, ekamantaṃ nisinno kho yaṃ ovaṭṭikasāraṃ katvā āgato lokanissaraṇabhavokkantipañhaṃ satthu sammāsambuddhataṃ pucchituṃ bhavampi notiādimāha.

1. In the first sutta of the Kosala Saṃyutta, regarding the phrase 'he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One': Just as the Blessed One, inquiring about his well-being and so forth, had a mutually agreeable exchange of joy with him, so too did he have a mutually agreeable exchange of joy with the Blessed One. Like cool water mixed with hot water, it reached a state of oneness. And the conversation with which he exchanged greetings—beginning with, “I hope, Venerable Gotama, you are well? I hope you are keeping on? I hope that for you, Venerable Gotama, and for your disciples, there is little illness, little affliction, lightness, strength, and a comfortable abiding?”—is called 'a greeting' (sammodanīyaṃ) because it generates the joy and gladness known as 'sammoda' and because it is suitable for exchanging greetings. It is called 'memorable' (sāraṇīyaṃ) because of the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, because it is worthy of being remembered and continued without interruption for a long time, and because it ought to be remembered. It is a 'greeting' because it is pleasant to hear, and 'memorable' because it is pleasant to recollect. Likewise, it is a 'greeting' because of the purity of its phrasing, and 'memorable' because of the purity of its meaning. Thus, having in these many ways concluded the delightful and memorable conversation, he—not knowing whether the Tathāgata's nature was profound or superficial in terms of his qualities, on account of not having seen him before—sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, in order to ask about the Teacher's perfect enlightenment, he posed the question concerning escape from the world and transcending existence—which he had come having made into a precious, concealed treasure—beginning with the words, 'Does the Venerable Gotama...'

Tattha bhavampīti pi-kāro sampiṇḍanatthe nipāto, tena ca cha satthāre sampiṇḍeti. Yathā pūraṇādayo “sammāsambuddhamhā”ti paṭijānanti, evaṃ bhavampi nu paṭijānātīti attho. Idaṃ pana rājā na attano laddhiyā, loke mahājanena [P 1.0130] gahitapaṭiññāvasena pucchati. Atha bhagavā buddhasīhanādaṃ nadanto yaṃ hi taṃ mahārājātiādimāha. Tattha ahaṃ hi mahārājāti anuttaraṃ sabbaseṭṭhaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇasaṅkhātaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ ahaṃ abhisambuddhoti attho. Samaṇabrāhmaṇāti [V 1.0116] pabbajjūpagamanena [M 1.0120] samaṇā, jātivasena brāhmaṇā. Saṅghinotiādīsu pabbajitasamūhasaṅkhāto saṅgho etesaṃ atthīti saṅghino. Sveva gaṇo etesaṃ atthīti gaṇino. Ācārasikkhāpanavasena tassa gaṇassa ācariyāti gaṇācariyā. Ñātāti paññātā pākaṭā. “Appicchā santuṭṭhā appicchatāya vatthampi na nivāsentī”ti evaṃ samuggato yaso etesaṃ atthīti yasassino. Titthakarāti laddhikarā. Sādhusammatāti “santo sappurisā”ti evaṃ sammatā. Bahujanassāti assutavato andhabālaputhujjanassa. Pūraṇotiādīni tesaṃ nāmagottāni. Pūraṇoti hi nāmameva. Tathā, makkhalīti. So pana gosālāya jātattā gosāloti vutto. Nāṭaputtoti nāṭassa putto. Belaṭṭhaputtoti belaṭṭhassa putto. Kaccāyanoti pakudhassa gottaṃ. Kesakambalassa dhāraṇato ajito kesakambaloti vutto.

1. Herein, in `bhavampīti`, the particle `pi` is an indeclinable in the sense of grouping together, and by it, the six teachers are grouped together. The meaning is: just as Pūraṇa and others profess, 'We are Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones,' in the same way, does the venerable one also profess this? The king, however, does not ask this based on his own view, but asks according to the claim accepted by the great populace in the world. Then the Blessed One, roaring the Buddha's lion's roar, spoke the words beginning with, 'Indeed, O great king...' Therein, 'I, indeed, O great king' means: 'I have fully awakened to the unsurpassed, most excellent perfect self-enlightenment, which is designated as the knowledge of omniscience.' 'Monks and brahmins' means: they are monks by having undertaken the going forth, and they are brahmins by birth. In `saṅghino` and so on: they are `saṅghino` (possessors of a community) because they have a `saṅgha`, which is defined as an assembly of those who have gone forth. That same group is a `gaṇa`, and because they have it, they are `gaṇino` (possessors of a group). They are `gaṇācariyā` (teachers of a group) because they are teachers of that group by way of instructing them in conduct. `Ñātā` (known) means well-known, famous. They are called `yasassino` (the famous ones) because they have fame (`yaso`) that has arisen in this way: 'They have few wishes and are contented; due to having few wishes, they do not even wear a cloth.' `Titthakarā` (founders of sects) means makers of doctrines. `Sādhusammatā` (deemed good) means they are considered thus: 'They are good, true men.' `Bahujanassa` (of the many people) means of the unlearned, blind, ordinary worldling. Pūraṇa and so on are their names and clans. Indeed, `Pūraṇa` is just a name. Likewise, `Makkhalī`. But he was called `Gosāla` because he was born in a cowshed (`gosālā`). `Nāṭaputta` means the son of Nāṭa. `Belaṭṭhaputta` means the son of Belaṭṭha. `Kaccāyana` is the clan name of Pakudha. Ajita was called `Kesakambala` because he wore a blanket of human hair (`kesakambala`).

Tepi mayāti kappakolāhalaṃ buddhakolāhalaṃ cakkavattikolāhalanti tīṇi kolāhalāni. Tattha “vassasatasahassamatthake kappuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti kappakolāhalaṃ nāma hoti – “ito vassasatasahassamatthake loko vinassissati, mettaṃ mārisā, bhāvetha, karuṇaṃ muditaṃ upekkha”nti manussappathe devatā ghosentiyo vicaranti. “Vassasahassamatthake pana buddho uppajjissatī”ti buddhakolāhalaṃ nāma hoti – “ito vassasahassamatthake buddho uppajjitvā dhammānudhammapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannena saṅgharatanena parivārito dhammaṃ desento vicarissatī”ti devatā ugghosenti. “Vassasatamatthake pana cakkavattī uppajjissatī”ti cakkavattikolāhalaṃ nāma hoti – “ito vassasatamatthake sattaratanasampanno catuddīpissaro [P 1.0131] sahassa puttaparivāro vehāsaṅgamo cakkavattirājā uppajjissatī”ti devatā ugghosenti.

There are these three uproars: the eon-uproar, the Buddha-uproar, and the wheel-turning monarch-uproar. Among them, the proclamation, 'After one hundred thousand years, the destruction of the eon will occur,' is called the eon-uproar. Deities wander in the paths of humankind, proclaiming: 'From now, after one hundred thousand years, the world will perish. O sirs, cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity!' The proclamation, 'After a thousand years, a Buddha will arise,' is called the Buddha-uproar. Deities proclaim: 'From now, after a thousand years, a Buddha will arise and, surrounded by the jewel of the Sangha practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, he will wander while teaching the Dhamma.' The proclamation, 'After a hundred years, a wheel-turning monarch will arise,' is called the wheel-turning monarch-uproar. Deities proclaim: 'From now, after a hundred years, a wheel-turning monarch will arise—endowed with the seven treasures, lord of the four great continents, surrounded by a thousand sons, and able to travel through the sky.'

Imesu tīsu kolāhalesu ime cha satthāro buddhakolāhalaṃ sutvā ācariye payirupāsitvā cintāmāṇivijjādīni uggaṇhitvā – “mayaṃ buddhamhā”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā mahājanaparivutā janapadaṃ vicarantā anupubbena sāvatthiyaṃ pattā. Tesaṃ upaṭṭhākā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā, “mahārāja, pūraṇo kassapo…pe… ajito kesakambalo buddho kira sabbaññū kirā”ti ārocesuṃ. Rājā “tumheva ne nimantetvā ānethā”ti āha[M 1.0121]. Te gantvā tehi, “rājā vo nimanteti. Rañño gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vuttā gantuṃ na ussahanti, punappunaṃ vuccamānā upaṭṭhākānaṃ cittānurakkhaṇatthāya adhivāsetvā sabbe ekatova agamaṃsu. Rājā āsanāni paññāpetvā [V 1.0117] “nisīdantū”ti āha. Nigguṇānaṃ attabhāve rājusmā nāma pharati, te mahārahesu āsanesu nisīdituṃ asakkontā phalakesu ceva bhūmiyaṃ ca nisīdiṃsu.

Among these three uproars, these six teachers, having heard the Buddha-uproar, approached their own teachers, learned the Cintāmaṇi spell and other arts, made the declaration, “We are Buddhas,” and, surrounded by a great crowd, wandered through the country until they gradually arrived at Sāvatthī. Their supporters approached the king and reported, “Great King, it is said that Pūraṇa Kassapa... Ajita Kesakambala is a Buddha, an all-knowing one.” The king said, “You yourselves invite them and bring them here.” They went and told them, “The king invites you. Receive alms in the king’s house.” When this was said, they did not dare to go; but, being repeatedly urged, they consented in order to protect the minds of their supporters, and all went together. The king had seats prepared and said, “Be seated.” The royal majesty pervades the persons of the virtueless; they, being unable to sit on the excellent seats, sat on planks and on the ground.

Rājā “ettakeneva natthi tesaṃ anto sukkadhammo”ti vatvā āhāraṃ adatvāva tālato patitaṃ muggarena pothento viya “tumhe buddhā, na buddhā”ti pañhaṃ pucchi. Te cintayiṃsu – “sace ‘buddhamhā’ti vakkhāma, rājā buddhavisaye pañhaṃ pucchitvā kathetuṃ asakkonte ‘tumhe mayaṃ buddhāti mahājanaṃ vañcetvā āhiṇḍathā’ti jivhampi chindāpeyya, aññampi anatthaṃ kareyyā”ti sakapaṭiññāya eva ‘na mayaṃ buddhā’ti vadiṃsu. Atha ne rājā gehato nikaḍḍhāpesi. Te rājagharato nikkhante upaṭṭhākā pucchiṃsu – “kiṃ ācariyā rājā tumhe pañhaṃ pucchitvā sakkārasammānaṃ akāsī”ti? Rājā “buddhā tumhe”ti pucchi, tato mayaṃ – “sace ayaṃ rājā buddhavisaye pañhaṃ kathiyamānaṃ ajānanto amhesu manaṃ padosessati, bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavissatī”ti rañño anukampāya ‘na mayaṃ buddhā’ti vadimhā, mayaṃ pana buddhā eva, amhākaṃ buddhabhāvo, udakena dhovitvāpi harituṃ na sakkāti. Iti bahiddhā ‘buddhamhā’ti [P 1.0132] āhaṃsu – rañño santike ‘na mayaṃ buddhā’ti vadiṃsūti, idaṃ gahetvā rājā evamāha. Tattha kiṃ pana bhavaṃ gotamo daharo ceva jātiyā, navo ca pabbajjāyāti idaṃ attano paṭiññaṃ gahetvā vadati. Tattha kinti paṭikkhepavacanaṃ. Ete jātimahallakā ca cirapabbajitā ca “buddhamhā”ti na paṭijānanti, bhavaṃ gotamo jātiyā ca daharo pabbajjāya ca navo kiṃ paṭijānāti? Mā paṭijānāhīti attho.

The king, knowing, “With just this, there is no pure dhamma within them,” without giving them food, asked the question, “Are you Buddhas or not Buddhas?” as if striking a person who had fallen from a palm tree with a club. They thought: “If we say, ‘We are Buddhas,’ the king, after asking a question on the subject of Buddhahood, might, when we are unable to answer, say, ‘You wander about deceiving the great populace, claiming, “We are Buddhas,”’ and he might have our tongues cut off or do us other harm.” Thus, by their own admission, they said, “We are not Buddhas.” Then the king had them expelled from the palace. As they were leaving the king's palace, their supporters asked them, “Teachers, did the king, after asking you a question, make offerings and show you honor?” They replied, “The king asked, ‘Are you Buddhas?’ Thereupon, thinking, ‘If, while a question on the subject of Buddhahood is being explained, this king, not understanding, should become hostile towards us, he will generate much demerit,’ out of compassion for the king, we said, ‘We are not Buddhas.’ But we are indeed Buddhas. Our Buddhahood cannot be taken away even by washing it with water.” Thus, outside they said, “We are Buddhas,” but in the king's presence they said, “We are not Buddhas.” Taking this up, the king spoke thus. Therein, he says this—“But what of the venerable Gotama, who is young in birth and new to the going forth?”—taking up the declaration made before him. Therein, ‘kiṃ’ is a word of rejection. These teachers, who are old in birth and long gone forth, do not claim, “We are Buddhas.” The venerable Gotama is young in birth and new to the going forth; why does he make this claim? He should not make this claim—this is the meaning.

Na uññātabbāti na avajānitabbā. Na paribhotabbāti na paribhavitabbā. Katame cattāroti kathetukamyatāpucchā. Khattiyoti rājakumāro. Uragoti āsīviso. Aggīti aggiyeva. Bhikkhūti imasmiṃ pana pade desanākusalatāya attānaṃ abbhantaraṃ katvā sīlavantaṃ pabbajitaṃ dasseti. Ettha [M 1.0122] ca daharaṃ rājakumāraṃ disvā, ukkamitvā maggaṃ adento, pārupanaṃ anapanento, nisinnāsanato anuṭṭhahanto, hatthipiṭṭhādīhi anotaranto, heṭṭhā katvā maññanavasena aññampi evarūpaṃ anācāraṃ karonto khattiyaṃ avajānāti nāma. “Bhaddako vatāyaṃ rājakumāro, mahākaṇḍo mahodaro – kiṃ nāma yaṃkiñci corūpaddavaṃ vūpasametuṃ yattha katthaci ṭhāne rajjaṃ anusāsituṃ sakkhissatī”tiādīni vadanto paribhoti nāma. Añjanisalākamattampi āsīvisapotakaṃ kaṇṇādīsu piḷandhanto aṅgulimpi jivhampi ḍaṃsāpento uragaṃ avajānāti nāma[V 1.0118]. “Bhaddako vatāyaṃ āsīviso udakadeḍḍubho viya kiṃ nāma kiñcideva ḍaṃsituṃ kassacideva kāye visaṃ pharituṃ sakkhissatī”tiādīni vadanto paribhoti nāma. Khajjopanakamattampi aggiṃ gahetvā hatthena kīḷanto bhaṇḍukkhalikāya khipanto cūḷāya vā sayanapiṭṭhasāṭakapasibbakādīsu vā ṭhapento aggiṃ avajānāti nāma. “Bhaddako vatāyaṃ aggi kataraṃ nu kho yāgubhattaṃ pacissati, kataraṃ macchamaṃsaṃ, kassa sītaṃ vinodessatī”tiādīni vadanto paribhoti nāma. Daharasāmaṇerampi pana disvā ukkamitvā maggaṃ adentoti [P 1.0133] rājakumāre vuttaṃ anācāraṃ karonto bhikkhuṃ avajānāti nāma. “Bhaddako vatāyaṃ sāmaṇero mahākaṇṭho mahodaro yaṃkiñci buddhavacanaṃ uggahetuṃ yaṃkiñci araññaṃ ajjhogāhetvā vasituṃ sakkhissati, saṅghattherakāle manāpo bhavissatī”tiādīni vadanto paribhoti nāma. Taṃ sabbampi na kātabbanti dassento na uññātabbo na paribhotabboti āha.

“They should not be disdained” means they should not be scorned. “They should not be treated with contempt” means they should not be disparaged. The question ‘What are the four?’ is one prompted by the desire to explain. ‘Khattiya’ means a prince. ‘Uraga’ means a viper. ‘Aggi’ means fire itself. However, in this word ‘bhikkhu’, due to His skill in teaching, He includes Himself and indicates a virtuous renunciant. Here, upon seeing a young prince, by not moving aside to give way, not removing one's upper garment, not rising from one's seat, not dismounting from an elephant's back and so on, and by performing other such improper conduct through considering him inferior, one is said to scorn a khattiya. By saying such things as, “This prince is indeed a fine fellow, with a thick neck and a big belly—how will he be able to quell any danger from thieves or rule the kingdom in any place whatsoever?” one is said to disparage him. One who wears a young viper, even one the size of an eyeliner stick, on one's ear and so on, or who causes it to bite one's finger or tongue, is said to scorn a viper. By saying such things as, “This viper is indeed a fine fellow, like a water snake—how will it be able to bite anyone at all, or spread its poison in anyone's body?” one is said to disparage it. One who takes a fire even the size of a firefly and plays with it in their hand, throws it into a container for goods, or places it on their topknot, or on a bed, chair, robe, bag, and so on, is said to scorn fire. By saying such things as, “This fire is indeed a fine fellow—what rice-gruel or meal will it cook? What fish or meat? Whose cold will it dispel?” one is said to disparage it. Furthermore, upon seeing even a young novice, by performing the improper conduct spoken of in the case of the prince—such as not moving aside to give way—one is said to scorn a monk. By saying such things as, “This novice is indeed a fine fellow, with a thick neck and a big belly—will he be able to learn any of the Buddha's words? Will he be able to enter any forest and dwell there? When he becomes a senior monk, will he be agreeable?” one is said to disparage him. Showing that none of this should be done, He said: ‘They should not be scorned, nor should they be disparaged.’”

Etadavocāti etaṃ gāthābandhaṃ avoca. Gāthā ca nāmetā tadatthadīpanāpi honti visesatthadīpanāpi, tatrimā tadatthampi visesatthampi dīpentiyeva. Tattha khattiyanti khettānaṃ adhipatiṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “khettānaṃ adhipatīti kho, vāseṭṭha, ‘khattiyo khattiyo’tveva dutiyaṃ akkharaṃ upanibbatta”nti (dī. ni. 3.131). Jātisampannanti tāyeva khattiyajātiyā jātisampannaṃ. Abhijātanti tīṇi kulāni atikkamitvā jātaṃ.

He spoke thus means: He spoke this verse composition. And these verses are illuminators of that meaning and also illuminators of a special meaning; herein, these verses indeed illuminate both that meaning and a special meaning. Therein, khattiya means: lord of the fields. For this was said: 'Because he is the lord of the fields, Vāseṭṭha, the second designation "khattiya" indeed arose.' Endowed with birth means: endowed with birth by that very khattiya birth. High-born means: born having transcended the three families.

Ṭhānaṃ hīti kāraṇaṃ vijjati. Manujindoti manussajeṭṭhako. Rājadaṇḍenāti rañño uddhaṭadaṇḍena, so appako nāma na hoti, dasasahassavīsatisahassappamāṇo hotiyeva. Tasmiṃ pakkamate bhusanti [M 1.0123] tasmiṃ puggale balavaupakkamaṃ upakkamati. Rakkhaṃ jīvitamattanoti attano jīvitaṃ rakkhamāno taṃ khattiyaṃ parivajjeyya na ghaṭṭeyya.

There is indeed a reason means: a reason exists. Lord of men means: foremost among men. By the king's punishment means: by the king's raised rod of authority; it is by no means small, it indeed amounts to ten or twenty thousand. When he proceeds with force means: he launches a strong attack upon that person. Protecting one's own life means: while protecting one's own life, one should avoid that khattiya, one should not provoke him.

Uccāvacehīti nānāvidhehi. Vaṇṇehīti saṇṭhānehi. Yena yena hi vaṇṇena caranto gocaraṃ labhati, yadi sappavaṇṇena, yadi deḍḍubhavaṇṇena, yadi dhamanivaṇṇena, antamaso kalandakavaṇṇenapi caratiyeva. Āsajjāti patvā. Bālanti yena bālena ghaṭṭito, taṃ bālaṃ naraṃ vā nāriṃ vā ḍaṃseyya.

Of high and low kinds means: of various kinds. By appearances means: by forms. For by whatever form it gets its prey while moving about—if by the form of a cobra, if by the form of a water snake, if by the form of a grass snake—it moves about by that very form, even down to the form of a squirrel. Having assailed means: having approached. A fool means: by whichever fool it is provoked, it might bite that fool, whether man or woman.

Pahūtabhakkhanti bahubhakkhaṃ. Aggissa hi abhakkhaṃ nāma natthi. Jālinanti jālavantaṃ. Pāvakanti [V 1.0119] aggiṃ. Pāvagantipi pāṭho. Kaṇhavattaninti vattanīti maggo, agginā gatamaggo kaṇho hoti kāḷako, tasmā “kaṇhavattanī”ti vuccati.

Having abundant fuel means: having much fuel. For there is nothing called non-fuel for a fire. Flaming means: possessing flames. Purifier means: fire. There is also the reading pāvagaṃ. Having a dark path: herein, vattanī means path; the path traversed by fire becomes black, dark, therefore it is called kaṇhavattanī (having a dark path).

Mahā hutvānāti mahanto hutvā. Aggi hi ekadā yāvabrahmalokappamāṇopi hoti. Jāyanti [P 1.0134] tattha pārohāti tattha agginā daḍḍhavane pārohā jāyanti. Pārohāti tiṇarukkhādayo vuccanti. Te hi agginā daḍḍhaṭṭhāne mūlamattepi avasiṭṭhe pādato rohanti jāyanti vaḍḍhanti, tasmā “pārohā”ti vuccanti. Puna rohanatthena vā pārohā. Ahorattānamaccayeti rattindivānaṃ atikkame. Nidāghepi deve vuṭṭhamatte jāyanti.

‘Having become great’ means having become vast. For fire sometimes becomes as vast as the Brahma world. ‘Shoots are born there’ means that shoots are born in the forest burned by fire. ‘Shoots’ refers to grass, trees, and the like. For even when burned by fire, if only the roots remain in the burned place, they sprout from the base, are born, and grow; therefore, they are called ‘shoots’. Or, they are ‘shoots’ because of their growing again. ‘With the passing of days and nights’ means the passing of days and nights. Even in the hot season, they grow as soon as rain falls.

Bhikkhu ḍahati tejasāti ettha akkosantaṃ paccakkosanto bhaṇḍantaṃ paṭibhaṇḍanto paharantaṃ paṭipaharanto bhikkhu nāma kiñci bhikkhutejasā ḍahituṃ na sakkoti. Yo pana akkosantaṃ na paccakkosati, bhaṇḍantaṃ na paṭibhaṇḍati. Paharantaṃ na paṭipaharati, tasmiṃ vippaṭipanno tassa sīlatejena ḍayhati. Tenevetaṃ vuttaṃ. Na tassa puttā pasavoti tassa puttadhītaropi gomahiṃsakukkuṭasūkarādayo pasavopi na bhavanti, vinassantīti attho. Dāyādā vindare dhananti tassa dāyādāpi dhanaṃ na vindanti. Tālāvatthū bhavanti teti te bhikkhutejasā daḍḍhā vatthumattāvasiṭṭho matthakacchinnatālo viya bhavanti, puttadhītādivasena na vaḍḍhantīti attho.

‘A monk burns with power’: here, a monk who retaliates against one who abuses, argues back when argued with, or strikes back when struck, is not able to burn anything with a monk's power. But one who does not retaliate when abused, does not argue back when argued with, and does not strike back when struck—one who acts wrongly towards such a monk is burned by the power of his virtue. For that very reason, this was said: ‘For him there are no sons or livestock’ means that for such a person, neither his sons and daughters, nor his livestock such as cattle, buffaloes, chickens, and pigs, prosper; they perish—this is the meaning. ‘Heirs would not find wealth’ means his heirs do not obtain wealth. ‘They become like palmyra stumps’ means that those persons, burned by the power of the monk, become like a palmyra tree with its top cut off, with only the base remaining; they do not prosper by way of sons, daughters, and the like—this is the meaning.

Tasmāti [M 1.0124] yasmā samaṇatejena daḍḍhā matthakacchinnatālo viya aviruḷhidhammā bhavanti, tasmā. Sammadeva samācareti sammā samācareyya. Sammā samācarantena pana kiṃ kātabbanti? Khattiyaṃ tāva nissāya laddhabbaṃ gāmanigamayānavāhanādiānisaṃsaṃ, uragaṃ nissāya tassa kīḷāpanena laddhabbaṃ vatthahiraññasuvaṇṇādiānisaṃsaṃ aggiṃ nissāya tassānubhāvena pattabbaṃ yāgubhattapacanasītavinodanādiānisaṃsaṃ, bhikkhuṃ nissāya tassa vasena pattabbaṃ asutasavanasutapariyodapana-saggamaggādhigamādiānisaṃsaṃ sampassamānena “ete nissāya pubbe vuttappakāro ādīnavo atthi. Kiṃ imehī”ti? Na sabbaso pahātabbā. Issariyatthikena pana vuttappakāraṃ avajānanañca paribhavanañca akatvā pubbuṭṭhāyipacchānipātitādīhi [P 1.0135] upāyehi khattiyakumāro tosetabbo, evaṃ tato issariyaṃ adhigamissati. Ahituṇḍikena urage vissāsaṃ akatvā nāgavijjaṃ parivattetvā ajapadena daṇḍena gīvāya gahetvā visaharena mūlena dāṭhā dhovitvā peḷāyaṃ pakkhipitvā kīḷāpentena caritabbaṃ. Evaṃ taṃ nissāya ghāsacchādanādīni labhissati. Yāgupacanādīni [V 1.0120] kattukāmena aggiṃ vissāsena bhaṇḍukkhalikādīsu apakkhipitvā hatthehi anāmasantena gomayacuṇṇādīhi jāletvā yāgupacanādīni kattabbāni, evaṃ taṃ nissāya ānisaṃsaṃ labhissati. Asutasavanādīni patthayantenapi bhikkhuṃ ativissāsena vejjakammanavakammādīsu ayojetvā catūhi paccayehi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhātabbo, evaṃ taṃ nissāya asutapubbaṃ buddhavacanaṃ asutapubbaṃ pañhāvinicchayaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ atthaṃ tisso kulasampattiyo cha kāmasaggāni nava ca brahmaloke patvā amatamahānibbānadassanampi labhissatīti imamatthaṃ sandhāya sammadeva samācareti āha.

As for 'Therefore': because those scorched by the fire of an ascetic's power become of a nature not to grow again, like a palmyra tree with its crown cut off, therefore. As for 'One should act rightly indeed,' it means one should act rightly. But what should be done by one who acts rightly? One who sees well the benefits to be obtained by relying on a royal, such as villages, towns, chariots, and vehicles; the benefits to be obtained by relying on a serpent and making it play, such as cloth, silver, and gold; the benefits to be attained by relying on fire and its power, such as cooking gruel and rice and dispelling cold; and the benefits to be attained by relying on a virtuous monk and his influence, such as hearing what has not been heard, the purification of what has been heard, and the attainment of heaven and the path, might think: 'By relying on these, there is the danger of the kind previously mentioned. What is to be done with them?' They should not be abandoned altogether. However, one desiring sovereignty and wealth, without showing contempt or abuse of the kind mentioned, should please the young royal by means such as being the first to rise and the last to lie down; thus, from him, one will obtain sovereignty and wealth. A snake charmer should proceed by not placing trust in the serpent, but by reciting the snake charm, seizing it by the neck with a goat-foot staff, washing its fangs with an antidote root, placing it in a basket, and making it play. Thus, by relying on it, one will obtain food, clothing, and so forth. One who wishes to cook gruel and so forth should not, out of over-familiarity, place the fire in containers for goods and the like, nor touch it with the hands, but should kindle it with cow-dung powder and the like, and then do the cooking of gruel and so forth. Thus, by relying on it, one will obtain the benefit. Even one desiring such things as hearing what has not been heard should not, with excessive familiarity, engage a virtuous monk in acts such as medical practice or construction work, but should attend to him respectfully with the four requisites. Thus, by relying on him, one will obtain the word of the Buddha not heard before, the resolution of questions not heard before, the benefit that brings about welfare in the present and in the future, the three accomplishments of family, the six sense-sphere heavens, and the nine Brahma worlds, and having reached them, one will also obtain the vision of the deathless, great Nibbāna. Having this meaning in mind, He said, 'One should act rightly indeed.'

Etadavocāti dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasanno pasādaṃ āvikaronto etaṃ “abhikkanta”ntiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha abhikkantanti abhikantaṃ atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ, atisundaranti attho. Ettha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi “abhikkantaṃ, bhante, yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanā”ti. Ekena attano [M 1.0125] pasādaṃ “abhikkantaṃ, bhante, yadidaṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādo”ti.

As for 'He said this': having heard the Dhamma teaching, being delighted and wishing to make his delight manifest, he spoke this utterance beginning with 'Excellent.' Herein, 'excellent' (abhikkantaṃ) means exceedingly desirable, exceedingly pleasing, exceedingly agreeable, and exceedingly beautiful—such is the meaning. Here, with one utterance of 'excellent,' he praises the teaching: 'Excellent, venerable sir, is this Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One.' With another, he praises his own delight: 'Excellent, venerable sir, is the delight that has been obtained by me on account of the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching.'

Tato paraṃ catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti uparimukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādichāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti [P 1.0136] hatthe gahetvā “esa maggo”ti vadeyya. Andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasī aḍḍharattaghanavanasaṇḍa meghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tame. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentena, yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya, evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānā pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggapaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ āvikarontena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāre nimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotaṃ dhārentena mayhaṃ bhagavatā etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti.

Thereafter, he praises the teaching itself with four similes. Herein, 'overturned' (nikkujjitaṃ) means placed face down, or naturally being face down. 'Would turn upright' (ukkujjeyya) means would make it face up. 'Covered' (paṭicchannaṃ) means covered with grass, leaves, and the like. 'Would uncover' (vivareyya) means would open it up. 'To one bewildered' (mūḷhassa) means to one who has lost their direction. 'Would show the path' (maggaṃ ācikkheyya) means, taking them by the hand, one would say, 'This is the path.' 'In the darkness' (andhakāre) refers to the four-factored darkness: the fourteenth day of the waning moon, midnight, a dense forest grove, and a layer of clouds. This is what is meant: just as someone would turn upright what has been overturned, so too, by raising me up from the false Dhamma—me who had turned away from the true Dhamma and had fallen into the false Dhamma; just as one would uncover what is covered, so too, by uncovering the Dispensation which, since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, had been covered by the thicket of wrong views; just as one would show the path to one who is lost, so too, by making manifest the path to heaven and liberation for me, who had entered upon a bad path, a wrong path; just as one would hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so too, for me who, being plunged in the darkness of delusion, did not see the forms of the gems such as the Buddha, by holding up the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which obscures them—because the Dhamma was illuminated for me by the Blessed One through these methods, the Dhamma has been illuminated in many ways.

Evaṃ desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattaye pasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto esāhantiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti [V 1.0121] bhagavantañca dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti imaṃ ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi. Upāsakaṃ maṃ, bhante, bhagavā dhāretūti maṃ bhagavā ‘upāsako aya’nti evaṃ dhāretu, jānātūti attho. Ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvā. Ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho, da-kāro padasandhikaro, ajja aggaṃ katvāti attho. Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretūti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya sāmaññaphalasutte sabbākārena vuttoti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Having praised the teaching in this way, with a mind delighted in the Triple Gem on account of this teaching, and wishing to express his reverence, he spoke the words beginning with 'This I...' Herein, 'This I' (esāhaṃ) means 'This I am.' 'I go for refuge to the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and the Sangha of bhikkhus'—that is, 'I go for refuge to this Triple Gem: the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and the Sangha of bhikkhus.' 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower'—that is, may the Blessed One remember me, knowing, 'This is a lay follower,' such is the meaning. 'From this day forward' (ajjatagge) means 'making today the beginning.' Or alternatively, the reading is 'ajjadagge,' where the letter 'da' is a euphonic conjunction, meaning 'making today the beginning.' As for 'endowed with life' (pāṇupetaṃ), it means: 'May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower and suitable attendant who has gone for refuge with the threefold taking of refuge, endowed with life for as long as my life continues, and having no other teacher.' This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, is given in every respect in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta of the Dīghanikāya commentary, the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. The first [discourse].

2. Purisasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Discourse about the Person

113. Dutiye [M 1.0126][P 1.0137] abhivādetvāti purimasutte saraṇagatattā idha abhivādesi. Ajjhattanti niyakajjhattaṃ, attano santāne uppajjantīti attho. Lobhādīsu lubbhanalakkhaṇo lobho, dussanalakkhaṇo doso, muyhanalakkhaṇo mohoti. Hiṃsantīti viheṭhenti nāsenti vināsenti. Attasambhūtāti attani sambhūtā. Tacasāraṃva samphalanti yathā tacasāraṃ veḷuṃ vā naḷaṃ vā attano phalaṃ hiṃsati vināseti, evaṃ hiṃsanti vināsentīti. Dutiyaṃ.

113. In the second discourse, regarding 'having paid homage' (`abhivādetvā`): because he had gone for refuge in the previous discourse, here he pays homage. 'Internally' (`ajjhattaṃ`) means one's own internal, that is, arising in one's own continuum. Regarding greed and so on: greed has the characteristic of craving, hatred has the characteristic of corrupting, and delusion has the characteristic of bewilderment. 'They harm' (`hiṃsanti`) means they afflict, destroy, and ruin. 'Self-born' (`attasambhūtā`) means born in oneself. 'Just as its own fruit destroys the plant with pith in its bark' (`tacasāraṃva samphalanti`): just as its own fruit harms and destroys a plant whose strength is in its bark, such as bamboo or a reed, so too do they harm and ruin. The second.

3. Jarāmaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Aging and Death

114. Tatiye aññatra jarāmaraṇāti jarāmaraṇato mutto nāma atthīti vuccati. Khattiyamahāsālāti khattiyamahāsālā nāma mahāsārappattā khattiyā. Yesaṃ hi khattiyānaṃ heṭṭhimantena koṭisataṃ nidhānagataṃ hoti, tayo kahāpaṇakumbhā valañjanatthāya gehamajjhe rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapitā honti, te khattiyamahāsālā nāma. Yesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ asītikoṭidhanaṃ nihitaṃ hoti, diyaḍḍho kahāpaṇakumbho valañjanatthāya gehamajjhe rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapito hoti, te brāhmaṇamahāsālā nāma. Yesaṃ gahapatīnaṃ cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ nihitaṃ hoti, kahāpaṇakumbho valañjanatthāya gehamajjhe rāsiṃ katvā ṭhapito hoti, te gahapatimahāsālā nāma.

114. In the third discourse, regarding the phrase 'apart from aging and death,' it is asked thus: 'Is there anyone, indeed, who is freed from aging and death?' Regarding 'Khattiya magnates': khattiyas who have attained great substance are called khattiya magnates. Indeed, those khattiyas for whom, at the lowest limit, one hundred crores of wealth is buried, and three pots of kahāpaṇas are placed in a pile in the middle of the house for their use, are called khattiya magnates. Those brahmins for whom eighty crores of wealth is buried, and one and a half pots of kahāpaṇas are placed in a pile in the middle of the house for their use, are called brahmin magnates. Those householders for whom forty crores of wealth is buried, and one pot of kahāpaṇas is placed in a pile in the middle of the house for their use, are called householder magnates.

Aḍḍhāti issarā. Nidhānagatadhanassa mahantatāya mahaddhanā. Suvaṇṇarajatabhājanādīnaṃ upabhogabhaṇḍānaṃ mahantatāya mahābhogā. Anidhānagatassa jātarūparajatassa pahūtatāya, pahūtajātarūparajatā[V 1.0122]. Vittūpakaraṇassa tuṭṭhikaraṇassa pahūtatāya pahūtavittūpakaraṇā. Godhanādīnañca sattavidhadhaññānañca pahūtatāya pahūtadhanadhaññā. Tesampi jātānaṃ natthi aññatra jarāmaraṇāti tesampi evaṃ issarānaṃ jātānaṃ nibbattānaṃ natthi aññatra jarāmaraṇā, jātattāyeva jarāmaraṇato mokkho nāma natthi, antojarāmaraṇeyeva hoti.

Regarding 'affluent' (`aḍḍhā`): they are masters. Because of the greatness of their buried wealth, they are of great wealth. Because of the greatness of their articles for use, such as gold and silver vessels, they have great possessions. Because of the abundance of their unburied gold and silver, they have abundant gold and silver. Because of the abundance of their delightful ornaments, they have abundant delightful ornaments. Because of the abundance of their wealth, such as cattle and other livestock, and of the seven kinds of grain, they have abundant wealth and grain. Regarding the phrase 'For even those who are born, there is nothing apart from aging and death': for even those masters who are thus born and have come into being, there is nothing apart from aging and death. Merely because of being born, there is no liberation from aging and death; they are only within aging and death.

Arahantotiādīsu [M 1.0127][P 1.0138] ārakā kilesehīti arahanto. Khīṇā etesaṃ cattāro āsavāti khīṇāsavā. Brahmacariyavāsaṃ vuṭṭhā pariniṭṭhitavāsāti vusitavanto. Catūhi maggehi karaṇīyaṃ etesaṃ katanti katakaraṇīyā. Khandhabhāro kilesabhāro abhisaṅkhārabhāro kāmaguṇabhāroti, ime ohitā bhārā etesanti ohitabhārā. Anuppatto arahattasaṅkhāto sako attho etesanti anuppattasadatthā. Dasavidhampi parikkhīṇaṃ bhavasaṃyojanaṃ etesanti parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanā. Sammā kāraṇehi jānitvā vimuttāti sammadaññāvimuttā. Maggapaññāya catusaccadhammaṃ ñatvā phalavimuttiyā vimuttāti attho. Bhedanadhammoti bhijjanasabhāvo. Nikkhepanadhammoti nikkhipitabbasabhāvo. Khīṇāsavassa hi ajīraṇadhammopi atthi, ārammaṇato paṭividdhaṃ nibbānaṃ, taṃ hi na jīrati. Idha panassa jīraṇadhammaṃ dassento evamāha. Atthuppattiko kirassa suttassa nikkhepo. Sivikasālāya nisīditvā kathitanti vadanti. Tattha bhagavā citrāni rathayānādīni disvā diṭṭhameva upamaṃ katvā, “jīranti ve rājarathā”ti gāthamāha.

In the terms beginning with 'Arahant': they are called Arahants because they are far (`ārakā`) from defilements. 'Their four taints (`āsavā`) are destroyed (`khīṇā`)'—thus, they are called Khīṇāsavā. 'They have lived the holy life, their dwelling is completed'—thus, they are called Vusitavanto. 'What had to be done by the four paths has been done by them'—thus, they are called Katakaraṇīyā. 'The burden of the aggregates, the burden of defilements, the burden of volitional formations, the burden of sensual pleasures—these burdens have been laid down (`ohitā`) by them'—thus, they are called Ohitabhārā. 'They have attained their own goal (`sako attho`), which is known as Arahantship'—thus, they are called Anuppattasadatthā. 'The tenfold fetter of existence has been completely destroyed for them'—thus, they are called Parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanā. 'Having known through right reasons, they are liberated'—thus, they are called Sammadaññāvimuttā. The meaning is: having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths by the wisdom of the path, they are liberated by the liberation of fruition. 'Of a nature to break' (`bhedanadhammo`) means having a nature of breaking up. 'Of a nature to be laid down' (`nikkhepanadhammo`) means having a nature that must be laid aside. For one whose taints are destroyed, there is indeed also a quality that does not decay: Nibbāna, which has been penetrated as an object, for that does not decay. Here, however, showing that this one has a quality that decays, he said thus. Reportedly, the exposition of this discourse arose from a specific occasion. They say it was spoken while he was seated in the Sivika hall. There, the Blessed One, having seen various painted chariots and vehicles, and having made a simile of the very thing he had seen, spoke the verse: 'Indeed, the royal chariots wear out.'

Tattha jīrantīti jaraṃ pāpuṇanti. Rājarathāti rañño abhirūhanarathā. Sucittāti suvaṇṇarajatādīhi suṭṭhu cittitā. Atho sarīrampi jaraṃ upetīti evarūpesu anupādiṇṇakesu sāradārumayesu rathesu jīrantesu imasmiṃ ajjhattike upādiṇṇake maṃsalohitādimaye sarīre kiṃ vattabbaṃ? Sarīrampi jaraṃ upetiyevāti attho. Santo have sabbhi pavedayantīti santo sabbhīhi saddhiṃ sataṃ dhammo na jaraṃ upetīti evaṃ pavedayanti. “Sataṃ dhammo nāma nibbānaṃ, taṃ na jīrati, ajaraṃ amatanti evaṃ kathentī”ti attho. Yasmā vā nibbānaṃ āgamma sīdanasabhāvā kilesā bhijjanti, tasmā taṃ sabbhīti vuccati. Iti purimapadassa kāraṇaṃ dassento “santo have sabbhi pavedayantī”ti āha. Idaṃ hi vuttaṃ hoti – sataṃ dhammo na jaraṃ upeti, tasmā santo sabbhi pavedayanti. Ajaraṃ nibbānaṃ sataṃ dhammoti [P 1.0139] ācikkhantīti attho. Sundarādhivacanaṃ vā etaṃ sabbhīti. Yaṃ sabbhidhammabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ santo pavedayanti kathayanti, so sataṃ dhammo na jaraṃ upetītipi attho. Tatiyaṃ.

Therein, 'they decay' (`jīranti`) means they reach old age. 'Royal chariots' (`rājarathā`) means the king's riding chariots. 'Well-adorned' (`sucittā`) means beautifully decorated with gold, silver, and so on. Regarding 'Moreover, the body also reaches old age' (`atho sarīrampi jaraṃ upeti`): when such unappropriated chariots made of heartwood decay, what is to be said of this internal, appropriated body made of flesh and blood? The body also certainly reaches old age; this is the meaning. Regarding 'The good, indeed, declare with the virtuous' (`santo have sabbhi pavedayanti`): the good, together with the virtuous, declare thus: 'The Dhamma of the good does not reach decay.' The meaning is: 'The Dhamma of the good is Nibbāna; it does not decay; it is ageless and deathless.' Thus they speak. Alternatively, because defilements, which have the nature of sinking down, are destroyed by reaching Nibbāna, therefore it is called `sabbhi`. Thus, showing the reason for the previous phrase, it is said, 'The good, indeed, declare with the virtuous.' For this is what is said: The Dhamma of the good does not reach decay; therefore, the good declare `sabbhi` (i.e., Nibbāna). The meaning is that they proclaim: 'Nibbāna, the ageless, is the Dhamma of the good.' Alternatively, this word `sabbhi` is a term for what is excellent. This is also the meaning: that Nibbāna which is the true Dhamma, which the good declare and speak of, that Dhamma of the good does not reach decay. The third.

4. Piyasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Piyasutta.

115. Catutthe [V 1.0123][M 1.0128] rahogatassāti rahasi gatassa. Paṭisallīnassāti nilīnassa ekībhūtassa. Evametaṃ, mahārājāti idha bhagavā imaṃ suttaṃ sabbaññubhāsitaṃ karonto āha. Antakenādhipannassāti maraṇena ajjhotthaṭassa. Catutthaṃ.

115. In the fourth discourse, 'gone to seclusion' (`rahogatassa`) means gone to a secluded place. 'Withdrawn' (`paṭisallīnassa`) means secluded, having become solitary. Regarding 'Thus it is, great king': here the Blessed One spoke, presenting this discourse as one spoken by the Omniscient One. 'Overcome by the Ender' (`antakenādhipannassa`) means overwhelmed by death. The fourth.

5. Attarakkhitasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Attarakkhita Sutta.

116. Pañcame hatthikāyoti hatthighaṭā. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Saṃvaroti pidahanaṃ. Sādhu sabbattha saṃvaroti iminā kammapathabhedaṃ apattassa kammassa saṃvaraṃ dasseti. Lajjīti hirimā. Lajjīgahaṇena cettha ottappampi gahitameva hoti. Pañcamaṃ.

116. In the fifth discourse, 'a troop of elephants' (`hatthikāya`) means a multitude of elephants. This same method applies to the remaining terms. 'Restraint' (`saṃvara`) means covering or restraining. By the phrase 'Restraint everywhere is good,' he shows the restraint of kamma that has not reached the level of a distinct path of kamma. 'Conscientious' (`lajjī`) means one who has moral shame (`hiri`). And here, by the inclusion of 'conscientious,' moral dread (`ottappa`) is also understood to be included. The fifth.

6. Appakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Appaka Sutta.

117. Chaṭṭhe uḷāre uḷāreti paṇīte ca bahuke ca. Majjantīti mānamajjanena majjanti. Atisāranti atikkamaṃ. Kūṭanti pāsaṃ. Pacchāsanti pacchā tesaṃ. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

117. In the sixth [discourse], 'excellent, excellent' (uḷāre uḷāre) means refined and abundant. 'They are intoxicated' (majjanti) means they are intoxicated by the intoxication of pride. 'They transgress' (atisāranti) refers to transgression. 'A snare' (kūṭaṃ) means a trap. 'Afterwards for them' (pacchā tesaṃ) means afterwards for them. The sixth [discourse].

7. Aḍḍakaraṇasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Aḍḍakaraṇa Sutta.

118. Sattame kāmahetūti kāmamūlakaṃ. Kāmanidānanti kāmapaccayā. Kāmādhikaraṇanti kāmakāraṇā. Sabbāni hetāni aññamaññavevacanāneva. Bhadramukhoti sundaramukho. Ekadivasaṃ kira rājā aḍḍakaraṇe nisīdi. Tattha paṭhamataraṃ lañjaṃ gahetvā nisinnā amaccā assāmikepi sāmike kariṃsu. Rājā taṃ ñatvā – “mayhaṃ tāva pathavissarassa sammukhāpete evaṃ karonti, parammukhā kiṃ nāma na karissanti? Paññāyissati dāni viṭaṭūbho senāpati sakena [P 1.0140] rajjena, kiṃ mayhaṃ evarūpehi lañjakhādakehi musāvādīhi saddhiṃ ekaṭṭhāne nisajjāyā”ti cintesi. Tasmā evamāha. Khippaṃva oḍḍitanti kuminaṃ viya oḍḍitaṃ. Yathā macchā oḍḍitaṃ kuminaṃ pavisantā na jānanti, evaṃ sattā kilesakāmena vatthukāmaṃ vītikkamantā na jānantīti attho. Sattamaṃ.

118. In the seventh [discourse], 'because of desire' (kāmahetu) means rooted in desire. 'Originating from desire' (kāmanidāna) means caused by desire. 'On account of desire' (kāmādhikaraṇa) means due to desire. All these terms are merely synonyms for one another. 'Fair-faced' (bhadramukha) means beautiful-faced. It is said that one day the king sat in the hall of judgment. There, the ministers, having first taken bribes, made those who were not owners into owners. The king, knowing this, thought: 'Even in my presence, the lord of the earth, they act thus—what will they not do behind my back? Now the commander, Prince Viṭaṭūbha, will be known by his own governance. What benefit is there for me in sitting in the same place with such bribe-taking liars?' Therefore, he spoke thus. 'Quickly set' (khippaṃva oḍḍitaṃ) means set like a fish trap. Just as fish entering a set fish trap do not know, so beings, transgressing against the object of desire with the desire that is a defilement, do not know—this is the meaning. The seventh [discourse].

8. Mallikāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Mallikā Sutta.

119. Aṭṭhame [V 1.0124][M 1.0129] atthi nu kho te malliketi kasmā pucchati? Ayaṃ kira mallikā duggatamālākārassa dhītā, ekadivasaṃ āpaṇato pūvaṃ gahetvā “mālārāmaṃ gantvāva khādissāmī”ti gacchantī paṭipathe bhikkhusaṅghaparivāraṃ bhagavantaṃ bhikkhācāraṃ pavisantaṃ disvā pasannacittā taṃ bhagavato adāsi. Satthā nisīdanākāraṃ dassesi. Ānandatthero cīvaraṃ paññāpetvā adāsi. Bhagavā tattha nisīditvā taṃ pūvaṃ paribhuñjitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Thero “imissā, bhante, ko vipāko bhavissatī”ti pucchi. Ānanda, ajjesā tathāgatassa paṭhamabhojanaṃ adāsi, ajjeva kosalarañño aggamahesī bhavissatīti. Taṃdivasameva ca rājā kāsigāme bhāgineyyena yuddhena parājito palāyitvā nagaraṃ āgacchanto mālārāmaṃ pavisitvā balakāyassa āgamanaṃ āgamesi. Tassa sā vattaṃ akāsi. So tāya vatte pasīditvā taṃ antepūraṃ atihārāpetvā taṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

119. In the eighth [discourse], 'Is there for you, Mallikā...?' (atthi nu kho te mallike) — why does he ask this? It is said that this Mallikā was the daughter of a poor garland-maker. One day, having taken a cake from the market, she thought, 'I will go to the flower garden and eat it.' On her way, she saw the Blessed One, surrounded by a company of monks, entering for the alms-round. With a mind of faith, she offered it to the Blessed One. The Teacher indicated a place to sit. The venerable Ānanda spread out a robe and offered it. The Blessed One sat there, ate the cake, rinsed his mouth, and smiled. The elder asked, 'What will be the result for her, Lord?' 'Ānanda, today she gave the Tathāgata his first meal; this very day she will become the chief queen of the Kosala king.' That very day, the king, defeated in battle by his nephew at a village in Kāsī, fled and, while coming towards the city, entered the flower garden to await the arrival of his army. She attended to his needs. Pleased with her service, he had her brought to the inner palace and established her in the position of chief queen.

Athekadivasaṃ cintesi – “mayā imissā duggatakulassa dhītuyā mahantaṃ issariyaṃ dinnaṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ puccheyyaṃ ‘ko te piyo’ti? Sā ‘tvaṃ me, mahārāja, piyo’ti vatvā puna maṃ pucchissati. Athassāhaṃ ‘mayhampi tvaṃyeva piyā’ti vakkhāmī”ti. Iti so aññamaññaṃ vissāsajananatthaṃ sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathento pucchati. Sā pana devī paṇḍitā buddhupaṭṭhāyikā dhammupaṭṭhāyikā saṅghupaṭṭhāyikā mahāpaññā[P 1.0141], tasmā evaṃ cintesi – “nāyaṃ pañho rañño mukhaṃ oloketvā kathetabbo”ti. Sā saraseneva kathetvā rājānaṃ pucchi. Rājā tāya sarasena kathitattā nivattituṃ alabhanto sayampi saraseneva kathetvā “sakāraṇaṃ idaṃ, tathāgatassa naṃ ārocessāmī”ti gantvā bhagavato ārocesi. Nevajjhagāti nādhigacchati. Evaṃ piyo puthu attā paresanti yathā ekassa attā piyo, evaṃ paresaṃ puthusattānampi attā piyoti attho. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Then one day he thought: 'I have given great sovereignty to this daughter of a poor family. What if I were to ask her, “Who is dear to you?” She will say, “You, great king, are dear to me,” and then she will ask me in return. Then I will say to her, “You alone are dear to me too.”' Thus, while making pleasant conversation for the purpose of generating mutual trust, he asked. But that queen was wise, a supporter of the Buddha, and of great wisdom; therefore, she thought thus: 'This question should not be answered by looking at the king's face.' She spoke from her own conviction and asked the king. The king, unable to make her retract since she had spoken from her own conviction, also replied from his own conviction and, thinking, 'This has a reason; I will report it to the Tathāgata,' he went and reported it to the Blessed One. 'He did not find' (nevajjhagā) means he did not comprehend. 'Thus the self is dear to others' (evaṃ piyo puthu attā paresaṃ) means: just as one's own self is dear, so too is the self dear to other many beings—this is the meaning. The eighth [discourse].

9. Yaññasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Explanation of the Yañña Sutta.

120. Navame [M 1.0130] thūṇūpanītānīti thūṇaṃ upanītāni, thūṇāya baddhāni honti. Parikammāni karontīti ettāvatā tehi bhikkhūhi rañño āraddhayañño tathāgatassa ārocito. Kasmā pana raññā ayaṃ yañño āraddho? Dussupinapaṭighātāya. Ekadivasaṃ kira rājā sabbālaṅkārappaṭimaṇḍito [V 1.0125] hatthikkhandhavaragato nagaraṃ anusañcaranto vātapānaṃ vivaritvā olokayamānaṃ ekaṃ itthiṃ disvā tassā paṭibaddhacitto tatova paṭinivattitvā antepuraṃ pavisitvā ekassa purisassa tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “gaccha tassā sassāmikabhāvaṃ vā assāmikabhāvaṃ vā jānāhī”ti pesesi. So gantvā pucchi. Sā “eso me sāmiko āpaṇe nisinno”ti dassesi. Rājapuriso rañño tamatthaṃ ācikkhi. Rājā taṃ purisaṃ pakkosāpetvā “maṃ upaṭṭhahā”ti āha. “Nāhaṃ, deva, upaṭṭhahituṃ jānāmī”ti ca vutte “upaṭṭhānaṃ nāma na ācariyassa santike uggahetabba”nti balakkārena āvudhaphalakaṃ gāhāpetvā upaṭṭhākaṃ akāsi. Upaṭṭhahitvā gehaṃ gatamattameva ca naṃ puna pakkosāpetvā “upaṭṭhākena nāma rañño vacanaṃ kattabbaṃ, gaccha ito yojanamatte amhākaṃ sīsadhovanapokkharaṇī atthi, tato aruṇamattikañca lohituppalamālañca gaṇhitvā ehi. Sace ajjeva nāgacchasi, rājadaṇḍaṃ karissāmī”ti vatvā pesesi. So rājabhayena nikkhamitvā [P 1.0142] gato.

120. In the ninth [discourse], 'brought to the pillar' (thūṇūpanītāni) means they were brought to the sacrificial pillar and were bound at the pillar. 'They are making preparations' (parikammāni karonti)—by this much, the sacrifice initiated by the king was reported to the Tathāgata by those monks. Now, why was this sacrifice initiated by the king? To counteract a bad dream. It is said that one day, the king, adorned with all ornaments and mounted on the back of a fine elephant, was touring the city when he saw a woman who had opened a window and was looking out. His mind became attached to her, so he turned back from that very spot, entered the inner palace, and related the matter to a certain man, sending him with the words, “Go and find out whether she has a husband or not.” That man went and asked. She pointed and said, “This is my husband, sitting in the shop.” The king’s man reported the matter to the king. The king had that man summoned and said, “Attend to me.” And when it was said, “Your Majesty, I do not know how to attend,” the king replied, “Service, so-called, is not something to be learned in the presence of a teacher.” Then, by force, he had the man take up a weapon and shield and made him an attendant. After the man had attended and had just gone home, the king had him summoned again and sent him away, saying: “An attendant must carry out the king’s word. Go. At a distance of a yojana from here is our head-washing pond. From there, take reddish clay and a garland of red water lilies and come back. If you do not return this very day, I will inflict the royal punishment upon you.” So, out of fear of the king, he went out from the city and departed.

Rājāpi tasmiṃ gate dovārikaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “ajja sāyanheyeva dvāraṃ pidahitvā ‘ahaṃ rājadūto’ti vā ‘uparājadūto’ti vā bhaṇantānampi mā vivarī”ti āha. So puriso mattikañca uppalāni ca gahetvā dvāre pihitamatte āgantvā bahuṃ vadantopi dvāraṃ alabhitvā parissayabhayena jetavanaṃ gato. Rājāpi rāgapariḷāhena abhibhūto kāle nisīdati, kāle tiṭṭhati, kāle nipajjati, sanniṭṭhānaṃ alabhanto yattha katthaci nisinnakova makkaṭaniddāya niddāyati.

The king, too, when that man had gone, summoned the gatekeeper and said, 'Close the gate this very evening, and do not open it even for those who say, "I am the king's envoy" or "I am the viceroy's envoy."' That man, taking the clay and the water lilies, arrived just as the gate was being closed. Though he pleaded much, he could not get the gate opened. Fearing peril, he went to Jetavana. The king, too, overcome by the torment of lust, sometimes sat, sometimes stood, and sometimes lay down. Unable to come to a decision, he dozed off wherever he sat, with the sleep of a monkey.

Pubbe [M 1.0131] ca tasmiṃyeva nagare cattāro seṭṭhiputtā paradārikakammaṃ katvā nandopanandāya nāma lohakumbhiyā nibbattiṃsu. Te pheṇuddehakaṃ paccamānā tiṃsavassasahassāni heṭṭhā gacchantā kumbhiyā talaṃ pāpuṇanti, tiṃsavassasahassāni upari gacchantā matthakaṃ pāpuṇanti. Te taṃ divasaṃ ālokaṃ oloketvā attano dukkaṭabhayena ekekaṃ gāthaṃ vattukāmā vattuṃ asakkontā ekekaṃ akkharameva āhaṃsu. Eko sa-kāraṃ, eko so-kāraṃ, eko na-kāraṃ, eko du-kāraṃ āha. Rājā tesaṃ nerayikasattānaṃ saddaṃ sutakālato paṭṭhāya sukhaṃ avindamānova taṃrattāvasesaṃ vītināmesi.

And previously, in that very city, four sons of wealthy men, having committed adultery, were reborn in the iron cauldron named Nandopananda. Being cooked and bubbling up like foam, they spend thirty thousand years descending to reach the bottom of the cauldron, and thirty thousand years ascending to reach the top. On that day, seeing the light and wishing to speak a verse each out of fear of their own evil deeds, but being unable to speak, they uttered only a single syllable each. One uttered the syllable 'sa,' another the syllable 'so,' another the syllable 'na,' and another the syllable 'du.' The king, from the time he heard the sound of those beings in hell, found no happiness at all and passed the remainder of that night.

Aruṇe uṭṭhite purohito āgantvā taṃ sukhaseyyaṃ pucchi. So “kuto me, ācariya, sukha”nti[V 1.0126]? Vatvā, “supine evarūpe sadde assosi”nti ācikkhi. Brāhmaṇo – “imassa rañño iminā supinena vuḍḍhi vā hāni vā natthi, apica kho pana yaṃ imassa gehe atthi, taṃ samaṇassa gotamassa hoti, gotamasāvakānaṃ hoti, brāhmaṇā kiñci na labhanti, brāhmaṇānaṃ bhikkhaṃ uppādessāmī”ti, “bhāriyo ayaṃ, mahārāja, supino tīsu jānīsu ekā paññāyati, rajjantarāyo vā bhavissati jīvitantarāyo vā, devo vā na vassissatī”ti āha. Kathaṃ sotthi bhaveyya ācariyāti? “Mantetvā ñātuṃ sakkā, mahārājāti. Gacchatha ācariyehi saddhiṃ mantetvā amhākaṃ sotthiṃ karothā”ti.

When dawn arose, the royal chaplain came and asked him about his pleasant sleep. The king replied, “Teacher, whence is there pleasure for me?” and recounted, “In a dream, I heard sounds of such a nature.” The brahmin thought to himself: “For this king, this dream signifies neither prosperity nor decline. However, whatever is in his palace will go to the ascetic Gotama and to the disciples of Gotama; the brahmins will receive nothing. I shall cause alms to arise for the brahmins.” He then said to the king, “Great king, this dream is serious. Of three kinds of calamities, one is indicated. There will be either danger to the kingdom, or danger to life, or the sky will not rain.” The king asked, “Teacher, how might there be safety?” The brahmin replied, “Great king, it is possible to know by deliberating.” The king said, “Go, deliberate with the teachers, and bring about our safety.”

So sivikasālāyaṃ brāhmaṇe sannipātetvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā, “visuṃ visuṃ gantvā evaṃ vadathā”ti tayo vagge akāsi[P 1.0143]. Brāhmaṇā pavisitvā rājānaṃ sukhaseyyaṃ pucchiṃsu. Rājā purohitassa kathitaniyāmeneva kathetvā “kathaṃ sotthi bhaveyyā”ti pucchi. Mahābrāhmaṇā – “sabbapañcasataṃ yaññaṃ yajitvā etassa kammassa sotthi bhaveyya, evaṃ, mahārāja, ācariyā kathentī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ sutvā anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā tuṇhī ahosi. Atha dutiyavaggabrāhmaṇāpi āgantvā tattheva kathesuṃ. Tathā tatiyavaggabrāhmaṇāpi. Atha rājā “yaññaṃ karontū”ti āṇāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya brāhmaṇā usabhādayo pāṇe āharāpesuṃ. Nagare mahāsaddo udapādi[M 1.0132]. Taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā mallikā rājānaṃ tathāgatassa santikaṃ pesesi. So gantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha naṃ bhagavā – “handa kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divādivassā”ti āha. Rājā – “ajja me, bhante, supinake cattāro saddā sutā, sohaṃ brāhmaṇe pucchiṃ. Brāhmaṇā ‘bhāriyo, mahārāja, supino, sabbapañcasataṃ yaññaṃ yajitvā paṭikammaṃ karomāti āraddhā’”ti āha. Kinti te, mahārāja, saddā sutāti. So yathāsutaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ bhagavā āha – pubbe, mahārāja, imasmiṃyeva nagare cattāro seṭṭhiputtā paradārikā hutvā nandopanandāya lohakumbhiyā nibbattā saṭṭhivassasahassamatthake uggacchiṃsu.

That chaplain, having assembled the brahmins in the hall for the royal palanquins and informed them of that matter, formed them into three groups, saying, 'Go separately and speak thus.' The brahmins entered and asked the king about his pleasant sleep. The king, speaking only in the manner instructed by the chaplain, asked, 'How can there be well-being?' The great brahmins said, 'Great King, by performing a sacrifice of five hundred of each kind, there would be well-being from this evil deed. Thus the teachers declare.' Having heard their words, the king, neither approving nor rejecting, became silent. Then the brahmins of the second group also came and spoke in the very same way. Likewise, the brahmins of the third group. Then the king ordered, 'Let them perform the sacrifice.' From then on, the brahmins had bulls and other living beings brought.
