A great uproar arose in the city. Having learned of this matter, Queen Mallikā sent the king to the presence of the Tathāgata. He went, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Now, Great King, from where do you come in the middle of the day?' The king said, 'Venerable Sir, today four sounds were heard by me in a dream, and I asked the brahmins. The brahmins have begun, saying, "Great King, the dream is ominous. Having performed a sacrifice of five hundred of each kind, we will perform a remedy."' 'What sounds were heard by you, Great King?' He related them as he had heard. Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Formerly, Great King, in this very city, four merchant's sons, having been adulterers, were reborn in the Lohakumbhī hell named Nandopananda. At the end of sixty thousand years, they rose to the surface.'

Tattha eko –

Among them, one—

“Saṭṭhivassasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni sabbaso;

Niraye paccamānānaṃ, kadā anto bhavissatī”ti.(pe. va. 802; jā. 1.4.54) –

"Sixty thousand years, all fully complete; For those being cooked in hell, when will there be an end?"

Imaṃ [V 1.0127] gāthaṃ vatthukāmo ahosi. Dutiyo –

He was desirous of speaking this verse. The second—

“Sohaṃ nūna ito gantvā, yoniṃ laddhāna mānusiṃ;

Vadaññū sīlasampanno, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahu”nti. (pe. va. 805; jā. 1.4.56) –

Indeed, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, generous and endowed with virtue, I will perform much that is meritorious.

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatthukāmo ahosi. Tatiyo –

He was desirous of uttering this verse. The third:

“Natthi anto kuto anto, na anto paṭidissati;

Tadā hi pakataṃ pāpaṃ, mama tuyhañca mārisā”ti. (pe. va. 803; jā. 1.4.55) –

There is no end; from where is the end? No end is apparent. For then, indeed, the evil deed was done by me and by you, O sirs.

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatthukāmo ahosi. Catuttho –

He was desirous of uttering this verse. The fourth:

“Dujjīvitamajīvimhā, ye sante na dadamhase;

Vijjamānesu bhogesu, dīpaṃ nākamha attano”ti. (pe. va. 804; jā. 1.4.53) –

We have lived a wretched life, we who did not give when there were possessions; with wealth available, we made no refuge for ourselves.

Imaṃ[P 1.0144]. Te imā gāthā vattuṃ asakkontā ekekaṃ akkharaṃ vatvā tattheva nimuggā. Iti, mahārāja, te nerayikasattā yathākammena viraviṃsu. Tassa saddassa sutapaccayā tuyhaṃ hāni vā vuḍḍhi vā natthi. Ettakānaṃ pana pasūnaṃ ghātanakammaṃ nāma bhāriyanti nirayabhayena tajjetvā dhammakathaṃ [M 1.0133] kathesi. Rājā dasabale pasīditvā, “muñcāmi, nesaṃ jīvitaṃ dadāmi, haritāni ceva tiṇāni khādantu, sītalāni ca pānīyāni pivantu, sīto ca nesaṃ vāto upavāyatū”ti vatvā, “gacchatha hārethā”ti manusse āṇāpesi. Te gantvā brāhmaṇe palāpetvā taṃ pāṇasaṅghaṃ bandhanato mocetvā nagare dhammabheriṃ carāpesuṃ.

Unable to utter these verses, they said one syllable each and sank right there. Thus, great king, those beings in hell cried out in accordance with their kamma. From the hearing of that sound, there is neither loss nor gain for you. However, the act of killing so many animals is indeed a heavy deed. Thus, having frightened him with the fear of hell, he gave a discourse on the Dhamma. The king, gaining faith in the One of Ten Powers, said, "I release them, I give them their lives. Let them eat green grass and drink cool water, and let a cool wind blow upon them." Having spoken thus, he commanded his men, saying, "Go, bring them away." They went, drove away the brahmins, freed that multitude of living beings from their bonds, and had the drum of the Dhamma beaten throughout the city.

Atha rājā dasabalassa santike nisinno āha – “bhante, ekaratti nāma tiyāmā hoti, mayhaṃ pana ajja dve rattiyo ekato ghaṭitā viya ahesu”nti. Sopi puriso tattheva nisinno [V 1.0128] āha – “bhante, yojanaṃ nāma catugāvutaṃ hoti, mayhaṃ pana ajja dve yojanāni ekato katāni viya ahesu”nti. Atha bhagavā – “jāgarassa tāva rattiyā dīghabhāvo pākaṭo, santassa yojanassa dīghabhāvo pākaṭo, vaṭṭapatitassa pana bālaputhujjanassa anamataggasaṃsāravaṭṭaṃ ekantadīghamevā”ti rājānañca tañca purisaṃ nerayikasatte ca ārabbha dhammapade imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then the king, seated in the presence of the Ten-Powered One, said: 'Venerable Sir, a single night is three watches, but for me today, it was as if two nights were joined into one.' That man, also seated right there, said: 'Venerable Sir, a yojana is four gāvutas, but for me today, it was as if two yojanas were made into one.' Then the Blessed One, reflecting, 'For one who is awake, the length of the night is evident; for one who is weary, the length of a yojana is evident; but for the foolish worldling who has fallen into the cycle, the round of saṃsāra with its unknown beginning is exceedingly long indeed,' and making the king, that man, and the beings in hell the subject, spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

“Dīghā jāgarato ratti, dīghaṃ santassa yojanaṃ;

Dīgho bālānaṃ saṃsāro, saddhammaṃ avijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 60);

Long is the night for one who is awake; long is a yojana for one who is weary; long is saṃsāra for fools who do not know the true Dhamma.

Gāthāpariyosāne so itthisāmiko puriso sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ jānitvā.

At the end of the verse, that man, the husband of the woman, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The phrase 'Etamatthaṃ viditvā' means 'having known this reason'.

Assamedhantiādīsu – porāṇarājakāle kira sassamedhaṃ purisamedhaṃ sammāpāsaṃ vācāpeyyanti cattāri saṅgahavatthūni ahesuṃ, yehi rājāno lokaṃ saṅgaṇhiṃsu. Tattha nipphannasassato [P 1.0145] dasamabhāgaggahaṇaṃ sassamedhaṃ nāma, sassasampādane medhāvitāti attho. Mahāyodhānaṃ chamāsikaṃ bhatta-vetanānuppadānaṃ purisamedhaṃ nāma, purisasaṅgaṇhane medhāvitāti attho. Daliddamanussānaṃ hatthato lekhaṃ gahetvā tīṇi vassāni vināva vaḍḍhiyā sahassadvisahassamattadhanānuppadānaṃ sammāpāsaṃ nāma. Tañhi sammā manusse pāseti, hadaye bandhitvā viya ṭhapeti, tasmā sammāpāsanti vuccati. “Tāta mātulā”tiādinā nayena saṇhavācābhaṇanaṃ vācāpeyyaṃ nāma, piyavācāti attho. Evaṃ catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi saṅgahitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ iddhañceva [M 1.0134] hoti phītañca pahūtaannapānaṃ khemaṃ nirabbudaṃ. Manussā mudā modamānā ure putte naccentā apārutagharadvārā viharanti. Idaṃ gharadvāresu aggaḷānaṃ abhāvato niraggaḷanti vuccati. Ayaṃ porāṇikā paveṇī.

Regarding 'assamedha' and so on—in ancient royal times, it is said there were four bases of sympathy: sassamedha, purisamedha, sammāpāsa, and vācāpeyya, by which kings won over the populace. Therein, the taking of the tenth part from the ripened crop is called sassamedha; the meaning is 'skill in the production of crops.' The giving of food and wages for six months to great warriors is called purisamedha; the meaning is 'skill in gathering men.' For poor people, having taken a written pledge from them, the giving of wealth amounting to one or two thousand for three years without interest is called sammāpāsa. For it rightly ensnares people, establishing them as if bound in the heart; therefore, it is called sammāpāsa. The speaking of gentle words in the manner of 'Dear father, uncle,' and so on, is called vācāpeyya; the meaning is 'affectionate speech.' Thus, a kingdom supported by these four bases of sympathy became prosperous and flourishing, abundant in food and drink, safe, and free from scourge. People, delighted and rejoicing, lived with their doors open, making their children dance on their laps. This is called 'without bars' because of the absence of bolts on the house doors. This is the ancient tradition.

Aparabhāge pana okkākarājakāle brāhmaṇā imāni cattāri saṅgahavatthūni imañca raṭṭhasampattiṃ parivattetvā uddhaṃmūlakaṃ katvā assamedhaṃ purisamedhanti ādike pañca yaññe nāma akaṃsu. Tesu assamettha medhanti vadhantīti assamedho. Dvīhi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa ekavīsatiyūpassa ekasmiṃ majjhimadivaseyeva sattanavutipañcapasusataghātabhiṃsanassa ṭhapetvā bhūmiñca [V 1.0129] purise ca avasesasabbavibhavadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Purisamettha medhantīti purisamedho. Catūhi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa saddhiṃ bhūmiyā assamedhe vuttavibhavadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sammamettha pāsentīti sammāpāso. Divase divase sammaṃ khipitvā tassa [P 1.0146] patitokāse vediṃ katvā saṃhārimehi yūpādīhi sarassatinadiyā nimuggokāsato pabhuti paṭilomaṃ gacchantena yajitabbassa satrayāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vājamettha pivantīti vājapeyyo. Ekena pariyaññena sattarasahi pasūhi yajitabbassa beluvayūpassa sattarasakadakkhiṇassa yaññassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Natthi ettha aggaḷāti niraggaḷo. Navahi pariyaññehi yajitabbassa saddhiṃ bhūmiyā ca purisehi ca assamedhe vuttavibhavadakkhiṇassa sabbamedhapariyāyanāmassa assamedhavikappassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Mahārambhāti mahākiccā mahākaraṇīyā. Sammaggatāti sammā paṭipannā buddhādayo. Nirārambhāti appatthā appakiccā. Yajanti anukulanti anukulesu yajanti, yaṃ niccabhattādi pubbapurisehi paṭṭhapitaṃ, taṃ aparāparaṃ anupacchinnattā manussā dadantīti attho. Navamaṃ.

Later, however, during the time of King Okkāka, the brahmins, having inverted these four bases of sympathy and this prosperity of the kingdom, and having uprooted them, performed five sacrifices named the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, and so on. Among these, the 'horse sacrifice' (assamedha) is so called because in it they slay (medhanti) a horse (assa). This is the designation for a sacrifice to be performed with two surrounding sacrifices and twenty-one sacrificial posts, in which on just a single middle day, there is the terrifying slaughter of five hundred and ninety-seven animals, and in which, excluding the land and the people, all remaining wealth is given as an offering. The 'human sacrifice' (purisamedha) is so called because in it they slay (medhanti) a person (purisa). This is the designation for a sacrifice to be performed with four surrounding sacrifices, together with the land, in which the offering of wealth is as stated in the horse sacrifice. The 'Sammāpāsa' is so called because in it they cast (pāsenti) the yoke-pin (sammaṃ). This is the designation for the Satrayāga sacrifice, which is to be performed by one who, day by day, throws the yoke-pin and makes an altar at the place where it has fallen, using transportable sacrificial posts and so on, and who proceeds upstream, starting from the place of immersion in the Sarassatī river. The 'Vājapeyya' is so called because in it they drink (pivanti) the honey-elixir prepared with mantras (vājaṃ). This is the designation for a sacrifice to be performed with one surrounding sacrifice and seventeen animals, having a sacrificial post of beluva wood, and in which seventeen kinds of offerings are given. The 'Niraggaḷa' (Without Bars) is so called because in it there are no bolts (aggaḷā). This is the designation for a variation of the horse sacrifice itself, which has the alternative name 'Sabbamedha' (All-Sacrifice), and is to be performed with nine surrounding sacrifices, together with the land and the people, and in which the offering of wealth is as stated in the horse sacrifice. 'Of great undertaking' (mahārambhā) means having great tasks, having great duties. 'Well-gone' (sammaggatā) means rightly practiced, like the Buddhas and other noble ones. 'Of no undertaking' (nirārambhā) means having few aims, having few tasks. The phrase 'they sacrifice in a suitable manner' (yajanti anukulaṃ) means they sacrifice in suitable families; whatever perpetual alms, etc., were established by the ancestors, people give from generation to generation because it is uninterrupted. This is the meaning. Ninth.

10. Bandhanasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Bondage Discourse

121. Dasame idha, bhante, raññāti idaṃ te bhikkhū tesu manussesu ānandattherassa sukatakāraṇaṃ ārocentā ārocesuṃ. Rañño kira sakkena kusarājassa dinno aṭṭhavaṅko maṇi paveṇiyā āgato. Rājā alaṅkaraṇakāle taṃ maṇiṃ āharathāti āha. Manussā “ṭhapitaṭṭhāne [M 1.0135] na passāmā”ti ārocesuṃ. Rājā antogharacārino “maṇiṃ pariyesitvā dethā”ti bandhāpesi. Ānandatthero te disvā maṇipaṭisāmakānaṃ ekaṃ upāyaṃ ācikkhi[P 1.0147]. Te rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā “paṇḍito thero, therassa vacanaṃ karothā”ti. Paṭisāmakamanussā rājaṅgaṇe udakacāṭiṃ ṭhapetvā sāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā te manusse āhaṃsu – “sāṭakaṃ pārupitvā ettha gantvā hatthaṃ otārethā”ti. Maṇicoro cintesi – “rājabhaṇḍaṃ vissajjetuṃ vā valañjetuṃ vā na sakkā”ti. So gehaṃ gantvā maṇiṃ upakacchake ṭhapetvā sāṭakaṃ pārupitvā āgamma udakacāṭiyaṃ pakkhipitvā pakkāmi. Mahājane paṭikkante rājamanussā cāṭiyaṃ hatthaṃ otāretvā maṇiṃ disvā āharitvā rañño adaṃsu. “Ānandattherena kira dassitanayena maṇi diṭṭho”ti mahājano kolāhalaṃ akāsi. Te bhikkhū taṃ kāraṇaṃ tathāgatassa ārocentā imaṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā – “anacchariyaṃ, bhikkhave, yaṃ ānando manussānaṃ hatthāruḷhamaṇiṃ āharāpeyya[V 1.0130], yattha pubbe paṇḍitā attano ñāṇe ṭhatvā ahetukapaṭisandhiyaṃ nibbattānaṃ tiracchānagatānampi hatthāruḷhaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ āharāpetvā rañño adaṃsū”ti vatvā –

121. In the tenth discourse, regarding the words 'Here, venerable sir, by the king,' those bhikkhus, wishing to report the good deed done by the Elder Ānanda concerning those people, related it. It is said that an eight-faceted jewel, given to King Kusa by Sakka, had come to the king by way of royal lineage. At the time of adornment, the king said, 'Bring that jewel.' The men reported, 'We do not see it in the place where it was kept.' The king had those who move about within the palace bound, saying, 'Search for the jewel and give it.' Seeing them, the Elder Ānanda told a stratagem to the jewel-keepers. They reported it to the king. The king said, 'The Elder is wise; do as the Elder says.' The jewel-keepers placed a large water pot in the royal courtyard, had it surrounded with a curtain, and said to those people, 'Covering yourselves with a garment, go there and dip your hands in.' The jewel thief thought, 'It is not possible to dispose of or to use the king's property.' He went home, placed the jewel in his armpit, covered himself with a garment, came, dropped it into the large water pot, and departed. When the great crowd had departed, the king's men dipped their hands into the pot, saw the jewel, brought it, and gave it to the king. The great crowd made an uproar, saying, 'It is said the jewel was found by the method shown by the Elder Ānanda.' Those bhikkhus, wishing to report the matter to the Tathāgata, related this event. The Teacher said, 'It is not surprising, bhikkhus, that Ānanda could cause a jewel that had come into people's hands to be brought back. For, in the past, wise men, standing firm in their own wisdom, having caused goods that had come into the hands even of animals born through a causeless rebirth-linking to be brought back, gave them to the king.' Having said this—

“Ukkaṭṭhe sūramicchanti, mantīsu akutūhalaṃ;

Piyañca annapānamhi, atthe jāte ca paṇḍita”nti. (jā. 1.1.92) –

“In conflict, they desire a hero; in counsel, one who is unperplexed; in food and drink, someone agreeable; and when a matter has arisen, a wise person.”

Mahāsārajātakaṃ kathesi.

He told the Mahāsāra Jātaka.

Na taṃ daḷhanti taṃ bandhanaṃ thiranti na kathenti. Yadāyasanti yaṃ āyasā kataṃ. Sārattarattāti suṭṭhu rattarattā, sārattena vā rattā sārattarattā, sāraṃ idanti maññanāya rattāti attho. Apekkhāti ālayo nikanti. Āhūti kathenti. Ohārinanti catūsu apāyesu ākaḍḍhanakaṃ. Sithilanti na āyasādibandhanaṃ viya iriyāpathaṃ nivāretvā ṭhitaṃ. Tena hi bandhanena baddhā paradesampi gacchantiyeva. Duppamuñcanti aññatra lokuttarañāṇena muñcituṃ asakkuṇeyyanti. Dasamaṃ.

Regarding `Na taṃ daḷhaṃ`: The wise do not say that that bond is a strong one. Regarding `Yadāyasaṃ`: It is the bond which is made of iron. Regarding `Sārattarattā`: It means intensely infatuated; or, infatuated by thinking, 'This is the essence.' This is the meaning. `Apekhā` is craving as clinging, craving as delight. `Āhu` means: they say. `Ohārinaṃ` means: that which has the nature of dragging one down into the four woeful states. `Sithilaṃ` means: it is not one that remains fixed by preventing the four postures, like a bond of iron and so on. For, those bound by that bond of craving indeed go even to a foreign country. `Duppamuñcaṃ` should be understood thus: one would be unable to be freed except by supramundane knowledge. Tenth.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

End of the First Chapter.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Sattajaṭilasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Seven Matted-Hair Ascetics

122. Dutiyavaggassa [M 1.0136] paṭhame [P 1.0148] pubbārāme migāramātupāsādeti pubbārāmasaṅkhāte vihāre migāramātuyā pāsāde. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – atīte satasahassakappamatthake ekā upāsikā padumuttaraṃ bhagavantaṃ nimantetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa satasahassadānaṃ datvā bhagavato pādamūle nipajjitvā – “anāgate tumhādisassa buddhassa aggupaṭṭhāyikā homī”ti patthanaṃ akāsi. Sā kappasatasahassaṃ devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsaritvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle bhaddiyanagare meṇḍakaputtassa dhanañcayaseṭṭhino gehe sumanadeviyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi[V 1.0131]. Jātakāle cassā visākhāti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Sā yadā bhagavā bhaddiyanagaraṃ agamāsi, tadā pañcahi dārikāsatehi saddhiṃ bhagavato paccuggamanaṃ gatā paṭhamadassanamhiyeva sotāpannā ahosi. Aparabhāge sāvatthiyaṃ migāraseṭṭhiputtassa puṇṇavaḍḍhanakumārassa gehaṃ gatā. Tattha naṃ migāraseṭṭhi mātiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi, tasmā migāramātāti vuccati. Tāya kārite pāsāde.

1. In the first discourse of the second chapter, regarding `pubbārāme migāramātupāsāde`: in the mansion of Migāramātā, in the monastery known as the Pubbārāma. Herein, this is the sequential narrative: In the past, a hundred thousand aeons ago, a certain female lay disciple, having invited the Blessed One Padumuttara, gave an alms-offering to the Saṅgha of one hundred thousand bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head. Lying prostrate at the Blessed One's feet, she made an aspiration, saying: 'In the future, may I become the chief female lay supporter of a Buddha like you.' That female lay disciple, having wandered for a hundred thousand aeons among devas and humans, in the time of our Blessed One, took conception in the womb of Sumanādevī in the house of the treasurer Dhanañjaya, son of the treasurer Meṇḍaka, in the city of Bhaddiya. And at the time of her birth, they gave her the name Visākhā. When the Blessed One came to the city of Bhaddiya, she went to welcome the Blessed One together with five hundred young maidens, and became a stream-enterer at the very first sight. At a later time, she went to the house of the young man Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, son of the treasurer Migāra, in Sāvatthī. There, the treasurer Migāra established her in the position of a mother; therefore, she is called Migāramātā. In the mansion caused to be built by her.

Bahi dvārakoṭṭhaketi pāsādadvārakoṭṭhakassa bahi, na vihāradvārakoṭṭhakassa. So kira pāsādo lohapāsādo viya samantā catudvārakoṭṭhakayuttena pākārena parikkhitto. Tesu pācīnadvārakoṭṭhakassa bahi pāsādacchāyāyaṃ pācīnalokadhātuṃ olokento paññatte varabuddhāsane nisinno hoti.

122. “Outside the gatehouse” means outside the palace gatehouse, not the monastery gatehouse. It is said that the palace was surrounded on all sides by a wall endowed with four gatehouses, like the Lohapāsāda. Among them, outside the eastern gatehouse, in the shade of the palace, he was seated on the prepared excellent Buddha-seat, gazing toward the eastern world-sphere.

Parūḷhakacchanakhalomāti parūḷhakacchā parūḷhanakhā parūḷhalomā, kacchādīsu dīghalomā dīghanakhā cāti attho. Khārivividhanti vividhakhāriṃ nānappakārakaṃ pabbajitaparikkhārabhaṇḍakaṃ. Avidūre atikkamantīti avidūramaggena nagaraṃ pavisanti. Rājāhaṃ[P 1.0149], bhanteti ahaṃ, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo, mayhaṃ nāmaṃ tumhe jānāthāti. Kasmā pana rājā loke aggapuggalassa santike nisinno evarūpānaṃ naggabhogganissirikānaṃ añjaliṃ paggaṇhātīti. Saṅgaṇhanatthāya. Evaṃ hissa ahosi – “sacāhaṃ ettakampi etesaṃ na karissāmi[M 1.0137], ‘mayaṃ puttadāraṃ pahāya etassatthāya dubbhojanadukkhaseyyādīni anubhoma, ayaṃ amhākaṃ añjalimattampi na karotī’ti attanā diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ paṭicchādetvā na katheyyuṃ. Evaṃ kate pana anigūhitvā kathessantī”ti. Tasmā evamakāsi. Apica satthu ajjhāsayajānanatthaṃ evamakāsi.

“With overgrown armpit hair, nails, and body hair” means having overgrown armpit hair, overgrown nails, and overgrown body hair; that is, long hair in the armpits and so on, and long nails. “Various ascetic equipment” means various kinds of an ascetic's equipment and belongings. “Passing not far away” means they enter the city by a nearby road. “I am the king, venerable sirs” means: “Venerable sirs, I am King Pasenadi of Kosala; you should know my name.” But why does the king, while seated in the presence of the foremost person in the world, raise his hands in reverence to such naked ascetics of broken practice and without splendor? For the purpose of winning them over. For this was his thought: “If I do not do even this much for them, they might think, ‘We have abandoned our children and wives and for his sake endure poor food, uncomfortable lodging, and so on, yet this king does not even show us the respect of raising his hands,’ and concealing what they have seen and heard, they would not speak of it. But if this is done, they will speak without concealing anything.” Therefore, he did so. Moreover, he did so to understand the Teacher’s inclination.

Kāsikacandananti saṇhacandanaṃ. Mālāgandhavilepananti vaṇṇagandhatthāya mālaṃ, sugandhabhāvatthāya gandhaṃ, vaṇṇagandhatthāya vilepanañca dhārentena.

“Kāsika sandalwood” means fine sandalwood. “Garlands, perfumes, and unguents” means by wearing garlands for the sake of beauty and fragrance, using perfumes for the sake of a good fragrance, and using unguents for the sake of beauty and fragrance.

Saṃvāsenāti sahavāsena. Sīlaṃ veditabbanti ayaṃ susīlo vā dussīlo vāti saṃvasantena upasaṅkamantena jānitabbo. Tañca kho dīghena addhunā na ittaranti tañca sīlaṃ dīghena kālena veditabbaṃ, na ittarena. Dvīhatīhañhi saṃyatākāro ca saṃvutindriyākāro ca na sakkā dassetuṃ. Manasikarotāti sīlamassa pariggahessāmīti manasikarontena paccavekkhanteneva sakkā [V 1.0132] jānituṃ, na itarena. Paññavatāti tampi sappaññeneva paṇḍitena. Bālo hi manasikarontopi jānituṃ na sakkoti.

‘By living together’ means by dwelling together. ‘Virtue is to be known’ means that whether this person is virtuous or unvirtuous is to be known by one who lives with and approaches them. ‘And that over a long period, not a short one’ means that this virtue is to be known over a long period of time, not a short one. For in only two or three days, it is not possible to show an appearance of being restrained and an appearance of having controlled faculties. ‘By paying attention’ means that it is possible to know only by one who pays attention and reflects with the thought, ‘I will investigate their virtue’; not otherwise. ‘By one with wisdom’ means that this virtue, too, can be known only by a wise, intelligent person. For a fool, even while paying attention, is not able to know.

Saṃvohārenāti kathanena.

‘By conversation’ means by speaking.

“Yo hi koci manussesu, vohāraṃ upajīvati;

Evaṃ vāseṭṭha jānāhi, vāṇijo so na brāhmaṇo”ti. (ma. ni. 2.457) –

“Whoever among humans makes a living by trade, know this, Vāseṭṭha, he is a trader, not a Brahmin.”

Ettha hi byavahāro vohāro nāma. “Cattāro ariyavohārā cattāro anariyavohārā”ti (dī. ni. 3.313) ettha cetanā. “Saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro”ti (dha. sa. 1313-1315) ettha paññatti. “Vohāramattena so vohareyyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.25) ettha kathā vohāro. Idhāpi esova adhippeto. Ekaccassa hi sammukhā kathā parammukhāya kathāya na sameti, parammukhā [P 1.0150] kathā ca sammukhāya kathāya, tathā purimakathā ca pacchimakathāya, pacchimakathā ca purimakathāya. So kathenteneva sakkā jānituṃ “asuci eso puggalo”ti. Sucisīlassa pana purimaṃ pacchimena, pacchimañca purimena sameti, sammukhākathitaṃ parammukhākathitena, parammukhākathitañca sammukhākathitena, tasmā kathentena sakkā sucibhāvo jānitunti pakāsento evamāha.

Here, transaction is called ‘vohāro’. In the passage, ‘Four noble usages, four ignoble usages’ (Dī. Ni. 3.313), here ‘vohāro’ is intention. In the passage, ‘Perception, term, concept, usage’ (Dha. Sa. 1313-1315), here it is concept. In the passage, ‘By mere usage he would use’ (Saṃ. Ni. 1.25), here speech is the ‘vohāro’. Here too, this very one is intended. Indeed, for a certain person, speech in one's presence does not agree with speech in one's absence, and speech in one's absence does not agree with speech in one's presence; likewise, former speech does not agree with later speech, and later speech with former speech. That person can be known through their speaking: ‘This person is impure.’ But for one of pure virtue, the former speech agrees with the latter, and the latter with the former; what is said in one's presence agrees with what is said in one's absence, and what is said in one's absence agrees with what is said in one's presence. Therefore, by speaking, the state of purity can be known. Thus, wishing to explain this, he spoke thus.

Thāmoti [M 1.0138] ñāṇathāmo. Yassa hi ñāṇathāmo natthi, so uppannesu upaddavesu gahetabbaggahaṇaṃ katabbakiccaṃ apassanto advāragharaṃ paviṭṭho viya carati. Tenāha āpadāsu kho, mahārāja, thāmo veditabboti. Sākacchāyāti saṃkathāya. Duppaññassa hi kathā udake geṇḍu viya uppalavati, paññavato kathentassa paṭibhānaṃ anantaraṃ hoti. Udakavipphanditeneva hi maccho khuddako vā mahanto vāti ñāyati. Ocarakāti heṭṭhācarakā. Carā hi pabbatamatthakena carantāpi heṭṭhā – carakāva honti. Ocaritvāti avacaritvā vīmaṃsitvā, taṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvāti attho. Rajojallanti rajañca jallañca. Vaṇṇarūpenāti vaṇṇasaṇṭhānena. Ittaradassanenāti lahukadassanena. Viyañjanenāti parikkhārabhaṇḍakena. Patirūpako mattikākuṇḍalovāti suvaṇṇakuṇḍalapatirūpako mattikākuṇḍalova. Lohaḍḍhamāsoti lohaḍḍhamāsako. Paṭhamaṃ.

By 'strength' is meant the strength of wisdom. For one who lacks the strength of wisdom, when troubles arise, not seeing what should be taken up or what task should be done, they act like one who has entered a house without a door. Therefore He said: 'Great king, strength is to be known in times of adversity.' 'By discussion' means by conversation. For the speech of the unwise floats on water like a ball, while the ready wit of the wise who is speaking is limitless. Indeed, just by the stirring of the water, a fish is known as small or large. 'Spies' means those who move below. For spies, even while moving on a mountain peak, are indeed those who move below. 'Having spied' means having investigated, examined, and known that particular course of events; this is the meaning. 'Dust and grime' means dust and grime. 'By appearance' means by color and form. 'By a brief seeing' means by a quick glance. 'By outward appearance' means by requisite-goods. 'Like a counterfeit clay earring' means like a clay earring that is a counterfeit of a golden one. 'A half-māsa of bronze' means a half-māsaka of bronze. The first.

2. Pañcarājasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Five Kings Sutta

123. Dutiye [V 1.0133] rūpāti nīlapītādibhedaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ. Kāmānaṃ agganti etaṃ kāmānaṃ uttamaṃ seṭṭhanti rūpagaruko āha. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Yatoti yadā. Manāpapariyantanti [P 1.0151] manāpanipphattikaṃ manāpakoṭikaṃ. Tattha dve manāpāni puggalamanāpaṃ sammutimanāpañca. Puggalamanāpaṃ nāma yaṃ ekassa puggalassa iṭṭhaṃ kantaṃ hoti, tadeva aññassa aniṭṭhaṃ akantaṃ. Paccantavāsīnañhi gaṇḍuppādāpi iṭṭhā honti kantā manāpā, majjhimadesavāsīnaṃ atijegucchā. Tesañca moramaṃsādīni iṭṭhāni honti, itaresaṃ tāni atijegucchāni. Idaṃ puggalamanāpaṃ. Itaraṃ sammutimanāpaṃ.

2. In the second sutta, 'form' refers to the sense-object of form, differentiated by blue, yellow, and so on. 'The highest of sensual pleasures' means 'this is the supreme and best of sensual pleasures'—so says one who esteems form. The same method applies in the remaining cases. 'Yato' means 'yadā' (when). 'Bounded by the agreeable' means perfected by the agreeable, having the agreeable as its limit. In this context, there are two kinds of agreeableness: personal agreeableness and conventional agreeableness. Personal agreeableness is that which is wished for and liked by one person, but that very thing is unwished for and disliked by another. For instance, even earthworms are wished for, liked, and agreeable to border-dwellers, while they are utterly repulsive to those in the middle country. And for those of the middle country, peacock flesh and so on are wished for, while for the others, those things are utterly repulsive. This is personal agreeableness. The other is conventional agreeableness.

Iṭṭhāniṭṭhārammaṇaṃ nāma loke paṭivibhattaṃ natthi, vibhajitvā pana dassetabbaṃ. Vibhajantena ca na atiissarānaṃ mahāsammatamahāsudassanadhammāsokādīnaṃ vasena vibhajitabbaṃ. Tesañhi dippakappampi ārammaṇaṃ amanāpaṃ upaṭṭhāti. Atiduggatānaṃ dullabhannapānānaṃ vasenapi na vibhajitabbaṃ. Tesañhi kaṇājakabhattasitthānipi pūtimaṃsassa rasopi atimadhuro amatasadiso hoti. Majjhimānaṃ pana gaṇakamahāmattaseṭṭhi kuṭumbikavāṇijādīnaṃ kālena [M 1.0139] iṭṭhaṃ kālena aniṭṭhaṃ labhamānānaṃ vasena vibhajitabbaṃ. Tañca panetaṃ ārammaṇaṃ javanaṃ paricchindituṃ na sakkoti. Javanañhi iṭṭhepi rajjati aniṭṭhepi, iṭṭhepi dussati aniṭṭhepi. Ekantato pana vipākacittaṃ iṭṭhāniṭṭhaṃ paricchindati. Kiñcāpi hi micchādiṭṭhikā buddhaṃ vā saṅghaṃ vā mahācetiyādīni vā uḷārāni ārammaṇāni disvā akkhīni pidahanti domanassaṃ āpajjanti, dhammasaddaṃ sutvā kaṇṇe thakenti, cakkhuviññāṇasotaviññāṇāni pana tesaṃ kusalavipākāneva honti. Kiñcāpi gūthasūkarādayo gūthagandhaṃ ghāyitvā khādituṃ labhissāmāti somanassajātā honti, gūthadassane pana nesaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, tassa gandhaghāyane ghānaviññāṇaṃ, rasasāyane jivhāviññāṇañca akusalavipākameva hoti. Bhagavā pana puggalamanāpataṃ sandhāya te ca, mahārāja, rūpātiādimāha.

123. In the world, what is called an agreeable or disagreeable object is not definitively distinguished; however, it should be explained by making a distinction. And one who makes this distinction should not do so based on those with excessive sovereignty, such as Mahāsammata, Mahāsudassana, or Dhammāsoka, for to them, even a divine-like object appears as disagreeable. Nor should the distinction be made based on the extremely destitute who have difficulty obtaining food and drink, for to them, even grains of rice from broken rice and the taste of rotten meat are exceedingly sweet, like nectar. Instead, the distinction should be made based on intermediate persons—such as accountants, high-ranking officials, bankers, householders, and merchants—who at times obtain what is agreeable and at other times what is disagreeable. And yet, this object cannot determine the impulsion (javana), for the impulsion is attached to what is agreeable and also to what is disagreeable, and it is averse to what is agreeable and also to what is disagreeable. Definitively, however, it is resultant consciousness (vipākacitta) that determines what is agreeable and disagreeable. For even though those with wrong views may close their eyes in distress upon seeing the Buddha, the Saṅgha, or great stupas—exalted objects—or block their ears upon hearing the Dhamma, their eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness are nevertheless only wholesome results. And even though pigs and the like, upon smelling feces, may feel joyful, thinking, 'We will get to eat it!', their eye-consciousness upon seeing the feces, their nose-consciousness upon smelling it, and their tongue-consciousness upon tasting it are only unwholesome results. The Blessed One, however, spoke with reference to personal agreeableness when he said, 'Great king, those forms...' and so on.

Candanaṅgalikoti idaṃ tassa upāsakassa nāmaṃ. Paṭibhāti maṃ bhagavāti bhagavā mayhaṃ ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ upaṭṭhāti paññāyati. Tassa te pañca rājāno āmuttamaṇikuṇḍale sajjitāya [P 1.0152] āpānabhūmiyā nisinnavaseneva mahatā rājānubhāvena paramena issariyavibhavena āgantvāpi dasabalassa [V 1.0134] santike ṭhitakālato paṭṭhāya divā padīpe viya udakābhisitte aṅgāre viya sūriyuṭṭhāne khajjopanake viya ca hatappabhe hatasobhe taṃ tathāgatañca tehi sataguṇena sahassaguṇena virocamānaṃ disvā, “mahantā vata bho buddhā nāmā”ti paṭibhānaṃ udapādi. Tasmā evamāha.

'Candanaṅgalika' is that lay follower's name. 'The Blessed One occurs to me' (paṭibhāti maṃ bhagavā) means: 'O Blessed One, a certain reason occurs to me; it becomes clear.' Those five kings, adorned with jeweled earrings, having been seated in the prepared drinking place, even though they had come with great royal power and supreme lordly splendor, from the moment they stood in the presence of the Ten-Powered One, they became like lamps in daylight, like embers sprinkled with water, and like fireflies at sunrise—their radiance destroyed, their splendor destroyed. Seeing the Tathāgata shining a hundredfold, a thousandfold more than them, the inspiration arose: 'Oh, how great indeed are the Buddhas!' Therefore, he spoke thus.

Kokanadanti padumassevetaṃ vevacanaṃ. Pātoti kālasseva. Siyāti bhaveyya. Avītagandhanti avigatagandhaṃ. Aṅgīrasanti sammāsambuddhaṃ. Bhagavato hi aṅgato rasmiyo nikkhamanti, tasmā aṅgīrasoti vuccati. Yathā kokanadasaṅkhātaṃ padumaṃ pātova phullaṃ avītagandhaṃ siyā, evameva bhagavantaṃ aṅgīrasaṃ tapantaṃ ādiccamiva antalikkhe virocamānaṃ passāti ayamettha saṅkhepattho. Bhagavantaṃ acchādesīti bhagavato adāsīti attho. Lokavohārato panettha īdisaṃ vacanaṃ hoti. So kira upāsako – “ete tathāgatassa guṇesu pasīditvā mayhaṃ pañca uttarāsaṅge [M 1.0140] denti, ahampi te bhagavatova dassāmī”ti cintetvā adāsi. Dutiyaṃ.

'Kokanada' is a synonym for the lotus. 'Pāto' means 'early.' 'Siyā' means 'it might be.' 'Avītagandhaṃ' means 'with unfaded scent.' 'Aṅgīrasa' refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One. For from the Blessed One's body, rays emanate; therefore, he is called Aṅgīrasa. Just as a lotus known as a kokanada, blooming early, might be of unfading scent, even so, behold the Blessed One, the Aṅgīrasa, blazing, shining in the sky like the sun—this is the concise meaning here. 'He clothed the Blessed One' means 'he gave to the Blessed One.' In terms of worldly usage, such a phrase occurs here. It is said that the lay follower, having gained faith in the qualities of the Tathāgata, thought, 'They give me five upper robes. I, too, will give these to the Blessed One,' and so he gave. The second.

3. Doṇapākasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Doṇapāka Sutta.

124. Tatiye doṇapākakuranti doṇapākaṃ kuraṃ, doṇassa taṇḍulānaṃ pakkabhattaṃ tadūpiyañca sūpabyañjanaṃ bhuñjatīti attho. Bhuttāvīti pubbe bhattasammadaṃ vinodetvā muhuttaṃ vissamitvā buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, taṃdivasaṃ pana bhuñjantova dasabalaṃ saritvā hatthe dhovitvā agamāsi. Mahassāsīti tassa gacchato balavā bhattaparīḷāho udapādi, tasmā mahantehi assāsehi assasati, gattatopissa sedabindūni muccanti, tamenaṃ ubhosu passesu ṭhatvā yamakatālavaṇṭehi bījanti, buddhagāravena pana nipajjituṃ na ussahatīti idaṃ sandhāya “mahassāsī”ti vuttaṃ. Imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsīti, rājā bhojane [P 1.0153] amattaññutāya kilamati, phāsu vihāraṃ dānissa karissāmīti cintetvā abhāsi. Manujassāti sattassa. Kahāpaṇasatanti pātarāse paṇṇāsaṃ sāyamāse paṇṇāsanti evaṃ kahāpaṇasataṃ. Pariyāpuṇitvāti raññā saddhiṃ thokaṃ gantvā “imaṃ maṅgalaasiṃ kassa dammi, mahārājā”ti? Asukassa nāma dehīti so taṃ asiṃ datvā dasabalassa santikaṃ āgamma vanditvā ṭhitakova “gāthaṃ vadatha, bho gotamā”ti vatvā bhagavatā vuttaṃ pariyāpuṇitvāti attho.

124. In the third, 'doṇapākakuraṃ' means that he eats the cooked rice from one doṇa of rice grains and the soups and curries suitable for it—this is the meaning. 'Bhuttāvī' means: on a previous day, after dispelling the weariness from the meal and resting for a moment, he would go to attend upon the Buddha. But on that day, while still eating, he remembered the One with Ten Powers, and just after washing his hands, he went. 'Mahassāsī' means: as he was going, a strong affliction from the meal arose in him. Therefore, he breathes with great breaths, and drops of sweat are released from his body. Standing on both sides of him, they fan him with a pair of palm-leaf fans. But out of reverence for the Buddha, he did not dare to lie down. With reference to this, it was said, 'mahassāsī'. 'He spoke this verse' means: thinking, "The king is weary from not knowing the measure in eating. Now I will create a comfortable abiding for him," he spoke. 'Manujassa' means 'of a being.' 'A hundred kahāpaṇas' means: fifty for the morning meal and fifty for the evening meal, thus a hundred kahāpaṇas. 'Having learned' means: having gone a short distance with the king, he asked, "To whom shall I give this auspicious sword, great king?" When it was said, "Give it to so-and-so," he gave that sword away, approached the One with Ten Powers, paid homage, and while still standing there, said, "Please speak the verse, Venerable Gotama." Having learned what was spoken by the Blessed One—this is the meaning.

Bhattābhihāre [V 1.0135] sudaṃ bhāsatīti kathaṃ bhāsati? Bhagavatā anusiṭṭhiniyāmena. Bhagavā hi naṃ evaṃ anusāsi – “māṇava, imaṃ gāthaṃ naṭo viya pattapattaṭṭhāne mā avaca, rañño bhuñjanaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā paṭhamapiṇḍādīsupi avatvā vosānapiṇḍe gahite vadeyyāsi, rājā sutvāva bhattapiṇḍaṃ chaḍḍessati. Atha rañño hatthesu dhotesu pātiṃ apanetvā sitthāni gaṇetvā tadupiyaṃ byañjanaṃ ñatvā punadivase tāvatake taṇḍule hāreyyāsi, pātarāse ca vatvā sāyamāse mā vadeyyāsī”ti. So sādhūti paṭissuṇitvā taṃdivasaṃ rañño pātarāsaṃ bhutvā gatattā sāyamāse bhagavato anusiṭṭhiniyāmena gāthaṃ abhāsi[M 1.0141]. Rājā dasabalassa vacanaṃ saritvā bhattapiṇḍaṃ pātiyaṃyeva chaḍḍesi. Rañño hatthesu dhotesu pātiṃ apanetvā sitthāni gaṇetvā tadupiyaṃ byañjanaṃ ñatvā punadivase tattake taṇḍule hariṃsu.

“He spoke during the meal offering”—how did he speak? According to the instruction of the Blessed One. For the Blessed One instructed him thus: “Young man, do not recite this verse like an actor in any and every place. Standing in the king's dining place, do not recite it during the first morsels, but you should recite when the final morsel is taken. The king, upon hearing it, will discard the morsel of food. Then, when the king’s hands are washed, remove the bowl, count the grains of rice, and having discerned the appropriate relish, the next day you should bring that many grains of rice. Recite at the morning meal, but do not recite at the evening meal.” He agreed, saying, “Very well.” On that day, because he had gone after the king's morning meal was finished, he recited the verse at the evening meal according to the Blessed One’s instruction. The king, recalling the words of the Ten-Powered One, discarded the morsel of food right in the bowl. When the king’s hands were washed, they removed the bowl, counted the grains of rice, and having discerned the appropriate relish, the next day they brought that many grains of rice.

Nāḷikodanaparamatāya saṇṭhāsīti so kira māṇavo divase divase tathāgatassa santikaṃ gacchati, dasabalassa vissāsiko ahosi. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ pucchi “rājā kittakaṃ bhuñjatī”ti? So “nāḷikodana”nti āha. Vaṭṭissati ettāvatā purisabhāgo esa, ito paṭṭhāya gāthaṃ mā vadīti. Iti rājā tattheva saṇṭhāsi. Diṭṭhadhammikena ceva atthena samparāyikena cāti ettha sallikhitasarīratā diṭṭhadhammikattho nāma, sīlaṃ samparāyikattho. Bhojane mattaññutā hi sīlaṅgaṃ nāma hotīti. Tatiyaṃ.

“He was established with a maximum of one nāḷika of rice.” It is said that the young man went daily to the presence of the Tathāgata and became a trusted follower of the Ten-Powered One. Then one day, the Buddha asked him, “How much does the king eat?” He replied, “He eats one nāḷika of rice.” The Buddha said, “Young man, that much will be sufficient. This is a man's portion. From now on, do not recite the verse.” Thus, the king was established in just that measure. Here, regarding “with benefits visible in this life and benefits in the life to come,” bodily leanness is the benefit visible in this life, and virtue is the benefit in the life to come. For moderation in food is indeed a factor of virtue. The Third.

4. Paṭhamasaṅgāmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the First Battle Sutta.

125. Catutthe [P 1.0154] vedehiputtoti vedehīti paṇḍitādhivacanametaṃ, paṇḍititthiyā puttoti attho. Caturaṅgininti hatthiassarathapattisaṅkhātehi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgataṃ. Sannayhitvāti cammapaṭimuñcanādīhi sannāhaṃ kāretvā. Saṅgāmesunti yujjhiṃsu. Kena kāraṇena? Mahākosalaraññā kira bimbisārassa dhītaraṃ dentena dvinnaṃ rajjānaṃ antare satasahassuṭṭhāno kāsigāmo nāma dhītu dinno. Ajātasattunā ca pitari mārite mātāpissa rañño viyogasokena nacirasseva matā. Tato rājā pasenadi kosalo – “ajātasattunā mātāpitaro māritā, mayhaṃ pitu santako gāmo”ti tassatthāya aḍḍaṃ karoti. Ajātasattupi “mayhaṃ mātu santako”ti tassa gāmassatthāya dvepi mātulabhāgineyyā yujjhiṃsu.

125. In the fourth, regarding vedehiputto (son of the Videhan queen): Vedehī is a term for a wise person; the meaning is 'son of a wise woman.' Regarding caturaṅginiṃ (with four divisions): it means endowed with the four divisions, namely, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. Regarding sannayhitvā (having arrayed): it means having caused the army to be arrayed by means of donning leather armor and so forth. Regarding saṅgāmesuṃ (they fought in battle): it means they fought. For what reason? It is said that when King Mahākosala gave his daughter to Bimbisāra, a village in the Kāsī country, which yielded a revenue of one hundred thousand, was given to his daughter, lying between the two kingdoms. And when Ajātasattu killed his father, his mother also died not long after from sorrow over the separation from the king. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, thinking, 'Ajātasattu has killed his mother and father; this village belongs to my father,' made it a point of contention for its sake. Ajātasattu also, saying, 'It belongs to my mother,' fought for the sake of that village; thus the two, the maternal uncle and the nephew, fought.

Pāpā [V 1.0136] devadattādayo mittā assāti pāpamitto. Teyevassa sahāyāti pāpasahāyo. Tesvevassa cittaṃ ninnaṃ sampavaṅkanti pāpasampavaṅko. Pasenadissa sāriputtattherādīnaṃ vasena kalyāṇamittāditā veditabbā. Dukkhaṃ setīti jitāni hatthiādīni anusocanto dukkhaṃ sayissati. Idaṃ bhagavā puna tassa jayakāraṇaṃ disvā āha. Jayaṃ veraṃ pasavatīti jinanto veraṃ pasavati, veripuggalaṃ labhati. Catutthaṃ.

He is pāpamitto (one with evil friends) because he has evil friends such as Devadatta. He is pāpasahāyo (one with evil companions) because they alone are his associates. He is pāpasampavaṅko (one inclined towards evil) because his mind is inclined and devoted only to them. In the case of Pasenadi, it should be understood that he had good friends and so on, by the influence of the Venerable Sāriputta Thera and others. Regarding dukkhaṃ seti (he sleeps in misery): lamenting the elephants and so on that were conquered, he will sleep in misery. The Blessed One, seeing again the cause of his (Pasenadi's) victory, said this. Regarding jayaṃ veraṃ pasavati (victory begets enmity): one who conquers begets enmity; he gains an enemy. The Fourth (Sutta).

5. Dutiyasaṅgāmasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Second Battle Sutta

126. Pañcame [M 1.0142] abbhuyyāsīti parājaye garahappatto “ārāmaṃ gantvā bhikkhūnaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ suṇāthā”ti rattibhāge buddharakkhitena nāma vuḍḍhapabbajitena dhammarakkhitassa vuḍḍhapabbajitassa “sace rājā imañca upāyaṃ katvā gaccheyya, puna jineyyā”ti vuttajayakāraṇaṃ sutvā abhiuyyāsi.

126. In the fifth, regarding abbhuyyāsi (he marched out again): Having been defeated and thus incurred blame, he (the king) commanded, 'Go to the monastery and listen to the conversation of the monks.' In the nighttime, having heard the stated cause for victory spoken by an elder monk named Buddharakkhita—'Friend, if the king were to employ this very strategy and go forth, he would surely win again'—he marched out again to confront the enemy.

Yāvassa upakappatīti yāva tassa upakappati sayhaṃ hoti. Yadā caññeti yadā aññe. Vilumpantīti taṃ vilumpitvā [P 1.0155] ṭhitapuggalaṃ vilumpanti. Vilumpatīti vilumpiyati. Ṭhānaṃ hi maññatīti “kāraṇa”nti hi maññati. Yadāti yasmiṃ kāle. Jetāraṃ labhate jayanti jayanto puggalo pacchā jetārampi labhati. Rosetāranti ghaṭṭetāraṃ. Rosakoti ghaṭṭako. Kammavivaṭṭenāti kammapariṇāmena, tassa vilumpanakammassa vipākadānena. So vilutto viluppatīti so vilumpako vilumpiyati. Pañcamaṃ.

Regarding yāvassa upakappati (for as long as it is possible for him): it means for as long as he can successfully oppress another and is able to do so. Regarding yadā caññe (and when others): it means when others. Regarding vilumpanti (they plunder): it means they plunder that person who, having plundered, was established. Regarding vilumpati (he plunders): it means he is plundered. Regarding ṭhānaṃ hi maññati (he considers it an opportunity): it means he considers it a 'cause'. Regarding yadā (when): it means at which time. Regarding jetāraṃ labhate jayaṃ (the victor finds victory): it means the person who was defeated before later also obtains victory. Regarding rosetāraṃ (one who provokes): it means one who afflicts. Regarding rosako (a provoker): it means one who afflicts. Regarding kammavivaṭṭena (by the turning of kamma): it means by the ripening of kamma, by the giving of the result of that kamma of plundering. Regarding so vilutto vilumpati (that plundered one plunders): it means that plunderer is plundered. Fifth.

6. Mallikāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta

127. Chaṭṭhe upasaṅkamīti mallikāya deviyā gabbhavuṭṭhānakāle sūtigharaṃ paṭijaggāpetvā ārakkhaṃ datvā upasaṅkami. Anattamano ahosīti, “duggatakulassa me dhītu mahantaṃ issariyaṃ dinnaṃ, sace puttaṃ alabhissa, mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ adhigamissa, tato dāni parihīnā”ti anattamano ahosi. Seyyāti dandhapaññasmā elamūgaputtato ekaccā itthīyeva seyyā. Posāti posehi. Janādhipāti janādhibhuṃ rājānaṃ ālapati. Sassudevāti sassusasuradevatā. Disampatīti disājeṭṭhakā. Tādisā subhagiyāti tādisāya subhariyāya. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

127. In the sixth, regarding upasaṅkami (he approached): at the time when Queen Mallikā's pregnancy was coming to term, having had the delivery room prepared and a guard provided, he approached. Regarding anattamano ahosi (he was displeased): he was displeased, thinking: 'I have given great sovereignty to a daughter from a poor family. If she had obtained a son, she would have received great honor; now she has fallen short of that.' Regarding seyyā (better): a certain woman is indeed better than a slow-witted, mute son. Regarding posa (nourish): it means you should raise her. Regarding janādhipa (O lord of people): it is how she addresses the king, the ruler of people. Regarding sassudevā (having her mother-in-law as a deva): it means having her mother-in-law and father-in-law as revered devas. Regarding disampati (lord of the land): it means the chief of the directions. Regarding tādisā subhariyā (of such a good wife): it means of such a good wife endowed with conduct, virtue, and wisdom. Sixth.

7. Appamādasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Heedfulness Sutta

128. Sattame [V 1.0137] samadhiggayhāti samadhiggaṇhitvā, ādiyitvāti attho. Appamādoti kārāpakaappamādo. Samodhānanti samavadhānaṃ upakkhepaṃ. Evameva khoti hatthipadaṃ viya hi kārāpakaappamādo, sesapadajātāni viya avasesā catubhūmakā kusaladhammā. Te hatthipade sesapadāni viya [M 1.0143][P 1.0156] appamāde samodhānaṃ gacchanti, appamādassa anto parivattanti. Yathā ca hatthipadaṃ sesapadānaṃ aggaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, evaṃ appamādo sesadhammānanti dasseti. Mahaggatalokuttaradhammānampi hesa paṭilābhakaṭṭhena lokiyopi samāno aggova hoti.

128. In the seventh, regarding samadhiggayha: it means having grasped well and exceedingly, having undertaken. Regarding appamādo: it refers to the heedfulness that accomplishes. Regarding samodhānaṃ: it means inclusion, being placed within. The meaning of the phrase evameva kho should be understood thus: for the heedfulness that accomplishes is like an elephant's footprint, and the remaining wholesome states of the four planes are like the collection of other footprints. Just as the other footprints come to be included within the elephant's footprint, those wholesome states come to be included in heedfulness; they revolve within heedfulness. And just as the elephant's footprint is foremost and best among the other footprints, so too is heedfulness foremost and best among the other states—this He shows. For this heedfulness, by reason of being the means for attainment of the sublime and supramundane states, although it is mundane, is indeed foremost.

Appamādaṃ pasaṃsantīti “etāni āyuādīni patthayantena appamādova kātabbo”ti appamādameva pasaṃsanti. Yasmā vā puññakiriyāsu paṇḍitā appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti, tasmā āyuādīni patthayantena appamādova kātabboti attho. Atthābhisamayāti atthapaṭilābhā. Sattamaṃ.

Regarding appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti (they praise heedfulness): the wise praise heedfulness alone, saying, 'One who desires such benefits as long life and so on should practice only heedfulness.' Alternatively, because the wise praise heedfulness in meritorious deeds, therefore one who desires such benefits as long life and so on should practice only heedfulness; this is the meaning. Regarding atthābhisamayā (through the full understanding of the goal): because of the attainment of benefits, one is called wise. The seventh.

8. Kalyāṇamittasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Good Friendship Sutta

129. Aṭṭhame so ca kho kalyāṇamittassāti so cāyaṃ dhammo kalyāṇamittasseva svākkhāto nāma hoti, na pāpamittassāti. Kiñcāpi hi dhammo sabbesampi svākkhātova, kalyāṇamittassa pana sussūsantassa saddahantassa atthaṃ pūreti bhesajjaṃ viya vaḷañjantassa na itarassāti. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Dhammoti cettha desanādhammo veditabbo.

129. In the eighth, regarding so ca kho kalyāṇamittassa: this Dhamma is called 'well-proclaimed' only for one who has a good friend, not for one who has a bad friend. For although the Dhamma is indeed well-proclaimed for all, it fulfills its purpose only for one with a good friend who listens attentively and has faith, just as medicine fulfills its purpose for one who uses it, but not for the other. For that reason, this was said. And here, by 'Dhamma' the teaching-Dhamma should be understood.

Upaḍḍhamidanti thero kira rahogato cintesi – “ayaṃ samaṇadhammo nāma ovādake anusāsake kalyāṇamitte sati paccattapurisakāre ṭhitassa sampajjati, upaḍḍhaṃ kalyāṇamittato hoti, upaḍḍhaṃ paccattapurisakārato”ti. Athassa etadahosi – “ahaṃ padesañāṇe ṭhito nippadesaṃ cintetuṃ na sakkomi, satthāraṃ pucchitvā nikkaṅkho bhavissāmī”ti. Tasmā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāha. Brahmacariyassāti ariyamaggassa. Yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatāti yā esā kalyāṇamittatā nāma, sā upaḍḍhaṃ, tato upaḍḍhaṃ āgacchatīti attho. Iti therena “upaḍḍhupaḍḍhā sammādiṭṭhiādayo kalyāṇamittato āgacchanti, upaḍḍhupaḍḍhā paccattapurisakārato”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi [V 1.0138] therassa ayaṃ manoratho, yathā pana bahūhi silāthambhe ussāpite, “ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ asukena ussāpitaṃ, ettakaṃ asukenā”ti vinibbhogo natthi, yathā ca mātāpitaro nissāya uppannesu puttesu “ettakaṃ mātito [P 1.0157] nibbattaṃ, ettakaṃ pitito”ti vinibbhogo natthi, evaṃ idhāpi avinibbhogadhammo hesa, “ettakaṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnaṃ [M 1.0144] kalyāṇamittato nibbattaṃ, ettakaṃ paccattapurisakārato”ti na sakkā laddhuṃ, kalyāṇamittatāya pana upaḍḍhaguṇo labbhatīti therassa ajjhāsayena upaḍḍhaṃ nāma jātaṃ, sakalaguṇo paṭilabbhatīti bhagavato ajjhāsayena sakalaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Kalyāṇamittatāti cetaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭilābhaṅgaṃ nāmāti gahitaṃ. Atthato kalyāṇamittaṃ nissāya laddhā sīlasamādhivipassanāvasena cattāro khandhā. Saṅkhārakkhandhotipi vadantiyeva.

Upaḍḍhamidanti: The elder, it is said, having gone to a secluded place, thought: 'This so-called practice of a recluse is accomplished for one who is established in their own individual manly effort when there is an advisor, an instructor, and a good friend. Half is from a good friend, half is from one's own individual manly effort.' Then this occurred to him: 'I, being established in partial knowledge, am not able to think this through completely. Having asked the Teacher, I will become free from doubt.' Therefore, having approached the Teacher, he spoke thus. Brahmacariyassa means of the Noble Path. Yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā means: whatever this is that is called the state of having a good friend, that is half; from that, half comes—this is the meaning. Thus it was said by the elder: 'Half of right view and the other factors come from a good friend, and half come from one's own individual manly effort.' Although this was the elder's wish, it is like when a stone pillar is erected by many men, there is no division such as, 'This much was erected by so-and-so, and this much by so-and-so.' And just as in the case of children born depending on a mother and father, there is no division such as, 'This much was produced from the mother, and this much from the father.' So too here, this is an indivisible principle. It is not possible to determine, 'This much of right view and the other factors was produced from a good friend, and this much from one's own individual manly effort.' However, since half the virtue is obtained through the state of having a good friend, it came to be called 'half' according to the elder's intention. Since the entire virtue is obtained, it came to be called 'the whole' according to the Blessed One's intention. And this 'good friendship' is taken as being a factor for the preliminary part of the attainment. In reality, it is the four aggregates obtained by relying on a good friend, by way of virtue, concentration, and insight. They also say it is the aggregate of formations.

Mā hevaṃ, ānandāti, ānanda, mā evaṃ abhaṇi, bahussuto tvaṃ sekhapaṭisambhidappatto aṭṭha vare gahetvā maṃ upaṭṭhahasi, catūhi acchariyabbhutadhammehi samannāgato, tādisassa evaṃ kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sakalameva hidaṃ, ānanda, brahmacariyaṃ, yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatāti idaṃ bhagavā – “cattāro maggā cattāri phalāni tisso vijjā cha abhiññā sabbaṃ kalyāṇamittamūlakameva hotī”ti sandhāyāha. Idāni vacībhedeneva kāraṇaṃ dassento kalyāṇamittassetantiādimāha. Tattha pāṭikaṅkhanti pāṭikaṅkhitabbaṃ icchitabbaṃ, avassaṃbhāvīti attho.

Mā hevaṃ, ānanda: Do not speak thus, Ānanda. You are of great learning, have attained the analytical knowledges as a trainee, you attend upon me having taken the eight boons, and are endowed with the four marvelous and wonderful qualities. It is not fitting for one such as you to speak in this way. Sakalameva hidaṃ, ānanda, brahmacariyaṃ, yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā: For indeed, Ānanda, this entire holy life is this: good friendship. The Blessed One said this with reference to the fact that ‘the four paths, the four fruits, the three knowledges, the six supernormal knowledges—all have good friendship as their root.’ Now, wishing to show the reason merely by verbal expression, he spoke the words beginning with ‘kalyāṇamittassa etaṃ’. Therein, pāṭikaṅkhaṃ means it is to be expected, to be desired; it is inevitable—this is the meaning.

Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāvetītiādīsu aṭṭhannaṃ ādipadānaṃyeva tāva ayaṃ saṅkhepavaṇṇanā – sammā dassanalakkhaṇā sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā abhiniropanalakkhaṇo sammāsaṅkappo. Sammā pariggahaṇalakkhaṇā sammāvācā. Sammā samuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇo sammākammanto. Sammā vodāpanalakkhaṇā sammāājīvo. Sammā paggahalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo. Sammā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati. Sammā samādhānalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhi.

Idha means in this Dispensation. Regarding the phrases beginning with “one develops right view,” first, this is a brief explanation of just the eight initial terms: Right View has the characteristic of correct seeing. Right Thought has the characteristic of correct directing of the mind. Right Speech has the characteristic of correct restraint. Right Action has the characteristic of correct origination. Right Livelihood has the characteristic of correct purification. Right Effort has the characteristic of correct exertion. Right Mindfulness has the characteristic of correct establishment. Right Concentration has the characteristic of correct placement.

Tesu ekekassa tīṇi kiccāni honti. Seyyāthidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi tāva aññehipi attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhiṃ micchādiṭṭhiṃ pajahati, nirodhaṃ ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca passati tappaṭicchādakamohavidhamanavasena asammohato. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi tatheva micchāsaṅkappādīni ca pajahanti, nirodhañca ārammaṇaṃ karonti. Visesato panettha sammādiṭṭhi sahajātadhamme sammā dasseti[P 1.0158]. Sammāsaṅkappo sahajātadhamme abhiniropeti, sammāvācā sammā pariggaṇhāti, sammākammanto sammā [M 1.0145] samuṭṭhāpeti, sammāājīvo sammā vodāpeti[V 1.0139], sammāvāyāmo sammā paggaṇhāti, sammāsati sammā upaṭṭhāpeti, sammāsamādhi sammā dahati.

Among these, for each one there are three functions. Namely: first, Right View abandons wrong view together with its other opposing defilements, makes cessation its object, and, due to non-delusion, sees the associated states by means of dispelling the delusion that conceals them. Right Thought and the others, in the same way, abandon wrong thought and so forth, and make cessation their object. Specifically, among these, Right View correctly shows the co-arisen states. Right Thought correctly directs the co-arisen states. Right Speech correctly embraces the co-arisen states. Right Action correctly arouses the co-arisen states. Right Livelihood correctly purifies the co-arisen states. Right Effort correctly exerts the co-arisen states. Right Mindfulness correctly establishes the co-arisen states. Right Concentration correctly composes the co-arisen states.

Apicesā sammādiṭṭhi nāma pubbabhāge nānākhaṇā nānārammaṇā hoti, maggakāle ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā. Kiccato pana sammādiṭṭhi dukkhe ñāṇantiādīni cattāri nāmāni labhati. Sammāsaṅkappādayopi pubbabhāge nānākhaṇā nānārammaṇā honti, maggakāle ekakkhaṇā ekārammaṇā. Tesu sammāsaṅkappo kiccato nekkhammasaṅkappotiādīni tīṇi nāmāni labhati. Sammāvācādayo tayo viratiyopi honti cetanāyopi, maggakkhaṇe pana viratiyova. Sammāvāyāmo sammāsatīti idampi dvayaṃ kiccato sammappadhānasatipaṭṭhānavasena cattāri nāmāni labhati. Sammāsamādhi pana pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi sammāsamādhiyeva.

Furthermore, this which is called Right View, in the preliminary stage, has different moments and various objects; at the time of the path, it has a single moment and a single object. Functionally, however, Right View obtains four names, such as 'knowledge in suffering,' etc. Right Thought and the others also, in the preliminary stage, have different moments and various objects; at the time of the path, they have a single moment and a single object. Among them, Right Thought functionally obtains three names, such as 'thought of renunciation,' etc. The three beginning with Right Speech are both abstinences and volitions, but at the path moment, they are only abstinences. This pair, Right Effort and Right Mindfulness, functionally obtains four names by way of the Right Exertions and the Foundations of Mindfulness. As for Right Concentration, it is only Right Concentration both in the preliminary stage and at the path moment.

Evaṃ tāva “sammādiṭṭhi”ntiādinā nayena vuttānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ ādipadānaṃyeva atthavaṇṇanaṃ ñatvā idāni bhāveti vivekanissitantiādīsu evaṃ ñātabbo. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti, attano cittasantāne punappunaṃ janeti, abhinibbattetīti attho. Vivekanissitanti vivekaṃ nissitaṃ, viveke vā nissitanti vivekanissitaṃ. Vivekoti vivittatā. Vivittatā cāyaṃ tadaṅgaviveko, vikkhambhana-samuccheda-paṭippassaddhi-nissaraṇavivekoti pañcavidho. Evametasmiṃ pañcavidhe viveke. Vivekanissitanti tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ samucchedavivekanissitaṃ nissaraṇavivekanissitañca sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāvetīti ayamattho veditabbo. Tathā hi ayaṃ ariyamaggabhāvanānuyutto yogī vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ, ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ, maggakāle pana kiccato samucchedavivekanissitaṃ, ārammaṇato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti. Esa nayo virāganissitādīsu. Vivekatthā eva hi virāgādayo[P 1.0159].

Thus, firstly, having known the explanation of the meaning of the eight initial terms according to the method beginning with 'Right View,' it should now be understood thus regarding the terms beginning with 'develops, based on seclusion.' 'Develops' means increases, repeatedly generates in one’s own mental continuum, produces—this is the meaning. 'Based on seclusion' means relying on seclusion or established in seclusion. 'Seclusion' means secludedness. And this secludedness is fivefold: seclusion by substitution of opposites, seclusion by suppression, seclusion by eradication, seclusion by tranquillization, and seclusion by escape. Thus, among these five kinds of seclusion, 'based on seclusion' means one develops Right View that is based on seclusion by substitution of opposites, seclusion by eradication, and seclusion by escape—this meaning should be understood. For this yogī, devoted to the development of the noble path, develops Right View thus: at the moment of insight, it is functionally based on seclusion by substitution of opposites and, by inclination, on seclusion by escape; at the time of the path, however, it is functionally based on seclusion by eradication and, as its object, on seclusion by escape. This is the method for 'based on dispassion,' etc., for dispassion and the others indeed have the meaning of seclusion.

Kevalañcettha vossaggo duvidho pariccāgavossaggo ca pakkhandanavossaggo cāti. Tattha pariccāgavossaggoti vipassanākkhaṇe ca tadaṅgavasena, maggakkhaṇe ca samucchedavasena kilesappahānaṃ. Pakkhandanavossaggoti vipassanākkhaṇe tanninnabhāvena, maggakkhaṇe pana ārammaṇakaraṇena nibbānapakkhandanaṃ, tadubhayampi imasmiṃ lokiyalokuttaramissake [V 1.0140] atthavaṇṇanānaye [M 1.0146] vaṭṭati. Tathā hi ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhi yathāvuttena pakārena kilese ca pariccajati, nibbānañca pakkhandati.

Moreover, herein, relinquishment is twofold: relinquishment as abandonment and relinquishment as leaping forward. Therein, 'relinquishment as abandonment' is the abandonment of defilements by way of temporary abandonment at the moment of insight, and by way of eradication at the moment of the path. 'Relinquishment as leaping forward' is the leaping forward to Nibbāna, which occurs at the moment of insight through inclination towards it, and at the moment of the path by making it the object. Both of these are applicable in this method of explanation, which is a mixture of the mundane and supramundane. For this Right View, in the way described, both abandons defilements and leaps forward to Nibbāna.

Vossaggapariṇāminti iminā pana sakalena vacanena vossaggatthaṃ pariṇamantaṃ pariṇatañca, paripaccantaṃ paripakkañcāti idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi ariyamaggabhāvanānuyutto bhikkhu yathā sammādiṭṭhi kilesapariccāgavossaggatthaṃ nibbānapakkhandanavossaggatthañca paripaccati, yathā ca paripakkā hoti, tathā naṃ bhāvetīti. Esa nayo sesamaggaṅgesu.

By this entire phrase, 'ending in relinquishment,' this is said: that which is ripening for the sake of relinquishment and has ripened, that which is maturing and has matured. Indeed, this monk, devoted to the cultivation of the noble path, cultivates Right View in such a way that it matures for the sake of the relinquishment that is the abandonment of defilements and for the sake of the relinquishment that is the leaping into Nibbāna, and in such a way that it becomes mature. This method should be applied to the remaining path factors.

Āgammāti ārabbha sandhāya paṭicca. Jātidhammāti jātisabhāvā jātipakatikā. Tasmāti yasmā sakalo ariyamaggopi kalyāṇamittaṃ nissāya labbhati, tasmā. Handāti vavassaggatthe nipāto. Appamādaṃ pasaṃsantīti appamādaṃ vaṇṇayanti, tasmā appamādo kātabbo. Atthābhisamayāti atthapaṭilābhā. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

'Having come' means concerning, with reference to, depending on. 'Subject to birth' means having the nature of birth, having the characteristic of birth. 'Therefore' means: because the entire noble path is also obtained by relying on a spiritual friend, therefore. 'Handa' is a particle in the sense of relinquishment. 'They praise heedfulness' means they extol heedfulness; therefore, heedfulness should be practiced. 'Understanding the meaning' means the attainment of the goal. The eighth.

9. Paṭhamaaputtakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Heirless

130. Navame divā divassāti divasassa divā, majjhanhikasamayeti attho. Sāpateyyanti dhanaṃ. Ko pana vādo rūpiyassāti suvaṇṇarajatatambalohakāḷalohaphālakacchapakādibhedassa ghanakatassa ceva paribhogabhājanādibhedassa ca rūpiyabhaṇḍassa pana ko vādo? “Ettakaṃ nāmā”ti kā paricchedakathāti attho. Kaṇājakanti sakuṇḍakabhattaṃ. Bilaṅgadutiyanti kañjikadutiyaṃ. Sāṇanti sāṇavākamayaṃ[P 1.0160]. Tipakkhavasananti tīṇi khaṇḍāni dvīsu ṭhānesu sibbitvā katanivāsanaṃ.

130. In the ninth sutta, 'by day of the day' means during the day, at the time of midday; this is the meaning. 'Property' means wealth. 'What then is to be said of money?' means: what is to be said of goods made of gold, silver, copper, iron, dark metal, ploughshares, turtle-shell shapes, and so on, whether made into solid ingots or into various utensils for use? What talk of limitation is there, saying, 'It is this much'?; this is the meaning. 'Broken rice' means rice with bran. 'With sour gruel as a second' means having sour gruel as the second item. 'Hemp-cloth' means made of hemp fiber. 'A lower garment of three cloths' means a lower garment made by sewing three pieces together in two places.

Asappurisoti lāmakapuriso. Uddhaggikantiādīsu uparūparibhūmīsu phaladānavasena uddhaṃ aggamassāti uddhaggikā. Saggassa hitā tatrupapattijananatoti sovaggikā. Nibbattaṭṭhānesu sukho vipāko assāti sukhavipākā. Suṭṭhu aggānaṃ dibbavaṇṇādīnaṃ visesānaṃ nibbattanato saggasaṃvattanikā. Evarūpaṃ dakkhiṇadānaṃ na patiṭṭhāpetīti.

'An unworthy person' means a base person. Regarding 'uddhaggika' and so on: because it has a supreme state that is upward by way of yielding fruit in higher and higher planes, it is called 'having a supreme upward destiny' (uddhaggikā); because it is for the welfare of heaven by generating rebirth there, it is called 'heavenly' (sovaggikā); because it has a pleasant result in the places where it arises, it is called 'having a pleasant result' (sukhavipākā); because it brings about exceedingly supreme, special qualities beginning with divine complexion, it is called 'conducive to heaven' (saggasaṃvattanikā). He does not establish such a worthy gift.

Sātodakāti madhurodakā. Settodakāti vīcīnaṃ bhinnaṭṭhāne udakassa setatāya setodakā. Supatitthāti [V 1.0141] sundaratitthā. Taṃ janoti [M 1.0147] yena udakena sātodakā, taṃ udakaṃ jano bhājanāni pūretvā neva hareyya. Na yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyyāti, yaṃ yaṃ udakena udakakiccaṃ kātabbaṃ, taṃ taṃ na kareyya. Tadapeyyamānanti taṃ apeyyamānaṃ. Kiccakaro ca hotīti attanā kattabbakiccakaro ceva kusalakiccakaro ca, bhuñjati ca, kammante ca payojeti, dānañca detīti attho. Navamaṃ.

'Sweet water' means having sweet water. 'White water' means having white water, due to the whiteness of the water in the place where the waves break. 'With a fine landing place' means having a beautiful landing place. 'People would not take that' means people would not fill their vessels with that sweet water and carry it away. 'Nor would they use it as needed' means they would not do with the water whatever task should be done with it. 'It not being drunk' means it is not drunk. 'And one is a doer of deeds' means one is a doer of deeds that ought to be done by oneself and a doer of skillful deeds; and one enjoys, engages in work, and gives gifts. This is the meaning. The ninth.

10. Dutiyaaputtakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Heirless

131. Dasame piṇḍapātena paṭipādesīti piṇḍapātena saddhiṃ saṃyojesi, piṇḍapātaṃ adāsīti attho. Pakkāmīti kenacideva rājupaṭṭhānādinā kiccena gato. Pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosīti so kira aññesupi divasesu taṃ paccekasambuddhaṃ passati, dātuṃ panassa cittaṃ na uppajjati. Tasmiṃ pana divase ayaṃ padumavatideviyā tatiyaputto taggarasikhī paccekabuddho gandhamādanapabbate phalasamāpattisukhena vītināmetvā pubbaṇhasamaye vuṭṭhāya anotattadahe mukhaṃ dhovitvā manosilātale nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā pattacīvaramādāya abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā iddhiyā vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā nagaradvāre oruyha cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattamādāya nagaravāsīnaṃ gharadvāresu sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ ṭhapento viya pāsādikehi abhikkantādīhi anupubbena seṭṭhino gharadvāraṃ sampatto. Taṃdivasañca [P 1.0161] seṭṭhi pātova uṭṭhāya paṇītabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā, gharadvārakoṭṭhake āsanaṃ paññāpetvā, dantantarāni sodhento nisinno hoti. So paccekabuddhaṃ disvā, taṃdivasaṃ pāto bhutvā nisinnattā dānacittaṃ uppādetvā, bhariyaṃ pakkosāpetvā, “imassa samaṇassa piṇḍapātaṃ dehī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

131. In the tenth sutta: 'He provided with alms-food' means he joined him with alms-food; the meaning is, he gave alms-food. 'He departed' means he went on account of some business, such as attending on the king. 'Later, he was remorseful'—it is said that on other days too he would see that Paccekasambuddha, but a mind to give would not arise in him. On that day, however, this Paccekabuddha Taggarasikhī, the third son of Queen Padumavatī, having passed the time on Gandhamādana Mountain in the bliss of the attainment of fruition, having arisen in the morning, having washed his face in Lake Anotatta, having put on his lower robe on the Manosilā terrace, having tied his waistband, having taken his bowl and robes, having entered the fourth jhāna which is the basis for higher knowledge, having ascended into the sky by psychic power, having descended at the city gate, having draped his outer robe, having taken his bowl, and—as if placing a purse of a thousand at the house-doors of the city-dwellers—with pleasing forward movements and so forth, he gradually arrived at the merchant's house-door. And on that day, the merchant, having risen very early and eaten a delicious meal, had a seat prepared in the gateway of his house and was seated, cleaning between his teeth. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, because on that day he had eaten early and was seated, he generated a mind for giving, had his wife summoned, and after saying, “Give alms-food to this ascetic,” he departed.

Seṭṭhibhariyā cintesi – “mayā ettakena kālena imassa ‘dethā’ti vacanaṃ na sutapubbaṃ, dāpentopi ca ajja na yassa vā tassa vā dāpeti, vītarāgadosamohassa vantakilesassa ohitabhārassa paccekabuddhassa dāpeti, yaṃ vā taṃ vā adatvā paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dassāmī”ti, gharā nikkhamma paccekabuddhaṃ pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā pattaṃ ādāya antonivesane paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā suparisuddhehi sālitaṇḍulehi bhattaṃ sampādetvā tadanurūpaṃ khādanīyaṃ byañjanaṃ supeyyañca sallakkhetvā pattaṃ pūretvā bahi gandhehi samalaṅkaritvā paccekabuddhassa hatthesu [M 1.0148] patiṭṭhapetvā vandi. Paccekabuddho – “aññesampi paccekabuddhānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti [V 1.0142] aparibhuñjitvāva anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sopi kho seṭṭhi bāhirato āgacchanto paccekabuddhaṃ disvā mayaṃ “tumhākaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dethā”ti vatvā pakkantā, api vo laddhoti? Āma, seṭṭhi laddhoti. “Passāmī”ti gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā olokesi. Athassa piṇḍapātagandho uṭṭhahitvā nāsāpuṭaṃ pahari. So cittaṃ saṃyametuṃ asakkonto pacchā vippaṭisārī āhosīti.

The merchant's wife thought: "In all this time, I have never before heard from him the words, 'Give alms.' And even when causing alms to be given today, he does not cause them to be given to just anyone, but he causes them to be given to a Paccekabuddha—one who is free from lust, hatred, and delusion, who has vomited out the defilements, who has laid down the burden. Instead of giving just any ordinary food, I will give exquisite alms-food." Having gone out from the house, she paid homage to the Paccekabuddha with the five-point prostration, took his bowl, had him sit on a prepared seat inside the residence, and prepared cooked rice with very pure Sāli rice grains. Having noted suitable hard food, curry, and soup, she filled the bowl, adorned the outside with perfumes, placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, and paid homage. The Paccekabuddha, thinking, "I will provide for other Paccekabuddhas as well," departed without having partaken of the food, after giving a blessing. That merchant, while coming from outside, saw the Paccekabuddha and asked: "We departed after saying, 'Give alms-food to you.' Did you receive it?" "Yes, merchant, it was received." Saying, "Let me see," he raised his neck and looked. Then the aroma of the alms-food arose and struck his nostrils. He, unable to restrain his mind, later became regretful.

Varametantiādi vippaṭisārassa uppannākāradassanaṃ. Bhātu ca pana ekaputtakaṃ sāpateyyassa kāraṇā jīvitā voropesīti tadā kirassa avibhatteyeva kuṭumbe mātāpitaro ca jeṭṭhabhātā ca kālamakaṃsu. So bhātujāyāya saddhiṃyeva saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Bhātu panassa eko putto hoti, taṃ vīthiyā kīḷantaṃ manussā vadanti – “ayaṃ dāso ayaṃ dāsī idaṃ yānaṃ idaṃ dhanaṃ tava santaka”nti. So tesaṃ kathaṃ gahetvā – “ayaṃ dāso mayhaṃ santaka”ntiādīni katheti.

The phrase beginning with 'Varam etaṃ' demonstrates the manner in which regret arose. 'And for the sake of property, he deprived his brother's only son of life.' It is said that at that time, while the family property was still undivided, his parents and elder brother passed away. He then lived together with his brother's wife. Now, his brother had one son. While that boy was playing in the street, people would say: "This male slave, this female slave, this vehicle, this wealth is your property." He, taking their words, would say such things as, "This male slave is my property."

Athassa cūḷapitā cintesi – “ayaṃ dārako idāneva evaṃ kathesi, mahallakakāle kuṭumbaṃ majjhe bhindāpeyya, idānevassa kattabbaṃ karissāmī”ti ekadivasaṃ vāsiṃ ādāya – “ehi putta, araññaṃ gacchāmā”ti taṃ araññaṃ netvā viravantaṃ viravantaṃ māretvā āvāṭe [P 1.0162] pakkhipitvā paṃsunā paṭicchādesi. Idaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sattakkhattunti sattavāre. Pubbapacchimacetanāvasena cettha attho veditabbo. Ekapiṇḍapātadānasmiñhi ekāva cetanā dve paṭisandhiyo na deti, pubbapacchimacetanāhi panesa sattakkhattuṃ sagge, sattakkhattuṃ seṭṭhikule nibbatto. Purāṇanti paccekasambuddhassa dinnapiṇḍapātacetanākammaṃ.

Then his paternal uncle thought: “This boy has spoken thus even now; when he is grown, he would cause the family estate to be split in half. I will do to him now what must be done.” One day, taking an adze, he said, “Come, son, let us go to the forest.” Having led him to the forest, he killed him while he was crying again and again, placed him in a pit, and covered him with dust. This was said in reference to this. 'Sattakkhattuṃ' means seven times. And here the meaning should be understood by way of the preceding and succeeding volitions. For in the giving of a single alms-meal, a single volition does not produce two rebirth-linkings; but by the power of the preceding and succeeding volitions, he was reborn seven times in heaven and seven times in a treasurer's family. 'Purāṇaṃ' means the kamma of the volition of giving an alms-meal to a Paccekasambuddha.

Pariggahanti pariggahitavatthu. Anujīvinoti ekaṃ mahākulaṃ nissāya paṇṇāsampi saṭṭhipi kulāni jīvanti, te manusse sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Sabbaṃ nādāya gantabbanti sabbametaṃ na ādiyitvā gantabbaṃ. Sabbaṃ nikkhippagāminanti sabbametaṃ nikkhippasabhāvaṃ, pariccajitabbasabhāvamevāti attho. Dasamaṃ.

'Pariggahaṃ' means a thing that is taken possession of. 'Anujīvino' means: relying on one great family, fifty or even sixty families make their living; this was said in reference to those people. 'Sabbaṃ nādāya gantabbaṃ' means one must depart without taking all this. 'Sabbaṃ nikkhippagāminaṃ' means all this has the nature of being laid down, that is, it has the very nature of being relinquished; this is the meaning. The tenth.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter.

1. Puggalasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Puggala Sutta

132. Tatiyavaggassa [V 1.0143][M 1.0149] paṭhame “nīce kule paccājāto”tiādikena tamena yuttoti tamo. Kāyaduccaritādīhi puna nirayatamūpagamanato tamaparāyaṇo. Iti ubhayenapi khandhatamova kathito hoti. “Ucce kule paccājāto”tiādikena jotinā yuttato joti, ālokībhūtoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kāyasucaritādīhi puna saggūpapattijotibhāvūpagamanato jotiparāyaṇo. Iminā nayena itarepi dve veditabbā.

1. In the first sutta of the third chapter: Regarding 'born in a low family,' etc., because he is endowed with that darkness (tamena), he is called 'tamo' (darkness). And because he goes to the darkness of hell through bodily misconduct and so on, he is 'tamaparāyaṇo' (one for whom darkness is the destination). Thus, by both terms, it is the darkness of the aggregates that is spoken of. Regarding 'born in a high family,' etc., because he is endowed with that light (jotinā), he is called 'joti' (light); it is said that he has become luminous. And because he goes to the state of light, which is rebirth in heaven, through good bodily conduct and so on, he is 'jotiparāyaṇo' (one for whom light is the destination). By this method, the other two persons should also be understood.

Venakuleti vilīvakārakule. Nesādakuleti migaluddakādīnaṃ kule. Rathakārakuleti cammakārakule. Pukkusakuleti pupphachaḍḍakakule. Kasiravuttiketi dukkhavuttike. Dubbaṇṇoti paṃsupisācako viya jhāmakhāṇuvaṇṇo. Duddasikoti vijātamātuyāpi amanāpadassano[P 1.0163]. Okoṭimakoti lakuṇḍako. Kāṇoti ekakkhikāṇo vā ubhayakkhikāṇo vā. Kuṇīti ekahatthakuṇī vā ubhayahatthakuṇī vā. Khañjoti ekapādakhañjo vā ubhayapādakhañjo vā. Pakkhahatoti hatapakkho pīṭhasappī. Padīpeyyassāti telakapallakādino padīpaupakaraṇassa. Evaṃ kho, mahārājāti ettha eko puggalo bahiddhā ālokaṃ adisvā mātukucchismiṃyeva kālaṃ katvā apāyesu nibbattanto sakalaṃ kappampi saṃsarati, sopi tamotamaparāyaṇova. So pana kuhakapuggalo bhaveyya. Kuhakassa hi evarūpā nibbatti hotīti vuttaṃ.

Venakula: the family of bamboo workers. Nesādakula: the family of hunters, such as deer hunters. Rathakārakula: the family of leather workers. Pukkusakuḷa: the family of flower scavengers. Kasiravuttika: one with a miserable livelihood. Dubbaṇṇa: ugly, like a dirt goblin, with the color of a charred stump. Duddasika: hard to look at, unpleasant even to one's own mother. Okoṭimaka: a dwarf. Kāṇa: blind in one eye or both eyes. Kuṇī: crippled in one hand or both hands. Khañja: lame in one foot or both feet. Pakkhahata: paralyzed on one side, lame. Of a lamp (padīpeyyassa): that is, of lamp accessories such as an oil pot and so on. Thus, great king, here a certain person, not seeing the light outside, dies in the mother's womb and is reborn in the lower worlds, wandering through an entire eon—he too is one destined for darkness upon darkness. That person might be a hypocrite. For it is said that such is the rebirth of a hypocrite.

Ettha ca “nīce kule paccājāto hoti caṇḍālakule vā”tiādīhi āgamanavipatti ceva pubbuppannapaccayavipatti ca dassitā. Daliddetiādīhi pavattapaccayavipatti. Kasiravuttiketiādīhi ājīvupāyavipatti. Dubbaṇṇotiādīhi [M 1.0150] attabhāvavipatti. Bavhābādhotiādīhi dukkhakāraṇasamāyogo. Na lābhītiādīhi sukhakāraṇavipatti ceva upabhogavipatti ca. Kāyena duccaritantiādīhi tamaparāyaṇabhāvassa kāraṇasamāyogo. Kāyassa bhedātiādīhi samparāyikatamūpagamo. Sukkapakkho vuttapaṭipakkhanayena veditabbo.

Here, by 'born in a low family, such as in an outcaste family' and so on, both the failure of destination (āgamanavipatti) and the failure of previously arisen conditions (pubbuppannapaccayavipatti) are shown. By 'poor' and so on, the failure of ongoing conditions (pavattapaccayavipatti) is shown. By 'having a difficult livelihood' and so on, the failure of means of livelihood (ājīvupāyavipatti) is shown. By 'afflicted with many diseases' and so on, the conjunction with the cause of suffering (dukkhakāraṇasamāyogo) is shown. By 'not gaining' and so on, both the failure of the cause of happiness (sukhakāraṇavipatti) and the failure of enjoyment (upabhogavipatti) are shown.
