By 'misconduct with the body' and so on, the conjunction with the cause of being destined for darkness (tamaparāyaṇabhāvassa kāraṇasamāyogo) is shown. By 'upon the breakup of the body' and so on, the going to darkness in the next life (samparāyikatamūpagamo) is shown. The bright side (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the method opposite to what has been stated.

Akkosatīti [V 1.0144] dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosati. Paribhāsatīti, “kasmā tiṭṭhatha? Kiṃ tumhehi amhākaṃ kasikammādīni katānī”tiādīhi? Paribhavavacanehi paribhāsati. Rosakoti ghaṭṭako. Abyaggamanasoti ekaggacitto. Paṭhamaṃ.

‘He abuses’ means he abuses with the ten grounds for abuse. ‘He reviles’ means he reviles with words of contempt, such as, ‘Why do you stand there? Have you done our farming and such?’ ‘Rosaka’ means one who is abrasive and quarrelsome. ‘Abyaggamanasa’ means one with a one-pointed mind. First.

2. Ayyikāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Ayyikā Sutta

133. Dutiye jiṇṇāti jarājiṇṇā. Vuḍḍhāti vayovuḍḍhā. Mahallikāti jātimahallikā. Addhagatāti addhaṃ cirakālaṃ atikkantā. Vayoanuppattāti pacchimavayaṃ sampattā. Piyā manāpāti rañño kira mātari matāya ayyikā mātuṭṭhāne ṭhatvā paṭijaggi, tenassa ayyikāya balavapemaṃ uppajji. Tasmā evamāha. Hatthiratanenāti [P 1.0164] satasahassagghanako hatthī satasahassagghanakena alaṅkārena alaṅkato hatthiratanaṃ nāma. Assaratanepi eseva nayo. Gāmavaropi satasahassuṭṭhānakagāmova. Sabbāni tāni bhedanadhammānīti tesu hi kiñci kariyamānameva bhijjati, kiñci katapariyositaṃ cakkato anapanītameva, kiñci apanetvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitamattaṃ, kiñci tato paraṃ, evameva sattesupi koci paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā marati, koci mūḷhagabbhāya mātari mātukucchito anikkhantova, koci nikkhantamatto, koci tato paranti. Tasmā evamāha. Dutiyaṃ.

133. In the second sutta, ‘aged’ (jiṇṇa) means aged and worn out. ‘Old’ (vuḍḍha) means advanced in age. ‘Ancient’ (mahallikā) means great by lineage. ‘Far gone’ (addhagata) means having passed a long period of time. ‘Reached old age’ (vayoanuppatta) means having arrived at the final stage of life. ‘Dear and beloved’ (piyā manāpā) — it seems that after the king's mother had died, his grandmother stood in the place of his mother and cared for him. Therefore, strong affection arose in him for his grandmother. Thus he spoke. ‘The elephant treasure’ (hatthiratana) is the name for an elephant worth a hundred thousand that has been adorned with ornaments worth a hundred thousand. The same applies to ‘the horse treasure.’ ‘The best village’ (gāmavara) is a village that produces a revenue of a hundred thousand. ‘All those are subject to breaking’ (sabbāni tāni bhedanadhammāni) — for among these, some break while being made; some break just as they are finished, even before being removed from the wheel; some break as soon as they are placed on the ground; some break after that. Similarly, among beings, some die after taking rebirth; some die as a miscarried embryo while still in the mother's womb; some die just after being born; some die after that. Therefore, He spoke thus. Second.

134. Tatiye sabbaṃ uttānameva. Tatiyaṃ.

134. In the third sutta, all is straightforward. Third.

4. Issattasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Issatta Sutta

135. Catutthassa aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo. Bhagavato kira paṭhamabodhiyaṃ mahālābhasakkāro udapādi bhikkhusaṅghassa ca. Titthiyā hatalābhasakkārā hutvā kulesu evaṃ kanthentā vicaranti – “samaṇo gotamo [M 1.0151] evamāha, ‘mayhameva dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, na aññesaṃ dānaṃ dātabbaṃ. Mayhameva sāvakānaṃ dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, na aññesaṃ sāvakānaṃ dānaṃ dātabbaṃ. Mayhameva dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, na aññesaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ. Mayhameva sāvakānaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, na aññesaṃ sāvakānaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphala’nti. Yuttaṃ nu kho sayampi bhikkhācāranissitena paresaṃ bhikkhācāranissitānaṃ catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ antarāyaṃ kātuṃ, ayuttaṃ karoti ananucchavika”nti. Sā [V 1.0145] kathā pattharamānā rājakulaṃ sampattā. Rājā sutvā cintesi – “aṭṭhānametaṃ yaṃ tathāgato paresaṃ lābhantarāyaṃ kareyya. Ete tathāgatassa alābhāya ayasāya parisakkanti. Sacāhaṃ idheva ṭhatvā ‘mā evaṃ avocuttha, na satthā evaṃ kathetī’ti vadeyyaṃ, evaṃ sā kathā nijjhattiṃ na gaccheyya, imassa mahājanassa sannipatitakāleyeva naṃ nijjhāpessāmī”ti ekaṃ chaṇadivasaṃ āgamento tuṇhī ahosi.

135. The exposition of the origin story for the fourth sutta. It is said that in the first period of enlightenment, great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One and also for the community of monks. The sectarians, deprived of gain and honor, went around among families complaining thus: “The ascetic Gotama says, ‘Gifts should be given only to me, not to others. Gifts should be given only to my disciples, not to the disciples of others. What is given to me bears great fruit, what is given to others does not. What is given to my disciples bears great fruit, what is given to the disciples of others does not.’ Is it proper for one who himself depends on the practice of alms-gathering to obstruct the requisites of others who also depend on the practice of alms-gathering? He does what is improper and unsuitable.” This talk spread widely and reached the royal court. The king, hearing it, thought: “It is impossible that the Tathāgata would obstruct the gains of others. These people are striving for the Tathāgata's loss of gain and dishonor. If I were to stay right here and say, ‘Do not speak thus; the Teacher does not speak thus,’ this talk would not be settled. I will have it settled only when this great crowd has gathered.” Awaiting a festival day, he remained silent.

Aparena [P 1.0165] samayena mahāchaṇe sampatte “ayaṃ imassa kālo”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpesi – “saddhā vā assaddhā vā sammādiṭṭhikā vā micchādiṭṭhikā vā geharakkhake dārake vā mātugāme vā ṭhapetvā avasesā ye vihāraṃ nāgacchanti, paññāsaṃ daṇḍo”ti. Sayampi pātova nhatvā katapātarāso sabbābharaṇapaṭimaṇḍito mahatā balakāyena saddhiṃ vihāraṃ agamāsi. Gacchanto ca cintesi – “bhagavā tumhe kira evaṃ vadatha ‘mayhameva dānaṃ dātabbaṃ…pe… na aññesaṃ sāvakānaṃ dinnaṃ mahapphala’nti evaṃ pucchituṃ ayuttaṃ, pañhameva pucchissāmi, pañhaṃ kathento ca me bhagavā avasāne titthiyānaṃ vādaṃ bhañjissatī”ti. So pañhaṃ pucchanto kattha nu kho, bhante, dānaṃ dātabbanti āha. Yatthāti yasmiṃ puggale cittaṃ pasīdati, tasmiṃ dātabbaṃ, tassa vā dātabbanti attho.

On another occasion, when a great festival was at hand, thinking, “This is the time,” he had a drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming: “Whether faithful or faithless, whether of right view or wrong view, excepting the young boys guarding the house and the womenfolk, whoever among the rest does not come to the monastery shall be fined fifty.” He himself, having bathed early in the morning, taken his morning meal, and adorned himself with all ornaments, went to the monastery with a great retinue. And while going, he thought: “It is improper to ask in this way: ‘Venerable sir, they say you speak thus: “A gift should be given only to me… a gift given to other disciples is not of great fruit.”’ I will just ask a question, and while answering my question, the Blessed One will, at the end, refute the doctrine of the sectarians.” So, wishing to ask the question, he said: “Venerable sir, where, indeed, should a gift be given?” The meaning of ‘Yattha’ (‘Wherever’) is this: in whatever person the mind is pleased, to that person it should be given, or for that one it should be given.

Evaṃ vutte rājā yehi manussehi titthiyānaṃ vacanaṃ ārocitaṃ, te olokesi. Te raññā olokitamattāva maṅkubhūtā adhomukhā pādaṅguṭṭhakena bhūmiṃ lekhamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Rājā – “ekapadeneva, bhante, hatā titthiyā”ti mahājanaṃ sāvento mahāsaddena abhāsi. Evañca pana bhāsitvā – “bhagavā cittaṃ nāma nigaṇṭhācelakaparibbājakādīsu yattha katthaci pasīdati[M 1.0152], kattha pana, bhante, dinnaṃ mahapphala”nti pucchi. Aññaṃ kho etanti, “mahārāja, aññaṃ tayā paṭhamaṃ pucchitaṃ, aññaṃ pacchā, sallakkhehi etaṃ, pañhākathanaṃ pana mayhaṃ bhāro”ti vatvā sīlavato khotiādimāha. Tattha idha tyassāti idha te assa. Samupabyūḷhoti rāsibhūto. Asikkhitoti dhanusippe asikkhito. Akatahatthoti muṭṭhibandhādivasena asampāditahattho. Akatayoggoti tiṇapuñjamattikāpuñjādīsu akataparicayo. Akatūpāsanoti rājarājamahāmattānaṃ adassitasarakkhepo. Chambhīti pavedhitakāyo.

When this was said, the king looked at those men who had reported the words of the sectarians. As soon as the king looked at them, they became crestfallen, hung their heads, and stood scratching the ground with their big toe. The king, making it heard by the great crowd, said with a loud voice, “Venerable sir, the sectarians are defeated with just one word!” Having spoken thus, he then asked, “Blessed One, the mind, it is said, becomes pleased with anyone among the Nigaṇṭhas, naked ascetics, wanderers, and so on; but where, venerable sir, does a gift given bear great fruit?” “Great king, you first asked one thing and afterwards another. Mark this well. But the burden of answering the question is mine.” Having said this, he spoke the words beginning with ‘sīlavato kho’ (‘Indeed, to one who is virtuous...’). Therein, ‘idha tyassa’ means ‘idha te assa’ (here, for you, it would be). ‘Samupabyūḷho’ means ‘formed into a mass.’ ‘Asikkhito’ means ‘untrained in the art of the bow.’ ‘Akatahattho’ means ‘one whose hand is not accomplished by means of clenching the fist and so on.’ ‘Akatayoggo’ means ‘one who has not practiced on heaps of grass, heaps of clay, and so on.’ ‘Akatūpāsano’ means ‘one who has not shown the shooting of an arrow to kings and great ministers of kings.’ ‘Chambhī’ means ‘one whose body trembles.’

Kāmacchando pahīnotiādīsu arahattamaggena kāmacchando pahīno hoti, anāgāmimaggena byāpādo[V 1.0146], arahattamaggeneva thinamiddhaṃ, tathā uddhaccaṃ, tatiyeneva kukkuccaṃ, paṭhamamaggena vicikicchā pahīnā hoti. Asekkhena [P 1.0166] sīlakkhandhenāti asekkhassa sīlakkhandho asekkho sīlakkhandho nāma. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ettha ca purimehi catūhi padehi lokiyalokuttarasīlasamādhipaññāvimuttiyo kathitā. Vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ hoti, taṃ lokiyameva.

In the phrases beginning with ‘Kāmacchando pahīno’ (‘sensual desire is abandoned’), sensual desire is abandoned by the path of Arahantship; ill will is abandoned by the path of non-returning; sloth and torpor are abandoned by the path of Arahantship alone; likewise, restlessness; worry is abandoned by the third path alone; doubt is abandoned by the first path. By ‘the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training’ (asekkhena sīlakkhandhena) is meant the aggregate of virtue of an Asekha. This is the method in all cases. And here, by the preceding four terms, mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation are taught. The knowledge and vision of liberation is reviewing knowledge, and that is only mundane.

Issattanti ususippaṃ. Balavīriyanti ettha balaṃ nāma vāyodhātu, vīriyaṃ kāyikacetasikavīriyameva. Bhareti bhareyya. Nāsūraṃ jātipaccayāti, “ayaṃ jātisampanno”ti evaṃ jātikāraṇā asūraṃ na bhareyya.

‘Issattaṃ’ means the art of the arrow. In ‘balavīriyaṃ,’ ‘bala’ (strength) is the wind element, and ‘vīriyaṃ’ (energy) is bodily and mental energy itself. ‘Bhare’ means one should support. ‘Nāsūraṃ jātipaccayā’ means: one should not support an unheroic person for the reason of birth, thinking, “This person is of high birth.”

Khantisoraccanti ettha khantīti adhivāsanakhanti, soraccanti arahattaṃ. Dhammāti ete dve dhammā. Assameti āvasathe. Vivaneti araññaṭṭhāne, nirudake araññe caturassapokkharaṇiādīni kārayeti attho. Duggeti visamaṭṭhāne. Saṅkamanānīti paṇṇāsahatthasaṭṭhihatthāni samokiṇṇaparisuddhavālikāni saṅkamanāni kareyya.

Regarding ‘Khantisoraccaṃ’: ‘khanti’ is the patience of forbearance; ‘soraccaṃ’ is Arahantship. ‘Dhammā’ refers to these two states. ‘Assame’ means in residences. ‘Vivane’ means in a forest place; the meaning is that in a waterless forest, one should have square ponds and so on made. ‘Dugge’ means in an uneven place. ‘Saṅkamanāni’ means one should make walking paths of fifty or sixty cubits, with evenly scattered, pure sand.

Idāni etesu araññasenāsanesu vasantānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhācāravattaṃ ācikkhanto annaṃ pānantiādimāha. Tattha senāsanānīti mañcapīṭhādīni. Vippasannenāti khīṇāsavassa dentopi sakaṅkhena kilesamalinena cittena adatvā vippasanneneva cittena dadeyya. Thanayanti gajjanto. Satakkakūti satasikharo, anekakūṭoti attho. Abhisaṅkhaccāti abhisaṅkharitvā samodhānetvā rāsiṃ katvā.

Now, wishing to explain the practice concerning the alms-round for monks dwelling in these forest lodgings, he spoke the words beginning with ‘annaṃ pānaṃ’ (‘food, drink’). Therein, ‘senāsanāni’ means beds, chairs, and the like. By ‘vippasannena’ is meant that even when giving to one whose taints are destroyed, one should not give with a mind stained by defilements and accompanied by doubt, but should give with a mind that is indeed especially clear. ‘Thanayanti’ means thundering. ‘Satakkakū’ means having a hundred summits; the meaning is ‘many-peaked.’ ‘Abhisaṅkhacca’ means having prepared, having brought together, and having made into a heap.

Āmodamānoti [M 1.0153] tuṭṭhamānaso hutvā. Pakiretīti dānagge vicirati, pakiranto viya vā dānaṃ deti. Puññadhārāti anekadānacetanāmayā puññadhārā. Dātāraṃ abhivassatīti yathā ākāse samuṭṭhitameghato nikkhantā udakadhārā pathaviṃ sinehayantī tementī kiledayantī abhivassati, evameva ayampi dāyakassa abbhantare uppannā puññadhārā tameva dātāraṃ anto sineheti pūreti abhisandeti. Tena vuttaṃ “dātāraṃ abhivassatī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

‘Āmodamāno’ means having a delighted mind. ‘Pakireti’ means he scatters at the place of giving, or alternatively, he gives a gift as if scattering it. ‘Puññadhārā’ means the stream of merit consisting of numerous volitions of giving. ‘Dātāraṃ abhivassati’ means: just as streams of water issuing from a cloud risen in the sky rain down upon the earth, making it sticky, wetting it, and moistening it, even so this stream of merit, arisen within the donor, moistens, fills, and suffuses that very donor within. Therefore, it was said, “It rains upon the giver.” The fourth.

5. Pabbatūpamasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Simile of the Mountain

136. Pañcame [V 1.0147] muddhāvasittānanti khattiyābhisekena muddhani avasittānaṃ katābhisekānaṃ. Kāmagedhapariyuṭṭhitānanti kāmesu gedhena pariyuṭṭhitānaṃ abhibhūtānaṃ. Janapadatthāvariyappattānanti [P 1.0167] janapade thirabhāvappattānaṃ. Rājakaraṇīyānīti rājakammāni rājūhi kattabbakiccāni. Tesu khvāhanti tesu ahaṃ. Usukkamāpannoti byāpāraṃ āpanno. Esa kira rājā divasassa tikkhattuṃ bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, antarāgamanāni bahūnipi honti. Tassa nibaddhaṃ gacchato balakāyo mahāpi hoti appopi. Athekadivasaṃ pañcasatā corā cintayiṃsu – “ayaṃ rājā avelāya appena balena samaṇassa gotamassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, antarāmagge naṃ gahetvā rajjaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti. Te andhavane nilīyiṃsu. Rājāno ca nāma mahāpuññā honti. Atha tesaṃyeva abbhantarato eko puriso nikkhamitvā rañño ārocesi. Rājā mahantaṃ balakāyaṃ ādāya andhavanaṃ parivāretvā te sabbe gahetvā andhavanato yāva nagaradvārā maggassa ubhosu passesu yathā aññamaññaṃ cakkhunā cakkhuṃ upanibandhitvā olokenti, evaṃ āsannāni sūlāni ropāpetvā sūlesu uttāsesi. Idaṃ sandhāya evamāha.

136. In the fifth discourse, 'of those anointed on the head' (muddhāvasittānaṃ) means of those consecrated with the khattiya-anointment poured on the head, for whom the anointment has been performed. 'Of those beset by greed for sensual pleasures' (kāmagedhapariyuṭṭhitānaṃ) means of those beset and overcome by greed for sensual pleasures. 'Of those who have attained stability in the country' (janapadatthāvariyappattānaṃ) means of those who have attained a state of stability in the country. 'Royal duties' (rājakaraṇīyāni) means royal affairs, duties to be performed by kings. 'In these matters, I' (tesu khvāhaṃ) is to be divided as 'in these, I' (tesu ahaṃ). 'Being occupied' (usukkamāpanno) means having become engaged in the task. It is said that this king goes to attend on the Blessed One three times a day, and there are also many visits in between. When he goes regularly, his retinue is sometimes large and sometimes small. Then one day, five hundred thieves thought: 'This king goes to attend on the ascetic Gotama at an unsuitable time with a small force. We will capture him on the way and seize the kingdom.' They hid in the Andhavana. And kings are indeed of great merit. Then, a man from their own group came out and informed the king. The king, taking a large force, surrounded the Andhavana and captured them all. Then, from the Andhavana up to the city gate, on both sides of the road, he had stakes planted so closely that they would be looking at each other eye to eye, and he had them impaled on those stakes. Referring to this, he spoke thus.

Atha satthā cintesi – “sacāhaṃ vakkhāmi, ‘mahārāja, mādise nāma sammāsambuddhe dhuravihāre vasante tayā evarūpaṃ dāruṇaṃ kammaṃ kataṃ, ayuttaṃ te kata’nti, athāyaṃ rājā maṅku hutvā santhambhituṃ na sakkuṇeyya, pariyāyena dhammaṃ kathentasseva me sallakkhessatī”ti dhammadesanaṃ ārabhanto [M 1.0154] taṃ kiṃ maññasītiādimāha. Tattha saddhāyikoti saddhātabbo, yassa tvaṃ vacanaṃ saddahasīti attho. Paccayikoti tasseva vevacanaṃ, yassa vacanaṃ pattiyāyasīti attho. Abbhasamanti ākāsasamaṃ. Nippothento āgacchatīti pathavitalato yāva akaniṭṭhabrahmalokā sabbe satte saṇhakaraṇīyaṃ tiṇacuṇṇaṃ viya karonto pisanto āgacchati.

Then the Teacher thought: 'If I were to say, "Great King, while a Perfectly Enlightened One like myself is dwelling in the principal monastery, you have committed such a cruel deed; what you have done is improper," then this king, becoming ashamed, would not be able to approach with familiarity. He will surely understand me only when I teach the Dhamma indirectly.' Thus, intending to begin the Dhamma discourse, he spoke the words beginning with, 'What do you think of this?' Therein, 'saddhāyiko' means one who should be believed; the meaning is 'one whose word you believe.' 'Paccayiko' is a synonym for that very word; the meaning is 'one whose word you trust.' 'Abbhasamaṃ' means like the sky. 'Nippothento āgacchati' means he comes crushing and grinding all beings from the surface of the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma world, making them like fine grass powder.

Aññatra dhammacariyāyāti ṭhapetvā dhammacariyaṃ aññaṃ kātabbaṃ natthi, dasakusalakammapathasaṅkhātā dhammacariyāva kattabbā, bhanteti – samacariyādīni tasseva vevacanāni. Ārocemīti ācikkhāmi. Paṭivedayāmīti jānāpemi. Adhivattatīti [P 1.0168] ajjhottharati. Hatthiyuddhānīti nāḷāgirisadise hemakappane nāge abhiruyha yujjhitabbayuddhāni. Gatīti nipphatti. Visayoti okāso, samatthabhāvo vā. Na hi sakkā tehi jarāmaraṇaṃ paṭibāhituṃ[V 1.0148]. Mantino mahāmattāti mantasampannā mahosadhavidhurapaṇḍitādisadisā mahāamaccā. Bhūmigatanti mahālohakumbhiyo pūretvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapitaṃ. Vehāsaṭṭhanti cammapasibbake pūretvā tulāsaṅghāṭādīsu laggetvā ceva niyyuhādīsu ca pūretvā ṭhapitaṃ. Upalāpetunti aññamaññaṃ bhindituṃ. Yathā dve janā ekena maggena na gacchanti evaṃ kātuṃ.

'Except for righteous conduct' means that, setting aside righteous conduct, there is nothing else to be done; only righteous conduct, known as the tenfold path of wholesome deeds, should be practiced. The terms 'even conduct' and so on are synonyms for that very word. 'I declare' means I proclaim. 'I make known' means I inform. 'Overcomes' means overwhelms. 'Elephant battles' refer to battles where one engages in combat by mounting a mighty elephant like Nālāgiri, adorned with golden trappings. 'Outcome' means result. 'Sphere' means opportunity or capability. For it is impossible to ward off old age and death by such means. 'Counselors, ministers' refers to great ministers endowed with counsel, like the wise Mahosadha and Vidhura. 'Buried in the ground' means filled into large bronze pots and buried in the earth. 'Suspended in the air' means filled into leather bags and hung from balance-beams, and also filled and placed in turrets. 'To sow discord' means to cause them to be divided from one another; to act in such a way that two people do not go by the same path.

Nabhaṃ āhaccāti ākāsaṃ pūretvā. Evaṃ jarā ca maccu cāti idha dveyeva pabbatā gahitā, rājovāde pana “jarā āgacchati sabbayobbanaṃ vilumpamānā”ti evaṃ jarā maraṇaṃ byādhi vipattīti cattāropete āgatāva. Tasmāti yasmā hatthiyuddhādīhi jarāmaraṇaṃ jinituṃ na sakkā, tasmā. Saddhaṃ nivesayeti saddhaṃ niveseyya, patiṭṭhāpeyyāti. Pañcamaṃ.

‘Reaching the sky’ (nabhaṃ āhacca) means ‘filling the sky.’ Thus, ‘old age and death’ (jarā ca maccu ca)—here only two mountains are taken, but in the Rājovāda, it is said: ‘Old age comes, plundering all youth,’ and so old age, death, sickness, and misfortune—these four mountains come. ‘Therefore’ (tasmā) means ‘because old age and death cannot be conquered by elephant battles and the like, therefore.’ ‘Establish faith’ (saddhaṃ nivesaye) means ‘one should establish faith, one should set it up.’ The fifth.

Tatiyo vaggo.

The Third Chapter.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Kosalasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Kosala Saṃyutta is concluded.

4. Mārasaṃyuttaṃ

4. The Māra Saṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Tapokammasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Tapokamma Sutta

137. Mārasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0149][P 1.0169][M 1.0155] paṭhame uruvelāyaṃ viharatīti paṭividdhasabbaññutaññāṇo uruvelagāmaṃ upanissāya viharati. Paṭhamābhisambuddhoti abhisambuddho hutvā paṭhamaṃ antosattāhasmiṃyeva. Dukkarakārikāyāti chabbassāni katāya dukkarakārikāya. Māro pāpimāti attano visayaṃ atikkamituṃ paṭipanne satte māretīti māro. Pāpe niyojeti, sayaṃ vā pāpe niyuttoti pāpimā. Aññānipissa kaṇho, adhipati, vasavattī, antako, namuci, pamattabandhūtiādīni bahūni nāmāni, idha pana nāmadvayameva gahitaṃ. Upasaṅkamīti – “ayaṃ samaṇo gotamo ‘muttosmī’ti maññati, amuttabhāvamassa kathessāmī”ti cintetvā upasaṅkami.

1. In the first sutta of the Māra Saṃyutta, ‘dwells at Uruvelā’ means: having penetrated the knowledge of omniscience, he dwells depending on the village of Uruvelā. ‘Newly fully enlightened’ means: having become fully enlightened, for the first time, within seven days. ‘By the difficult practice’ means: by the difficult practice performed for six years. ‘Māra the Evil One’: he oppresses beings who are practicing to transcend his realm, therefore he is called ‘Māra.’ He engages beings in evil, or he himself is engaged in evil, therefore he is called ‘Pāpimā’ (the Evil One). He also has many other names, such as Kaṇha, Adhipati, Vasavattī, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu, but here only the pair of names is taken. ‘He approached’ means: thinking, “This ascetic Gotama thinks, ‘I am liberated.’ I will tell him of his state of not being liberated,” he approached.

Tapokammā apakkammāti tapokammato apakkamitvā. Aparaddhoti “dūre tvaṃ suddhimaggā”ti vadati. Amaraṃ tapanti amaratapaṃ amarabhāvatthāya kataṃ lūkhatapaṃ, attakilamathānuyogo. Sabbānatthāvahaṃ hotīti, “sabbaṃ tapaṃ mayhaṃ atthāvahaṃ na bhavatī”ti ñatvā. Phiyārittaṃva dhammanīti araññe thale phiyārittaṃ viya. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā araññe thale nāvaṃ ṭhapetvā bhaṇḍassa pūretvā mahājanā abhirūhitvā phiyārittaṃ gahetvā saṃkaḍḍheyyuṃ ceva uppīleyyuṃ ca, so mahājanassa vāyāmo ekaṅguladvaṅgulamattampi nāvāya gamanaṃ asādhento niratthako bhaveyya [P 1.0170] na anatthāvaho, evameva ahaṃ ‘sabbaṃ amaraṃ tapaṃ anatthāvahaṃ hotī’ti ñatvā vissajjesinti.

“Having turned away from ascetic practices” means having turned away from the practice of austerity. “You have gone astray” means he says, “You are far from the path of purity.” “Austerity for immortality” means a harsh austerity, a repeated association with bodily fatigue, undertaken for the sake of the state of an immortal. “It is all unprofitable” means, knowing: “All austerity does not bring me benefit.” “Like an oar on dry land” means like an oar on dry land in the wilderness. This is what is said: Just as if a boat were placed on dry land in the wilderness, filled with goods, and many people, having boarded it and taken up oars, were to row and pole it, that effort of the many people, not accomplishing the boat's movement by even a finger's or two fingers' breadth, would be fruitless, not unprofitable; even so, I, knowing, “All austerity for immortality is unprofitable,” abandoned it.

Idāni [M 1.0156] taṃ amaraṃ tapaṃ pahāya yena maggena buddho jāto, taṃ dassento sīlantiādimāha[V 1.0150]. Tattha sīlanti vacanena sammāvācākammantājīvā gahitā, samādhinā sammāvāyāmasatisamādhayo, paññāya sammādiṭṭhisaṅkappā. Maggaṃ bodhāya bhāvayanti imaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikameva ariyamaggaṃ bodhatthāya bhāvayanto. Ettha ca bodhāyāti maggatthāya. Yathā hi yāgutthāya yāgumeva pacanti, pūvatthāya pūvameva pacanti, na aññaṃ kiñci karonti, evaṃ maggameva maggatthāya bhāveti. Tenāha “maggaṃ bodhāya bhāvaya”nti. Paramaṃ suddhinti arahattaṃ. Nihatoti tvaṃ mayā nihato parājito. Paṭhamaṃ.

Now, having abandoned that austerity for immortality, wishing to show the path by which one becomes a Buddha, he spoke the words beginning with “virtue.” Therein, by the word “virtue,” Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are taken; by “concentration,” Right Effort, Right Mindfulness, and Right Concentration are taken; by “wisdom,” Right View and Right Thought are taken. “Cultivating the path for awakening” means cultivating this very Noble Eightfold Path for the sake of awakening. And here, “for awakening” means for the sake of the path. For just as one cooks only gruel for the sake of gruel, and one bakes only cakes for the sake of cakes, and does not do anything else, even so, one cultivates only the path for the sake of the path. Therefore, he said, “Cultivate the path for awakening.” “The ultimate purity” means Arahantship. “Defeated” means: “You have been rendered harmless, defeated by me.” The first sutta.

2. Hatthirājavaṇṇasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Hatthirājavaṇṇa Sutta

138. Dutiye rattandhakāratimisāyanti rattiṃ andhabhāvakārake mahātame caturaṅge tamasi. Abbhokāse nisinno hotīti gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ pāsāṇaphalake mahācīvaraṃ sīse ṭhapetvā padhānaṃ pariggaṇhamāno nisinno hoti.

138. In the second sutta, “in the gloom and darkness of the night” means: in the great, four-factored darkness that causes blindness at night. “He was sitting in the open” means: having gone out from the perfumed chamber, he was sitting on a stone slab at the end of the walking path, having placed the great robe on his head while fully undertaking the striving.

Nanu ca tathāgatassa abhāvito vā maggo, appahīnā vā kilesā, appaṭividdhaṃ vā akuppaṃ, asacchikato vā nirodho natthi, kasmā evamakāsīti? Anāgate kulaputtānaṃ aṅkusatthaṃ. “Anāgate hi kulaputtā mayā gatamaggaṃ āvajjitvā abbhokāsavāsaṃ vasitabbaṃ maññamānā padhānakammaṃ karissantī”ti sampassamāno satthā evamakāsi. Mahāti mahanto. Ariṭṭhakoti kāḷako. Maṇīti pāsāṇo. Evamassa sīsaṃ hotīti evarūpaṃ tassa kāḷavaṇṇaṃ kūṭāgārappamāṇaṃ mahāpāsāṇasadisaṃ sīsaṃ hoti.

But is it not so that for the Tathāgata there is no undeveloped path, no unabandoned defilements, no unpenetrated unshakeable state, and no unrealized cessation? Why then did he act thus? For the sake of being a goad for future sons of good families. For, the Teacher, foreseeing that 'in the future, sons of good families, reflecting on the path I have taken, will think, "We should live in the open," and will undertake the work of striving,' acted thus. 'Great' (mahā) means large (mahanto). 'Ariṭṭhaka' means black (kāḷako). 'Jewel' (maṇi) means stone (pāsāṇo). 'Thus is its head' means: its head is of such a nature, black in color, the size of a gabled building, resembling a great stone.

Subhāsubhanti dīghamaddhānaṃ saṃsaranto sundarāsundaraṃ vaṇṇaṃ katvā āgatosīti vadati. Atha vā saṃsaranti saṃsaranto āgacchanto. Dīghamaddhānanti vasavattiṭṭhānato yāva uruvelāya dīghamaggaṃ, pure bodhāya vā chabbassāni [P 1.0171] dukkarakārikasamayasaṅkhātaṃ dīghakālaṃ. Vaṇṇaṃ katvā subhāsubhanti sundarañca asundarañca nānappakāraṃ vaṇṇaṃ katvā anekavāraṃ mama santikaṃ āgatosīti attho. So kira vaṇṇo nāma natthi, yena [M 1.0157] vaṇṇena māro vibhiṃsakatthāya bhagavato santikaṃ na āgatapubbo. Tena taṃ bhagavā evamāha. Alaṃ te tenāti alaṃ tuyhaṃ etena māravibhiṃsākāradassanabyāpārena. Dutiyaṃ.

Regarding 'beautiful and ugly' (subhāsubhaṃ), he says: 'Wandering for a long time, having created beautiful and unbeautiful forms, you have come.' Or alternatively, `saṃsaraṃ` means 'wandering, coming.' `Dīghamaddhānaṃ` (for a long time) means the long path from the abode of Vasavattī to Uruvelā; or, before awakening, the long time reckoned as the six years of the period of performing austerities. 'Having created forms, beautiful and ugly' (vaṇṇaṃ katvā subhāsubhaṃ) means: 'Having created various kinds of forms, both beautiful and unbeautiful, you have come into my presence many times.' This is the meaning. Indeed, there is no form by which Māra had not previously come into the presence of the Blessed One for the purpose of intimidation. Therefore, the Blessed One said this to him. 'Enough with that for you' (alaṃ te tena) means: enough for you with this effort of showing the intimidating forms of Māra. The second sutta.

3. Subhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Explanation of the Subha Sutta

139. Tatiye [V 1.0151] susaṃvutāti supihitā. Na te māravasānugāti, māra, te tuyhaṃ vasānugā na honti. Na te mārassa baddhagūti te tuyhaṃ mārassa baddhacarā sissā antevāsikā na honti. Tatiyaṃ.

139. In the third sutta, ‘well-restrained’ (susaṃvutā) means well-closed (supihitā). The phrase ‘they are not under Māra’s control’ (na te māravasānugā) means, ‘Māra, they do not come under your power.’ The phrase ‘they are not Māra’s bound followers’ (na te mārassa baddhagū) means, ‘They are not your, Māra's, bound followers, disciples, or pupils.’ The third sutta.

4. Paṭhamamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the First Māra's Snare Sutta

140. Catutthe yoniso manasikārāti upāyamanasikārena. Yoniso sammappadhānāti upāyavīriyena kāraṇavīriyena. Vimuttīti arahattaphalavimutti. Ajjhabhāsīti “ayaṃ attanā vīriyaṃ katvā arahattaṃ patvāpi na tussati, idāni aññesampi ‘pāpuṇāthā’ti ussāhaṃ karoti, paṭibāhessāmi na”nti cintetvā abhāsi.

140. In the fourth sutta, ‘wise attention’ (yoniso manasikāra) means attention with skillful means (upāyamanasikārena). ‘Wise right striving’ (yoniso sammappadhāna) means effort with skillful means (upāyavīriyena), effort through cause (kāraṇavīriyena). ‘Liberation’ (vimutti) means the liberation that is the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphalavimutti). ‘Addressed’ (ajjhabhāsi) means that, having thought, ‘This one, having striven by himself and attained arahantship, is still not satisfied; now he makes an effort for others too, saying, “May you attain it!” I will obstruct him,’ he thus spoke.

Mārapāsenāti kilesapāsena. Ye dibbā ye ca mānusāti ye dibbā kāmaguṇasaṅkhātā mānusā kāmaguṇasaṅkhātā ca mārapāsā nāma atthi, sabbehi tehi tvaṃ baddhoti vadati. Mārabandhanabaddhoti mārabandhanena baddho, mārabandhane vā baddho. Na me samaṇa mokkhasīti samaṇa tvaṃ mama visayato na muccissasi. Catutthaṃ.

‘By Māra’s snare’ (mārapāsena) means by the snare of defilements (kilesapāsena). ‘Those that are divine and those that are human’ means: he says, ‘Whatever snares of Māra there are, namely, those termed divine sensual pleasures and those termed human sensual pleasures, you are bound by all of them.’ ‘Bound by Māra’s bondage’ (mārabandhanabaddho) means bound by Māra’s bondage (mārabandhanena baddho), or bound in the place of Māra’s bondage (mārabandhane vā baddho). ‘Ascetic, you will not escape me’ (na me samaṇa mokkhasi) means, ‘Ascetic, you will not be freed from my domain.’ The fourth sutta.

5. Dutiyamārapāsasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Explanation of the Second Sutta on Māra’s Snare

141. Pañcame muttāhanti mutto ahaṃ. Purimaṃ suttaṃ antovasse vuttaṃ, idaṃ pana pavāretvā vuṭṭhavassakāle. Cārikanti anupubbagamanacārikaṃ. (Pavāretvā) divase divase yojanaparamaṃ [P 1.0172] gacchantā carathāti vadati. Mā ekena dveti ekamaggena dve janā mā agamittha. Evañhi gatesu ekasmiṃ dhammaṃ desente, ekena tuṇhībhūtena ṭhātabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā evamāha.

141. In the fifth sutta, ‘I am freed’ (muttāhaṃ) means I am freed (mutto ahaṃ). The previous sutta was spoken during the rains-retreat, but this one was spoken after performing the Pavāraṇā, at the time when the rains-retreat had ended. ‘Wandering’ (cārikaṃ) means wandering by going in sequence (anupubbagamanacārikaṃ). He says: ‘Having performed the Pavāraṇā, traveling at most a yojana day by day, you should wander.’ ‘Not two by one’ (mā ekena dve) means two persons should not go by one path (ekamaggena dve janā mā agamittha). For when they have gone thus, while one is teaching the Dhamma, the other has to remain silent. Therefore, he spoke thus.

Ādikalyāṇanti ādimhi kalyāṇaṃ sundaraṃ bhaddakaṃ. Tathā majjhapariyosānesu. Ādimajjhapariyosānañca nāmetaṃ sāsanassa ca desanāya ca [M 1.0158] vasena duvidhaṃ. Tattha sāsanassa sīlaṃ ādi, samathavipassanāmaggā majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ. Sīlasamādhayo vā ādi[V 1.0152], vipassanāmaggā majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ. Sīlasamādhivipassanā vā ādi, maggo majjhaṃ, phalanibbānāni pariyosānaṃ. Desanāya pana catuppadikāya gāthāya tāva paṭhamapādo ādi, dutiyatatiyā majjhaṃ, catuttho pariyosānaṃ. Pañcapadachappadānaṃ paṭhamapādo ādi, avasānapādo pariyosānaṃ, avasesā majjhaṃ. Ekānusandhikasuttassa nidānaṃ ādi, “idamavocā”ti pariyosānaṃ, sesaṃ majjhaṃ. Anekānusandhikassa majjhe bahūpi anusandhi majjhameva, nidānaṃ ādi, “idamavocā”ti pariyosānaṃ.

‘Beautiful in the beginning’ (ādikalyāṇaṃ) means beautiful, excellent, and auspicious at the beginning (ādimhi kalyāṇaṃ sundaraṃ bhaddakaṃ). Likewise, in the middle and at the end. This ‘beginning, middle, and end’ is twofold, by way of the Dispensation and by way of the teaching. Therein, with regard to the Dispensation, virtue is the beginning; serenity, insight, and the paths are the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end. Alternatively, virtue and concentration are the beginning; insight and the paths are the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end. Or, virtue, concentration, and insight are the beginning; the path is the middle; and the fruits and Nibbāna are the end. As for the teaching, for a four-line verse, the first line is the beginning; the second and third are the middle; and the fourth is the end. For five-line or six-line verses, the first line is the beginning; the last line is the end; and the remainder is the middle. For a discourse with a single connection, the introduction is the beginning; ‘This the Blessed One said’ (idamavoca) is the end; and the rest is the middle. For a discourse with multiple connections, though there are many connections in the middle, they are all the middle; the introduction is the beginning; and ‘This the Blessed One said’ (idamavoca) is the end.

Sātthanti sātthakaṃ katvā desetha. Sabyañjananti byañjanehi ceva padehi ca paripūraṃ katvā desetha. Kevalaparipuṇṇanti sakalaparipuṇṇaṃ. Parisuddhanti nirupakkilesaṃ. Brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ. Pakāsethāti āvikarotha.

‘Meaningful’ (sātthaṃ) means teach, making it meaningful (sātthakaṃ katvā desetha). ‘With the phrasing’ (sabyañjanaṃ) means teach, making it complete with both phrases and words (byañjanehi ceva padehi ca paripūraṃ katvā desetha). ‘Entirely complete’ (kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ) means entirely complete (sakalaparipuṇṇaṃ). ‘Pure’ (parisuddhaṃ) means free from defilements (nirupakkilesaṃ). ‘The holy life’ (brahmacariyaṃ) means the holy life of the Dispensation, which is comprised of the threefold training (sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanabrahmacariyaṃ). ‘Make known’ (pakāsetha) means reveal (āvikarotha).

Apparajakkhajātikāti paññācakkhumhi appakilesarajasabhāvā, dukūlasāṇiyā paṭicchannā viya catuppadikagāthāpariyosāne arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthā santīti attho. Assavanatāti assavanatāya. Parihāyantīti alābhaparihāniyā dhammato parihāyanti. Senānigamoti paṭhamakappikānaṃ senāya niviṭṭhokāse patiṭṭhitagāmo, sujātāya vā pitu senānī nāma nigamo. Tenupasaṅkamissāmīti nāhaṃ tumhe uyyojetvā pariveṇādīni kāretvā upaṭṭhākādīhi paricariyamāno [P 1.0173] viharissāmi, tiṇṇaṃ pana jaṭilānaṃ aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni dassetvā dhammameva desetuṃ upasaṅkamissāmīti. Tenupasaṅkamīti, “ayaṃ samaṇo gotamo mahāyuddhaṃ vicārento viya, ‘mā ekena dve agamittha, dhammaṃ desethā’ti saṭṭhi jane uyyojeti, imasmiṃ pana ekasmimpi dhammaṃ desente mayhaṃ cittassādaṃ natthi, evaṃ bahūsu desentesu kuto bhavissati, paṭibāhāmi na”nti cintetvā upasaṅkami. Pañcamaṃ.

‘Of little dust in their eyes’ (apparajakkhajātikā) means: there are beings with little dust of defilements in the eye of wisdom, who, as if covered by a fine linen curtain, are capable of attaining Arahantship at the end of a four-lined stanza—this is the meaning. ‘Due to not listening’ (assavanatā) means by the state of not listening. ‘They decline’ (parihāyanti) means they decline from the Dhamma through the loss of attainment. ‘Senānigama’ (senānigamo) is a village established in the place where the army of the first cosmic age was encamped, or the market town named Senā belonging to Sujātā's father. ‘I will approach’ (tenupasaṅkamissāmi) means: ‘I will not send you out and then remain here, having monasteries and so on prepared and being attended to by supporters. Rather, after showing the three matted-hair ascetics three and a half thousand miracles, I will approach only to teach the Dhamma.’ ‘He approached’ (tenupasaṅkami) means: having thought, ‘This ascetic Gotama, as if arranging a great battle, sends out sixty people, saying, “Do not go two by one path; teach the Dhamma.” But when even one of these teaches the Dhamma, my mind finds no delight; when many are teaching, how could there be? I will obstruct him,’ he thus approached. The fifth.

6. Sappasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Snake Sutta

142. Chaṭṭhe soṇḍikākilañjanti surākārakānaṃ piṭṭhapattharaṇakakilañjaṃ. Kosalikā kaṃsapātīti kosalarañño rathacakkappamāṇā paribhogapāti[M 1.0159]. Gaḷagaḷāyanteti gajjante. Kammāragaggariyāti kammāruddhanapaṇāḷiyā. Dhamamānāyāti bhastavātena pūriyamānāya. Iti viditvāti – “samaṇo gotamo padhānamanuyutto sukhena nisinno, ghaṭṭayissāmi na”nti vuttappakāraṃ [V 1.0153] attabhāvaṃ māpetvā niyāmabhūmiyaṃ ito cito ca sañcarantaṃ vijjulatālokena disvā, “ko nu kho eso satto”ti? Āvajjento, “māro aya”nti evaṃ viditvā.

6. Sixth, ‘soṇḍikākilañja’ is the mat for spreading flour paste belonging to liquor-makers. ‘Kosalikā kaṃsapātī’ is a bronze bowl for personal use belonging to the Kosalan king, the size of a chariot wheel. ‘Gaḷagaḷāyante’ means thundering. ‘Kammāragaggariyā’ is the blacksmith’s bellows pipe. ‘Dhamamānāya’ means being filled by the wind from the bellows. ‘Having known thus’ (iti viditvā): having seen with a flash of lightning one who was moving about here and there in the place of his solitude—who, thinking, ‘The ascetic Gotama is devoted to striving, seated comfortably; I will disturb him,’ had created an appearance of the kind described—the Buddha wondered, ‘Who indeed is this being?’ Reflecting, he thus knew, ‘This is Māra.’

Suññagehānīti suññāgārāni. Seyyāti seyyatthāya. Ṭhassāmi caṅkamissāmi nisīdissāmi nipajjissāmīti etadatthāya yo suññāgārāni sevatīti attho. So muni attasaññatoti so buddhamuni hatthapādakukkuccābhāvena saṃyatattabhāvo. Vossajja careyya tattha soti so tasmiṃ attabhāve ālayaṃ nikantiṃ vossajjitvā pahāya careyya. Patirūpaṃ hi tathāvidhassa tanti tādisassa taṃsaṇṭhitassa buddhamunino taṃ attabhāve nikantiṃ vossajjitvā caraṇaṃ nāma patirūpaṃ yuttaṃ anucchavikaṃ.

142. ‘Empty dwellings’ (suññagehāni) means secluded places (suññāgārāni). ‘Abiding’ (seyyā) means for the purpose of abiding (seyyatthāya). The meaning is: one who frequents secluded places for this purpose, thinking, ‘I will stand, I will walk, I will sit, I will lie down.’ ‘That sage is self-restrained’ (so muni attasaññato) means that Buddha-sage has a restrained nature due to the absence of fidgeting with hands and feet. ‘Having abandoned, he should conduct himself there’ (vossajja careyya tattha so) means in that state of being, having abandoned and relinquished attachment and craving, he should conduct himself. ‘Indeed, for such a one, it is fitting’ (patirūpaṃ hi tathāvidhassa taṃ) means for such a Buddha-sage, who is so constituted, the conduct called abandoning craving for that state of being is fitting, suitable, and appropriate.

Carakāti sīhabyagghādikā sañcaraṇasattā. Bheravāti saviññāṇakaaviññāṇakabheravā. Tattha saviññāṇakā sīhabyagghādayo, aviññāṇakā rattibhāge khāṇuvammikādayo. Tepi hi tasmiṃ kāle yakkhā viya upaṭṭhahanti, rajjuvalliyādīni sabbāni sappā viya upaṭṭhahanti. Tatthāti tesu bheravesu suññāgāragato [P 1.0174] buddhamuni lomacalanamattakampi na karoti.

‘Moving creatures’ (carakā) means moving creatures such as lions and tigers. ‘Terrifying things’ (bheravā) means terrifying things with consciousness and without consciousness. Among them, those with consciousness are lions, tigers, and so forth; those without consciousness are tree stumps, anthills, and so forth at nighttime. Indeed, at that time, even these appear like yakkhas, and all things like ropes and vines appear like snakes. ‘There’ (tattha) means amidst those terrifying objects, the Buddha-sage, having gone to a secluded place, does not make even the slightest movement of a body-hair.

Idāni aṭṭhānaparikappaṃ dassento nabhaṃ phaleyyātiādimāha. Tattha phaleyyāti kākapadaṃ viya hīrahīraso phaleyya. Caleyyāti pokkharapatte vātāhato udakabindu viya caleyya. Sallampi ce urasi pakappayeyyunti tikhiṇasattisallaṃ cepi urasmiṃ cāreyeyyuṃ. Upadhīsūti khandhūpadhīsu. Tāṇaṃ na karontīti tikhiṇe salle urasmiṃ cāriyamāne bhayena gumbantarakandarādīni pavisantā tāṇaṃ karonti nāma. Buddhā pana samucchinnasabbabhayā evarūpaṃ tāṇaṃ nāma na karonti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Now, wishing to show conjecture on what is impossible, he spoke the words beginning with, ‘The sky might split.’ Therein, ‘might split’ (phaleyya) means it might split into shreds like a crow's foot. ‘Might shake’ (caleyya) means it might shake like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, struck by the wind. ‘Even if they should drive a spear into the chest’ (sallampi ce urasi pakappayeyyuṃ) means even if they were to drive a sharp spear-shaft into the chest. ‘In the upadhis’ (upadhīsu) means in the upadhis which are the aggregates. ‘They do not make a refuge’ (tāṇaṃ na karonti) means: when a sharp spear is being driven into the chest, those who, out of fear, enter into thickets, mountain clefts, chasms, and so forth, are said to make a refuge. But the Buddhas, having completely cut off all fear, do not make such a thing called a refuge. Sixth.

7. Supatisuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Supati Sutta

143. Sattame [M 1.0160] pāde pakkhāletvāti utugāhāpanatthaṃ dhovitvā. Buddhānaṃ pana sarīre rajojallaṃ na upalimpati, udakampi pokkharapatte pakkhittaṃ viya vivaṭṭitvā gacchati. Apica kho dhotapādake gehe pāde dhovitvā pavisanaṃ pabbajitānaṃ vattaṃ. Tattha buddhānaṃ vattabhedo nāma natthi, vattasīse pana ṭhatvā dhovanti. Sace hi tathāgato neva nhāyeyya, na pāde dhoveyya, “nāyaṃ [V 1.0154] manusso”ti vadeyyuṃ. Tasmā manussakiriyaṃ amuñcanto dhovati. Sato sampajānoti soppapariggāhakena satisampajaññena samannāgato. Upasaṅkamīti samaṇo gotamo sabbarattiṃ abbhokāse caṅkamitvā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā niddāyati, ativiya sukhasayito bhavissati, ghaṭṭayissāmi nanti cintetvā upasaṅkami.

143. In the seventh (sutta), 'having washed his feet' means washing them in order to take on the warmth. However, dust and grime do not cling to the bodies of the Buddhas, and water also rolls off and departs, like water placed on a lotus leaf. Moreover, it is the duty for renunciates to wash their feet before entering a house where it is proper to tread with washed feet. In this regard, there is no such thing as a breaking of the duty for the Buddhas; rather, standing at the head of the duty, they wash. For if the Tathāgata were neither to bathe nor wash his feet, they would say, 'This is not a human.' Therefore, not abandoning human conduct, he washes. 'Mindful and clearly comprehending' means endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension that takes hold of sleep. 'He approached' means, thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama, having walked in the open air all night, has entered the fragrant chamber and is sleeping; he will be sleeping very comfortably. I will harass him,' he approached.

Kiṃ soppasīti kiṃ supasi, kiṃ soppaṃ nāmidaṃ tavāti vadati. Kiṃ nu soppasīti kasmā nu supasi? Dubbhago viyāti mato viya, visaññī viya ca. Suññamagāranti suññaṃ me gharaṃ laddhanti soppasīti vadati. Sūriye uggateti sūriyamhi uṭṭhite. Idāni hi aññe bhikkhū sammajjanti[P 1.0175], pānīyaṃ upaṭṭhapenti, bhikkhācāragamanasajjā bhavanti, tvaṃ kasmā soppasiyeva.

‘Why are you sleeping?’ means he says: ‘Why do you sleep? What is this sleep of yours?’ ‘Why then are you sleeping?’ means: ‘For what reason do you sleep?’ ‘Like an unfortunate one’ means: like one who is dead, and like one who is unconscious. ‘An empty dwelling’ means he says: ‘Are you sleeping, thinking, “I have obtained an empty dwelling”?’ ‘When the sun has risen’ means: when the sun is up. For now other monks are sweeping, setting out drinking water and water for use, and are ready for the alms-round; why do you just keep sleeping?

Jālinīti tayo bhave ajjhottharitvā ṭhitena “ajjhattikassupādāya aṭṭhārasataṇhāvicaritānī”tiādinā (vibha. 842) tena tena attano koṭṭhāsabhūtena jālena jālinī. Visattikāti rūpādīsu tattha tattha visattatāya visamūlatāya visaparibhogatāya ca visattikā. Kuhiñci netaveti katthaci netuṃ. Sabbūpadhi parikkhayāti sabbesaṃ khandhakilesābhisaṅkhārakāmaguṇabhedānaṃ upadhīnaṃ parikkhayā. Kiṃ tavettha, mārāti, māra, tuyhaṃ kiṃ ettha? Kasmā tvaṃ uṇhayāguyaṃ nilīyituṃ asakkontī khuddakamakkhikā viya antanteneva ujjhāyanto āhiṇḍasīti. Sattamaṃ.

'Jālinī' (Net-like) is so called because, having overwhelmed the three existences, it is established; and in accordance with the passage beginning, “the eighteen courses of craving that arise depending on the internal,” etc. (Vibh. 842), it is 'net-like' (jālinī) by that very net (jāla) which is its own portion. 'Visattikā' (Clinging) is so called because of its special attachment to forms and so on in various places, because of its being a root of suffering, and because of its partaking of suffering. 'Kuhiñci netave' (to lead anywhere) means to lead to some existence. 'By the complete destruction of all attachments' means because of the complete destruction of all attachments, which are divided into the aggregates, defilements, formations, and sensual pleasures. 'What is there for you here, Māra?' means: Māra, what is there for you here? Why do you, like a small fly unable to rest in hot gruel, wander about, reviling only from the vicinity? The seventh.

8. Nandatisuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Nandati Sutta

144. Aṭṭhamaṃ devatāsaṃyutte vuttatthameva. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

144. The eighth has the meaning already stated in the Devatāsaṃyutta. The eighth.

9. Paṭhamaāyusuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the First Āyu Sutta

145. Navame [M 1.0161] appaṃ vā bhiyyoti bhiyyo jīvanto aparaṃ vassasataṃ jīvituṃ na sakkoti, paṇṇāsaṃ vā saṭṭhi vā vassāni jīvati. Ajjhabhāsīti samaṇo gotamo “manussānaṃ appamāyū”ti katheti, dīghabhāvamassa kathessāmīti paccanīkasātatāya abhibhavitvā abhāsi.

145. In the ninth (sutta): 'A little or more' means that one who lives for a long time is not able to live for another hundred years; one lives for fifty or sixty years. 'He addressed' means: The ascetic Gotama says, 'The lifespan of humans is short.' Thinking, 'I will tell him about its long duration,' he spoke, seeking to overwhelm him out of a delight in opposition.

Na [V 1.0155] naṃ hīḷeti taṃ āyuṃ “appakamida”nti na hīḷeyya. Khīramatto vāti yathā daharo kumāro uttānaseyyako khīraṃ pivitvā dukūlacumbaṭake nipanno asaññī viya niddāyati, kassaci āyuṃ appaṃ vā dīghaṃ vāti na cinteti, evaṃ sappuriso. Careyyādittasīso vāti āyuṃ parittanti ñatvā pajjalitasīso viya careyya. Navamaṃ.

'One should not despise it': One should not despise that life, thinking, 'This is short.' 'Like one fed on milk': Just as a young infant lying on its back, having drunk milk, lies on a bundle of fine cloth and sleeps as if without perception, not thinking whether anyone's life is short or long, so it is with a good person. 'One should fare as if one's head were on fire': Knowing that life is short, one should fare like a person whose head is ablaze. The ninth.

10. Dutiyaāyusuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Second Āyu Sutta

146. Dasame nemīva rathakubbaranti yathā divasaṃ gacchantassa rathassa cakkanemi kubbaraṃ anupariyāyati na vijahati, evaṃ āyu anupariyāyatīti. Dasamaṃ.

146. In the tenth (sutta): 'Like the wheel-rim the chariot's pole-box' means: just as the wheel-rim of a chariot that travels for a day follows the pole-box and does not abandon it, so too life follows. The tenth.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Pāsāṇasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Pāsāṇa Sutta

147. Dutiyavaggassa [P 1.0176] paṭhame nisinnoti pubbe vuttanayeneva padhānaṃ pariggaṇhanto nisinno. Māropissa sukhanisinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā ghaṭṭayissāmīti upasaṅkamanto. Padālesīti pabbatapiṭṭhe ṭhatvā pavijjhi. Pāsāṇā nirantarā aññamaññaṃ abhihanantā patanti. Kevalanti sakalaṃ. Sabbanti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ.

147. In the first (sutta) of the second chapter, 'seated' is: he was seated, having fully undertaken the meditative development, in the very manner previously stated. Māra, too, knowing his state of being comfortably seated, approached, thinking, 'I will harass him.' 'He caused to split' means: standing on the mountain plateau, he hurled great stones. The stones, without interval, striking one another, fell. 'Kevalaṃ' means 'all'. The word 'sabbaṃ' is a synonym for that very word. The first (sutta).

2. Kinnusīhasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Kinnusīha Sutta.

148. Dutiye vicakkhukammāyāti parisāya paññācakkhuṃ vināsetukamyatāya. Buddhānaṃ panesa paññācakkhuṃ vināsetuṃ na sakkoti, parisāya bheravārammaṇaṃ [M 1.0162] sāvento vā dassento vā sakkoti. Vijitāvī nu maññasīti kiṃ nu tvaṃ “vijitavijayo aha”nti maññasi? Mā evaṃ maññi, natthi te jayo. Parisāsūti, aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Balappattāti dasabalappattā. Dutiyaṃ.

148. In the second (sutta), 'for the sake of blinding' means: with the desire to destroy the wisdom-eye of the assembly. However, this Māra is not able to destroy the wisdom-eye of the Buddhas; he is able to do so for the assembly by causing them to hear or by showing them a terrifying object. 'Do you think you are a victor?' means: 'Why do you think, “I am one who has won the victory”?' Do not think so; you have no victory. 'In the assemblies' means: in the eight assemblies. 'Attained to power' means: attained to the ten powers. The second (sutta).

3. Sakalikasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sakalika Sutta.

149. Tatiye [V 1.0156] mandiyā nūti mandabhāvena momūhabhāvena. Udāhu kāveyyamattoti udāhu yathā kavi kabbaṃ cintento tena kabbakaraṇena matto sayati, evaṃ sayasi. Sampacurāti bahavo. Kimidaṃ soppase vāti kasmā idaṃ soppaṃ soppasiyeva? Atthaṃ sameccāti atthaṃ samāgantvā pāpuṇitvā. Mayhaṃ hi asaṅgaho nāma saṅgahavipanno vā attho natthi. Sallanti tikhiṇaṃ sattisallaṃ. Jaggaṃ na saṅketi yathā ekacco sīhapathādīsu jagganto saṅkati, tathā ahaṃ jaggantopi na saṅkāmi. Napi bhemi sottunti yathā ekacco sīhapathādīsuyeva supituṃ bhāyati, evaṃ ahaṃ supitumpi na bhāyāmi. Nānutapanti māmanti yathā ācariyassa vā antevāsikassa vā aphāsuke jāte uddesaparipucchāya [P 1.0177] ṭhitattā antevāsiṃ rattindivā atikkamantā anutapanti, evaṃ maṃ nānutapanti. Na hi mayhaṃ kiñci apariniṭṭhitakammaṃ nāma atthi. Tenevāha hāniṃ na passāmi kuhiñci loketi. Tatiyaṃ.

149. In the third (sutta), 'Are you sluggish?' means: due to a state of dullness, due to a state of utter delusion. 'Or intoxicated with poetry?' means: or else, just as a poet contemplating a poem might sleep as if intoxicated by that task of creating poetry, in that way, do you sleep? 'Many' means: numerous. 'Why this sleeping?' means: 'Why do you just sleep this sleep?' 'Having realized the goal' means: having well arrived at and attained the goal. For me, there is indeed no goal that is ungrasped or lost to grasping. 'Dart' means: a sharp spear-dart. 'I am not anxious while vigilant' means: just as a certain person, while keeping watch in places like a lion's path, is apprehensive, in that way, I, even while keeping watch, am not apprehensive. 'Nor do I fear to sleep' means: just as a certain person fears to sleep in those very places like a lion's path, in that way, I do not fear even to sleep. 'They do not grieve for me' means: just as when a teacher or a resident pupil becomes unwell, the resident pupils grieve as the days and nights pass because they are established in recitation and inquiry, in that way, they do not grieve for me. For me, there is indeed no such thing as an unfinished task. Therefore, he said, 'I see no decline anywhere in the world.' The third (sutta).

4. Patirūpasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Patirūpa Sutta

150. Catutthe anurodhavirodhesūti rāgapaṭighesu. Mā sajjittho tadācaranti evaṃ dhammakathaṃ ācaranto mā laggi. Dhammakathaṃ kathentassa hi ekacce sādhukāraṃ dadanti, tesu rāgo uppajjati. Ekacce asakkaccaṃ suṇanti, tesu paṭigho uppajjati. Iti dhammakathiko anurodhavirodhesu sajjati nāma. Tvaṃ evaṃ mā sajjitthoti vadati. Yadaññamanusāsatīti yaṃ aññaṃ anusāsati, taṃ. Sambuddho hitānukampī hitena anupakampati. Yasmā ca hitānukampī[M 1.0163], tasmā anurodhavirodhehi vippamutto tathāgatoti. Catutthaṃ.

150. In the fourth, 'regarding attraction and repulsion' means with respect to lust and aversion. 'Do not be attached while acting thus' means: while thus giving a Dhamma talk, do not cling. For when one teaches the Dhamma, some give approval, and lust arises in him toward them. Some listen without respect, and aversion arises in him toward them. Thus, the Dhamma speaker is said to be attached to attraction and repulsion. He says, 'You should not be attached in this way.' 'When instructing another' means that with which he instructs another. The Fully Enlightened One, being compassionate for their welfare, shows compassion with what is for their welfare. And because he is compassionate for their welfare, therefore the Tathāgata is freed from attraction and repulsion; thus it should be understood. The fourth.

5. Mānasasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Mānasa Sutta

151. Pañcame ākāse carantepi bandhatīti antalikkhacaro. Pāsoti rāgapāso. Mānasoti manasampayutto. Pañcamaṃ.

151. In the fifth, it is a 'sky-farer' because it binds even those who travel in the sky. 'The snare' means the snare of lust. 'Mental' means associated with the mind. The fifth.

6. Pattasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Patta Sutta

152. Chaṭṭhe [V 1.0157] pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ upādāyāti pañca upādānakkhandhe ādiyitvā, sabhāvasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena nānappakārato vibhajitvā dassento. Sandassetīti khandhānaṃ sabhāvalakkhaṇādīni dasseti. Samādapetīti gaṇhāpeti. Samuttejetīti samādānamhi ussāhaṃ janeti. Sampahaṃsetīti paṭividdhaguṇena vodāpeti jotāpeti. Aṭṭhiṃ katvāti atthikaṃ katvā, “ayaṃ no adhigantabbo attho”ti evaṃ sallakkhetvā tāya desanāya atthikā hutvā. Manasi katvāti citte ṭhapetvā. Sabbacetaso samannāharitvāti sabbena [P 1.0178] tena kammakārakacittena samannāharitvā. Ohitasotāti ṭhapitāsotā. Abbhokāse nikkhittāti otāpanatthāya ṭhapitā.

152. In the sixth, 'by grasping the five aggregates of clinging' means: taking up the five aggregates of clinging, and showing them by differentiating them in various ways according to their specific and general characteristics. 'He shows' means he shows the specific characteristics, etc., of the aggregates. 'He induces' means he makes them grasp. 'He inspires' means he generates enthusiasm in the undertaking. 'He gladdens' means he purifies and illuminates with the quality of penetration. 'Having made it a goal' means: having made it a need, and having considered, 'This is the goal we must achieve,' they become desirous of that teaching. 'Having attended' means having placed it in the mind. 'With complete mental focus' means having brought it all together with the whole of that operative mind. 'With ears attentive' means with ears set. 'Set out in the open' means placed for the purpose of sunning.

Rūpaṃ vedayitaṃ saññānti, ete rūpādayo tayo khandhā. Yañca saṅkhatanti iminā saṅkhārakkhandho gahito. Evaṃ tattha virajjatīti “eso ahaṃ na homi, etaṃ mayhaṃ na hotī”ti passanto evaṃ tesu khandhesu virajjati. Khemattanti khemībhūtaṃ attabhāvaṃ. Iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Anvesanti bhavayonigatiṭhitisattāvāsasaṅkhātesu sabbaṭṭhānesu pariyesamānā. Nājjhagāti na passīti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

'Form, feeling, perception'—these are the three aggregates beginning with form. 'And whatever is conditioned'—by this, the aggregate of formations is included. Thus, 'he becomes dispassionate there'—seeing, 'This I am not, this is not mine,' he thus becomes dispassionate towards those aggregates. 'The state of security'—the state of existence that has become secure. By this, he indicates the moment of fruition. 'They seek'—that is, searching in all places designated as existence, birth, destiny, station, and abode of beings. 'He did not find'—that is, I do not see. The sixth.

7. Chaphassāyatanasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Chaphassāyatana Sutta

153. Sattame phassāyatanānanti sañjātisamosaraṇaṭṭhena chadvārikassa phassassa āyatanānaṃ. Bhayabheravaṃ saddanti meghadundubhiasanipātasaddasadisaṃ bhayajanakaṃ saddaṃ. Pathavī maññe undrīyatīti ayaṃ mahāpathavī paṭapaṭasaddaṃ [M 1.0164] kurumānā viya ahosi. Ettha loko vimucchitoti etesu chasu ārammaṇesu loko adhimucchito. Māradheyyanti mārassa ṭhānabhūtaṃ tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ. Sattamaṃ.

153. In the seventh, 'the sense bases of contact'—that is, the bases of contact of the six doors, in the sense of their arising and converging. 'The terrifying sound'—that is, a fear-inducing sound similar to the sound of thunder, storm clouds, and lightning strikes. 'The earth, it seems, is splitting open'—that is, this great earth seemed to be as if making a cracking sound. Here, 'the world is utterly infatuated'—that is, the world is strongly infatuated with these six sense-objects. 'The domain of Māra'—that is, the threefold round of existence, which is the place of Māra. The seventh.

8. Piṇḍasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Piṇḍa Sutta

154. Aṭṭhame pāhunakāni bhavantīti tathārūpe nakkhatte tattha tattha pesetabbāni pāhunakāni bhavanti, āgantukapaṇṇākāradānāni vā. Sayaṃcaraṇadivase samavayajātigottā kumārakā [V 1.0158] tato tato sannipatanti. Kumārikāyopi attano attano vibhavānurūpena alaṅkatā tahaṃ tahaṃ vicaranti. Tatra kumārikāyopi yathārucikānaṃ kumārakānaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ pesenti, kumārakāpi kumārikānaṃ aññasmiṃ asati antamaso mālāguḷenapi parikkhipanti. Anvāviṭṭhāti anu āviṭṭhā. Taṃdivasaṃ kira pañcasatā [P 1.0179] kumārikāyo uyyānakīḷaṃ gacchantiyo paṭipathe satthāraṃ disvā chaṇapūvaṃ dadeyyuṃ. Satthā tāsaṃ dānānumodanatthaṃ pakiṇṇakadhammadesanaṃ deseyya, desanāpariyosāne sabbāpi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhaheyyuṃ. Māro tāsaṃ sampattiyā antarāyaṃ karissāmīti anvāvisi. Pāḷiyaṃ pana mā samaṇo gotamo piṇḍamalatthāti ettakaṃyeva vuttanti.

154. In the eighth, as for the phrase 'gifts come into being': on such a festival day of the constellation, gifts to be sent come into being, or presents are given to arriving guests. On this day of free association, young men of the same age, birth, and clan gather from various places. Young girls, too, adorned according to their own means, wander here and there. There, the young girls send a token gift to the young men they fancy, and the young men, if there is nothing else, at the very least adorn the young girls with a garland. 'He possessed' means he entered into. It is said that on that day, five hundred young girls, going to the park for amusement, would have seen the Teacher on the path and offered him festival cakes. The Teacher, for the purpose of rejoicing in their gift, would have delivered a miscellaneous Dhamma discourse, and at the conclusion of the discourse, all of them would have been established in the fruit of stream-entry. Māra, thinking, 'I will create an obstacle to their accomplishment,' possessed them. In the Pāḷi text, however, only this much is said: 'May the ascetic Gotama not obtain alms-food!'

Kiṃ pana satthā mārāvaṭṭanaṃ ajānitvā paviṭṭhoti? Āma ajānitvā. Kasmā? Anāvajjanatāya. Buddhānañhi – “asukaṭṭhāne bhattaṃ labhissāma, na labhissāmā”ti āvajjanaṃ na ananucchavikaṃ. Paviṭṭho pana manussānaṃ upacārabhedaṃ disvā, “kiṃ ida”nti? Āvajjento ñatvā, “āmisatthaṃ mārāvaṭṭanaṃ bhindituṃ ananucchavika”nti abhinditvāva nikkhanto.

Now, did the Teacher enter without knowing of Māra's deception? Yes, without knowing. Why? Due to not adverting. Indeed, for Buddhas, it is not fitting to advert to the thought: 'In such-and-such a place we will receive alms-food, or we will not.' Having entered, however, and seeing the people's breach of respectful conduct, he adverted, 'What is this?' Upon adverting, he knew, and thinking, 'It is not fitting to destroy Māra's deception for the sake of material gain,' he departed without having destroyed it.

Upasaṅkamīti amittavijayena viya tuṭṭho sakalagāme kaṭacchumattampi bhattaṃ alabhitvā gāmato nikkhamantaṃ bhagavantaṃ gāmiyamanussavesena upasaṅkami. Tathāhaṃ karissāmīti idaṃ so musā bhāsati. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “mayā evaṃ vutte puna pavisissati, atha naṃ gāmadārakā ‘sakalagāme caritvā kaṭacchubhikkhampi alabhitvā gāmato nikkhamma puna paviṭṭhosī’tiādīni [M 1.0165] vatvā uppaṇḍessantī”ti. Bhagavā pana – “sacāyaṃ maṃ evaṃ viheṭhessati muddhamasseva sattadhā phalissatī”ti tasmiṃ anukampāya apavisitvā gāthādvayamāha.

'He approached': As if delighted by the conquest of an enemy, Māra, in the guise of a villager, approached the Blessed One who, not having obtained even a spoonful of food in the entire village, was departing from the village. 'I will do thus'—this Māra speaks falsely. It is said that this thought occurred to him: 'When I have spoken thus, he will re-enter. Then the village boys, saying, “Having wandered the entire village and not having obtained even a spoonful of alms, you departed from the village and have now re-entered,” and so on, will mock him.' But the Blessed One, thinking, 'If this one should harass me thus, his head will split into seven pieces,' out of compassion for him, did not re-enter and spoke two verses.

Tattha pasavīti janesi nipphādesi. Āsajjāti āsādetvā ghaṭṭetvā. Na me pāpaṃ vipaccatīti mama pāpaṃ na paccati. Nipphalaṃ etanti kiṃ nu tvaṃ evaṃ maññasi? Mā evaṃ maññi, atthi tayā katassa pāpassa phalanti dīpeti. Kiñcananti maddituṃ samatthaṃ rāgakiñcanādi kilesajātaṃ. Ābhassarā yathāti yathā ābhassarā devā sappītikajjhānena yāpentā pītibhakkhā nāma honti, evaṃ bhavissāmāti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Therein, pasavī means: he generated, he accomplished. Āsajjā means: having assailed, having provoked. Na me pāpaṃ vipaccati means: my evil does not ripen. 'This is fruitless'—why do you think thus? Do not think so; there is indeed a fruit for the evil done by you—thus he explains. Kiñcana means: that which is capable of crushing, the mass of defilements such as the impediment of lust. Ābhassarā yathā means: just as the Ābhassarā devas, sustaining themselves by means of jhāna accompanied by rapture, are called 'rapture-feeders,' so shall we be. The eighth.

9. Kassakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Kassaka Sutta

155. Navame [V 1.0159][P 1.0180] nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttāyāti nibbānaṃ apadisitvā pavattāya. Haṭahaṭakesoti purimakese pacchato, pacchimakese purato vāmapassakese dakkhiṇato, dakkhiṇapassakese vāmato pharitvā pharitvā vippakiṇṇakeso. Mama cakkhusamphassaviññāṇāyatananti cakkhuviññāṇena sampayutto cakkhusamphassopi viññāṇāyatanampi mamevāti. Ettha ca cakkhusamphassena viññāṇasampayuttakā dhammā gahitā, viññāṇāyatanena sabbānipi cakkhudvāre uppannāni āvajjanādiviññāṇāni. Sotadvārādīsupi eseva nayo. Manodvāre pana manoti sāvajjanakaṃ bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Dhammāti ārammaṇadhammā. Manosamphassoti sāvajjanena bhavaṅgena sampayuttaphasso. Viññāṇāyatananti javanacittaṃ tadārammaṇampi vaṭṭati.

155. In the ninth: Connected with Nibbāna means that which has arisen by taking Nibbāna as a support. With disheveled hair means with hair scattered about, by spreading the front hair to the back, the back hair to the front, the hair on the left side to the right, and the hair on the right side to the left. My eye-contact-consciousness-base means that eye-contact associated with eye-consciousness, and also the consciousness-base, are mine. And here, by eye-contact are taken the phenomena associated with eye-consciousness; by consciousness-base are taken all the consciousnesses that have arisen at the eye-door, such as adverting and so on. This same method applies to the ear-door and so on. At the mind-door, however, mind refers to the bhavaṅga-consciousness together with adverting. Phenomena are the object-phenomena. Mind-contact is the contact associated with the bhavaṅga together with adverting. The base of consciousness refers to the javana consciousness; the tadārammaṇa consciousness is also appropriate.

Taveva pāpima, cakkhūti yaṃ loke timirakācādīhi upaddutaṃ anekarogāyatanaṃ upakkavipakkaṃ antamaso kāṇacakkhupi, sabbaṃ taṃ taveva bhavatu. Rūpādīsupi eseva nayo.

'O Evil One, let the eye be yours alone' means: whatever eye in the world is afflicted by worms and so on, is a basis for many diseases, is festering and inflamed, even a blind eye at the very least—let all that be yours alone. The same method applies to forms and so on.

Yaṃ vadantīti yaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ “mama ida”nti vadanti. Ye vadanti mamanti cāti ye ca puggalā “mama”nti vadanti. Ettha ce te mano atthīti etesu ca ṭhānesu yadi cittaṃ atthi. Na me samaṇa mokkhasīti samaṇa mayhaṃ visayato na muccissasi. Yaṃ vadantīti yaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ vadanti, na taṃ mayhaṃ. Ye vadantīti yepi puggalā evaṃ vadanti, na te ahaṃ. Na me maggampi dakkhasīti bhavayonigatiādīsu mayhaṃ gatamaggampi na passasi. Navamaṃ.

'What they say' refers to whatever goods they speak of as 'this is mine.' And 'those who say "mine"' refers to those persons who speak of 'mine.' 'And if your mind is in this' means: if your mind is in these things. 'You will not escape me, ascetic' means: O ascetic, you will not be freed from my domain. 'What they say' means: whatever goods they speak of, that is not mine. 'Those who say' means: those persons who speak thus, I am not they. 'You will not even see my path' means: you will not see even the path I have gone upon through existences, origins, destinations, and so on. The ninth.

10. Rajjasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Rajja Sutta

156. Dasame [M 1.0166] ahanaṃ aghātayanti ahanantena aghātayantena. Ajinaṃ ajāpayanti parassa dhanajāniṃ akarontena akārāpentena. Asocaṃ asocāpayanti asocantena asocāpayantena. Iti bhagavā adhammikarājūnaṃ rajje vijite daṇḍakarapīḷite manusse disvā kāruññavasena evaṃ cintesi. Upasaṅkamīti [P 1.0181] “samaṇo gotamo ‘sakkā nu kho rajjaṃ kāretu’nti cintesi, rajjaṃ kāretukāmo bhavissati, rajjañca nāmetaṃ pamādaṭṭhānaṃ, rajjaṃ kārente sakkā otāraṃ labhituṃ, gacchāmi ussāhamassa janessāmī”ti cintetvā upasaṅkami. Iddhipādāti ijjhanakakoṭṭhāsā[V 1.0160]. Bhāvitāti vaḍḍhitā. Bahulīkatāti punappunaṃ katā. Yānīkatāti yuttayānaṃ viya katā. Vatthukatāti patiṭṭhaṭṭhenavatthukatā. Anuṭṭhitāti avijahitā niccānubaddhā. Paricitāti sātaccakiriyāya suparicitā katā issāsassa avirādhitavedhihattho viya. Susamāraddhāti suṭṭhu samāraddhā paripuṇṇabhāvanā. Adhimucceyyāti cinteyya.

156. In the tenth, 'not killing' means not killing, nor causing another to kill. 'Not causing loss' means not causing loss of wealth to others, nor causing others to cause loss of wealth. 'Not grieving' means not grieving, nor causing another to grieve. Thus, the Blessed One, seeing people oppressed by unjust kings in conquered lands, afflicted by punishments and taxation, out of compassion, thought thus. 'He approached' means: thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama may have thought, "Is it not possible to rule a kingdom?" He may desire to rule, but kingship is a place of negligence. If he rules, it might be possible to find an opportunity. I will go and generate enthusiasm in him,' he approached. 'Bases of psychic power' refers to the constituents of accomplishment. 'Developed' means increased. 'Cultivated' means done repeatedly. 'Made a vehicle' means made like a yoked chariot. 'Established' means established as a base. 'Pursued' means not abandoned, constantly attended. 'Familiarized' means well-practiced through continuous action, like the unerring hand of an archer. 'Well undertaken' means thoroughly undertaken with complete development. 'He could resolve' means he could think.

Pabbatassāti pabbato bhaveyya. Dvittāvāti tiṭṭhatu eko pabbato, dvikkhattumpi tāva mahanto suvaṇṇapabbato ekassa nālaṃ, na pariyattoti attho. Iti vidvā samañcareti evaṃ jānanto samaṃ careyya. Yatonidānanti dukkhaṃ nāma pañcakāmaguṇanidānaṃ, taṃ yatonidānaṃ hoti, evaṃ yo adakkhi. Kathaṃ nameyyāti so jantu tesu dukkhassa nidānabhūtesu kāmesu kena kāraṇena nameyya. Upadhiṃ viditvāti kāmaguṇaupadhiṃ “saṅgo eso, lagganameta”nti evaṃ viditvā. Tasseva jantu vinayāya sikkheti tasseva upadhissa vinayāya sikkheyya. Dasamaṃ.

'Of a mountain' means it would be a mountain. 'Twice as much' means: let one mountain stand; even a golden mountain twice as large would not be enough, would not suffice for one person—this is the meaning. 'Thus, a wise one should fare evenly' means: knowing thus, one should fare evenly. Regarding 'from what source': suffering, indeed, has the five strands of sensual pleasure as its cause. A being has seen truly that it arises from this source. Regarding 'how would they incline?': for what reason would that being incline towards those sensual pleasures that have become the source of suffering? 'Having understood the substrate' means: having understood the substrate of sensual pleasures thus: 'This is an attachment, this is a clinging.' 'A being should train for its removal' means: a being should train for the removal of that very substrate. The tenth.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter

1. Sambahulasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Sambahula Sutta

157. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhame jaṭaṇḍuvenāti jaṭācumbaṭakena. Ajinakkhipanivatthoti sakhuraṃ ajinacammaṃ ekaṃ nivattho ekaṃ pāruto. Udumbaradaṇḍanti [M 1.0167] appicchabhāvappakāsanatthaṃ īsakaṃ vaṅkaṃ udumbaradaṇḍaṃ gahetvā. Etadavocāti loke brāhmaṇassa vacanaṃ nāma sussūsanti, brāhmaṇesupi pabbajitassa, pabbajitesupi mahallakassāti mahallakabrāhmaṇassa pabbajitavesaṃ gahetvā padhānabhūmiyaṃ kammaṃ karonte te bhikkhū upasaṅkamitvā hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā etaṃ “daharā bhavanto”tiādivacanaṃ [P 1.0182] avoca. Okampetvāti hanukena uraṃ paharanto adhonataṃ katvā. Jivhaṃ nillāletvāti kabaramahājivhaṃ nīharitvā uddhamadho ubhayapassesu ca lāletvā. Tivisākhanti tisākhaṃ. Nalāṭikanti bhakuṭiṃ, nalāṭe uṭṭhitaṃ valittayanti attho. Pakkāmīti tumhe jānantānaṃ [V 1.0161] vacanaṃ akatvā attanova tele paccissathāti vatvā ekaṃ maggaṃ gahetvā gato. Paṭhamaṃ.

157. In the first of the third chapter: 'with a coil of matted hair' means with a coil of matted hair. 'Clad in an antelope hide' means wearing a black antelope skin, complete with its hooves—one as an undergarment, one as an upper garment. 'Carrying an udumbara staff' means holding a slightly crooked udumbara staff to show a state of having few wants. 'He spoke thus' means: in the world, people listen to the word of a brahmin; among brahmins, to one who has gone forth; and among those who have gone forth, to an elder. Thus, having taken the guise of an elder brahmin renunciant, he approached those monks who were practicing in a place of exertion, raised his hand, and spoke this speech beginning with, 'You are young, sirs...'. 'Shaking' means striking his chest with his chin, having bent down low. 'Lolling his tongue' means sticking out his large, variegated tongue and moving it up, down, and to both sides. 'Three-pronged' means having three forks. 'On the forehead' means a frown; that is, the set of three wrinkles that has arisen on the forehead. 'He departed' means, having said, 'Since you do not follow the word of those who know, you will be scorched in your own place!', he took a certain path and went away. The first.

2. Samiddhisuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Samiddhi Sutta

158. Dutiye lābhā vata me, suladdhaṃ vata meti evarūpassa satthu ceva dhammassa ca sabrahmacārīnañca laddhattā mayhaṃ lābhā mayhaṃ suladdhanti. So kirāyasmā pacchā mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ sammasitvā “arahattaṃ gahessāmī”ti pāsādikaṃ tāva kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇe āvajjetvā cittakallataṃ uppādetvā cittaṃ hāsetvā tosetvā nisinno. Tenassa evamahosi. Upasaṅkamīti “ayaṃ samiddhi bhikkhu pāsādikaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā nisinnasadiso, yāva mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā arahattaṃ na gaṇhāti, tāvassa antarāyaṃ karissāmī”ti upasaṅkami. Gaccha tvanti satthā sakalajambudīpaṃ olokento “tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne tassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ sappāyaṃ bhavissatī”ti addasa, tasmā evamāha. Satipaññā ca me buddhāti mayā sati ca paññā ca ñātā. Karassu rūpānīti bahūnipi vibhiṃsakārahāni rūpāni karassu. Neva maṃ byādhayissasīti maṃ neva vedhayissasi na kampassesi. Dutiyaṃ.

158. In the second sutta, ‘Gains indeed for me, well-gained indeed for me’ means: ‘Because of having gained such a Teacher, Dhamma, and holy companions, it is a gain for me, it is well-gained for me.’ It is said that the venerable one, having later reflected on his fundamental meditation subject, thinking, ‘I will attain arahantship,’ first took up a pleasing meditation subject. After recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha, he aroused mental readiness, gladdened and satisfied his mind, and sat down. Therefore, it occurred to him thus. ‘Approached’ means Māra approached, thinking: ‘This monk Samiddhi seems to be sitting having taken up a pleasing meditation subject. As long as he does not attain arahantship by taking up his fundamental meditation subject, I will create an obstacle for him.’ ‘Go!’ means the Teacher, surveying the entire Jambudīpa, saw that the meditation subject would be suitable for him in that very place, and therefore spoke thus. ‘Mindfulness and wisdom are known to me’ means mindfulness and wisdom have been known by me. ‘Make forms’ means make many forms that are fit to cause terror. ‘You will not afflict me’ means you will not pierce me, you will not shake me. The second.

3. Godhikasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Godhika Sutta.

159. Tatiye [M 1.0168] isigilipasseti isigilissa nāma pabbatassa passe. Kāḷasilāyanti kāḷavaṇṇāya silāyaṃ. Sāmayikaṃ cetovimuttinti [P 1.0183] appitappitakkhaṇe paccanīkadhammehi vimuccati, ārammaṇe ca adhimuccatīti lokiyasamāpatti sāmayikā cetovimutti nāma. Phusīti paṭilabhi. Parihāyīti kasmā yāva chaṭṭhaṃ parihāyi? Sābādhattā. Therassa kira vātapittasemhavasena anusāyiko ābādho atthi, tena samādhissa sappāye upakārakadhamme pūretuṃ na sakkoti, appitappitāya samāpattiyā parihāyati.

159. In the third sutta, ‘at the side of Isigili’ means on the slope of the mountain named Isigili. ‘At Black Rock’ means on a rock of black color. ‘Temporary liberation of mind’ means that at the moment of each application, one is freed from opposing states and becomes absorbed in the object; thus, a mundane attainment is called temporary liberation of mind. ‘He touched’ means he attained. ‘He declined’ means why did he decline up to the sixth time? Due to illness. It is said that the elder had a persistent illness caused by wind, bile, and phlegm. Because of this, he was unable to fulfill the supportive factors conducive to concentration, and thus he declined from the attainment each time it was reached.

Yaṃnūnāhaṃ satthaṃ āhareyyanti so kira cintesi, yasmā parihīnajjhānassa kālaṅkaroto anibaddhā gati hoti, aparihīnajjhānassa nibaddhā gati hoti, brahmaloke nibbattati, tasmā satthaṃ āharitukāmo ahosi. Upasaṅkamīti – “ayaṃ samaṇo satthaṃ āharitukāmo, satthāharaṇañca [V 1.0162] nāmetaṃ kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhassa hoti. Yo evaṃ kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkho hoti, so mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ sammasitvā arahattampi gahetuṃ samattho hoti, mayā pana paṭibāhitopi esa na oramissati, satthārā paṭibāhito oramissatī”ti therassa atthakāmo viya hutvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.

‘What if I were to bring a weapon?’ means: it is said that he thought thus, because for one who dies having declined from jhāna, their destination is uncertain, whereas for one who has not declined from jhāna, their destination is certain, for they are reborn in the Brahma world. Therefore, he desired to bring a weapon. ‘He approached’ means: Māra, as if desiring the elder’s welfare, approached the Blessed One, thinking: ‘This ascetic wishes to bring a weapon, and this act of bringing a weapon is for one who has no concern for body and life. One who is thus without concern for body and life, having contemplated the fundamental meditation subject, is capable of attaining even Arahantship. However, even if forbidden by me, he will not desist. Only if forbidden by the Teacher will he desist.’

Jalāti jalamānā. Pāde vandāmi cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā tava pāde vandāmi. Jutindharāti ānubhāvadharā. Appattamānasoti appattaarahatto. Sekhoti sīlādīni sikkhamāno sakaraṇīyo. Jane sutāti jane vissutā. Satthaṃ āharitaṃ hotīti thero kira “kiṃ mayhaṃ iminā jīvitenā”ti? Uttāno nipajjitvā satthena galanāḷiṃ chindi, dukkhā vedanā uppajjiṃsu. Thero vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā taṃyeva vedanaṃ pariggahetvā satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā mūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ sammasanto arahattaṃ patvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi. Samasīsī nāma tividho hoti iriyāpathasamasīsī, rogasamasīsī, jīvitasamasīsīti.

‘Blazing forth’ means shining brightly. ‘I bow at the feet of the One with Vision’ means: ‘O One with Vision, possessing the five eyes, I bow at your feet.’ ‘Bearer of Radiance’ means possessor of power. ‘One whose mind has not attained’ means one who has not attained Arahantship. ‘A trainee’ means one who is still training in virtue and other practices, still having something to be done. ‘Renowned among people’ means well-known among the populace. ‘The weapon was brought forth’ means: it is said that the elder, thinking, ‘What is this life to me?’, lay down on his back and cut his throat with the weapon. Painful feelings arose. The elder, having suppressed the painful feeling, took up that very feeling, established mindfulness, and while contemplating his fundamental meditation subject, attained Arahantship and, becoming one of equal-headedness (samasīsī), attained Parinibbāna. One of equal-headedness (samasīsī) is of three kinds: equal in posture, equal in illness, and equal in life.

Tattha [M 1.0169] yo ṭhānādīsu iriyāpathesu aññataraṃ adhiṭṭhāya – “imaṃ akopetvāva arahattaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti, athassa arahattappatti ca iriyāpathakopanañca ekappahāreneva hoti. Ayaṃ iriyāpathasamasīsī nāma. Yo pana cakkhurogādīsu aññatarasmiṃ [P 1.0184] sati – “ito anuṭṭhitova arahattaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti, athassa arahattappatti ca rogato vuṭṭhānañca ekappahāreneva hoti. Ayaṃ rogasamasīsī nāma. Keci pana tasmiṃyeva iriyāpathe tasmiñca roge parinibbānavasenettha samasīsitaṃ paññāpenti. Yassa pana āsavakkhayo ca jīvitakkhayo ca ekappahāreneva hoti. Ayaṃ jīvitasamasīsī nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ – “yassa puggalassa apubbaṃ acarimaṃ āsavapariyādānañca hoti jīvitapariyādānañca, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo samasīsī”ti (pu. pa. 16).
