Among these, a person who, having resolved upon one of the postures such as standing, establishes insight thinking, ‘Without breaking this posture, I will attain Arahantship’; for him, the attainment of Arahantship and the breaking of the posture occur at the very same instant. This one is called iriyāpathasamasīsī. Furthermore, a person who, while afflicted with an eye disease or the like, establishes insight thinking, ‘Without rising from this illness, I will attain Arahantship’; for him, the attainment of Arahantship and the recovery from the illness occur at the very same instant. This one is called rogasamasīsī. Some teachers, however, designate the state of being samasīsī in this context by way of final Nibbāna in that very posture and in that very illness. Furthermore, for whichever person the destruction of the cankers and the destruction of life occur at the very same instant, this one is called jīvitasamasīsī. And this was also stated: ‘The person for whom the complete ending of the cankers and the ending of life occur not one before the other, that person is called samasīsī.’

Ettha ca pavattisīsaṃ kilesasīsanti dve sīsāni. Tattha pavattisīsaṃ nāma jīvitindriyaṃ, kilesasīsaṃ nāma avijjā. Tesu jīvitindriyaṃ cuticittaṃ khepeti, avijjā maggacittaṃ. Dvinnaṃ cittānaṃ ekato uppādo natthi. Maggānantaraṃ pana phalaṃ, phalānantaraṃ bhavaṅgaṃ, bhavaṅgato vuṭṭhāya paccavekkhaṇaṃ, taṃ paripuṇṇaṃ vā hoti aparipuṇṇaṃ vā. Tikhiṇena asinā sīse chijjantepi [V 1.0163] hi eko vā dve vā paccavekkhaṇavārā avassaṃ uppajjantiyeva, cittānaṃ pana lahuparivattitāya āsavakkhayo ca jīvitapariyādānañca ekakkhaṇe viya paññāyati.

Here, there are two ‘heads’: the head of existence and the head of defilements. Among them, the head of existence is the life faculty, and the head of defilements is ignorance. Of these, the death-consciousness destroys the life faculty, and the path-consciousness destroys ignorance. The simultaneous arising of these two consciousnesses does not occur. However, immediately after the path is fruition; immediately after fruition is the life-continuum; and rising from the life-continuum, there is reviewing. That reviewing may be complete or incomplete. Indeed, even when one's head is being severed by a sharp sword, one or two rounds of reviewing inevitably arise. However, due to the swift changing of consciousnesses, the destruction of the cankers and the complete ending of life appear as if in a single moment.

Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyhāti avijjāmūlena samūlakaṃ taṇhaṃ arahattamaggena uppāṭetvā. Parinibbutoti anupādisesanibbānena parinibbuto.

‘Having pulled out craving with its root’ means having uprooted craving, which has ignorance as its root, by means of the path of Arahantship. ‘Is fully extinguished’ means is fully extinguished by means of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining.

Vivattakkhandhanti parivattakkhandhaṃ. Semānanti uttānaṃ hutvā sayitaṃ hoti. Thero pana kiñcāpi uttānako sayito, tathāpissa dakkhiṇena passena paricitasayanattā sīsaṃ dakkhiṇatova parivattitvā ṭhitaṃ. Dhūmāyitattanti dhūmāyitabhāvaṃ. Tasmiṃ hi khaṇe dhūmavalāhakā viya timiravalāhakā viya ca uṭṭhahiṃsu. Viññāṇaṃ samanvesatīti paṭisandhicittaṃ pariyesati. Appatiṭṭhitenāti paṭisandhiviññāṇena appatiṭṭhitena, appatiṭṭhitakāraṇāti attho. Beluvapaṇḍuvīṇanti beluvapakkaṃ viya paṇḍuvaṇṇaṃ suvaṇṇamahāvīṇaṃ. Ādāyāti kacche ṭhapetvā. Upasaṅkamīti [P 1.0185] “godhikattherassa nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ na [M 1.0170] jānāmi, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ pucchitvā nikkaṅkho bhavissāmī”ti khuddakadārakavaṇṇī hutvā upasaṅkami. Nādhigacchāmīti na passāmi. Sokaparetassāti sokena phuṭṭhassa. Abhassathāti pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ patitā. Tatiyaṃ.

‘A rolled-back bundle’ means a bundle that has been turned over. ‘Lying’ means lying stretched out on one's back. Though the elder was lying on his back, because he was accustomed to lying on his right side, his head remained turned to the right. ‘Smoke-like’ refers to the state of being smoky. At that moment, clouds like smoke and clouds like darkness arose. ‘Seeking consciousness’ means searching for the rebirth-linking consciousness. ‘Unestablished’ means that the rebirth-linking consciousness is unestablished; this is the meaning of ‘having no basis’. ‘A pale-beluva-colored harp’ means a great golden harp, pale in color like a ripe beluva fruit. ‘Taking it’ means placing it in the armpit. ‘Approached’ means, thinking, ‘I do not know the place where the elder Godhika was reborn; I will ask the ascetic Gotama and be free from doubt,’ he took the form of a young boy and approached. ‘I do not find’ means I do not see. ‘Of one afflicted by sorrow’ means of one touched by sorrow. ‘Fell’ means it fell on the top of his foot. The third.

4. Sattavassānubandhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Discourse on the Seven-Year Pursuit

160. Catutthe satta vassānīti pure bodhiyā chabbassāni, bodhito pacchā ekaṃ vassaṃ. Otārāpekkhoti “sace samaṇassa gotamassa kāyadvārādīsu kiñcideva ananucchavikaṃ passāmi, codessāmi na”nti evaṃ vivaraṃ apekkhamāno. Alabhamānoti rathareṇumattampi avakkhalitaṃ apassanto. Tenāha –

160. In the fourth, “for seven years” refers to six years before his enlightenment and one year after his enlightenment. “Looking for an opening” means, “If I see anything at all unbecoming in the doors of body, etc., of the ascetic Gotama, I will reproach him,” thus seeking an opportunity. “Not finding” means not seeing even a fault the size of a speck of chariot dust. Hence it is said:

“Satta vassāni bhagavantaṃ, anubandhiṃ padāpadaṃ;

Otāraṃ nādhigacchissaṃ, sambuddhassa satīmato”ti. (su. ni. 448);

“For seven years I followed the Blessed One, step by step; I found no opening in the mindful, fully awakened one.”

Upasaṅkamīti “ajja samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ atigahetvā gamissāmī”ti upasaṅkami.

‘Approached’ means he approached, thinking: “Today, having feigned compliance with the ascetic Gotama's way, I will depart.”

Jhāyasīti [V 1.0164] jhāyanto avajjhāyanto nisinnosīti vadati. Vittaṃ nu jīnoti sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā jitosi nu. Āguṃ nu gāmasminti, kiṃ nu antogāme pamāṇātikkantaṃ pāpakammaṃ akāsi, yena aññesaṃ mukhaṃ oloketuṃ avisahanto araññe vicarasi? Sakkhinti mittabhāvaṃ.

“Are you meditating?” means: he says, “Are you sitting here brooding?” “Have you lost wealth?” means: “Have you lost a hundred or a thousand?” “Or have you committed a fault in the village?” means: “Have you committed some evil deed beyond measure within the village, on account of which, being unable to look others in the face, you wander in the forest?” “Friendship” is the meaning of ‘sakkhi’.

Palikhāyāti khaṇitvā. Bhavalobhajappanti bhavalobhasaṅkhātaṃ taṇhaṃ. Anāsavo jhāyāmīti nittaṇho hutvā dvīhi jhānehi jhāyāmi. Pamattabandhūti māraṃ ālapati. So hi yekeci loke pamattā, tesaṃ bandhu.

“Having dug up” means having uprooted. “The muttering of greed for existence” means the craving known as greed for existence. “I meditate free from taints” means: being without craving, I meditate with the two kinds of meditation. By “Friend of the heedless,” he addresses Māra. For indeed, whoever in the world is heedless, Māra is their friend.

Sace maggaṃ anubuddhanti yadi tayā maggo anubuddho. Apehīti apayāhi. Amaccudheyyanti [P 1.0186] maccuno anokāsabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ. Pāragāminoti yepi pāraṃ gatā, tepi pāragāmino. Yepi pāraṃ gacchissanti, yepi pāraṃ gantukāmā, tepi pāragāmino.

“If you have understood the path” means: if the path has been understood by you. “Go away!” means: depart. “Beyond the domain of death” means Nibbāna, which is not a domain for Death. “Those who go to the far shore” means: those who have gone to the far shore are ‘those who go to the far shore’; those who will go to the far shore, and those who wish to go to the far shore, they too are ‘those who go to the far shore’.

Visūkāyikānīti [M 1.0171] māravisūkāni. Visevitānīti viruddhasevitāni, “appamāyu manussānaṃ, accayanti ahorattā”ti vutte. “Dīghamāyu manussānaṃ, nāccayanti ahorattā”tiādīni paṭilomakāraṇāni. Vipphanditānīti, tamhi tamhi kāle hatthirājavaṇṇasappavaṇṇādidassanāni. Nibbejanīyāti ukkaṇṭhanīyā.

‘Spasmodic displays’ means Māra's darts. ‘Wrongly practiced’ means practiced in a contrary way; for when it is said, ‘Short is the life of humans; days and nights pass by,’ there are contrary reasons, such as, ‘Long is the life of humans; days and nights do not pass by.’ ‘Struggles’ means the showing of appearances at various times, such as the form of a king of elephants or the form of a snake. ‘Causing revulsion’ means wearisome.

Anupariyagātiādīsu kiñcāpi atītavacanaṃ kataṃ, attho pana vikappavasena veditabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā medavaṇṇaṃ pāsāṇaṃ vāyaso disvā – “api nāmettha muduṃ vindeyyāma, api assādo siyā”ti anuparigaccheyya, atha so tattha assādaṃ alabhitvāva vāyaso etto apakkameyya, tato pāsāṇā apagaccheyya, evaṃ mayampi so kāko viya selaṃ gotamaṃ āsajja assādaṃ vā santhavaṃ vā alabhantā gotamā nibbinditvā apagacchāma. Catutthaṃ.

In “he went around” and so on, although a past tense form is used, the meaning should be understood by way of supposition. This is what is said: Just as a crow, seeing a rock the color of fat, might circle it thinking, “Perhaps we might find something soft here, perhaps there might be a taste.” Then that crow, not getting any taste there, would retreat from that place; it would go away from that rock. In the same way, we too, like that crow, having approached Gotama who is like a rock, and not getting any taste or intimacy, becoming disenchanted with Gotama, depart. The fourth.

5. Māradhītusuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse on Māra's Daughters

161. Pañcame abhāsitvāti ettha a-kāro nipātamattaṃ, bhāsitvāti attho. Abhāsayitvātipi [V 1.0165] pāṭho. Upasaṅkamiṃsūti “gopālakadārakaṃ viya daṇḍakena bhūmiṃ lekhaṃ datvā ativiya dummano hutvā nisinno. ‘Kinnu kho kāraṇa’nti? Pucchitvā, jānissāmā”ti upasaṅkamiṃsu.

161. In the fifth, regarding ‘abhāsitvā,’ here the letter ‘a-’ is merely a particle, and the meaning is ‘having spoken.’ There is also the reading ‘abhāsayitvā,’ meaning ‘not having spoken.’ ‘They approached’ means: “Like a young cowherd drawing a line on the ground with a stick, he sat, having become extremely dejected. They approached with the intention, ‘What could be the reason? Having inquired, we will know.’”

Socasīti cintesi. Āraññamiva kuñjaranti yathā araññato pesitagaṇikārahatthiniyo āraññakaṃ kuñjaraṃ itthikuttadassanena palobhetvā bandhitvā ānayanti, evaṃ ānayissāma. Māradheyyanti tebhūmakavaṭṭaṃ.

‘You grieve’ means ‘he was grieving.’ Regarding ‘like a forest elephant’: Just as trained female elephants, sent from the forest, entice a wild bull elephant by displaying feminine wiles, and having bound him, bring him back, in the same way, “We will bring him.” ‘Māra's domain’ means the round of existence in the three realms.

Upasaṅkamiṃsūti – “tumhe thokaṃ adhivāsetha, mayaṃ taṃ [P 1.0187] ānessāmā”ti pitaraṃ samassāsetvā upasaṅkamiṃsu. Uccāvacāti nānāvidhā. Ekasataṃ ekasatanti ekekaṃ sataṃ sataṃ katvā. Kumārivaṇṇasatanti iminā nayena kumāriattabhāvānaṃ sataṃ.

‘They approached’ means: Having consoled their father, saying, “May you be patient for a little while; we will bring him,” they approached. ‘High and low’ means ‘of various kinds.’ ‘One hundred, one hundred’ means ‘making each one a hundred, a hundred.’ ‘A hundred maidenly forms’ means, by this method, a hundred maidenly states of being.

Atthassa [M 1.0172] pattiṃ hadayassa santinti, dvīhipi padehi arahattameva kathesi. Senanti kilesasenaṃ. Sā hi piyarūpasātarūpā nāma. Ekāhaṃ jhāyanti eko ahaṃ jhāyanto. Sukhamanubodhinti arahattasukhaṃ anubujjhiṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ senaṃ jinitvā ahaṃ eko jhāyanto “atthassa pattiṃ hadayassa santi”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ arahattasukhaṃ anubujjhiṃ. Tasmā janena mittasanthavaṃ na karomi, teneva ca me kāraṇena kenaci saddhiṃ sakkhī na sampajjatīti.

With the two phrases “the attainment of the goal, the peace of heart,” he spoke only of Arahantship. ‘Army’ means the army of defilements. For it is indeed called “of pleasing form and of delightful form.” ‘I, alone, meditating’ is the meaning of ‘ekāhaṃ jhāyanti.’ ‘I awakened to bliss’ means ‘I awakened to the bliss of Arahantship.’ This is what is said: Having conquered the army of pleasing and delightful form, I, alone and meditating, awakened to the bliss of Arahantship, which has reached the state designated as “the attainment of the goal, the peace of heart.” Therefore, I do not form friendly association with people, and for that very reason, friendship with anyone is not accomplished for me.

Kathaṃvihārībahuloti katamena vihārena bahulaṃ viharanto. Aladdhāti alabhitvā. Yoti nipātamattaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – katamena jhānena bahulaṃ jhāyantaṃ taṃ puggalaṃ kāmasaññā alabhitvāva paribāhirā hontīti.

“Kathaṃvihārībahulo” means “abiding frequently in which abiding?” “Aladdhā” means “not having obtained.” “Yo” is merely a particle. This is what is said: By which jhāna does that person frequently enter jhāna, such that perceptions of sensuality, not having obtained him, become external?

Passaddhakāyoti catutthajjhānena assāsapassāsakāyassa passaddhattā passaddhakāyo. Suvimuttacittoti arahattaphalavimuttiyā suṭṭhu vimuttacitto. Asaṅkharānoti tayo kammābhisaṅkhāre anabhisaṅkharonto. Anokoti anālayo. Aññāya dhammanti catusaccadhammaṃ jānitvā. Avitakkajhāyīti avitakkena catutthajjhānena jhāyanto. Na kuppatītiādīsu dosena na kuppati, rāgena na sarati, mohena na thīno. Imesu tīsu mūlakilesesu gahitesu diyaḍḍhakilesasahassaṃ [V 1.0166] gahitameva hoti. Paṭhamapadena vā byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ gahitaṃ, dutiyena kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, tatiyena thinaṃ ādiṃ katvā sesanīvaraṇāni. Iti iminā nīvaraṇappahānena khīṇāsavaṃ dasseti.

“Passaddhakāyo” means the body is calmed because the body of in-and-out breathing is calmed by the fourth jhāna. “Suvimuttacitto” means the mind is well-liberated, thoroughly liberated by the liberation that is the fruit of Arahantship. “Asaṅkharāno” means not forming the three kamma-formations. “Anoko” means without abode, that is, without attachment. “Aññāya dhammaṃ” means having known the Dhamma of the Four Truths. “Avitakkajhāyī” means meditating with the fourth jhāna, which is without initial thought. Regarding “Na kuppati,” and so on: he is not angered by aversion, does not recollect with lust, and is not torpid due to delusion. When these three root defilements are taken, the one thousand five hundred defilements are indeed taken. Alternatively, by the first phrase, the hindrance of ill will is taken; by the second, the hindrance of sensual desire; by the third, the hindrance of sloth and torpor and the remaining hindrances. Thus, by this abandonment of the hindrances, he shows the state of one whose taints are destroyed.

Pañcoghatiṇṇoti pañcadvārikaṃ kilesoghaṃ tiṇṇo. Chaṭṭhanti manodvārikampi chaṭṭhaṃ kilesoghaṃ atari. Pañcoghaggahaṇena vā pañcorambhāgiyāni saṃyojanāni[P 1.0188], chaṭṭhaggahaṇena pañcuddhambhāgiyāni veditabbāni. Gaṇasaṅghacārīti gaṇe ca saṅghe ca caratīti satthā gaṇasaṅghacārī nāma. Addhā carissantīti aññepi saddhā bahujanā ekaṃsena carissanti. Ayanti ayaṃ satthā. Anokoti anālayo.

“Pañcoghatiṇṇo” means having crossed the flood of defilements at the five sense doors. “The sixth” means he also crossed the sixth flood of defilements at the mind door. Alternatively, by the mention of the five floods, the five lower fetters are to be understood; by the mention of the sixth, the five higher fetters. “Gaṇasaṅghacārī” means the Teacher is called “one who moves among groups and assemblies” because he moves among groups and assemblies. “Surely they will practice” means that many other faithful people will also practice with certainty. “Ayaṃ” means this Teacher. “Anoko” means without attachment.

Acchejja [M 1.0173] nessatīti acchinditvā nayissati, maccurājassa hatthato acchinditvā nibbānapāraṃ nayissatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Nayamānānanti nayamānesu.

“Acchejja nessati” means “he will lead by snatching away”; it is said that he will snatch them away from the hand of the King of Death and lead them to the far shore of Nibbāna. “Nayamānānaṃ” means “among those being led.”

Selaṃva sirasūhacca, pātāle gādhamesathāti mahantaṃ kūṭāgārappamāṇaṃ silaṃ sīse ṭhapetvā pātāle patiṭṭhagavesanaṃ viya. Khāṇuṃva urasāsajjāti urasi khāṇuṃ paharitvā viya. Apethāti apagacchatha. Imasmiṃ ṭhāne saṅgītikārā “idamavocā”ti desanaṃ niṭṭhapetvā daddallamānāti gāthaṃ āhaṃsu. Tattha daddallamānāti ativiya jalamānā sobhamānā. Āgañchunti āgatā. Panudīti nīhari. Tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃva mālutoti yathā phalato bhaṭṭhaṃ simbalitūlaṃ vā poṭakitūlaṃ vā vāto panudati nīharati, evaṃ panudīti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Like a stone placed on the head, seeking a foothold in the abyss” means like placing a large rock the size of a gabled mansion on one's head and searching for a firm footing in the abyss. “Like a stump struck against the chest” means like striking a tree stump against the chest. “Depart!” means “go away!” At this point, the compilers of the council, having concluded the discourse with “thus he spoke,” uttered the verse beginning with “Daddallamānā.” Therein, “daddallamānā” means exceedingly blazing and shining. “Āgañchuṃ” means “they came.” “Panudi” means “he drove away.” “Like cotton burst from its pod by the wind” means just as the wind blows away and removes silk-cotton or grass-cotton that has burst from its fruit, so he drove them away. The fifth.

Tatiyo vaggo.

The Third Chapter.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Mārasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the explanation of the Māra Saṃyutta is concluded.

5. Bhikkhunīsaṃyuttaṃ

5. 5. The Bhikkhunī Saṃyutta, 1. The Bhikkhunī Chapter

1. Āḷavikāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. 1. The Commentary on the Āḷavikā Sutta

162. Bhikkhunīsaṃyuttassa [V 1.0167][P 1.0189][M 1.0174] paṭhame āḷavikāti āḷaviyaṃ jātā āḷavinagaratoyeva ca nikkhamma pabbajitā. Andhavananti kassapasammāsambuddhassa cetiye navakammatthāya dhanaṃ samādapetvā āgacchantassa yasodharassa nāma dhammabhāṇakassa ariyapuggalassa akkhīni uppāṭetvā tattheva akkhibhedappattehi pañcahi corasatehi nivutthattā tato paṭṭhāya “andhavana”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ vanaṃ. Taṃ kira sāvatthito dakkhiṇapasse gāvutamatte hoti rājārakkhāya guttaṃ. Tattha pavivekakāmā bhikkhū ca bhikkhuniyo ca gacchanti. Tasmā ayampi kāyavivekatthinī yena taṃ vanaṃ, tenupasaṅkami. Nissaraṇanti nibbānaṃ. Paññāyāti paccavekkhaṇañāṇena. Na tvaṃ jānāsi taṃ padanti tvaṃ etaṃ nibbānapadaṃ vā nibbānagāmimaggapadaṃ vā na jānāsi. Sattisūlūpamāti vinivijjhanatthena sattisūlasadisā. Khandhāsaṃ adhikuṭṭanāti khandhā tesaṃ adhikuṭṭanabhaṇḍikā. Paṭhamaṃ.

162. In the first sutta of the Bhikkhunīsaṃyutta: Āḷavikā means she who was born in Āḷavī and, having gone forth from that very city of Āḷavī, was ordained. Andhavana (Blind Forest): The forest came to be known as 'Andhavana' from that time onwards because it was inhabited by five hundred thieves, who had become blind in that very place after having gouged out the eyes of the noble person, the Dhamma-reciter named Yasodhara, who was returning after having collected funds for new work at the cetiya of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa. It is said that this forest is located about a gāvuta to the south of Sāvatthī and is protected by the king's guard. Monks and nuns desiring seclusion go there. Therefore, this bhikkhunī too, desiring bodily seclusion, approached that forest. Nissaraṇaṃ means Nibbāna. Paññāya means by the knowledge of reviewing. Na tvaṃ jānāsi taṃ padaṃ means: you do not know this state of Nibbāna or the path-state leading to Nibbāna. Sattisūlūpamā means they are like a spear or stake because of their quality of piercing through. Khandhāsaṃ adhikuṭṭanā means for those beings, the aggregates are like a chopping block. The first.

2. Somāsuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Somā Sutta

163. Dutiye ṭhānanti arahattaṃ. Durabhisambhavanti duppasahaṃ. Dvaṅgulapaññāyāti parittapaññāya. Yasmā vā dvīhi aṅgulehi kappāsavaṭṭiṃ gahetvā suttaṃ kantanti, tasmā [P 1.0190] itthī “dvaṅgulapaññā”ti vuccati. Ñāṇamhi vattamānamhīti phalasamāpattiñāṇe pavattamāne. Dhammaṃ vipassatoti catusaccadhammaṃ vipassantassa, pubbabhāge vā vipassanāya ārammaṇabhūtaṃ khandhapañcakameva. Kiñci vā pana aññasmīti aññaṃ vā kiñci “ahaṃ asmī”ti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhivasena yassa siyā. Dutiyaṃ.

163. In the second sutta, ṭhāna means arahantship. Durabhisambhava means difficult to attain. Dvaṅgulapaññāya means by means of limited wisdom. Alternatively, because women spin thread by holding a cotton wick with two fingers, a woman is therefore called 'dvaṅgulapaññā.' Ñāṇamhi vattamānamhi means when the knowledge of fruition attainment is occurring. Dhammaṃ vipassato means for one contemplating the Dhamma of the four truths, or, in the preliminary stage, the five aggregates themselves which are the object of insight. Kiñci vā pana aññasmī means or if for anyone there might be some other thing regarded as 'I am' by way of craving, conceit, or wrong view. The second.

3. Kisāgotamīsuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Kisāgotamī Sutta

164. Tatiye [V 1.0168] kisāgotamīti appamaṃsalohitatāya kisā, gotamīti panassā nāmaṃ. Pubbe kira sāvatthiyaṃ ekasmiṃ kule asītikoṭidhanaṃ sabbaṃ aṅgārāva jātaṃ. Kuṭumbiko aṅgārajātāni anīharitvā [M 1.0175] – “avassaṃ koci puññavā bhavissati, tassa puññena puna pākatikaṃ bhavissatī”ti suvaṇṇahiraññassa cāṭiyo pūretvā āpaṇe ṭhapetvā samīpe nisīdi. Athekā duggatakulassa dhītā – “aḍḍhamāsakaṃ gahetvā dārusākaṃ āharissāmī”ti vīthiṃ gatā taṃ disvā kuṭumbikaṃ āha – “āpaṇe tāva dhanaṃ ettakaṃ, gehe kittakaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Kiṃ disvā amma evaṃ kathesīti? Imaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇanti. So “puññavatī esā bhavissatī”ti tassā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitvā āpaṇe bhaṇḍaṃ paṭisāmetvā tassā mātāpitaro upasaṅkamitvā evamāha – “amhākaṃ gehe vayappatto dārako atthi, tassetaṃ dārikaṃ dethā”ti. Kiṃ sāmi duggatehi saddhiṃ keḷiṃ karosīti? Mittasanthavo nāma duggatehipi saddhiṃ hoti, detha naṃ, kuṭumbasāminī bhavissatīti naṃ gahetvā gharaṃ ānesi. Sā saṃvāsamanvāya puttaṃ vijātā. Putto padasā āhiṇḍanakāle kālamakāsi. Sā duggatakule uppajjitvā mahākulaṃ gantvāpi “puttavināsaṃ pattāmhī”ti uppannabalavasokā puttassa sarīrakiccaṃ vāretvā taṃ matakaḷevaraṃ ādāya nagare vippalapantī carati.

164. In the third sutta, regarding Kisāgotamī: she was thin (kisā) due to her lack of flesh and blood, and Gotamī was her name. It is said that formerly in Sāvatthī, in one family, eighty crores of wealth all turned to charcoal. The householder, without removing the things that had turned to charcoal, thought: 'Surely, there must be someone meritorious, and through their merit, it will be restored to its original state.' He filled pots with gold and silver, placed them in his shop, and sat nearby. Then a daughter of a poor family, having gone to the street intending to fetch firewood and greens for half a māsaka, saw it and said to the householder: 'If there is so much wealth in the shop, how much must there be at home?' 'Having seen what, my dear, do you speak thus?' 'This gold and silver.' Thinking, 'She must be meritorious,' he inquired about her residence, packed up his goods from the shop, and approached her parents, saying thus: 'We have a son of marriageable age in our house; give this girl to him.' 'Sir, why do you jest with the poor?' 'Friendship, you see, can exist even with the poor. Give her to us; she will be the mistress of the household.' Taking her, he brought her home. Through their life together, she gave birth to a son. When the son was at the age of toddling about on foot, he died. She, having been born into a poor family and then gone to a great family, thought, 'I have met with the destruction of my son!' and with powerful grief having arisen, she prevented the funeral rites for her son, took up the dead body, and wandered through the city, wailing.

Ekadivasaṃ mahatiyā buddhavīthiyā dasabalassa [P 1.0191] santikaṃ gantvā – “puttassa me arogabhāvatthāya bhesajjaṃ detha bhagavā”ti āha. Gaccha sāvatthiṃ āhiṇḍitvā yasmiṃ gehe matapubbo natthi, tato siddhatthakaṃ āhara, puttassa te bhesajjaṃ bhavissatīti. Sā nagaraṃ pavisitvā dhuragehato paṭṭhāya bhagavatā vuttanayena gantvā siddhatthakaṃ yācantī ghare ghare, “kuto tvaṃ evarūpaṃ gharaṃ passissasī”ti vuttā katipayāni gehāni āhiṇḍitvā – “sabbesampi kirāyaṃ dhammatā, na mayhaṃ puttassevā”ti sālāyaṃ chavaṃ chaḍḍetvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Satthā “imaṃ pabbājetū”ti bhikkhuniupassayaṃ pesesi. Sā khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Imaṃ theriṃ sandhāya “atha kho kisāgotamī”ti vuttaṃ.

One day, going to the presence of the Ten-Powered One by way of the great road to the Buddha, she said: 'Blessed One, give me medicine for my son's health.' He replied: 'Go, wander through Sāvatthī, and from any house where no one has previously died, bring back a mustard seed; that will be the medicine for your son.' She entered the city and, starting from the very first house, went as instructed by the Blessed One, asking for a mustard seed. In house after house, she was told, 'Where will you find such a house?' After wandering through several houses, she reflected: 'Indeed, this is the nature of things for all beings; it is not for my son alone.' She abandoned the corpse in a public hall and asked for the going forth. The Teacher, saying, 'Let her go forth,' sent her to the nuns' residence. She attained arahantship at the very tip of the razor. It is with reference to this elder nun that 'Then Kisāgotamī...' was said.

Ekamāsīti ekā āsi. Rudammukhīti rudamānamukhī viya. Accantaṃ mataputtāmhīti ettha [V 1.0169] antaṃ atītaṃ accantaṃ, bhāvanapuṃsakametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā puttamaraṇaṃ antaṃ atītaṃ hoti, evaṃ mataputtā ahaṃ, idāni mama puna puttamaraṇaṃ nāma natthi. Purisā etadantikāti purisāpi me etadantikāva[M 1.0176]. Yo me puttamaraṇassa anto, purisānampi me esevanto, abhabbā ahaṃ idāni purisaṃ gavesitunti. Sabbattha vihatā nandīti sabbesu khandhāyatanadhātubhavayonigatiṭhitinivāsesu mama taṇhānandī vihatā. Tamokkhandhoti avijjākkhandho. Padālitoti ñāṇena bhinno. Tatiyaṃ.

Ekamāsi means: she was one alone. Rudammukhī means: as if with a weeping face. Regarding 'Accantaṃ mataputtāmhi' (I am one whose son is dead beyond measure), here the analysis is: 'antaṃ atītaṃ' (gone beyond the end) is 'accantaṃ'; this is a neuter noun of state. This is what is meant: just as the death of a son, the end, is surpassed, so I am one whose son is dead. Now, for me, there is no more a 'death of a son.' 'Purisā etadantikā' (men are at this end) means: for me, men too are at this same end. The end that was my son's death is for me the end of men also. Now I am incapable of seeking a man. 'Sabbattha vihatā nandī' (delight is destroyed everywhere) means: in all aggregates, sense bases, elements, states of existence, births, destinations, stations, and abodes, my delight in craving is destroyed. 'Tamokkhandho' (mass of darkness) means: the mass of ignorance. 'Padālito' (shattered) means: shattered by knowledge. The third.

4. Vijayāsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vijayā Sutta

165. Catutthe pañcaṅgikenāti ātataṃ vitataṃ ātatavitataṃ ghanaṃ susiranti evaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgatena. Niyyātayāmi tuyhevāti sabbe tuyhaṃyeva demi. Nāhaṃ tenatthikāti nāhaṃ tena atthikā. Pūtikāyenāti suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kāyo niccaṃ uggharitapaggharitaṭṭhena pūtikāyova, tasmā evamāha. Bhindanenāti bhijjanasabhāvena. Pabhaṅgunāti cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ āpajjanadhammena. Aṭṭīyāmīti aṭṭā pīḷitā homi. Harāyāmīti lajjāmi. Santā samāpattīti [P 1.0192] aṭṭhavidhā lokiyasamāpatti ārammaṇasantatāya aṅgasantatāya ca santāti vuttā. Sabbatthāti sabbesu rūpārūpabhavesu, tesaṃ dvinnaṃ bhavānaṃ gahitattā gahite kāmabhave aṭṭhasu ca samāpattīsūti etesu sabbesu ṭhānesu mayhaṃ avijjātamo vihatoti vadati. Catutthaṃ.

165. In the fourth sutta, 'pañcaṅgikena' (by means of the five-factored) means: by that which is endowed with five constituents, thus: that which is covered (ātata), that which is covered all over (vitata), that which is covered and covered all over (ātatavitata), that which is solid (ghana), and that which is hollow (susira). 'Niyyātayāmi tuyheva' (I hand over to you) means: I give all to you alone. 'Nāhaṃ tenatthikā' (I am not in need of it) means: I am not in need of it. 'Pūtikāyena' (by means of a putrid body): even a body with a complexion like gold is indeed a putrid body, because of its nature of constantly oozing and dripping; therefore, he spoke thus. 'Bhindanena' (by its breaking) means: by its nature of breaking. 'Pabhaṅgunā' (by its fragility) means: by its nature of becoming powder and dust. 'Aṭṭīyāmi' (I am distressed) means: I am afflicted and oppressed. 'Harāyāmi' (I am ashamed) means: I am ashamed. 'Santā samāpatti' (peaceful attainments): the eight kinds of mundane attainments are called 'peaceful' because of the peacefulness of their object and the peacefulness of their factors. 'Sabbattha' (everywhere) means: in all form and formless existences; since those two existences are included, and when the sense-sphere existence is included, and in the eight attainments—thus, in all these places, my darkness of ignorance has been dispelled, so she says. The fourth.

5. Uppalavaṇṇāsuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Uppalavaṇṇā Sutta

166. Pañcame supupphitagganti aggato paṭṭhāya suṭṭhu pupphitaṃ sālarukkhaṃ. Na catthi te dutiyā vaṇṇadhātūti tava vaṇṇadhātusadisā dutiyā vaṇṇadhātu natthi, tayā sadisā aññā bhikkhunī natthīti vadati. Idhāgatā tādisikā bhaveyyunti yathā tvaṃ idhāgatā kiñci santhavaṃ vā sinehaṃ vā na labhasi, evamevaṃ tepi tayāva sadisā bhaveyyuṃ. Pakhumantarikāyanti dvinnaṃ akkhīnaṃ majjhe nāsavaṃsepi tiṭṭhantiṃ maṃ na passasi. Vasībhūtamhīti vasībhūtā asmi. Pañcamaṃ.

166. In the fifth sutta, 'supupphitaggaṃ' (with a beautifully blossomed top) means: a sāl tree beautifully blossomed starting from the top. 'Na catthi te dutiyā vaṇṇadhātu' (There is no second element of complexion for you) means: there is no second element of complexion similar to your element of complexion; there is no other nun similar to you, so he says. 'Idhāgatā tādisikā bhaveyyuṃ' (Those who have come here would be of such a kind) means: just as you, having come here, do not obtain any familiarity or affection, in the very same way they too would be similar only to you. 'Pakhumantarikāyaṃ' (between the eyelashes): you do not see me standing even on the bridge of the nose between your two eyes. 'Vasībhūtamhi' (I have mastery) means: I have attained mastery. The fifth.

6. Cālāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Cālā Sutta

167. Chaṭṭhe [V 1.0170] ko nu taṃ idamādapayīti ko nu mandabuddhi bālo taṃ evaṃ gāhāpesi? Pariklesanti aññampi nānappakāraṃ upaddavaṃ. Idāni yaṃ māro āha [M 1.0177] – “ko nu taṃ idamādapayī”ti, taṃ maddantī – “na maṃ andhabālo ādapesi, loke pana aggapuggalo satthā dhammaṃ desesī”ti dassetuṃ, buddhotiādimāha. Tattha sacce nivesayīti paramatthasacce nibbāne nivesesi. Nirodhaṃ appajānantāti nirodhasaccaṃ ajānantā. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

167. In the sixth sutta, 'ko nu taṃ idamādapayī' (who indeed incited you to this?) means: what dull-witted fool persuaded you thus? 'Pariklesaṃ' (affliction) means: also other various kinds of trouble. Now, to show that she was refuting what Māra said—'Who indeed incited you to this?'—by saying, 'No blind fool incited me, but in the world the Supreme Person, the Teacher, taught the Dhamma,' she spoke the verse beginning with 'Buddho'. Therein, 'sacce nivesayī' (he established in the truth) means: he established in the ultimate truth, Nibbāna. 'Nirodhaṃ appajānantā' (not understanding cessation) means: not understanding the truth of cessation. The sixth.

7. Upacālāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Upacālā Sutta

168. Sattame [P 1.0193] enti māravasaṃ punāti punappunaṃ maraṇamārakilesamāradevaputtamārānaṃ vasaṃ āgacchanti. Padhūpitoti santāpito. Agati yattha mārassāti yattha tuyhaṃ mārassa agati. Tatthāti tasmiṃ nibbāne. Sattamaṃ.

168. In the seventh sutta, 'they repeatedly fall into the power of Māra' (enti māravasaṃ puna) means 'they repeatedly come into the power of the Māra of death, the Māra of defilements, and the Māra of the divine son.' 'Tormented' (padhūpita) means 'afflicted.' 'Where Māra has no access' (agati yattha mārassā) means 'where you, Māra, have no access.' 'There' (tattha) means 'in that Nibbāna.' The seventh.

8. Sīsupacālāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Exposition of the Sīsupacālā Sutta

169. Aṭṭhame samaṇī viya dissasīti samaṇisadisā dissasi. Kimiva carasi momūhāti kiṃ kāraṇā momūhā viya carasi? Ito bahiddhāti imamhā sāsanā bahi. Pāsaṃ ḍentīti pāsaṇḍā, sattānaṃ cittesu diṭṭhipāsaṃ khipantīti attho. Sāsanaṃ pana pāse moceti, tasmā pāsaṇḍoti na vuccati, ito bahiddhāyeva pāsaṇḍā honti. Pasīdantīti saṃsīdanti lagganti.

169. In the eighth sutta, 'You appear like a female ascetic' (samaṇī viya dissasi) means 'you appear similar to a female ascetic.' 'Why do you wander about so utterly deluded?' (kimiva carasi momūhā) means 'for what reason do you wander about as if utterly deluded?' 'Outside of this' (ito bahiddhā) means 'outside of this dispensation.' 'Casting the noose' (pāsaṃ ḍenti) refers to sectarians (pāsaṇḍā); the meaning is that they cast the noose of views into the minds of beings. But the dispensation releases from the noose; therefore, it is not called sectarian. Only those outside of this are sectarians. 'They sink down' (pasīdanti) means 'they sink and cling.'

Idāni “kaṃ nu uddissa muṇḍāsī”ti pañhaṃ kathentī atthi sakyakule jātotiādimāha. Tattha sabbābhibhūti sabbāni khandhāyatanadhātubhavayonigatiādīni abhibhavitvā ṭhito. Maraṇamārādayo nudi nīharīti māranudo. Sabbatthamaparājitoti sabbesu rāgādīsu vā mārayuddhe vā ajito. Sabbattha muttoti sabbesu khandhādīsu mutto. Asitoti taṇhādiṭṭhinissayena [V 1.0171] anissito. Sabbakammakkhayaṃ pattoti sabbakammakkhayasaṅkhātaṃ arahattaṃ patto. Upadhisaṅkhayeti upadhisaṅkhayasaṅkhāte nibbāne ārammaṇato vimutto. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Now, explaining the question, 'For whom have you shaved your head?' (kaṃ nu uddissa muṇḍāsi), she begins with 'born in the Sakya clan' and so on. Therein, 'all-conquering' (sabbābhibhū) means he stands having conquered all—all aggregates, sense bases, elements, existences, origins, destinies, and so on. 'Dispeller of Māra' (māranudo) is so called because he drove away and removed death-Māra and so on (maraṇamārādayo nudi nīhari). 'Unconquered in everything' (sabbatthamaparājito) means 'unconquered in all lust and so on, or in the battle with Māra.' 'Everywhere free' (sabbattha mutto) means 'free from all aggregates and so on.' 'Unattached' (asito) means 'not dependent on craving and views.' 'Having reached the destruction of all kamma' (sabbakammakkhayaṃ patto) means 'having attained arahantship, which is called the destruction of all kamma.' 'With the cessation of attachments' (upadhisaṅkhaye) means 'liberated by way of object in Nibbāna, which is called the cessation of attachments.' The eighth.

9. Selāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Exposition of the Selā Sutta

170. Navame kenidaṃ pakatanti kena idaṃ kataṃ. Bimbanti attabhāvaṃ sandhāya vadati. Aghanti dukkhapatiṭṭhānattā attabhāvameva vadati. Hetubhaṅgāti hetunirodhena paccayavekallena. Navamaṃ.

170. In the ninth sutta: 'By whom was this made?' (kenidaṃ pakataṃ) means 'by whom was this made?' 'Figure' (bimbaṃ) is said with reference to the individual existence. 'Misery' (aghaṃ) refers to the individual existence itself, because it is the foundation of suffering. 'With the breaking of the cause' (hetubhaṅgā) means 'through the cessation of the cause, through the deficiency of the condition.' The ninth.

10. Vajirāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Exposition of the Vajirā Sutta

171. Dasame [M 1.0178][P 1.0194] nayidha sattupalabbhatīti imasmiṃ suddhasaṅkhārapuñje paramatthato satto nāma na upalabbhati. Khandhesu santesūti pañcasu khandhesu vijjamānesu tena tenākārena vavatthitesu. Sammutīti sattoti samaññāmattameva hoti. Dukkhanti pañcakkhandhadukkhaṃ. Nāññatra dukkhāti ṭhapetvā dukkhaṃ añño neva sambhoti na nirujjhatīti. Dasamaṃ.

171. In the tenth sutta: 'No being is found here' (nayidha sattupalabbhati) means that in this heap of mere formations, a so-called being is not found in an ultimate sense. 'When the aggregates are present' (khandhesu santesu) means when the five aggregates are present, established in this or that manner. 'Convention' (sammuti) means that 'a being' is merely a designation. 'Suffering' (dukkhaṃ) means the suffering that is the five aggregates. 'Apart from suffering' (nāññatra dukkhā) means that apart from suffering, nothing else arises or ceases. The tenth.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Bhikkhunīsaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the Exposition of the Bhikkhunīsaṃyutta is concluded.

6. Brahmasaṃyuttaṃ

6. The Brahmasaṃyutta

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Brahmāyācanasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition of the Brahmā's Entreaty Sutta

172. Brahmasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0172][P 1.0195][M 1.0179] paṭhame parivitakko udapādīti sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo ayaṃ cetaso vitakko udapādi. Kadā udapādīti? Buddhabhūtassa aṭṭhame sattāhe rājāyatanamūle sakkena devānamindena ābhataṃ dantakaṭṭhañca osadhaharītakañca khāditvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā catūhi lokapālehi upanīte paccagghe selamayapatte tapussabhallikānaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñjitvā puna paccāgantvā ajapālanigrodhe nisinnamattassa.

172. In the first sutta of the Brahmasaṃyutta: 'A reflection arose' (parivitakko udapādi) means that this thought, well-practiced by all Buddhas, arose. When did it arise? In the eighth week after he had become a Buddha, at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, after chewing the tooth-stick and medicinal myrobalan brought by Sakka, king of the devas, and washing his mouth; after consuming the almsfood of Tapussa and Bhallika in a valuable stone bowl offered by the four world-guardians; and after returning and just as he was sitting down at the Ajapāla banyan tree.

Adhigatoti paṭividdho. Dhammoti catusaccadhammo. Gambhīroti uttānapaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ. Duddasoti gambhīrattāva duddaso dukkhena daṭṭhabbo, na sakkā sukhena daṭṭhuṃ. Duddasattāva duranubodho dukkhena avabujjhitabbo, na sakkā sukhena avabujjhituṃ. Santoti nibbuto. Paṇītoti atappako. Idaṃ dvayaṃ lokuttarameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Atakkāvacaroti takkena avacaritabbo ogāhitabbo na hoti, ñāṇeneva avacaritabbo. Nipuṇoti saṇho. Paṇḍitavedanīyoti sammāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipannehi paṇḍitehi veditabbo. Ālayarāmāti sattā pañcasu kāmaguṇesu allīyanti, tasmā te ālayāti vuccanti. Aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni vā allīyanti, tasmāpi ālayāti vuccanti. Tehi ālayehi ramantīti ālayarāmā. Ālayesu ratāti ālayaratā. Ālayesu [P 1.0196] suṭṭhu muditāti ālayasammuditā. Yatheva hi susajjitaṃ pupphaphalabharitarukkhādisampannaṃ uyyānaṃ paviṭṭho rājā tāya tāya sampattiyā ramati, sammudito āmoditapamodito hoti, na ukkaṇṭhati, sāyampi nikkhamituṃ na icchati, evamimehipi kāmālayataṇhālayehi [V 1.0173] sattā ramanti, saṃsāravaṭṭe sammuditā anukkaṇṭhitā vasanti. Tena tesaṃ bhagavā duvidhaṃ ālayaṃ uyyānabhūmiṃ viya dassento “ālayarāmā”tiādimāha.

‘Attained’ (adhigato) means penetrated. ‘Dhamma’ (dhammo) refers to the Dhamma of the Four Truths. ‘Profound’ (gambhīro) is a word that rejects superficiality. ‘Hard to see’ (duddaso) means that because it is profound, it is hard to see, to be seen with difficulty; it cannot be seen easily. Because it is hard to see, it is ‘hard to understand’ (duranubodho), to be understood with difficulty; it cannot be understood easily. ‘Peaceful’ (santo) means extinguished. ‘Sublime’ (paṇīto) means that which brings contentment. These two terms are stated solely with reference to the supramundane. ‘Beyond the scope of logic’ (atakkāvacaro) means that it is not to be traversed or fathomed by reasoning; it is to be traversed only by wisdom. ‘Subtle’ (nipuṇo) means refined. ‘To be understood by the wise’ (paṇḍitavedanīyo) means it is to be known by the wise who have undertaken the right practice. ‘Delighting in attachment’ (ālayarāmā): beings cling to the five strands of sensual pleasure; therefore these are called ‘attachments’ (ālayā). Or, beings cling to the one hundred and eight applications of craving; therefore, these are also called ‘attachments’. They delight in these attachments, thus they are ‘delighting in attachment’ (ālayarāmā). They are fond of attachments, thus they are ‘fond of attachment’ (ālayaratā). They are greatly pleased with attachments, thus they are ‘greatly pleased with attachment’ (ālayasammuditā). For just as a king, entering a well-adorned park abundant with flowers, fruits, trees, and so on, delights in its various splendors, is greatly pleased, joyful and delighted, is not discontented, and does not wish to leave even in the evening; so too do beings delight in these attachments of sensual pleasure and craving, dwelling greatly pleased and contented in the round of rebirths. Therefore, the Blessed One, showing them the twofold attachment as if it were park grounds, spoke the words beginning with ‘delighting in attachment’.

Tattha yadidanti nipāto, tassa ṭhānaṃ sandhāya “yaṃ ida”nti, paṭiccasamuppādaṃ sandhāya “yo aya”nti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādoti imesaṃ [M 1.0180] paccayā idappaccayā, idappaccayā eva idappaccayatā, idappaccayatā ca sā paṭiccasamuppādo cāti idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo. Saṅkhārādipaccayānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sabbasaṅkhārasamathotiādi sabbaṃ nibbānameva. Yasmā hi taṃ āgamma sabbasaṅkhāravipphanditāni samanti, vūpasammanti, tasmā sabbasaṅkhārasamathoti vuccati. Yasmā ca taṃ āgamma sabbe upadhayo paṭinissaṭṭhā honti, sabbā taṇhā khīyanti, sabbe kilesarāgā virajjanti, sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ nirujjhati, tasmā sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodhoti vuccati. Yā panesā taṇhā bhavena bhavaṃ, phalena vā saddhiṃ kammaṃ vinati saṃsibbatīti katvā vānanti vuccati, tato nikkhantaṃ vānatoti nibbānaṃ. So mamassa kilamathoti yā ajānantānaṃ desanā nāma, so mama kilamatho assa, sā mama vihesā assāti attho. Kāyakilamatho ceva kāyavihesā ca assāti vuttaṃ hoti. Citte pana ubhayampetaṃ buddhānaṃ natthi. Apissūti anubrūhanatthe nipāto. So “na kevalaṃ ayaṃ parivitakko udapādi, imāpi gāthā paṭibhaṃsū”ti dīpeti. Anacchariyāti anuacchariyā. Paṭibhaṃsūti [P 1.0197] paṭibhānasaṅkhātassa ñāṇassa gocarā ahesuṃ, parivitakkayitabbataṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

Herein, ‘whatever this is’ (yadidaṃ) is a particle. With reference to its place, it means ‘that which is this’ (yaṃ idaṃ); with reference to dependent origination, it means ‘that which is this’ (yo ayaṃ)—thus the meaning should be understood. ‘Dependent origination through this-conditionality’ (idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo) is thus: the conditions of these are ‘these conditions’ (idappaccayā); ‘these conditions’ themselves are ‘this-conditionality’ (idappaccayatā); and that this-conditionality is also dependent origination—thus, ‘dependent origination through this-conditionality’. This is a designation for the conditions beginning with formations. ‘The calming of all formations’ (sabbasaṅkhārasamatho) and so on, all refer solely to Nibbāna. For it is by relying on it that all agitations of formations cease and are stilled; hence it is called ‘the calming of all formations’. And because by relying on it, all substrates of existence are relinquished, all craving is destroyed, all defilements of passion fade away, and all suffering ceases, it is therefore called ‘the relinquishment of all substrates, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation’. Furthermore, that craving which weaves existence to existence, or which binds action together with its result, is called ‘weaving’ (vāna); that which has departed from this ‘weaving’ is Nibbāna. ‘This would be a weariness for me’ (so mamassa kilamatho) means: the teaching for those who do not understand, ‘that would be a weariness for me; that would be an affliction for me’. It is said that it would be bodily weariness and bodily affliction. But for the Buddhas, neither of these exists in the mind. ‘Moreover’ (apissu) is a particle in the sense of amplification. It clarifies: ‘Not only did this reflection arise, but these verses also occurred to him’. `Anacchariyā` is to be divided as `anu-acchariyā`, meaning 'repeatedly wonderful'. ‘Occurred to him’ (paṭibhaṃsu) means they became the domain of the knowledge known as ‘inspired understanding’ (paṭibhāna); they attained a state fit to be reflected upon.

Kicchenāti dukkhena, na dukkhāya paṭipadāya. Buddhānaṃ hi cattāropi maggā sukhapaṭipadāva honti. Pāramīpūraṇakāle pana sarāgasadosasamohasseva sato āgatāgatānaṃ yācakānaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ sīsaṃ kantitvā galalohitaṃ nīharitvā suañjitāni akkhīni uppāṭetvā kulavaṃsappadīpaṃ puttaṃ manāpacāriniṃ bhariyanti evamādīni dentassa aññāni ca khantivādisadisesu attabhāvesu chejjabhejjādīni pāpuṇantassa āgamanīyapaṭipadaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Halanti ettha ha-kāro nipātamatto, alanti attho. Pakāsitunti desituṃ, evaṃ kicchena adhigatassa alaṃ desituṃ pariyattaṃ desituṃ. Ko attho desitenāti vuttaṃ hoti? Rāgadosaparetehīti rāgadosaphuṭṭhehi rāgadosānugatehi vā.

‘With difficulty’ (kicchena) means with suffering, not by a difficult practice. For the Buddhas, all four paths are indeed of easy practice. However, this was said with reference to the practice leading to Buddhahood during the time of fulfilling the perfections, when, while still being with lust, hatred, and delusion, the Bodhisatta would give his adorned and prepared head to beggars who came again and again, cutting it off and bringing forth blood from his neck; would pluck out his well-anointed eyes; would give his son, the lamp of the lineage, and his wife of pleasing conduct, and other such things; and who, in other existences similar to that of Khantivādi, would encounter cutting, breaking, and the like. Here, in the word ‘halaṃ’, the letter ‘ha’ is a mere particle; the meaning is ‘alaṃ’ (enough). ‘To declare’ (pakāsituṃ) means to teach. Thus, it is said: “It is not fitting to teach what has been attained with such difficulty. I am not able to teach it. What would be the use of teaching it?” ‘By those overcome by lust and hatred’ (rāgadosaparetehi) means by those afflicted by lust and hatred, or by those who follow after lust and hatred.

Paṭisotagāminti [V 1.0174] niccādīnaṃ paṭisotaṃ, “aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā asubha”nti evaṃ gataṃ catusaccadhammaṃ. Rāgarattāti kāmarāgena bhavarāgena diṭṭhirāgena ca rattā. Na dakkhantīti aniccaṃ dukkhamanattā asubhanti iminā sabhāvena na passissanti[M 1.0181], te apassante ko sakkhissati evaṃ gāhāpetuṃ. Tamokhandhena āvuṭāti avijjārāsinā ajjhotthaṭā.

‘Going against the stream’ (paṭisotagāmiṃ) means going against the stream of such things as permanence; it is the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which is understood as ‘impermanent, suffering, non-self, and unattractive.’ ‘Stained by lust’ (rāgarattā) means stained by sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. ‘They will not see’ (na dakkhanti) means they will not see it with its true nature as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and unattractive. When they do not see it, who will be able to make them grasp it in this way? ‘Covered by a mass of darkness’ (tamokhandhena āvuṭā) means they are overwhelmed by a heap of ignorance.

Appossukkatāyāti nirussukkabhāvena, adesetukāmatāyāti attho. Kasmā panassa evaṃ cittaṃ nami? Nanu esa mutto mocessāmi, tiṇṇo tāressāmi –

‘Due to lack of enthusiasm’ (appossukkatāya) means due to the state of being without enthusiasm; that is, the desire not to teach. But why did his mind incline thus? Did he not think: ‘Being freed, I shall free others; having crossed over, I shall help others cross over’—

“Kiṃ me aññātavesena, dhammaṃ sacchikatenidha;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, tārayissaṃ sadevaka”nti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.56) –

‘What is the use to me of realizing the Dhamma here in an unknown guise? Having attained omniscience, I shall help the world with its devas to cross over.’ (Buddhavaṃsa 2.56) –

Patthanaṃ katvā pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ pattoti? Saccametaṃ, tadevaṃ paccavekkhaṇānubhāvena panassa [P 1.0198] evaṃ cittaṃ nami. Tassa hi sabbaññutaṃ patvā sattānaṃ kilesagahanataṃ, dhammassa ca gambhīrataṃ paccavekkhantassa sattānaṃ kilesagahanatā ca dhammagambhīratā ca sabbākārena pākaṭā jātā. Athassa – “ime sattā kañjiyapuṇṇā lābu viya, takkabharitā cāṭi viya, vasātelapītapilotikā viya, añjanamakkhitahattho viya ca kilesabharitā atisaṃkiliṭṭhā rāgarattā dosaduṭṭhā mohamūḷhā, te kiṃ nāma paṭivijjhissantī”ti? Cintayato kilesagahanapaccavekkhaṇānubhāvenāpi evaṃ cittaṃ nami.

Having made the aspiration and fulfilled the perfections, did he not attain Omniscience? This is true. However, it was through the power of that very reflection that his mind inclined thus. For when he, having attained Omniscience, reflected upon the density of defilements in beings and the profundity of the Dhamma, the density of defilements in beings and the profundity of the Dhamma became apparent to him in every way. Then it occurred to him: “These beings are like a gourd full of rice-gruel, like a pot filled with buttermilk, like a worn-out cloth soaked in fat and oil, and like a hand smeared with lampblack; they are filled with defilements, exceedingly defiled, impassioned with lust, corrupted by hatred, and deluded by ignorance. What indeed will they penetrate?” As he was thus thinking, through the power of reflecting on the density of defilements, his mind also inclined in this way.

“Ayañca dhammo pathavīsandhārakaudakakkhandho viya gambhīro, pabbatena paṭicchādetvā ṭhapito sāsapo viya duddaso, satadhā bhinnassa vālassa koṭiyā koṭipaṭipādanaṃ viya duranubodho. Nanu mayā hi imaṃ dhammaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ vāyamantena adinnaṃ dānaṃ nāma natthi, arakkhitaṃ sīlaṃ nāma natthi, aparipūritā kāci pāramī nāma natthi, tassa me nirussāhaṃ viya mārabalaṃ vidhamantassāpi pathavī na kampittha, paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussarantassāpi na kampittha, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhentassāpi na kampittha, pacchimayāme pana paṭiccasamuppādaṃ paṭivijjhantasseva me dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha. Iti mādisenāpi tikkhañāṇena kicchenevāyaṃ dhammo paṭividdho. Taṃ lokiyamahājanā kathaṃ paṭivijjhissantī”ti? Dhammagambhīrapaccavekkhaṇānubhāvenāpi evaṃ cittaṃ namīti veditabbaṃ.

“And this Dhamma is as profound as the earth-supporting mass of water, as difficult to see as a mustard seed placed and covered by a mountain, and as difficult to comprehend as rejoining the tip of a hair that has been split a hundred times. Surely, as I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift I had not given, no virtue I had not guarded, no perfection I had not fulfilled. For me, even when scattering the army of Māra as if without exertion, the earth did not tremble. In the first watch of the night, even as I recollected past lives, it did not tremble. In the middle watch, even as I purified the divine eye, it did not tremble. But in the last watch, it was only when I penetrated Dependent Origination that the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled. Thus, this Dhamma was penetrated with difficulty even by one such as myself, possessed of keen wisdom. How then will the worldly populace penetrate it?” It should be understood that through the power of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, his mind also inclined in this way.

Apica [V 1.0175] brahmunā yācite desetukāmatāyapissa evaṃ cittaṃ nami. Jānāti hi bhagavā – “mama appossukkatāya citte namamāne maṃ mahābrahmā dhammadesanaṃ [M 1.0182] yācissati, ime ca sattā brahmagarukā. Te ‘satthā kira dhammaṃ na desetukāmo ahosi. Atha naṃ mahābrahmā yācitvā desāpesi. Santo vata bho dhammo, paṇīto vata bho dhammo’ti maññamānā sussūsissantī”ti. Idampissa kāraṇaṃ paṭicca appossukkatāya cittaṃ nami, no dhammadesanāyāti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, when entreated by Brahmā, his mind inclined thus toward disinclination, also out of a desire to teach. For the Blessed One knew: 'When my mind inclines toward disinclination, Mahābrahmā will entreat me to teach the Dhamma, and these beings revere Brahmā. They will think: “It seems the Teacher was unwilling to teach the Dhamma. Then Mahābrahmā, having entreated him, caused him to teach. Truly, sirs, the Dhamma is excellent! Truly, sirs, the Dhamma is sublime!”—and thinking thus, they will listen respectfully.' It should be understood that on account of this reason also his mind inclined toward disinclination, not toward teaching the Dhamma.

Sahampatissāti [P 1.0199] so kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane sahako nāma thero paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ kappāyukabrahmā hutvā nibbatto. Tatra naṃ “sahampatibrahmā”ti paṭisañjānanti. Taṃ sandhāyāha “brahmuno sahampatissā”ti. Nassati vata bhoti so kira imaṃ saddaṃ tathā nicchāresi, yathā dasasahassilokadhātubrahmāno sutvā sabbe sannipatiṃsu. Yatra hi nāmāti yasmiṃ nāma loke. Purato pāturahosīti tehi dasahi brahmasahassehi saddhiṃ pāturahosi. Apparajakkhajātikāti paññāmaye akkhimhi appaṃ parittaṃ rāgadosamoharajaṃ etesaṃ evaṃsabhāvāti apparajakkhajātikā. Assavanatāti assavanatāya. Bhavissantīti purimabuddhesu dasapuññakiriyavasena katādhikārā paripākagatā padumāni viya sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ, dhammadesanaṃyeva ākaṅkhamānā catuppadikagāthāvasāne ariyabhūmiṃ okkamanārahā na eko, na dve, anekasatasahassā dhammassa aññātāro bhavissantīti dasseti.

Sahampati: It is said that a senior monk named Sahaka, in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, having developed the first jhāna, was reborn as a Brahmā with a lifespan of an eon in the realm of the first jhāna. There, they recognized him as 'Brahmā Sahampati.' Referring to him, the text says, 'of Brahmā Sahampati.' Regarding 'Nassati vata bho': It is said that he uttered this sound in such a way that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world-system heard it and all gathered together. Yatra hi nāma: 'in whatever world,' means 'in whatever world.' Purato pāturahosi: 'appeared before,' means he appeared with those ten thousand Brahmās. Apparajakkhajātikā: 'with little dust in their eyes,' means that in their wisdom-eye there is little, a mere trace, of the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion; thus, they are of such a nature. Assavanatā: 'due to not hearing,' means due to not hearing. Bhavissanti: 'there will be,' shows that there will be beings who, in the time of previous Buddhas, established their foundation of merit through the ten bases of meritorious action. Having reached maturity, like lotuses awaiting the touch of the sun's rays, they long only for the teaching of the Dhamma. At the conclusion of a four-line verse, they are worthy of entering the noble stage. Not one, not two, but many hundreds of thousands of knowers of the Dhamma will there be.

Pāturahosīti pātubhavi. Samalehi cintitoti samalehi chahi satthārehi cintito. Te hi puretaraṃ uppajjitvā sakalajambudīpe kaṇṭake pattharamānā viya, visaṃ siñcamānā viya ca samalaṃ micchādiṭṭhidhammaṃ desayiṃsu. Apāpuretanti vivaraṃ etaṃ. Amatassa dvāranti amatassa nibbānassa dvārabhūtaṃ ariyamaggaṃ. Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhanti ime sattā rāgādimalānaṃ abhāvato vimalena sammāsambuddhena anubuddhaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ suṇantu tāva bhagavāti yācati.

Pāturahosi: 'he has appeared,' means he has become manifest. Samalehi cintito: 'conceived by the stained ones,' means conceived by the six teachers stained with wrong views. For they arose earlier and spread their stained, false doctrine across the whole of Jambudīpa as if strewing thorns, and as if pouring out poison. Apāpuretaṃ: 'open,' means 'open this'. Amatassa dvāraṃ: 'the door to the Deathless,' means the Noble Path that serves as the door to the Deathless, Nibbāna. Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhaṃ: 'May they listen to the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One,' means: 'May these beings listen, O Blessed One, to the Dhamma of the Four Truths awakened to by the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who is stainless due to the absence of stains such as lust.' Thus he entreats.

Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhitoti selamaye ekagghane pabbatamuddhani yathāṭhitova. Na hi tassa ṭhitassa dassanatthaṃ gīvukkhipanapasāraṇādikiccaṃ atthi. Tathūpamanti tappaṭibhāgaṃ selapabbatūpamaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – yathā selapabbatamuddhani ṭhitova cakkhumā puriso samantato janataṃ passeyya[M 1.0183], tathā tvampi sumedha sundarapañña sabbaññutañāṇena samantacakkhu bhagavā dhammamayaṃ pāsādamāruyha sayaṃ apetasoko sokāvatiṇṇaṃ [P 1.0200] jātijarābhibhūtaṃ janataṃ avekkhassu [V 1.0176] upadhāraya upaparikkha. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – yathā hi pabbatapāde samantā mahantaṃ khettaṃ katvā, tattha kedārapāḷīsu kuṭikāyo katvā rattiṃ aggiṃ jāleyyuṃ, caturaṅgasamannāgatañca andhakāraṃ assa, atha tassa pabbatassa matthake ṭhatvā cakkhumato purisassa bhūmiṃ olokayato neva khettaṃ na kedārapāḷiyo na kuṭiyo na tattha sayitamanussā paññāyeyyuṃ. Kuṭikāsu pana aggijālāmattakameva paññāyeyya, evaṃ dhammapāsādaṃ āruyha sattanikāyaṃ olokayato tathāgatassa ye te akatakalyāṇā sattā, te ekavihāre dakkhiṇajāṇupasse nisinnāpi buddhacakkhussa āpāthaṃ nāgacchanti, rattiṃ khittā sarā viya honti. Ye pana katakalyāṇā veneyyapuggalā, te evassa dūrepi ṭhitā āpāthaṃ āgacchanti so aggi viya himavantapabbato viya ca. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito: 'Just as one stands on a mountain peak,' means just as one stands on a solid, single-mass rock mountain peak. For one standing there, there is no need to stretch or crane the neck to see. Tathūpamaṃ: 'This is the simile,' means a simile comparable to a rock mountain. Herein is the brief meaning: Just as a clear-sighted person standing on a rocky mountain peak sees people all around, so too, O you of good and beautiful wisdom, the All-Seeing Blessed One, by means of your Omniscience, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, yourself free from sorrow, should look upon, observe, and scrutinize the populace plunged in sorrow, oppressed by birth and old age. Herein is the intended meaning: Suppose a vast field is laid out around the foot of a mountain, with huts built along the borders of the rice fields. At night, fires are lit, and there is fourfold darkness. Yet, if a clear-sighted person stands on the mountain’s summit and looks down upon the ground, neither the field, nor the borders, nor the huts, nor the people sleeping there would be discernible. Only the mere flame of the fire in the huts would be discernible. Similarly, when the Tathāgata ascends the palace of Dhamma and surveys the host of beings, those beings who have done no good—though seated even in the same monastery, near his right knee—do not come into the range of the Buddha’s eye; they are like arrows shot in the night. But those who have done good, the teachable individuals, even if far away, come into his range, like a fire or the Himavanta mountain. And this has also been said:

“Dūre santo pakāsenti, himavantova pabbato;

Asantettha na dissanti, rattiṃ khittā yathā sarā”ti. (dha. pa. 304);

"From afar the good are manifest, like the Himavanta mountain; the bad are not seen here, like arrows shot at night."

Ajjhesananti yācanaṃ. Buddhacakkhunāti indriyaparopariyattañāṇena ca āsayānusayañāṇena ca. Imesaṃ hi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ “buddhacakkhū”ti nāmaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇassa “samantacakkhū”ti, tiṇṇaṃ maggañāṇānaṃ “dhammacakkhū”ti. Apparajakkhetiādīsu yesaṃ vuttanayeneva paññācakkhumhi rāgādirajaṃ appaṃ, te apparajakkhā. Yesaṃ taṃ mahantaṃ, te mahārajakkhā. Yesaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni tikkhāni, te tikkhindriyā. Yesaṃ tāni mudūni, te mudindriyā. Yesaṃ teyeva saddhādayo ākārā sundarā, te svākārā. Ye kathitakāraṇaṃ sallakkhenti, sukhena sakkā honti viññāpetuṃ, te suviññāpayā. Ye paralokañceva vajjañca bhayato passanti, te paralokavajjabhayadassāvino nāma.

Ajjhesanaṃ means a request. Buddhacakkhunā, 'by the Buddha's eye,' means by the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties and by the knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies. Indeed, for these two knowledges, the name is 'the Buddha's eye'; for the knowledge of omniscience, the name is 'the all-encompassing eye'; for the three path-knowledges, the name is 'the eye of the Dhamma'. Regarding 'apparajakkhā', and so on: those for whom the dust of passion, and so on, is little in the eye of wisdom, by the method already stated, are 'those with little dust'. Those for whom it is great are 'those with much dust'. Those whose faculties of faith, and so on, are keen are 'those with keen faculties'. Those for whom they are soft are 'those with soft faculties'. Those whose very aspects of faith, and so on, are beautiful are 'those with beautiful aspects'. Those who reflect on the stated reason and can be easily made to understand are 'those who are easy to instruct'. Those who see the next world and faults as fearful are called 'those who see fear in the next world and in faults'.

Ayaṃ panettha pāḷi – “saddho puggalo apparajakkho, assaddho [P 1.0201] puggalo mahārajakkho. Āraddhavīriyo, kusīto. Upaṭṭhitassati, muṭṭhassati. Samāhito[M 1.0184], asamāhito. Paññavā, duppañño puggalo mahārajakkho. Tathā saddho puggalo tikkhindriyo…pe… paññavā puggalo paralokavajjabhayadassāvī, duppañño puggalo na paralokavajjabhayadassāvī. Lokoti khandhaloko, āyatanaloko, dhātuloko, sampattibhavaloko, sampattisambhavaloko, vipattibhavaloko, vipattisambhavaloko. Eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Dve lokā nāmañca rūpañca. Tayo [V 1.0177] lokā tisso vedanā. Cattāro lokā cattāro āhārā. Pañca lokā pañcupādānakkhandhā. Cha lokā cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni. Satta lokā satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Aṭṭha lokā aṭṭha lokadhammā. Nava lokā nava sattāvāsā. Dasa lokā dasāyatanāni. Dvādasa lokā dvādasāyatanāni. Aṭṭhārasa lokā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo. Vajjanti sabbe kilesā vajjā, sabbe duccaritā vajjā, sabbe abhisaṅkhārā vajjā, sabbe bhavagāmikammā vajjā, iti imasmiñca loke imasmiñca vajje tibbā bhayasaññā paccupaṭṭhitā hoti, seyyathāpi ukkhittāsike vadhake. Imehi paññāsāya ākārehi imāni pañcindriyāni jānāti passati aññāsi paṭivijjhi. Idaṃ tathāgatassa indriyaparopariyatte ñāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.112).

Herein, this is the Pāli text: 'A person with faith is one with little dust; a person without faith is one with much dust. A person with aroused energy is one with little dust; a lazy person is one with much dust. A person with established mindfulness is one with little dust; a person with lapsed mindfulness is one with much dust. A concentrated person is one with little dust; an unconcentrated person is one with much dust. A wise person is one with little dust; a person of little wisdom is one with much dust. Similarly, a person with faith has keen faculties... a wise person sees the danger of what is blameworthy in the next world; a person of little wisdom does not see the danger of what is blameworthy in the next world. ‘The world’ means: the world of aggregates, the world of sense bases, the world of elements, the world of fortunate existence, the world of fortunate becoming, the world of unfortunate existence, the world of unfortunate becoming. One world: all beings are sustained by nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds: three feelings. Four worlds: four nutriments. Five worlds: five aggregates subject to clinging. Six worlds: six internal sense bases. Seven worlds: seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: ten sense bases. Twelve worlds: twelve sense bases. Eighteen worlds: eighteen elements. ‘Blameworthy’ means: all defilements are blameworthy, all misconduct is blameworthy, all volitional formations are blameworthy, all actions leading to becoming are blameworthy. Thus, in this world and in what is blameworthy, a keen perception of danger is present, just as with an executioner with a raised sword. With these fifty aspects, one knows, sees, has understood, and has penetrated these five faculties. This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of others.'

Uppaliniyanti uppalavane. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Antonimuggaposīnīti yāni anto nimuggāneva posiyanti. Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitānī ti udakaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitāni. Tattha yāni accuggamma ṭhitāni, tāni sūriyarasmisamphassaṃ āgamayamānāni ṭhitāni ajja pupphanakāni. Yāni pana samodakaṃ ṭhitāni, tāni sve pupphanakāni. Yāni udakānuggatāni antonimuggaposīni, tāni tatiyadivase pupphanakāni. Udakā pana anuggatāni aññānipi sarogauppalādīni nāma atthi, yāni neva pupphissanti, macchakacchapabhakkhāneva bhavissanti, tāni pāḷiṃ nāruḷhāni. Āharitvā pana dīpetabbānīti dīpitāni. Yatheva hi tāni catubbidhāni pupphāni, evamevaṃ ugghaṭitaññū [P 1.0202] vipañcitaññū neyyo padaparamoti cattāro puggalā.

In the lotus grove. The same method applies to the others. ‘Nourished while submerged’ means those that are nourished only when submerged. ‘Standing above the water’ means they stand having gone beyond the water. Among them, those that stand having gone beyond the water, awaiting contact with the sun's rays, are to bloom today. But those that stand level with the water are to bloom tomorrow. Those that have not emerged from the water, nourished while submerged within, are to bloom on the third day. Furthermore, there are other lotuses that have not emerged from the water, such as the diseased ones, which will never bloom and will only become food for fish and turtles; these are not mentioned in the Pāli. However, they are brought forth to be explained, and thus they are explained. Just as there are these four kinds of lotuses, so too are there four kinds of persons: one of swift understanding, one who understands after detailed exposition, one who is to be guided, and one for whom the text is the limit.

Tattha “yassa puggalassa saha udāhaṭavelāya dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ugghaṭitaññū. Yassa puggalassa saṃkhittena bhāsitassa [M 1.0185] vitthārena atthe vibhajiyamāne dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo vipañcitaññū. Yassa puggalassa uddesato paripucchato yoniso manasikaroto kalyāṇamitte sevato bhajato payirupāsato anupubbena dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo neyyo. Yassa puggalassa bahumpi suṇato bahumpi bhaṇato bahumpi dhārayato bahumpi vācayato na tāya jātiyā dhammābhisamayo hoti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo padaparamo (pu. pa. 148-151). Tattha bhagavā uppalavanādisadisaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ olokento – “ajja pupphanakāni viya ugghaṭitaññū, sve pupphanakāni viya [V 1.0178] vipañcitaññū, tatiyadivase pupphanakāni viya neyyo, macchakacchapabhakkhāni pupphāni viya padaparamo”ti addassa. Passanto ca “ettakā apparajakkhā, ettakā mahārajakkhā, tatrāpi ettakā ugghaṭitaññū”ti evaṃ sabbākāratova addasa.

Here, ‘a person for whom there is the realization of the Dhamma at the very time it is uttered is called one of swift understanding. A person for whom there is the realization of the Dhamma when the meaning of a concise statement is analyzed in detail is called one who understands after detailed exposition. A person for whom there is the realization of the Dhamma gradually through study, inquiry, proper application of mind, and by associating with, attending on, and waiting upon good friends is called one who is to be guided. A person for whom, despite much listening, much speaking, much memorizing, and much teaching, there is no realization of the Dhamma in that life is called one for whom the text is the limit.’ There, the Blessed One, looking upon the ten-thousandfold world-system as if it were a lotus grove, saw: ‘Like lotus buds that will bloom today are those of swift understanding; like lotus buds that will bloom tomorrow are those who understand after detailed exposition; like lotus buds that will bloom on the third day are those who are to be guided; and like lotus buds that are food for fish and turtles are those for whom the text is the limit.’ And in seeing, he discerned: ‘This many have little dust, this many have much dust; and even among them, this many are of swift understanding’—thus he saw in all aspects.

Tattha tiṇṇaṃ puggalānaṃ imasmiṃyeva attabhāve bhagavato dhammadesanā atthaṃ sādheti. Padaparamānaṃ anāgatatthāya vāsanā hoti. Atha bhagavā imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ atthāvahaṃ dhammadesanaṃ viditvā desetukamyataṃ uppādetvā puna sabbepi tīsu bhavesu satte bhabbābhabbavasena dve koṭṭhāse akāsi. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ – “katame sattā abhabbā? Ye te sattā kammāvaraṇena samannāgatā kilesāvaraṇena samannāgatā vipākāvaraṇena samannāgatā assaddhā acchandikā duppaññā abhabbā niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ, ime te sattā abhabbā. Katame sattā bhabbā? Ye te sattā na kammāvaraṇena…pe… ime te sattā bhabbā”ti (vibha. 827; paṭi. ma. 1.115). Tattha sabbepi abhabbapuggale pahāya bhabbapuggaleyeva ñāṇena pariggahetvā, “ettakā rāgacaritā ettakā dosa-mohacaritā [P 1.0203] vitakka-saddhā-buddhicaritā”ti cha koṭṭhāse akāsi. Evaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desessāmīti cintesi.

Among these, the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma bears fruit in this very life for three types of persons. For those for whom the text is the limit, it serves as an impression for the future. Then, knowing the teaching of the Dhamma is beneficial for these four types of persons, the Blessed One generated the desire to teach and further divided all beings in the three realms into two categories based on their capability: those capable and those incapable. This was stated in reference to them: ‘Which beings are incapable? Those beings who are obstructed by the kamma-obstruction, the defilement-obstruction, and the result-obstruction, who are faithless, without desire, and of little wisdom—these are incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome qualities; these beings are incapable. Which beings are capable? Those beings who are not obstructed by the kamma-obstruction... these beings are capable.’ There, having abandoned all incapable persons, he encompassed only the capable ones with his knowledge and divided them into six categories: ‘So many are of a greedy character, so many of a hating and deluded character, so many of a speculative, faithful, and intellectual character.’ Having done so, he thought: ‘Thus, I will teach the Dhamma.’

Paccabhāsīti patiabhāsi. Apārutāti vivaṭā. Amatassa dvārāti ariyamaggo. So hi amatasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa dvāraṃ, so mayā vivaritvā ṭhapitoti dasseti. Pamuñcantu saddhanti sabbe attano saddhaṃ pamuñcantu [M 1.0186] vissajjentu. Pacchimapadadvaye ayamattho – ahañhi attano paguṇaṃ suppavattitampi imaṃ paṇītaṃ uttamaṃ dhammaṃ kāyavācākilamathasaññī hutvā na bhāsiṃ. Idāni pana sabbo jano saddhābhājanaṃ upanetu, pūressāmi tesaṃ saṅkappanti.

`Paccabhāsi` means he replied. `Apārutā` means 'they are opened by me.' `Amatassa dvārā` refers to the Noble Path. For it is the door to Nibbāna, called the Deathless; 'it has been opened and established by me'—this is what is shown. `Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ` means let all release their faith. The meaning of the last two phrases is this: 'Being of the perception that I was weary in body and speech, I did not teach this excellent, supreme Dhamma, even though it was well-practiced and familiar to me. But now, let all people bring near the vessel of faith; I will fulfill their aspiration.'

Antaradhāyīti satthāraṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā antarahito, sakaṭṭhānameva gatoti attho. Gate ca pana tasmiṃ bhagavā “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya”nti? Āḷārudakānaṃ kālaṅkatabhāvaṃ, pañcavaggiyānañca bahūpakārabhāvaṃ ñatvā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desetukāmo bārāṇasiyaṃ isipatanaṃ gantvā dhammacakkaṃ pavattesīti. Paṭhamaṃ.

As for 'He disappeared' (antaradhāyi): this means that having honored the Teacher with perfumes, garlands, and so on, he vanished and went to his own place. This is the meaning. And when he had gone, the Blessed One reflected: 'To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma?' Knowing that Āḷāra and Uddaka had passed away and that the group of five had been of great assistance, he, wishing to teach them the Dhamma, went to Isipatana in Bārāṇasī and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. The first [sutta].

2. Gāravasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Gārava Sutta.

173. Dutiye [V 1.0179] udapādīti ayaṃ vitakko pañcame sattāhe udapādi. Agāravoti aññasmiṃ gāravarahito, kañci garuṭṭhāne aṭṭhapetvāti attho. Appatissoti patissayarahito, kañci jeṭṭhakaṭṭhāne aṭṭhapetvāti attho.

173. In the second [sutta], as for 'arose' (udapādi): this thought arose in the fifth week. As for 'without reverence' (agāravo): it means being devoid of reverence for another, not placing anyone in a position of esteem. This is the meaning. As for 'without deference' (appatisso): it means being devoid of deference, not placing anyone in a position of seniority. This is the meaning.

Sadevaketiādīsu saddhiṃ devehi sadevake. Devaggahaṇena cettha mārabrahmesu gahitesupi māro nāma vasavattī sabbesaṃ upari vasaṃ vatteti, brahmā nāma mahānubhāvo ekaṅguliyā ekasmiṃ cakkavāḷasahasse ālokaṃ pharati. Dvīhi dvīsu…pe… dasahi aṅgulīhi dasasupi cakkavāḷasahassesu ālokaṃ pharati, so iminā sīlasampannataroti vattuṃ mā labhatūti samārake sabrahmaketi visuṃ vuttaṃ. Tathā samaṇā nāma ekanikāyādivasena bahussutā sīlavanto paṇḍitā, brāhmaṇāpi vatthuvijjādivasena bahussutā paṇḍitā, te iminā sīlasampannatarāti vattuṃ mā labhantūti sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāyāti vuttaṃ. Sadevamanussāyāti [P 1.0204] idaṃ pana nippadesato dassanatthaṃ gahitameva gahetvā vuttaṃ. Apicettha purimāni tīṇi padāni lokavasena vuttāni, pacchimāni dve pajāvasena. Sīlasampannataranti sīlena sampannataraṃ, adhikataranti attho. Sesesupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca sīlādayo cattāro dhammā lokiyalokuttarā kathitā, vimuttiñāṇadassanaṃ lokiyameva. Paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ hetaṃ.

In the phrases beginning with `sadevake`: `sadevake` means 'together with the devas.' And here, although Māra and Brahmā are included by the term 'deva'—Māra is known as Vasavattī, who exercises power over all, and Brahmā is known as one of great power, who with one finger can illuminate a thousand world-systems, with two... up to ten fingers can illuminate ten thousand world-systems—lest one should get to say of them, 'He is more accomplished in virtue than this one [the Buddha],' the phrase 'with Māra, with Brahmā' is stated separately. Similarly, ascetics are learned, virtuous, and wise by way of the various Nikāyas, etc., and brahmins are also learned and wise by way of the science of sites, etc. Lest one should get to say of them, 'They are more accomplished in virtue than this one [the Buddha],' the phrase 'the populace with its ascetics and brahmins' is stated. As for the phrase 'with its devas and humans,' this is stated by taking what has already been included, in order to show it without remainder. Furthermore, here the first three terms are stated with reference to the world, and the last two with reference to beings. 'More accomplished in virtue' means more endowed with virtue, that is, more superior; this is the meaning. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. And here, the four qualities beginning with virtue are described as both mundane and supramundane, while the knowledge and vision of liberation is described as only mundane. For this is the knowledge of reviewing.

Pāturahosīti [M 1.0187] – “ayaṃ satthā avīcito yāva bhavaggā sīlādīhi attanā adhikataraṃ apassanto ‘mayā paṭividdhaṃ navalokuttaradhammameva sakkatvā garuṃ katvā upanissāya viharissāmī’ti cinteti, kāraṇaṃ bhagavā cinteti, atthaṃ vuḍḍhivisesaṃ cinteti, gacchāmissa ussāhaṃ janessāmī”ti cintetvā purato pākaṭo ahosi, abhimukhe aṭṭhāsīti attho.

'He appeared' (pāturahosi) means: This Sahampati Brahmā, having thought thus: 'This Teacher, not seeing anyone more accomplished than himself in virtue and so forth from Avīci up to the summit of existence, thinks, “I will dwell honoring, revering, and relying upon only the nine supramundane Dhammas that I have penetrated.” The Blessed One reflects on the cause, reflects on the unerring meaning, and on the special cause for growth. I shall go and generate enthusiasm for him.'—having thus thought, he became manifest before him; he stood face to face. This is the meaning.

Viharanti cāti ettha yo vadeyya “viharantīti vacanato paccuppannepi bahū buddhā”ti, so “bhagavāpi, bhante, etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti iminā vacanena paṭibāhitabbo.

'And they dwell' (viharanti ca) – here, if someone should say, 'Since it is said “they dwell” (viharantīti) in the plural, there are many Buddhas even in the present,' they should be refuted with the statement, 'But, venerable sir, even now the Blessed One is the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.'

“Na [V 1.0180] me ācariyo atthi, sadiso me na vijjati;

Sadevakasmiṃ lokasmiṃ, natthi me paṭipuggalo”ti. (mahāva. 11; ma. ni. 1.285) –

“I have no teacher; one like me does not exist. In this world with its devas, there is no counterpart to me.”

Ādīhi cassa suttehi aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ abhāvo dīpetabbo. Tasmāti yasmā sabbepi buddhā saddhammagaruno, tasmā. Mahattamabhikaṅkhatāti mahantabhāvaṃ patthayamānena. Saraṃ buddhāna-sāsananti buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ sarantena. Dutiyaṃ.

And by these and other suttas, the absence of other Buddhas should be demonstrated to him. `Tasmā`: because all Buddhas hold the good Dhamma in reverence, therefore... `Mahattamabhikaṅkhatā` means by one aspiring to a state of greatness. `Saraṃ buddhāna-sāsanaṃ` means by one remembering the teaching of the Buddhas. The second [sutta].

3. Brahmadevasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Brahmadeva Sutta

174. Tatiye ekoti ṭhānādīsu iriyāpathesu ekako, ekavihārīti attho. Vūpakaṭṭhoti kāyena vūpakaṭṭho nissaṭo. Appamattoti satiyā avippavāse ṭhito. Ātāpīti vīriyātāpena samannāgato. Pahitattoti pesitatto. Kulaputtāti ācārakulaputtā. Sammadevāti na iṇaṭṭā na bhayaṭṭā na jīvitapakatā hutvā, yathā vā tathā vā pabbajitāpi ye anulomapaṭipadaṃ pūrenti, te sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti nāma. Brahmacariyapariyosānanti maggabrahmacariyassa [P 1.0205] pariyosānabhūtaṃ ariyaphalaṃ. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti sāmaṃ jānitvā paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upasampajjāti paṭilabhitvā sampādetvā vihāsi. Evaṃ viharanto ca khīṇā jāti…pe… abbhaññāsīti. Etenassa paccavekkhaṇabhūmi dassitā.

3. In the third [sutta], `eko` means solitary in the postures such as standing; the meaning is one who dwells alone. `Vūpakaṭṭho` means secluded in body, detached from company. `Appamatto` means established in the state of not being parted from mindfulness. `Ātāpī` means endowed with the energy that torments the defilements. `Pahitatto` means one whose mind is sent forth to Nibbāna. `Kulaputtā` means sons of good family by way of conduct. `Sammadeva` means: not having gone forth because of being oppressed by debt, by fear, or for lack of a livelihood, but rather, those who fulfill the practice that is in conformity with the supramundane Dhamma, even if they have gone forth in whatever way, they are said to have rightly gone forth from the home life to homelessness. `Brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ` means the noble fruit, which is the culmination of the holy life that is the path. `Diṭṭheva dhamme` means in this very existence. `Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā` means having known by oneself and having realized it directly. `Upasampajja` means having attained and having accomplished, he dwelt. And dwelling thus, he knew: 'Birth is destroyed...' and so on. By this, his stage of reviewing knowledge is shown.

Katamā [M 1.0188] panassa jāti khīṇā, kathañca naṃ abbhaññāsīti? Vuccate, na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā tattha vāyāmābhāvato, na paccuppannā vijjamānattā. Maggassa pana abhāvitattā yā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti. Sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā. Taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā – “kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ hotī”ti jānanto jānāti.

174. But what birth of his is destroyed, and how did he know it? It is said: First, his past birth is not destroyed, because it was already destroyed before the attainment of the path; nor the future birth, because of the absence of effort regarding it; nor the present birth, because of its existing.
