However, because the path had not been developed, whatever birth would arise—differentiated into one, four, and five aggregates in the one-, four-, and five-constituent existences—that birth is destroyed by reaching the state of non-arising because the path has been developed. He knows that by reviewing the defilements abandoned through the development of the path, knowing thus: 'In the absence of defilements, even though kamma exists, in the future it is without rebirth-linking.'

Vusitanti vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ[V 1.0181]. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyabhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya, evaṃ soḷasakiccabhāvāya, kilesakkhayāya vā katamaggabhāvanā natthīti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthattabhāvato, imasmā evaṃpakārā idāni vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ natthi, ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlako rukkho viyāti abbhaññāsi. Aññataroti eko. Arahatanti arahantānaṃ, bhagavato sāvakānaṃ arahataṃ abbhantaro ahosi.

'Vusitaṃ' means: lived, fully lived; the practice has been undertaken and brought to completion; this is the meaning. 'Brahmacariyaṃ' means the holy life which is the path. 'Kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ' means the sixteen-fold task in relation to the four noble truths—namely, comprehending, abandoning, realizing, and developing by means of the four paths—has been brought to completion; this is the meaning. 'Nāparaṃ itthattāya' means: now there is no further cultivation of the path that has been undertaken for the sake of this state of being, that is, for the sake of the sixteen-fold task, or for the destruction of the defilements. Or alternatively, 'itthattāya' means: from this state of being, that is, from this present continuum of aggregates of this kind, there is no further continuum of aggregates; but these five aggregates, having been fully comprehended, remain like a tree with its root cut off—thus he understood. 'Aññataro' means one. 'Arahataṃ' means he was among the Arahants, an Arahant among the Blessed One’s disciples.

Sapadānanti sapadānacāraṃ, sampattagharaṃ anukkamma paṭipāṭiyā caranto. Upasaṅkamīti upasaṅkamanto. Mātā panassa puttaṃ disvāva gharā nikkhamma pattaṃ gahetvā antonivesanaṃ pavesetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpesi.

'Sapadānaṃ' means: undertaking the ascetic practice of systematic alms-round, going from house to house in succession without skipping any. 'Upasaṅkami' means approaching. His mother, however, upon seeing her son, came out of the house, took his bowl, led him into the inner dwelling, and had him sit on a prepared seat.

Āhutiṃ niccaṃ paggaṇhātīti niccakāle āhutipiṇḍaṃ paggaṇhāti. Taṃ divasaṃ pana tasmiṃ ghare bhūtabalikammaṃ hoti. Sabbagehaṃ haritupalittaṃ vippakiṇṇalājaṃ [P 1.0206] vanamālaparikkhittaṃ ussitaddhajapaṭākaṃ tattha tattha puṇṇaghare ṭhapetvā daṇḍadīpikā jāletvā gandhacuṇṇamālādīhi alaṅkataṃ, samantato sañchādiyamānā dhūmakaṭacchu ahosi. Sāpi brāhmaṇī kālasseva vuṭṭhāya soḷasahi gandhodakaghaṭehi nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkārena attabhāvaṃ alaṅkari. Sā tasmiṃ samaye mahākhīṇāsavaṃ nisīdāpetvā, yāguuḷuṅkamattampi adatvā, “mahābrahmaṃ bhojessāmī”ti suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ pāyāsaṃ [M 1.0189] pūretvā sappimadhusakkharādīhi yojetvā nivesanassa pacchābhāge haritupalittabhāvādīhi alaṅkatā bhūtapīṭhikā atthi. Sā taṃ pātiṃ ādāya, tattha gantvā, catūsu koṇesu majjhe ca ekekaṃ pāyāsapiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā, ekaṃ piṇḍaṃ hatthena gahetvā, yāva kapparā sappinā paggharantena pathaviyaṃ jāṇumaṇḍalaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā “bhuñjatu bhavaṃ mahābrahmā, sāyatu bhavaṃ mahābrahmā, tappetu bhavaṃ mahābrahmā”ti vadamānā brahmānaṃ bhojeti.

‘Āhutiṃ niccaṃ paggaṇhāti’ means she always makes an offering of sacrificial food. On that day, however, a ritual offering to the spirits was being performed in that house. The entire house was smeared with fresh cow-dung, scattered with parched rice, surrounded by forest and household garlands, and had flags and banners raised. Full water pots were placed here and there, oil-lamp stands were lit, and it was decorated with perfumed powders, garlands, and the like. All around, there was a smoke-ladle from which smoke was circulating. That brahmin woman, too, rising early, bathed with sixteen pots of fragrant water and adorned her body with all ornaments. At that time, having caused the great Arahant to be seated, but without giving even a ladleful of gruel, she thought, 'I will feed the Great Brahmā.' She filled a golden bowl with milk-rice, combined it with ghee, honey, sugar, and the like. In the back part of the house, there was a spirit-platform, decorated by being smeared with fresh cow-dung and so on. She, taking that bowl, went there, placed one lump of milk-rice in each of the four corners and in the middle, then took one lump in her hand. With ghee dripping down to her elbow, she placed her knees on the ground and, saying, 'May the Venerable Great Brahmā eat, may the Venerable Great Brahmā savor, may the Venerable Great Brahmā be satiated,' she fed Brahmā.

Etadahosīti mahākhīṇāsavassa sīlagandhaṃ chadevaloke ajjhottharitvā brahmalokaṃ upagataṃ ghāyamānassa etaṃ ahosi. Saṃvejeyyanti codeyyaṃ, sammāpaṭipattiyaṃ yojeyyaṃ. ‘Ayaṃ hi evarūpaṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyaṃ mahākhīṇāsavaṃ nisīdāpetvā yāguuḷuṅkamattampi adatvā, “mahābrahmaṃ bhojessāmī”ti tulaṃ pahāya hatthena tulayantī viya, bheriṃ pahāya kucchiṃ vādentī viya, aggiṃ [V 1.0182] pahāya khajjopanakaṃ dhamamānā viya bhūtabaliṃ kurumānā āhiṇḍati. Gacchāmissā micchādassanaṃ bhinditvā apāyamaggato uddharitvā yathā asītikoṭidhanaṃ buddhasāsane vippakiritvā saggamaggaṃ ārohati, tathā karomīti vuttaṃ hoti.

This thought occurred to Mahābrahmā, as he smelled the fragrance of the great Arahant's virtue, which had pervaded the six deva worlds and reached the Brahma-world. 'Should I arouse a sense of urgency?'—meaning, 'Should I admonish her, should I engage her in right practice?' 'For this woman, having seated such a supreme recipient of offerings—the great one whose taints were destroyed—without giving even a ladleful of rice gruel, thinks, "I will feed the Mahābrahmā," and wanders about making an offering to Brahmā, like one who, having abandoned a scale, weighs with the hand; like one who, having abandoned a drum, beats their belly; and like one who, having abandoned a fire, blows on a firefly. I will go and shatter her wrong view, lift her from the path to the lower realms, and act so that she scatters eighty crores of wealth in the Buddha’s Dispensation and ascends the path to heaven.' Thus it is said.

Dūre itoti imamhā ṭhānā dūre brahmaloko. Tato hi kūṭāgāramattā silā pātitā ekena ahorattena aṭṭhacattālīsayojanasahassāni khepayamānā catūhi māsehi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhaheyya, sabbaheṭṭhimopi brahmaloko evaṃ dūre. Yassāhutinti yassa brahmuno āhutiṃ paggaṇhāsi, tassa brahmaloko [P 1.0207] dūreti attho. Brahmapathanti ettha brahmapatho nāma cattāri kusalajjhānāni, vipākajjhānāni pana nesaṃ jīvitapatho nāma, taṃ brahmapathaṃ ajānantī tvaṃ kiṃ jappasi vippalapasi? Brahmāno hi sappītikajjhānena yāpenti, na etaṃ tiṇabījāni pakkhipitvā randhaṃ goyūsaṃ khādanti, mā akāraṇā kilamasīti.

'Dūre ito' means, from this place the Brahma-world is far away. For if a rock the size of a peaked house were to fall from there, traveling forty-eight thousand yojanas in a single day and night, it would take four months to come to rest on the earth. Even the lowest Brahma-world is thus far away. 'Yassāhutiṃ' means, the Brahma-world of whichever Brahmā you offer oblations to is far away; this is the meaning. 'Brahmapathaṃ'—here, the path to Brahmā means the four wholesome jhānas. However, the resultant jhānas are called their path of life. Not knowing that path to Brahmā, why do you mutter and babble? For the Brahmās sustain themselves with jhānas accompanied by rapture; they do not eat this cow-broth cooked with grass seeds. Do not weary yourself needlessly.

Evaṃ vatvā puna so mahābrahmā añjaliṃ paggayha avakujjo hutvā theraṃ upadisanto eso hi te brāhmaṇi brahmadevotiādimāha. Tattha nirūpadhikoti kilesābhisaṅkhārakāmaguṇopadhīhi virahito. Atidevapattoti devānaṃ atidevabhāvaṃ brahmānaṃ atibrahmabhāvaṃ patto. Anaññaposīti [M 1.0190] ṭhapetvā imaṃ attabhāvaṃ aññassa attabhāvassa vā puttadārassa vā aposanatāya anaññaposī.

Having said this, that Mahābrahmā again raised his joined hands, bowed down, and, pointing to the Thera, spoke the words beginning with, 'This, O brahmin woman, is your Brahmadeva.' Therein, `nirūpadhiko` means devoid of the substrata of defilements, volitional formations, and sensual pleasures. `Atidevapatto` means having attained a state surpassing devas and a state surpassing brahmās. `Anaññaposī` means one who does not support another, because, setting aside this personal existence, he does not support another being or a wife and children.

Āhuneyyoti āhunapiṇḍaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ yutto. Vedagūti catumaggasaṅkhātehi vedehi dukkhassantaṃ gato. Bhāvitattoti attānaṃ bhāvetvā vaḍḍhetvā ṭhito. Anūpalittoti taṇhādīhi lepehi ālitto. Ghāsesanaṃ iriyatīti āhārapariyesanaṃ carati.

`Āhuneyyo` means worthy to receive offerings. `Vedagū` means one who has gone to the end of suffering by means of the wisdoms known as the four paths. `Bhāvitatto` means one who stands firm, having developed and augmented the self with virtues such as morality. `Anūpalitto` means unsmeared by smearing agents such as craving. `Ghāsesanaṃ iriyati` means he wanders in search of food.

Na tassa pacchā na puratthamatthīti pacchā vuccati atītaṃ, puratthaṃ vuccati anāgataṃ, atītānāgatesu khandhesu chandarāgavirahitassa pacchā vā puratthaṃ vā natthīti vadati. Santotiādīsu rāgādisantatāya santo. Kodhadhūmavigamā vidhūmo, dukkhābhāvā anīgho, kattaradaṇḍādīni gahetvā vicarantopi vadhakacetanāya abhāvā nikkhittadaṇḍo. Tasathāvaresūti ettha pana puthujjanā tasā nāma, khīṇāsavā thāvarā nāma. Satta pana sekhā tasāti vattuṃ na [V 1.0183] sakkā, thāvarā na honti, bhajamānā pana thāvarapakkhameva bhajanti. So tyāhutinti so te āhutiṃ.

Regarding `Na tassa pacchā na puratthamatthīti`: `pacchā` (behind) is said of the past, and `puratthaṃ` (before) is said of the future. For one who is devoid of desire and lust for past and future aggregates, there is nothing 'behind' or 'before'—thus it is said. In `Santo`, etc.: `santo` (peaceful) because of being pacified from lust and so on. `Vidhūmo` (smokeless) due to the departure of the smoke of anger. `Anīgho` (trouble-free) due to the absence of suffering. `Nikkhittadaṇḍo` (one who has laid down the rod) because, even while wandering about holding a cutting-stick, a rod, and so on, there is an absence of the intention to kill. Now, in `Tasathāvaresu`: worldlings are called `tasā` (trembling ones); Arahants, whose cankers are destroyed, are called `thāvarā` (steadfast ones). But the seven trainees cannot be called `tasā`, nor are they `thāvarā`; however, when classified, they belong only to the faction of the steadfast. `So tyāhutiṃ` means: May he partake of your (`te`) offering (`āhutiṃ`).

Visenibhūtoti kilesasenāya viseno jāto. Anejoti nittaṇho. Susīloti khīṇāsavasīlena susīlo. Suvimuttacittoti phalavimuttiyā suṭṭhu vimuttacitto. Oghatiṇṇanti cattāro [P 1.0208] oghe tiṇṇaṃ. Ettakena kathāmaggena brahmā therassa vaṇṇaṃ kathento āyatane brāhmaṇiṃ niyojesi. Avasānagāthā pana saṅgītikārehi ṭhapitā. Patiṭṭhapesi dakkhiṇanti catupaccayadakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhapesi. Sukhamāyatikanti sukhāyatikaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ, sukhāvahanti attho. Tatiyaṃ.

'Disarmed' (Visenibhūto) means one who has become disarmed of the army of defilements. 'Undisturbed' (Anejo) means free from craving. 'Of excellent virtue' (Susīlo) means one who is of excellent virtue through the virtue of one whose taints are destroyed. 'One whose mind is well-liberated' (Suvimuttacitto) means one whose mind is well-liberated through the liberation of fruition. 'Crossed the flood' (Oghatiṇṇaṃ) means one who has crossed the four floods. With this much discourse, Brahmā, praising the elder, urged the brahmin woman to exertion. The concluding verse, however, was placed by the compilers of the Council. 'He established the offering' (Patiṭṭhapesi dakkhiṇaṃ) means he established the offering of the four requisites. 'Bringing happiness in the future' (Sukhamāyatikaṃ) means having a pleasant future, a future of pleasant result, bringing happiness—this is the meaning. The third.

4. Bakabrahmasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Bakabrahma Sutta

175. Catutthe pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigatanti lāmikā sassatadiṭṭhi. Idaṃ niccanti idaṃ saha kāyena brahmaṭṭhānaṃ aniccaṃ “nicca”nti vadati. Dhuvādīni tasseva vevacanāni. Tattha dhuvanti thiraṃ. Sassatanti sadā vijjamānaṃ. Kevalanti akhaṇḍaṃ sakalaṃ. Acavanadhammanti acavanasabhāvaṃ. Idaṃ hi na jāyatītiādīsu imasmiṃ ṭhāne koci jāyanako vā jīyanako vā mīyanako vā cavanako [M 1.0191] vā upapajjanako vā natthi, taṃ sandhāya vadati. Ito ca panaññanti ito sahakāyā brahmaṭṭhānā uttari aññaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nāma natthīti. Evamassa thāmagatā sassatadiṭṭhi uppannā hoti. Evaṃvādī ca pana so upari tisso jhānabhūmiyo cattāro magge cattāri phalāni nibbānanti sabbaṃ paṭibāhati. Kadā panassa sā diṭṭhi uppannāti? Paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ nibbattakāle. Dutiyajjhānabhūmiyanti eke.

175. In the fourth, 'an evil view' (pāpakaṃ diṭṭhigataṃ) means the base eternalist view. 'This is permanent' (Idaṃ niccaṃ) means he says this Brahma-abode, which along with the body is impermanent, is 'permanent'. 'Permanent' and so on (Dhuvādīni) are synonyms for that very word. Therein, 'stable' (dhuvaṃ) means firm. 'Eternal' (sassataṃ) means always existing. 'Absolute' (kevalaṃ) means undivided, whole. 'Not subject to passing away' (acavanadhammaṃ) means of a nature that does not pass away. In 'For this does not come to be born' (Idaṃ hi na jāyati) and so on, he speaks with reference to the fact that in this place there is no one who is born, or ages, or dies, or passes away, or is reborn. 'And there is no other beyond this' (Ito ca panaññaṃ) means that beyond this Brahma-abode together with the body, there is no other escape. Thus a strong eternalist view has arisen for him. And he who speaks thus rejects all that is higher: the three jhāna-realms, the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna. When, then, did that view arise for him? At the time of arising in the first jhāna-realm. Some say in the second jhāna-realm.

Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – heṭṭhupapattiko kiresa brahmā anuppanne buddhuppāde isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā samāpattiyo nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā catutthajjhānabhūmiyaṃ vehapphalabrahmaloke pañcakappasatikaṃ āyuṃ gahetvā nibbatti. Tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā heṭṭhupapattikaṃ katvā tatiyajjhānaṃ paṇītaṃ bhāvetvā subhakiṇhabrahmaloke catusaṭṭhikappaṃ āyuṃ gahetvā nibbatti. Tattha dutiyajjhānaṃ bhāvetvā ābhassare aṭṭha kappe āyuṃ gahetvā nibbatti. Tattha paṭhamajjhānaṃ bhāvetvā, paṭhamajjhānabhūmiyaṃ kappāyuko hutvā nibbatti[V 1.0184]. So paṭhamakāle attanā katakammañca nibbattaṭṭhānañca [P 1.0209] aññāsi, kāle pana gacchante gacchante ubhayaṃ pamussitvā sassatadiṭṭhiṃ uppādesi.

Here is the sequential discourse: It is said that this Brahmā is one who is reborn in lower realms. Before the arising of a Buddha, having gone forth into the ascetic life, having done the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, having brought forth the attainments, and being one whose jhāna had not declined, he passed away and was reborn in the fourth jhāna plane, in the Vehapphala Brahma-world, having taken a lifespan of five hundred great aeons. Having remained there for the full extent of his lifespan, having developed the jhāna that is a cause for rebirth in a lower realm, and having developed the third jhāna to a sublime state, he was reborn in the Subhakiṇha Brahma-world, having taken a lifespan of sixty-four great aeons. There, having developed the second jhāna, he was reborn in the Ābhassara world, having taken a lifespan of eight great aeons. There, having developed the first jhāna, he was reborn in the first jhāna plane, having become one with a lifespan of a great aeon. In the initial period, he knew both the deeds he had done and the place of his rebirth, but as time went on, he forgot both and gave rise to the eternalist view.

Avijjāgatoti avijjāya gato samannāgato aññāṇī andhībhūto. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma. Vakkhatīti bhaṇati. “Yatrā”ti nipātayogena pana anāgatavacanaṃ kataṃ.

'Avijjāgato' means: gone with ignorance, endowed with it, ignorant, become blind. 'Yatra hi nāma' means: whoever. 'Vakkhati' means: he says. However, the future tense form was used because of its connection with the particle 'yatrā'.

Evaṃ vutte so brahmā yathā nāma maggacoro dve tayo pahāre adhivāsento sahāye anācikkhitvāpi uttariṃ pahāraṃ pahariyamāno “asuko ca asuko ca mayhaṃ sahāyo”ti ācikkhati, evameva bhagavatā santajjiyamāno satiṃ labhitvā, “bhagavā mayhaṃ padānupadaṃ pekkhanto maṃ nippīḷitukāmo”ti bhīto attano sahāye ācikkhanto dvāsattatītiādimāha. Tassattho – bho gotama, mayaṃ dvāsattati janā puññakammā tena puññakammena idha nibbattā. Vasavattino sayaṃ aññesaṃ vase avattitvā pare attano vase vattema, jātiñca jarañca atītā, ayaṃ no vedehi gatattā “vedagū”ti saṅkhaṃ gatā bhagavā antimā brahmupapatti. Asmābhijappanti janā anekāti anekajanā amhe [M 1.0192] abhijappanti. “Ayaṃ kho bhavaṃ brahmā, mahābrahmā, abhibhū, anabhibhūto, aññadatthudaso, vasavattī, issaro, kattā, nimmātā, seṭṭho, sajitā, vasī, pitā bhūtabhabyāna”nti evaṃ patthenti pihentīti.

When this was said, that Brahmā—just as a road thief who, after enduring two or three blows, when struck further without having pointed out his companions, cries out, 'This one and that one are my companions!'—in the same way, being rebuked by the Blessed One and regaining his mindfulness, he became frightened, thinking, 'The Blessed One is watching my every step, intending to crush me.' Revealing his companion Brahmās, he said, 'Seventy-two,' and so on. The meaning of that is this: 'Venerable Gotama, we seventy-two beings, having performed meritorious deeds, have been reborn here by that meritorious deed. Wielding power, not being subject to the power of others, we make others subject to our power. We have transcended birth and old age. O Blessed One, because we have attained it through knowledges, we have reached the designation ‘Vedagū’; this is our final Brahma-rebirth. Many beings long for us'—that is, many beings long for and cherish us, saying, 'This honorable Brahmā is Mahābrahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the Sovereign, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Best, the Ordainer, the Master, the Father of all that have been and will be.' Thus they long for and cherish him.

Atha naṃ bhagavā appaṃ hi etantiādimāha. Tattha etanti yaṃ tvaṃ idha tava āyuṃ “dīgha”nti maññasi, etaṃ appaṃ parittakaṃ. Sataṃ sahassānaṃ nirabbudānanti nirabbudagaṇanāya satasahassanirabbudānaṃ. Āyuṃ pajānāmīti, “idāni tava avasiṭṭhaṃ ettakaṃ āyū”ti ahaṃ jānāmi. Anantadassī bhagavā hamasmīti, bhagavā, tumhe “ahaṃ anantadassī jātiādīni upātivatto”ti vadatha. Kiṃ me purāṇanti, yadi tvaṃ anantadassī, evaṃ sante idaṃ me ācikkha, kiṃ mayhaṃ purāṇaṃ? Vatasīlavattanti sīlameva vuccati. Yamahaṃ vijaññāti yaṃ ahaṃ [P 1.0210] tayā kathitaṃ jāneyyaṃ, taṃ me ācikkhāti vadati.

Then the Blessed One said to him, 'Indeed, this is little,' and so on. Herein, 'this' means: that which you, O Baka Brahmā, consider here as your lifespan to be 'long'—this is little, insignificant. 'A hundred thousand Nirabbudas' refers to one hundred thousand Nirabbudas by that count. As for 'I know the lifespan': it means, 'I know that this much of your lifespan, amounting to one hundred thousand Nirabbudas, is what now remains.' As for 'I am the Blessed One of infinite vision': The Blessed One says, 'I am one of infinite vision, having transcended birth and so forth.' As for 'What was my past?': The Brahmā asks, 'If you are one of infinite vision, that being so, tell me this: what was my past practice and virtue?' 'Vow and virtuous conduct' refers to virtue alone. As for 'That I may know': 'That which is spoken by you, I would know. Tell me that,' thus the Brahmā speaks.

Idānissa ācikkhanto bhagavā yaṃ tvaṃ apāyesītiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – pubbe kiresa kulaghare nibbattitvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā – “jātijarāmaraṇassa antaṃ karissāmī”ti nikkhamma isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā samāpattiyo nibbattetvā abhiññāpādakajjhānassa [V 1.0185] lābhī hutvā gaṅgātīre paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā jhānaratiyā vītināmeti. Tadā ca kālenakālaṃ satthavāhā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi marukantāraṃ paṭipajjanti. Marukantāre pana divā na sakkā gantuṃ, rattiṃ gamanaṃ hoti. Atha purimasakaṭassa aggayuge yuttabalibaddā gacchantā gacchantā nivattitvā āgatamaggābhimukhā ahesuṃ, sabbasakaṭāni tatheva nivattitvā aruṇe uggate nivattitabhāvaṃ jāniṃsu. Tesañca tadā kantāraṃ atikkamanadivaso ahosi. Sabbaṃ dārudakaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ – tasmā “natthi dāni amhākaṃ jīvita”nti cintetvā, goṇe cakkesu bandhitvā, manussā sakaṭacchāyaṃ pavisitvā nipajjiṃsu.

Now, explaining this to him, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning, 'That you gave to drink...' In that, this is the meaning: It is said that previously this one, having been born in a family home and having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, thought, 'I will make an end of birth, aging, and death.' He then went forth into the ascetic life of a sage. Having produced the worldly meditative attainments and having become a recipient of the jhāna that is the basis for the supernormal knowledges, he had a leaf-hut made on the bank of the Ganges and passed the time with the delight of jhāna. And at that time, from time to time, caravan merchants traveled the Maru wilderness with five hundred carts. But in the Maru wilderness, it is not possible to travel by day; the journey is at night. Then, the bullocks yoked to the front yoke of the first cart, while going along, turned back and faced the path by which they had come. All the carts turned back in the same way, and when dawn rose, they realized that they had turned back. And for them, that was the day for crossing the wilderness. All the firewood and water was exhausted. Therefore, thinking, 'Now there is no life for us,' they tied the oxen to the wheels, and the men, having entered the shade of the carts, lay down.

Tāpasopi kālasseva paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā paṇṇasāladvāre nisinno gaṅgaṃ olokayamāno addasa gaṅgaṃ mahatā udakoghena pūriyamānaṃ pavattitamaṇikkhandhaṃ viya āgacchantaṃ, disvā cintesi – “atthi nu kho imasmiṃ loke evarūpassa madhurodakassa alābhena kilissamānā sattā”ti? So evaṃ āvajjento marukantāre taṃ satthaṃ disvā ‘ime sattā mā nassantū’ti “ito cito ca mahāudakakkhandho chijjitvā marukantāre [M 1.0193] satthābhimukho gacchatū”ti abhiññācittena adhiṭṭhāsi. Saha cittuppādena mātikāruḷhaṃ viya udakaṃ tattha agamāsi. Manussā udakasaddena vuṭṭhāya udakaṃ disvā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā nhāyitvā pivitvā goṇepi pāyetvā sotthinā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Satthā taṃ brahmuno pubbakammaṃ dassento paṭhamaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha apāyesīti pāyesi. A-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Gammanīti gimhe. Sampareteti gimhātapena phuṭṭhe anugate.

The ascetic, too, having left his leaf-hut early in the morning, sat at its door gazing at the Ganges. He saw the Ganges coming, filled with a great flood of water, like a rolling mass of jewels. Seeing this, he thought: 'Are there any beings in this world suffering from the lack of such sweet water?' Reflecting thus, he saw that caravan in the desert. Thinking, 'May these beings not perish,' he resolved with his mind of higher knowledge: 'Let a great mass of water, having broken off from this Ganges, go toward the caravan in the desert.' As soon as the thought arose, the water, as if carried by a channel, went there. The people, awakened by the sound of the water, saw the water and, overjoyed, bathed, drank, and gave their oxen to drink. Then, safely, they went to their desired destination. The Teacher, revealing that past deed of the Brahmā, spoke the first verse. Therein, 'apāyesi' means 'you gave to drink.' The 'a-' is merely a particle. 'Gammani' means 'in the hot season.' 'Samparete' means 'those afflicted and overcome by the summer heat.'

Aparasmimpi samaye tāpaso gaṅgātīre paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā araññagāmakaṃ nissāya vasati. Tena ca samayena corā taṃ gāmaṃ paharitvā hatthasāraṃ gahetvā gāviyo ca karamare [P 1.0211] ca gahetvā gacchanti. Gāvopi sunakhāpi manussāpi mahāviravaṃ viravanti. Tāpaso taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kinnu kho eta”nti? Āvajjento “manussānaṃ bhayaṃ uppanna”nti ñatvā “mayi passante ime sattā mā nassantū”ti abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya abhiññācittena corānaṃ paṭipathe caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ māpesi. Kammasajjā āgacchantā corā disvā, “rājā maññe āgato”ti vilopaṃ chaḍḍetvā pakkamiṃsu. Tāpaso “yaṃ yassa santakaṃ, taṃ tasseva hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi, taṃ tatheva ahosi. Mahājano sotthibhāvaṃ pāpuṇi. Satthā idampi [V 1.0186] tassa pubbakammaṃ dassento dutiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha eṇikūlasminti gaṅgātīre. Gayhakaṃ nīyamānanti gahetvā nīyamānaṃ, karamaraṃ nīyamānantipi attho.

At another time, the ascetic, having fashioned a leaf-hut on the bank of the Ganges, dwelt relying on a small forest village. And at that time, robbers, having attacked that village, seized the valuable property, captured the cows and the people, and were departing. The cows, the dogs, and the people cried out with a great uproar. The ascetic, having heard that sound, reflected, 'What, indeed, is this?' Knowing that 'Danger has arisen for the people,' and thinking, 'While I am looking on, let not these beings perish,' he entered the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge. Having arisen from it, with a mind of direct knowledge, he created a four-divisioned army on the path directly ahead of the robbers. The robbers, approaching prepared for action, saw it and, thinking, 'The king, we suppose, has come,' abandoned their plunder and fled. The ascetic made a determination: 'Whatever belongs to whomever, let it be for that very owner.' And it was just so. The great populace attained a state of safety. The Teacher, also showing this past deed of his, spoke the second verse. Therein, 'eṇikūlasmiṃ' means 'on the bank of the Ganges.' 'Gayhakaṃ nīyamānaṃ' means 'being seized and led away'; the meaning should also be understood as 'captives being led away.'

Puna ekasmiṃ samaye uparigaṅgāvāsikaṃ ekaṃ kulaṃ heṭṭhāgaṅgāvāsikena kulena saddhiṃ mittasanthavaṃ katvā, nāvāsaṅghāṭaṃ bandhitvā, bahuṃ khādanīyañceva bhojanīyañca gandhamālādīni ca āropetvā gaṅgāsotena āgacchati. Manussā khādamānā bhuñjamānā naccantā gāyantā devavimānena gacchantā viya balavasomanassā ahesuṃ. Gaṅgeyyako nāgo disvā kupito “ime mayi saññampi na karonti. Idāni ne samuddameva pāpessāmī”ti mahantaṃ attabhāvaṃ māpetvā udakaṃ dvidhā bhinditvā uṭṭhāya phaṇaṃ katvā, susukāraṃ karonto aṭṭhāsi. Mahājano disvā bhīto vissaramakāsi. Tāpaso paṇṇasālāyaṃ nisinno sutvā, “ime gāyantā naccantā somanassajātā āgacchanti. Idāni pana bhayaravaṃ raviṃsu, kinnu kho”ti? Āvajjento [M 1.0194] nāgarājaṃ disvā, “mayi passante sattā mā nassantū”ti abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā attabhāvaṃ pajahitvā supaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ māpetvā nāgarājassa dassesi. Nāgarājā bhīto phaṇaṃ saṃharitvā udakaṃ paviṭṭho, mahājano sotthibhāvaṃ pāpuṇi. Satthā idampi tassa pubbakammaṃ dassento tatiyaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha luddenāti dāruṇena. Manussakamyāti manussakāmatāya, manusse viheṭhetukāmatāyāti attho.

Again, at one time, a family dwelling upstream on the Ganges formed a friendship with a family dwelling downstream. They tied a raft of boats together, loaded it with much hard and soft food, as well as perfumes, garlands, and so forth, and came along the current of the Ganges. The people, eating and feasting, dancing and singing, were filled with great joy, as if traveling in a divine mansion. The Nāga named Gaṅgeyyaka, seeing them, became angry, thinking: 'These people do not even acknowledge me. Now I shall make them reach the ocean itself!' He created a massive form, split the water in two, rose up, spread his hood, and stood hissing loudly. The great multitude, seeing this, became terrified and cried out in alarm. The ascetic, sitting in his leaf-hut, heard them and thought: 'These people were coming along singing and dancing, full of joy. But now they have cried out in fear—what could be the reason?' Reflecting, he saw the Nāga king. Thinking, 'May no beings perish while I am watching,' he entered the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge, abandoned his own form, created the appearance of a Supaṇṇa, and revealed himself to the Nāga king. The Nāga king, frightened, withdrew his hood and plunged into the water. The great multitude attained safety. The Teacher, also showing this past deed of his, spoke the third verse. Therein, 'luddena' means 'by the cruel one,' that is, 'by the harsh one.' 'Manussakamyā' means 'out of a desire for humans,' that is, 'with the wish to harm humans'—this is the meaning.

Aparasmimpi [P 1.0212] samaye esa isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā kesavo nāma tāpaso ahosi. Tena samayena amhākaṃ bodhisatto kappo nāma māṇavo kesavassa baddhacaro antevāsiko hutvā ācariyassa kiṃkārapaṭissāvī manāpacārī buddhisampanno atthacaro ahosi. Kesavo tena vinā vasituṃ na sakkoti, taṃ nissāyeva jīvikaṃ kappesi. Satthā idampi tassa pubbakammaṃ dassento catutthaṃ gāthamāha.

At another time, this one went forth into the ascetic life and became an ascetic named Kesava. At that time, our Bodhisatta, a young man named Kappa, became Kesava’s close attendant and resident pupil. He was obedient to his teacher's instructions, pleasing in his conduct, endowed with wisdom, and one who acted for his teacher's welfare. Kesava was not able to live without him; he maintained his livelihood relying only on him. The Teacher, also showing this past deed of his, spoke the fourth verse.

Tattha baddhacaroti antevāsiko, so pana jeṭṭhantevāsiko ahosi. Sambuddhimantaṃ vatinaṃ amaññīti, “sammā buddhimā vatasampanno aya”nti evaṃ maññamāno kappo tava antevāsiko ahosiṃ ahaṃ so tena samayenāti dasseti. Aññepi jānāsīti na kevalaṃ mayhaṃ āyumeva, aññepi tvaṃ jānāsiyeva. Tathā hi buddhoti tathā hi tvaṃ buddho, yasmā buddho, tasmā jānāsīti attho. Tathā hi tyāyaṃ jalitānubhāvoti yasmā ca tvaṃ buddho, tasmā [V 1.0187] te ayaṃ jalito ānubhāvo. Obhāsayaṃ tiṭṭhatīti sabbaṃ brahmalokaṃ obhāsayanto tiṭṭhati. Catutthaṃ.

Herein, 'a constant attendant' means a resident pupil; and he was the senior resident pupil. As for 'He thought him to be one endowed with perfect wisdom and vows': He shows, 'O Brahmā, at that time, I, thinking, “This one is truly possessed of right wisdom and accomplished in vows,” was your resident pupil named Kappa.' As for 'You know others too': You know not only my lifespan, but you certainly know others as well. As for 'For indeed you are the Buddha': Indeed, you are the Buddha; because you are the Buddha, therefore you know—this is the meaning. As for 'For indeed this radiant power of yours': And because you are the Buddha, therefore this radiant power is yours. As for 'Illuminating, he stands': Illuminating the entire Brahma-world, he stands. The Fourth.

5. Aññatarabrahmasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Discourse about a Certain Brahmā

176. Pañcame tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvāti tejokasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya, “sarīrato jālā nikkhamantū”ti adhiṭṭhahanto adhiṭṭhānacittānubhāvena sakalasarīrato jālā nikkhamanti, evaṃ tejodhātuṃ samāpanno nāma hoti, tathā samāpajjitvā. Tasmiṃ brahmaloketi kasmā thero tattha agamāsi? Therassa kira tejodhātuṃ samāpajjitvā tassa brahmuno upari nisinnaṃ tathāgataṃ disvā “aṭṭhivedhī [M 1.0195] ayaṃ puggalo, mayāpettha gantabba”nti ahosi, tasmā agamāsi. Sesānaṃ gamanepi [P 1.0213] eseva nayo. So hi brahmā tathāgatassa ceva tathāgatasāvakānañca ānubhāvaṃ adisvā abhabbo vinayaṃ upagantuṃ, tena so sannipāto ahosi. Tattha tathāgatassa sarīrato uggatajālā sakalabrahmalokaṃ atikkamitvā ajaṭākāse pakkhandā, tā ca pana chabbaṇṇā ahesuṃ, tathāgatassa sāvakānaṃ ābhā pakativaṇṇāva.

176. In the fifth discourse, as for 'having attained the fire element': Having performed the preliminary work for the fire kasiṇa, having emerged from the basic jhāna, and resolving, 'Let flames issue from my body,' by the power of the mind of resolution, flames issue from his entire body. Thus, one is said to have attained the fire element. Having attained it thus. As for 'in that Brahma-world': Why did the Elder go there? It is said that the Elder, having attained the fire element and having seen the Tathāgata seated above that Brahmā, thought, 'This person is one to be pierced to the marrow; I too must go there.' Therefore, he went. This is the same method for the going of the others as well. Indeed, that Brahmā, not having seen the power of the Tathāgata and the Tathāgata’s disciples, was incapable of coming to the discipline. For that reason, that assembly took place. There, the flames that had risen up from the Tathāgata’s body, having surpassed the entire Brahma-world, leapt into the unformed space, and they were of six colors. The radiance of the Tathāgata’s disciples was of its natural color.

Passasi vītivattantanti imasmiṃ brahmaloke aññabrahmasarīravimānālaṅkārādīnaṃ pabhā atikkamamānaṃ buddhassa bhagavato pabhassaraṃ pabhaṃ passasīti pucchati. Na me, mārisa, sā diṭṭhīti yā mesā, “idhāgantuṃ samattho añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā natthī”ti pure diṭṭhi, natthi me sā. Kathaṃ vajjanti kena kāraṇena vadeyyaṃ. Niccomhi sassatoti imassa kira brahmuno laddhidiṭṭhi sassatadiṭṭhi cāti dve diṭṭhiyo. Tatrāssa tathāgatañceva tathāgatasāvake ca passato laddhidiṭṭhi pahīnā. Bhagavā panettha mahantaṃ dhammadesanaṃ desesi. Brahmā desanāpariyosāne sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Itissa maggena sassatadiṭṭhi pahīnā, tasmā evamāha.

As for 'Do you see it surpassing?': He asks, 'Do you see the radiant light of the Blessed One, the Buddha, surpassing the splendor of the bodies, mansions, ornaments, and so forth, of other Brahmās in this Brahma-world?' As for 'No, sir, I do not have that view': 'That view which I formerly held, that “there is no other ascetic or brahmin capable of coming here,” I no longer have that view.' As for 'How could I say so?': 'For what reason should I say so?' As for 'I am eternal, permanent': It is said that this Brahmā had two views: the acquired view and the eternalist view. Therein, upon seeing the Tathāgata and his disciples, his acquired view was abandoned. The Blessed One then gave a great discourse there. At the end of the discourse, the Brahmā became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Thus, his eternalist view was abandoned by the path, and so he spoke thus.

Brahmapārisajjanti brahmapāricārikaṃ. Therānañhi bhaṇḍagāhakadaharā viya brahmānampi pārisajjā brahmāno nāma honti. Tenupasaṅkamāti kasmā therasseva santikaṃ pesesi? There kirassa tattakeneva kathāsallāpena vissāso udapādi, tasmā tasseva santikaṃ pesesi aññepīti yathā tumhe cattāro janā, kinnu kho evarūpā aññepi atthi, udāhu tumhe cattāro eva mahiddhikāti? Tevijjāti pubbenivāsadibbacakkhuāsavakkhayasaṅkhātāhi tīhi vijjāhi [V 1.0188] samannāgatā. Iddhipattāti iddhividhañāṇaṃ pattā. Cetopariyāyakovidāti paresaṃ cittācāre kusalā. Evamettha pañca abhiññāpi sarūpena vuttā. Dibbasotaṃ pana tāsaṃ vasena āgatameva hoti. Bahūti evarūpā chaḷabhiññā buddhasāvakā bahū gaṇanapathaṃ atikkantā, sakalaṃ jambudīpaṃ kāsāvapajjotaṃ katvā vicarantīti. Pañcamaṃ.

As for 'Brahmā’s retinue': It means 'Brahmā’s attendants.' For just as there are young monks who are attendants carrying the requisites of the elders, so too there are Brahmās called 'attendants' who serve the Great Brahmās. As for 'He approached him': Why did he send him to the elder alone? It is said that confidence arose in him toward the elder through just that conversation; therefore, he sent him to the elder alone. As for 'Are there others too?': 'Just as you four people are of great psychic power, are there others of such a nature, or are only you four of great psychic power?' As for 'Possessed of the three knowledges': Endowed with the three knowledges known as the recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints. As for 'Attained to psychic power': Having attained the knowledge of psychic power. As for 'Skilled in understanding the minds of others': Skilled in discerning the conduct of others’ minds. Thus, here the five superknowledges are mentioned specifically. But the divine ear is included by way of them. As for 'Many': Such disciples of the Buddha endowed with the six superknowledges are many, beyond the path of counting, wandering and making the whole of Jambudīpa a blaze of saffron robes. Fifth.

6. Brahmalokasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Brahmaloka Sutta

177. Chaṭṭhe [M 1.0196][P 1.0214] paccekaṃ dvārabāhanti ekeko ekekaṃ dvārabāhaṃ nissāya dvārapālā viya aṭṭhaṃsu. Iddhoti jhānasukhena samiddho. Phītoti abhiññāpupphehi supupphito. Anadhivāsentoti asahanto. Etadavocāti etesaṃ nimmitabrahmānaṃ majjhe nisinno etaṃ “passasi me”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

177. In the sixth discourse, as for 'each at a doorpost': Each Brahmā stood relying on a single doorpost like a doorkeeper. As for 'powerful': Endowed with the bliss of jhāna. As for 'prosperous': Well-blossomed with the flowers of direct knowledge. As for 'unable to endure': Not being able to endure. As for 'he spoke thus': Seated among those created Brahmās, he spoke this statement beginning with, 'Do you see me?'

Tayo supaṇṇāti gāthāya pañcasatāti satapadaṃ rūpavasena vā pantivasena vā yojetabbaṃ. Rūpavasena tāva tayo supaṇṇāti tīṇi supaṇṇarūpasatāni. Caturo ca haṃsāti cattārihaṃsarūpasatāni. Bugghīnisā pañcasatāti byagghasadisā ekacce migā byagghīnisā nāma, tesaṃ byagghīnisārūpakānaṃ pañcasatāni, pantivasena tayo supaṇṇāti tīṇi supaṇṇapantisatāni, caturo haṃsāti cattāri haṃsapantisatāni. Byagghīnisā pañcasatāti pañca byagghīnisā pantisatāni. Jhāyinoti jhāyissa mayhaṃ vimāne ayaṃ vibhūtīti dasseti. Obhāsayanti obhāsayamānaṃ. Uttarassaṃ disāyanti taṃ kira kanakavimānaṃ tesaṃ mahābrahmānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānato uttaradisāyaṃ hoti. Tasmā evamāha. Ayaṃ panassa adhippāyo – evarūpe kanakavimāne vasanto ahaṃ kassa aññassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmīti. Rūpe raṇaṃ disvāti rūpamhi jātijarābhaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ dosaṃ disvā. Sadā pavedhitanti sītādīhi ca niccaṃ pavedhitaṃ calitaṃ ghaṭṭitaṃ rūpaṃ disvā. Tasmā na rūpe ramati sumedhoti yasmā rūpe raṇaṃ passati, sadā pavedhitañca rūpaṃ passati, tasmā sumedho sundarapañño so satthā rūpe na ramatīti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

In the verse beginning 'Three supaṇṇas,' the word 'hundred' in the phrase 'five hundred' should be connected either by way of form or by way of line. By way of form, first, 'three supaṇṇas' means three hundred supaṇṇa-forms. 'And four haṃsas' means four hundred haṃsa-forms. 'Five hundred byagghīnisās': certain beasts resembling tigers are called byagghīnisā; five hundred of their byagghīnisā-forms. By way of line, 'three supaṇṇas' means three hundred lines of supaṇṇa-forms; 'four haṃsas' means four hundred lines of haṃsa-forms. 'Five hundred byagghīnisās' means five hundred lines of byagghīnisā-forms. As for 'of the meditator': It shows, 'This is the splendor in the mansion of me, the meditator.' As for 'illuminating': It means illuminating. As for 'in the northern direction': That golden celestial mansion is in the northern direction from the place where those great Brahmās were standing. Therefore, he spoke thus. This, however, is his intention: 'I, dwelling in such a golden celestial mansion, to what other should I go to attend upon?' As for 'having seen the fault in form': Having seen the fault in form, designated as birth, aging, and dissolution. As for 'always agitated': Having seen form as constantly agitated, shaken, and struck by things such as cold. As for 'therefore, the one of good wisdom does not delight in form': Because that Teacher, the one of good wisdom, sees the fault in form and sees form as constantly agitated, therefore he does not delight in form. The Sixth.

7. Kokālikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Kokālika Sutta

178. Sattame appameyyaṃ paminantoti appameyyaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalaṃ “ettakaṃ sīlaṃ, ettako [V 1.0189] samādhi, ettakā paññā”ti evaṃ minanto. Kodhavidvā vikappayeti ko idha vidvā [P 1.0215] medhāvī vikappeyya, khīṇāsavova khīṇāsavaṃ minanto kappeyyāti dīpeti. Nivutaṃ taṃ maññeti yo pana puthujjano taṃ pametuṃ ārabhati, taṃ nivutaṃ avakujjapaññaṃ maññāmīti. Sattamaṃ.

178. In the seventh sutta: 'He who measures the immeasurable' (appameyyaṃ paminanto) means one who measures the immeasurable, that is, an individual whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavapuggalaṃ), thinking, 'Virtue is this much, concentration is this much, wisdom is this much.' 'Who here, being wise, would assess?' (ko idha vidvā vikappeyya) shows that: who here, being wise and intelligent, would assess? Only one whose taints are destroyed, when measuring another whose taints are destroyed, could assess them. 'I consider that one to be veiled' (nivutaṃ taṃ maññe) means: whichever ordinary person (puthujjano) attempts to measure that one, I consider him to be veiled, with wisdom turned downward (avakujjapaññaṃ). The seventh.

8. Katamodakatissasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Katamodakatissa Sutta

179. Aṭṭhame [M 1.0197] akissavanti kissavā vuccati paññā, nippaññoti attho. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

179. In the eighth sutta: 'Akissava' (akissavaṃ): 'kissavā' is said to be wisdom; the meaning is 'without wisdom' (nippañño). The eighth.

9. Turūbrahmasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Turūbrahma Sutta

180. Navame ābādhikoti “sāsapamattīhi pīḷakāhī”tiādinā nayena anantarasutte āgatena ābādhena ābādhiko. Bāḷhagilānoti adhimattagilāno. Turūti kokālikassa upajjhāyo turutthero nāma anāgāmiphalaṃ patvā brahmaloke nibbatto. So bhūmaṭṭhakadevatā ādiṃ katvā, “ayuttaṃ kokālikena kataṃ aggasāvake antimavatthunā abbhācikkhantenā”ti paramparāya brahmalokasampattaṃ kokālikassa pāpakammaṃ sutvā – “mā mayhaṃ passantasseva varāko nassi, ovadissāmi naṃ theresu cittapasādatthāyā”ti āgantvā tassa purato aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “turū paccekabrahmā”ti. Pesalāti piyasīlā. Kosi tvaṃ, āvusoti nipannakova kabarakkhīni ummīletvā evamāha. Passa yāvañca teti passa yattakaṃ tayā aparaddhaṃ, attano nalāṭe mahāgaṇḍaṃ apassanto sāsapamattāya pīḷakāya maṃ codetabbaṃ maññasīti āha.

180. In the ninth sutta: 'Afflicted' (ābādhiko) means afflicted by the illness that is described in the immediately following sutta in the manner of 'with boils the size of mustard seeds,' and so on. 'Severely ill' (bāḷhagilāno) means extremely ill. 'Turu' (turū): Kokālika’s preceptor, an elder named Turu, who attained the fruit of non-returning and was reborn in the Brahma world. That Turu Brahmā, having heard of Kokālika's evil deed—slandering the chief disciples with the final matter—which had reached the Brahma world in succession, starting from the earth-bound deities, thought, 'Let not this wretched one perish while I am looking on! I will advise him for the sake of inspiring confidence in the elders.' Having come, he stood before him. With reference to that, it was said, 'Turu, the Paccekabrahmā.' 'Virtuous' (pesalā) means of amiable virtue. 'Who are you, friend?' (kosi tvaṃ, āvuso): lying down, he opened his mottled eyes and spoke thus. 'See how much you...' (passa yāvañca te): Kokālika said, 'See how much you have transgressed! Not seeing the great boil on your own forehead, you think to accuse me for a boil the size of a mustard seed.'

Atha naṃ “adiṭṭhippatto ayaṃ varāko, gilaviso viya kassaci vacanaṃ na karissatī”ti ñatvā purisassa hītiādimāha. Tattha kuṭhārīti kuṭhārisadisā pharusā vācā. Chindatīti kusalamūlasaṅkhāte mūleyeva nikantati. Nindiyanti ninditabbaṃ dussīlapuggalaṃ. Pasaṃsatīti uttamatthe sambhāvetvā khīṇāsavoti vadati. Taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyoti[P 1.0216], yo vā pasaṃsitabbo khīṇāsavo, taṃ antimavatthunā codento “dussīlo aya”nti vadati. Vacināti mukhena so kalinti, so taṃ aparādhaṃ mukhena vicināti nāma. Kalinā tenāti tena aparādhena sukhaṃ na vindati. Nindiyapasaṃsāya hi pasaṃsiyanindāya ca samakova vipāko.

Then, knowing of him, 'This wretch has not attained the right view; like one who has swallowed poison, he will not listen to anyone's words,' he spoke the words beginning with 'purisassa hi'. Therein, 'axe' (kuṭhārī) means harsh speech, like an axe. 'Cuts' (chindati) means it severs the very roots known as the wholesome roots. 'The blameworthy' (nindiyaṃ) means a blameworthy, immoral person. 'Praises' (pasaṃsati) means, having esteemed him in the highest attainment, he declares, 'He is one whose taints are destroyed.' Or, 'he blames one who is praiseworthy' (taṃ vā nindati yo pasaṃsiyo): that is, one who is praiseworthy, one whose taints are destroyed, he accuses with the final matter, saying, 'This one is immoral.' 'He seeks out misfortune with his mouth' (vicināti mukhena so kaliṃ): that person indeed seeks out that offense with his mouth. 'By that misfortune' (kalinā tena): by that offense, he does not find happiness. For by praising the blameworthy and by blaming the praiseworthy, the result is the very same.

Sabbassāpi [V 1.0190] sahāpi attanāti sabbena sakenapi attanāpi saddhiṃ yo akkhesu dhanaparājayo nāma, ayaṃ appamattako aparādho. Yo [M 1.0198] sugatesūti yo pana sammaggatesu puggalesu cittaṃ padusseyya, ayaṃ cittapadosova tato kalito mahantataro kali.

‘With all, and with oneself’ (sabbassāpi sahāpi attanā): The loss of wealth in gambling, together with all of one's own possessions and oneself—this is a minor offense. ‘Who towards the Sugatas’ (yo sugatesu): But whoever should corrupt their mind towards persons who have gone rightly (sammaggatesu), this very corruption of mind is a far greater misfortune than that loss.

Idāni tassa mahantatarabhāvaṃ dassento sataṃ sahassānantiādimāha. Tattha sataṃ sahassānanti nirabbudagaṇanāya satasahassaṃ. Chattiṃsatīti aparāni chattiṃsati nirabbudāni. Pañca cāti abbudagaṇanāya pañca abbudāni. Yamariyagarahīti yaṃ ariye garahanto nirayaṃ upapajjati, tattha ettakaṃ āyuppamāṇanti. Navamaṃ.

Now, to show its greater magnitude, he spoke the words beginning with 'a hundred thousand'. Therein, 'a hundred thousand' (sataṃ sahassānaṃ) means one hundred thousand by the reckoning of nirabbudas. 'Thirty-six' (chattiṃsati) means another thirty-six nirabbudas. 'And five' (pañca ca) means five abbudas by the reckoning of abbudas. The phrase 'one who reviles noble ones' (yam ariyagarahī) means: into whichever hell one who reviles noble ones is reborn, there the measure of the lifespan is this much. The ninth.

10. Kokālikasuttavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Kokālika Sutta

181. Dasame kokāliko bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti, ko ayaṃ kokāliko, kasmā ca upasaṅkami? Ayaṃ kira kokālikaraṭṭhe kokālikanagare kokālikaseṭṭhissa putto pabbajitvā pitarā kārāpite vihāre paṭivasati cūḷakokālikoti nāmena, na devadattassa sisso. So hi brāhmaṇaputto mahākokāliko nāma. Bhagavati pana sāvatthiyaṃ viharante dve aggasāvakā pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ janapadacārikaṃ caramānā upakaṭṭhāya vassūpanāyikāya vivekāvāsaṃ vasitukāmā te bhikkhū uyyojetvā attano pattacīvaramādāya tasmiṃ janapade taṃ nagaraṃ patvā taṃ vihāraṃ agamaṃsu. Tattha nesaṃ kokāliko vattaṃ dassesi. Te tena saddhiṃ sammoditvā, “āvuso, mayaṃ idha temāsaṃ vasissāma, mā kassaci ārocehī”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā vasiṃsu. Vasitvā pavāraṇādivase pavāretvā, “gacchāma mayaṃ, āvuso”ti kokālikaṃ āpucchiṃsu. Kokāliko “ajjekadivasaṃ, āvuso, vasitvā sve gamissathā”ti vatvā dutiyadivase nagaraṃ pavisitvā manusse āmantesi – “āvuso, tumhe aggasāvake idhāgantvā [P 1.0217] vasamānepi na jānātha, na ne koci paccayenāpi nimantetī”ti. Nagaravāsino, “kahaṃ, bhante, therā, kasmā no na ārocayitthā”ti? Kiṃ āvuso ārocitena, kiṃ na passatha dve bhikkhū therāsane nisīdante, ete aggasāvakāti. Te khippaṃ sannipatitvā sappiphāṇitādīni ceva cīvaradussāni ca saṃhariṃsu.

181. In the tenth sutta, regarding the phrase 'the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One': who was this Kokālika, and why did he approach? It is said that this was the son of the merchant Kokālika in the city of Kokālika in the country of Kokālika who, after going forth, dwelt in a monastery built by his father and was known by the name Cūḷakokālika. He was not the disciple of Devadatta; for that one was the son of a brahmin, named Mahākokālika. Now, while the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, the two chief disciples, along with about five hundred bhikkhus, were traveling through the countryside. As the rains-residence approached, wishing to dwell in seclusion, they sent those bhikkhus away and, taking their own bowls and robes, arrived in that country, reached that city, and went to that monastery. There, Kokālika attended to their duties. After exchanging friendly greetings with him, they said, "Friend, we will stay here for the three months; do not inform anyone." Having obtained his promise, they stayed. After completing their stay, on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, having performed the Pavāraṇā, they said, "Friend, we are leaving," and took leave of Kokālika. Kokālika said, "Friends, stay just one more day, and you may leave tomorrow." The next day, he entered the city and addressed the people: "Friends, you do not even know that the chief disciples have come here and are staying, nor has anyone invited them even for requisites." The city dwellers said, "Where, venerable sir, are the elders? Why did you not inform us?" He replied, "Friends, what is the use of my informing you? Do you not see those two bhikkhus sitting on the elder's seat? They are the chief disciples." Quickly gathering, they collected items such as ghee and molasses, and also cloth for robes.

Kokāliko [M 1.0199] cintesi – “paramappicchā aggasāvakā payuttavācāya uppannaṃ lābhaṃ na sādiyissanti[V 1.0191], asādiyantā ‘āvāsikassa dethā’ti vakkhantī”ti. Taṃ taṃ lābhaṃ gāhāpetvā therānaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Therā disvāva “ime paccayā neva amhākaṃ, na kokālikassa kappantī”ti paṭikkhipitvā pakkamiṃsu. Kokāliko “kathaṃ hi nāma attanā agaṇhantā mayhampi adāpetvā pakkamissantī”ti? Āghātaṃ uppādesi. Tepi bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā puna attano parisaṃ ādāya janapadacārikaṃ carantā anupubbena tasmiṃ raṭṭhe tameva nagaraṃ paccāgamiṃsu. Nāgarā there sañjānitvā saha parikkhārehi dānaṃ sajjitvā nagaramajjhe maṇḍapaṃ katvā dānaṃ adaṃsu, therānañca parikkhāre upanāmesuṃ. Therā bhikkhusaṅghassa niyyādayiṃsu. Taṃ disvā kokāliko cintesi – “ime pubbe appicchā ahesuṃ, idāni pāpicchā jātā, pubbepi appicchasantuṭṭhapavivittasadisā maññe”ti there upasaṅkamitvā, “āvuso, tumhe pubbe appicchā viya, idāni pana pāpabhikkhū jātā”ti vatvā “mūlaṭṭhāneyeva nesaṃ patiṭṭhaṃ bhindissāmī”ti taramānarūpo nikkhamitvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami. Ayameva kokāliko iminā ca kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti veditabbo.

Kokālika thought: "The chief disciples are of extremely few desires; they will not accept a gain that has arisen from speech connected with intimation. Not accepting it, they will say, ‘Give it to the resident monk.’" Having had those gains taken, he went to the presence of the elders. The elders, upon seeing, and thinking, "These requisites are suitable neither for us nor for Kokālika," rejected them and departed. Kokālika generated resentment, thinking, "How indeed could they, not accepting for themselves, depart without having it given to me?" They also, having gone to the presence of the Blessed One and having paid homage to the Blessed One, again took their own retinue and, while wandering on tour in the country, in due course, returned to that very city in that country. The townspeople, recognizing the elders, prepared an alms-offering together with requisites, made a pavilion in the middle of the city, and gave the alms-offering. They also presented the requisites to the elders. The elders entrusted them to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Seeing this, Kokālika thought: "Previously, these ones were of few desires; now they have become of evil desires. Even previously, I think they were only semblances of those with few desires, of the contented, and of the secluded." Having approached the elders, he said, "Friends, previously you were as if of few desires, but now you have become evil bhikkhus." Then, thinking, "I will destroy their standing right at its foundation," he hurriedly departed, went to Sāvatthī, and approached the place where the Blessed One was. It should be known thus: This very Kokālika approached for this reason as well.

Bhagavā taṃ turitaturitaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvāva āvajjento aññāsi – “ayaṃ aggasāvake akkositukāmo āgato”ti. “Sakkā nu kho paṭisedhetu”nti ca āvajjento, “na sakkā paṭisedhetuṃ, theresu aparajjhitvā kālaṅkato ekaṃsena padumaniraye nibbattissatī”ti disvā, “sāriputtamoggallānepi nāma garahantaṃ sutvā na nisedhetī”ti vādamocanatthaṃ ariyūpavādassa ca mahāsāvajjabhāvadassanatthaṃ mā hevanti tikkhattuṃ paṭisedhesi. Tattha mā hevanti mā evaṃ abhaṇi. Saddhāyikoti saddhāya ākaro pasādāvaho saddhātabbavacano vā. Paccayikoti pattiyāyitabbavacano.

Seeing him coming in great haste, the Blessed One, reflecting, knew: "This one has come intending to revile the chief disciples." Reflecting further, "Is it possible to prevent him?" he saw, "It is not possible to prevent him. Having offended the elders, he will die and certainly be reborn in the Paduma hell." And for the purpose of being free from the accusation, 'Even after hearing him revile Sāriputta and Moggallāna, he did not prevent him,' and for showing the great blameworthiness of disparaging the noble ones, he restrained him three times, saying, "Do not speak thus." Therein, "Do not speak thus" means "Do not speak in this way." "Saddhāyiko" means a source of faith, one who inspires confidence, or one whose word is to be believed. "Paccayiko" means one whose word is to be trusted.

Pakkāmīti kammānubhāvena codiyamāno pakkāmi. Okāsakataṃ hi kammaṃ na sakkā paṭibāhituṃ, taṃ tassa tattha ṭhātuṃ na adāsi. Acirapakkantassāti pakkantassa [P 1.0218] sato na cireneva. Sabbo kāyo phuṭo [M 1.0200] ahosīti kesaggamattampi okāsaṃ āvajjetvā sakalasarīraṃ aṭṭhīni bhinditvā uggatāhi pīḷakāhi ajjhotthaṭaṃ ahosi. Yasmā pana buddhānubhāvena tathārūpaṃ kammaṃ buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve vipākaṃ na deti, dassanūpacāre vijahitamatte deti, tasmā tassa acirapakkantassa pīḷakā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Kalāyamattiyoti caṇakamattiyo. Beluvasalāṭukamattiyoti [V 1.0192] taruṇabeluvamattiyo. (Billamattiyoti mahābeluvamattiyo.) Pabhijjiṃsūti bhijjiṃsu. Tāsu bhinnāsu sakalasarīraṃ panasapakkaṃ viya ahosi. So pakkena gattena jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake visagilito maccho viya kadalipattesu sayi. Atha dhammasavanatthaṃ āgatāgatā manussā – “dhi kokālika, dhi kokālika, ayuttamakāsi, attanoyeva mukhaṃ nissāya anayabyasanaṃ patto”ti āhaṃsu. Tesaṃ sutvā ārakkhadevatā dhi-kāraṃ akaṃsu. Ārakkhakadevatānaṃ ākāsadevatāti iminā upāyena yāva akaniṭṭhabhavanā ekadhikāro udapādi. Athassa upajjhāyo āgantvā ovādaṃ agaṇhantaṃ ñatvā garahitvā pakkāmi.

He departed, meaning he departed, urged on by the power of his kamma. Indeed, kamma that has been given an opportunity cannot be resisted; it did not allow him to stay there. Acirapakkantassa means not long after he had departed. Sabbo kāyo phuṭo ahosi means his entire body, not sparing even the space of a hair's tip, was overwhelmed by tumors that had erupted, shattering his bones. For, due to the power of the Buddhas, such kamma does not yield its result in the presence of the Buddhas; it yields its result only when one has just moved beyond the range of sight. Therefore, soon after he left, the tumors arose. Kalāyamattiyo means the size of chickpeas. Beluvasalāṭukamattiyo means the size of tender beluva fruits. (Billamattiyoti means the size of large beluva fruits.) Pabhijjiṃsu means they burst. When they burst, his entire body became like a ripe jackfruit. With his festering body, he lay on banana leaves at the gatehouse of Jetavana like a fish that has swallowed poison. Then, people who came to hear the Dhamma said, “Shame on you, Kokālika! Shame on you, Kokālika! You acted improperly; relying on your own mouth, you have attained ruin and disaster.” Hearing them, the guardian deities made a sound of contempt. Hearing the guardian deities, the sky deities also made a sound of contempt, and in this way, up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, a single sound of contempt arose. Then, his preceptor came, and knowing that he would not accept advice, rebuked him and departed.

Kālamakāsīti upajjhāye pakkante kālamakāsi. Padumaṃ nirayanti pāṭiyekko padumanirayo nāma natthi, avīcimahānirayamhiyeva pana padumagaṇanāya paccitabbe ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nibbatti.

Kālamakāsi means he died when his preceptor had departed. Regarding 'the Paduma hell,' there is no separate hell named Paduma; rather, he was reborn in a certain place within the great Avīci hell itself, to be tormented for a duration counted in padumas.

Vīsatikhārikoti māgadhakena patthena cattāro patthā kosalaraṭṭhe ekapattho hoti, tena patthena cattāro patthā āḷhakaṃ, cattāri āḷhakāni doṇaṃ, catudoṇā mānikā, catumānikā khārī, tāya khāriyā vīsatikhāriko. Tilavāhoti māgadhakānaṃ sukhumatilānaṃ tilasakaṭaṃ. Abbudo nirayoti abbudo nāma pāṭiyekko nirayo natthi. Avīcimhiyeva pana abbudagaṇanāya paccitabbaṭṭhānassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Nirabbudādīsupi [P 1.0219] eseva nayo.

Regarding `vīsatikhārika`: four `patthas` by the Magadhan measure are equivalent to one `pattha` in the Kosala country. By that `pattha`, four `patthas` are an `āḷhaka`; four `āḷhakas` are a `doṇa`; four `doṇas` are a `mānikā`; four `mānikās` are a `khārī`. A `vīsatikhārika` is a measure of twenty such `khārīs`. Regarding `tilavāha`: it is a cartload of the fine sesame seeds of the Magadhans. Regarding `Abbuda niraya`: there is no separate hell named Abbuda. Rather, in the Avīci hell itself, this is the name for a place where one is tormented for a duration counted in `abbudas`. This same method applies also to `Nirabbuda` and the others.

Vassagaṇanāpi panettha evaṃ veditabbā – yatheva hi sataṃ satasahassāni koṭi hoti, evaṃ sataṃ satasahassakoṭiyo pakoṭi nāma hoti, sataṃ satasahassapakoṭiyo koṭipakoṭi nāma, sataṃ satasahassakoṭipakoṭiyo [M 1.0201] nahutaṃ, sataṃ satasahassanahutāni ninnahutaṃ, sataṃ satasahassaninnahutāni ekaṃ abbudaṃ, tato vīsatiguṇaṃ nirabbudaṃ. Eseva nayo sabbatthāti. Dasamaṃ.

Here, the counting of years should also be understood thus: just as a hundred hundred-thousands is a `koṭi`, so a hundred thousand `koṭis` is called a `pakoṭi`; a hundred thousand `pakoṭis` is named `koṭipakoṭi`; a hundred thousand `koṭipakoṭis` is a `nahuta`; a hundred thousand `nahutas` is a `ninnahuta`; a hundred thousand `ninnahutas` is one `abbuda`; twenty times that is a `nirabbuda`. This is the method in all cases. The Tenth.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter.

1. Sanaṅkumārasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Sanaṅkumāra Sutta.

182. Dutiyavaggassa [V 1.0193] paṭhame sappinītīreti sappinīnāmikāya nadiyā tīre. Sanaṅkumāroti so kira pañcasikhakumārakakāle jhānaṃ bhāvetvā brahmaloke nibbatto kumārakavaṇṇeneva vicarati. Tena naṃ “kumāro”ti sañjānanti, porāṇakattā pana “sanaṅkumāro”ti vuccati. Janetasminti janitasmiṃ, pajāyāti attho. Ye gottapaṭisārinoti ye janetasmiṃ gottaṃ paṭisaranti tesu loke gottapaṭisārīsu khattiyo seṭṭho. Vijjācaraṇasampannoti bhayabheravasuttapariyāyena (ma. ni. 1.34 ādayo) pubbenivāsādīhi vā tīhi, ambaṭṭhasuttapariyāyena (dī. ni. 1.278 ādayo) vipassanāñāṇaṃ manomayiddhi cha abhiññāyoti imāhi vā aṭṭhahi vijjāhi, sīlesu paripūrakāritā indriyesu guttadvāratā bhojane mattaññutā jāgariyānuyogo satta saddhammā cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānānīti evaṃ pannarasadhammabhedena caraṇena ca samannāgato. So seṭṭho devamānuseti so khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo devesu ca manussesu ca seṭṭho uttamoti. Paṭhamaṃ.

182. In the first sutta of the second chapter, ‘Sappinītīre’ means on the bank of the river named Sappinī. ‘Sanaṅkumāra’: it is said that this Brahmā, having developed jhāna in the time when he was the youth Pañcasikha, was reborn in the Brahma-world and wanders about in the form of a youth. Therefore, they recognize him as ‘Kumāra’ (Youth), but due to his ancientness, he is called ‘Sanaṅkumāra’ (Eternal Youth). ‘Janetasminti’ means ‘in what is born,’ that is, ‘among creatures.’ ‘Ye gottapaṭisārino’ means: those who trace their lineage among creatures. Among those in the world who trace their lineage, the khattiya is the best. ‘Vijjācaraṇasampanno’ means endowed with the three knowledges (such as recollection of past lives) by way of the Bhayabheravasutta, or with these eight knowledges by way of the Ambaṭṭhasutta: insight knowledge, mind-made psychic power, and the six supernormal knowledges; and with the conduct of fifteen kinds: the practice of fulfilling the moral precepts, guardedness of the sense-doors, moderation in eating, the practice of wakefulness, the seven qualities of a good person, and the four form-sphere jhānas. ‘So seṭṭho devamānuse’ means: that arahant whose taints are destroyed is the best, the highest, among both devas and humans. The first sutta.

2. Devadattasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Devadatta Sutta

183. Dutiye [P 1.0220] acirapakkanteti saṅghaṃ bhinditvā nacirasseva veḷuvanato gayāsīsaṃ gate. Assatarinti gadrabhassa vaḷavāya jātaṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

183. In the second sutta, ‘acirapakkante’ means: when Devadatta, having split the Saṅgha, had gone from Veḷuvana to Gayāsīsa not long after. ‘Assatariṃ’ means that which is born from a female donkey. The second sutta.

3. Andhakavindasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Andhakavinda Sutta

184. Tatiye [M 1.0202] andhakavindanti evaṃnāmakaṃ gāmaṃ. Upasaṅkamīti “satthā idānipi vīriyaṃ karoti padhānamanuyuñjati, gacchāmissa santike ṭhatvā sāsanānucchavikaṃ vīriyapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ gāthaṃ vakkhāmī”ti upasaṅkami.

184. In the third sutta, ‘Andhakavindaṃ’ means the village so named. ‘Upasaṅkami’ means he approached, thinking: “The Teacher is even now making an effort, he is engaged in striving. I will go to his presence and speak a verse suitable to the teaching and connected with effort.”

Pantānīti [V 1.0194] janataṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāre ṭhitāni. Saṃyojanavippamokkhāti tāni ca senāsanāni sevamāno na cīvarādīnaṃ atthāya seveyya, atha kho dasasaṃyojanavippamokkhatthāya careyya. Saṅghe vaseti tesu senāsanesu ratiṃ alabhanto upaṭṭhākādīnaṃ cittānurakkhaṇatthaṃ gadrabhapiṭṭhe rajaṃ viya uppatanto araññe acaritvā saṅghamajjhe vaseyya. Rakkhitatto satīmāti tattha ca vasanto sagavacaṇḍo goṇo viya sabrahmacārino avijjhanto aghaṭṭento rakkhitatto satipaṭṭhānaparāyaṇo hutvā vaseyya.

‘Pantāni’ means established in places not frequented by people, having gone beyond the crowd. ‘Saṃyojanavippamokkha’ means that while frequenting such dwellings, one should not do so for the sake of robes and so on; but rather, one should practice for the purpose of release from the ten fetters. ‘Saṅghe vase’ means that if one does not obtain delight in those dwellings, then for the sake of protecting the minds of supporters and so on, with a scattered mind like dust on a donkey’s back, without having wandered in the forest, one should dwell in the midst of the Saṅgha. ‘Rakkhitatto satīmā’ means that while dwelling there, like a fierce bull among the herd, not goring or striking one's fellow monastics, one should dwell with a guarded mind, having the foundations of mindfulness as one's resort.

Idāni saṅghe vasamānassa bhikkhuno bhikkhācāravattaṃ ācikkhanto kulākulantiādimāha. Tattha piṇḍikāya carantoti piṇḍatthāya caramāno. Sevetha pantāni senāsanānīti saṅghamajjhaṃ otaritvā vasamānopi dhurapariveṇe tālanāḷikeraādīni ropetvā upaṭṭhākādisaṃsaṭṭho na vaseyya, cittakallataṃ pana janetvā cittaṃ hāsetvā tosetvā puna pantasenāsane vaseyyāti araññasseva vaṇṇaṃ katheti. Bhayāti vaṭṭabhayato. Abhayeti nibbāne. Vimuttoti adhimutto hutvā vaseyya.

Now, explaining the duty of going for alms for a monk dwelling in the Saṅgha, he speaks beginning with ‘kulākulaṃ’. Therein, ‘piṇḍikāya caranto’ means walking for the sake of alms-food. ‘Sevetha pantāni senāsanāni’ means that even a monk who dwells having descended into the midst of the Saṅgha should not dwell associated with supporters and so on, planting palm trees, coconut trees, etc., in the main monastic compound. But rather, having generated mental readiness, having gladdened and pleased the mind, one should again dwell in a secluded dwelling. Thus, he speaks in praise of the forest dwelling itself. ‘Bhayā’ means from the fear of the round of existence. ‘Abhaye’ means in Nibbāna. ‘Vimutto’ means one should dwell with a mind intent upon it.

Yattha bheravāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne bhayajanakā saviññāṇakā sīhabyagghādayo, aviññāṇakā rattibhāge khāṇuvalliādayo bahū atthi. Sarīsapāti dīghajātikādisarīsapā. Nisīdi tattha bhikkhūti [P 1.0221] tādise ṭhāne bhikkhu nisinno. Iminā idaṃ dīpeti – bhagavā yathā tumhe etarahi tatraṭṭhakabheravārammaṇāni ceva sarīsape ca vijjunicchāraṇādīni ca amanasikatvā nisinnā, evamevaṃ padhānamanuyuttā bhikkhū nisīdantīti.

‘Yattha bheravā’ means in which place there are many fear-inducing things: sentient beings such as lions and tigers, and insentient things in the nighttime, such as tree stumps, vines, and so on. ‘Sarīsapā’ means creeping things such as long-bodied snakes. ‘Nisīdi tattha bhikkhu’ means in such a place a monk is seated. By this, he explains the following: 'O Blessed One, just as you now sit, not paying attention to the terrifying objects present in this place, to the creeping things, and to the flashes of lightning and so on, in the very same way, monks devoted to the striving sit.'

Jātu me diṭṭhanti ekaṃsena mayā diṭṭhaṃ. Na yidaṃ itihītihanti idaṃ itiha itihāti na takkahetu vā nayahetu vā piṭakasampadānena vā [M 1.0203] ahaṃ vadāmi. Ekasmiṃ brahmacariyasminti ekāya dhammadesanāya. Dhammadesanā hi idha brahmacariyanti adhippetā. Maccuhāyinanti maraṇapariccāginaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ.

‘Jātu me diṭṭhanti’: it has been definitively seen by me. ‘Na yidaṃ itihītihanti’: I do not speak of this based on hearsay—‘thus it was, thus it was’—nor by reason of logic, nor by reason of inference, nor by scriptural transmission. ‘Ekasmiṃ brahmacariyasminti’: in one teaching of the Dhamma. For here, the teaching of the Dhamma is intended by ‘the holy life’. ‘Maccuhāyinanti’: of the arahants, who have completely abandoned death.

Dasā ca dasadhā dasāti ettha dasāti daseva, dasadhā dasāti sataṃ, aññe ca dasuttaraṃ sekhasataṃ passāmīti vadati. Sotasamāpannāti maggasotaṃ samāpannā. Atiracchānagāminoti desanāmattametaṃ, avinipātadhammāti attho. Saṅkhātuṃ nopi sakkomīti musāvādabhayena ettakā nāma [V 1.0195] puññabhāgino sattāti gaṇetuṃ na sakkomīti bahuṃ brahmadhammadesanaṃ sandhāya evamāha. Tatiyaṃ.

In ‘Dasā ca dasadhā dasāti’: ‘dasāti’ means just ten; ‘dasadhā dasāti’ means one hundred. And besides these, he says, “I see one hundred and ten trainees.” ‘Sotasamāpannāti’: those who have attained the stream of the path. ‘Atiracchānagāminoti’: this is merely a way of teaching; the meaning is ‘not subject to downfall’. ‘Saṅkhātuṃ nopi sakkomīti’: out of fear of false speech, he says, “I am not able to count that there are such-and-such a number of beings who share in merit,” referring to the extensive Dhamma teaching of the Brahmā. The third.

4. Aruṇavatīsuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Aruṇavatī Sutta

185. Catutthe abhibhūsambhavanti abhibhū ca sambhavo ca. Tesu abhibhūthero sāriputtatthero viya paññāya aggo, sambhavatthero mahāmoggallāno viya samādhinā aggo. Ujjhāyantīti avajjhāyanti, lāmakato vā cintenti. Khiyyantīti, kinnāmetaṃ kinnāmetanti? Aññamaññaṃ kathenti. Vipācentīti vitthārayantā punappunaṃ kathenti. Heṭṭhimena upaḍḍhakāyenāti nābhito paṭṭhāya heṭṭhimakāyena. Pāḷiyaṃ ettakameva āgataṃ. Thero pana “pakativaṇṇaṃ vijahitvā nāgavaṇṇaṃ gahetvā dasseti, supaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ gahetvā vā dassetī”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.13) nayena āgataṃ anekappakāraṃ iddhivikubbanaṃ dassesi. Imā gāthāyo abhāsīti thero kira cintesi – “kathaṃ desitā nu kho dhammadesanā sabbesaṃ piyā assa manāpā”ti. Tato āvajjento – “sabbepi pāsaṇḍā sabbe devamanussā attano attano samaye purisakāraṃ [P 1.0222] vaṇṇayanti, vīriyassa avaṇṇavādī nāma natthi, vīriyapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ katvā desessāmi, evaṃ ayaṃ dhammadesanā sabbesaṃ piyā bhavissati manāpā”ti ñatvā tīsu piṭakesu vicinitvā imā gāthā abhāsi.

185. In the fourth, Abhibhūsambhava means Abhibhū and Sambhava. Among them, the Elder Abhibhū is foremost in wisdom, like the Elder Sāriputta, and the Elder Sambhava is foremost in concentration, like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Ujjhāyanti means they criticize or think badly. Khiyyanti means they say to one another, “What kind of conduct is this? What kind of conduct is this?” Vipācenti means they elaborate and speak of it repeatedly. Heṭṭhimena upaḍḍhakāyena means with the lower half of the body, starting from the navel. Only this much has come in the Pāli text. However, the Elder displayed many kinds of psychic transformations that are mentioned in the manner of, “Having abandoned his natural form and taken on the form of a nāga, he displays it; or having taken on the form of a supaṇṇa, he displays it,” and so on. He spoke these verses means that the Elder, it is said, thought: “How might a Dhamma discourse, when delivered, be dear and agreeable to all?” Then, while reflecting, he knew: “All sectarians, and all devas and humans, praise human effort in their own respective doctrines; there is no one who speaks in dispraise of effort. I will teach by making it connected with effort. In this way, this Dhamma discourse will be dear and agreeable to all.” Having known this, and having investigated in the three Piṭakas, he spoke these verses.

Tattha ārambhathāti ārambhavīriyaṃ karotha. Nikkamathāti nikkamavīriyaṃ karotha. Yuñjathāti payogaṃ karotha parakkamatha. Maccuno senanti maccuno senā nāma kilesasenā, taṃ dhunātha. Jātisaṃsāranti jātiñca [M 1.0204] saṃsārañca, jātisaṅkhātaṃ vā saṃsāraṃ. Dukkhassantaṃ karissatīti vaṭṭadukkhassa paricchedaṃ karissati. Kiṃ pana katvā thero sahassilokadhātuṃ viññāpesīti? Nīlakasiṇaṃ tāva samāpajjitvā sabbattha ālokaṭṭhāne andhakāraṃ phari, odātakasiṇaṃ samāpajjitvā andhakāraṭṭhāne obhāsaṃ. Tato “kimidaṃ andhakāra”nti? Sattānaṃ ābhoge uppanne ālokaṃ dassesi. Ālokaṭṭhāne ālokakiccaṃ natthi, “kiṃ āloko aya”nti? Vicinantānaṃ attānaṃ dassesi. Atha tesaṃ theroti vadantānaṃ imā gāthāyo abhāsi, sabbe osaṭāya parisāya majjhe nisīditvā dhammaṃ desentassa viya saddaṃ suṇiṃsu. Atthopi nesaṃ pākaṭo ahosi. Catutthaṃ.

Therein, 'Begin!' means: make the effort of beginning. 'Strive!' means: make the effort of striving. 'Apply yourselves!' means: make an application, endeavor. 'The army of Death' means: the army of Death is the army of defilements—destroy it. 'Birth and the round of rebirth' means: birth and the round of rebirth, or the round of rebirth known as birth. 'He will make an end of suffering' means: he will make an end to the suffering of the round. But how did the elder make the thousandfold world-system aware? First, he attained the blue kasiṇa and spread darkness in all places of light; then he attained the white kasiṇa and spread light in places of darkness. Then, when the thought "What is this darkness?" arose in the beings, he showed them light. In places of light there is no function for light. To those investigating, "What is this light?" he revealed himself. Then, as they were saying, "It is the elder!", he spoke these verses. They all heard the sound as if he were sitting in the middle of the gathered assembly, teaching the Dhamma. The meaning also became clear to them. The fourth.

5. Parinibbānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Parinibbāna Sutta

186. Pañcame [V 1.0196] upavattane mallānaṃ sālavaneti yatheva hi kadambanadītīrato rājamātuvihāradvārena thūpārāmaṃ gantabbaṃ hoti, evaṃ hiraññavatikāya nāma nadiyā pārimatīrato sālavanaṃ uyyānaṃ. Yathā anurādhapurassa thūpārāmo, evaṃ taṃ kusinārāya hoti. Yathā thūpārāmato dakkhiṇadvārena nagaraṃ pavisanamaggo pācīnamukho gantvā uttarena nivattati, evaṃ uyyānato sālapanti pācīnamukhā gantvā uttarena nivattā. Tasmā taṃ “upavattana”nti vuccati. Tasmiṃ upavattane mallānaṃ sālavane. Antarena [P 1.0223] yamakasālānanti mūlakkhandhaviṭapapattehi aññamaññaṃ saṃsibbitvā ṭhitasālānaṃ antarikāya. Appamādena sampādethāti satiavippavāsena kattabbakiccāni sampādayatha. Iti bhagavā yathā nāma maraṇamañce nipanno mahaddhano kuṭumbiko puttānaṃ dhanasāraṃ ācikkheyya, evamevaṃ parinibbānamañce nipanno pañcacattālīsa vassāni dinnaṃ ovādaṃ sabbaṃ ekasmiṃ appamādapadeyeva pakkhipitvā abhāsi. Ayaṃ tathāgatassa pacchimā vācāti idaṃ pana saṅgītikārānaṃ vacanaṃ.

186. In the fifth section, regarding the Mallās' sāla grove at Upavattana: Indeed, just as one would go from the Kadamba riverbank through the Rājamātā vihāra gate to reach the Thūpārāma, so too from the far bank of the Hiraññavatī river lies the sāla grove park. As the Thūpārāma is to Anurādhapura, so is this to Kusinārā. Just as the path from the Thūpārāma's southern gate enters the city by going eastward and then turning north, so from the park, the row of sāla trees goes eastward and then turns north. Therefore, it is called 'Upavattana.' In that Upavattana, in the sāla grove of the Mallas. 'Between the twin sāla trees' means the space between the sāla trees whose roots, trunks, branches, and leaves were intertwined. 'Strive diligently' means: fulfill your duties without loss of mindfulness. Thus, the Blessed One, just as a wealthy householder lying on his deathbed would instruct his sons on the essence of wealth, in the same way, lying on his Parinibbāna-bed, he gathered all the instruction given over forty-five years into the single term of diligence, and spoke. 'This was the Tathāgata's last word'—this, however, is the statement of the Council Reciters.

Ito paraṃ yaṃ parinibbānaparikammaṃ katvā bhagavā parinibbuto, taṃ dassetuṃ, atha kho bhagavā paṭhamaṃ jhānantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanne bhagavati assāsapassāsānaṃ appavattiṃ disvā, “parinibbuto satthā”ti saññāya devamanussā ekappahārena viraviṃsu, ānandattheropi – “parinibbuto nu kho, bhante, anuruddha bhagavā”ti theraṃ [M 1.0205] pucchi. Thero “na kho, āvuso ānanda, tathāgato parinibbuto, apica saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpanno”ti āha. Kathaṃ pana so aññāsi? Thero kira satthārā saddhiṃyeva taṃ taṃ samāpattiṃ samāpajjanto yāva nevasaññānāsaññāyatanavuṭṭhānaṃ, tāva gantvā, “idāni bhagavā nirodhaṃ samāpanno, antonirodhe ca kālaṃkiriyā nāma natthī”ti aññāsi.

After this, to show the preliminary work for Parinibbāna which the Blessed One performed before attaining Parinibbāna, the passage beginning, 'Then, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna...' was spoken. Therein, when the Blessed One had attained the cessation of perception and feeling, the devas and humans, seeing the non-occurrence of his in-breaths and out-breaths, cried out at once with the perception, 'The Teacher has attained Parinibbāna!' Venerable Ānanda also asked the Elder, 'Venerable Anuruddha, has the Blessed One indeed attained Parinibbāna?' The Elder replied, 'No, friend Ānanda, the Tathāgata has not attained Parinibbāna; but indeed, he has attained the cessation of perception and feeling.' But how did he know? It is said that the Elder, entering into those respective meditative attainments together with the Teacher and proceeding in sequence as far as the emergence from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, knew thus: 'Now the Blessed One has attained cessation, and within cessation, there is no such thing as dying.'

Atha kho bhagavā saññāvedayitanirodhasamāpattito vuṭṭhahitvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpajji…pe… tatiyajjhānā vuṭṭhahitvā catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajjīti ettha pana bhagavā catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji, terasasu ṭhānesu dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ… tathā tatiyaṃ… pannarasasu ṭhānesu catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji. Kathaṃ? Dasasu asubhesu dvattiṃsākāre aṭṭhasu [V 1.0197] kasiṇesu mettākaruṇāmuditesu ānāpāne paricchedākāseti imesu tāva catuvīsatiyā ṭhānesu paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji. Ṭhapetvā pana dvattiṃsākārañca dasa ca asubhāni sesesu terasasu dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ… tesuyeva tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji. Aṭṭhasu pana kasiṇesu upekkhābrahmavihāre ānāpāne paricchedākāse catūsu arūpesūti imesu [P 1.0224] pannarasasu ṭhānesu catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpajji. Ayampi ca saṅkhepakathāva. Nibbānapuraṃ pavisanto pana bhagavā dhammassāmi sabbāpi catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassasaṅkhā samāpattiyo pavisitvā videsaṃ gacchanto ñātijanaṃ āliṅgetvā viya sabbasamāpattisukhaṃ anubhavitvā paviṭṭho.

Then the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception…pe… having emerged from the third jhāna, he entered the fourth jhāna. In this regard, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna in twenty-four instances, the second jhāna in thirteen instances… similarly the third jhāna… and the fourth jhāna in fifteen instances. How? In the ten impurities, the thirty-two parts, the eight kasiṇas, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, mindfulness of breathing, and the limited space—in these twenty-four instances, he entered the first jhāna. But excluding the thirty-two parts and the ten impurities, in the remaining thirteen instances, he entered the second jhāna… in those very instances, he entered the third jhāna. But in the eight kasiṇas, the divine abiding of equanimity, mindfulness of breathing, the limited space, and the four formless states—in these fifteen instances, he entered the fourth jhāna. And this is just a condensed account. When entering the city of Nibbāna, the Blessed One, the Lord of the Dhamma, having entered all the attainments numbering twenty-four hundred thousand crores, entered after having experienced the bliss of all the attainments, just as one going to a foreign land embraces his relatives.

Catutthajjhānā vuṭṭhahitvā samanantarā bhagavā parinibbāyīti ettha ca jhānasamanantaraṃ paccavekkhaṇasamanantaranti, dve samanantarāni. Catutthajjhānā vuṭṭhāya bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇassa tattheva parinibbānaṃ jhānasamanantaraṃ nāma, catutthajjhānā vuṭṭhahitvā puna jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhitvā bhavaṅgaṃ otiṇṇassa tattheva parinibbānaṃ paccavekkhaṇasamanantaraṃ nāma. Imāni dvepi samanantarāneva. Bhagavā pana jhānaṃ samāpajjitvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya jhānaṅgāni paccavekkhitvā bhavaṅgacittena abyākatena dukkhasaccena parinibbāyi. Ye hi keci buddhā vā paccekabuddhā vā ariyasāvakā vā antamaso kunthakipillikaṃ upādāya sabbe bhavaṅgacitteneva abyākatena dukkhasaccena kālaṃ karonti.

‘Having arisen from the fourth jhāna, immediately thereafter the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna.’ In this statement, there are two immediacies: immediacy after jhāna and immediacy after reviewing. Having arisen from the fourth jhāna and descended into the life-continuum, the attainment of Parinibbāna right there is called ‘immediacy after jhāna.’ Having arisen from the fourth jhāna, again reviewed the jhāna factors, and descended into the life-continuum, the attainment of Parinibbāna right there is called ‘immediacy after reviewing.’ These two are indeed immediacies. The Blessed One, however, having attained the jhāna, having arisen from the jhāna, and having reviewed the jhāna factors, attained Parinibbāna with the life-continuum consciousness, which is undeclared and included in the truth of suffering. For indeed, all beings—be they Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or noble disciples, down to the very last, beginning with insects and ants—pass away only with the life-continuum consciousness, which is undeclared and included in the truth of suffering.

Bhūtāti [M 1.0206] sattā. Appaṭipuggaloti paṭibhāgapuggalavirahito. Balappattoti dasavidhaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ patto. Uppādavayadhamminoti uppādavayasabhāvā. Tesaṃ vūpasamoti tesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ vūpasamo. Sukhoti asaṅkhataṃ nibbānameva sukhanti attho. Tadāsīti “saha parinibbānā mahābhūmicālo ahosī”ti evaṃ mahāparinibbāne (dī. ni. 2.220) vuttaṃ bhūmicālaṃ sandhāyāha. So hi lomahaṃsanako ca bhiṃsanako ca āsi. Sabbākāravarūpeteti sabbākāravaraguṇūpete. Nāhu assāsapassāsoti na jāto assāsapassāso. Anejoti taṇhāsaṅkhātāya ejāya abhāvena anejo.
