Santimārabbhāti anupādisesaṃ nibbānaṃ ārabbha paṭicca sandhāya. Cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Parinibbutoti khandhaparinibbānena parinibbuto. Asallīnenāti anallīnena asaṅkuṭitena suvikasiteneva cittena. Vedanaṃ ajjhavāsayīti [P 1.0225] vedanaṃ adhivāsesi, na vedanānuvattī hutvā ito cito samparivatti. Vimokkhoti [V 1.0198] kenaci dhammena anāvaraṇavimokkho sabbaso apaññattibhāvūpagamo pajjotanibbānasadiso jātoti. Pañcamaṃ.

‘Beings’ (bhūtā) means living beings. ‘Without a counterpart’ (appaṭipuggala) means devoid of an equal individual. ‘Attained to strength’ (balappatta) means having attained the tenfold knowledge-power. ‘Subject to arising and passing away’ (uppādavayadhammino) means having the nature of arising and passing away. ‘Their cessation’ (tesaṃ vūpasamo) means the cessation of those formations. ‘Happiness’ (sukha) means that the unconditioned Nibbāna itself is happiness; this is the meaning. ‘At that time’ (tadāsi): He said this referring to the great earthquake mentioned in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, which occurred simultaneously with the Parinibbāna. For that earthquake was both hair-raising and terrifying. ‘Endowed with all excellent qualities’ (sabbākāravarūpeta) means endowed with all kinds of excellent virtues. ‘There was no in-breath or out-breath’ (nāhu assāsapassāso) means no in-breath or out-breath occurred. ‘Unshaken’ (aneja) means unshaken due to the absence of the agitation called craving. ‘With reference to peace’ (santimārabbha) means with reference to, based on, and concerning Nibbāna without remaining residue. ‘Endowed with vision’ (cakkhumā) means endowed with vision through the five eyes. ‘Fully extinguished’ (parinibbuta) means fully extinguished by the parinibbāna of the aggregates. ‘With an unshrinking mind’ (asallīnena) means with a mind that was not clinging, not contracted, but fully blossomed. ‘He endured the feeling’ (vedanaṃ ajjhavāsayī) means he endured the feeling; not following after the feeling, he did not toss and turn hither and thither. ‘Liberation’ (vimokkha) means a liberation unobstructed by any state, the complete attainment of a state beyond designation, like the extinguishing of a lamp, has occurred. Fifth.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Brahmasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the Exposition of the Brahmasaṃyutta is concluded.

7. Brāhmaṇasaṃyuttaṃ

7. The Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta

1. Arahantavaggo

1. The Arahant Chapter

1. Dhanañjānīsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Dhanañjānī Sutta

187. Brāhmaṇasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0199][P 1.0226][M 1.0207] paṭhame dhanañjānīti dhanañjānigottā. Ukkaṭṭhagottā kiresā. Sesabrāhmaṇā kira brahmuno mukhato jātā, dhanañjānigottā matthakaṃ bhinditvā nikkhantāti tesaṃ laddhi. Udānaṃ udānesīti kasmā udānesi? So kira brāhmaṇo micchādiṭṭhiko “buddho dhammo saṅgho”ti vutte kaṇṇe pidahati, thaddho khadirakhāṇusadiso. Brāhmaṇī pana sotāpannā ariyasāvikā. Brāhmaṇo dānaṃ dento pañcasatānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ appodakaṃ pāyāsaṃ deti, brāhmaṇī buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa nānārasabhojanaṃ. Brāhmaṇassa dānadivase brāhmaṇī tassa vasavattitāya pahīnamaccheratāya ca sahatthā parivisati. Brāhmaṇiyā pana dānadivase brāhmaṇo pātova gharā nikkhamitvā palāyati. Athekadivasaṃ brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇiyā saddhiṃ asammantetvā pañcasate brāhmaṇe nimantetvā brāhmaṇiṃ āha – “sve bhoti amhākaṃ ghare pañcasatā brāhmaṇā bhuñjissantī”ti. Mayā kiṃ kātabbaṃ brāhmaṇāti? Tayā aññaṃ kiñci kātabbaṃ natthi, sabbaṃ pacanaparivesanaṃ aññe karissanti. Yaṃ pana tvaṃ ṭhitāpi nisinnāpi khipitvāpi ukkāsitvāpi “namo buddhassā”ti tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa namakkāraṃ karosi, taṃ sve ekadivasamattaṃ mā akāsi. Taṃ hi sutvā brāhmaṇā anattamanā honti, mā maṃ brāhmaṇehi bhindasīti. Tvaṃ brāhmaṇehi [P 1.0227] vā bhijja devehi vā, ahaṃ pana satthāraṃ anussaritvā na sakkomi anamassamānā saṇṭhātunti. Bhoti kulasatike gāme gāmadvārampi tāva pidahituṃ vāyamanti, tvaṃ dvīhaṅgulehi pidahitabbaṃ mukhaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ bhojanakālamattaṃ pidahituṃ na sakkosīti. Evaṃ punappunaṃ kathetvāpi so nivāretuṃ asakkonto ussīsake ṭhapitaṃ maṇḍalaggakhaggaṃ [V 1.0200] gahetvā – “bhoti sace sve brāhmaṇesu nisinnesu taṃ [M 1.0208] muṇḍasamaṇakaṃ namassasi, iminā taṃ khaggena pādatalato paṭṭhāya yāva kesamatthakā kaḷīraṃ viya koṭṭetvā rāsiṃ karissāmī”ti imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

187. In the first sutta of the Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta, 'Dhanañjānī' refers to one of the Dhanañjānī clan. It is said that this is a noble clan. It is said that other brahmins were born from Brahmā’s mouth, but those of the Dhanañjānī clan broke through the top of his head and emerged—such was their belief. Regarding the phrase 'she uttered an inspired utterance': why did she utter it? It is said that the brahmin held wrong views. When 'The Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha' was said, he would cover his ears; he was stubborn, like an acacia stake. The brahmin woman, however, was a stream-enterer, a noble female disciple. When the brahmin gave alms, he offered thick rice-porridge with little water to five hundred brahmins, while the brahmin woman served the Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, with food of various flavors. On the brahmin’s almsgiving day, the brahmin woman, being under his authority and having abandoned stinginess, served the meal with her own hands. But on her almsgiving day, the brahmin would leave the house early in the morning and flee. Then one day, without consulting his wife, the brahmin invited five hundred brahmins and told her, 'Tomorrow, lady, five hundred brahmins will eat in our house.' 'What should I do, brahmin?' 'You need not do anything else; others will handle all the cooking and serving. But that you, whether standing, sitting, sneezing, or coughing, pay homage to that shaveling ascetic, saying, “Homage to the Buddha”—do not do that for even a single day tomorrow. For hearing it, the brahmins become displeased. Do not cause me to be divided from the brahmins!' 'Be you divided from the brahmins or from the gods, but I, while recollecting the Teacher, am unable to remain without paying homage.' 'Lady, in a family-owned village, they manage to close even the village gate. Yet you are unable to close your mouth, which can be closed with two fingers, for just the duration of the brahmins' meal?' Thus, though he spoke repeatedly, being unable to restrain her, he took the sword with a circular tip that was kept at the head of the bed and threatened, 'Lady, if tomorrow, while the brahmins are seated, you pay homage to that shaveling ascetic, with this sword I will chop you from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head like a bamboo shoot and make a pile of you!' Then he spoke this verse:

“Iminā maṇḍalaggena, pādato yāva matthakā;

Kaḷīramiva chejjāmi, yadi micchaṃ na kāhasi.

With this circular-tipped sword, from foot to head, I will cut you like a bamboo shoot, if you do not do my will.

“Sace buddhoti bhaṇasi, sace dhammoti bhāsasi;

Sace saṅghoti kittesi, jīvantī me nivesane”ti.

If you say 'Buddha,' if you speak of 'Dhamma,' if you praise the 'Saṅgha,' while living in my house.

Ariyasāvikā pana pathavī viya duppakampā, sineru viya dupparivattiyā. Sā tena naṃ evamāha –

But the noble female disciple is like the earth, difficult to shake; like Mount Sineru, difficult to move. She, therefore, said this to him:

“Sace me aṅgamaṅgāni, kāmaṃ chejjasi brāhmaṇa;

Nevāhaṃ viramissāmi, buddhaseṭṭhassa sāsanā.

O brahmin, though you may cut my major and minor limbs at will, I will not desist from the teaching of the Supreme Buddha.

“Nāhaṃ okkā varadharā, sakkā rodhayituṃ jinā;

Dhītāhaṃ buddhaseṭṭhassa, chinda vā maṃ vadhassu vā”ti.

I do not yet bear the final, most excellent body; it is possible to be made to grow by the Conqueror. I am the daughter of the Supreme Buddha. Cut me or kill me as you will.

Evaṃ dhanañjānigajjitaṃ nāma gajjantī pañca gāthāsatāni abhāsi. Brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇiṃ parāmasituṃ vā paharituṃ vā asakkonto “bhoti yaṃ te ruccati, taṃ karohī”ti vatvā khaggaṃ sayane khipi. Punadivase gehaṃ haritupalittaṃ kārāpetvā lājāpuṇṇaghaṭamālāgandhādīhi tattha tattha alaṅkārāpetvā pañcannaṃ brāhmaṇasatānaṃ navasappisakkharamadhuyuttaṃ appodakapāyāsaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā kālaṃ ārocāpesi.

In this way, roaring what is called the 'Roar of Dhanañjānī,' she spoke five hundred stanzas. The brahmin, not daring to touch or strike the brahmin woman, said, 'Madam, do as you please,' and threw the sword onto the bed. The next day, he had the house smeared with fresh cow-dung and adorned in various places with parched grain, full water-pots, garlands, perfumes, and so on. He had a thick milk-rice prepared with little water, mixed with fresh ghee, sugar, and honey, for five hundred brahmins and had the time announced.

Brāhmaṇīpi pātova gandhodakena sayaṃ nhāyitvā sahassagghanakaṃ ahatavatthaṃ nivāsetvā pañcasatagghanakaṃ ekaṃsaṃ katvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā [P 1.0228] suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gahetvā bhattagge brāhmaṇe [V 1.0201] parivisamānā tehi saddhiṃ ekapantiyaṃ nisinnassa tassa brāhmaṇassa bhattaṃ upasaṃharantī dunnikkhitte dārubhaṇḍe pakkhali. Pakkhalanaghaṭṭanāya dukkhā vedanā uppajji. Tasmiṃ samaye dasabalaṃ sari. Satisampannatāya pana pāyāsapātiṃ achaḍḍetvā saṇikaṃ otāretvā bhūmiyaṃ saṇṭhapetvā pañcannaṃ brāhmaṇasatānaṃ majjhe sirasi añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā yena veḷuvanaṃ, tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi.

The brahmin woman also, having bathed herself early in the morning with scented water, put on an unused garment worth a thousand, draped another worth five hundred over one shoulder, and, adorned with all her ornaments, took a golden ladle. While serving the brahmins in the dining hall, as she was bringing food to her brahmin husband who was seated in the same row with them, she stumbled on a carelessly placed wooden item. A painful feeling arose from the stumble and impact. At that moment, she recollected the Ten-Powered One. Due to her mindfulness, instead of dropping the bowl of milk-rice, she slowly lowered it and placed it firmly on the ground. Then, in the midst of the five hundred brahmins, she placed her joined hands on her head, and bowing with her joined hands in the direction of the Veḷuvana monastery, she uttered this inspired utterance.

Tasmiñca [M 1.0209] samaye tesu brāhmaṇesu keci bhuttā honti, keci bhuñjamānā, keci hatthe otāritamattā, kesañci bhojanaṃ purato ṭhapitamattaṃ hoti. Te taṃ saddaṃ sutvāva sinerumattena muggarena sīse pahaṭā viya kaṇṇesu sūlena viddhā viya dukkhadomanassaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamānā “iminā aññaladdhikena mayaṃ gharaṃ pavesitā”ti kujjhitvā hatthe piṇḍaṃ chaḍḍetvā mukhena gahitaṃ niṭṭhubhitvā dhanuṃ disvā kākā viya brāhmaṇaṃ akkosamānā disāvidisā pakkamiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo evaṃ bhijjitvā gacchante brāhmaṇe disvā brāhmaṇiṃ sīsato paṭṭhāya oloketvā, “idameva bhayaṃ sampassamānā mayaṃ hiyyo paṭṭhāya bhotiṃ yācantā na labhimhā”ti nānappakārehi brāhmaṇiṃ akkositvā, etaṃ “evamevaṃ panā”tiādivacanaṃ avoca.

And at that time, among those brahmins, some had eaten, some were in the middle of eating, some had just put their hands to the food, and for some the food had just been placed before them. As soon as they heard that sound, experiencing pain and displeasure as if they had been struck on the head with a club the size of Mount Sineru or pierced in the ears with a stake, they became angry, thinking, 'We have been brought into this house by this holder of a different view!' They threw away the lump of food in their hands, spat out what they had taken into their mouths, and, like crows that have seen a bow, they reviled the brahmin and departed in all directions. Seeing the brahmins thus breaking up and leaving, the brahmin looked at his wife from head to toe and, after scolding her in various ways, saying, 'It was because I foresaw this very danger that I have been begging you since yesterday, but I did not succeed!', he spoke those words beginning, 'Is it thus...'

Upasaṅkamīti “samaṇo gotamo gāmanigamaraṭṭhapūjito, na sakkā gantvā yaṃ vā taṃ vā vatvā santajjetuṃ, ekameva naṃ pañhaṃ pucchissāmī”ti gacchantova “kiṃsu chetvā”ti gāthaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā – “sace ‘asukassa nāma vadhaṃ rocemī’ti vakkhati, atha naṃ ‘ye tuyhaṃ na ruccanti, te māretukāmosi, lokavadhāya uppanno, kiṃ tuyhaṃ samaṇabhāvenā’ti? Niggahessāmi. Sace ‘na kassaci vadhaṃ rocemī’ti vakkhati, atha naṃ ‘tvaṃ rāgādīnampi vadhaṃ na icchasi. Kasmā samaṇo hutvā āhiṇḍasī’ti? Niggahessāmī. Iti imaṃ ubhatokoṭikaṃ pañhaṃ samaṇo gotamo neva gilituṃ na uggilituṃ sakkhissatī”ti cintetvā upasaṅkami[P 1.0229]. Sammodīti attano paṇḍitatāya kuddhabhāvaṃ adassetvā madhurakathaṃ kathento sammodi. Pañho devatāsaṃyutte kathito. Sesampi heṭṭhā vitthāritamevāti. Paṭhamaṃ.

He approached: Thinking, 'The ascetic Gotama is honored by villages, market-towns, and countries; it is not possible to go and threaten him by saying just anything. I will ask him just one question,' and while still on his way, he composed the verse 'What having cut off...' and planned thus: 'If he says, “I approve of the killing of such-and-such,” then I will refute him, saying: “You wish to kill those who do not please you; you have arisen for the destruction of the world. What is the use of your asceticism?” If he says, “I do not approve of the killing of anyone,” then I will refute him, saying: “You do not desire the destruction even of passion and so forth. Why then, having become an ascetic, do you wander about?” Thus, the ascetic Gotama will be able neither to swallow nor to spit out this two-pronged question.' Thinking thus, he approached. He exchanged friendly greetings: due to his own cleverness, he did not show his state of anger, but spoke sweet words. The question is spoken of in the Devatāsaṃyutta. The remainder has already been explained in detail below. The first.

2. Akkosasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Akkosaka Sutta.

188. Dutiye [V 1.0202] akkosakabhāradvājoti bhāradvājova so, pañcamattehi pana gāthā satehi tathāgataṃ akkosanto āgatoti. “Akkosakabhāradvājo”ti tassa saṅgītikārehi nāmaṃ gahitaṃ. Kupito anattamanoti “samaṇena gotamena mayhaṃ jeṭṭhakabhātaraṃ pabbājentena [M 1.0210] jāni katā, pakkho bhinno”ti kodhena kupito domanassena ca anattamano hutvāti attho. Akkosatīti “corosi, bālosi, mūḷhosi, thenosi, oṭṭhosi, meṇḍosi, goṇosi, gadrabhosi, tiracchānagatosi, nerayikosī”ti dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosati. Paribhāsatīti “hotu muṇḍakasamaṇaka, ‘adaṇḍo aha’nti karosi, idāni te rājakulaṃ gantvā daṇḍaṃ āropessāmī”tiādīni vadanto paribhāsati nāma.

188. In the second sutta, Akkosaka Bhāradvāja: he was that very Bhāradvāja, but he came intending to abuse the Tathāgata with five hundred stanzas. Thus, the compilers of the canon gave him the name 'Akkosaka Bhāradvāja.' Angry and displeased: this means he became angry with anger and displeased with grief, thinking, 'By giving the going forth to my elder brother, the ascetic Gotama has caused the decline of our clan; our faction has been broken.' He abuses: he abuses with the ten grounds for abuse, saying, 'You are a thief, you are a fool, you are deluded, you are a cheat, you are a camel, you are a ram, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are an animal, you are one destined for hell.' He reviles: he is said to revile when saying such things as, 'So be it, you shaveling, you wretched ascetic! Do you act thinking, “I am beyond punishment”? Now I will go to the royal court and have a penalty imposed on you.'

Sambhuñjatīti ekato bhuñjati. Vītiharatīti katassa paṭikāraṃ karoti. Bhagavantaṃ kho, gotamanti kasmā evamāha? “Tavevetaṃ, brāhmaṇa, tavevetaṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti kirassa sutvā. “Isayo nāma kupitā sapanaṃ denti kisavacchādayo viyā”ti anussavavasena “sapati maṃ maññe samaṇo gotamo”ti bhayaṃ uppajji. Tasmā evamāha.

He eats with means he eats together. He exchanges means he retaliates for what was done. Why did he say, 'Venerable Gotama...'? It is said that upon hearing, 'This is yours, brahmin, this is yours, brahmin,' fear arose in him. Based on hearsay—having heard that 'Sages, when angered, utter curses, like Kisavaccha and others'—he thought, 'I think the ascetic Gotama is cursing me.' Therefore, he spoke thus.

Dantassāti nibbisevanassa. Tādinoti tādilakkhaṇaṃ pattassa. Tasseva tena pāpiyoti tasseva puggalassa tena kodhena pāpaṃ hoti. Sato upasammatīti satiyā samannāgato hutvā adhivāseti. Ubhinnaṃ tikicchantānanti ubhinnaṃ tikicchantaṃ. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Yo puggalo sato upasammati, ubhinnamatthaṃ carati tikicchati sādheti, taṃ puggalaṃ janā bāloti maññanti. Kīdisā janā? Ye dhammassa akovidā. Dhammassāti pañcakkhandhadhammassa vā catusaccadhammassa vā. Akovidāti tasmiṃ dhamme akusalā andhabālaputhujjanā. Dutiyaṃ.

Of the tamed means of one who is unperturbed. Of such a one means of one who has attained the characteristic of being 'such a one.' For him it is worse means for that very person, it is evil because of that anger. Being mindful, he is calm means, being endowed with mindfulness, he endures. Of one who is a physician to both means of one who is a physician to both. Or this is the reading: The person who, being mindful, is calm, and who practices for the welfare of both, who cures and accomplishes it—people regard that person as a fool. What kind of people? Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma. Of the Dhamma means of the Dhamma of the five aggregates or of the Dhamma of the Four Truths. Unskilled means those who are unskillful in that Dhamma, who are blind, foolish worldlings. The second.

3. Asurindakasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Asurindaka Sutta.

189. Tatiye [P 1.0230] asurindakabhāradvājoti akkosakabhāradvājassa kaniṭṭho. Kupitoti teneva kāraṇena kuddho. Jayañcevassa taṃ hotīti asseva taṃ jayaṃ hoti, so jayo hotīti attho[V 1.0203]. Katamassāti? Yā titikkhā vijānato adhivāsanāya guṇaṃ vijānantassa titikkhā adhivāsanā, ayaṃ tassa vijānatova jayo. Bālo [M 1.0211] pana pharusaṃ bhaṇanto “mayhaṃ jayo”ti kevalaṃ jayaṃ maññati. Tatiyaṃ.

189. In the third sutta, Asurindakabhāradvāja is the younger brother of Akkosakabhāradvāja. Angry means he was angry for that very reason. And that is his victory means: for that very one, that is the victory; that victory comes to be. This is the meaning. For whom? For one who knows patience, who understands the virtue of endurance. Whatever patience, which is endurance, there is, this victory belongs to that very one who knows. But the fool, while speaking harshly, merely thinks, 'Mine is the victory.' The third.

4. Bilaṅgīkasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Bilaṅgika Sutta.

190. Catutthe bilaṅgikabhāradvājoti bhāradvājova so, nānappakāraṃ pana suddhañca sambhārayuttañca kañjikaṃ kāretvā vikkiṇāpento bahudhanaṃ saṅkharīti “bilaṅgikabhāradvājo”ti tassa saṅgītikārehi nāmaṃ gahitaṃ. Tuṇhībhūtoti “tayo me jeṭṭhakabhātaro iminā pabbājitā”ti ativiya kuddho kiñci vattuṃ asakkonto tuṇhībhūto aṭṭhāsi. Gāthā pana devatāsaṃyutte kathitāva. Catutthaṃ.

190. In the fourth sutta, Bilaṅgikabhāradvāja: he was indeed a Bhāradvāja. However, because he had various kinds of pure and mixed gruel prepared and sold, and amassed much wealth, the compilers of the canon gave him the name ‘Bilaṅgikabhāradvāja’. Remained silent means: being exceedingly angry, thinking, ‘My three elder brothers have been given the going forth by this one,’ and unable to say anything, he stood silent. The verse, however, has already been stated in the Devatāsaṃyutta. The fourth.

5. Ahiṃsakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ahiṃsaka Sutta.

191. Pañcame ahiṃsakabhāradvājoti bhāradvājovesa, ahiṃsakapañhaṃ pana pucchi, tenassetaṃ saṅgītikārehi nāmaṃ gahitaṃ. Nāmena vā esa ahiṃsako, gottena bhāradvājo. Ahiṃsakāhanti ahiṃsako ahaṃ, iti me bhavaṃ gotamo jānātūti āha. Tathā cassāti tathā ce assa, bhaveyyāsīti attho. Na hiṃsatīti na viheṭheti na dukkhāpeti. Pañcamaṃ.

191. In the fifth sutta, Ahiṃsakabhāradvāja: this one was a Bhāradvāja, but because he asked a question concerning non-violence, the compilers of the canon gave him this name. Alternatively, this one was Ahiṃsaka by name and Bhāradvāja by clan. Ahiṃsaka I am: he said, 'I am Ahiṃsaka; thus may the Venerable Gotama know me.' Regarding Tathā cassa, the word division is Tathā ce assa. The meaning is: 'May you be as your name is.' He does not harm means: he does not harass, he does not cause suffering. The fifth.

6. Jaṭāsuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Jaṭā Sutta.

192. Chaṭṭhe jaṭābhāradvājoti bhāradvājovesa, jaṭāpañhassa pana pucchitattā saṅgītikārehi evaṃ vutto. Sesaṃ devatāsaṃyutte kathitameva. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

192. In the sixth sutta, Jaṭābhāradvāja: this one was a Bhāradvāja, but because he asked the question concerning the tangle, he was thus referred to by the compilers of the canon. The rest has already been stated in the Devatāsaṃyutta. The sixth.

7. Suddhikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Suddhika Sutta.

193. Sattame [P 1.0231] suddhikabhāradvājoti ayampi bhāradvājova, suddhikapañhassa pana pucchitattā [V 1.0204] saṅgītikārehi evaṃ vutto. Sīlavāpi tapokaranti sīlasampannopi tapokammaṃ karonto. Vijjācaraṇasampannoti ettha vijjāti tayo vedā. Caraṇanti gottacaraṇaṃ. So sujjhati na aññā itarā pajāti so tevijjo brāhmaṇo sujjhati, ayaṃ pana aññā nāmikā [M 1.0212] pajā na sujjhatīti vadati. Bahumpi palapaṃ jappanti bahumpi palapaṃ jappanto, “brāhmaṇova sujjhatī”ti evaṃ vacanasahassampi bhaṇantoti attho. Antokasambūti anto kilesapūtisabhāvena pūtiko. Saṃkiliṭṭhoti kiliṭṭhehi kāyakammādīhi samannāgato. Sattamaṃ.

193. In the seventh sutta, Suddhikabhāradvāja: This one too was a Bhāradvāja, but because he asked the question concerning purity, he was thus called by the compilers of the scriptures. ‘Even one endowed with virtue, performing austerities’: Even though endowed with virtue, performing the act of austerity. ‘Endowed with knowledge and conduct’: Here, ‘knowledge’ means the three Vedas. ‘Conduct’ means lineage conduct. ‘He is purified, not other beings’: He says that the brahmin possessing the three Vedas is purified, but these other beings are not purified. ‘Though they utter much babble’: The meaning is, though uttering much babble, even speaking a thousand verses thus, ‘Only the brahmin is purified.’ ‘Foul within’: Putrid within, by the nature of being foul with defilements. ‘Defiled’: Endowed with defiled bodily actions and so forth. The seventh.

8. Aggikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Aggika Sutta

194. Aṭṭhame aggikabhāradvājoti ayampi bhāradvājova, aggi paricaraṇavasena panassa saṅgītikārehi etaṃ nāmaṃ gahitaṃ. Sannihito hotīti saṃyojito hoti. Aṭṭhāsīti kasmā tattha aṭṭhāsi? Bhagavā kira paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento imaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā cintesi – “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo evarūpaṃ aggapāyāsaṃ gahetvā ‘mahābrahmānaṃ bhojemī’ti aggimhi jhāpento aphalaṃ karoti apāyamaggaṃ okkamati, imaṃ laddhiṃ avissajjanto apāyapūrakova bhavissati, gacchāmissa dhammadesanāya, micchādiṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā pabbājetvā cattāro magge ceva cattāri ca phalāni demī”ti, tasmā pubbaṇhasamaye rājagahaṃ pavisitvā tattha aṭṭhāsi.

194. In the eighth sutta, Aggikabhāradvāja: This one too was a Bhāradvāja, but by means of his tending the fire, this name was adopted for him by the compilers of the scriptures. ‘It was prepared’: It was combined with ghee. ‘He stood’: Why did he stand there? It is said that the Blessed One, surveying the world at dawn, saw this brahmin and thought: ‘This brahmin, taking such excellent milk-rice and burning it in the fire, thinking, “I will feed the Great Brahmā,” is performing a fruitless act and is entering the path to the lower realms. Without abandoning this view, he will only be a filler of the lower realms. I shall go and, with a Dhamma teaching for him, I will shatter his wrong view, ordain him, and give him the four paths and the four fruits.’ Therefore, in the forenoon, he entered Rājagaha and stood there.

Tīhi vijjāhīti tīhi vedehi. Jātimāti yāva sattamā pitāmahayugā parisuddhāya jātiyā samannāgato. Sutavā bahūti bahu nānappakāre ganthe sutavā. Somaṃ bhuñjeyyāti so tevijjo brāhmaṇo imaṃ pāyāsaṃ bhuñjituṃ yutto, tumhākaṃ panesa pāyāso ayuttoti vadati.

‘With the three knowledges’: With the three Vedas. ‘Of high birth’: Endowed with a pure lineage up to the seventh generation of ancestors. ‘Much-learned’: Learned in many various kinds of texts. ‘He may eat this’: He says that the brahmin who has mastered the three Vedas is fit to eat this milk-rice, but for you, this milk-rice is not suitable.

Vedīti pubbenivāsañāṇena jāni paṭivijjhi. Saggāpāyanti dibbena cakkhunā saggampi apāyampi passati. Jātikkhayanti arahattaṃ. Abhiññāvositoti jānitvā vositavosāno. Brāhmaṇo [P 1.0232] bhavanti avīcito yāva bhavaggā bhotā gotamena sadiso jātisampanno khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇo natthi, bhavaṃyeva brāhmaṇoti.

‘The Knower’: He knew and penetrated with the knowledge of past lives. ‘Heaven and the Plane of Misery’: He sees both heaven and the plane of misery with the divine eye. ‘The Destruction of Birth’: Arahantship. ‘One who has reached the end through direct knowledge’: Having known, he has reached the final completion. ‘The Venerable Brahmin’: From the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence, there is no taintless brahmin accomplished in birth who is equal to the Venerable Gotama. The Venerable One alone is the Brahmin.

Evañca pana vatvā suvaṇṇapātiṃ pūretvā dasabalassa pāyāsaṃ upanāmesi. Satthā uppattiṃ dīpetvā [V 1.0205] bhojanaṃ paṭikkhipanto gāthābhigītaṃ metiādimāha. Tattha gāthābhigītanti gāthāhi abhigītaṃ. Abhojaneyyanti abhuñjitabbaṃ[M 1.0213]. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, mayhaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ bhikkhācāravattena ṭhitassa kaṭacchumattampi dātuṃ nāsakkhi, idāni pana mayā tuyhaṃ kilañjamhi tile vitthārentena viya sabbe buddhaguṇā pakāsitā, iti gāyanena gāyitvā laddhaṃ viya idaṃ bhojanaṃ hoti, tasmā idaṃ gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyanti. Sampassataṃ, brāhmaṇa, nesa dhammoti, brāhmaṇa, atthañca dhammañca sampassantānaṃ “evarūpaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjitabba”nti esa dhammo na hoti. Sudhābhojanampi gāthābhigītaṃ panudanti buddhā, gāthāhi gāyitvā laddhaṃ buddhā nīharantiyeva. Dhamme sati, brāhmaṇa, vuttiresāti, brāhmaṇa, dhamme sati dhammaṃ apekkhitvā dhamme patiṭṭhāya jīvitaṃ kappentānaṃ esā vutti ayaṃ ājīvo – evarūpaṃ nīharitvā dhammaladdhameva bhuñjitabbanti.

Having said this, he filled a golden bowl and offered the milk-rice to the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher, explaining the occasion, declined the food and spoke the words beginning with 'Gāthābhigītaṃ me...'. Herein, ‘gāthābhigītaṃ’ means obtained by singing verses. ‘Abhojaneyyaṃ’ means not to be eaten. This is what is meant: ‘You, brahmin, for so long, while I stood observing the practice of an alms-farer, were unable to give me even a spoonful; but now, it is as if this food has been obtained by me singing verses for you, like one scattering sesame seeds on a coarse mat, after all the Buddha's virtues were proclaimed. Therefore, this food obtained by singing verses is not to be eaten by me.’ ‘For those who see, brahmin, this is not the principle’: O brahmin, for those who clearly see the benefit and the cause, it is not the principle that ‘such food should be eaten’. ‘The Buddhas reject what is obtained by singing verses’: The Buddhas indeed reject what is obtained by singing with verses, even if it were the food of the gods. ‘When the Dhamma is present, brahmin, this is the mode of conduct’: O brahmin, when the Dhamma is present, for those who lead their life established in the Dhamma, with regard for the Dhamma, this is their mode of conduct, this is their livelihood—having rejected such, only what is obtained righteously should be eaten.

Atha brāhmaṇo cintesi – ahaṃ pubbe samaṇassa gotamassa guṇe vā aguṇe vā na jānāmi. Idāni panassāhaṃ guṇe ñatvā mama gehe asītikoṭimattaṃ dhanaṃ sāsane vippakiritukāmo jāto, ayañca “mayā dinnapaccayā akappiyā”ti vadati. Appaṭiggayho ahaṃ samaṇena gotamenāti. Atha bhagavā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pesetvā tassa cittācāraṃ vīmaṃsanto, “ayaṃ sabbepi attanā dinnapaccaye ‘akappiyā’ti sallakkheti. Yaṃ hi bhojanaṃ ārabbha kathā uppannā, etadeva na vaṭṭati, sesā niddosā”ti brāhmaṇassa catunnaṃ paccayānaṃ dānadvāraṃ dassento aññena cātiādimāha. Tattha kukkuccavūpasantanti hatthakukkuccādīnaṃ vasena vūpasantakukkuccaṃ. Annena pānenāti desanāmattametaṃ[P 1.0233]. Ayaṃ panattho – aññehi tayā “pariccajissāmī”ti sallakkhitehi cīvarādīhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahassu. Khettaṃ hi taṃ puññapekkhassa hotīti etaṃ tathāgatasāsanaṃ nāma puññapekkhassa puññatthikassa tuyhaṃ appepi bīje bahusassaphaladāyakaṃ sukhettaṃ viya paṭiyattaṃ hoti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

Then the brahmin thought: ‘Previously, I did not know the virtues or faults of the ascetic Gotama. But now, having known his virtues, I have become desirous of distributing wealth amounting to eighty crores in the Dispensation, yet he says, “Requisites given by me are improper.” I am not to be accepted by the ascetic Gotama.’ Then the Blessed One, sending forth his omniscient knowledge and examining the brahmin’s mental disposition, thought: ‘This one considers all requisites given by himself as “improper.” The discussion has arisen concerning the food; that alone is not allowable, the rest are blameless.’ Showing the brahmin the gateway to giving the four requisites, he spoke the words beginning with ‘aññena ca...’. Herein, ‘one whose fidgeting is calmed’ means one whose fidgeting, due to such things as restlessness of the hands, is calmed. ‘With food and drink’ is merely an indicative teaching. This, however, is the meaning: ‘You should serve with other requisites, such as robes and so on, which you have marked out, thinking, “I will give these up.”’ ‘For it is a field for one seeking merit’ means: this Dispensation of the Tathāgata is prepared for you, who seek and desire merit, like a fertile field that yields an abundant harvest of crops even from a little seed. The eighth.

9. Sundarikasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Sundarika Sutta

195. Navame sundarikabhāradvājoti sundarikāya nadiyā tīre aggijuhaṇena evaṃladdhanāmo. Sundarikāyāti evaṃnāmikāya nadiyā. Aggiṃ [M 1.0214] juhatīti āhutiṃ pakkhipanena jāleti[V 1.0206]. Aggihuttaṃ paricaratīti agyāyatanaṃ sammajjanupalepanabalikammādinā payirupāsati. Ko nu kho imaṃ habyasesaṃ bhuñjeyyāti so kira brāhmaṇo aggimhi hutāvasesaṃ pāyāsaṃ disvā cintesi – “aggimhi tāva pakkhittapāyāso mahābrahmunā bhutto, ayaṃ pana avaseso atthi, taṃ yadi brahmuno mukhato jātassa brāhmaṇassa dadeyyaṃ, evaṃ me pitarā saha puttopi santappito bhaveyya, suvisodhito cassa brahmalokagāmimaggo”ti. So brāhmaṇassa dassanatthaṃ uṭṭhāyāsanā catuddisā anuvilokesi, “ko nu kho imaṃ habyasesaṃ bhuñjeyyā”ti?

195. In the ninth (sutta), Sundarikabhāradvāja is so named because he obtained his name by offering fire sacrifices on the bank of the Sundarikā River. Sundarikā: a river of that name. He offers fire: he kindles it by placing offerings. He tends the sacred fire: he attends to the fire altar by sweeping, plastering, and performing bali offerings. “Who now might eat this remnant of the offering?”—it is said that the brahmin, seeing the remnant of the rice porridge after the fire sacrifice, thought: “The rice porridge offered into the fire has already been eaten by Mahābrahmā. But this remnant remains. If I were to give it to a brahmin born from Brahmā’s mouth, then my father together with my son would be satisfied, and the path to the Brahmā world would be thoroughly purified for me.” So, for the purpose of seeing a brahmin, he rose from his seat and looked around in the four directions, thinking, “Who now might eat this remnant of the offering?”

Rukkhamūleti tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe jeṭṭhakarukkhassa mūle. Sasīsaṃ pārutaṃ nisinnanti saha sīsena pārutakāyaṃ nisinnaṃ. Kasmā pana bhagavā tattha nisīdi? Bhagavā kira paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento imaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā cintesi – ayaṃ brāhmaṇo evarūpaṃ aggapāyāsaṃ gahetvā “mahābrahmānaṃ bhojemī”ti aggimhi jhāpento aphalaṃ karoti…pe… cattāro magge ceva cattāri ca phalāni demīti. Tasmā kālasseva vuṭṭhāya sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā pattacīvaraṃ ādāya gantvā vuttanayena tasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi. Atha kasmā sasīsaṃ pārupīti? Himapātassa ca sītavātassa ca paṭibāhaṇatthaṃ, paṭibalova etaṃ tathāgato adhivāsetuṃ. Sace pana apārupitvā [P 1.0234] nisīdeyya, brāhmaṇo dūratova sañjānitvā nivatteyya, evaṃ sati kathā nappavatteyya. Iti bhagavā – “brāhmaṇe āgate sīsaṃ vivarissāmi, atha maṃ so disvā kathaṃ pavattessati, tassāhaṃ kathānusārena dhammaṃ desessāmī”ti kathāpavattanatthaṃ evamakāsi.

At the foot of a tree: in that grove, at the foot of the chief tree. Seated wrapped up, head and all: sitting with his body covered, including his head. But why did the Blessed One sit there? It is said that at dawn, while surveying the world, the Blessed One saw this brahmin and thought: “This brahmin, taking such excellent rice porridge and burning it in the fire, thinking, ‘I will feed Mahābrahmā,’ is performing a fruitless act… I will give him the four paths and the four fruits.” Therefore, rising early, attending to his bodily needs, and taking his bowl and robe, he went and sat at the foot of that tree in the manner described. But why did he cover his head? To ward off the falling frost and the cold wind—the Tathāgata was indeed capable of enduring that. But if he had sat uncovered, the brahmin would have recognized him from afar and turned away; in that case, no conversation would have arisen. Thus, the Blessed One thought: “When the brahmin approaches, I will uncover my head. Then, upon seeing me, he will start a conversation, and I will teach him the Dhamma in accordance with that conversation.” For the purpose of a conversation arising, he acted thus.

Upasaṅkamīti brāhmaṇo – “ayaṃ sasīsaṃ pārupitvā sabbarattiṃ padhānamanuyutto. Imassa dakkhiṇodakaṃ datvā imaṃ habyasesaṃ dassāmī”ti, brāhmaṇasaññī hutvā upasaṅkami. Muṇḍo ayaṃ bhavaṃ, muṇḍako ayaṃ bhavanti sīse vivaritamatte nīcakesantaṃ disvā “muṇḍo”ti āha. Tato suṭṭhutaraṃ olokento pavattamattampi sikhaṃ adisvā hīḷento “muṇḍako”ti āha. Tatovāti yattha ṭhito addasa, tamhāva padesā. Muṇḍāpi hīti kenaci kāraṇena muṇḍitasīsāpi honti.

He approached: the brahmin, perceiving him to be a brahmin, approached, thinking: “This one, wrapped up head and all, has been devoted to striving all night. After giving him the water of dedication, I will give him this remnant of the offering.” “This venerable one is shaven, this venerable one is a shaveling”—as soon as the head was uncovered, seeing the short hair, he said, “shaven.” Then, looking more closely and not seeing even a trace of a topknot, he said scornfully, “a shaveling.” From there: from the very spot where he stood when he saw him. For there are also shaven ones: for some reason, there are also those with shaven heads.

Mā [M 1.0215] jātiṃ pucchāti yadi dānassa mahapphalataṃ paccāsīsasi, jātiṃ mā puccha. Akāraṇaṃ hi dakkhiṇeyyabhāvassa jāti. Caraṇañca pucchāti apica kho sīlādiguṇabhedaṃ caraṇaṃ puccha. Etaṃ hi dakkhiṇeyyabhāvassa kāraṇaṃ. Idānissa tamatthaṃ vibhāvento kaṭṭhā have jāyati jātavedotiādimāha[V 1.0207]. Tatrāyaṃ adhippāyo – idha kaṭṭhā aggi jāyati, na ca so sālādikaṭṭhā jātova aggikiccaṃ karoti, sāpāna-doṇiādikaṭṭhā jāto na karoti, attano pana acciyādiguṇasampattiyā yato vā tato vā jāto karotiyeva. Evaṃ na brāhmaṇakulādīsu jātova dakkhiṇeyyo hoti, caṇḍālakulādīsu jāto na hoti, apica kho nīcakulinopi uccakulinopi khīṇāsava-muni dhitimā hirīnisedho ājānīyo hoti. Imāya dhitihiripamokkhāya guṇasampattiyā jātimā uttamadakkhiṇeyyo hoti. So hi dhitiyā guṇe dhāreti, hiriyā dose nisedhetīti. Apicettha munīti monadhammena samannāgato. Dhitimāti vīriyavā. Ājānīyoti kāraṇākāraṇajānanako. Hirīnisedhoti hiriyā pāpāni nisedhetvā ṭhito.

Do not ask about birth: if you desire the great fruit of giving, do not ask about birth. For birth is not the cause of being worthy of offerings. And ask about conduct: moreover, you should ask about conduct, which is distinguished by qualities such as virtue, for this is the cause of being worthy of offerings. Now, making this meaning clear, he said the words beginning with, “From wood, indeed, fire is born.” Herein, this is the meaning: Here, fire is born from wood. It is not that only fire born from sal wood and the like performs the function of fire, nor that fire born from a dog-trough and the like does not perform it. Rather, by the accomplishment of its own qualities, such as its flame, fire born from any wood whatsoever certainly performs its function. Similarly, it is not that only one born in a brahmin family and so on is worthy of offerings, nor is one unworthy by being born in a caṇḍāla family and so on. Moreover, whether from a low family or a high family, a sage whose taints are destroyed is resolute, restrained by shame, and discerning. By this accomplishment of qualities, foremost among which are resolution and shame, he is one of true birth and becomes supremely worthy of offerings. For he, through resolution, upholds qualities, and through shame, restrains faults. Moreover, herein, sage means one endowed with the quality of sagacity. Resolute means energetic. Discerning means one who knows cause and non-cause. Restrained by shame means one who stands firm having restrained evils through shame.

Saccena dantoti [P 1.0235] paramatthasaccena danto. Damasā upetoti indriyadamena upeto. Vedantagūti catunnaṃ maggavedānaṃ antaṃ, catūhi vā maggavedehi kilesānaṃ antaṃ gato. Vusitabrahmacariyoti maggabrahmacariyavāsaṃ vuttho. Yaññopanītoti upanītayañño paṭiyāditayañño ca. Tamupavhayethāti yena yañño paṭiyādito, so taṃ paramatthabrāhmaṇaṃ avhayeyya. “Indamavhayāma, somamavhayāma, varuṇamavhayāma, īsānamavhayāma, yāmamavhayāmā”ti idaṃ pana avhānaṃ niratthakaṃ. Kālenāti avhayanto ca “kālo, bhante, niṭṭhitaṃ bhatta”nti antomajjhanhikakāleyeva taṃ upavhayeyya. So juhati dakkhiṇeyyeti yo evaṃ kāle khīṇāsavaṃ āmantetvā tattha catupaccayadakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhapeti, so dakkhiṇeyye juhati nāma, na acetane aggimhi pakkhipanto.

Restrained by truth: restrained by the ultimate truth. Endowed with self-control: endowed with control of the senses. Gone to the end of the Vedas: gone to the end of the four path-knowledges, or gone to the end of the defilements by means of the four path-knowledges. He has lived the spiritual life: he has lived the holy life of the path. One to whom the offering is brought: one for whom the offering has been brought near and prepared. He should invite him: he by whom the offering has been prepared should invite that ultimate brahmin. “We invoke Indra, we invoke Soma, we invoke Varuṇa, we invoke Īsāna, we invoke Yama”—but this invocation is meaningless. At the right time: when inviting, saying, “It is time, venerable sir, the meal is ready,” one should invite him only within the midday period. He sacrifices to the worthy: he who, at the right time, invites one whose taints are destroyed and establishes in him an offering of the four requisites, is said to sacrifice to the worthy, not one who throws it into the insentient fire.

Iti brāhmaṇo bhagavato kathaṃ suṇanto pasīditvā idāni attano pasādaṃ āvikaronto addhā suyiṭṭhantiādimāha. Tassattho – addhā mama yidaṃ idāni suyiṭṭhañca suhutañca bhavissati, pubbe pana aggimhi jhāpitaṃ niratthakaṃ ahosīti. Añño janoti “ahaṃ brāhmaṇo, ahaṃ brāhmaṇo”ti vadanto [M 1.0216] andhabālaputhujjano. Habyasesanti hutasesaṃ. Bhuñjatu bhavantiādi purimasutte vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Thus, the brahmin, hearing the Blessed One's discourse and gaining faith, now revealing his own faith, said the words beginning with, “Surely, well-sacrificed.” Its meaning is: “Surely, this gift of mine will now be well-sacrificed and well-offered; but previously, what was burnt in the fire was useless.” Another person: a blind, foolish worldling who says, “I am a brahmin, I am a brahmin.” Remnant of the offering: remnant of the sacrifice. “Let the venerable one eat,” etc., should be understood in the same way as explained in the previous sutta.

Na khvāhanti na kho ahaṃ. Kasmā panevamāhāti? Tasmiṃ kira bhojane upahaṭamatteva “satthā [V 1.0208] bhuñjissatī”ti saññāya catūsu mahādīpesu dvīsu parittadīpasahassesu devatā pupphaphalādīni ceva sappinavanītatelamadhuphāṇitādīni ca ādāya madhupaṭalaṃ pīḷetvā madhuṃ gaṇhantiyo viya dibbānubhāvena nibbattitojameva gahetvā pakkhipiṃsu. Tena taṃ sukhumattaṃ gataṃ, manussānañca oḷārikaṃ vatthūti tesaṃ tāva oḷārikavatthutāya sammā pariṇāmaṃ na gacchati. Goyūse pana tilabījāni pakkhipitvā pakkattā oḷārikamissakaṃ jātaṃ, devānañca sukhumaṃ vatthūti tesaṃ sukhumavatthutāya sammā pariṇāmaṃ na gacchati. Sukkhavipassakakhīṇāsavassāpi kucchiyaṃ na pariṇamati. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhīkhīṇāsavassa pana samāpattibalena [P 1.0236] pariṇāmeyya. Bhagavato pana pākatikeneva kammajatejena pariṇāmeyya.

The phrase 'Na khvāhaṃ' should be parsed as 'na kho ahaṃ.' Why, then, did he say so? It is said that at the very moment when the food was offered, thinking, “The Teacher will eat,” deities from the four great continents and two thousand minor islands, taking flowers, fruits, and the like, as well as ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses, with divine power took and infused the very essence that had been produced, just as one might take honey by squeezing a honeycomb. Thus, that food became subtle. And since the physical body of humans is coarse, it does not properly digest for them due to the coarseness of their physical body. But because sesame seeds were put into cow's milk and cooked, it became mixed with coarse matter. And for deities, their physical body is subtle, so due to the subtlety of their physical body, it does not properly digest for them. Even for a dry-insight arahant, it does not digest in the stomach. But for an arahant who has attained the eight meditative attainments, it would digest through the power of attainment. For the Blessed One, however, it would naturally digest through the power of kamma-born heat.

Appahariteti aharite. Sace hi haritesu tiṇesu pakkhipeyya, siniddhapāyāsena tiṇāni pūtīni bhaveyyuṃ. Buddhā ca bhūtagāmasikkhāpadaṃ na vītikkamanti, tasmā evamāha. Yattha pana galappamāṇāni mahātiṇāni, tādise ṭhāne pakkhipituṃ vaṭṭati. Appāṇaketi sappāṇakasmiṃ hi parittake udake pakkhitte pāṇakā maranti, tasmā evamāha. Yaṃ pana gambhīraṃ mahāudakaṃ hoti, pātisatepi pātisahassepi pakkhitte na āluḷati, tathārūpe udake vaṭṭati. Opilāpesīti suvaṇṇapātiyā saddhiṃyeva nimujjāpesi. Cicciṭāyati ciṭiciṭāyatīti evarūpaṃ saddaṃ karoti. Kiṃ panesa pāyāsassa ānubhāvo, udāhu tathāgatassāti? Tathāgatassa. Ayaṃ hi brāhmaṇo taṃ pāyāsaṃ opilāpetvā ummaggaṃ āruyha satthu santikaṃ anāgantvāva gaccheyya, atha bhagavā – “ettakaṃ acchariyaṃ disvā mama santikaṃ āgamissati. Athassāhaṃ dhammadesanāya micchādiṭṭhigahaṇaṃ bhinditvā sāsane otāretvā amatapānaṃ pāyessāmī”ti adhiṭṭhānabalena evamakāsi.

‘Not on fresh grass’ means on non-fresh grass. For if it were placed on green grass, the grass would become putrid because of the rich milk-rice. And the Buddhas do not transgress the training rule concerning plant life; therefore, he spoke thus. However, where there are large grasses the size of a throat, it is permissible to place it there. ‘Without living beings’ means that if it were placed in a small amount of water containing living beings, the living beings would die; therefore, he spoke thus. But in deep, large bodies of water, even if a hundred or a thousand bowls were placed in it, it would not be disturbed; in such water, it is permissible. ‘He sank it’ means he made it sink together with the golden bowl. ‘It made a hissing sound’ means it made a sound like ‘cicciṭāyati ciṭiciṭāyati.’ Now, was this the power of the milk-rice or of the Tathāgata? It was the power of the Tathāgata. For this brahmin, having sunk the milk-rice and taken another road, might have gone away without returning to the Teacher. Then the Blessed One, thinking, ‘Having seen such a wonder, he will come to me. Then I will break his thicket of wrong views with a discourse on the Dhamma, establish him in the Dispensation, and make him drink the Deathless,’ made it so through the power of his determination.

Dāru [M 1.0217] samādahānoti dāruṃ jhāpayamāno. Bahiddhā hi etanti etaṃ dārujjhāpanaṃ nāma ariyadhammato bahiddhā. Yadi etena suddhi bhaveyya, ye davaḍāhakādayo bahūni dārūni jhāpenti, te paṭhamataraṃ sujjheyyuṃ. Kusalāti khandhādīsu kusalā. Ajjhattamevujjalayāmi jotinti niyakajjhatte attano santānasmiṃyeva ñāṇajotiṃ jālemi. Niccagginīti āvajjanapaṭibaddhena sabbaññutaññāṇena niccaṃ pajjalitaggi. Niccasamāhitattoti niccaṃ sammā ṭhapitacitto. Brahmacariyaṃ carāmīti bodhimaṇḍe caritaṃ brahmacariyaṃ gahetvā evaṃ vadati.

‘Piling up wood’ means setting fire to wood. ‘For this is external’ means this burning of wood is external to the Noble Dhamma. If purity could be achieved by this, then those who burn many logs, such as those who start forest fires and the like, would be the first to become pure. ‘Skilled’ means skilled in the aggregates and so on. ‘I kindle the light within’ means I ignite the light of knowledge within my own self, in my own continuum. ‘Ever aflame’ means constantly blazing with the all-knowing knowledge connected with advertence. ‘Ever concentrated’ means with a mind constantly well-established. ‘I live the holy life’ means he speaks thus, referring to the holy life lived at the Bodhi-maṇḍa.

Māno [V 1.0209] hi te, brāhmaṇa, khāribhāroti yathā khāribhāro khandhena vayhamāno upari ṭhitopi akkantakkantaṭṭhāne pathaviyā saddhiṃ phuseti, evameva jātigottakulādīni mānavatthūni nissāya ussāpito mānopi tattha tattha issaṃ uppādento catūsu apāyesu saṃsīdāpeti. Tenāha “māno hi te, brāhmaṇa, khāribhāro”ti[P 1.0237]. Kodho dhūmoti tava ñāṇaggissa upakkilesaṭṭhena kodho dhumo. Tena hi te upakkiliṭṭho ñāṇaggi na virocati. Bhasmani mosavajjanti nirojaṭṭhena musāvādo chārikā nāma. Yathā hi chārikāya paṭicchanno aggi na joteti, evaṃ te musāvādena paṭicchannaṃ ñāṇanti dasseti. Jivhā sujāti yathā tuyhaṃ suvaṇṇarajatalohakaṭṭhamattikāsu aññataramayā yāgayajanatthāya sujā hoti, evaṃ mayhaṃ dhammayāgaṃ yajanatthāya pahūtajivhā sujāti vadati. Hadayaṃ jotiṭṭhānanti yathā tuyhaṃ nadītīre jotiṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ mayhaṃ dhammayāgassa yajanaṭṭhānatthena sattānaṃ hadayaṃ jotiṭṭhānaṃ. Attāti cittaṃ.

‘Pride is your burden, brahmin’: Just as a khārī load carried on the shoulder, even though situated on top, makes contact with the earth in every place that is stepped upon, in the very same way, pride, hoisted up depending on the bases of pride such as birth, clan, and lineage, causes one to sink into the four states of misery by causing envy to arise in those various bases. Therefore, He said, ‘Pride is your burden, brahmin.’ ‘Anger is smoke’: Anger is smoke in the sense of being a defilement of your fire of knowledge. Indeed, being defiled by it, your fire of knowledge does not shine. ‘False speech is ashes’: False speech is called ashes in the sense of not blazing. For just as a fire covered by ashes does not blaze, in the same way, He shows that your knowledge, covered by false speech, does not blaze. ‘The tongue is the ladle’: Just as for you there is a ladle made of one or another of gold, silver, bronze, wood, or clay for the purpose of offering a sacrifice, in the same way, my broad tongue is the ladle for the purpose of offering the Dhamma-sacrifice, He says. ‘The heart is the place for kindling the fire’: Just as for you the place for kindling the fire is on the riverbank, in the same way, for me, the heart of beings is the place for kindling the fire in the sense of being the place of offering for the Dhamma-sacrifice. ‘The self’ means the mind.

Dhammo rahadoti yathā tvaṃ aggiṃ paricaritvā dhūmachārikasedakiliṭṭhasarīro sundarikaṃ nadiṃ otaritvā nhāyasi, evaṃ mayhaṃ sundarikāsadisena bāhirena rahadena attho natthi, aṭṭhaṅgikamaggadhammo pana mayhaṃ rahado, tatrāhaṃ pāṇasatampi pāṇasahassampi caturāsītipāṇasahassānipi ekappahārena nhāpemi. Sīlatitthoti tassa pana me dhammarahadassa catupārisuddhisīlaṃ titthanti dasseti. Anāviloti yathā tuyhaṃ sundarikā nadī catūhi pañcahi ekato nhāyantehi heṭṭhupariyavālikā āluḷā hoti[M 1.0218], na evaṃ mayhaṃ rahado, anekasatasahassesupi pāṇesu otaritvā nhāyantesu so anāvilo vippasannova hoti. Sabbhi sataṃ pasatthoti paṇḍitehi paṇḍitānaṃ pasaṭṭho. Uttamatthena vā so sabbhīti vuccati, paṇḍitehi pasatthattā sataṃ pasattho. Taranti pāranti nibbānapāraṃ gacchanti.

‘The Dhamma is a lake’: Just as you, having attended to the fire, with a body soiled by smoke, ash, and sweat, descend into the Sundarikā river to bathe, so I have no need for an external lake like the Sundarikā. The Dhamma of the Eightfold Path, however, is my lake, wherein I bathe hundreds, thousands, even eighty-four thousand beings all at once. ‘The ford of virtue’: this shows that the fourfold purity of virtue is the ford of my Dhamma-lake. ‘Unstirred’: Unlike your Sundarikā river, which becomes turbid when four or five people bathe together, stirring up the sand below and above, my lake is not so. Even when countless hundreds of thousands of beings descend and bathe in it, it remains unstirred and exceedingly clear. ‘Praised by the good’: It is praised by the wise among the wise. Or, in the highest sense, one is called ‘good’; because it is praised by the wise, it is praised by the good. ‘They cross over to the far shore’: This means they go to the far shore of Nibbāna.

Idāni ariyamaggarahadassa aṅgāni uddharitvā dassento saccaṃ dhammotiādimāha. Tattha saccanti vacīsaccaṃ. Dhammoti iminā diṭṭhisaṅkappavāyāmasatisamādhayo dasseti. Saṃyamoti iminā kammantājīvā gahitā. Saccanti vā iminā maggasaccaṃ gahitaṃ. Sā atthato sammādiṭṭhi. Vuttañhetaṃ – “sammādiṭṭhi maggo ceva hetu cā”ti (dha. sa. 1039). Sammādiṭṭhiyā pana gahitāya taggatikattā sammāsaṅkappo gahitova hoti. Dhammoti iminā vāyāmasatisamādhayo. Saṃyamoti iminā vācākammantājīvā. Evampi aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo dassito [V 1.0210] hoti. Atha vā saccanti paramatthasaccaṃ[P 1.0238], taṃ atthato nibbānaṃ. Dhammotipadena diṭṭhi saṅkappo vāyāmo sati samādhīti pañcaṅgāni gahitāni. Saṃyamoti vācā kammanto ājīvoti tīṇi. Evampi aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo dassito hoti. Brahmacariyanti etaṃ brahmacariyaṃ nāma. Majjhe sitāti sassatucchede vajjetvā majjhe nissitā. Brahmapattīti seṭṭhapatti. Sa tujjubhūtesu namo karohīti ettha ta-kāro padasandhikaro, sa tvaṃ ujubhūtesu khīṇāsavesu namo karohīti attho. Tamahaṃ naraṃ dhammasārīti brūmīti yo evaṃ paṭipajjati, tamahaṃ puggalaṃ “dhammasārī eso dhammasāriyā paṭicchanno”ti ca “kusaladhammehi akusaladhamme sāretvā ṭhito”ti vāti vadāmīti. Navamaṃ.

Now, wishing to show the factors of the great lake that is the Noble Path by extracting them, he spoke the words beginning with 'truth, Dhamma,' and so on. Therein, ‘truth’ means verbal truthfulness. By ‘Dhamma’ he indicates right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. By ‘restraint’ right action and right livelihood are taken. Alternatively, by ‘truth’ the path-truth is taken. This, in the sense of being a forerunner, is right view. For it has been said: ‘Right view is both the path and the cause’ (Dhs. 1039). When right view is taken, right intention is also taken because it has a similar nature. By ‘Dhamma’ are meant right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. By ‘restraint’ are meant right speech, right action, and right livelihood. In this way too the Noble Eightfold Path is shown. Or alternatively, ‘truth’ means ultimate truth, which in substance is Nibbāna. By the term ‘Dhamma’ five factors are taken: view, intention, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. By ‘restraint’ are meant three: speech, action, and livelihood. In this way too the Noble Eightfold Path is shown. ‘The holy life’ refers to the holy life of the path. ‘Sits in the middle’ means relying on the middle, avoiding eternalism and annihilationism. ‘Attainment of Brahmā’ means the supreme attainment. In `Sa tujjubhūtesu namo karohi`, the letter `ta` is a euphonic connector; the meaning is: 'That you should pay homage to the Arahants who have become upright'. ‘Him I call a man who lives by Dhamma’—whoever practices in this way, I call that person ‘one who lives by Dhamma,’ and ‘this one is covered by the movement that is the Dhamma,’ or ‘one who stands having made unwholesome states move by means of wholesome states.’ The ninth.

10. Bahudhītarasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Many Daughters Sutta

196. Dasame aññatarasmiṃ vanasaṇḍeti paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento tassa brāhmaṇassa arahattassa upanissayaṃ disvā “gacchāmissa saṅgahaṃ karissāmī”ti gantvā tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe viharati. Naṭṭhā hontīti kasitvā vissaṭṭhā aṭavimukhā caramānā brāhmaṇe bhuñjituṃ gate palātā honti. Pallaṅkanti samantato ūrubaddhāsanaṃ. Ābhujitvāti bandhitvā[M 1.0219]. Ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāyāti uparimaṃ sarīraṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapetvā, aṭṭhārasa piṭṭhikaṇṭake koṭiyā koṭiṃ paṭipādetvā. Parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāti kammaṭṭhānābhimukhaṃ satiṃ ṭhapayitvā, mukhasamīpe vā katvāti attho. Teneva vibhaṅge vuttaṃ – “ayaṃ sati upaṭṭhitā hoti sūpaṭṭhitā nāsikagge vā mukhanimitte vā, tena vuccati parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti (vibha. 537). Atha vā “parīti pariggahaṭṭho. Mukhanti niyyānaṭṭho. Satīti upaṭṭhānaṭṭho. Tena vuccati parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā”ti evaṃ paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.164) vuttanayenapettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepo – “pariggahitaniyyānaṃ satiṃ katvā”ti. Evaṃ nisīdanto ca pana chabbaṇṇā ghanabuddharasmiyo vissajjetvā nisīdi. Upasaṅkamīti domanassābhibhūto āhiṇḍanto, “sukhena vatāyaṃ samaṇo nisinno”ti cintetvā upasaṅkami.

196. In the tenth sutta, 'in a certain forest grove' means: while surveying the world at dawn, he saw the supporting condition for the brahmin's attainment of Arahantship. Thinking, 'I will go and support him,' he went and dwelled in that forest grove. 'They are lost' means: having been released after plowing and wandering towards the forest, they fled when the brahmin went to eat. 'Cross-legged posture' means a seat with the thighs bound together all around. 'Having folded' means having bound. 'Having held the body erect' means setting the upper body straight, making the eighteen vertebrae of the spine meet end to end. 'Having established mindfulness before him' means establishing mindfulness facing the meditation subject, or placing it near the mouth. For that very reason, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'This mindfulness is established, well-established, either at the tip of the nose or at the sign of the mouth; therefore it is said, "having established mindfulness before him"' (Vibh 537). Or alternatively, the meaning here should also be understood according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: '"Pari" has the meaning of encompassing. "Mukha" has the meaning of release. "Sati" has the meaning of establishment. Therefore it is said, "having established mindfulness before him"' (Paṭis I 164). Therein, this is the summary: 'having made mindfulness the comprehended means of release.' And while sitting thus, he emitted the six-colored, dense Buddha-rays and sat down. 'He approached' means: being overwhelmed by displeasure and wandering about, he approached, thinking, 'Oh, how peacefully this ascetic sits!'

Ajjasaṭṭhiṃ [P 1.0239] na dissantīti ajja chadivasamattakā paṭṭhāya na dissanti. Pāpakāti lāmakā tilakhāṇukā. Tena kira tilakhette vapite tadaheva devo vassitvā tile paṃsumhi osīdāpesi[V 1.0211], pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā gahetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Yepi vaḍḍhiṃsu, tesaṃ upari pāṇakā patitvā paṇṇāni khādiṃsu, ekapaṇṇadupaṇṇā khāṇukā avasissiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo khettaṃ oloketuṃ gato te disvā – “vaḍḍhiyā me tilā gahitā, tepi naṭṭhā”ti domanassajāto ahosi, taṃ gahetvā imaṃ gāthamāha.

“For sixty days now they are not seen” means: starting from today, for a period of six days, they are not seen. “Wretched” means the inferior sesame stumps. It is said that when that brahmin sowed the sesame field, on that very day the rain-god rained, causing the sesame seeds to sink into the dust; they were unable to produce flowers or fruit. And upon those that did grow, insects fell and ate the leaves; only stumps with one or two leaves remained. The brahmin went to inspect the field, and seeing them, he became distressed, thinking, “My sesame was taken up for a profit, yet even that is destroyed.” Taking this matter to heart, he spoke this verse.

Ussoḷhikāyāti ussāhena kaṇṇanaṅguṭṭhādīni ukkhipitvā vicarantā uppatanti. Tassa kira anupubbena bhogesu parikkhīṇesu pakkhipitabbassa abhāvena tucchakoṭṭhā ahesuṃ. Tassa ito cito ca sattahi gharehi āgatā mūsikā te tucchakoṭṭhe pavisitvā uyyānakīḷaṃ kīḷantā viya naccanti, taṃ gahetvā evamāha.

“With frisking bodies” means: with effort, lifting up their ears, tails, and so on, they leap about while running around. It is said that for that brahmin, as his wealth gradually dwindled, due to the absence of anything to be put in, his granaries became empty. Mice, having come from seven houses here and there, entered those empty granaries and danced as if playing a garden-game. Taking this matter to heart, he spoke thus.

Uppāṭakehi sañchannoti uppāṭakapāṇakehi sañchanno. Tassa kira brāhmaṇassa sayanatthāya santhataṃ tiṇapaṇṇasanthāraṃ koci antarantarā paṭijagganto natthi. So divasaṃ araññe kammaṃ katvā sāyaṃ āgantvā tasmiṃ nipajjati. Athassa uppāṭakapāṇakā sarīraṃ ekacchannaṃ karontā khādanti, taṃ gahetvā evamāha.

“Covered with skin-flayers” means: covered with skin-flaying pests. It is said that for that brahmin, there was no one who would from time to time maintain the spread of grass and leaves laid out for his bedding. Having done his work in the forest during the day, he would come in the evening and lie down on it. Then, the skin-flaying pests, making his body completely covered, would bite him. Taking this matter to heart, he spoke thus.

Vidhavāti [M 1.0220] matapatikā. Yāva kira tassa brāhmaṇassa gehe vibhavamattā ahosi, tāva tā vidhavāpi hutvā patikulesu vasituṃ labhiṃsu. Yadā pana so niddhano jāto, tadā tā “pitugharaṃ gacchathā”ti sassusasurādīhi nikkaḍḍhitā tato tasseva gharaṃ āgantvā vasantiyo brāhmaṇassa bhojanakāle “gacchatha ayyakena saddhiṃ bhuñjathā”ti putte pesenti, tehi pātiyaṃ hatthesu otāritesu brāhmaṇo hatthassa okāsaṃ na labhati. Taṃ gahetvā imaṃ gāthamāha.

“Widows” means: those whose husbands are dead. It is said that for as long as there was some measure of wealth in that brahmin's house, for that long they, though being widows, were able to live in their husbands' families. But when he became poor, they were driven out by their mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and so on, who said, “Go to your father's house.” Having come from there to his very house and staying, at the brahmin's mealtime they would send their children, saying, “Go, eat with your grandfather.” When those children put their hands into the bowl, the brahmin could not find space for his own hand. Taking this matter to heart, he spoke this verse.

Piṅgalāti kaḷārapiṅgalā. Tilakāhatāti kāḷasetādivaṇṇehi tilakehi āhatagattā. Sottaṃ pādena bodhetīti niddaṃ okkantaṃ pādena paharitvā pabodheti. Ayaṃ kira brāhmaṇo mūsikasaddena ubbāḷho uppāṭakehi ca khajjamāno sabbarattiṃ [P 1.0240] niddaṃ alabhitvā paccūsakāle niddāyati. Atha naṃ akkhīsu nimmilitamattesveva – “kiṃ karosi, brāhmaṇa, pacchā ca pubbe ca gahitassa iṇassa? Vaḍḍhi matthakaṃ pattā, satta dhītaro posetabbā. Idāni iṇāyikā āgantvā [V 1.0212] gehaṃ parivāressanti, gaccha kammaṃ karohī”ti pādena paharitvā pabodheti. Taṃ gahetvā imaṃ gāthamāha.

Piṅgalā means one with protruding, tawny-colored eyes. Tilakāhatā means her body was speckled all over with spots of colors such as black and white. 'She wakes him with her foot' means she rouses the brahmin who has fallen asleep by kicking him with her foot. It is said that this brahmin, tormented by the sound of mice and being bitten by bedbugs, could not get any sleep the whole night and would fall asleep at dawn. Then, just as his eyes were closing, she would awaken him by kicking him with her foot, saying: 'What are you doing, brahmin? The interest on the debt taken both before and after has reached its peak. Seven daughters must be supported. Now the creditors will come and surround the house. Go and do your work!' Taking that matter into account, he spoke this verse.

Iṇāyikāti yesaṃ anena hatthato iṇaṃ gahitaṃ. So kira kassaci hatthato ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ kassaci dve kassaci dasa…pe… kassaci satanti evaṃ bahūnaṃ hatthato iṇaṃ aggahesi. Te divā brāhmaṇaṃ apassantā “gehato taṃ nikkhantameva gaṇhissāmā”ti balavapaccūse gantvā codenti. Taṃ gahetvā imaṃ gāthamāha.

Iṇāyikā means those from whose hand he had taken a debt. It is said that he had taken a debt from the hands of many: from someone one kahāpaṇa, from someone two, from someone ten, and so on, up to a hundred from someone. Not seeing the brahmin during the day, those creditors would go at early dawn and demand payment, thinking, 'We will seize him just as he leaves the house.' Taking that matter into account, he spoke this verse.

Bhagavā tena brāhmaṇena imāhi sattahi gāthāhi dukkhe kathite “yaṃ yaṃ, brāhmaṇa, tayā dukkhaṃ kathitaṃ, sabbametaṃ mayhaṃ natthī”ti dassento paṭigāthāhi brāhmaṇassa dhammadesanaṃ vaḍḍhesi. Brāhmaṇo tā gāthā sutvā bhagavati pasanno saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Taṃ dassetuṃ evaṃ vutte bhāradvājagottotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha alatthāti labhi.

When that brahmin had spoken of suffering to the Blessed One with these seven verses, the Blessed One, showing, 'Brahmin, whatever suffering you have spoken of, none of that exists for me,' expanded the Dhamma teaching for the brahmin with responsive verses. The brahmin, having heard those verses, with faith in the Blessed One, having been established in the refuges, went forth and attained arahantship. To show this, the passage beginning, 'When this was said, he of the Bhāradvāja clan...' was spoken. Therein, alatthā means 'he obtained'.

Tañca pana brāhmaṇaṃ bhagavā pabbājetvā ādāya jetavanaṃ gantvā punadivase tena therena pacchāsamaṇena kosalarañño gehadvāraṃ agamāsi[M 1.0221]. Rājā “satthā āgato”ti sutvā pāsādā oruyha vanditvā hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā tathāgataṃ uparipāsādaṃ āropetvā varāsane nisīdāpetvā gandhodakena pāde dhovitvā satapākatelena makkhetvā yāguṃ āharāpetvā rajatadaṇḍaṃ suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gahetvā satthu upanāmesi. Satthā pattaṃ pidahi. Rājā tathāgatassa pādesu patitvā, “sace me, bhante, doso atthi, khamathā”ti āha. Natthi, mahārājāti. Atha kasmā yāguṃ na gaṇhathāti? Palibodho atthi, mahārājāti. Kiṃ pana, bhante, yāguṃ agaṇhanteheva labhitabbo esa palibodho, paṭibalo ahaṃ palibodhaṃ dātuṃ, gaṇhatha, bhanteti. Satthā aggahesi. Mahallakattheropi dīgharattaṃ chāto yāvadatthaṃ yāguṃ pivi. Rājā khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ datvā bhattakiccāvasāne bhagavantaṃ [P 1.0241] vanditvā āha – “bhagavā tumhe paveṇiyā āgate okkākavaṃse uppajjitvā cakkavattisiriṃ pahāya pabbajitvā loke aggataṃ patto, ko nāma, bhante, tumhākaṃ palibodho”ti? Mahārāja, etassa mahallakattherassa palibodho amhākaṃ palibodhasadisovāti.

Then, having ordained that brahmin, the Blessed One took him and went to Jetavana. On the next day, the Blessed One, with that elder as his attendant monk, went to the door of King Kosala's palace. Hearing, "The Teacher has come," the king descended from his palace, paid homage, took the bowl from the Teacher's hand, led the Tathāgata up to the upper palace, seated him on a splendid seat, washed his feet with fragrant water, anointed them with oil refined a hundred times, had rice gruel brought, and taking a golden ladle with a silver handle, offered it to the Teacher. The Teacher covered his bowl. The king, falling at the Tathāgata's feet, said, "Venerable sir, if there is any fault in me, please forgive me." "There is none, great king." "Then why do you not accept the gruel?" "There is an impediment, great king." "But, venerable sir, is this an impediment that can only be addressed by not accepting the gruel? I am able to provide for the impediment. Please accept, venerable sir." The Teacher accepted. The great elder, who had been hungry for a long time, also drank as much gruel as he desired. The king, having offered hard and soft food, at the conclusion of the meal, paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Blessed One, you were born in the Okkāka lineage which has come down in succession, and having renounced the glory of a universal monarch and gone forth, you have attained the highest state in the world. What, venerable sir, could be your impediment?" "Great king, the impediment of this great elder is like our own impediment."

Rājā [V 1.0213] theraṃ vanditvā – “ko, bhante, tumhākaṃ palibodho”ti pucchi? Iṇapalibodho, mahārājāti. Kittako, bhanteti? Gaṇehi, mahārājāti. Rañño “ekaṃ dve sataṃ sahassa”nti gaṇentassa aṅguliyo nappahonti. Athekaṃ purisaṃ pakkositvā, “gaccha, bhaṇe, nagare bheriṃ carāpehi ‘sabbe bahudhītikabrāhmaṇassa iṇāyikā rājaṅgaṇe sannipatantū”ti. Manussā bheriṃ sutvā sannipatiṃsu. Rājā tesaṃ hatthato paṇṇāni āharāpetvā sabbesaṃ anūnaṃ dhanamadāsi. Tattha suvaṇṇameva satasahassagghanakaṃ ahosi. Puna rājā pucchi – “aññopi atthi, bhante, palibodho”ti. Iṇaṃ nāma, mahārāja, datvā muccituṃ sakkā, etā pana satta dārikā mahāpalibodhā mayhanti. Rājā yānāni pesetvā tassa dhītaro āharāpetvā attano dhītaro katvā taṃ taṃ kulagharaṃ pesetvā, “aññopi, bhante, atthi palibodho”ti pucchi? Brāhmaṇī, mahārājāti. Rājā yānaṃ pesetvā, tassa brāhmaṇiṃ āharāpetvā, ayyikaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā puna pucchi – “aññopi, bhante, atthi palibodho”ti? Natthi[M 1.0222], mahārājāti vutte rājāpi cīvaradussāni dāpetvā, “bhante, mama santakaṃ tumhākaṃ bhikkhubhāvaṃ jānāthā”ti āha. Āma, mahārājāti. Atha naṃ rājā āha – “bhante, cīvarapiṇḍapātādayopi sabbe paccayā amhākaṃ santakā bhavissanti. Tumhe tathāgatassa manaṃ gahetvā samaṇadhammaṃ karothā”ti. Thero tatheva appamatto samaṇadhammaṃ karonto nacirasseva āsavakkhayaṃ pattoti. Dasamaṃ.

The king paid homage to the elder and asked, 'Venerable sir, what is your impediment?' 'The impediment of debt, great king.' 'How much, venerable sir?' 'Calculate it, great king.' As the king was counting, 'one, two, a hundred, a thousand,' his fingers were not sufficient. Then he summoned a man and said, 'Go, good man, have a drum beaten in the city: "Let all the creditors of the brahmin Bahudhītika assemble in the royal courtyard."' Having heard the drum, the people assembled. The king had the account documents brought from their hands and gave the full amount of money to all of them. Therein, the gold alone was worth a hundred thousand. Again the king asked, 'Venerable sir, is there any other impediment?' 'A debt, great king, can be paid and one can be freed from it, but these seven daughters are a great impediment to me.' The king sent carriages, had his daughters brought, made them his own daughters, and sent them to suitable noble families. Then he asked, 'Venerable sir, is there any other impediment?' 'The brahmin woman, great king.' The king sent a carriage, had the brahmin woman brought, and established her in the position of a grandmother. Then he asked again, 'Venerable sir, is there any other impediment?' 'There is none, great king.' When this was said, the king had robes and cloth given, and said, 'Venerable sir, know that your state as a bhikkhu is my responsibility.' 'Yes, great king.' Then the king said to him, 'Venerable sir, all the requisites, such as robes and alms-food, will be our responsibility. You, having taken to heart the teaching of the Tathāgata, should practice the duty of an ascetic.' The elder, just so, being diligent while practicing the duty of an ascetic, before long attained the destruction of the taints. The Tenth Sutta.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

2. Upāsakavaggo

2. The Chapter on Lay Followers

1. Kasibhāradvājasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary to the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta

197. Dutiyavaggassa [P 1.0242] paṭhame magadhesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. Dakkhiṇāgirisminti rājagahaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitassa girino dakkhiṇabhāge janapado atthi, tasmiṃ janapade, tattha vihārassāpi tadeva nāmaṃ. Ekanāḷāyaṃ brāhmaṇagāmeti ekanāḷāti tassa gāmassa nāmaṃ. Brāhmaṇā [V 1.0214] panettha sambahulā paṭivasanti, brāhmaṇabhogo eva vā so. Tasmā “brāhmaṇagāmo”ti vuccati.

197. In the first sutta of the second chapter: `magadhesu` means in a country so named. `Dakkhiṇāgirismiṃ`: there is a country in the southern part of the mountain that stands surrounding Rājagaha; in that country. There, the monastery also has that very name. Regarding `Ekanāḷāyaṃ brāhmaṇagāme`: `Ekanāḷā` is the name of that village. Many brahmins reside here, or it is indeed a brahmin estate. Therefore, it is called 'the brahmin village'.

Tena kho pana samayenāti yaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā magadharaṭṭhe ekanāḷaṃ brāhmaṇagāmaṃ upanissāya dakkhiṇagirimahāvihāre brāhmaṇassa indriyaparipākaṃ āgamayamāno viharati, tena samayena. Kasibhāradvājassāti so brāhmaṇo kasiṃ nissāya jīvati, bhāradvājoti cassa gottaṃ. Pañcamattānīti pañca pamāṇāni, anūnāni anadhikāni pañcanaṅgalasatānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Payuttānīti yojitāni, balībaddānaṃ khandhesu ṭhapetvā yuge yottehi yojitānīti attho.

`Tena kho pana samayena` means: at the time when the Blessed One was dwelling near the brahmin village of Ekanāḷa in the Magadha country, in the Dakkhiṇagiri Great Monastery, awaiting the maturation of the brahmin's faculties. `Kasibhāradvājassa` means: that brahmin makes his living by means of agriculture, and `Bhāradvāja` is his clan name. `Pañcamattāni` means: five measures, neither less nor more; it is said to mean five hundred ploughs. `Payuttāni` means: yoked. The meaning is: having placed yokes on the necks of the oxen, they were yoked with ropes.

Vappakāleti vappanakāle bījanikkhepasamaye. Tattha dve vappāni kalalavappañca paṃsuvappañca. Paṃsuvappaṃ idha adhippetaṃ, tañca kho paṭhamadivase maṅgalavappaṃ. Tatthāyaṃ upakaraṇasampadā – tīṇi balibaddasahassāni upaṭṭhāpitāni honti, sabbesaṃ suvaṇṇamayāni siṅgāni paṭimukkāni, rajatamayā khurā, sabbe [M 1.0223] setamālāhi ceva gandhapañcaṅgulīhi ca alaṅkatā paripuṇṇapañcaṅgā sabbalakkhaṇasampannā, ekacce kāḷā añjanavaṇṇā, ekacce setā phalikavaṇṇā, ekacce rattā pavāḷavaṇṇā, ekacce kammāsā masāragallavaṇṇā. Evaṃ pañcasatā kassakā sabbe ahatasetavatthā gandhamālālaṅkatā dakkhiṇaaṃsakūṭesu patiṭṭhitapupphacumbaṭakā haritālamanosilālañjanujjalagattā dasa dasa naṅgalā ekekagumbā hutvā gacchanti. Naṅgalānaṃ sīsañca yugañca patodā ca suvaṇṇakhacitā[P 1.0243]. Paṭhamanaṅgale aṭṭha balībaddā yuttā, sesesu cattāro cattāro, avasesā kilantaparivattanatthaṃ ānītā. Ekekagumbe ekekabījasakaṭaṃ ekeko kasati, ekeko vappati.

`Vappakāle` means at the time of sowing, the moment of depositing the seeds. Therein, there are two kinds of sowing: sowing in mud and sowing in fine soil. Here, sowing in fine soil is intended, and that, indeed, on the first day, is the auspicious sowing. Therein, this is the accomplishment of the equipment: three thousand bulls are made ready. For all of them, golden horns and silver hooves are fitted. All are adorned with white garlands and fragrant five-finger marks; they possess the five perfect limbs and are endowed with all auspicious marks. Some are black, the color of collyrium; some are white, the color of crystal; some are red, the color of coral; and some are dappled, the color of a masāragalla gem. Thus, five hundred farmers—all clad in fresh white garments, adorned with fragrant garlands, with wreaths of flowers well-placed on their right shoulder-tips, their bodies radiant, anointed with yellow orpiment, red arsenic, and collyrium—proceed in groups of ten plows each. The heads of the plows, the yokes, and the goads are inlaid with gold. To the first plow, eight bulls are yoked; to the remaining ones, four each. The rest are brought for the purpose of replacing the tired ones. In each group, there is one seed-cart; one man plows, and one man sows.

Brāhmaṇo pana pageva massukammaṃ kārāpetvā nhāyitvā sugandhagandhehi vilitto pañcasatagghanakaṃ vatthaṃ nivāsetvā sahassagghanakaṃ ekaṃsaṃ karitvā ekekissā aṅguliyā dve dveti vīsati aṅgulimuddikāyo kaṇṇesu sīhakuṇḍalāni sīse brahmaveṭhanaṃ paṭimuñcitvā suvaṇṇamālaṃ kaṇṭhe katvā brāhmaṇagaṇaparivuto kammantaṃ vosāsati. Athassa brāhmaṇī anekasatabhājanesu pāyāsaṃ pacāpetvā mahāsakaṭesu āropetvā gandhodakena nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitā brāhmaṇīgaṇaparivutā kammantaṃ agamāsi. Gehampissa haritupalittaṃ vippakiṇṇalājaṃ [V 1.0215] puṇṇaghaṭakadalidhajapaṭākāhi alaṅkataṃ gandhapupphādīhi sukatabalikammaṃ, khettañca tesu tesu ṭhānesu samussitaddhajapaṭākaṃ ahosi. Parijanakammakārehi saddhiṃ osaṭaparisā aḍḍhateyyasahassā ahosi, sabbe ahatavatthā, sabbesaṃ pāyāsabhojanameva paṭiyattaṃ.

The brahmin, however, first having had his beard and mustache shaved, having bathed, and being anointed with very fragrant perfumes, having worn a garment worth five hundred, having draped a cloth worth a thousand over one shoulder, having put on twenty finger-rings—two on each finger—earrings in the shape of a lion's mouth in his ears, and a turban like the crown of Brahmā on his head, and having placed a golden garland on his neck, surrounded by a group of brahmins, supervised the work. Then his brahmin wife, having had rice-porridge cooked in countless hundreds of vessels and having loaded it onto large carts, having bathed with scented water, and being adorned with all ornaments, surrounded by a group of brahmin women, went to the place of work. His house also was smeared with fresh cow-dung, had parched rice scattered about, was decorated with full water-pots, banana trees, banners, and flags, and had offerings well-prepared with perfumes, flowers, and so on. And the field, in various places, had banners and flags well-erected. The assembled company, together with attendants and workers, was two thousand five hundred. All had new clothes, and for all of them, only a meal of rice-porridge was prepared.

Atha brāhmaṇo suvaṇṇapātiṃ dhovāpetvā pāyāsassa pūretvā sappimadhuphāṇitehi abhisaṅkharitvā naṅgalabalikammaṃ kārāpesi. Brāhmaṇī pañcannaṃ kassakasatānaṃ suvaṇṇarajatakaṃsatambalohamayāni bhājanāni dāpetvā suvaṇṇakaṭacchuṃ gahetvā pāyāsena parivisantī gacchati. Brāhmaṇo pana balikammaṃ kāretvā rattabandhikāyo upāhanāyo ārohitvā rattasuvaṇṇadaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā, “idha pāyāsaṃ detha, idha sappiṃ [M 1.0224] detha, idha sakkharaṃ dethā”ti vosāsamāno vicarati. Ayaṃ tāva kammante pavatti.

Then the brahmin, having had a golden bowl washed, having had it filled with rice-porridge, and having seasoned it with ghee, honey, and molasses, had the plowing-offering ceremony performed. The brahmin woman, having had vessels made of gold, silver, bronze, copper, and iron given to the five hundred farmers, took a golden ladle and went about serving the rice-porridge. The brahmin, however, having had the offering made, having put on sandals with red instep-coverings, and having taken a red-gold staff, wandered about directing, “Give rice-porridge here! Give ghee here! Give sugar here!” This, for now, is the account of the proceedings at the work-site.

Vihāre pana yattha yattha buddhā vasanti, tattha tattha nesaṃ devasikaṃ pañca kiccāni bhavanti, seyyathidaṃ – purebhattakiccaṃ pacchābhattakiccaṃ purimayāmakiccaṃ majjhimayāmakiccaṃ pacchimayāmakiccanti.

In the monastery, however, wherever the Buddhas reside, there daily arise for them five duties. They are as follows: the duty of the forenoon, the duty of the afternoon, the duty of the first watch, the duty of the middle watch, and the duty of the last watch.

Tatridaṃ purebhattakiccaṃ [P 1.0244] – bhagavā hi pātova uṭṭhāya upaṭṭhākānuggahatthaṃ sarīraphāsukatthañca mukhadhovanādiparikammaṃ katvā yāva bhikkhācāravelā, tāva vivittāsane vītināmetvā bhikkhācāravelāya nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattamādāya kadāci ekako kadāci bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya pavisati kadāci pakatiyā, kadāci anekehi pāṭihāriyehi vattamānehi. Seyyathidaṃ – piṇḍāya pavisato lokanāthassa purato purato gantvā mudugatiyo vātā pathaviṃ sodhenti, valāhakā udakaphusitāni muñcantā magge reṇuṃ vūpasametvā upari vitānaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhanti, apare vātā pupphāni upaharitvā magge okiranti. Unnatā bhūmippadesā onamanti, onatā unnamanti. Pādanikkhepasamaye samāva bhūmi hoti, sukhasamphassāni padumapupphāni vā pāde sampaṭicchanti. Indakhīlassa anto ṭhapitamatte dakkhiṇapāde sarīrā chabbaṇṇarasmiyo nikkhamitvā suvaṇṇarasasiñcanāni viya citrapaṭaparikkhittāni viya ca pāsādakūṭāgārādīni karontiyo ito cito ca vidhāvanti. Hatthiassavihaṅgādayo sakasakaṭṭhānesu ṭhitāyeva madhurenākārena saddaṃ karonti[V 1.0216], tathā bherivīṇādīni tūriyāni manussānañca kāyūpagāni ābharaṇāni. Tena saññāṇena manussā jānanti “ajja bhagavā idha piṇḍāya paviṭṭho”ti. Te sunivatthā supārutā gandhapupphādīni ādāya gharā nikkhamitvā antaravīthiṃ paṭipajjitvā bhagavantaṃ gandhapupphādīhi sakkaccaṃ pūjetvā vanditvā – “amhākaṃ, bhante, dasa bhikkhū, amhākaṃ vīsati, amhākaṃ bhikkhusataṃ dethā”ti yācitvā bhagavatopi pattaṃ gahetvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā sakkaccaṃ piṇḍapātena paṭimānenti.

Herein is the forenoon duty: Indeed, the Blessed One rises early in the morning and, for the sake of favoring his attendants and for bodily comfort, performs preliminary duties such as washing his face. Until the time for the alms round, he passes the time in a secluded seat. At the time for the alms round, having put on his lower robe, fastened his waistband, draped his outer robe, and taken his bowl, he enters a village or a town for alms—sometimes alone, sometimes surrounded by the community of bhikkhus; sometimes in his ordinary form, sometimes with many miracles occurring. This is how it is: when the Protector of the World enters for alms, gentle winds, going before him, cleanse the earth. Clouds, releasing drops of water, settle the dust on the path and stand above, having become a canopy. Other winds bring flowers and scatter them on the path. Elevated regions of the earth lower, and low regions rise. At the time of placing his foot, the ground becomes even, and lotus blossoms, pleasant to the touch, receive his feet. Just as his right foot is placed inside the threshold, six-colored rays emanate from his body and dart hither and thither, adorning palaces, pinnacled buildings, and so forth, as if they were sprinkled with liquid gold or surrounded by colorful cloths. Elephants, horses, birds, and so forth, while remaining in their respective places, make sweet sounds; likewise do musical instruments such as drums and lutes, and the ornaments worn on the bodies of people. By that sign, people know: 'Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms.' They, well-dressed and well-cloaked, take perfumes, flowers, and so forth, leave their homes, proceed to the middle of the street, reverently honor the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, pay homage to him, and request: 'Venerable sir, give us ten bhikkhus, give us twenty, give us a hundred bhikkhus!' Then, taking the Blessed One's bowl as well, they prepare a seat and respectfully honor him with almsfood.

Bhagavā [M 1.0225] katabhattakicco tesaṃ santānāni oloketvā tathā dhammaṃ deseti, yathā keci saraṇagamane patiṭṭhahanti, keci pañcasu sīlesu, keci sotāpattisakadāgāmianāgāmiphalānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ, keci pabbajitvā aggaphale arahatteti[P 1.0245]. Evaṃ mahājanaṃ anuggahetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ gacchati. Tattha gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdati bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosānaṃ āgamayamāno. Tato bhikkhūnaṃ bhattakiccapariyosāne upaṭṭhāko bhagavato nivedeti. Atha bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisati. Idaṃ tāva purebhattakiccaṃ.

The Blessed One, having completed his meal-duty, observes their mental continuums and teaches the Dhamma in such a way that some are established in the refuges, some in the five precepts, some in one of the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning, and some, having gone forth, are established in the supreme fruit, Arahantship. Having thus favored the great multitude, he rises from his seat and goes to the monastery. There, in the perfumed pavilion, he sits on the excellent Buddha-seat that has been prepared, awaiting the conclusion of the bhikkhus' meal-duty. Then, when the bhikkhus' meal-duty is finished, the attendant informs the Blessed One. Thereupon, the Blessed One enters the perfumed chamber. This, for now, is the forenoon duty.
