Atha bhagavā evaṃ katapurebhattakicco gandhakuṭiyā upaṭṭhāne nisīditvā pāde pakkhāletvā pādapīṭhe ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ovadati – “bhikkhave, appamādena sampādetha, dullabho buddhuppādo lokasmiṃ, dullabho manussattapaṭilābho, dullabhā saddhāsampatti, dullabhā pabbajjā, dullabhaṃ saddhammassavana”nti. Tattha keci bhagavantaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pucchanti. Bhagavā tesaṃ attano cariyānurūpaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ deti. Tato sabbepi bhagavantaṃ vanditvā attano attano rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni gacchanti, keci araññaṃ, keci rukkhamūlaṃ, keci pabbatādīnaṃ aññataraṃ, keci cātumahārājikabhavanaṃ…pe… keci vasavattibhavananti. Tato bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā sace ākaṅkhati, dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno muhuttaṃ sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti. Atha samassāsitakāyo uṭṭhahitvā dutiyabhāge lokaṃ voloketi. Tatiyabhāge yaṃ gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā upanissāya viharati, tattha mahājano purebhattaṃ dānaṃ datvā pacchābhattaṃ sunivattho supāruto gandhapupphādīni ādāya vihāre sannipatati. Tato bhagavā sampattaparisāya anurūpena pāṭihāriyena gantvā dhammasabhāyaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane [V 1.0217] nisajja dhammaṃ deseti kālayuttaṃ samayayuttaṃ. Atha kālaṃ viditvā parisaṃ uyyojeti, manussā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pakkamanti. Idaṃ pacchābhattakiccaṃ.

Then the Blessed One, having thus completed his forenoon duties, sat down at the entrance of the perfumed chamber, washed his feet, stood on the footstool, and exhorted the community of monks: “Monks, strive with diligence. Rare is the arising of a Buddha in the world; rare is the attainment of the human state; rare is the accomplishment of faith; rare is the going forth; rare is the hearing of the True Dhamma.” There, some asked the Blessed One for a meditation subject. The Blessed One gave them a meditation subject suitable to their own temperaments. Then all, having paid homage to the Blessed One, went to their respective places for the night and for the day—some to a forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to one of the mountains and so on, some to the realm of the Cātumahārājika devas... and so on... some to the realm of the Vasavattī devas. Then the Blessed One entered the perfumed chamber, and if he so desired, he would assume the lion’s posture on his right side, mindful and fully aware, for a moment. Then, his body having become refreshed, he would arise and, in the second part of the day, survey the world. In the third part of the day, in whatever village or town he was dwelling in dependence upon, there the great populace, having given alms in the forenoon, would assemble at the monastery in the afternoon, well-dressed, well-cloaked, and taking perfumes, flowers, and so on. Then the Blessed One, having gone by means of a miracle suitable for the assembled congregation, would sit on the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared in the Dhamma hall and teach the Dhamma that is suitable for the time and suitable for the occasion. Then, knowing the time, he would dismiss the congregation. The people, having paid homage to the Blessed One, would depart. This is the duty after the meal.

So evaṃ niṭṭhitapacchābhattakicco sace gattāni osiñcitukāmo hoti, buddhāsanā vuṭṭhāya nhānakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisitvā upaṭṭhākena paṭiyāditaudakena gattāni utuṃ gāhāpeti[P 1.0246]. Upaṭṭhākopi buddhāsanaṃ ānetvā papphoṭetvā gandhakuṭipariveṇe paññāpeti. Bhagavā surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā tattha āgantvā nisīdati [M 1.0226] ekakova muhuttaṃ paṭisallīno. Atha bhikkhū tato tato āgamma bhagavato upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanti. Tattha ekacce pañhaṃ pucchanti, ekacce kammaṭṭhānaṃ, ekacce dhammassavanaṃ yācanti. Bhagavā tesaṃ adhippāyaṃ sampādento purimayāmaṃ vītināmeti. Idaṃ purimayāmakiccaṃ.

Thus, having completed his post-meal duties, if he was desirous of pouring water over his limbs, he would rise from the Buddha-seat, enter the bathing chamber, and have his limbs bathed with water prepared by the attendant to suit the season. The attendant also, having brought the Buddha-seat, shaken it out, spreads it in the precinct of the Perfumed Chamber. The Blessed One, having put on a bright-red double-layered robe, fastened his waistband, and properly arranged his upper robe, comes there and sits, abiding alone in seclusion for a moment. Then, bhikkhus, coming from various places, go to attend upon the Blessed One. There, some ask questions, some ask for a meditation subject, and some request to hear the Dhamma. The Blessed One, fulfilling their intentions, passes the first watch. This is the duty of the first watch.

Purimayāmakiccapariyosāne pana bhikkhūsu bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pakkamantesu sakaladasasahassilokadhātudevatāyo okāsaṃ labhamānā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchanti yathābhisaṅkhataṃ antamaso caturakkharampi. Bhagavā tāsaṃ tāsaṃ devatānaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjento majjhimayāmaṃ vītināmeti. Idaṃ majjhimayāmakiccaṃ.

Now, at the conclusion of the duty of the first watch, when the bhikkhus, having paid homage to the Blessed One, are departing, the devas from the entire ten-thousand world-systems, obtaining the opportunity, approach the Blessed One and ask a question as they have formulated it, even one of as few as four syllables. The Blessed One, answering the questions of those various devas, passes the middle watch. This is the duty of the middle watch.

Pacchimayāmaṃ pana tayo koṭṭhāse katvā purebhattato paṭṭhāya nisajjāpīḷitassa sarīrassa kilāsubhāvamocanatthaṃ ekaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ caṅkamena vītināmeti. Dutiyakoṭṭhāse gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā dakkhiṇena passena sato sampajāno sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti. Tatiyakoṭṭhāse paccuṭṭhāya nisīditvā purimabuddhānaṃ santike dānasīlādivasena katādhikārapuggaladassanatthaṃ buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ oloketi. Idaṃ pacchimayāmakiccaṃ.

As for the last watch, having divided it into three portions, He passes one portion pacing, for the sake of relieving the fatigue of His body, which has been oppressed by sitting since the forenoon. In the second portion, having entered the Perfumed Chamber, He adopts the lion's reclining posture on His right side, mindful and fully aware. In the third portion, having arisen and sat down, He surveys the world with the Buddha-eye, for the sake of seeing persons who have made an aspiration in the presence of past Buddhas by way of giving, virtue, and so forth. This is the duty of the last watch.

Tadāpi evaṃ olokento kasibhāradvājaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ arahattassa upanissayasampannaṃ disvā – “tattha mayi gate kathā pavattissati, kathāvasāne dhammadesanaṃ sutvā eso brāhmaṇo saputtadāro tīsu saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya asītikoṭidhanaṃ mama sāsane vippakiritvā aparabhāge nikkhamma pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇissatī”ti ñatvā tattha gantvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ atha kho bhagavātiādi vuttaṃ.

At that time also, while looking about in this manner, He saw the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, who was endowed with the supporting condition for Arahantship. Knowing: “When I go there, a conversation will arise. At the end of the conversation, having heard the Dhamma teaching, this brahmin, together with his wife and children, will become established in the three refuges, distribute his wealth of eighty crores in my Dispensation, and later, having gone forth from home and become ordained, will attain Arahantship,” He went there, initiated the conversation, and taught the Dhamma. To show this meaning, the passage beginning, “Then, the Blessed One…” was spoken.

Tattha [V 1.0218] pubbaṇhasamayanti bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ, pubbaṇhasamayeti attho. Nivāsetvāti paridahitvā. Vihāracīvaraparivattanavasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Pattacīvaramādāyāti pattaṃ hatthehi, cīvaraṃ kāyena ādiyitvā, sampaṭicchitvā [P 1.0247] dhāretvāti attho. Bhagavato kira piṇḍāya pavisitukāmassa bhamaro viya vikasitapadumadvayamajjhaṃ, indanīlamaṇivaṇṇaselamayapatto hatthadvayamajjhaṃ āgacchati. Taṃ evamāgataṃ pattaṃ hatthehi sampaṭicchitvā cīvarañca parimaṇḍalaṃ pārutaṃ kāyena dhāretvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tenupasaṅkamīti [M 1.0227] yena maggena kammanto gantabbo, tena ekakova upasaṅkami. Kasmā pana naṃ bhikkhū nānubandhiṃsūti? Yadā hi bhagavā ekakova katthaci gantukāmo hoti, yāva bhikkhācāravelā dvāraṃ pidahitvā antogandhakuṭiyaṃ nisīdati. Bhikkhū tāya saññāya jānanti “ajja bhagavā ekakova piṇḍāya caritukāmo, addhā kañci eva vinetabbapuggalaṃ addasā”ti. Te attano pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā gandhakuṭiṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā vanditvā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchanti. Tadā ca bhagavā evamakāsi, tasmā bhikkhū nānubandhiṃsūti.

Therein, the word `pubbaṇhasamayaṃ` is an accusative term used in the locative sense; the meaning is `pubbaṇhasamaye`, ‘in the morning time.’ `Nivāsetvā` means having put on the under-robe. This is said with reference to changing the lower garment worn in the monastery. `Pattacīvaramādāya` means: having taken the bowl with the hands and the robe with the body, having received and carried it. It is said that when the Blessed One is desirous of entering for alms, just as a bee approaches the middle of two opened lotuses, the bowl made of stone the color of a sapphire gem comes into the middle of his pair of hands. It is meant that he received with his hands that bowl which had come in this manner, and carried on his body the robe which was worn perfectly round. `Tenupasaṅkami` means: by whichever path the workplace was to be reached, by that path he approached, all alone. But why did the monks not follow him? For when the Blessed One is desirous of going somewhere all alone, until it is time for the alms-round, he closes the door and sits inside the fragrant chamber. By that sign, the monks know: “Today the Blessed One is desirous of going for alms all alone; surely, he has seen some person who is to be trained.” Taking their own bowls and robes, they circumambulate the fragrant chamber keeping it to their right, pay homage, and go for alms. And on that occasion, the Blessed One did so; therefore, the monks did not follow him.

Parivesanā vattatīti tesaṃ suvaṇṇabhājanādīni gahetvā nisinnānaṃ pañcasatānaṃ kassakānaṃ parivisanā vippakatā hoti. Ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsīti yattha ṭhitaṃ brāhmaṇo passati, tathārūpe dassanūpacāre kathāsavanaphāsuke uccaṭṭhāne aṭṭhāsi. Ṭhatvā ca rajatasuvaṇṇarasapiñjaraṃ candimasūriyānaṃ pabhaṃ atirocamānaṃ samantato sarīrappabhaṃ muñci, yāya ajjhotthaṭattā brāhmaṇassa kammantasālābhittirukkhakasitamattikapiṇḍādayo suvaṇṇamayā viya ahesuṃ. Atha manussā bhuñjantā ca kasantā ca sabbakiccāni pahāya asītianubyañjanaparivāraṃ dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sarīraṃ byāmappabhāparikkhepavibhūsitaṃ bāhuyugalaṃ jaṅgamaṃ viya padumasaraṃ, rasmijālasamujjalitatārāgaṇamiva gaganatalaṃ, vijjulatāvinaddhamiva ca kanakasikharaṃ siriyā jalamānaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ disvā hatthapāde dhovitvā añjaliṃ paggayha samparivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Evaṃ tehi samparivāritaṃ addasā kho kasibhāradvājo brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ piṇḍāya ṭhitaṃ, disvāna bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ahaṃ kho, samaṇa, kasāmi ca vapāmi cāti.

The serving was taking place, but for the five hundred farmers who had taken their golden bowls and were seated, the serving was incomplete. He stood to one side: He stood in a high place, within sight and where conversation could be easily heard, a place where the brahmin could see Him standing. And standing there, He released from His body a radiance of molten silver and gold that outshone the light of the moon and sun, illuminating all around. By its pervasive brilliance, the brahmin’s work hall, walls, trees, plowed clods of earth, and so on, appeared as if made of gold. Then the people, whether eating or plowing, abandoned all their tasks. They saw the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One standing to one side, blazing with splendor: His body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and surrounded by the eighty minor characteristics, beautified by a surrounding aura of a fathom's length, and possessing a noble pair of arms; He was like a moving lotus pond, like the expanse of the sky with its host of stars brilliantly shining with a net of rays, and like a golden peak entwined with vines of lightning. Having seen Him, they washed their hands and feet, raised their joined palms in reverence, surrounded Him, and stood there. Thus surrounded by them, the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja indeed saw the Blessed One standing for alms-food. And having seen the Blessed One, he said this: “Indeed, ascetic, I plow and I sow.”

Kasmā [P 1.0248] panāyaṃ evamāha, kiṃ samantapāsādike pasādanīye uttamadamathasamathamanuppattepi tathāgate appasādena, udāhu aḍḍhatiyānaṃ janasahassānaṃ pāyāsaṃ paṭiyādetvāpi kaṭacchubhikkhāya maccherenāti? Ubhayathāpi no, bhagavato panassa dassanena atittaṃ nikkhittakammantaṃ janaṃ disvā “kammabhaṅgaṃ [V 1.0219] me kātuṃ āgato”ti anattamanatā ahosi, tasmā [M 1.0228] evamāha. Bhagavato ca lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā – “sacāyaṃ kammante appayojayissa, sakalajambudīpe manussānaṃ sīse cūḷāmaṇi viya abhavissa, ko nāmassa attho na sampajjissati, evamevaṃ alasatāya kammante appayojetvā vappamaṅgalādīsu piṇḍāya caratī”tipissa anattamanatā ahosi. Tenāha – “ahaṃ kho, samaṇa, kasāmi ca vapāmi ca, kasitvā ca vapitvā ca bhuñjāmī”ti.

But why did he say this? Was it due to a lack of faith in the Tathāgata, who is altogether inspiring, worthy of confidence, and has attained the highest taming and calm? Or was it due to miserliness concerning a single ladleful of alms, even after having prepared milk-rice for two and a half thousand people? It was for neither reason. Rather, seeing the crowd of people who, upon seeing the Blessed One, were insatiable and had set aside their work, he became displeased, thinking, 'He has come to disrupt my work.' That is why he spoke thus. Furthermore, upon seeing the perfection of the Blessed One’s marks, he became displeased, thinking: 'If this man were to apply himself to work, he would be like a crest-jewel on the heads of all people in the entire Jambudīpa. What benefit would not be accomplished for him? Yet, just so, out of laziness, he does not apply himself to work and wanders for alms at the plowing festival and so forth.' This too displeased him. Therefore, he said, 'I, ascetic, plow and sow. Having plowed and sown, I eat.'

Ayaṃ kirassa adhippāyo – mayhampi tāva kammantā na byāpajjanti, na camhi yathā tvaṃ evaṃ lakkhaṇasampanno, tvampi kasitvā ca vapitvā ca bhuñjassu, ko te attho na sampajjeyya evaṃ lakkhaṇasampannassāti. Apicāyaṃ assosi – “sakyarājakule kira kumāro uppanno, so cakkavattirajjaṃ pahāya pabbajito”ti. Tasmā idāni “ayaṃ so”ti ñatvā “cakkavattirajjaṃ pahāya kilantosī”ti upārambhaṃ āropento evamāha. Apica tikkhapañño esa brāhmaṇo, na bhagavantaṃ apasādento bhaṇati, bhagavato pana rūpasampattiṃ disvā puññasampattiṃ sambhāvayamāno kathāpavattanatthampi evamāha. Atha bhagavā veneyyavasena sadevake loke aggakassakavappakabhāvaṃ attano dassento ahampi kho brāhmaṇotiādimāha.

This, it seems, was his intention: 'Even I must still strive at my work, and I am not endowed with marks as you are. You too, having plowed and sown, should eat. For one endowed with such marks, what benefit would not be accomplished?' Moreover, he had heard: 'A prince, it is said, has been born in the Sakyan royal clan, and he, having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, has gone forth.' Therefore, now recognizing him as 'This is he,' he spoke thus, intending a reproach: 'Having renounced the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch, you are now weary.' Furthermore, this brahmin is sharp-witted. He does not speak out of disrespect for the Blessed One; rather, seeing the Blessed One’s physical perfection and esteeming his abundance of merit, he also speaks thus to initiate a conversation. Then the Blessed One, in accordance with the disposition of the one to be trained, revealing his own status as the foremost plowman and sower in the world with its gods, said, 'I too, O brahmin,' and so forth.

Atha brāhmaṇo cintesi – “ayaṃ samaṇo” ‘ahampi kasāmi ca vapāmi cā’ti bhaṇati. Na cassa oḷārikāni yuganaṅgalādīni kasibhaṇḍāni passāmi, kiṃ nu kho musā bhaṇatī”ti? Bhagavantaṃ pādatalato paṭṭhāya yāva kesaggā olokayamāno, aṅgavijjāya katādhikārattā dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇasampattimassa ñatvā, “aṭṭhānametaṃ yaṃ evarūpo musā bhaṇeyyā”ti sañjātabahumāno [P 1.0249] bhagavati samaṇavādaṃ pahāya gottena bhagavantaṃ samudācaramāno na kho pana mayaṃ passāma bhoto gotamassātiādimāha. Bhagavā pana yasmā pubbadhammasabhāgatāya kathanaṃ nāma buddhānaṃ ānubhāvo, tasmā buddhānubhāvaṃ dīpento saddhā bījantiādimāha.

Then the brahmin thought: 'This ascetic says, "I too plow and sow," but I do not see any of his gross implements for plowing, such as a yoke and plow. Could he be speaking falsely?' Observing the Blessed One from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair, and being proficient in the science of bodily marks, he recognized his perfection in the thirty-two excellent marks. He thought: 'It is impossible that one of such a nature would speak falsely.' Filled with great respect for the Blessed One, he abandoned addressing him as 'ascetic' and, using his clan name, said: 'But we do not see Master Gotama's...' and so on. The Blessed One, however, since teaching in correspondence with the preceding topic is a power of the Buddhas, therefore, revealing the power of the Buddhas, said: 'Faith is the seed...' and so forth.

Kā panettha pubbadhammasabhāgatā? Nanu brāhmaṇena bhagavā naṅgalādikasisambhārasamāyogaṃ puṭṭho apucchitassa bījassa sabhāgatāya āha “saddhā bīja”nti, evañca sati kathāpi ananusandhikā hoti? Na hi buddhānaṃ ananusandhikakathā [M 1.0229] nāma atthi, napi pubbadhammassa asabhāgatāya [V 1.0220] kathenti. Evaṃ panettha anusandhi veditabbā – brāhmaṇena hi bhagavā yuganaṅgalādikasisambhāravasena kasiṃ pucchito. So tassa anukampāya “idaṃ apucchita”nti aparihāpetvā samūlaṃ saupakāraṃ sasambhāraṃ saphalaṃ kasiṃ paññāpetuṃ mūlato paṭṭhāya dassento “saddhā bīja”ntiādimāha. Tattha bījaṃ kasiyā mūlaṃ, tasmiṃ sati kattabbato, asati akattabbato, tappamāṇena ca kattabbato. Bīje hi sati kasiṃ karonti, na asati. Bījappamāṇena ca kusalā kassakā khettaṃ kasanti, na ūnaṃ “mā no sassaṃ parihāyī”ti, na adhikaṃ “mā no mogho vāyāmo ahosī”ti. Yasmā ca bījameva mūlaṃ, tasmā bhagavā mūlato paṭṭhāya kasisambhāraṃ dassento tassa brāhmaṇassa kasiyā pubbadhammassa bījassa sabhāgatāya attano kasiyā pubbadhammaṃ dassento āha “saddhā bīja”nti. Evamettha pubbadhammasabhāgatāpi veditabbā.

What, here, is the correspondence with the preceding teaching? Was not the Blessed One asked by the brahmin about the association with farming equipment beginning with the plow? He said, 'Faith is the seed,' in correspondence with the unasked-for seed. This being so, does not the discourse become disconnected? For disconnected speech is not found in Buddhas, nor do they speak without correspondence to the preceding teaching. Here, the connection should be understood thus: the brahmin asked the Blessed One about farming based on the equipment beginning with the yoke and plow. He, out of compassion for him, not setting aside 'this is unasked,' in order to make known farming with its root, with its benefit, with its implements, and with its fruit, showing it beginning from the root, said, 'Faith is the seed,' and so forth. Therein, the seed is the root of farming, because when it exists, farming is to be done; when it does not exist, it is not to be done; and because it is to be done according to its measure. For when the seed exists, farmers farm; not when it does not exist. And skilled farmers plow the field according to the measure of the seed—not too little, thinking, 'May our crop not diminish,' nor too much, thinking, 'May our effort not be in vain.' And since the seed itself is the root, therefore the Blessed One, showing the equipment for farming beginning from the root, and showing the preceding element of His own farming in correspondence with the seed—the preceding element of that brahmin's farming—said, 'Faith is the seed.' Thus, here, the correspondence with the preceding teaching should also be known.

Pucchitaṃyeva vatvā apucchitaṃ pacchā kiṃ na vuttanti ce? Tassa upakārabhāvato ca dhammasambandhasamatthabhāvato ca. Ayaṃ hi brāhmaṇo paññavā, micchādiṭṭhikule pana jātattā saddhārahito, saddhārahito ca paññavā paresaṃ saddhāya attano avisaye apaṭipajjamāno visesaṃ nādhigacchati, kilesakālussiyaparāmaṭṭhāpi cassa dubbalā saddhā balavatiyā paññāya sahasā vattamānā atthasiddhiṃ na karoti hatthinā saddhiṃ ekadhure yutto goṇo [P 1.0250] viya. Itissa saddhā upakārikāti taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ saddhāya patiṭṭhāpentena pacchāpi vattabbo ayamattho desanākusalatāya pubbe vutto. Bījassa ca upakārikā vuṭṭhi, sā tadanantaraṃyeva vuccamānā samatthā hoti. Evaṃ dhammasambandhasamatthabhāvato pacchāpi vattabbo ayamattho, añño ca evarūpo īsāyottādi pubbe vuttoti veditabbo.

If it is said, 'Why was the unasked-for matter not spoken of later, after having addressed what was asked?' It is because of its benefit to him and because of its ability to connect the teaching to its result. Indeed, this brahmin is wise, but because he was born in a family of wrong view, he is devoid of faith. A wise person who is devoid of faith, not undertaking the practice in his proper domain through faith in others, does not attain a special attainment. And his weak faith, though afflicted by the stain of defilements, when proceeding together with powerful wisdom, does not bring about the accomplishment of the goal, just like an ox yoked to a single shaft together with an elephant. Thus, 'faith is beneficial to him.' Therefore, by Him who was establishing that brahmin in faith, this meaning, which should have been spoken later, was spoken earlier due to His skill in exposition. Rain is beneficial to a seed, and it is effective when spoken of immediately after the seed. Similarly, it should be understood that because of its ability to connect the teaching to its result, this meaning which should have been spoken later, and other similar meanings such as the plough-pole and yoke-rope, were spoken earlier.

Tattha sampasādalakkhaṇā saddhā, okappanalakkhaṇā vā. Bījanti pañcavidhaṃ bījaṃ mūlabījaṃ khandhabījaṃ phalubījaṃ aggabījaṃ bījabījameva pañcamanti. Taṃ sabbampi viruhaṇaṭṭhena bījanteva saṅkhaṃ gacchati.

Therein, faith has the characteristic of serene confidence, or it has the characteristic of conviction. As for 'seed', a seed is fivefold: root-seed, stem-seed, joint-seed, shoot-seed, and the fifth is seed-seed itself. All of these are designated as 'seed' because of their meaning of sprouting.

Tattha [M 1.0230] yathā brāhmaṇassa kasiyā mūlabhūtaṃ bījaṃ dve kiccāni karoti, heṭṭhā mūlena patiṭṭhāti, upari aṅkuraṃ uṭṭhāpeti, evaṃ bhagavato kasiyā mūlabhūtā saddhā heṭṭhā sīlamūlena patiṭṭhāti[V 1.0221], upari samathavipassanaṅkuraṃ uṭṭhāpeti. Yathā ca taṃ mūlena pathavirasaṃ āporasaṃ gahetvā nāḷena dhaññaparipākagahaṇatthaṃ vaḍḍhati, evamayaṃ sīlamūlena samathavipassanārasaṃ gahetvā ariyamagganāḷena ariyaphaladhaññaparipākagahaṇatthaṃ vaḍḍhati. Yathā ca taṃ subhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahitvā mūlaṅkurapaṇṇanāḷakaṇḍapasavehi vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ patvā khīraṃ janetvā anekasāliphalabharitaṃ sālisīsaṃ nipphādeti, evamesā cittasantāne patiṭṭhahitvā chahi visuddhīhi vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ patvā ñāṇadassanavisuddhikhīraṃ janetvā anekapaṭisambhidābhiññābharitaṃ arahattaphalaṃ nipphādeti. Tena vuttaṃ “saddhā bīja”nti.

In this context, just as for a brahmin’s cultivation, the seed, being the fundamental cause, performs two functions: below, it is established by the root, and above, it causes a sprout to arise. So too, for the Blessed One’s cultivation, faith, being the fundamental cause, is established below by the root that is virtue, and above, it causes the sprout of serenity and insight to arise. And just as that seed, having taken the earth-essence and the water-essence by its root, grows by its stalk for the purpose of attaining the ripening of the grain, so too this faith, having taken the essence of serenity and insight by the root that is virtue, grows by the stalk that is the noble path for the purpose of attaining the ripening of the grain that is the noble fruit. And just as that seed, having been established in good soil, having attained growth, sprouting, and abundance through its root, sprout, leaf, stalk, and joint, and having produced milk-sap, brings to completion an ear of rice filled with countless grains; so too this faith, having been established in the mental continuum, having attained growth, sprouting, and abundance through the six purifications, and having produced the milk-sap that is the purification of knowledge and vision, brings to completion the fruit of Arahantship filled with numerous analytical knowledges and direct knowledges. Therefore, it was said, “Faith is the seed.”

Kasmā pana aññesu paropaññāsāya kusaladhammesu ekato uppajjamānesu saddhāva “bīja”nti vuttāti ce? Bījakiccakaraṇato. Yathā hi tesu viññāṇaṃyeva vijānanakiccaṃ karoti, evaṃ saddhā bījakiccaṃ. Sā ca sabbakusalānaṃ mūlabhūtā. Yathāha – “saddhājāto upasaṅkamati, upasaṅkamanto payirupāsati…pe… paññāya ca naṃ ativijjha passatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.183).

If it is asked, “But why, when the other fifty-odd wholesome states arise together, is faith alone said to be ‘the seed’?” Because it performs the function of a seed. For just as among those states, consciousness alone performs the function of cognizing, so too faith performs the function of a seed. And it is the fundamental cause of all wholesome states. As it was said: “Having been born of faith, one approaches; approaching, one pays respect… and one penetrates it with wisdom and sees.”

Akusaladhamme [P 1.0251] ceva kāyañca tapatīti tapo. Indriyasaṃvaravīriyadhutaṅgadukkarakārikānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ, idha pana indriyasaṃvaro adhippeto. Vuṭṭhīti vassavuṭṭhi vātavuṭṭhītiādi anekavidhā, idha vassavuṭṭhi adhippetā. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa vassavuṭṭhisamanuggahitaṃ bījaṃ bījamūlakañca sassaṃ viruhati na milāyati nipphattiṃ gacchati, evaṃ bhagavato indriyasaṃvarasamanuggahitā saddhā, saddhāmūlā ca sīlādayo dhammā viruhanti, na milāyanti nipphattiṃ gacchanti. Tenāha “tapo vuṭṭhī”ti.

Tapa is that which torments unwholesome qualities and the body. This is a designation for those who undertake restraint of the senses, energy, ascetic practices, and difficult deeds; here, however, restraint of the senses is intended. Vuṭṭhi is of many kinds, such as rain and wind-rain; here, however, rain is intended. Just as for a brahmin, the seed and the crop rooted in the seed, supported by rain, grow, do not wither, and reach maturity, so too for the Blessed One, faith, which is supported by restraint of the senses, and the qualities rooted in faith—such as virtue and so on—grow, do not wither, and reach maturity. Therefore, He said, “Austerity is the rain.”

Paññā meti ettha vutto me-saddo purimapadesupi yojetabbo “saddhā me bījaṃ, tapo me vuṭṭhī”ti tena kiṃ dīpeti? Yathā, brāhmaṇa, tayā vapite khette sace vuṭṭhi atthi, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce atthi, udakampi tāva dātabbaṃ hoti. Tathā mayā hiriīse paññāyuganaṅgale manoyottena ekābaddhe kate vīriyabalībadde yojetvā satipācanena vijjhitvā attano cittasantānakhettamhi saddhābīje vapite [M 1.0231] vuṭṭhiyā abhāvo nāma natthi, ayaṃ pana me niccakālaṃ indriyasaṃvaratapo vuṭṭhīti.

“Wisdom is mine”—here the word “mine” should be applied to the previous phrases as well: “faith is my seed, austerity is my rain.” What does this illustrate? Just as, brahmin, if in the field you have sown, there is rain, that is good. If not, water must still be given. Similarly, when I have fashioned the yoke-plow of wisdom with the pole of moral shame, bound as one with the yoke-rope of mind, having yoked the two oxen of energy, and having prodded them with the goad of mindfulness, in the field of my own mental continuum where the seed of faith is sown, there is no such thing as an absence of rain. Rather, this restraint of the senses as austerity is my constant rain.

Paññāti [V 1.0222] kāmāvacarādibhedato anekavidhā. Idha pana saha vipassanāya maggapaññā adhippetā. Yuganaṅgalanti yugañca naṅgalañca yuganaṅgalaṃ. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa yuganaṅgalaṃ, evaṃ bhagavato duvidhāpi vipassanā paññā ca. Tattha yathā yugaṃ īsāya upanissayaṃ hoti, purato ca īsābaddhaṃ hoti, yottānaṃ nissayaṃ hoti, balībaddānaṃ ekato gamanaṃ dhāreti, evaṃ paññā hirippamukhānaṃ dhammānaṃ upanissayā hoti. Yathāha – “paññuttarā sabbe kusalā dhammā”ti (a. ni. 8.83; 10.58) ca, “paññā hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadanti, nakkhattarājāriva tārakāna”nti (jā. 2.17.81) ca. Kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pubbaṅgamaṭṭhena purato ca hoti. Yathāha – “sīlaṃ sirī cāpi satañca dhammo, anvāyikā paññavato bhavantī”ti hirivippayogena anuppattito pana īsābaddho hoti. Manosaṅkhātassa samādhiyottassa nissayapaccayato yottānaṃ [P 1.0252] nissayo hoti. Accāraddhātilīnabhāvapaṭisedhanato vīriyabalībaddānaṃ ekato gamanaṃ dhāreti, yathā ca naṅgalaṃ phālayuttaṃ kasanakāle pathavighanaṃ bhindati, mūlasantānakāni padāleti, evaṃ satiyuttā paññā vipassanākāle dhammānaṃ santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanaṃ bhindati, sabbakilesamūlasantānakāni padāleti. Sā ca kho lokuttarāva, itarā pana lokikāpi siyā. Tenāha “paññā me yuganaṅgala”nti.

Wisdom is of many kinds, such as that pertaining to the sense-sphere and so forth. Here, however, path-wisdom together with insight is intended. Yuganaṅgalaṃ means a yoke and a plow. Just as for a brahmin there is a yoke-plow, so too for the Blessed One, insight-wisdom is twofold. Therein, just as the yoke is a support for the pole, is fastened to the pole in front, is a support for the harnesses, and enables the oxen to move together; so too, wisdom is a support for moral qualities headed by moral shame. As it is said: “All wholesome states are led by wisdom,” and “The wise declare wisdom to be the best of wholesome qualities, like the king of stars among the stars.” Wisdom stands at the forefront due to being the forerunner of wholesome qualities. As it is said: “Virtue, glory, and the Dhamma of the good become attendants of the wise.” And because it does not arise apart from moral shame, it is fastened to the pole. Because it is the support-condition for the harness of concentration, which is designated as mind, it is a support for the harnesses. By preventing excessive exertion or sluggishness, it enables the oxen of energy to move together. And just as the plow, fitted with a share, breaks up the hard ground when plowing and tears apart the root networks; so too, wisdom, yoked with mindfulness, at the time of insight, breaks up the solid mass of continuity, collection, function, and object of phenomena, and tears apart all the root networks of defilements. That which tears apart is exclusively supramundane, but the other may be mundane too. Therefore, He said: “Wisdom is my yoke-plow.”

Hirīyati pāpakehi dhammehīti hirī. Taggahaṇena tāya avippayuttaṃ ottappampi gahitameva hoti. Īsāti yuganaṅgalasandhārikā rukkhalaṭṭhi. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa īsā yuganaṅgalaṃ dhāreti, evaṃ bhagavatopi hirī lokiyalokuttarapaññāsaṅkhātaṃ yuganaṅgalaṃ dhāreti hiriabhāve paññāya abhāvato. Yathā ca īsāpaṭibaddhayuganaṅgalaṃ kiccakaraṃ hoti acalaṃ asithilaṃ, evaṃ hiripaṭibaddhā ca paññā kiccakārī hoti acalā asithilā abbokiṇṇā ahirikena. Tenāha “hirī īsā”ti. Munātīti mano, cittassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Idha pana manosīsena taṃsampayutto samādhi adhippeto. Yottanti rajjubandhanaṃ. Taṃ tividhaṃ īsāya saha yugassa [M 1.0232] bandhanaṃ, yugena saha balībaddānaṃ bandhanaṃ, sārathinā saha balībaddānaṃ ekābandhananti. Tattha yathā brāhmaṇassa yottaṃ īsāyugabalībadde ekābaddhe katvā sakakicce paṭipādeti, evaṃ bhagavato samādhi sabbeva te hiripaññāvīriyadhamme ekārammaṇe avikkhepasabhāvena bandhitvā sakakicce paṭipādeti. Tenāha “mano yotta”nti.

Because one is ashamed of evil states, it is called hirī (moral shame). By the taking of this term, ottappa (moral dread), which is inseparable from it, is also indeed taken. Īsā (pole) is the wooden shaft that holds the yoke and plow firmly. For just as a brahmin's pole carries the yoke-plow, so too the Blessed One's moral shame carries the yoke-plow known as mundane and supramundane wisdom, because in the absence of moral shame, there is an absence of wisdom. And just as the yoke-plow bound by the pole is unmoving, unslackened, and accomplishes its task, so too wisdom bound by moral shame is unmoving, unslackened, performs its task, and is unmixed with the shameless. Therefore, He said, “Moral shame is the pole.” Because it knows, it is mano (mind); this is a name for citta (consciousness). Here, however, the concentration associated with it, with mind as the lead, is intended. Yottaṃ (yoke-rope) is a rope-binding. It is threefold: the binding of the yoke together with the pole, the binding of the oxen together with the yoke, and the single binding of the oxen together with the plowman. Therein, just as a brahmin's yoke-rope, having bound the pole, yoke, and oxen as one, accomplishes its own tasks, so too the Blessed One's concentration, having bound all those states—moral shame, wisdom, and energy—to a single object by its nature of non-distraction, accomplishes their respective tasks. Therefore, He said, “The mind is the yoke-rope.”

Cirakatādimatthaṃ [V 1.0223] saratīti sati. Phāletīti phālo. Pājenti etenāti pājanaṃ. Taṃ idha “pācana”nti vuttaṃ. Patodassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Phālo ca pācanañca phālapācanaṃ. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa phālapācanaṃ, evaṃ bhagavato vipassanāsampayuttā maggasampayuttā ca sati. Tattha yathā phālo naṅgalaṃ [P 1.0253] anurakkhati, purato cassa gacchati, evaṃ sati kusalākusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ gatiyo samanvesamānā ārammaṇe vā upaṭṭhāpayamānā paññānaṅgalaṃ rakkhati. Tenevesā “satārakkhena cetasā viharatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 10.20) viya ārakkhāti vuttā. Appamussanavasena cassā purato hoti. Satiparicite hi dhamme paññā pajānāti, no pamuṭṭhe. Yathā ca pācanaṃ balībaddānaṃ vijjhanabhayaṃ dassentaṃ saṃsīdituṃ na deti, uppathagamanaṃ vāreti, evaṃ sati vīriyabalībaddānaṃ apāyabhayaṃ dassentī kosajjasaṃsīdanaṃ na deti, kāmaguṇasaṅkhāte agocare cāraṃ nivāretvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojentī uppathagamanaṃ vāreti. Tenāha “sati me phālapācana”nti.

Because it remembers the meaning of what was done long ago, etc., it is sati (mindfulness). Because it splits, it is a phāla (plowshare). Because they drive with it, it is a pājana (goad). Here, that is called a 'pācana' (goad). This is a name for a goad. The plowshare and the goad are the phālapācana (plowshare-and-goad). For just as a brahmin has a plowshare-and-goad, so the Blessed One has mindfulness that is associated with insight and associated with the path. Therein, just as the plowshare protects the plow and goes before it, so mindfulness, while investigating the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, or while establishing them in the object, protects the plow of wisdom. For that very reason, it is called a 'guardian,' as in passages such as 'he dwells with a mind guarded by mindfulness.' And by way of non-forgetfulness, it is before it. For wisdom discerns a state made familiar by mindfulness, not one that is forgotten. And just as the goad, showing the danger of being pierced to the oxen, does not allow them to sink down and prevents them from going astray, so mindfulness, showing the danger of the lower realms to the oxen of energy, does not allow the sinking down into laziness; having prevented wandering in the unsuitable pasture consisting of sensual pleasures and yoking them to the meditation subject, it prevents them from going astray. Therefore, He said, 'Mindfulness is my plowshare-and-goad.'

Kāyaguttoti tividhena kāyasucaritena gutto. Vacīguttoti catubbidhena vacīsucaritena gutto. Ettāvatā pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Āhāre udare yatoti ettha āhāramukhena sabbapaccayānaṃ gahitattā catubbidhepi paccaye yato saṃyato nirupakkilesoti attho. Iminā ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Udare yatoti udare yato saṃyato mitabhojī, āhāre mattaññūti vuttaṃ hoti. Iminā bhojane mattaññutāmukhena paccayapaṭisevanasīlaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena kiṃ dīpeti? Yathā tvaṃ, brāhmaṇa, bījaṃ vapitvā sassaparipālanatthaṃ kaṇṭakavatiṃ vā rukkhavatiṃ vā pākāraparikkhepaṃ vā karosi, tena te gomahiṃsamigagaṇā pavesaṃ alabhantā sassaṃ na vilumpanti, evamahampi taṃ saddhābījaṃ vapitvā nānappakārakusalasassaparipālanatthaṃ kāyavacīāhāraguttimayaṃ tividhaṃ parikkhepaṃ karomi[M 1.0233], tena me rāgādiakusaladhammagomahiṃsamigagaṇā pavesaṃ alabhantā nānappakārakaṃ kusalasassaṃ na vilumpantīti.

As for 'guarded in body,' it means guarded by the threefold good bodily conduct. As for 'guarded in speech,' it means guarded by the fourfold good verbal conduct. By this much, the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha is stated. As for 'restrained in food, in the belly,' here, because all requisites are included under the heading of food, the meaning is: restrained, well-restrained, and undefiled regarding the fourfold requisites. By this, the virtue of purity of livelihood is stated. As for 'restrained in the belly,' it means restrained and well-restrained in the belly, moderate in eating; it is said to be 'knowing the measure in food.' By this, through knowing the measure in food, the virtue of using requisites reflectively is stated. By that, what does he illustrate? 'Brahmin, just as you, having sown seed, make a thorn fence, a wooden fence, or a surrounding wall to protect the crop, whereby herds of cattle, buffalo, and deer, not gaining entry, do not plunder the crop; even so, I too, having sown that seed of faith, make a threefold fence consisting of the guarding of body, speech, and food to protect the crop of various kinds of wholesome states, whereby the herds of cattle, buffalo, and deer that are the unwholesome states such as lust, not gaining entry, do not plunder my crop of various kinds of wholesome states.' This is what he illustrates.

Saccaṃ karomi niddānanti ettha dvīhākārehi avisaṃvādanaṃ saccaṃ. Niddānanti chedanaṃ lunanaṃ uppāṭanaṃ[P 1.0254]. Karaṇatthe cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ hettha attho “saccena karomi niddāna”nti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “yathā tvaṃ bāhiraṃ kasiṃ katvā sassadūsakānaṃ tiṇānaṃ hatthena vā asitena vā niddānaṃ karosi, evaṃ ahampi ajjhattikaṃ kasiṃ katvā kusalasassadūsakānaṃ [V 1.0224] visaṃvādanatiṇānaṃ saccena niddānaṃ karomī”ti. Yathābhūtañāṇaṃ vā ettha saccanti veditabbaṃ. Tena attasaññādīnaṃ tiṇānaṃ niddānaṃ karomīti dasseti. Atha vā niddānanti chedakaṃ lāvakaṃ uppāṭakanti attho. Yathā tvaṃ dāsaṃ vā kammakaraṃ vā niddānaṃ karosi, “niddehi tiṇānī”ti tiṇānaṃ chedakaṃ lāvakaṃ uppāṭakaṃ karosi, evamahaṃ saccaṃ karomīti dasseti, atha vā saccanti diṭṭhisaccaṃ. Tamahaṃ niddānaṃ karomi, chinditabbaṃ lunitabbaṃ uppāṭetabbaṃ karomīti. Iti imesu dvīsu vikappesu upayogenevattho yujjati.

Herein, regarding 'Saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ' (I perform the weeding), truth is non-deception in two ways. 'Weeding' means severing, reaping, and uprooting. And this should be understood as a term of application in the instrumental sense. This is the meaning here: 'I perform the weeding by means of truth.' What is being said? 'Just as you, having done external farming, perform the weeding of the weeds that spoil the crops with your hand or a sickle, so too I, having done internal farming, perform the weeding with truth of the weeds of deception that spoil the wholesome crops.' Or, herein, truth should be understood as knowledge of things as they really are. By that, he shows, 'I perform the weeding of the weeds of the perception of self, etc.' Alternatively, 'weeding' means a weeder: a severer, a reaper, an uprooter. Just as you make a slave or a worker a weeder, saying, 'Weed the weeds!'—making them a severer, a reaper, an uprooter of weeds—so he shows, 'I make truth my weeder.' Or, 'truth' refers to the truth of (wrong) view. That I make a weeding, meaning I make it to be severed, to be reaped, to be uprooted. Thus, in these two alternatives, the meaning is suitable only through its use as a term of application.

Soraccaṃ me pamocananti ettha yaṃ taṃ “kāyiko avītikkamo vācasiko avītikkamo”ti sīlameva “soracca”nti vuttaṃ, na taṃ adhippetaṃ. “Kāyagutto”tiādinā hi taṃ vuttameva. Arahattaphalaṃ pana adhippetaṃ. Taṃ hi sundare nibbāne ratattā “soracca”nti vuccati. Pamocananti yogavissajjanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā tava pamocanaṃ punapi sāyanhe vā dutiyadivase vā anāgatasaṃvacchare vā yojetabbato appamocanameva hoti, na mama evaṃ. Na hi mama antarā mocanaṃ nāma atthi. Ahaṃ hi dīpaṅkaradasabalakālato paṭṭhāya paññānaṅgale vīriyabalībadde yojetvā kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni mahākasiṃ kasanto tāva na muñciṃ, yāva na sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhiṃ. Yadā ca me sabbaṃ taṃ kālaṃ khepetvā bodhimūle aparājitapallaṅke nisinnassa sabbaguṇaparivāraṃ arahattaphalaṃ udapādi, tadā mayā taṃ [P 1.0255] sabbussukkapaṭippassaddhiyā pamuttaṃ, na dāni puna yojetabbaṃ bhavissatīti. Etamatthaṃ sandhāyāha “soraccaṃ me pamocana”nti.

As to 'Gentleness is my release,' here, what is called 'gentleness' is the virtue of 'non-transgression by body or speech,' but that is not what is intended. For that has already been stated by 'guarded in body,' and so on. Rather, the fruit of Arahantship is intended. That is called 'gentleness' because it delights in the beautiful Nibbāna. 'Release' means the relinquishing of application. This is what is said: 'Just as your release, because it must be applied again in the evening or on the next day or in a future year, is in fact not a release, it is not so for me. For there is no such thing as an intermittent release for me. For I, beginning from the time of Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, having yoked the oxen of energy to the plow of wisdom and tilling the great field for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand great aeons, was not released so long as I had not fully awakened to perfect self-awakening. And when, for me, having spent all that time, while seated on the unconquered seat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the fruit of Arahantship, attended by all virtues, arose, then I was released with the complete calming of all striving, and now it will not have to be applied again.' It is with reference to this meaning that he said, 'Gentleness is my release.'

Vīriyaṃ [M 1.0234] me dhuradhorayhanti ettha vīriyanti kāyikacetasiko vīriyārambho. Dhuradhorayhanti dhurāyaṃ dhorayhaṃ, dhurāvahanti attho. Yathā hi brāhmaṇassa dhurāyaṃ dhorayhākaḍḍhitaṃ naṅgalaṃ bhūmighanaṃ bhindati, mūlasantānakāni ca padāleti, evaṃ bhagavato vīriyākaḍḍhitaṃ paññānaṅgalaṃ yathā vuttaṃ ghanaṃ bhindati, kilesasantānakāni ca padāleti. Tenāha “vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayha”nti. Atha vā purimadhurāvahattā dhurā, mūladhurāvahattā dhorayhā, dhurā ca dhorayhā ca dhuradhorayhā. Iti yathā brāhmaṇassa ekekasmiṃ naṅgale catubalībaddapabhedaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ vahantaṃ uppannuppannaṃ tiṇamūlaghātañceva sassasampattiñca sādheti, evaṃ bhagavato catusammappadhānavīriyabhedaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ vahantaṃ uppannuppannaṃ akusalaghātañceva kusalasampattiñca sādheti. Tenāha “vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayha”nti.

Regarding 'My energy is the burden-bearer,' herein, 'energy' is the bodily and mental exertion of effort. 'Burden-bearer' means like a strong ox at the front of the yoke; it means one who is capable of bearing the burden. For example, just as a plow, pulled by a brahmin's strong, burden-bearing oxen, breaks up the solid earth and tears apart the networks of roots, so too the plow of wisdom, pulled by the Blessed One’s energy, breaks up the solid mass as has been stated and tears apart the networks of defilements. Therefore, He said: 'My energy is the burden-bearer.' Alternatively, 'dhurā' is so called because it bears the first burden, and 'dhorayhā' because it bears the root burden. 'Dhurā' and 'dhorayhā' together form 'dhuradhorayhā'. Thus, just as for a brahmin, a burden-bearing team comprising four oxen for each plow, while pulling, accomplishes both the destruction of the roots of whatever grass arises and the perfection of the crop, so too the Blessed One’s burden-bearing energy, comprising the four right strivings, while being exerted, accomplishes both the destruction of whatever unwholesome states arise and the perfection of wholesome states. Therefore, He said: 'My energy is the burden-bearer.'

Yogakkhemādhivāhananti [V 1.0225] ettha yogehi khemattā nibbānaṃ yogakkhemaṃ nāma, taṃ adhikicca vāhīyati, abhimukhaṃ vā vāhīyatīti adhivāhanaṃ, yogakkhemassa adhivāhanaṃ yogakkhemādhivāhananti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā tava dhuradhorayhaṃ puratthimādīsu aññataradisābhimukhaṃ vāhīyati, tathā mama dhuradhorayhaṃ nibbānābhimukhaṃ vāhīyatīti. Evaṃ vāhīyamānaṃva gacchati anivattantaṃ. Yathā tava naṅgalaṃ vahantaṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ khettakoṭiṃ patvā puna nivattati, evaṃ anivattantaṃ dīpaṅkarakālato paṭṭhāya gacchateva. Yasmā vā tena tena maggena pahīnā kilesā na punappunaṃ pahātabbā honti, yathā tava naṅgalena chinnāni tiṇāni puna aparasmiṃ samaye chinditabbāni honti, tasmāpi evaṃ paṭhamamaggavasena diṭṭhekaṭṭhe [P 1.0256] kilese, dutiyavasena oḷārike, tatiyavasena aṇusahagate, catutthavasena sabbakilese pajahantaṃ gacchati anivattantaṃ. Atha vā gacchati anivattanti nivattanarahitaṃ hutvā gacchatīti attho. Tanti taṃ dhuradhorayhaṃ. Evamettha attho veditabbo. Evaṃ gacchantañca yathā tava dhuradhorayhaṃ na taṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati, yattha gantvā kassako asoko virajo hutvā na socati. Etaṃ pana taṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchati yattha gantvā na socati. Yattha satipācanena etaṃ vīriyadhuradhorayhaṃ codento gantvā mādiso kassako asoko virajo hutvā na socati, taṃ sabbasokasallasamugghātabhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma asaṅkhataṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchatīti.

Regarding 'the carrier to security from the yokes,' herein, because of its security from the yokes, Nibbāna is called 'security from the yokes.' It is carried with reference to that, or it is carried towards it; therefore, it is called the 'carrier.' The carrier to security from the yokes is 'yogakkhemādhivāhana.' This is what is said: Just as your beast of burden is carried towards one of the eastern or other directions, so my beast of burden is carried towards Nibbāna. Thus, being carried, it goes without turning back. Just as your beast of burden, while carrying the plow, turns back again after reaching the edge of the field, so this one goes on without turning back, ever since the time of Dīpaṅkara. Or, because the defilements abandoned by their respective paths do not need to be abandoned again and again—just as the grasses cut by your plow need to be cut again at another time—therefore also, it goes without turning back, abandoning the defilements in the same group as wrong view by means of the first path, the gross ones by means of the second, the subtle ones by means of the third, and all defilements by means of the fourth. Alternatively, 'it goes without turning back' means it goes having become free from turning back. 'That' refers to that beast of burden. Thus should the meaning here be understood. And as it goes, just as your beast of burden does not go to that place where, having gone, the farmer becomes sorrowless, passionless, and does not grieve; this one, however, goes to that place where, having gone, one does not grieve. It goes to that unconditioned place called Nibbāna, the ground for uprooting all darts of sorrow, where a farmer such as myself, having gone there by urging on this beast of burden of energy with the goad of mindfulness, becomes sorrowless, passionless, and does not grieve.

Idāni [M 1.0235] nigamanaṃ karonto evamesā kasīti gāthamāha. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yassa, brāhmaṇa, esā saddhābījā tapovuṭṭhiyā anuggahitā kasī paññāmayaṃ yuganaṅgalaṃ hirimayañca īsaṃ manomayena yottena ekābaddhaṃ katvā paññānaṅgalena satiphālaṃ ākoṭetvā satipācanaṃ gahetvā kāyavacīāhāraguttiyā gopetvā saccaṃ niddānaṃ katvā soraccapamocanaṃ vīriyadhuradhorayhaṃ yogakkhemābhimukhaṃ anivattantaṃ vāhantena kaṭṭhā kasī kammapariyosānaṃ catubbidhaṃ sāmaññaphalaṃ pāpitā, sā hoti amatapphalā, sā esā kasī amatapphalā hoti. Amataṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ, nibbānānisaṃsā hotīti attho. Sā kho panesā kasī na mamevekassa amatapphalā hoti, atha kho yo koci khattiyo vā brāhmaṇo vā vesso vā suddo vā gahaṭṭho vā pabbajito vā etaṃ kasiṃ kasati, so sabbopi etaṃ kasitvāna sabbadukkhā pamuccatīti.

Now, wishing to make a conclusion, he spoke the verse beginning 'evamesā kasī.' This is its summary meaning: O brahmin, for one whose cultivation is supported by the seed of faith and the rain of austerity; having bound together a yoke and plow made of wisdom with a plowshaft made of conscience by means of a mind-made rope; having fixed the plowshare of mindfulness to the plow of wisdom; having taken the goad of mindfulness; having guarded with bodily, verbal, and dietary restraint; having done the weeding with truth; with gentleness as the unyoking; this cultivation—tilled by the beast of burden of energy that pulls without turning back towards security from the yokes—is brought to the fourfold fruit of recluseship as its completion of work, and it has a deathless fruit. This cultivation has a deathless fruit. The Deathless is called Nibbāna; it has the benefit of Nibbāna, this is the meaning. Moreover, this cultivation does not have a deathless fruit for me alone. But whoever, whether a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, a laborer, a householder, or a renunciant, cultivates this cultivation, all of them, having cultivated it, are freed from all suffering.

Evaṃ bhagavā brāhmaṇassa arahattanikūṭena nibbānapariyosānaṃ katvā desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Tato [V 1.0226] brāhmaṇo gambhīratthaṃ desanaṃ sutvā – “mama kasiphalaṃ bhuñjitvā punapi divaseyeva chāto hoti, imassa pana kasī amatapphalā, tassa phalaṃ bhuñjitvā sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti ñatvā pasanno pasannākāraṃ karonto bhuñjatu bhavaṃ gotamotiādimāha. Taṃ sabbaṃ tato parañca vuttatthamevāti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Thus, the Blessed One concluded his teaching for the brahmin, making arahantship its peak and Nibbāna its conclusion. Then the brahmin, having heard the teaching of profound meaning, knowing, “Having eaten the fruit of my cultivation, one becomes hungry again on that very day, but the cultivation of this one is of deathless fruit; having eaten its fruit, one is freed from all suffering,” was pleased, and making a gesture of pleasure, he spoke the words beginning with, “Let the venerable Gotama eat.” All of that, and what follows it, has the same meaning as what has already been said. The first.

2. Udayasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Udaya Sutta

198. Dutiye [P 1.0257] odanena pūresīti attano atthāya sampāditena sūpabyañjanena odanena pūretvā adāsi. Bhagavā kira paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokentova taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ disvā, pātova sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā, gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā, dvāraṃ pidhāya, nisinno tassa bhojanaṃ upasaṃhariyamānaṃ disvā, ekakova pattaṃ aṃsakūṭe laggetvā, gandhakuṭito nikkhamma, nagaradvāre pattaṃ nīharitvā, antonagaraṃ pavisitvā, paṭipāṭiyā gacchanto brāhmaṇassa dvārakoṭṭhake aṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ disvā, attano sajjitaṃ bhojanaṃ adāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Dutiyampīti dutiyadivasepi. Tatiyampīti tatiyadivasepi. Tāni kira tīṇi divasāni nirantaraṃ [M 1.0236] brāhmaṇassa gharadvāraṃ gacchantassa bhagavato antarā añño koci uṭṭhāya pattaṃ gahetuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi, mahājano olokentova aṭṭhāsi.

198. In the second sutta, “he filled with rice” means he filled it with rice along with curries and condiments prepared for his own use, and gave it. It is said that the Blessed One, surveying the world in the early morning, saw that brahmin. After attending to his bodily needs at dawn, he entered the fragrant hut, closed the door, and sat down. Seeing his food being brought near, he alone, having hung his bowl on his shoulder, came out from the fragrant hut, took out his bowl at the city gate, entered the city, and going in sequence, stood at the brahmin’s doorpost. The brahmin, seeing the Blessed One, gave him his own prepared meal. This was said with reference to that. “On the second day too” means also on the second day. “On the third day too” means also on the third day. It is said that for those three consecutive days, while the Blessed One was going to the brahmin’s house door, no one else was able to rise and take the bowl. The great multitude just stood watching.

Etadavocāti brāhmaṇo tīṇi divasāni pattaṃ pūretvā dentopi na saddhāya adāsi, “gharadvāraṃ āgantvā ṭhitassa pabbajitassa bhikkhāmattampi adatvā bhuñjatī”ti upārambhabhayena adāsi. Dadanto ca dve divasāni datvā kiñci avatvāva nivatto. Bhagavāpi kiñci avatvāva pakkanto. Tatiyadivase pana adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto etaṃ “pakaṭṭhako”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Bhagavāpi etaṃ vacanaṃ nicchārāpanatthameva yāva tatiyamagamāsi. Tattha pakaṭṭhakoti rasagiddho.

“He said this” means: the brahmin, although giving for three days by filling the bowl, did not give with faith. He gave out of fear of reproach, thinking, “He eats without giving even a morsel of almsfood to the ascetic who has come and stands at his door.” And while giving, having given for two days, he turned back without saying anything. The Blessed One also departed without saying anything. But on the third day, being unable to endure it, he spoke this utterance beginning with “Pakaṭṭhaka!” The Blessed One also went there for the third time precisely to draw forth that utterance. Therein, “pakaṭṭhaka” means one who is greedy for flavors.

Punappunaṃ ceva vapanti bījanti satthā brāhmaṇassa vacanaṃ sutvā, “brāhmaṇa, tvaṃ tīṇi divasāni piṇḍapātaṃ datvā osakkasi, punappunaṃ kātabbā nāma lokasmiṃ soḷasa dhammā”ti vatvā te dhamme dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha punappunaṃ ceva vapantīti ekasmiṃ sassavāre vuttaṃ [V 1.0227] “alamettāvatā”ti anosakkitvā aparāparesupi sassavāresu ca vapantiyeva. Punappunaṃ vassatīti na ekadivasaṃ vassitvā tiṭṭhati, punappunadivasesupi punappunasaṃvaccharesupi vassatiyeva, evaṃ janapadā iddhā honti. Etenupāyena sabbattha nayo veditabbo.

Regarding 'Again and again they sow the seed': The Teacher, having heard the brahmin's words, said, 'Brahmin, you withdrew after giving almsfood for three days. In this world, there are sixteen principles that should be acted upon again and again.' Having said this, he began this teaching to show those principles. Therein, 'again and again they sow' means that without withdrawing, thinking 'This much is enough' regarding what was sown in one crop season, they sow again and again in subsequent crop seasons. 'Again and again it rains' means it does not rain for just one day and stop, but rains repeatedly on subsequent days and in subsequent years. Thus, the country becomes prosperous. By this method, the principle should be understood everywhere.

Yācakāti [P 1.0258] imasmiṃ pade satthā desanākusalatāya attānampi pakkhipitvā dasseti. Khīranikāti khīrakārakā godohakā. Na hi te ekavārameva thanaṃ añchanti, punappunaṃ añchantā dhenuṃ duhantīti attho. Kilamati phandati cāti ayaṃ satto tena iriyāpathena kilamati ceva phandati ca. Gabbhanti soṇasiṅgālādīnampi tiracchānagatānaṃ kucchiṃ. Sivathikanti susānaṃ, mataṃ mataṃ sattaṃ tattha punappunaṃ harantīti attho. Maggañca laddhā apunabbhavāyāti apunabbhavāya maggo nāma nibbānaṃ, taṃ labhitvāti attho.

In this term `yācakā` (alms-seekers): due to his skill in teaching, the Teacher includes himself to illustrate. `Khīranikā` (milk-seekers) means milk-procurers, cow-milkers. For they do not pull from the udder just once; pulling again and again, they milk the cow—this is the meaning. `Kilamati phandati ca` (one toils and trembles) means this being both toils and trembles through that mode of deportment. `Gabbhaṃ` (womb) means the bellies of animals such as dogs, jackals, and so on. `Sivathikaṃ` (cemetery) means the charnel ground; the meaning is that they carry each and every dead being there again and again. `Maggañca laddhā apunabbhavāya` (and having found the path to no more rebirth) means the path to no more rebirth is Nibbāna; 'having attained it' is the meaning.

Evaṃ vutteti evaṃ bhagavatā antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhatvāva soḷasa punappunadhamme desentena vutte. Etadavocāti desanāpariyosāne pasanno saddhiṃ [M 1.0237] puttadāramittañātivaggena bhagavato pāde vanditvā etaṃ “abhikkantaṃ bho”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Dutiyaṃ.

As for `evaṃ vutte` (when this was said): when this was said by the Blessed One, who was teaching the sixteen principles of repetition while standing in the middle of the street. As for `etadavoca` (he said this): at the end of the teaching, being pleased, he paid homage at the Blessed One’s feet along with his retinue of sons, wife, friends, and relatives, and spoke these words, beginning with “Excellent, venerable sir!” The second.

3. Devahitasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Devahita Sutta

199. Tatiye vātehīti udaravātehi. Bhagavato kira chabbassāni dukkarakārikaṃ karontassa pasatamuggayūsādīni āhārayato dubbhojanena ceva dukkhaseyyāya ca udaravāto kuppi. Aparabhāge sambodhiṃ patvā paṇītabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassāpi antarantarā so ābādho attānaṃ dassetiyeva. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Upaṭṭhāko hotīti paṭhamabodhiyaṃ anibaddhupaṭṭhākakāle upaṭṭhāko hoti. Tasmiṃ kira kāle satthuasītimahātheresu upaṭṭhāko abhūtapubbo nāma natthi. Nāgasamālo upavāno sunakkhatto cundo samaṇuddeso sāgato bodhi meghiyoti ime pana pāḷiyaṃ āgatupaṭṭhākā. Imasmiṃ pana kāle upavānatthero pātova uṭṭhāya pariveṇasammajjanaṃ dantakaṭṭhadānaṃ nhānodakapariyādanaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā anugamananti sabbaṃ bhagavato upaṭṭhānamakāsi. Upasaṅkamīti paṭhamabodhiyaṃ kira vīsati vassāni niddhūmaṃ [P 1.0259] araññameva hoti, bhikkhusaṅghassa udakatāpanampi na bhagavatā anuññātaṃ. So ca brāhmaṇo uddhanapāḷiṃ bandhāpetvā [V 1.0228] mahācāṭiyo uddhanamāropetvā uṇhodakaṃ kāretvā, nhānīyacuṇṇādīhi saddhiṃ taṃ vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappeti. Nhāyitukāmā tattha gantvā mūlaṃ datvā nhāyitvā gandhe vilimpitvā mālaṃ piḷandhitvā pakkamanti. Tasmā thero tattha upasaṅkami.

199. In the third sutta, 'by winds' means by abdominal winds. It is said that for six years, while the Blessed One was undertaking severe austerities, consuming food such as a handful of bean soup and the like, his abdominal winds became disturbed through unrefined food and an uncomfortable bed. In the later part, even after attaining full enlightenment and partaking of refined food, that ailment would occasionally manifest itself. It is with reference to this that it was said. 'He was an attendant' means that during the first twenty years of his ministry, at the time when there was no permanently assigned attendant, he served as an attendant. Indeed, it is said that at that time, among the eighty great elders, there was no one who had not previously served as an attendant. However, Nāgasamāla, Upavāna, Sunakkhatta, Cunda the novice, Sāgata, Bodhi, and Meghiya are the attendants mentioned in the Pāḷi texts. But at this time, the Elder Upavāna would rise early, sweep the monastery precincts, offer a tooth-stick and water for washing, prepare bathing water, and follow behind carrying the bowl and robe—he performed all these services for the Blessed One. 'He approached' means that during the first twenty years of his ministry, it is said that the forest was indeed smokeless, and even the heating of water for the monastic community was not permitted by the Blessed One. And that brahmin, having had a row of furnaces built and large pots placed on them, would have water heated and sell it along with bathing powders and the like, thus making a living. Those who wished to bathe would go there, pay the price, bathe, anoint themselves with perfumes, adorn themselves with garlands, and depart. Therefore, the elder approached there.

Kiṃ patthayānoti kiṃ icchanto. Kiṃ esanti kiṃ gavesanto. Pūjito pūjaneyyānanti idaṃ thero dasabalassa vaṇṇaṃ kathetumārabhi. Gilānabhesajjatthaṃ gatena kira gilānassa vaṇṇo kathetabboti vattametaṃ. Vaṇṇaṃ hi sutvā manussā sakkaccaṃ bhesajjaṃ dātabbaṃ maññanti. Sappāyabhesajjaṃ laddhā gilāno khippameva vuṭṭhāti. Kathentena ca jhānavimokkhasamāpattimaggaphalāni ārabbha kathetuṃ na vaṭṭati. “Sīlavā lajjī kukkuccako bahussuto āgamadharo vaṃsānurakkhako”ti evaṃ pana āgamanīyapaṭipadaṃyeva kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pūjaneyyānanti asītimahātherā sadevakena lokena [M 1.0238] pūjetabbāti pūjaneyyā. Teyeva sakkātabbāti sakkareyyā. Tesaṃyeva apaciti kattabbāti apaceyyā. Bhagavā tesaṃ pūjito sakkato apacito ca, iccassa taṃ guṇaṃ pakāsento thero evamāha. Hātaveti harituṃ.

‘What is he desiring?’ means ‘what is he wishing for?’ ‘What is he seeking?’ means ‘what is he searching for?’ ‘Honored by those worthy of honor’—this the Elder began to state as a quality of the Ten-Powered One. It is said to be a duty that when one goes for medicine for the sick, the quality of the sick person should be spoken of. For, having heard of the quality, people think that medicine should be given respectfully. Having obtained suitable medicine, the sick person quickly recovers. And when speaking, it is not proper to speak concerning jhāna, liberations, attainments, paths, and fruits. But it is proper to speak only of the preliminary practice, thus: ‘He is virtuous, has a sense of shame, is scrupulous, is learned, a bearer of the tradition, a guardian of the lineage.’ ‘Worthy of honor’ (pūjaneyyā) means the eighty great elders are worthy of being honored by the world with its devas. They themselves are worthy of being revered (sakkareyyā). Homage is to be paid to them (apaceyyā). The Blessed One is honored, revered, and paid homage to by them; thus, proclaiming this quality of his, the Elder spoke thus. ‘Hātave’ means ‘to take’.

Phāṇitassa ca puṭanti mahantaṃ nicchārikaṃ guḷapiṇḍaṃ. So kira “kiṃ samaṇassa gotamassa aphāsuka”nti? Pucchitvā, “udaravāto”ti sutvā, “tena hi mayamettha bhesajjaṃ jānāma, ito thokena udakena idaṃ phāṇitaṃ āloḷetvā nhānapariyosāne pātuṃ detha, iti uṇhodakena bahi parisedo bhavissati, iminā antoti evaṃ samaṇassa gotamassa phāsukaṃ bhavissatī”ti vatvā therassa patte pakkhipitvā adāsi.

And ‘a bundle of molasses’ means a large lump of jaggery without ash applied. It is said that he asked, ‘What is the ascetic Gotama’s discomfort?’ Having heard, ‘It is an abdominal wind,’ he said, ‘If so, then we know a medicine for this. Dissolve this jaggery in a little of this hot water and give it to him to drink at the end of his bath. Thus, because of the hot water, there will be perspiration on the outside of the body. By this, there will be an end to the disease. In this way, the ascetic Gotama will become comfortable.’ Having said this, he placed it in the Elder’s bowl and gave it.

Upasaṅkamīti tasmiṃ kira ābādhe paṭippassaddhe “devahitena tathāgatassa bhesajjaṃ dinnaṃ, teneva rogo vūpasanto, aho dānaṃ paramadānaṃ brāhmaṇassā”ti kathā vitthāritā jātā. Taṃ sutvā kittikāmo brāhmaṇo “ettakenapi [P 1.0260] tāva me ayaṃ kittisaddo abbhuggato”ti somanassajāto attanā katabhāvaṃ jānāpetukāmo tāvatakeneva dasabale vissāsaṃ āpajjitvā upasaṅkami.

‘He approached’ means: It is said that when that illness had subsided, the talk became widespread: ‘Medicine was given to the Tathāgata by Devahita, and by that very medicine the disease was calmed. Oh, the brahmin’s gift is the highest gift!’ Hearing that, the brahmin, who desired fame, became joyful, thinking, ‘Even by so little, this sound of fame has arisen for me.’ Desiring to make known the deed he had done, and having gained confidence in the Ten-Powered One with just that much, he approached.

Dajjāti dadeyya. Kathaṃ hi yajamānassāti kena kāraṇena yajantassa. Ijjhatīti samijjhati mahapphalo hoti. Yovedīti yo avedi aññāsi, viditaṃ pākaṭamakāsi “yovetī”tipi [V 1.0229] pāṭho, yo aveti jānātīti attho. Passatīti dibbacakkhunā passati. Jātikkhayanti arahattaṃ. Abhiññāvositoti jānitvā vosito vosānaṃ katakiccataṃ patto. Evaṃ hi yajamānassāti iminā khīṇāsave yajanākārena yajantassa. Tatiyaṃ.

‘Let him give’ means ‘he should give.’ ‘For how for the sacrificer?’ means ‘for what reason for one who sacrifices?’ ‘It succeeds’ means ‘it prospers, it becomes of great fruit.’ ‘Who knows’ means ‘who understood, who knew, who made it known and clear.’ There is also the reading ‘yoveti,’ which means ‘who knows, who understands.’ ‘He sees’ means ‘he sees with the divine eye.’ ‘The end of birth’ means ‘arahantship.’ ‘Mastered by direct knowledge’ means ‘having known, completed, attained the state of having the task completed.’ Thus, ‘for the sacrificer’ means for one who sacrifices in this manner of sacrificing to one whose cankers are destroyed. The third sutta.

4. Mahāsālasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Mahāsāla Sutta

200. Catutthe lūkho lūkhapāvuraṇoti jiṇṇo jiṇṇapāvuraṇo. Upasaṅkamīti kasmā upasaṅkami? Tassa kira ghare aṭṭhasatasahassadhanaṃ ahosi. So catunnaṃ puttānaṃ āvāhaṃ katvā cattāri satasahassāni adāsi[M 1.0239]. Athassa brāhmaṇiyā kālaṅkatāya puttā sammantayiṃsu – “sace aññaṃ brāhmaṇiṃ ānessati, tassā kucchiyaṃ nibbattavasena kulaṃ bhijjissati. Handa naṃ mayaṃ saṅgaṇhāmā”ti. Te cattāropi paṇītehi ghāsacchādanādīhi upaṭṭhahantā hatthapādasambāhanādīni karontā saṅgaṇhitvā ekadivasaṃ divā niddāyitvā vuṭṭhitassa hatthapāde sambāhamānā pāṭiyekkaṃ gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ vatvā – “mayaṃ tumhe iminā nīhārena yāvajīvaṃ upaṭṭhahissāma, sesadhanampi no dethā”ti yāciṃsu. Brāhmaṇo puna ekekassa satasahassaṃ satasahassaṃ datvā attano nivatthapārupanamattaṃ ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ cattāro koṭṭhāse katvā niyyādesi. Taṃ jeṭṭhaputto katipāhaṃ upaṭṭhahi.

200. In the fourth, ‘coarse, with a coarse outer robe’ means ‘aged, with a worn-out outer robe.’ Why did he approach? It is said that in his house there was wealth of eight hundred thousand. Having arranged marriages for his four sons, he gave four hundred thousand. Then, when his brahmin wife passed away, the sons consulted among themselves: ‘If he brings another brahmin woman, the family will be divided by means of offspring in her womb. Come, let us take care of him.’ All four of them, attending to him with fine food, clothing, and so forth, and doing things like massaging his hands and feet, took care of him. One day, after he had slept during the day and arisen, while they were massaging his hands and feet, they each separately spoke of the drawbacks of household life and requested, ‘We will attend to you in this manner for as long as you live; give us the remaining wealth as well.’ The brahmin, again giving one hundred thousand to each, and keeping only what was sufficient for his own wearing and covering, made four portions of all his possessions for use and enjoyment and handed them over. The eldest son attended to him for a few days.

Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ nhatvā āgacchantaṃ dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhatvā suṇhā evamāha – “kiṃ tayā jeṭṭhaputtassa sataṃ vā sahassaṃ vā atirekaṃ dinnamatthi? Nanu sabbesaṃ dve dve satasahassāni dinnāni, kiṃ sesaputtānaṃ gharassa maggaṃ na jānāsī”ti? So “nassa vasalī”ti [P 1.0261] kujjhitvā aññassa gharaṃ agamāsi, tatopi katipāhaccayena imināva upāyena palāpito aññassāti evaṃ ekagharepi pavesanaṃ alabhamāno paṇḍaraṅgapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā bhikkhāya caranto kālānamaccayena jarājiṇṇo dubbhojanadukkhaseyyāhi milātasarīro bhikkhācārato āgamma, pīṭhakāya nipanno niddaṃ okkamitvā vuṭṭhāya nisinno attānaṃ oloketvā puttesu patiṭṭhaṃ apassanto cintesi – “samaṇo kira gotamo abbhākuṭiko uttānamukho sukhasambhāso paṭisanthārakusalo, sakkā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paṭisanthāraṃ labhitu”nti nivāsanapāvuraṇaṃ saṇṭhapetvā bhikkhābhājanamādāya yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami.

Then one day, as he was returning from bathing, his daughter-in-law, standing at the gateway, said to him: ‘What, have you given anything extra—a hundred or a thousand—to your eldest son? Were not two hundred thousand given to each of all your sons? Do you not know the way to the houses of the remaining sons?’ Enraged, he said, ‘Perish, vile woman!’ and went to another son’s house. From there also, after a few days had passed, he was made to flee by this same means, and so to another’s. Thus, not obtaining entry into even one house, he undertook the going-forth of a white-robed ascetic. Wandering for alms, with the passing of time he became old and decrepit, his body withered from poor food and uncomfortable lodging. Having returned from his alms-round, he lay down on a bench and fell asleep. Upon waking and sitting up, he looked at himself and, seeing no support in his sons, he thought: ‘The ascetic Gotama, it is said, is without a frown, with an open face, of pleasant speech, and skilled in friendly greeting. It should be possible to approach the ascetic Gotama and receive a friendly greeting.’ Having arranged his lower and upper garments and taken his alms bowl, he approached the Blessed One where he was.

Dārehi [V 1.0230] saṃpuccha gharā nikkhāmentīti sabbaṃ mama santakaṃ gahetvā mayhaṃ niddhanabhāvaṃ ñatvā attano bhariyāhi saddhiṃ mantayitvā maṃ gharā nikkaḍḍhāpenti.

‘Having consulted with their wives, they expel me from the house’ means: Having taken all my possessions and knowing my state of poverty, they consult with their own wives and have me driven out from the house.

Nandissanti nandijāto tuṭṭho pamudito ahosiṃ. Bhavamicchisanti vuḍḍhiṃ patthayiṃ. Sāva vārenti sūkaranti yathā sunakhā vaggavaggā hutvā bhussantā [M 1.0240] bhussantā sūkaraṃ vārenti, punappunaṃ mahāravaṃ ravāpenti, evaṃ dārehi saddhiṃ maṃ bahuṃ vatvā viravantaṃ palāpentīti attho.

'Nandissaṃ' means: I was joyful, pleased, and delighted. 'Bhavamicchisaṃ' means: I desired their prosperity. 'Sāva vārenti sūkaraṃ' means: Just as dogs, having formed into packs and barking repeatedly, ward off a pig and cause it to make a great noise again and again, so too they, together with their wives, having said much to me, make me flee while I am crying out. This is the meaning.

Asantāti asappurisā. Jammāti lāmakā. Bhāsareti bhāsanti. Puttarūpenāti puttavesena. Vayogatanti tayo vaye gataṃ atikkantaṃ pacchimavaye ṭhitaṃ maṃ. Jahantīti pariccajanti.

'Asantā' means 'unvirtuous men'. 'Jammā' means 'base ones'. 'Bhāsare' means 'they speak'. 'Puttarūpena' means 'in the guise of a son'. 'Vayogataṃ' means 'me, who has passed beyond the three ages and is established in the final age'. 'Jahanti' means 'they abandon'.

Nibbhogoti nipparibhogo. Khādanā apanīyatīti asso hi yāvadeva taruṇo hoti javasampanno, tāvassa nānārasaṃ khādanaṃ dadanti, jiṇṇaṃ nibbhogaṃ tato apanenti, antimavaye taṃ vattaṃ na labhati, gāvīhi saddhiṃ aṭaviyaṃ sukkhatiṇāni khādanto carati. Yathā so asso, evaṃ jiṇṇakāle viluttasabbadhanattā nibbhogo mādisopi bālakānaṃ pitā thero paragharesu bhikkhati.

'Without enjoyment' means unfit for use. 'Is removed from food' means: indeed, for as long as a horse is young and endowed with swiftness, they give it food of various tastes; but when it is old and unfit for use, they remove it from that food. In its final age, it does not receive that regular provision; instead, it wanders in the forest with cows, eating dry grass. Just like that horse, so too in old age, on account of all wealth having been plundered and thus being without possessions, a father of foolish sons like me, even though an elder, begs in others' homes.

Yañceti nipāto. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ye mama puttā anassavā appatissā avasavattino, tehi daṇḍova kira seyyo sundarataroti. Idānissa seyyabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ caṇḍampi goṇantiādi vuttaṃ.

'Yañca' is a particle. This is what is said: 'As for those sons of mine who are disobedient, disrespectful, and not under my control—a staff is indeed better, more excellent, than them.' Now, to show its superiority, 'even a fierce bull' and so forth was said.

Pure hotīti aggato hoti, taṃ purato katvā gantuṃ sukhaṃ hotīti attho[P 1.0262]. Gādhamedhatīti udakaṃ otaraṇakāle gambhīre udake patiṭṭhaṃ labhati.

'It is at the forefront' means it is foremost. The meaning is that it is pleasant to go, having placed it in front. 'It finds a firm footing' means that at the time of descending into water, one obtains a foothold in deep water.

Pariyāpuṇitvāti uggaṇhitvā vā vācuggatā katvā. Sannisinnesūti tathārūpe brāhmaṇānaṃ samāgamadivase sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitesu puttesu taṃ sabhaṃ ogāhetvā brāhmaṇānaṃ majjhe mahārahe āsane nisinnesu. Abhāsīti ‘ayaṃ me kālo’ti sabhāya majjhe pavisitvā hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā[V 1.0231], “bho ahaṃ tumhākaṃ gāthā bhāsitukāmo, bhāsite suṇissathā”ti vatvā – “bhāsa, brāhmaṇa, suṇomā”ti vutto ṭhitakova abhāsi. “Tena ca samayena manussānaṃ vattaṃ hoti yo mātāpitūnaṃ santakaṃ khādanto mātāpitaro na poseti, so māretabbo”ti. Tasmā te brāhmaṇaputtā pitupādesu nipatitvā “jīvitaṃ no tāta, dehī”ti yāciṃsu. So pituhadayassa puttānaṃ muduttā “mā me, bho, bālake vināsayittha, posissanti ma”nti āha.

'Having thoroughly learned' means having learned or having committed to recitation. 'When they were seated' means: on such a day of assembly for the brahmins, when their sons, adorned with all ornaments, had entered that assembly and were seated on great seats in the midst of the brahmins. 'He spoke' means: thinking, 'This is my time,' he entered the middle of the assembly, raised his hand, and after saying, 'Sirs, I wish to recite a verse to you; will you listen when it is recited?'—when he was told, 'Speak, brahmin, we will listen'—he spoke while standing. And at that time, there was a custom among the people: 'Whoever, while consuming his parents' property, does not support his parents, should be killed.' Therefore, those sons of the brahmin fell at their father's feet and begged, 'Father, give us our lives!' He, because of the tenderness of a father's heart for his sons, said, 'Sirs, do not destroy my foolish children; they will support me.'

Athassa [M 1.0241] putte manussā āhaṃsu – “sace, bho, ajja paṭṭhāya pitaraṃ na sammā paṭijaggissatha, ghātessāma vo”ti. Te bhītā gharaṃ netvā paṭijaggiṃsu. Taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho naṃ brāhmaṇamahāsālantiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha netvāti pīṭhe nisīdāpetvā sayaṃ ukkhipitvā nayiṃsu. Nhāpetvāti sarīraṃ telena abbhañjitvā ubbaṭṭetvā gandhacuṇṇādīhi nhāpesuṃ. Brāhmaṇiyopi pakkosāpetvā, “ajja paṭṭhāya amhākaṃ pitaraṃ sammā paṭijaggatha. Sace pamādaṃ āpajjissatha, gharato vo nikkaḍḍhissāmā”ti vatvā, paṇītabhojanaṃ bhojesuṃ.

Then the people said to his sons, 'If, good sirs, from today onwards you do not properly look after your father, we will kill you.' Frightened, they took him home and looked after him. To show this, the passage beginning 'Then, the great brahmin householder...' was spoken. There, 'having taken him' means having made him sit on their back, they themselves lifted and carried him. 'Having bathed him' means having anointed his body with oil and rubbed it with fragrant powders and so on, they bathed him. Having also summoned their wives, the brahmin women, they said, 'From today onwards, properly look after our father. If you become negligent, we will drive you out of the house.' Having said this, they fed him with excellent food.

Brāhmaṇo subhojanañca sukhaseyyañca āgamma katipāhaccayena sañjātabalo pīṇitindriyo attabhāvaṃ oloketvā, “ayaṃ me sampatti samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ nissāya laddhā”ti paṇṇākāraṃ ādāya bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ dassetuṃ atha kho sotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha etadavocāti dussayugaṃ pādamūle ṭhapetvā etaṃ avoca. Saraṇagamanāvasāne cāpi bhagavantaṃ evamāha – “bho gotama, mayhaṃ puttehi cattāri dhurabhattāni dinnāni[P 1.0263], tato ahaṃ dve tumhākaṃ dammi, dve sayaṃ paribhuñjissāmī”ti. Kalyāṇaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pāṭiyekkaṃ pana mā niyyādehi, amhākaṃ ruccanaṭṭhānameva gamissāmāti. “Evaṃ, bho”ti kho brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṃ vanditvā gharaṃ gantvā putte āmantesi “tātā, samaṇo gotamo mayhaṃ sahāyo, tassa dve dhurabhattāni dinnāni, tumhe tasmiṃ sampatte mā pamajjathā”ti. Sādhu, tātāti. Punadivase bhagavā pubbaṇhasamaye pattacīvaraṃ ādāya jeṭṭhaputtassa nivesanadvāraṃ gato. So satthāraṃ disvāva hatthato pattaṃ gahetvā gharaṃ pavesetvā mahārahe pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā paṇītabhojanamadāsi. Satthā punadivase itarassa, punadivase itarassāti paṭipāṭiyā sabbesaṃ gharāni agamāsi. Sabbe tatheva sakkāraṃ akaṃsu.

The brahmin, on account of the fine food and comfortable lodging, gained strength within a few days. His faculties were refreshed, and upon observing his own condition, he thought, 'This prosperity of mine was attained through reliance on the ascetic Gotama.' Taking a gift, he went to the presence of the Blessed One. To show this, the passage beginning 'Then...' and so forth was said. There, 'he spoke thus' means that after placing a pair of cloths at the Blessed One's feet, he spoke this. At the conclusion of taking refuge, he also said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Gotama, my sons have given me four portions of food. From these, I give two to you, and I will consume two myself.' The Buddha replied, 'Good, brahmin, but do not assign them specifically; we will go only to a place that is agreeable to us.' 'So be it, venerable sir,' said the brahmin. After paying homage to the Blessed One, he went home and addressed his sons: 'Dear sons, the ascetic Gotama is my friend. I have given him two portions of food. When he arrives, do not be negligent.' 'Good, Father,' they said. The next day, in the morning, the Blessed One took his bowl and robe and went to the door of the eldest son’s house. As soon as he saw the Teacher, the son took the bowl from his hand, led him into the house, seated him on a worthy seat, and offered him excellent food. On the next day, the Teacher went to the house of the next son, and on the day after that to the next; in this sequence, he went to the houses of all of them. All of them honored him in the same way.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0232] jeṭṭhaputtassa ghare maṅgalaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ. So pitaraṃ āha – “tāta, kassa maṅgalaṃ demā”ti. Amhe aññaṃ na jānāma? Nanu samaṇo gotamo mayhaṃ sahāyoti? Tena hi tumhe pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ svātanāya samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ nimantethāti. Brāhmaṇo tathā akāsi[M 1.0242]. Bhagavā adhivāsetvā punadivase bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto tassa gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. So haritupalittaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ gehaṃ satthāraṃ pavesetvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paññattāsanesu nisīdāpetvā appodakapāyāsañceva khajjakavikatiñca adāsi. Antarabhattasmiṃyeva brāhmaṇassa cattāropi puttā satthu santike nisīditvā āhaṃsu – “bho gotama, mayaṃ amhākaṃ pitaraṃ paṭijaggāma nappamajjāma, passathassa attabhāva”nti. Satthā “kalyāṇaṃ vo kataṃ, mātāpituposakaṃ nāma porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ āciṇṇamevā”ti vatvā mahānāgajātakaṃ (jā. 1.11.1 ādayo; cariyā. 2.1 ādayo) nāma kathetvā, cattāri saccāni dīpetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Desanāpariyosāne brāhmaṇo saddhiṃ catūhi puttehi catūhi ca suṇhāhi desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito. Tato paṭṭhāya satthā na sabbakālaṃ tesaṃ gehaṃ agamāsīti. Catutthaṃ.

Then one day, a festive occasion arose in the house of the eldest son. He asked his father, 'Father, for whom shall we hold this celebration?' 'We know no other. Is not the ascetic Gotama my friend?' 'In that case, you should invite the ascetic Gotama with five hundred monks for tomorrow.' The brahmin did so. The Blessed One consented, and the next day, surrounded by the Sangha of monks, he arrived at the door of his son's house. He ushered the Teacher into the house, which was smeared with fresh cow-dung and adorned with all kinds of ornaments, seated the Sangha of monks, headed by the Buddha, on prepared seats, and offered them thick rice-gruel and various kinds of confections. During the meal, the brahmin's four sons sat near the Teacher and said, 'Venerable Gotama, we look after our father and are not negligent; look at his physical state.' The Teacher replied, 'You have done well. Indeed, supporting one’s parents is the practice of the ancient wise ones.' Then he narrated the Mahānāga Jātaka and, illuminating the Four Noble Truths, expounded the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, the brahmin, along with his four sons and four daughters-in-law, directed his knowledge in accordance with the teaching and was established in the fruit of stream-entry. From then on, the Teacher did not always visit their house. Fourth.

5. Mānatthaddhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Discourse on Conceit and Obstinacy.

201. Pañcame [P 1.0264] mānatthaddhoti vātabharitabhastā viya mānena thaddho. Ācariyanti sippuggahaṇakāle ācariyo anabhivādentassa sippaṃ na deti, aññasmiṃ pana kāle taṃ na abhivādeti, atthibhāvampissa na jānāti. Nāyaṃ samaṇoti evaṃ kirassa ahosi – “yasmā ayaṃ samaṇo mādise jātisampannabrāhmaṇe sampatte paṭisanthāramattampi na karoti, tasmā na kiñci jānātī”ti.
