201. In the fifth discourse, 'stiff with conceit' means as stiff with conceit as a leather bag filled with wind. Regarding 'teacher': at the time of learning a craft, a teacher does not impart the craft to one who does not pay respects. At other times, however, that person does not pay respects to him, nor does he acknowledge his existence. 'This is no ascetic'—thus it occurred to him: 'Since this ascetic does not show even the slightest friendly greeting to one like me, a brahmin endowed with noble birth, therefore he knows nothing.'

Abbhutavittajātāti abhūtapubbāya tuṭṭhiyā samannāgatā. Kesu cassāti kesu bhaveyya. Kyassāti ke assa puggalassa. Apacitā assūti apacitiṃ dassetuṃ yuttā bhaveyyuṃ. Arahanteti imāya gāthāya desanākusalattā attānaṃ antokatvā pūjaneyyaṃ dasseti. Pañcamaṃ.

'Filled with wonder and joy' means possessed of a joy never before experienced. 'In whom would it be?' means: in whom would it be? 'For whom' means: for that person, who... 'They would be revered' means: they would be suitable to show reverence to. 'Arahant'—by this verse, due to his skill in teaching, having included himself, he shows a person worthy of veneration. Fifth.

6. Paccanīkasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Paccanīka Sutta.

202. Chaṭṭhe [V 1.0233] “sabbaṃ seta”nti vutte “sabbaṃ kaṇha”ntiādinā nayena paccanīkaṃ karontassevassa sātaṃ sukhaṃ hotīti paccanīkasāto. Yo [M 1.0243] ca vineyya sārambhanti yo karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇaṃ sārambhaṃ vinetvā suṇātīti attho. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

202. In the sixth discourse: when it is said, 'all is white,' one for whom pleasure and happiness arise only by making an opposition in the manner of, 'all is black,' and so on, is thus one who delights in opposition. 'And who, having subdued contentiousness' means: one who listens after having subdued the contentiousness that is characterized by excessiveness. This is the meaning. Sixth.

7. Navakammikasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Navakammika Sutta.

203. Sattame navakammikabhāradvājoti so kira araññe rukkhaṃ chindāpetvā tattheva pāsādakūṭāgārādīni yojetvā nagaraṃ āharitvā vikkiṇāti, iti navakammaṃ nissāya jīvatīti navakammiko, gottena bhāradvājoti navakammikabhāradvājo. Disvānassa etadahosīti chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajjetvā nisinnaṃ bhagavantaṃ disvāna assa etaṃ ahosi. Vanasminti imasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe. Ucchinnamūlaṃ me vananti mayhaṃ kilesavanaṃ ucchinnamūlaṃ. Nibbanathoti nikkilesavano. Eko rameti ekako abhiramāmi. Aratiṃ vippahāyāti pantasenāsanesu ceva bhāvanāya ca ukkaṇṭhitaṃ jahitvā. Sattamaṃ.

203. In the seventh discourse, 'Navakammika Bhāradvāja' means: it is said that he, having had trees cut in the forest, and right there having assembled tiered mansions, peaked buildings, and so on, brought them to the city and sold them. Thus, because he lives by means of new work, he is called 'Navakammika'; by clan, he is 'Bhāradvāja'; therefore, he is 'Navakammikabhāradvāja'. 'Having seen him, this occurred to him' means: having seen the Blessed One seated, emitting the six-colored rays, this thought occurred to him. 'In the forest' means: in this great grove. 'My forest has its roots cut off' means: my forest of defilements has its roots completely cut off. 'Devoid of forest-thicket' means: devoid of the forest of defilements. 'He delights alone' means: I, alone, greatly delight. 'Having abandoned discontent' means: having abandoned discontent with remote lodging places and with meditation. Seventh.

8. Kaṭṭhahārasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāra Sutta.

204. Aṭṭhame [P 1.0265] antevāsikāti veyyāvaccaṃ katvā sippuggaṇhanakā dhammantevāsikā. Nisinnanti chabbaṇṇarasmiyo vissajjetvā nisinnaṃ. Gambhīrarūpeti gambhīrasabhāve.

204. In the eighth discourse, 'pupils' means: pupils who learn a craft after having rendered service, and pupils in the Dhamma. 'Seated' means: the one seated, having emitted the six-colored rays. 'Of profound form' means: of a profound nature.

Bahubheraveti tatraṭṭhakasaviññāṇakaaviññāṇakabheravehi bahubherave. Vigāhiyāti anupavisitvā. Aniñjamānenātiādīni kāyavisesanāni, evarūpena kāyenāti attho. Sucārurūpaṃ vatāti atisundaraṃ vata jhānaṃ jhāyasīti vadati.

'Full of many terrors' means: full of many terrors on account of the animate and inanimate terrors existing there. 'Having entered' means: having entered into. 'Unmoving' and so on are qualifiers of the body; the meaning is: with a body of such a nature. 'Oh, what a very lovely form!' means: he says, 'Oh, how exceedingly beautiful is the jhāna you are absorbed in!'

Vanavassito munīti vanaṃ avassito buddhamuni. Idanti idaṃ tumhākaṃ evaṃ vane nisinnakāraṇaṃ mayhaṃ accherarūpaṃ paṭibhāti. Pītimanoti tuṭṭhacitto. Vane vaseti vanamhi vasi.

‘The sage dwelling in the forest’ (vanavassito munī) means the Buddha-sage who dwells in the forest. ‘This’ (idaṃ) means ‘this reason for your sitting thus in the forest seems astonishing to me.’ ‘Joyful’ (pītimano) means with a delighted mind. ‘He dwells in the forest’ (vane vaseti) means he dwelt in the forest.

Maññāmahanti [V 1.0234] maññāmi ahaṃ. Lokādhipatisahabyatanti lokādhipatimahābrahmunā sahabhāvaṃ. Ākaṅkhamānoti icchamāno. Tidivaṃ anuttaranti idaṃ brahmalokameva sandhāyāha. Kasmā bhavaṃ vijanamaraññamassitoti ahaṃ tāva brahmalokaṃ ākaṅkhamānoti maññāmi. Yadi evaṃ na hoti, atha me ācikkha, kasmā bhavanti? Pucchati. Brahmapattiyāti seṭṭhapattiyā[M 1.0244]. Idha idaṃ tapo kasmā karosīti aparenapi ākārena pucchati.

‘I think’ (maññāmahaṃ) means ‘I think.’ ‘Companionship with the Lord of the World’ (lokādhipatisahabyataṃ) means companionship with Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the World. ‘Desiring’ (ākaṅkhamāno) means wishing. ‘The unsurpassed triple heaven’ (tidivaṃ anuttaraṃ): this he spoke referring to the Brahmā world itself. ‘Why do you, venerable sir, resort to the lonely forest?’ (kasmā bhavaṃ vijanamaraññamassito) means: I first think that you are one who desires the Brahmā world. If it is not so, then tell me, why do you dwell in the forest? Thus he asks. ‘For attainment of Brahma’ (brahmapattiyā) means for the highest attainment. ‘Here, why do you practice this austerity?’ (idha idaṃ tapo kasmā karosīti): thus he asks also in another way.

Kaṅkhāti taṇhā. Abhinandanāti abhinandanavasena taṇhāva vuttā. Anekadhātūsūti anekasabhāvesu ārammaṇesu. Puthūti nānappakārā taṇhā sesakilesā vā. Sadāsitāti niccakālaṃ avassitā. Aññāṇamūlappabhavāti avijjāmūlā hutvā jātā. Pajappitāti taṇhāva “idampi mayhaṃ, idampi mayha”nti pajappāpanavasena pajappitā nāmāti vuttā. Sabbā mayā byantikatāti sabbā taṇhā mayā aggamaggena vigatantā nirantā katā. Samūlikāti saddhiṃ aññāṇamūlena.

‘Doubt’ (kaṅkhā) means craving. ‘Delight’ (abhinandana) means craving itself is spoken of by way of delight. ‘In various elements’ (anekadhātūsu) means in objects of various natures. ‘Diverse’ (puthū) means cravings of various kinds, or the remaining defilements. ‘Always attached’ (sadāsitā) means constantly dependent. ‘Rooted in ignorance’ (aññāṇamūlappabhavā) means having arisen with ignorance as their root. ‘Longing’ (pajappitā) means craving itself, by way of causing the utterance ‘This is mine, this too is mine,’ is called ‘longing.’ ‘All have been eradicated by me’ (sabbā mayā byantikatā) means all craving has been made to be without end, to be ceased, by me through the supreme path. ‘With its root’ (samūlikā) means together with the root that is ignorance.

Anūpayoti anupagamano. Sabbesu dhammesu visuddhadassanoti iminā sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dīpeti. Sambodhimanuttaranti arahattaṃ sandhāyāha. Sivanti seṭṭhaṃ[P 1.0266]. Jhāyāmīti dvīhi jhānehi jhāyāmi. Visāradoti vigatasārajjo. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

‘Without clinging’ (anūpayo) means not approaching. By ‘having pure vision in all phenomena’ (sabbesu dhammesu visuddhadassano), he indicates the knowledge of omniscience. ‘Supreme enlightenment’ (sambodhimanuttaraṃ) refers to the fruit of Arahantship. ‘Auspicious’ (sivaṃ) means the best. ‘I contemplate’ (jhāyāmi) means ‘I contemplate with the two kinds of contemplation: contemplation on an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna) and contemplation on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna).’ ‘Confident’ (visārado) means devoid of timidity. The eighth (sutta).

9. Mātuposakasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Mātuposaka Sutta

205. Navame peccāti ito paṭigantvā. Navamaṃ.

205. In the ninth (sutta), ‘having departed’ (pecca) means having departed from this human existence. The ninth (sutta).

10. Bhikkhakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Bhikkhaka Sutta

206. Dasame idhāti imasmiṃ bhikkhubhāve. Vissaṃ dhammanti duggandhaṃ akusaladhammaṃ. Bāhitvāti aggamaggena jahitvā. Saṅkhāyāti ñāṇena. Sa ve bhikkhūti vuccatīti so ve bhinnakilesattā bhikkhu nāma vuccati. Dasamaṃ.

206. In the tenth sutta, 'here' means in this state of being a bhikkhu. 'A foul thing' means the unwholesome dhamma which is foul-smelling. 'Having banished' means having utterly abandoned by means of the highest path. 'Having comprehended' means by means of wisdom. 'He is indeed called a bhikkhu' means: he indeed, because of having broken the defilements, is called a bhikkhu. The tenth.

11. Saṅgāravasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Saṅgārava Sutta

207. Ekādasame [V 1.0235] paccetīti icchati pattheti. Sādhu, bhanteti āyācamāno āha. Therassa kiresa gihisahāyo, tasmā thero “ayaṃ varāko maṃ sahāyaṃ labhitvāpi micchādiṭṭhiṃ gahetvā mā apāyapūrako ahosī”ti āyācati. Apicesa mahāparivāro, tasmiṃ [M 1.0245] pasanne pañcakulasatāni anuvattissantīti maññamānopi āyācati. Atthavasanti atthānisaṃsaṃ atthakāraṇaṃ. Pāpanti pāṇātipātādiakusalaṃ. Pavāhemīti galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ otaritvā pavāhemi palāpemi. Dhammoti gāthā vuttatthāva. Ekādasamaṃ.

207. In the eleventh sutta, 'he desires' (pacceti) means he wishes, he longs for. 'Good, sir,' he said, making a request. It is said that this person was the Elder's friend from his lay life; therefore, the Elder requests, thinking: 'May this wretched person, even after getting me as a friend, not take up wrong view and become one who fills the planes of misery.' Furthermore, thinking, 'This person has a large retinue; when he gains confidence, five hundred families will follow his example,' he also makes the request. 'For the sake of the goal' means for the sake of the benefit, for the sake of the reason. 'Evil' means the unwholesome, such as the destruction of life. 'I wash away' means: having descended into water up to the neck, I cause it to float away, I cause it to flee. The verse beginning with 'Dhamma' has the meaning already stated in the Sundarikabhāradvāja Sutta. The eleventh.

12. Khomadussasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Khomadussa Sutta

208. Dvādasame khomadussaṃ nāmāti khomadussānaṃ ussannattā evaṃladdhanāmaṃ. Sabhāyanti sālāyaṃ. Phusāyatīti phusitāni muñcati vassati. Satthā kira taṃ sabhaṃ upasaṅkamitukāmo – “mayi evamevaṃ upasaṅkamante aphāsukadhātukaṃ hoti, ekaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca upasaṅkamissāmī”ti adhiṭṭhānavasena vuṭṭhiṃ uppādesi. Sabhādhammanti sukhanisinne kira asañcāletvā ekapassena pavisanaṃ tesaṃ sabhādhammo [P 1.0267] nāma, na mahājanaṃ cāletvā ujukameva pavisanaṃ. Bhagavā ca ujukameva āgacchati, tena te kupitā bhagavantaṃ hīḷentā “ke ca muṇḍakā samaṇakā, ke ca sabhādhammaṃ jānissantī”ti āhaṃsu. Santoti paṇḍitā sappurisā. Pahāyāti ete rāgādayo jahitvā rāgādivinayāya dhammaṃ bhaṇanti, tasmā te santo nāmāti. Dvādasamaṃ.

208. In the twelfth sutta, 'Khomadussa' is so named because of the abundance of linen cloths. 'In the assembly hall' means in the hall. 'It rains' means it releases drops, it rains. It is said the Teacher wished to approach that assembly hall. Thinking, 'If I approach just like this, it will be uncomfortable. I shall approach depending on a certain reason,' by the power of his determination, he caused rain to arise. 'Assembly custom' means: it is said their assembly custom is to enter by one side without disturbing those seated comfortably; it is not to enter straight on, making the crowd move. And the Blessed One came straight on. For that reason, they became angry and, reviling the Blessed One, said: 'Who are these shaveling ascetics, and what would they know of assembly custom?' 'The good' means the wise, the good persons. 'Having abandoned': having abandoned these things such as lust, they speak the Dhamma for the removal of lust and so on; therefore, they are called 'the good'. The twelfth.

Upāsakavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter: The Lay Followers.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Brāhmaṇasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Saṃyutta is concluded.

8. Vaṅgīsasaṃyuttaṃ

8. The Connected Discourses with Vaṅgīsa

1. Nikkhantasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Nikkhanta Sutta

209. Vaṅgīsasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0236][M 1.0246] paṭhame [P 1.0268] aggāḷave cetiyeti āḷaviyaṃ aggacetiye. Anuppanne buddhe aggāḷavagotamakādīni yakkhanāgādīnaṃ bhavanāni, cetiyāni ahesuṃ. Uppanne buddhe tāni apanetvā manussā vihāre kariṃsu. Tesaṃ tāneva nāmāni jātāni. Nigrodhakappenāti nigrodharukkhamūlavāsinā kappattherena. Ohiyyakoti ohīnako. Vihārapāloti so kira tadā avassiko hoti pattacīvaraggahaṇe akovido. Atha naṃ therā bhikkhū – “āvuso, imāni chattupāhanakattarayaṭṭhiādīni olokento nisīdā”ti vihārarakkhakaṃ katvā piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ “vihārapālo”ti. Samalaṅkaritvāti attano vibhavānurūpena alaṅkārena alaṅkaritvā. Cittaṃ anuddhaṃsetīti kusalacittaṃ viddhaṃseti vināseti. Taṃ kutettha labbhāti etasmiṃ rāge uppanne taṃ kāraṇaṃ kuto labbhā. Yaṃ me paroti yena me kāraṇena añño puggalo vā dhammo vā anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā idāneva abhiratiṃ uppādeyya ācariyupajjhāyāpi maṃ vihāre ohāya gatā.

209. In the first [discourse] of the Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta, 'at the Aggāḷava Shrine' means: at the chief shrine near Āḷavī. Before the Buddha arose, the dwellings of yakkhas, nāgas, and others, named Aggāḷava, Gotamaka, and so on, were shrines. When the Buddha arose, people removed those [shrines] and built monasteries, but the old names remained. 'With Nigrodhakappa' means: with the Elder Kappa, his preceptor, who dwelt at the foot of a banyan tree. 'Left behind' (ohiyyako) means one who was left behind. 'Monastery-guardian' (vihārapālo): it is said that at that time he had not yet completed a rains-residence and was unskilled in taking the bowl and robes. Then the elder monks, having made him the monastery-guardian, said: 'Friend, sit watching these umbrellas, sandals, staffs, and so forth,' and entered [the village] for alms-food. Therefore, it was said, 'monastery-guardian'. 'Having adorned' (samalaṅkaritvā) means: having adorned oneself with ornaments befitting one's own wealth. 'It destroys the mind' (cittaṃ anuddhaṃseti) means: it corrupts and ruins the wholesome mind. 'From where could that be obtained here?' (taṃ kutettha labbhā) means: when this lust has arisen, from where can that reason be obtained? 'That which for me another...' (yaṃ me paro) means: by which reason another person or teaching might dispel my discontent and arouse delight right now? Even my teachers and preceptors have left me in the monastery and gone.

Agārasmāti agārato nikkhantaṃ. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ upagatanti attho. Kaṇhatoti kaṇhapakkhato mārapakkhato ādhāvanti. Uggaputtāti uggatānaṃ puttā mahesakkhā rājaññabhūtā. Daḷhadhamminoti daḷhadhanuno, uttamappamāṇaṃ ācariyadhanuṃ dhārayamānā. Sahassaṃ apalāyinanti ye te samantā sarehi parikireyyuṃ, tesaṃ apalāyīnaṃ saṅkhaṃ dassento “sahassa”nti āha. Etato [P 1.0269] bhiyyoti etasmā sahassā atirekatarā. Neva maṃ byādhayissantīti maṃ cāletuṃ na sakkhissanti. Dhamme samhi patiṭṭhitanti anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā abhiratiṃ uppādanasamatthe sake sāsanadhamme patiṭṭhitaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – issāsasahasse tāva samantā sarehi parikirante sikkhito [V 1.0237] puriso daṇḍakaṃ gahetvā sabbe sare sarīre apatamāne antarāva paharitvā pādamūle pāteti. Tattha [M 1.0247] ekopi issāso dve sare ekato na khipati, imā pana itthiyo rūpārammaṇādivasena pañca pañca sare ekato khipanti. Evaṃ khipantiyo etā sacepi atirekasahassā honti, neva maṃ cāletuṃ sakkhissantīti.

'From home' (agārasmā) means: having gone forth from home. 'Into homelessness' (anagāriyaṃ): the meaning is having undertaken the going forth. 'From the dark' (kaṇhato) means: they run to the dark faction, to Māra's faction. 'Sons of the eminent' (uggaputtā) means: sons of the prominent, royal warriors of great power. 'Of strong Dhamma' (daḷhadhammino) means: those with strong bows, bearing a master's bow of the highest measure. 'A thousand who do not flee' (sahassaṃ apalāyinaṃ): he said 'a thousand' indicating the number of those who do not flee who would surround him with arrows from all sides. 'More than that' (etato bhiyyo) means: more than that thousand. 'They will not afflict me' (neva maṃ byādhayissanti) means: they will not be able to unsettle me. 'Established in one's own Dhamma' (dhamme samhi patiṭṭhitaṃ) means: established in one's own teaching, in the Dhamma which is capable of dispelling discontent and arousing delight. This is what is meant: even if a thousand archers were to surround him with arrows from all sides, a trained man could take a staff and, before all the arrows hit his body, strike them mid-air, causing them to fall at his feet. There, not even one archer shoots two arrows at once. But these women shoot five arrows at once, by way of sense objects such as forms. Even if these who shoot were more than a thousand, they would not be able to unsettle me.

Sakkhī hi me sutaṃ etanti mayā hi sammukhā etaṃ sutaṃ. Nibbānagamanaṃ magganti vipassanaṃ sandhāyāha. So hi nibbānassa pubbabhāgamaggo, liṅgavipallāsena pana “magga”nti āha. Tattha meti tasmiṃ me attano taruṇavipassanāsaṅkhāte nibbānagamanamagge mano nirato. Pāpimāti kilesaṃ ālapati. Maccūtipi tameva ālapati. Na me maggampi dakkhasīti yathā me bhavayoniādīsu gatamaggampi na passasi, tathā karissāmīti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Sakkhī hi me sutaṃ etaṃ means: for I have heard this directly. Nibbānagamanaṃ maggaṃ means: this was said referring to insight. For that is the preliminary path to Nibbāna, but through an inversion of gender, it is called 'maggaṃ'. Tattha me means: in that path leading to Nibbāna, known as my own youthful insight, my mind is intent. Pāpimā: this addresses defilement. Maccu also: this addresses the same. Na me maggampi dakkhasi means: I shall act in such a way that you will not see even the path where I have gone in the wombs of existence and so forth. The first [discourse].

2. Aratīsuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Arati Sutta.

210. Dutiye nikkhamatīti vihārā nikkhamati. Aparajju vā kāleti dutiyadivase vā bhikkhācārakāle. Vihāragaruko kiresa thero. Aratiñca ratiñcāti sāsane aratiṃ kāmaguṇesu ca ratiṃ. Sabbaso gehasitañca vitakkanti pañcakāmaguṇagehanissitaṃ pāpavitakkañca sabbākārena pahāya. Vanathanti kilesamahāvanaṃ. Kuhiñcīti kismiñci ārammaṇe. Nibbanathoti nikkilesavano. Aratoti taṇhāratirahito.

210. In the second [sutta], `nikkhamati` (he goes out) means: he goes out from the monastery. `Aparajju vā kāle` (on the next day or at the time) means: on the second day at the time for the alms-round. It is said this elder reveres the monastery. `Aratiñca ratiñca` (discontent and delight) means: discontent in the Dispensation and delight in sensual pleasures. `Sabbaso gehasitañca vitakkaṃ` (and entirely thoughts connected with the household) means: having in every way abandoned the evil thought based on the household of the five strands of sensual pleasure. `Vanathaṃ` (the thicket) means: the great forest of defilements. `Kuhiñci` (anywhere) means: in any object. `Nibbanatho` (free from the thicket) means: free from the forest of defilements. `Arato` (devoid of delight) means: devoid of the delight of craving.

Pathaviñca vehāsanti pathaviṭṭhitañca [P 1.0270] itthipurisavatthālaṅkārādivaṇṇaṃ, vehāsaṭṭhakañca candasūriyobhāsādi. Rūpagatanti rūpameva. Jagatogadhanti jagatiyā ogadhaṃ, antopathaviyaṃ nāgabhavanagatanti attho. Parijīyatīti parijīrati. Sabbamaniccanti sabbaṃ taṃ aniccaṃ. Ayaṃ therassa mahāvipassanāti vadanti. Evaṃ samaccāti evaṃ samāgantvā. Caranti mutattāti viññātattabhāvā viharanti.

`Pathaviñca vehāsaṃ` (earth and sky) means: the appearance of women, men, clothes, ornaments, and so on, situated on the earth, and the radiance of the moon, sun, and so on, situated in the sky. `Rūpagataṃ` (form-bound) means: only form. `Jagatogadhaṃ` (immersed in the world) means: submerged in the world, that is, gone to the nāga-abode beneath the earth. `Parijīyati` (it decays) means: it decays. `Sabbamaniccaṃ` (all is impermanent) means: all that is impermanent. This is the elder’s great insight, they say. `Evaṃ samacca` means: thus having comprehended. `Caranti mutattā` means: they dwell having understood their own existence.

Upadhīsūti khandhakilesābhisaṅkhāresu. Gadhitāti giddhā. Diṭṭhasuteti cakkhunā diṭṭhe rūpe, sotena sute sadde. Paṭighe ca mute cāti ettha paṭighapadena gandharasā gahitā, mutapadena phoṭṭhabbārammaṇaṃ[V 1.0238]. Yo ettha na limpatīti yo etesu pañcakāmaguṇesu taṇhādiṭṭhilepehi na limpati.

`Upadhīsu` (in the attachments) means: in the aggregates, defilements, and volitional formations. `Gadhitā` (greedy) means: greedy. `Diṭṭhasute` (in the seen and heard) means: in a form seen with the eye, and in a sound heard with the ear. `Paṭighe ca mute ca` (and in the impinged and sensed) means: here, by the word ‘impinged’ (`paṭigha`), smells and tastes are included; by the word ‘sensed’ (`muta`), the tangible object is included. `Yo ettha na limpati` (one who is not stained here) means: one who is not stained by the stains of craving and views in these five strands of sensual pleasure.

Atha saṭṭhinissitā savitakkā, puthū janatāya adhammā niviṭṭhāti atha cha ārammaṇanissitā puthū adhammavitakkā janatāya niviṭṭhāti attho. Na [M 1.0248] ca vaggagatassa kuhiñcīti tesaṃ vasena na katthaci kilesavaggagato bhaveyya. No pana duṭṭhullabhāṇīti duṭṭhullavacanabhāṇīpi na siyā. Sa bhikkhūti so evaṃvidho bhikkhu nāma hoti.

`Atha saṭṭhinissitā savitakkā, puthū janatāya adhammā niviṭṭhā` (Then, sixty dependent, with thoughts, various unwholesome things are established among people) means: then, dependent on the six sense objects, various unwholesome thoughts are established among people. `Na ca vaggagatassa kuhiñci` (and not belonging to any faction anywhere) means: he would not belong to any faction of defilements anywhere under their influence. `No pana duṭṭhullabhāṇī` (nor speaking coarse words) means: nor should he be a speaker of coarse words. `Sa bhikkhu` (that monk) means: such a one is called a bhikkhu.

Dabboti dabbajātiko paṇḍito. Cirarattasamāhitoti dīgharattaṃ samāhitacitto. Nipakoti nepakkena samannāgato pariṇatapañño. Apihālūti nittaṇho. Santaṃ padanti nibbānaṃ. Ajjhagamā munīti adhigato muni. Paṭicca parinibbuto kaṅkhati kālanti nibbānaṃ paṭicca kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto parinibbānakālaṃ āgameti. Dutiyaṃ.

`Dabbo` (wise) means: of a wise nature, wise. `Cirarattasamāhito` (long composed) means: for a long time with a composed mind. `Nipako` (prudent) means: endowed with prudence, having mature wisdom. `Apihālu` (without craving) means: without craving. `Santaṃ padaṃ` (the peaceful state) means: Nibbāna. `Ajjhagamā muni` (the sage attained) means: the sage who has attained. `Paṭicca parinibbuto kaṅkhati kālaṃ` (having realized, fully extinguished, he awaits the time) means: having realized Nibbāna, being fully extinguished by the final extinguishment of defilements, he awaits the time of final Nibbāna. The second [discourse].

3. Pesalasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Pesala Sutta.

211. Tatiye [P 1.0271] atimaññatīti “kiṃ ime mahallakā? Na etesaṃ pāḷi, na aṭṭhakathā, na padabyañjanamadhuratā, amhākaṃ pana pāḷipi aṭṭhakathāpi nayasatena nayasahassena upaṭṭhātī”ti atikkamitvā maññati. Gotamāti gotamabuddhasāvakattā attānaṃ ālapati. Mānapathanti mānārammaṇañceva mānasahabhuno ca dhamme. Vippaṭisārīhuvāti vippaṭisārī ahuvā, ahosīti attho. Maggajinoti maggena jitakileso. Kittiñca sukhañcāti vaṇṇabhaṇanañca kāyikacetasikasukhañca. Akhilodha padhānavāti akhilo idha padhānavā vīriyasampanno. Visuddhoti visuddho bhaveyya. Asesanti nissesaṃ navavidhaṃ. Vijjāyantakaroti vijjāya kilesānaṃ antakaro. Samitāvīti rāgādīnaṃ samitatāya samitāvī. Tatiyaṃ.

211. In the third [sutta], `atimaññati` (he looks down) means: thinking, “What are these elders? For them, the Pāli canon does not appear, the commentary does not appear, the sweetness of words and phrases does not appear. But for us, the Pāli canon and the commentary appear with a hundred methods, with a thousand methods.” Thus, despising them, he conceives. `Gotama` means: because of being a disciple of the Buddha Gotama, he addresses himself. `Mānapathaṃ` (the path of conceit) means: both the objects of conceit and the states associated with conceit. `Vippaṭisārīhuvā` (he was regretful) means: he was regretful; this is the meaning of ‘he was.’ `Maggajino` (the path-victor) means: one who has conquered the defilements by the four paths. `Kittiñca sukhañca` (fame and happiness) means: praise, and bodily and mental happiness. `Akhilodha padhānavā` (without mental barrenness here, striving) means: being free from the five mental barrennesses here, endowed with energy. `Visuddho` (pure) means: he would be pure. `Asesaṃ` (without remainder) means: without remainder, the ninefold conceit. `Vijjāyantakaro` (the end-maker by knowledge) means: one who makes an end of the defilements by the knowledge of the Arahant path. `Samitāvī` (the calmed one) means: one who is calmed because of the calming of lust and so on. The third [discourse].

4. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta.

212. Catutthe rāgoti āyasmā ānando mahāpuñño sambhāvito, taṃ rājarājamahāmattādayo [V 1.0239] nimantetvā antonivesane nisīdāpenti. Sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitāpi itthiyo theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā tālavaṇṭena bījenti, upanisīditvā pañhaṃ pucchanti dhammaṃ suṇanti. Tattha āyasmato vaṅgīsassa navapabbajitassa ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetuṃ asakkontassa itthirūpārammaṇe rāgo cittaṃ anuddhaṃseti. So saddhāpabbajitattā ujujātiko kulaputto “ayaṃ me rāgo vaḍḍhitvā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ atthaṃ nāseyyā”ti [M 1.0249] cintetvā anantaraṃ nisinnova therassa attānaṃ āvikaronto kāmarāgenātiādimāha.

212. In the fourth [sutta], regarding `rāgo` (lust): The Venerable Ānanda, being of great merit and esteemed, was invited by the king's chief ministers and others and was seated inside the residence. Women adorned with all ornaments approached the Elder, paid homage, fanned him with a palm-leaf fan, sat nearby, asked questions, and listened to the Dhamma. There, the mind of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, who was newly ordained and unable to comprehend the meditation object, was assailed by lust for the object of the female form. He, a clansman of upright nature who had gone forth out of faith, thought, “If this lust of mine grows, it will destroy my welfare in both the present and future lives.” Thus thinking, while still seated nearby, revealing himself to the Elder, he spoke the words beginning with, ‘With sensual lust…’

Tattha nibbāpananti rāganibbānakāraṇaṃ. Vipariyesāti vipallāsena. Subhaṃ rāgūpasañhitanti rāgaṭṭhāniyaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. Parato passāti aniccato passa. Mā ca attatoti [P 1.0272] attato mā passa. Kāyagatā tyatthūti kāyagatā te atthu. Animittañca bhāvehīti niccādīnaṃ nimittānaṃ ugghāṭitattā vipassanā animittā nāma, taṃ bhāvehīti vadati. Mānābhisamayāti mānassa dassanābhisamayā ceva pahānābhisamayā ca. Upasantoti rāgādisantatāya upasanto. Catutthaṃ.

Therein, `nibbāpanaṃ` (for extinguishing) means: the cause for the extinguishing of lust. `Vipariyesā` (by means of perversion) means: through the perversion of perception. `Subhaṃ rāgūpasañhitaṃ` (beautiful, connected with lust) means: a desirable object that is a basis for lust. `Parato passā` (see it as other) means: see it as impermanent. `Mā ca attato` (and not as self) means: do not see it as self. `Kāyagatā tyatthū` (let there be for you mindfulness directed to the body) means: let mindfulness directed to the body be for you. `Animittañca bhāvehi` (and develop the signless) means: because it has removed the signs of permanence and so on, insight is called ‘signless’; develop that, is what is said. `Mānābhisamayā` (through the breakthrough to conceit) means: through the breakthrough of seeing and the breakthrough of abandoning conceit. `Upasanto` (peaceful) means: peaceful through the pacification of lust and so on. The fourth [discourse].

5. Subhāsitasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Subhāsita Sutta.

213. Pañcame aṅgehīti kāraṇehi, avayavehi vā. Musāvādāveramaṇiādīni hi cattāri subhāsitavācāya kāraṇāni, saccavacanādayo cattāro avayavā. Kāraṇatthe ca aṅgasadde “catūhī”ti nissakkavacanaṃ hoti, avayavatthe karaṇavacanaṃ. Samannāgatāti samanuāgatā pavattā yuttā ca. Vācāti samullapanavācā, yā “vācā girā byappatho”ti (dha. sa. 636) ca, “nelā kaṇṇasukhā”ti (dī. ni. 1.9) ca āgatā. “Yā pana vācāya ce kataṃ kamma”nti evaṃ viññatti ca “yā catūhi vacīduccaritehi ārati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati sammāvācā”ti (vibha. 206) evaṃ virati ca, “pharusavācā, bhikkhave, āsevitā bhāvitā bahulīkatā nirayasaṃvattanikā hotī”ti (a. ni. 8.40) evaṃ cetanā ca vācāti āgatā, na sā idha adhippetā. Kasmā? Abhāsitabbato. Subhāsitāti suṭṭhu bhāsitā. Tenassā atthāvahataṃ dīpeti. No dubbhāsitāti na duṭṭhu bhāsitā. Tenassā anatthāvahanapahānataṃ dīpeti. Anavajjāti rāgādivajjarahitā. Imināssā kāraṇasuddhiṃ catudosābhāvañca dīpeti. Ananuvajjāti anuvādavimuttā[V 1.0240]. Imināssā sabbākārasampattiṃ dīpeti. Viññūnanti paṇḍitānaṃ. Tena nindāpasaṃsāsu bālā appamāṇāti dīpeti.

213. “By factors” means by causes or by components. For abstaining from false speech and so on are the four causes of well-spoken speech, while truthful speech and so on are the four components. In the sense of cause, the word “factor” takes the ablative case (“by four”), while in the sense of component, it takes the instrumental case. “Endowed” means associated with, occurring, and connected. “Speech” means articulate speech, which is described as “speech, utterance, expression” (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 636) and “eloquent, pleasant to the ear.” Also, “whatever action is done by speech” refers to verbal intimation, and “abstaining from the four kinds of verbal misconduct… this is called right speech” (Vibhaṅga 206) refers to abstinence, and “harsh speech, monks, when cultivated, developed, and frequently practiced, leads to hell” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.40) refers to intention—these are all called speech, but that is not intended here. Why? Because it is not to be spoken. “Well-spoken” means spoken well. This shows that it brings benefit. “Not ill-spoken” means not spoken badly. This shows the abandonment of what is harmful. “Faultless” means free from the faults of lust and so on. This shows the purity of its cause and the absence of four faults. “Blameless” means free from blame. This shows its perfection in all aspects. “By the wise” means by the learned. This shows that fools are no measure in blame and praise.

Subhāsitaṃyeva [M 1.0250][P 1.0273] bhāsatīti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya catūsu vācaṅgesu aññataraniddosavacanametaṃ. No dubbhāsitanti tasseva vācaṅgassa paṭipakkhabhāsananivāraṇaṃ. No dubbhāsitanti iminā micchāvācappahānaṃ dīpeti. Subhāsitanti iminā pahīnamicchāvācena bhāsitabbavacanalakkhaṇaṃ. Aṅgaparidīpanatthaṃ panettha abhāsitabbaṃ pubbe avatvā bhāsitabbamevāha. Esa nayo dhammaṃyevātiādīsupi. Ettha ca paṭhamena pisuṇadosarahitaṃ samaggakaraṇaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ, dutiyena samphappalāpadosarahitaṃ dhammato anapetaṃ mantāvacanaṃ, itarehi dvīhi pharusālikarahitāni piyasaccavacanāni. Imehi khoti ādinā tāni aṅgāni paccakkhato dassento taṃ vācaṃ nigameti. Yañca aññe paṭiññādīhi avayavehi, nāmādīhi padehi, liṅgavacanavibhattikālakārakasampattīhi ca samannāgataṃ musāvādādivācampi subhāsitanti maññanti, taṃ paṭisedheti. Avayavādisamannāgatāpi hi tathārūpī vācā dubbhāsitāva hoti attano ca paresañca anatthāvahattā. Imehi pana catūhaṅgehi samannāgatā sacepi milakkhubhāsāpariyāpannā ghaṭaceṭikāgītikapariyāpannāpi hoti, tathāpi subhāsitāva lokiyalokuttarahitasukhāvahattā. Tathā hi maggapasse sassaṃ rakkhantiyā sīhaḷaceṭikāya sīhaḷakeneva jātijarāmaraṇayuttaṃ gītikaṃ gāyantiyā saddaṃ sutvā maggaṃ gacchantā saṭṭhimattā vipassakā bhikkhū arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tathā tisso nāma āraddhavipassako bhikkhu padumasarasamīpena gacchanto padumasare padumāni bhañjitvā –

“He speaks only what is well-spoken”—this, in the teaching based on the individual, is a faultless statement relating to one of the four aspects of speech. “He does not speak what is ill-spoken”—this is the prevention of speaking the opposite of that very aspect of speech. By “He does not speak what is ill-spoken,” he indicates the abandoning of wrong speech. By “He speaks what is well-spoken,” he shows the characteristic of speech that should be spoken by one who has abandoned wrong speech. Here, for the purpose of clarifying the aspects, without first stating what should not be spoken, he speaks only of what should be spoken. This same method applies in passages such as, “He speaks only the Dhamma.” And here, by the first, speech that is free from the fault of slander and creates harmony is stated. By the second, consultative speech that is free from the fault of idle chatter and does not deviate from what is beneficial is stated. By the other two, pleasant and truthful words that are free from harshness and falsehood are stated. With the passage beginning, “By these,” he concludes his statement on speech by directly pointing out those aspects. And he refutes what others consider “well-spoken,” even speech such as falsehood that is complete with logical components like a proposition, with words such as nouns, and with the perfections of gender, number, case, tense, and syntax. For such speech, even if complete with logical components and so on, is indeed ill-spoken because it brings harm to oneself and to others. But speech that is endowed with these four aspects, even if it is in a foreign tongue or is in the category of a potter-servant’s song, is still well-spoken because it brings worldly and supramundane benefit and happiness. For so it was: sixty monks practicing insight meditation, while walking along a path, heard the sound of a Sinhalese servant woman guarding the crops by the wayside, singing a song in the Sinhalese language about birth, aging, and death, and they attained Arahantship. Similarly, a monk named Tissa, who was practicing insight meditation, was walking near a lotus pond and, having plucked lotuses in the pond—

“Pātova [P 1.0274] phullitakokanadaṃ, sūriyālokena bhijjiyate;

Evaṃ manussattaṃ gatā sattā, jarābhivegena maddiyantī”ti. –

“Just as a blooming red lotus in the morning is broken apart by sunlight, so beings who have attained human existence are crushed by the onrush of old age.”

Imaṃ gītikaṃ gāyantiyā ceṭikāya sutvā arahattaṃ patto.

Hearing this song sung by a servant girl, he attained Arahantship.

Buddhantarepi aññataro puriso sattahi puttehi saddhiṃ aṭavito āgamma aññatarāya itthiyā musalena taṇḍule koṭṭentiyā –

Also in the interval between Buddhas, a certain man, having come from the forest together with his seven sons, heard a certain woman pounding rice with a pestle sing:

“Jarāya [V 1.0241][M 1.0251] parimadditaṃ etaṃ, milātachavicammanissitaṃ;

Maraṇena bhijjati etaṃ, maccussa ghāsamāmisaṃ.

“This body is crushed by old age, dependent on withered skin, thick and thin; this body is broken by death, it is the food and flesh for Death.

“Kimīnaṃ ālayaṃ etaṃ, nānākuṇapena pūritaṃ;

Asucissa bhājanaṃ etaṃ, kadalikkhandhasamaṃ ida”nti. –

“This is a dwelling for worms, filled with various corpses; this is a vessel of the impure, this is like a plantain trunk.”

Imaṃ gītikaṃ sutvā paccavekkhanto saha puttehi paccekabodhiṃ patto. Evaṃ imehi catūhi aṅgehi samannāgatā vācā sacepi milakkhubhāsāpariyāpannā ghaṭaceṭikāgītikapariyāpannāpi hoti, tathāpi subhāsitāti veditabbā. Subhāsitattā eva ca anavajjā ca ananuvajjā ca viññūnaṃ atthatthikānaṃ atthapaṭisaraṇānaṃ, no byañjanapaṭisaraṇānanti.

Having heard this song and reflecting on it, he attained the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha together with his sons. Thus, speech that is endowed with these four factors, even if it is included in a barbarian language or included in the song of a potter's female servant, should still be known as well-spoken. And just because it is well-spoken, it is both faultless and irreproachable by the wise—those who desire the benefit, who have meaning as their refuge, and not the letter.

Sāruppāhīti anucchavikāhi. Abhitthavīti pasaṃsi. Na tāpayeti vippaṭisārena na tāpeyya na vibādheyya. Pareti parehi bhindanto nābhibhaveyya na bādheyya. Iti imāya gāthāya apisuṇavācāvasena bhagavantaṃ thometi. Paṭinanditāti piyāyitā. Yaṃ anādāyāti yaṃ vācaṃ bhāsanto paresaṃ pāpāni appiyāni pharusavacanāni anādāya atthabyañjanamadhuraṃ piyameva bhāsati, taṃ vācaṃ bhāseyyāti [P 1.0275] piyavācāvasena abhitthavi.

`Sāruppāhi` means: by suitable words. `Abhitthavi` means: he praised. `Na tāpaye` means: one should not cause torment with remorse, nor should one oppress. `Pare` means: one should not overwhelm or oppress others by causing division. Thus, with this verse, he extols the Blessed One by way of speech free from slander. `Paṭinanditā` means: beloved. `Yaṃ anādāya` means: whichever speech one speaks, not taking up evil, unendearing, and harsh words towards others, one speaks only what is endearing, sweet in meaning and expression. One should speak such speech. Thus, he praised the Blessed One by way of endearing speech.

Amatāti sādhubhāvena amatasadisā. Vuttampi hetaṃ – “saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ rasāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.246) nibbānāmatapaccayattā vā amatā. Esa dhammo sanantanoti yā ayaṃ saccavācā nāma, esa porāṇo dhammo cariyā paveṇī. Idameva hi porāṇānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ, na te alikaṃ bhāsiṃsu. Tenevāha – sacce atthe ca dhamme ca, āhu santo patiṭṭhitāti.

`Amatā` means: like the deathless nectar due to its quality of goodness. For it has been said: “Truth, indeed, is the sweetest of tastes.” Or, it is deathless because it is a condition for the deathless, Nibbāna. `Esa dhammo sanantano` means: this which is called true speech is an ancient principle, a practice, a tradition. Indeed, this very thing was the constant practice of the ancients; they did not speak falsehood. For that reason, He said: “The good, they say, are established in truth, in meaning, and in the Dhamma.”

Tattha sacce patiṭṭhitattāva attano ca paresañca atthe patiṭṭhitā, atthe patiṭṭhitattā eva dhamme patiṭṭhitā hontīti veditabbā. Saccavisesanameva vā etaṃ. Idaṃ hi vuttaṃ hoti – sacce patiṭṭhitā, kīdise? Atthe ca dhamme ca, yaṃ paresaṃ atthato anapetattā atthaṃ anuparodhakaraṃ[V 1.0242], dhammato anapetattā dhammaṃ dhammikameva atthaṃ sādhetīti. Iti imāya gāthāya saccavacanavasena abhitthavi.

Herein, because of being established in truth, they are established in their own welfare and the welfare of others. It should be known that precisely by being established in welfare, they are established in the Dhamma. Or, this phrase 'in welfare and in the Dhamma' is merely a qualifier of 'truth'. For this is what is said: 'Established in truth'—of what kind? 'In welfare and in the Dhamma.' That which, not being devoid of the welfare of others, is a welfare that causes no opposition; and not being devoid of the Dhamma, is a Dhamma that accomplishes a righteous welfare. Thus, by means of this third verse, he praised him by way of truthful speech.

Khemanti [M 1.0252] abhayaṃ nirupaddavaṃ. Kena kāraṇenāti ce. Nibbānapattiyā dukkhassantakiriyāya, yasmā kilesanibbānaṃ pāpeti, vaṭṭadukkhassa ca antakiriyāya saṃvattatīti attho. Atha vā yaṃ buddho nibbānapattiyā dukkhassantakiriyāyāti dvinnaṃ nibbānadhātūnaṃ atthāya khemamaggappakāsanato khemaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, sā ve vācānamuttamāti sā vācā sabbavācānaṃ seṭṭhāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Iti imāya gāthāya mantāvacanavasena bhagavantaṃ abhitthavanto arahattanikūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhapesīti. Pañcamaṃ.

'Safe' (khemaṃ) means fearless, free from danger. If it is asked, 'For what reason is it free from danger?' Because it is for the attainment of Nibbāna, for making an end of suffering; for it leads to the Nibbāna of defilements and conduces to making an end of the suffering of the cycle—this is the meaning. Or alternatively, because the Buddha, for the sake of the two Nibbāna elements—that is, for the attainment of Nibbāna and for making an end of suffering—speaks a safe speech by revealing the safe path, 'that speech is truly the highest of speeches' (sā ve vācānamuttamā). Thus, in this context, the meaning should be understood as: 'that speech is the best of all speeches.' Thus, by means of this fourth verse, praising the Blessed One by way of consultative speech, he concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship. The fifth sutta.

6. Sāriputtasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta

214. Chaṭṭhe poriyāti akkharādiparipuṇṇāya. Vissaṭṭhāyāti avibaddhāya apalibuddhāya. Dhammasenāpatissa hi kathentassa pittādīnaṃ vasena apalibuddhavacanaṃ hoti, ayadaṇḍena pahatakaṃsatālato saddo viya niccharati. Anelagalāyāti anelāya agalāya niddosāya ceva akkhalitapadabyañjanāya ca. Therassa hi kathayato padaṃ vā byañjanaṃ vā na parihāyati. Atthassa viññāpaniyāti atthassa viññāpanasamatthāya. Bhikkhunanti [P 1.0276] bhikkhūnaṃ.

214. In the sixth sutta, 'urbane' (poriyā) means complete in letters and so forth. 'Articulate' (vissaṭṭhā) means unobstructed and unhindered. For when the General of the Dhamma speaks, his words are unimpeded by such things as bile, and they issue forth like the sound from a bronze cymbal struck by an iron rod. 'Without fault or stammer' (anelagalā) means faultless (anelā) and not stammering (agalā); that is, both faultless and with non-stumbling words and letters. For when the Elder speaks, neither a word nor a letter is deficient. 'Making the meaning known' (atthassa viññāpaniyā) means capable of making the meaning known. 'To the bhikkhus' (bhikkhunaṃ) means 'for the bhikkhus'.

Saṃkhittenapīti “cattārimāni, āvuso, ariyasaccāni. Katamāni cattāri? Dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ…pe… imāni kho, āvuso, cattāri ariyasaccāni, tasmātiha, āvuso, idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasaccanti yogo karaṇīyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1096-1098) evaṃ saṃkhittenapi deseti. Vitthārenapīti “katamaṃ, āvuso, dukkhaṃ ariyasacca”ntiādinā (ma. ni. 3.373) nayena tāneva vibhajanto vitthārenapi bhāsati. Khandhādidesanāsupi eseva nayo. Sāḷikāyiva nigghosoti yathā madhuraṃ ambapakkaṃ sāyitvā pakkhehi vātaṃ datvā madhurassaraṃ nicchārentiyā sāḷikasakuṇiyā nigghoso, evaṃ therassa dhammaṃ kathentassa madhuro nigghoso hoti. Paṭibhānaṃ udīrayīti samuddato ūmiyo viya anantaṃ paṭibhānaṃ uṭṭhahati. Odhentīti odahanti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

'In brief' (saṃkhittenapi): "Friends, there are these four Noble Truths. What four? The Noble Truth of suffering... and so on... These, friends, are the four Noble Truths. Therefore, friends, in this Teaching, effort should be made thus: 'This is the Noble Truth of suffering.'" Thus, he teaches even in brief. 'In detail' (vitthārenapi): "Friends, what is the Noble Truth of suffering?" and so on. By this method, analyzing those very truths, he speaks even in detail. This same method applies to teachings on the aggregates and so forth. 'Like the melodious call of a sāḷikā bird' (sāḷikāyiva nigghoso): just as a sāḷikā bird, having tasted a sweet ripe mango and fanning with its wings, emits a sweet sound, so too is the Elder’s voice sweet when he teaches the Dhamma. 'His eloquence arose' (paṭibhānaṃ udīrayi): infinite eloquence arises like waves from the ocean. 'They pay attention' (odhenti): they pay attention (odahanti). The sixth.

7. Pavāraṇāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Pavāraṇā Sutta

215. Sattame [V 1.0243][M 1.0253] tadahūti tasmiṃ ahu, tasmiṃ divaseti attho. Upavasanti etthāti uposatho. Upavasantīti ca sīlena vā anasanena vā upetā hutvā vasantīti attho. So panesa uposathadivaso aṭṭhamīcātuddasīpannarasībhedena tividho, tasmā sesadvayanivāraṇatthaṃ pannaraseti vuttaṃ. Pavāraṇāyāti vassaṃ-vuṭṭha-pavāraṇāya. Visuddhipavāraṇātipi etissāva nāmaṃ. Nisinno hotīti sāyanhasamaye sampattaparisāya kālayuttaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā udakakoṭṭhake gattāni parisiñcitvā nivatthanivāsano ekaṃsaṃ sugatamahācīvaraṃ katvā majjhimatthambhaṃ nissāya paññatte varabuddhāsane puratthimadisāya uṭṭhahato candamaṇḍalassa siriṃ siriyā abhibhavamāno nisinno hoti. Tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtanti yato yato anuviloketi, tato tato tuṇhībhūtameva. Tattha hi ekabhikkhussāpi hatthakukkuccaṃ vā pādakukkuccaṃ vā natthi, sabbe niravā santena iriyāpathena nisīdiṃsu. Anuviloketvāti dissamānapañcapasādehi nettehi anuviloketvā. Handāti vossaggatthe nipāto. Na ca me kiñci garahathāti ettha na ca kiñcīti pucchanatthe na-kāro. Kiṃ me kiñci [P 1.0277] garahatha? Yadi garahatha, vadatha, icchāpemi vo vattunti attho. Kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vāti iminā kāyavacīdvārāneva pavāreti, na manodvāraṃ. Kasmā? Apākaṭattā. Kāyavacīdvāresu hi doso pākaṭo hoti, na manodvāre. “Ekamañce sayatopi hi kiṃ cintesī”ti? Pucchitvā cittācāraṃ jānāti. Iti manodvāraṃ apākaṭattā na pavāreti, no aparisuddhattā. Bodhisattabhūtassāpi hi tassa bhūridattachaddantasaṅkhapāladhammapālādikāle manodvāraṃ parisuddhaṃ, idānettha vattabbameva natthi.

215. In the seventh sutta, 'on that day' (tadahū) means 'on that day,' that is, 'on that date.' 'Uposatha' is so called because 'they observe (upavasanti) on it (ettha).' And 'they observe' (upavasanti) means 'they dwell, having undertaken virtue or fasting'—this is the meaning. This Uposatha day is of three kinds, distinguished as the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth. Therefore, to exclude the other two, 'the fifteenth' is stated. 'For the Pavāraṇā' (pavāraṇāya) means for the Pavāraṇā after having resided for the rains. 'Purity-Pavāraṇā' (Visuddhipavāraṇā) is also a name for it. 'He is seated' (nisinno hoti) means: in the evening, after teaching the Dhamma suitable for the time to the assembled gathering, having bathed his limbs in the bathing chamber, wearing his lower robe and having arranged the Sugata’s great outer robe over one shoulder, he sits on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat, leaning against the central pillar, overpowering with his own splendor the splendor of the moon-disc rising in the eastern direction. 'Utterly silent' (tuṇhībhūtaṃ): wherever he looks around, it is utterly silent there. For there, not even one bhikkhu has fidgeting of hands or feet; all sat soundlessly, with peaceful deportment. 'Having looked around' (anuviloketvā) means having looked around with his eyes possessing the fivefold clarity. 'Come now' (handa) is a particle in the sense of invitation. In 'Do you find any fault in me?' (na ca me kiñci garahatha), the particle 'na' is in the sense of a question. The meaning is: 'Do you find any fault in me? If you do find fault, speak; I grant you leave to speak.' By 'bodily or verbal' (kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vā), he invites criticism only regarding the doors of body and speech, not the door of mind. Why? Because it is not manifest. For a fault in the doors of body and speech is manifest, not in the door of mind. For, even of one lying on the same couch, only by asking, 'What are you thinking?' does one know the conduct of the mind. Thus, he does not invite criticism regarding the door of mind because it is not manifest, not because it is impure. For even when he was a Bodhisatta, his door of mind was pure in the times of Bhūridatta, Chaddanta, Saṅkhapāla, and Dhammapāla. Now, in this regard, there is nothing at all to be said.

Etadavocāti dhammasenāpatiṭṭhāne ṭhitattā bhikkhusaṅghassa bhāraṃ vahanto etaṃ avoca. Na kho mayaṃ, bhanteti, bhante, mayaṃ bhagavato na kiñci garahāma. Kāyikaṃ vā vācasikaṃ vāti idaṃ catunnaṃ arakkhiyataṃ sandhāya thero āha. Bhagavato hi cattāri arakkhiyāni. Yathāha –

'He spoke thus' (etadavoca): Being established in the position of the General of the Dhamma and bearing the burden of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, he spoke this. 'Indeed, we do not, venerable sir' (na kho mayaṃ, bhante): Venerable sir, we find no fault whatsoever in the Blessed One. The Elder said this—'bodily or verbal'—with reference to the four things that need no guarding. For the Blessed One has four things that need no guarding. As it is said:

“Cattārimāni[M 1.0254], bhikkhave, tathāgatassa arakkhiyāni. Katamāni cattāri? Parisuddhakāyasamācāro, bhikkhave, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa kāyaduccaritaṃ, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’ti. Parisuddhavacīsamācāro, bhikkhave, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa [V 1.0244] vacīduccaritaṃ, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya, ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’ti. Parisuddhamanosamācāro, bhikkhave, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa manoduccaritaṃ, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya, ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’ti. Parisuddhājīvo, bhikkhave, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa micchāājīvo, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya “mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī”ti (a. ni. 7.58).

Bhikkhus, these are the four things of the Tathāgata that need no guarding. What four? Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is of pure bodily conduct; there is no bodily misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would guard, thinking, 'May another not know this of me.' Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is of pure verbal conduct; there is no verbal misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would guard, thinking, 'May another not know this of me.' Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is of pure mental conduct; there is no mental misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would guard, thinking, 'May another not know this of me.' Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is of pure livelihood; there is no wrong livelihood of the Tathāgata that he would guard, thinking, 'May another not know this of me.'

Idāni bhagavato yathābhūtaguṇe kathento bhagavā hi, bhantetiādimāha. Tattha anuppannassāti kassapasammāsambuddhato paṭṭhāya aññena samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā anuppāditapubbassa. Asañjātassāti idaṃ anuppannavevacanameva. Anakkhātassāti aññena adesitassa. Pacchā samannāgatāti paṭhamagatassa bhagavato pacchā samanuāgatā. Iti thero yasmā sabbepi bhagavato sīlādayo guṇā arahattamaggameva nissāya āgatā, tasmā arahattamaggameva nissāya guṇaṃ kathesi. Tena sabbaguṇā kathitāva honti. Ahañca kho, bhanteti idaṃ thero sadevake loke aggapuggalassa attano ceva saṅghassa ca kāyikavācasikaṃ pavārento āha.

Now, wishing to speak of the Blessed One’s true qualities, he uttered the words beginning with, 'Indeed, the Blessed One, venerable sir.' Therein, 'of the unarisen' (anuppannassa) means of that which had not been previously produced by any other ascetic or brahmin since the time of Kassapa the Fully Enlightened One. 'Of the ungenerated' (asañjātassa) is simply a synonym for 'unarisen.' 'Of the undeclared' (anakkhātassa) means of that which was not taught by another. 'Followed after' (pacchā samannāgatā) means having followed in succession after the Blessed One who went first. Thus, since all the qualities of the Blessed One, such as virtue and so on, arise in dependence on the path to Arahantship, the Elder therefore spoke of the qualities in dependence on the path to Arahantship. By this, all qualities are indeed spoken of. 'And I, venerable sir' (Ahañca kho, bhante): The Elder said this while inviting scrutiny, toward the foremost person in the world with its devas, of the bodily and verbal conduct of both himself and the Saṅgha.

Pitarā [P 1.0278] pavattitanti cakkavattimhi kālaṅkate vā pabbajite vā sattāhaccayena cakkaṃ antaradhāyati, tato dasavidhaṃ dvādasavidhaṃ cakkavattivattaṃ pūretvā nisinnassa puttassa aññaṃ pātubhavati, taṃ so pavatteti. Ratanamayattā pana sadisaṭṭhena tadeva vattaṃ katvā “pitarā pavattita”nti vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā so “appossukko tvaṃ, deva, hohi, ahamanusāsissāmī”ti āha, tasmā pitarā pavattitaṃ āṇācakkaṃ anuppavatteti nāma. Sammadeva anuppavattesīti sammā nayena hetunā kāraṇeneva anuppavattesi. Bhagavā hi catusaccadhammaṃ katheti, thero tameva anukatheti, tasmā evamāha. Ubhatobhāgavimuttāti dvīhi bhāgehi vimuttā[M 1.0255], arūpāvacarasamāpattiyā rūpakāyato vimuttā, aggamaggena nāmakāyatoti. Paññāvimuttāti paññāya vimuttā tevijjādibhāvaṃ appattā khīṇāsavā.

'Set in motion by the father' (pitarā pavattitaṃ): when a wheel-turning monarch dies or goes forth, after seven days the wheel-treasure disappears. Then, for his son who is seated having fulfilled the tenfold and twelvefold duties of a wheel-turning monarch, another appears, and he sets it in motion. But because it is made of gems and because of its similarity, having performed that very same duty, it is said, 'set in motion by the father.' Or because he said, 'Be without anxiety, Your Majesty, I will instruct,' therefore, he is one who sets in motion subsequently the wheel of command set in motion by the father. 'He rightly set it in motion subsequently' (sammadeva anuppavattesi): he set it in motion subsequently by the right method, by reason and cause alone. Indeed, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma of the Four Truths, and the Elder teaches that very same Dhamma subsequently; therefore, he spoke thus. 'Released in both parts' (ubhatobhāgavimuttā): released by two parts—released from the form-body by means of the formless sphere attainments, and from the name-body by means of the supreme path. 'Released by wisdom' (paññāvimuttā): released by wisdom, they are canker-destroyed ones who have not attained the state of the triple knowledge and so on.

Visuddhiyāti visuddhatthāya. Saṃyojanabandhanacchidāti saṃyojanasaṅkhāte ceva bandhanasaṅkhāte ca kilese chinditvā ṭhitā. Vijitasaṅgāmanti vijitarāgadosamohasaṅgāmaṃ, mārabalassa vijitattāpi [V 1.0245] vijitasaṅgāmaṃ. Satthavāhanti aṭṭhaṅgikamaggarathe āropetvā veneyyasatthaṃ vāheti saṃsārakantāraṃ uttāretīti bhagavā satthavāho, taṃ satthavāhaṃ. Palāpoti antotuccho dussīlo. Ādiccabandhunanti ādiccabandhuṃ satthāraṃ dasabalaṃ vandāmīti vadati. Sattamaṃ.

'For purity' means for the sake of purity. 'Having cut the fetters and bonds' means: having cut the defilements designated as fetters and also as bonds, they are established. 'Victor in battle' means one who has conquered the battle against lust, hatred, and delusion; also, victor in battle because of having conquered Māra's army. 'Caravan leader' means: having placed the multitude of trainable beings on the chariot of the Eightfold Path, he leads them and makes them cross over the wilderness of saṃsāra; thus, the Blessed One is the Caravan Leader; to that Caravan Leader. 'Chaff' means empty within, one of bad moral conduct. 'Kinsman of the Sun' means he says, 'I pay homage to the Kinsman of the Sun, the Teacher, the Possessor of the Ten Powers.' The seventh sutta.

8. Parosahassasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Parosahassa Sutta.

216. Aṭṭhame parosahassanti atirekasahassaṃ. Akutobhayanti nibbāne kutoci bhayaṃ natthi, nibbānappattassa vā kutoci bhayaṃ natthīti nibbānaṃ akutobhayaṃ nāma. Isīnaṃ isisattamoti vipassito paṭṭhāya isīnaṃ sattamako isi.

216. In the eighth sutta, 'more than a thousand' means exceeding a thousand. 'Without fear from anywhere' means: in Nibbāna, there is no fear from anywhere; or, for a person who has attained Nibbāna, there is no fear from anywhere; thus, Nibbāna is called 'without fear from anywhere.' 'The seventh sage among sages' means: starting from the Buddha Vipassī, he is the seventh sage among the sages.

Kiṃ nu te vaṅgīsāti idaṃ bhagavā atthuppattivasena āha. Saṅghamajjhe kira kathā udapādi “vaṅgīsatthero vissaṭṭhavatto[P 1.0279], neva uddese, na paripucchāya, na yonisomanasikāre kammaṃ karoti, gāthā bandhanto cuṇṇiyapadāni karonto vicaratī”ti. Atha bhagavā cintesi – “ime bhikkhū vaṅgīsassa paṭibhānasampattiṃ na jānanti, cintetvā cintetvā vadatīti maññanti, paṭibhānasampattimassa jānāpessāmī”ti cintetvā, “kiṃ nu te vaṅgīsā”tiādimāha.

The Blessed One spoke this, 'What is it with you, Vaṅgīsa?' in connection with the arising of the matter. It is said that in the midst of the Saṅgha, a discussion arose: 'The Elder Vaṅgīsa has abandoned his duties, engaging neither in recitation, nor in questioning, nor in the task of proper attention; he wanders about composing verses and prose passages.' Then the Blessed One thought: 'These bhikkhus do not know Vaṅgīsa's accomplishment in ready wit; they think he speaks after pondering and pondering. I will make them aware of his accomplishment in ready wit.' Having thought thus, he uttered the words beginning with, 'What is it with you, Vaṅgīsa?'

Ummaggapathanti anekāni kilesummujjanasatāni, vaṭṭapathattā pana pathanti vuttaṃ. Pabhijja khilānīti rāgakhilādīni pañca bhinditvā carasi. Taṃ passathāti taṃ evaṃ abhibhuyya bhinditvā carantaṃ buddhaṃ passatha. Bandhapamuñcakaranti bandhanamocanakaraṃ. Asitanti anissitaṃ. Bhāgaso pavibhajanti satipaṭṭhānādikoṭṭhāsavasena dhammaṃ vibhajantaṃ. Pavibhajjāti vā pāṭho, aṅgapaccaṅgakoṭṭhāsavasena vibhajitvā vibhajitvā passathāti attho.

As for 'the path of emergence', it means the many hundreds of emergences from defilements; however, because it is the path of the cycle, it is called a 'path'. As for 'having shattered the stakes', it means you wander after shattering the five stakes, such as the stake of lust. As for 'see him', it means see that Buddha who wanders, having thus overcome and shattered them. As for 'the one who releases from bonds', it means the one who brings about release from bondage. As for 'unattached', it means unreliant. As for 'dividing into portions', it means one who divides the Dhamma by way of sections such as the foundations of mindfulness. Alternatively, there is the reading 'having divided'; the meaning is: see after dividing and re-dividing by way of sections of major and minor limbs.

Oghassāti [M 1.0256] caturoghassa. Anekavihitanti satipaṭṭhānādivasena anekavidhaṃ. Tasmiṃ ca amate akkhāteti tasmiṃ tena akkhāte amate. Dhammaddasāti dhammassa passitāro. Ṭhitā asaṃhīrāti asaṃhāriyā hutvā patiṭṭhitā.

'Of the flood' means of the four floods. 'Manifold' means of many kinds, by way of the foundations of mindfulness and so on. 'And when that deathless state was proclaimed' means when that deathless state was proclaimed by him. 'Seers of the Dhamma' means seers of the Dhamma. 'Established, unshakeable' means they are established, having become unshakeable.

Ativijjhāti ativijjhitvā. Sabbaṭṭhitīnanti sabbesaṃ diṭṭhiṭṭhānānaṃ viññāṇaṭṭhitīnaṃ vā[V 1.0246]. Atikkamamaddasāti atikkamabhūtaṃ nibbānamaddasa. Agganti uttamadhammaṃ. Aggeti vā pāṭho, paṭhamataranti attho. Dasaddhānanti pañcannaṃ, aggadhammaṃ pañcavaggiyānaṃ, agge vā pañcavaggiyānaṃ dhammaṃ desesīti attho. Tasmāti yasmā esa dhammo sudesitoti jānantena ca pamādo na kātabbo, tasmā. Anusikkheti tisso sikkhā sikkheyya. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

'Having pierced through' means having pierced through and known. 'Of all standpoints' means of all standpoints of views or stations of consciousness. 'I saw the transcendence' means I saw Nibbāna, which is transcendence. 'Supreme' means the supreme Dhamma. Alternatively, there is the reading 'foremost,' the meaning of which is 'first of all.' As for 'of half of ten,' it means 'of the five'; the meaning is either that he taught the supreme Dhamma to the group of five monks, or that he taught the Dhamma foremost to the group of five monks. As for 'therefore': since this Dhamma is well-taught, one who knows this should not be negligent; therefore. 'One should train accordingly' means one should train in the three trainings. The eighth.

9. Koṇḍaññasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Koṇḍañña Sutta

217. Navame [P 1.0280] aññāsikoṇḍaññoti paṭhamaṃ dhammassa aññātattā evaṃ gahitanāmo thero. Sucirassevāti kīvacirassa? Dvādasannaṃ saṃvaccharānaṃ. Ettakaṃ kālaṃ kattha vihāsīti. Chaddantabhavane mandākinipokkharaṇiyā tīre paccekabuddhānaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne. Kasmā? Vihāragarutāya. So hi paññavā mahāsāvako. Yatheva bhagavato, evamassa dasasahassacakkavāḷe devamanussānaṃ abbhantare guṇā patthaṭāva. Devamanussā tathāgatassa santikaṃ gantvā gandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ katvā “aggadhammaṃ paṭividdhasāvako”ti anantaraṃ theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā pūjenti. Santikaṃ āgatānañca nāma tathārūpā dhammakathā vā paṭisanthāro vā kātabbo hoti. Thero ca vihāragaruko, tenassa so papañco viya upaṭṭhāti. Iti vihāragarutāya tattha gantvā vihāsi.

217. In the ninth, 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña' means the elder was so named because he was the first to understand the Dhamma. 'For a very long time' means for how long? For twelve years. For such a long time, where did he dwell? On the shore of the Mandākinī pond in the Chaddanta forest, the dwelling place of Paccekabuddhas. Why? Due to his reverence for dwelling in seclusion. For he was a wise great disciple. Just as the Blessed One's virtues were spread among gods and humans throughout the ten-thousand world-systems, so too were his. Gods and humans, having gone to the Tathāgata's presence and paid homage with perfumes, garlands, and the like, would immediately after approach the elder and pay homage, praising him as 'the disciple who has penetrated the supreme Dhamma.' And for those who came to his presence, a suitable Dhamma talk or a friendly reception had to be undertaken. But the elder revered dwelling in seclusion, so this appeared to him like a complication. Thus, out of reverence for dwelling in seclusion, he went there and dwelled.

Aparampi kāraṇaṃ – bhikkhācāravelāyaṃ tāva sabbasāvakā vassaggena gacchanti. Dhammadesanākāle pana majjhaṭṭhāne alaṅkatabuddhāsanamhi satthari nisinne dakkhiṇahatthapasse dhammasenāpati, vāmahatthapasse mahāmoggallānatthero nisīdati, tesaṃ piṭṭhibhāge aññāsikoṇḍaññattherassa āsanaṃ paññāpenti. Sesā bhikkhū taṃ parivāretvā nisīdanti. Dve aggasāvakā aggadhammapaṭividdhattā ca mahallakattā ca there sagāravā theraṃ mahābrahmaṃ [M 1.0257] viya aggikkhandhaṃ viya āsīvisaṃ viya ca maññamānā dhurāsane nisīdantā ottappanti harāyanti. Thero cintesi – “imehi dhurāsanatthāya kappasatasahassādhikaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ pāramiyo pūritā, te idāni dhurāsane nisīdantā mama ottappanti harāyanti, phāsuvihāraṃ nesaṃ karissāmī”ti. So patirūpe kāle tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā “icchāmahaṃ, bhante, janapade vasitu”nti āha, satthā anujāni.

Another reason is this: At the time of the alms round, all the disciples go out in order of seniority. But during the teaching of the Dhamma, when the Teacher is seated on the adorned Buddha-seat in the middle, the General of the Dhamma sits on his right side, while the Elder Mahāmoggallāna sits on his left. Behind them, a seat is arranged for the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. The remaining monks sit surrounding him. The two chief disciples, respectful towards the Elder both because he had penetrated the foremost Dhamma and because of his great age, felt moral dread and shame while sitting in the seats of honor, regarding him as if he were a great Brahmā, a mass of fire, or a venomous snake. The Elder thought: 'For the sake of these seats of honor, they have fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable and a hundred thousand aeons. Now, while sitting in the seats of honor, they feel moral dread and shame because of me. I shall bring about a comfortable abiding for them.' At an appropriate time, he approached the Tathāgata and said, 'Venerable sir, I wish to dwell in the countryside.' The Teacher gave his permission.

Thero [V 1.0247] senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā pattacīvaramādāya chaddantabhavane mandākinitīraṃ gato. Pubbe paccekabuddhānaṃ pāricariyāya kataparicayā aṭṭhasahassā hatthināgā theraṃ disvāva “amhākaṃ puññakkhettaṃ āgata”nti nakhehi [P 1.0281] caṅkamanaṃ nittiṇaṃ katvā āvaraṇasākhā haritvā therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggitvā vattaṃ katvā sabbe sannipatitvā mantayiṃsu – “sace hi mayaṃ ‘ayaṃ therassa kattabbaṃ karissati, ayaṃ karissatī’ti paṭipajjissāma, thero bahuñātikagāmaṃ gato viya yathādhoteneva pattena gamissati, vārena naṃ paṭijaggissāma, ekassa pana vāre patte sesehipi nappamajjitabba”nti vāraṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Vārikanāgo pātova therassa mukhodakañca dantakaṭṭhañca ṭhapeti, vattaṃ karoti.

The Elder, having put his lodging in order, took his bowl and robe and went to the bank of the Mandākini Lake in the abode of Chaddanta. In the past, having become familiar through serving Paccekabuddhas, eight thousand great elephants, upon the very sight of the Elder, thought, 'Our field of merit has arrived.' Having made the walking path free of grass with their nails, removed obstructing branches, prepared the Elder's dwelling place, and performed their duties, they all gathered and conferred: 'If we act with the thought, "This one will do what is needed for the Elder, that one will do it," the Elder will depart like one who has gone to a village with many relatives—with his bowl as clean as when he arrived. Let us attend to him in turns. And when it is one's turn, the others must not be negligent.' Thus, they established a rotation. The elephant on duty would place water for the Elder's morning ablutions and a tooth-cleansing stick early in the morning and perform its duties.

Mandākinipokkharaṇī nāma cesā paṇṇāsayojanā hoti. Tassā pañcavīsatiyojanamatte ṭhāne sevālo vā paṇakaṃ vā natthi, phalikavaṇṇaṃ udakameva hoti. Tato paraṃ pana kaṭippamāṇe udake aḍḍhayojanavitthataṃ sesapadumavanaṃ paṇṇāsayojanaṃ saraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ. Tadanantaraṃ tāva mahantameva rattapadumavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ rattakumudavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ setakumudavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ nīluppalavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ rattuppalavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ sugandharattasālivanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ eḷālukalābukumbhaṇḍādīni madhurarasāni valliphalāni, tadanantaraṃ aḍḍhayojanavitthārameva ucchuvanaṃ, tattha pūgarukkhakkhandhappamāṇā ucchū, tadanantaraṃ kadalivanaṃ, yato duve pakkāni khādantā kilamanti, tadanantaraṃ cāṭippamāṇaphalaṃ panasavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ jambuvanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ ambavanaṃ, tadanantaraṃ kapitthavananti. Saṅkhepato tasmiṃ dahe khāditabbayuttakaṃ phalaṃ nāma natthīti na vattabbaṃ. Kusumānaṃ pupphanasamaye vāto reṇuvaṭṭiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā paduminipattesu ṭhapeti, tattha udakaphusitāni patanti. Tato ādiccapākena paccitvā pakkapayoghanikā viya tiṭṭhati, etaṃ pokkharamadhu nāma[M 1.0258], taṃ therassa āharitvā denti. Muḷālaṃ naṅgalasīsamattaṃ hoti, tampi āharitvā denti. Bhisaṃ mahābheripokkharappamāṇaṃ hoti, tassa ekasmiṃ pabbe pādaghaṭakappamāṇaṃ khīraṃ hoti, taṃ āharitvā denti. Pokkharaṭṭhīni madhusakkharāya yojetvā [P 1.0282] denti. Ucchuṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhe ṭhapetvā pādena akkamanti. Tato raso paggharitvā soṇḍiāvāṭe pūretvā, ādiccapākena paccitvā khīrapāsāṇapiṇḍo viya tiṭṭhati, taṃ āharitvā denti. Panasakadaliambapakkādīsu kathāva natthi.

This lake named Mandākinī is fifty yojanas in extent. In an area of it measuring twenty-five yojanas, there is no moss or algae; there is only water the color of crystal. Beyond that, however, in waist-deep water, a forest of white lotuses, half a yojana in width, stands surrounding the fifty-yojana lake. Next to that is a forest of red lotuses of the same great size, then a forest of red water lilies, followed by a forest of white water lilies, then a forest of blue water lilies, then a forest of red water lilies, then a forest of fragrant red sāli rice. Next are sweet-tasting vine fruits such as cucumbers, gourds, and pumpkins. Next is a sugarcane grove just half a yojana in width, where the sugarcane stalks are the size of an areca palm's trunk. Next is a banana grove, from which eating two ripe fruits causes one to become fatigued. Then comes a jackfruit grove with fruit the size of a large pot, followed by a rose-apple grove, then a mango grove, and finally a wood-apple grove. In brief, it should not be said that in that lake there is no such thing as edible fruit. At the time of the flowers' blooming, the wind raises up a mass of pollen and places it on the lotus leaves, whereon drops of water fall. Then, being cooked by the sun's heat, it becomes like a thickened milk-curd. This is called lotus-honey, and they bring it and offer it to the Elder. The lotus root is the size of a plow-head; that too, they bring and offer. The lotus stalk is the size of the head of a great drum; in each one of its joints, there is milk the measure of a pādaghaṭaka, which they bring and offer. They mix the lotus seeds with honey-sugar and offer them. They place the sugarcane on a stone slab and press it with their feet. The juice then flows out and fills small hollows, where, being cooked by the sun's heat, it solidifies like a lump of milk-stone, which they bring and offer. As for the ripe jackfruits, bananas, mangoes, and so on, there is nothing to be said.

Kelāsapabbate [V 1.0248] nāgadatto nāma devaputto vasati. Thero kālena kālaṃ tassa vimānadvāraṃ gacchati. So navasappipokkharamadhucuṇṇayuttassa nirudakapāyāsassa pattaṃ pūretvā deti. So kira kassapabuddhakāle vīsativassasahassāni sugandhasappinā khīrasalākaṃ adāsi. Tenassetaṃ bhojanaṃ uppajjati. Evaṃ thero dvādasa vassāni vasitvā attano āyusaṅkhāraṃ olokento parikkhīṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā “kattha parinibbāyissāmī”ti cintetvā – “hatthināgehi maṃ dvādasa vassāni upaṭṭhahantehi dukkaraṃ kataṃ, satthāraṃ anujānāpetvā etesaṃyeva santike parinibbāyissāmī”ti ākāsena bhagavato santikaṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ “sucirasseva yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamī”ti.

On Mount Kelāsa lives a deity named Nāgadatta. The Elder, from time to time, goes to the door of his celestial mansion. He fills a bowl with milk-rice without water, mixed with fresh ghee, lotus honey, and powder, and gives it. It is said that during the time of Kassapa Buddha, for twenty thousand years, he gave ticket-food of milk-rice with fragrant ghee. Because of that, this food arises for him. Thus, the Elder, having dwelt for twelve years, reviewing his life-formation and realizing it was exhausted, thought, "Where shall I attain final Nibbāna?" Considering, "A difficult thing has been done by the great elephants attending upon me for twelve years. Having obtained the Teacher's permission, I shall attain final Nibbāna in their very presence," he went through the air to the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: "After a very long time, he approached where the Blessed One was."

Nāmañcāti kasmā nāmaṃ sāveti? Therañhi keci sañjānanti, keci na sañjānanti. Tattha thero cintesi – “ye maṃ ajānantā ‘ko esa paṇḍarasīso obhaggo gopānasivaṅko mahallako satthārā saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ karotī’ti cittaṃ padūsessanti, te apāyapūrakā bhavissanti. Ye pana maṃ jānantā – ‘dasasahassacakkavāḷe satthā viya paññāto pākaṭo mahāsāvako’ti cittaṃ pasādessanti, te saggūpagā bhavissantī”ti, sattānaṃ apāyamaggaṃ pidahitvā saggamaggaṃ vivaranto nāmaṃ sāveti.

Regarding 'And his name': why does he announce his name? For some recognize the Elder, while others do not. There, the Elder reflected: "Those who do not know me will corrupt their minds, thinking, 'Who is this white-headed, broken-down, hunchbacked old man engaging in conversation with the Teacher?' They will become fillers of the woeful states. But those who know me will gladden their minds, thinking, 'This is the great disciple, renowned and famous throughout the ten-thousandfold world-system, like the Teacher.' They will be bound for heaven." Thus, closing off the path to the woeful states for beings and opening the path to heaven, he announces his name.

Buddhānubuddhoti paṭhamaṃ satthā cattāri saccāni bujjhi, pacchā thero, tasmā buddhānubuddhoti, vuccati. Tibbanikkamoti bāḷhavīriyo. Vivekānanti tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ. Tevijjo, cetopariyāyakovidoti chasu abhiññāsu catasso vadati. Itarā dve kiñcāpi na vuttā, thero pana chaḷabhiññova. Imissā ca gāthāya pariyosāne parisā sannisīdi. Parisāya [M 1.0259] sannisinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā thero satthārā saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “parikkhīṇā me, bhante, āyusaṅkhārā, parinibbāyissāmī”ti, parinibbānakālaṃ anujānāpesi[P 1.0283]. Kattha parinibbāyissasi koṇḍaññāti? Upaṭṭhākehi me, bhante, hatthināgehi dukkaraṃ kataṃ, tesaṃ santiketi. Satthā anujāni.

As for 'awakened after the Buddha': first, the Teacher awakened to the four truths; afterwards, the Elder awakened. Therefore, he is called 'awakened after the Buddha.' As for 'of keen exertion': he was of strong energy. As for 'of seclusions': of the three seclusions. As for 'possessed of the three knowledges, skilled in penetrating the minds of others': among the six higher knowledges, he speaks of only four. Although the other two are not mentioned, the Elder, however, was indeed possessed of the six higher knowledges. And at the end of this verse, the assembly was well-seated. Knowing that the assembly was seated, the Elder, after exchanging a friendly greeting with the Teacher, requested permission for the time of his final Nibbāna, saying: 'Venerable sir, my life-formations are exhausted; I will attain final Nibbāna.' 'Where will you attain final Nibbāna, Koṇḍañña?' 'Venerable sir, a difficult service has been rendered by my attendants, the great elephants; it will be in their presence.' The Teacher gave permission.

Thero dasabalaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā – “pubbaṃ taṃ me, bhante, paṭhamadassanaṃ, idaṃ pacchimadassana”nti paridevante mahājane satthāraṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā, dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhito – “mā [V 1.0249] socittha, mā paridevittha, buddhā vā hontu buddhasāvakā vā, uppannā saṅkhārā abhijjanakā nāma natthī”ti mahājanaṃ ovaditvā passantasseva mahājanassa vehāsaṃ abbhuggamma mandākinitīre otaritvā pokkharaṇiyaṃ nhatvā nivatthanivāsano katuttarāsaṅgo senāsanaṃ saṃsāmetvā phalasamāpattiyā tayo yāme vītināmetvā balavapaccūsasamaye parinibbāyi. Therassa sahaparinibbānā himavati sabbarukkhā pupphehi ca phalehi ca onatavinatā ahesuṃ. Vārikanāgo therassa parinibbutabhāvaṃ ajānanto pātova mukhodakadantakaṭṭhāni upaṭṭhapetvā vattaṃ katvā khādanīyaphalāni āharitvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. So yāva sūriyuggamanā therassa nikkhamanaṃ apassanto “kiṃ nu kho etaṃ? Pubbe ayyo pātova caṅkamati, mukhaṃ dhovati. Ajja pana paṇṇasālatopi na nikkhamatī”ti kuṭidvāraṃ kampetvā olokento theraṃ nisinnakameva disvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā parāmasitvā assāsapassāse pariyesanto tesaṃ appavattibhāvaṃ ñatvā – “parinibbuto thero”ti soṇḍaṃ mukhe pakkhipitvā mahāravaṃ viravi. Sakalahimavanto ekaninnādo ahosi. Aṭṭhanāgasahassāni sannipatitvā theraṃ jeṭṭhakanāgassa kumbhe nisīdāpetvā supupphitarukkhasākhā gahetvā parivāretvā sakalahimavantaṃ anuvicaritvā sakaṭṭhānameva āgatā.

The Elder, having circumambulated the One with Ten Powers, spoke thus: 'Venerable Sir, that former seeing was my first seeing; this is the last seeing.' Then, while the great assembly was lamenting, he paid homage to the Teacher and departed. Standing at the gateway, he admonished the great assembly, saying: 'Do not grieve, do not lament. Whether they be Buddhas or disciples of the Buddha, there are no arisen formations whatsoever that do not break up.' While the great assembly watched, he rose into the sky and descended on the bank of the Mandākinī Lake. After bathing in the lotus pond, having put on his lower robe and arranged his upper robe, and having tidied his lodging, he spent the three watches of the night in the attainment of fruition and attained Parinibbāna at the very break of dawn. Simultaneously with the Elder's attainment of Parinibbāna, all the trees in the Himavanta became bent and bowed down with flowers and fruits. The attendant elephant, unaware that the Elder had attained Parinibbāna, early in the morning prepared water for washing the face and tooth-sticks, performed his duties, brought edible fruits, and stood at the end of the walking path. Not seeing the Elder emerge by sunrise, he wondered: 'What can this be? Previously, the noble one would walk early and wash his face. But today he has not even come out of the leaf-hut.' Shaking the hut door and looking inside, he saw the Elder seated just as he was. He stretched out his trunk, touched him, and searching for his in-breaths and out-breaths, realized their absence and knew: 'The Elder has attained Parinibbāna.' Placing his trunk in his mouth, he let out a great cry. The entire Himavanta became a single resounding echo. Eight thousand elephants gathered, seated the Elder on the head of the chief elephant, and holding branches of fully blossomed trees, they surrounded him. They roamed the entire Himavanta before returning to their own place.

Sakko vissakammaṃ āmantesi – “tāta, amhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātā parinibbuto, sakkāraṃ karissāma, navayojanikaṃ sabbaratanamayaṃ kūṭāgāraṃ māpehī”ti. So tathā katvā theraṃ tattha nipajjāpetvā hatthināgānaṃ adāsi. Te kūṭāgāraṃ ukkhipitvā tiyojanasahassaṃ himavantaṃ punappunaṃ āvijjhiṃsu[M 1.0260]. Tesaṃ hatthato ākāsaṭṭhakā devā gahetvā [P 1.0284] sādhukīḷitaṃ kīḷiṃsu. Tato vassavalāhakā sītavalāhakā uṇhavalāhakā cātumahārājikā tāvatiṃsāti etenupāyena yāva brahmalokā kūṭāgāraṃ agamāsi, puna brahmāno devānanti anupubbena hatthināgānaṃyeva kūṭāgāraṃ adaṃsu. Ekekā devatā caturaṅgulamattaṃ candanaghaṭikaṃ āhari, citako navayojaniko ahosi. Kūṭāgāraṃ citakaṃ āropayiṃsu. Pañca bhikkhusatāni ākāsenāgantvā sabbarattiṃ sajjhāyamakaṃsu. Anuruddhatthero dhammaṃ kathesi, bahūnaṃ devatānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Punadivase aruṇuggamanavelāyameva citakaṃ nibbāpetvā sumanamakuḷavaṇṇānaṃ dhātūnaṃ parisāvanaṃ pūretvā bhagavati nikkhamitvā veḷuvanavihārakoṭṭhakaṃ sampatte āharitvā satthu hatthe ṭhapayiṃsu. Satthā dhātuparisāvanaṃ gahetvā pathaviyā hatthaṃ pasāresi, mahāpathaviṃ bhinditvā rajatabubbuḷasadisaṃ cetiyaṃ [V 1.0250] nikkhami. Satthā sahatthena cetiye dhātuyo nidhesi. Ajjāpi kira taṃ cetiyaṃ dharatiyevāti. Navamaṃ.

Sakka addressed Vissakamma: 'My dear, our eldest brother has attained Parinibbāna. We shall pay him homage. Create a nine-yojana pinnacled casket made of all kinds of precious gems.' Having done so, Vissakamma laid the Elder there and gave it to the elephant kings. They lifted the pinnacled casket and repeatedly dragged it through the three-thousand-yojana Himavanta. The devas dwelling in the sky took it from the hands of the elephants and played a sacred game. Then, the Vassavalāhaka devas, Sītavalāhaka devas, Uṇhavalāhaka devas, Cātumahārājika devas, and Tāvatiṃsa devas—in this manner, the pinnacled casket reached as far as the Brahmā world. Again, the Brahmās gave it to the devas, and thus, in succession, they gave the pinnacled casket back to none other than the elephant kings. Each and every deva brought a piece of sandalwood four finger-breadths in size. The funeral pyre was nine yojanas in extent. They placed the pinnacled casket upon the pyre. Five hundred bhikkhus arrived through the sky and recited throughout the entire night. The Elder Anuruddha taught the Dhamma, and for many devas, there was the realization of the Dhamma. On the next day, at the very time of sunrise, they extinguished the pyre and filled a water-strainer with the relics, which were the color of jasmine buds. When the Blessed One, having gone forth, arrived at the gatehouse of the Veḷuvana monastery, they brought the strainer and placed it in the Teacher’s hands. The Teacher took the relic-strainer and extended his hand toward the earth. The great earth split open, and a cetiya resembling a silver bubble emerged. The Teacher, with his own hand, enshrined the relics in the cetiya. It is said that even to this day, that cetiya indeed still exists. The ninth.

10. Moggallānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta

218. Dasame samannesatīti pariyesati paccavekkhati. Nagassāti pabbatassa. Muninti buddhamuniṃ. Dukkhassa pāragunti dukkhapāraṃ gataṃ. Samannesanti samannesanto. Evaṃ sabbaṅgasampannanti evaṃ sabbaguṇasampannaṃ. Anekākārasampannanti anekehi guṇehi samannāgataṃ. Dasamaṃ.

10. In the tenth sutta: `samannesati` means he searches, he reflects. `Nagassa` means of the mountain, that is, of the Isigili mountain. `Muniṃ` means the Buddha-sage. `Dukkhassa pāraguṃ` means one who has gone to the far shore of suffering. `Samannesanti` means searching. `Evaṃ sabbaṅgasampannaṃ` means thus endowed with all virtues. `Anekākārasampannaṃ` means endowed with numerous qualities. The tenth.

11. Gaggarāsuttavaṇṇanā

11. Commentary on the Gaggarā Sutta

219. Ekādasame tyāssudanti te assudaṃ. Assudanti nipātamattaṃ. Vaṇṇenāti sarīravaṇṇena. Yasasāti parivārena. Vigatamalova bhāṇumāti vigatamalo ādicco viya. Ekādasamaṃ.
