218. In the eleventh: `tyāssudaṃ` is divided as `te assudaṃ`. `Assudaṃ` is merely a particle. `Vaṇṇena` means by bodily complexion. `Yasasā` means by retinue. `Vigatamalova bhāṇumā` means like the sun free from stains. The eleventh.

12. Vaṅgīsasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Sutta

220. Dvādasame [P 1.0285] āyasmāti piyavacanaṃ. Vaṅgīsoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. So kira pubbe padumuttarakāle paṭibhānasampannaṃ sāvakaṃ disvā dānaṃ [M 1.0261] datvā patthanaṃ katvā kappasatasahassaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā amhākaṃ bhagavato kāle sakalajambudīpe vādakāmatāya jambusākhaṃ pariharitvā ekena paribbājakena saddhiṃ vādaṃ katvā vāde jayaparājayānubhāvena teneva paribbājakena saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappetvā vasamānāya ekissā paribbājikāya kucchimhi nibbatto vayaṃ āgamma mātito pañcavādasatāni, pitito pañcavādasatānīti vādasahassaṃ uggaṇhitvā vicarati. Ekañca vijjaṃ jānāti, yaṃ vijjaṃ parijappitvā matānaṃ sīsaṃ aṅguliyā paharitvā – “asukaṭṭhāne nibbatto”ti jānāti. So anupubbena gāmanigamādīsu vicaranto pañcahi māṇavakasatehi saddhiṃ sāvatthiṃ anuppatto nagaradvāre sālāya nisīdati.

11. In the twelfth: 'āyasmā' is an affectionate term. 'Vaṅgīsa' is the name of that elder. It is said that in a past life, during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, having seen a disciple endowed with ready wit, he gave alms and made an aspiration. After fulfilling the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons, during the time of our Blessed One, he was born in the womb of a certain female wanderer. She was living with a male wanderer after their cohabitation was established by the power of victory and defeat in a debate they held while wandering across the whole of Jambudīpa carrying a rose-apple branch, desiring a debate. Having come of age, he learned a thousand debating points—five hundred from his mother and five hundred from his father—and wandered about. He also knew a certain science: by reciting a spell and striking the head of a dead person with his finger, he would know, 'He has been reborn in such-and-such a place.' Gradually wandering through villages, towns, and so on, he arrived at Sāvatthī together with five hundred young students and sat down in a hall at the city gate.

Tadā [V 1.0251] ca nagaravāsino purebhattaṃ dānaṃ datvā pacchābhattaṃ suddhuttarāsaṅgā gandhamālādihatthā dhammassavanāya vihāraṃ gacchanti. Māṇavo disvā, “kahaṃ gacchathā”ti? Pucchi. Te “dasabalassa santikaṃ dhammassavanāyā”ti āhaṃsu. Sopi saparivāro tehi saddhiṃ gantvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ bhagavā āha – “vaṅgīsa, bhaddakaṃ kira sippaṃ jānāsī”ti. “Bho gotama, ahaṃ bahusippaṃ jānāmi. Tumhe kataraṃ sandhāya vadathā”ti? Chavadūsakasippanti. Āma, bho gotamāti. Athassa bhagavā attano ānubhāvena niraye nibbattassa sīsaṃ dassetvā, “vaṅgīsa, ayaṃ kahaṃ nibbatto”ti pucchi. So mantaṃ jappitvā aṅguliyā paharitvā “niraye”ti āha. “Sādhu, vaṅgīsa, sukathita”nti devaloke nibbattassa sīsaṃ dassesi. Tampi so tatheva byākāsi. Athassa khīṇāsavassa sīsaṃ dassesi. So punappunaṃ mantaṃ parivattetvāpi aṅguliyā paharitvāpi nibbattaṭṭhānaṃ na [P 1.0286] passati.

At that time, the city dwellers, having given alms in the morning, would go to the monastery in the afternoon, clad in clean upper robes and carrying perfumes and garlands in their hands, to listen to the Dhamma. Seeing them, the young man asked, “Where are you going?” They replied, “To the presence of the One with Ten Powers to hear the Dhamma.” He too, along with his retinue, went with them, exchanged courtesies, and stood to one side. Then the Blessed One said to him, “Vaṅgīsa, I hear you know a fine craft.” “Venerable Gotama, I know many crafts. To which one do you refer?” “The skull-tapping skill.” “Yes, Venerable Gotama,” he replied. Then the Blessed One, by his own power, showed him the head of one reborn in hell and asked, “Vaṅgīsa, where is this one reborn?” He recited his mantra, tapped it with his finger, and said, “In hell.” “Good, Vaṅgīsa, well spoken,” said the Blessed One, and then showed him the head of one reborn in the heavenly realm. He declared that one also in the same way. Then he showed him the head of one whose cankers were destroyed. Though he repeatedly recited his mantra and tapped it with his finger, he could not discern the place of rebirth.

Atha naṃ bhagavā “kilamasi, vaṅgīsā”ti āha? Āma bho, gotamāti. Punappunaṃ upadhārehīti. Tathā karontopi adisvā, “tumhe, bho gotama, jānāthā”ti āha. Āma, vaṅgīsa, maṃ nissāya cesa gato, ahamassa gatiṃ jānāmīti. Mantena jānāsi, bho gotamāti? Āma, vaṅgīsa, ekena manteneva jānāmīti. Bho gotama, mayhaṃ mantena imaṃ mantaṃ dethāti. Amūliko, vaṅgīsa, mayhaṃ mantoti. Detha, bho gotamāti. Na [M 1.0262] sakkā mayhaṃ santike apabbajitassa dātunti. So antevāsike āmantesi – “tātā samaṇo gotamo atirekasippaṃ jānāti, ahaṃ imassa santike pabbajitvā sippaṃ gaṇhāmi, tato sakalajambudīpe amhehi bahutaraṃ jānanto nāma na bhavissati. Tumhe yāva ahaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva anukkaṇṭhitvā vicarathā”ti te uyyojetvā “pabbājetha ma”nti āha. Satthā nigrodhakappassa paṭipādesi. Thero taṃ attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā pabbājesi. So pabbajitvā satthu santikaṃ āgamma vanditvā ṭhito “sippaṃ dethā”ti yāci. Vaṅgīsa, tumhe sippaṃ gaṇhantā aloṇabhojanathaṇḍilaseyyādīhi parikammaṃ katvā gaṇhatha, imassāpi sippassa parikammaṃ atthi, taṃ tāva karohīti. Sādhu, bhanteti. Athassa satthā dvattiṃsākārakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. So taṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasikaronto vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Then the Blessed One asked him, “Are you weary, Vaṅgīsa?” “Yes, Venerable Gotama.” “Keep applying your mind again and again.” Even as he did so, he could not see and said, “Do you know, Venerable Gotama?” “Yes, Vaṅgīsa, he has departed supported by me; I know his destination.” “Do you know by a mantra, Venerable Gotama?” “Yes, Vaṅgīsa, I know by a single mantra.” “Venerable Gotama, give me this mantra.” “Vaṅgīsa, my mantra is without a fee.” “Give it, Venerable Gotama.” “It cannot be given to one who has not gone forth in my presence.” He then addressed his pupils: “My good men, the ascetic Gotama knows an extraordinary skill. I will go forth in his presence and learn the skill. Then there will be no one in all of Jambudīpa who knows more than we do. Until I return, you should wander without being discontented.” Having dismissed them, he said, “Please give me the going forth.” The Teacher entrusted him to Nigrodhakappa. The Elder took him to his own dwelling place and gave him the going forth. After going forth, he approached the Teacher, paid homage, stood, and requested, “Give me the skill.” “Vaṅgīsa, when people learn a skill, they learn it after making preparations such as eating saltless food and sleeping on the bare ground. This skill of mine also has a preparation. First, undertake that.” “Very well, Venerable Sir.” Then the Teacher taught him the meditation subject on the thirty-two parts of the body. Applying his mind to it forwards and backwards, he developed insight and in due course attained Arahantship.

Vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedīti evaṃ arahattaṃ patvā vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedento. Kāveyyamattāti kāveyyena [V 1.0252] kabbakaraṇena mattā. Khandhāyatanadhātuyoti [P 1.0287] imāni khandhādīni pakāsento dhammaṃ desesi. Ye niyāmagataddasāti ye niyāmagatā ceva niyāmadassāti ca. Svāgatanti suāgamanaṃ. Iddhipattomhīti iminā iddhividhañāṇaṃ gahitaṃ. Cetopariyāyakovidoti iminā cetopariyañāṇaṃ. Dibbasotaṃ pana avuttampi gahitameva hoti. Evaṃ cha abhiññāpatto eso mahāsāvakoti veditabbo. Dvādasamaṃ.

He experiences the bliss of liberation—thus, having attained Arahantship, he experiences the bliss of liberation. Measured by poetry—measured by the composition of poetry. Aggregates, sense bases, and elements—thus, while explaining these aggregates and so forth, he taught the Dhamma. Those who have entered the fixed course and see it—meaning, those who have entered the fixed course and also see the fixed course. Welcome—a good arrival. “I have attained psychic power”—by this, the knowledge of the kinds of psychic power is taken. Skilled in knowledge of the minds of others—by this, knowledge of encompassing the minds of others is taken. The divine ear, though not mentioned, is also taken as included. Thus, this great disciple should be known as one who has attained the six super-knowledges. Twelfth.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary to the Connected Discourses,

Vaṅgīsasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

the Commentary on the Vaṅgīsa Saṃyutta is concluded.

9. Vanasaṃyuttaṃ

9. The Forest Connected Discourses

1. Vivekasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Discourse on Solitude

221. Vanasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0253][M 1.0263] paṭhame [P 1.0288] kosalesu viharatīti satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā tassa janapadassa sulabhabhikkhatāya tattha gantvā viharati. Saṃvejetukāmāti vivekaṃ paṭipajjāpetukāmā. Vivekakāmoti tayo viveke patthayanto. Niccharatī bahiddhāti bāhiresu puthuttārammaṇesu carati. Jano janasminti tvaṃ jano aññasmiṃ jane chandarāgaṃ vinayassu. Pajahāsīti pajaha. Bhavāsīti bhava. Sataṃ taṃ sārayāmaseti satimantaṃ paṇḍitaṃ taṃ mayampi sārayāma, sataṃ vā dhammaṃ mayaṃ taṃ sārayāmāti attho. Pātālarajoti appatiṭṭhaṭṭhena pātālasaṅkhāto kilesarajo. Mā taṃ kāmarajoti ayaṃ kāmarāgarajo taṃ mā avahari, apāyameva mā netūti attho. Paṃsukunthitoti paṃsumakkhito. Vidhunanti vidhunanto. Sitaṃ rajanti sarīralaggaṃ rajaṃ. Saṃvegamāpādīti devatāpi nāma maṃ evaṃ sāretīti vivekamāpanno, uttamavīriyaṃ vā paggayha paramavivekaṃ maggameva paṭipannoti. Paṭhamaṃ.

221. In the first (sutta) of the Forest Connected Discourses, 'he dwells among the Kosalans' means: having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher, he goes there and dwells in that country because of the easy availability of alms. Desiring to cause spiritual urgency—desiring to make one enter upon seclusion. Longing for seclusion—aspiring for the three kinds of seclusion. He strays outwardly—he wanders among external, diverse objects. Person to person—you, a person, should remove desire and lust for another person. Abandon—abandon. Become—become. We remind you, the mindful one—we remind you, the wise and mindful one; or, we remind you of the Dhamma of the good—this is the meaning. The dust of the abyss—the dust of defilements, called the abyss because it is unestablished. May this sensual dust not—this dust of sensual lust, may it not carry you away; may it not lead you to the plane of misery—this is the meaning. Covered in dust—smeared with dust. Shaking—shaking off. Clinging dust—the dust clinging to the body. He attained spiritual urgency—'Even a devatā reminds me thus,' so he attained seclusion; or, having exerted supreme energy, he entered upon the path itself, the ultimate seclusion. The first.

2. Upaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the Upaṭṭhānasutta

222. Dutiye supatīti ayaṃ kira khīṇāsavo, so dūre bhikkhācāragāmaṃ gantvā āgato paṇṇasālāya pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā avidūre jātassaraṃ otaritvā gattāni utuṃ gāhāpetvā divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā tattha nīcamañcakaṃ paññāpetvā [P 1.0289] niddaṃ anokkamantova nipanno. Khīṇāsavassāpi hi kāyadaratho hotiyevāti tassa vinodanatthaṃ, taṃ sandhāya supatīti vuttaṃ. Ajjhabhāsīti “ayaṃ bhikkhu satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā divā supati, divāsoppañca nāmetaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ atthaṃ nāsetī”ti maññamānā “codessāmi na”nti cintetvā abhāsi.

222. In the second sutta, as for 'he sleeps': This monk, it is said, is one whose cankers are destroyed. Having gone to a distant village for alms-round and returned, he put away his bowl and robe in the leaf-hut, descended into the Jātassara lake which was not far away, and had his limbs take on the cool temperature. Having swept the day-resting place, he prepared a low couch there and lay down without entering into sleep. Indeed, even for one whose cankers are destroyed, there is bodily fatigue; he was lying down for the purpose of dispelling it. With reference to that, it was said, 'he sleeps.' As for 'she addressed him': Thinking, 'This monk, having taken a meditation subject in the Teacher's presence, sleeps by day. And this, which is called sleeping by day, destroys the increased benefit pertaining to the present life and the future life,' and thinking, 'I will admonish him,' she spoke.

Āturassāti [V 1.0254] jarāturo rogāturo kilesāturoti tayo āturā, tesu kilesāturaṃ sandhāyevamāha. Sallaviddhassāti savisena [M 1.0264] sattisallena viya avijjāvisaviṭṭhena taṇhāsallena hadaye viddhassa. Ruppatoti ghaṭṭiyamānassa.

As for 'of the afflicted': there are three kinds of afflicted ones: one afflicted by old age, one afflicted by disease, and one afflicted by defilements. Among these, with reference to the one afflicted by defilements, He spoke thus. As for 'of one pierced by a dart': like one pierced by a poisoned spear-dart, this means of one pierced in the heart by the dart of craving which is smeared with the poison of ignorance. As for 'being tormented': of one being afflicted.

Idānissa kāmesu ādīnavaṃ kathayantī aniccātiādimāha. Tattha asitanti taṇhādiṭṭhinissayena anissitaṃ. Kasmā pabbajitaṃ tapeti evarūpaṃ khīṇāsavaṃ divāsoppaṃ na tapati, tādisaṃ pana kasmā na tapessatīti? Vadati. Therasseva vā etaṃ vacanaṃ, tasmā ayamettha attho – baddhesu muttaṃ asitaṃ mādisaṃ khīṇāsavapabbajitaṃ kasmā divāsoppaṃ tape, na tapessatīti? Sesagāthāsupi eseva nayo. Devatāya hi vacanapakkhe – “evarūpaṃ khīṇāsavapabbajitaṃ divāsoppaṃ na tapati, tādisaṃ pana kasmā na tapessati? Tapessatiyevā”ti attho. Therassa vacanapakkhe – “evarūpaṃ mādisaṃ khīṇāsavapabbajitaṃ kasmā divāsoppaṃ tape? Na tapatiyevā”ti attho. Ayaṃ panettha anuttānapadavaṇṇanā. Vinayāti vinayena. Samatikkamāti vaṭṭamūlikāya avijjāya samatikkamena. Taṃ ñāṇanti taṃ catusaccañāṇaṃ. Paramodānanti paramaparisuddhaṃ. Pabbajitanti evarūpena ñāṇena samannāgataṃ pabbajitaṃ. Vijjāyāti catutthamaggavijjāya. Āraddhavīriyanti paggahitavīriyaṃ paripuṇṇavīriyaṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

Now, speaking to that forest deity of the danger in sensual pleasures, the Elder uttered the words beginning with 'impermanent.' Therein, 'asitaṃ' means not dependent, by way of craving and wrong view as a support. Regarding 'Kasmā pabbajitaṃ tape', it means: 'Day-sleep does not torment such a taint-free one. Why would it torment such a one whose taints are destroyed? It certainly would not torment.' Thus he speaks. Or, this statement is the Elder's own utterance. Therefore, this is the meaning here: 'Why should day-sleep torment one like me, a taint-free renunciant who is liberated from the bonds of sensual pleasures and is not dependent? It will certainly not torment.' In the remaining verses, this is the same method. Indeed, from the perspective of the deity's statement, the meaning is: 'Day-sleep does not torment such a taint-free renunciant, but why would it not torment one such as you? It will indeed torment!' From the perspective of the Elder's statement, the meaning is: 'Why should day-sleep torment such a taint-free renunciant like me? It indeed does not torment!' Now, this is the explanation of the terms with non-obvious meanings herein. 'Vinayā' means by the removal of sensual desire. 'Samatikkamaṃ' means by transcending ignorance, which is the root of the cycle of existence. 'Taṃ ñāṇaṃ' means that knowledge of the Four Truths. 'Paramodānaṃ' means supremely pure. 'Pabbajitaṃ' means one who has gone forth endowed with such knowledge. 'Vijjāya' means by the knowledge of the fourth path. 'Āraddhavīriyaṃ' means one whose energy is exerted, whose energy is complete. The second sutta.

3. Kassapagottasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Kassapagotta Sutta

223. Tatiye chetanti ekaṃ migaluddakaṃ. Ovadatīti so kira migaluddako pātova bhuñjitvā “mige vadhissāmī”ti araññaṃ paviṭṭho ekaṃ rohitamigaṃ disvā “sattiyā naṃ paharissāmī”ti [P 1.0290] anubandhamāno therassa paṭhamasutte vuttanayeneva divāvihāraṃ nisinnassa avidūrena pakkamati. Atha naṃ thero – “upāsaka, pāṇātipāto nāmesa apāyasaṃvattaniko appāyukasaṃvattaniko, sakkā aññenapi kasivaṇijjādikammena dārabharaṇaṃ kātuṃ, mā evarūpaṃ kakkhaḷakammaṃ karohī”ti āha. Sopi “mahāpaṃsukūlikatthero kathetī”ti gāravena ṭhatvā sotuṃ āraddho. Athassa sotukāmataṃ janessāmīti thero aṅguṭṭhakaṃ jālāpesi. So akkhīhipi passati, kaṇṇehipi suṇāti, cittaṃ panassa “asukaṭṭhānaṃ [M 1.0265] migo gato bhavissati, asukatitthaṃ otiṇṇo, tattha naṃ gantvā ghātetvā yāvadicchakaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditvā sesaṃ kājenādāya [V 1.0255] gantvā puttake tosessāmī”ti evaṃ migasseva anupadaṃ dhāvati. Evaṃ vikkhittacittassa dhammaṃ desentaṃ theraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “ovadatī”ti. Ajjhabhāsīti “ayaṃ thero adāruṃ tacchanto viya akhette vappanto viya attanopi kammaṃ nāseti, etassāpi codessāmi na”nti abhāsi.

3. In the third sutta, 'chetaṃ' means a certain deer hunter. Regarding 'ovadati': It is said that this deer hunter, having eaten early in the morning and thinking, 'I will kill deer,' entered the forest. Seeing a red deer, he pursued it, thinking, 'I will strike it with a spear.' Just as described in the first sutta, the deer ran past, not far from where the elder was seated for his day's abiding. Then the elder said to him, 'Lay follower, the killing of living beings is conducive to the plane of misery and to a short life. It is possible to support a family through other means, such as farming or trade. Do not engage in such a harsh deed.' Out of respect, thinking, 'The great Paṃsukūlika elder is speaking,' he stood and began to listen. Then, wishing to make him eager to listen, the elder made his thumb blaze. The hunter saw with his eyes and heard with his ears, but his mind was running after the deer's tracks, thinking, 'The deer must have gone to such-and-such a place, crossed at such-and-such a ford. I will go there, kill it, eat as much meat as I want, take the rest on a carrying pole, and go and satisfy my children.' With reference to the elder teaching the Dhamma to one with such a distracted mind, it is said, 'ovadati.' Regarding 'ajjhabhāsi': The devatā spoke, thinking, 'This elder, like one carving non-wood or sowing in a non-field, destroys his own effort and this hunter's too. I will admonish him.'

Appapaññanti nippaññaṃ. Acetasanti kāraṇajānanasamatthena cittena rahitaṃ. Mandovāti andhabālo viya. Suṇātīti tava dhammakathaṃ suṇāti. Na vijānātīti atthamassa na jānāti. Āloketīti tava puthujjanikaiddhiyā jalantaṃ aṅguṭṭhakaṃ āloketi. Na passatīti ettha “neva telaṃ na vaṭṭi na dīpakapallikā, therassa pana ānubhāvenāyaṃ jalatī”ti imaṃ kāraṇaṃ na passati. Dasa pajjoteti dasasu aṅgulīsu dasa padīpe. Rūpānīti kāraṇarūpāni. Cakkhūti paññācakkhu. Saṃvegamāpādīti kiṃ me imināti? Vīriyaṃ paggayha paramavivekaṃ arahattamaggaṃ paṭipajji. Tatiyaṃ.

223. 'Appapaññanti' means without wisdom. 'Acetasanti' means devoid of a mind capable of knowing the cause, that is, a mind associated with the knowledge that kamma is one's own property. 'Mandovāti' is like a blind fool. 'Suṇātīti' means he merely hears your Dhamma talk. 'Na vijānātīti' means he does not understand its meaning. 'Āloketīti' means he looks at your glowing thumb, [glowing] by the psychic power of an ordinary person. 'Na passatīti' means he does not see this reason: 'Here, there is neither oil, nor wick, nor lamp vessel; rather, this burns by the elder’s power.' 'Dasa pajjoteti' refers to ten lamps on ten fingers. 'Rūpānīti' means causal forms. 'Cakkhūti' means the eye of wisdom. 'Saṃvegamāpādīti' means, 'What benefit is there for me from this hunter?' He exerted energy and attained the supreme solitude, the path to arahantship. Third.

4. Sambahulasuttavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Sambahula Sutta

224. Catutthe sambahulāti bahū suttantikā ābhidhammikā vinayadharā ca. Viharantīti satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā viharanti. Pakkamiṃsūti te kira tasmiṃ janapade aññataraṃ gāmaṃ upasaṅkamante disvā manussā pasannacittā [P 1.0291] āsanasālāya kojavattharaṇādīni paññāpetvā yāgukhajjakāni datvā upanisīdiṃsu. Mahāthero ekaṃ dhammakathikaṃ “dhammaṃ kathehī”ti āha. So cittaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathesi. Manussā pasīditvā bhojanavelāyaṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ adaṃsu. Mahāthero manuññaṃ bhattānumodanamakāsi. Manussā bhiyyosomattāya pasannā “idheva, bhante, temāsaṃ vasathā”ti paṭiññaṃ kāretvā gamanāgamanasampanne ṭhāne senāsanāni kāretvā catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Mahāthero vassūpanāyikadivase bhikkhū ovadi – “āvuso, tumhehi garukassa satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahitaṃ, buddhapātubhāvo nāma dullabho. Māsassa aṭṭha divase dhammassavanaṃ katvā gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya appamattā viharathā”ti. Te tato paṭṭhāya yuñjanti ghaṭenti. Kadāci sabbarattikaṃ dhammassavanaṃ [M 1.0266] karonti, kadāci pañhaṃ vissajjenti, kadāci padhānaṃ karonti. Tesaṃ dhammassavanadivase dhammaṃ kathentānaṃyeva aruṇo uggacchati. Pañhāvissajjanadivase [V 1.0256] byatto bhikkhu pañhaṃ pucchati, paṇḍito vissajjetīti pucchanavissajjanaṃ karontānaṃyeva. Padhānadivase sūriyatthaṅgamane gaṇḍiṃ paharitvāva caṅkamaṃ otaritvā padhānaṃ karontānaṃyeva. Te evaṃ vassaṃ vassitvā pavāretvā pakkamiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Paridevamānāti “idāni tathārūpaṃ madhuraṃ dhammassavanaṃ pañhākathanaṃ kuto labhissāmī”tiādīni vatvā rodamānā.

224. In the fourth, 'sambahulā' means many who are experts in the discourses, the Abhidhamma, and the Vinaya. 'Viharantī' means they dwelt near the Teacher after receiving meditation subjects. 'Pakkamiṃsu'—it is said that when those monks were approaching a certain village in that country, people with devout minds saw them, prepared seats with coverings such as felt rugs in a hall, offered rice gruel and solid food, and sat down nearby. The Great Elder told one Dhamma speaker, “Speak the Dhamma.” He gave a wondrous Dhamma talk. The people, delighted, offered excellent food at mealtime. The Great Elder gave a pleasing meal-blessing. The people, even more devout with joy, requested, “Venerable sirs, please stay here for the three months,” and having secured their promise, they had lodgings prepared in a place convenient for coming and going and attended to them with the four requisites. On the day of entering the rains retreat, the Great Elder advised the monks: “Friends, you have received meditation subjects from the presence of the revered Teacher. The appearance of a Buddha is rare. Having listened to the Dhamma for eight days a month, abandoning association in groups, dwell heedfully.” From then on, they applied themselves and strove. Sometimes they listened to the Dhamma all night, sometimes they answered questions, sometimes they made an effort in meditation. On the days of listening to the Dhamma, dawn broke while they were still speaking the Dhamma. On the days of answering questions, a skilled monk would ask a question, and a wise one would answer—dawn broke while they were still questioning and answering. On the days of making an effort, as soon as the sun set, they struck the gong, descended to the walking path, and made an effort in meditation—dawn broke while they were still making an effort. Thus, they spent the rains retreat, held the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and departed. This was said in reference to them. 'Paridevamānā' means weeping while saying, “Now, where will we find such a sweet listening to the Dhamma and discussion of questions again?” and so on.

Khāyatīti paññāyati upaṭṭhāti. Ko meti kahaṃ ime. Vajjibhūmiyāti vajjiraṭṭhābhimukhā gatā. Magā viyāti yathā magā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pabbatapāde vā vanasaṇḍe vā vicarantā – “idaṃ amhākaṃ mātusantakaṃ pitusantakaṃ paveṇiāgata”nti agahetvā, yattheva nesaṃ gocaraphāsutā ca hoti paripanthābhāvo ca, tattha vicaranti. Evaṃ aniketā agehā bhikkhavopi “ayaṃ, āvuso, amhākaṃ ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santako paveṇiāgato”ti agahetvā yattheva nesaṃ utusappāyaṃ bhojanasappāyaṃ puggalasappāyaṃ senāsanasappāyaṃ dhammassavanasappāyañca sulabhaṃ hoti, tattha viharanti. Catutthaṃ.

“Khāyati” means it appears, it becomes evident, it is established. “Ko me” means “Where are these?”. “Vajjibhūmiyā” means they have gone facing the Vajji country. “Magā viyā”: Just as deer, wandering at the foot of this or that mountain or in this or that forest grove, without taking it as, “This is our mother’s property, our father’s property, come down by lineage,” roam wherever for them there is ease of pasture and an absence of danger. Similarly, homeless monks, without fixed abodes, do not take it as, “This, friends, is the property of our teachers and preceptors, come down by lineage.” Instead, they dwell wherever a suitable climate, suitable food, suitable persons, suitable lodgings, and the suitability of hearing the Dhamma are easy for them to obtain. The Fourth.

5. Ānandasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Ānanda Sutta

225. Pañcame [P 1.0292] ānandoti dhammabhaṇḍāgārikatthero. Ativelanti atikkantaṃ velaṃ. Gihisaññattibahuloti rattiñca divā ca bahukālaṃ gihī saññāpayanto. Bhagavati parinibbute mahākassapatthero theraṃ āha – “āvuso, mayaṃ rājagahe vassaṃ upagantvā dhammaṃ saṅgāyissāma, gaccha tvaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā uparimaggattayatthāya vāyāmaṃ karohī”ti. So bhagavato pattacīvaramādāya kosalaraṭṭhaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ araññāvāse vasitvā punadivase ekaṃ gāmaṃ pāvisi. Manussā theraṃ disvā – “bhante ānanda, tumhe pubbe satthārā saddhiṃ āgacchatha. Ajja ekakāva āgatā. Kahaṃ satthāraṃ ṭhapetvā āgatattha? Idāni kassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vicaratha? Kassa mukhodakaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ detha, pariveṇaṃ sammajjatha, vattapaṭivattaṃ karothā”ti bahuṃ vatvā parideviṃsu. Thero – “mā, āvuso, socittha, mā [M 1.0267] paridevittha, aniccā saṅkhārā”tiādīni vatvā te saññāpetvā bhattakiccāvasāne vasanaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Manussā sāyampi tattha gantvā tatheva paridevanti. Theropi tatheva ovadati. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ajjhabhāsīti [V 1.0257] “ayaṃ thero bhikkhusaṅghassa kathaṃ sutvā ‘samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī’ti araññaṃ pavisitvā idāni gihī saññāpento viharati, satthu sāsanaṃ asaṅgahitapuppharāsi viya ṭhitaṃ, dhammasaṅgahaṃ na karoti, codessāmi na”nti cintetvā abhāsi.

225. In the fifth, 'Ānanda' refers to the Elder who was the treasurer of the Dhamma. 'Ativelaṃ' means for a time that has passed, i.e., for too long. 'Gihisaññattibahulo' means spending much time, day and night, instructing householders. After the Blessed One’s parinibbāna, the Elder Mahākassapa said to the Elder: “Friend, we will enter the rains residence in Rājagaha and chant the Dhamma. You go into the forest and strive for the sake of the three higher paths.” Taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, he went to the Kosala country. Dwelling in a forest hermitage, the next day he entered a village. Seeing the Elder, the people said: “Venerable Ānanda, you used to come with the Teacher. Today you have come alone. Where have you left the Teacher and come from? Whose bowl and robe are you carrying now? For whom do you give water for washing the face and a tooth-stick, sweep the precinct, and perform the major and minor duties?” Having said much, they lamented. The Elder said: “Do not grieve, friends, do not lament. Formations are impermanent,” and so on. Having instructed them, after the meal was finished, he went to his dwelling place. In the evening, the people went there and lamented in the same way. The Elder likewise advised them. This was said with reference to that. 'Ajjhabhāsi' means: Having thought, “This Elder, having heard the talk of the community of monks, entered the forest thinking, ‘I will practice the recluse’s duty.’ But now he dwells instructing householders. The Teacher’s Dispensation stands like a heap of unstrung flowers. He does not make a collection of the Dhamma. I will reprove him,” he spoke.

Pasakkiyāti pavisitvā. Hadayasmiṃ opiyāti kiccato ca ārammaṇato ca hadayamhi pakkhipitvā. “Nibbānaṃ pāpuṇissāmī”ti vīriyaṃ karonto nibbānaṃ kiccato hadayamhi opeti nāma, nibbānārammaṇaṃ pana samāpattiṃ appetvā nisīdanto ārammaṇato. Tadubhayampi sandhāyesā bhāsati. Jhāyāti dvīhi jhānehi jhāyiko bhava. Biḷibiḷikāti ayaṃ gihīhi saddhiṃ biḷibiḷikathā. Pañcamaṃ.

“Pasakkiya” means having entered. “Hadayasmiṃ opiya” means having placed it in the heart, both in terms of function and in terms of object. One who makes an effort, thinking, “I will attain Nibbāna,” is said to place Nibbāna in the heart in terms of function; but one who sits having entered into an attainment that has Nibbāna as its object does so in terms of the object. This deity speaks with reference to both. “Jhāya” means: become one who practices jhāna with the two jhānas. “Biḷibiḷikā” means this entangling talk with householders. Fifth.

6. Anuruddhasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Anuruddha Sutta

226. Chaṭṭhe [P 1.0293] purāṇadutiyikāti anantare attabhāve aggamahesī. Sobhasīti pubbepi sobhasi, idānipi sobhasi. Duggatāti na gatiduggatiyā duggatā. Tā hi sugatiyaṃ ṭhitā sampattiṃ anubhavanti, paṭipattiduggatiyā pana duggatā. Tato cutā hi tā nirayepi upapajjantīti duggatā. Patiṭṭhitāti sakkāyasmiṃ hi patiṭṭhahanto aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi patiṭṭhāti – ratto rāgavasena patiṭṭhāti, duṭṭho dosavasena… mūḷho mohavasena… vinibaddho mānavasena… parāmaṭṭho diṭṭhivasena… thāmagato anusayavasena… aniṭṭhaṅgato vicikicchāvasena… vikkhepagato uddhaccavasena patiṭṭhāti. Tāpi evaṃ patiṭṭhitāva. Naradevānanti devanarānaṃ.

226. In the sixth, 'the former consort' means the chief queen in the immediately preceding existence. 'You are radiant' means: you were radiant formerly, and you are radiant now. 'Unfortunate': not unfortunate because of an unfortunate destination. For they, being established in a good destination, experience prosperity, but they are unfortunate because of unfortunate practice. For having passed away from there, they are reborn in hell; thus, they are unfortunate. 'Established': for one establishing oneself in self-identity view is established for eight reasons: one who is impassioned is established by the power of lust; one who is corrupt, by the power of hatred; one who is deluded, by the power of delusion; one who is bound, by the power of conceit; one who misapprehends, by the power of views; one who is strong, by the power of underlying tendencies; one who is indecisive, by the power of doubt; one who is scattered, by the power of restlessness. They too are thus established. 'Of gods and men' means of devas and humans.

Natthi dānīti sā kira devadhītā there balavasinehā ahosi, paṭigantuṃ nāsakkhi. Kālena āgantvā pariveṇaṃ sammajjati, mukhodakaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ upaṭṭhapeti. Thero anāvajjanena paribhuñjati. Ekasmiṃ divase therassa jiṇṇacīvarassa coḷakabhikkhaṃ carato saṅkārakūṭe dibbadussaṃ ṭhapetvā pakkami. Thero taṃ disvā ukkhipitvā, olokento dussantaṃ [M 1.0268] disvā “dussameta”nti ñatvā, “alaṃ ettāvatā”ti aggahesi. Tenevassa cīvaraṃ niṭṭhāsi. Atha dve aggasāvakā anuruddhatthero cāti tayo janā cīvaraṃ kariṃsu. Satthā sūciṃ yojetvā [V 1.0258] adāsi. Niṭṭhitacīvarassa piṇḍāya carato devatā piṇḍapātaṃ samādapeti. Sā kālena ekikā, kālena attadutiyā therassa santikaṃ āgacchati. Tadā pana attatatiyā āgantvā divāṭṭhāne theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā – “mayaṃ manāpakāyikā nāma manasā icchiticchitarūpaṃ māpemā”ti āha. Thero – “etā evaṃ vadanti, vīmaṃsissāmi, sabbā nīlakā hontū”ti cintesi. Tā therassa manaṃ ñatvā sabbāva nīlavaṇṇā ahesuṃ, evaṃ pītalohitaodātavaṇṇāti. Tato cintayiṃsu – “thero amhākaṃ dassanaṃ assādetī”ti tā samajjaṃ kātuṃ āraddhā, ekāpi gāyi, ekāpi nacci, ekāpi accharaṃ pahari. Thero indriyāni okkhipi. Tato – “na amhākaṃ dassanaṃ thero assādetī”ti ñatvā sinehaṃ vā santhavaṃ vā alabhamānā nibbinditvā gantumāraddhā. Thero tāsaṃ gamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā – “mā [P 1.0294] punappunaṃ āgacchiṃsū”ti arahattaṃ byākaronto imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha vikkhīṇoti khīṇo. Jātisaṃsāroti tattha tattha jātisaṅkhāto saṃsāro. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Now there is none”: It is said that the divine daughter had strong affection for the Elder and was unable to go back. From time to time, she would come, sweep the monastic precinct, and set out water for washing the face, a tooth-stick, drinking water, and water for use. The Elder would partake of them without paying attention. One day, as the Elder, who had a worn-out robe, was searching for rag-cloth, she placed a celestial cloth on a rubbish heap and departed. The Elder saw it and picked it up. While examining it, he saw the edge of the cloth and, recognizing it as a cloth, he took it, thinking, “This much is sufficient.” With that very cloth, his set of three robes was completed. Then the two chief disciples and the Elder Anuruddha, three persons in all, made the robe. The Teacher threaded a needle and gave it to them. When his robe was finished and he was going for alms, the deity ensured that he received alms-food. Sometimes she came to the Elder’s presence alone, and sometimes with one companion. On this occasion, however, she came with two companions, approached the Elder at his day-dwelling, and said: “Venerable sir, we are called the Manāpakāyikā deities; with our minds, we can create any form whatsoever that we desire.” The Elder thought, “They say this; I will test them. Let them all be blue.” Knowing the Elder’s thought, they all became blue-colored, and likewise yellow, red, and white. Then they thought, “The Elder delights in the sight of us,” and they began to put on a performance: one sang, one danced, and one clapped her hands. The Elder cast down his sense faculties. Then, knowing, “The Elder does not delight in the sight of us,” and not receiving affection or intimacy, they became disenchanted and began to leave. The Elder, knowing their intention to depart, declared his arahantship so that they would not come again and again, and spoke this verse. Therein, as to vikkhīṇo: it means destroyed. As to jātisaṃsāro: it is the round of existence reckoned as birth in this or that state. The Sixth.

7. Nāgadattasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Nāgadatta Sutta

227. Sattame atikālenāti sabbarattiṃ niddāyitvā balavapaccūse koṭisammuñjaniyā thokaṃ sammajjitvā mukhaṃ dhovitvā yāgubhikkhāya pātova pavisati. Atidivāti yāguṃ ādāya āsanasālaṃ gantvā pivitvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne nipanno niddāyitvā – “manussānaṃ bhojanavelāya paṇītaṃ bhikkhaṃ labhissāmī”ti upakaṭṭhe majjhanhike uṭṭhāya dhammakaraṇena udakaṃ gahetvā akkhīni pamajjitvā piṇḍāya caritvā yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā majjhanhike vītivatte paṭikkamati. Divā ca āgantvāti atikāle paviṭṭhena nāma aññehi bhikkhūhi paṭhamataraṃ āgantabbaṃ hoti, tvaṃ pana ativiya divā āgantvā gatāsīti attho. Bhāyāmi nāgadattanti taṃ nāgadattaṃ ahaṃ bhāyāmi. Suppagabbhanti suṭṭhu pagabbhaṃ. Kulesūti khattiyakulādiupaṭṭhākakulesu. Sattamaṃ.

227. In the seventh, 'too early' means that having slept all night, at the time of strong dawn, having swept a little with the tip of a broom and having washed his face, one enters for alms of gruel very early in the morning. 'Too late in the day' means taking the gruel, going to the dining hall, drinking it, lying down in one place to sleep, thinking, 'When it is time for the people's meal, I will get excellent alms-food,' then rising when midday is near, taking water with a water strainer, rubbing the eyes, going for alms, eating as much as desired, and departing when midday has passed. 'And coming back late in the day' means that one who enters too early should return earlier than other monks, but you have come and gone excessively late in the day—this is the meaning. 'I fear Nāgadatta' means 'I am afraid of that Nāgadatta.' 'Very insolent' means 'thoroughly insolent.' 'Among families' means among the supporting families, such as those of the Khattiya clan. The Seventh.

8. Kulagharaṇīsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Exposition of the Discourse on the Lady of the House

228. Aṭṭhame [M 1.0269] ajjhogāḷhappattoti ogāhappatto. So kira satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā [V 1.0259] taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā dutiyadivase gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi pāsādikehi abhikkantādīhi. Aññataraṃ kulaṃ tassa iriyāpathe pasīditvā pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā piṇḍapātaṃ adāsi. Bhattānumodanaṃ puna sutvā atirekataraṃ pasīditvā, “bhante, niccakālaṃ idheva bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti nimantesi. Thero adhivāsetvā tesaṃ āhāraṃ paribhuñjamāno vīriyaṃ paggayha ghaṭento arahattaṃ patvā cintesi – “bahūpakāraṃ me etaṃ kulaṃ, aññattha gantvā kiṃ karissāmī”ti? Phalasamāpattisukhaṃ anubhavanto tattheva vasi. Ajjhabhāsīti sā kira therassa khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ ajānantī [P 1.0295] cintesi – “ayaṃ thero neva aññaṃ gāmaṃ gacchati, na aññaṃ gharaṃ, na rukkhamūlaāsanasālādīsu nisīdati, niccakālaṃ gharaṃ pavisitvāva nisīdati, ubhopete ogādhappattā paṭigādhappattā, kadāci esa imaṃ kulaṃ dūseyya, codessāmi na”nti. Tasmā abhāsi.

228. In the eighth, 'one who has plunged in' means 'one who has reached heartfelt intimacy.' It is said that he, after receiving a meditation subject from the Teacher, entered that grove and on the second day went to the village for alms, appearing pleasing with his deportment, such as his going forward. A certain family, pleased with his deportment, paid homage with the fivefold prostration and offered him almsfood. Hearing the blessing after the meal, they became exceedingly pleased and invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please always receive alms right here.' The elder consented and, while partaking of their food, exerted his energy and, striving, attained arahantship. He reflected, 'This family has been of great help to me; what would I gain by going elsewhere?' Enjoying the bliss of fruition attainment, he stayed right there. 'She addressed him' means that a certain deity, it is said, unaware of the elder's state as one whose taints were destroyed, thought, 'This elder neither goes to another village nor another house, nor does he sit at the foot of trees, in rest houses, or the like; he always enters the house and sits there. Both of them have become intimate and are mutually attached. What if he were to corrupt the lady of this house someday? I will reproach him!' Therefore, she spoke.

Saṇṭhāneti nagaradvārassa āsanne manussānaṃ bhaṇḍakaṃ otāretvā vissamanaṭṭhāne. Saṅgammāti samāgantvā. Mantentīti kathenti. Mañca tañcāti mañca kathenti tañca kathenti. Kimantaranti kiṃ kāraṇaṃ? Bahū hi saddā paccūhāti bahukā ete lokasmiṃ paṭilomasaddā. Na tenāti tena kāraṇena, tena vā tapassinā na maṅku hotabbaṃ. Na hi tenāti na hi tena parehi vuttavacanena satto kilissati, attanā katena pana pāpakammeneva kilissatīti dasseti. Vātamigo yathāti yathā vane vātamigo vāteritānaṃ paṇṇādīnaṃ saddena paritassati, evaṃ yo saddaparittāsī hotīti attho. Nāssa sampajjate vatanti tassa lahucittassa vataṃ na sampajjati. Thero pana khīṇāsavattā sampannavatoti veditabbo. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

'Saṇṭhāne' means at a resting place near the city gate where people unload their goods. 'Saṅgamma' means 'having come together.' 'Mantenti' means 'they speak.' 'Mañca tañca' means 'they speak of me and they speak of that.' 'Kimantaraṃ' means 'what is the cause?' 'Bahū hi saddā paccūhā' means 'these adverse sounds in the world are many.' 'Na tena' means 'not for that reason,' or 'that ascetic should not be dismayed by it.' 'Na hi tena' shows: 'for a being is not defiled by words spoken by others, but is defiled only by evil deeds done by oneself.' 'Like a wind-deer' (vātamigo yathā) means that just as a wind-deer in the forest is terrified by the sound of leaves and so forth stirred by the wind, so too is one who is terrified by sounds—this is the meaning. 'His practice is not accomplished' (nāssa sampajjate vataṃ) means that the practice of that fickle-minded one is not accomplished. But the Elder, being one whose taints are destroyed, should be understood as one whose practice is accomplished. The eighth.

9. Vajjiputtasuttavaṇṇanā

9. Explanation of the Vajjiputta Sutta

229. Navame vajjiputtakoti vajjiraṭṭhe rājaputto chattaṃ pahāya pabbajito. Sabbaratticāroti kattikanakkhattaṃ ghosetvā sakalanagaraṃ dhajapaṭākādīhi [M 1.0270] paṭimaṇḍetvā pavattito sabbaratticāro. Idañhi nakkhattaṃ yāva cātumahārājikehi ekābaddhaṃ hoti. Tūriyatāḷitavāditanigghosasaddanti bheriāditūriyānaṃ tāḷitānaṃ vīṇādīnañca vāditānaṃ nigghosasaddaṃ. Abhāsīti vesāliyaṃ kira satta rājasahassāni sattasatāni satta ca rājāno, tattakāva tesaṃ uparājasenāpatiādayo[V 1.0260]. Tesu alaṅkatapaṭiyattesu nakkhattakīḷanatthāya vīthiṃ otiṇṇesu saṭṭhihatthe mahācaṅkame caṅkamamāno nabhassa majjhe ṭhitaṃ candaṃ disvā caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ phalakaṃ nissāya ṭhito abhāsi. Apaviddhaṃva [P 1.0296] vanasmiṃ dārukanti vatthaveṭhanālaṅkārarahitattā vane chaḍḍitadārukaṃ viya jātaṃ. Pāpiyoti lāmakataro amhehi añño koci atthi. Pihayantīti thero āraññiko paṃsukūliko piṇḍapātiko sapadānacāriko appiccho santuṭṭhoti bahū tuyhaṃ patthayantīti attho. Saggagāminanti saggaṃ gacchantānaṃ gatānampi. Navamaṃ.

229. In the ninth, 'Vajjiputta' refers to a prince from the Vajji country who, abandoning his royal umbrella, went forth into homelessness. 'All-night observance' means the all-night observance that was held after announcing the Kattika constellation and decorating the entire city with flags, banners, and so forth. For this constellation is connected all the way up to the realm of the Four Great Kings. 'The sound of drums, beats, and instrumental music' refers to the resounding noise of drums and other instruments being beaten, and lutes and so forth being played. 'He spoke': It is said that in Vesālī there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings, along with just as many viceroys, generals, and others. When they, adorned and prepared, went out into the streets to celebrate the constellation, he saw the moon standing in the middle of the sky while walking on a great promenade sixty cubits in length. Leaning against a railing at the end of the walkway, he spoke. 'Like a discarded piece of wood in the forest': because he was devoid of clothing, ornaments, and adornments, he had become like a log thrown away in the woods. 'More wretched': Is there anyone else more wretched than us? 'They desire': The elder, being a forest-dweller, a rag-robe wearer, an alms-food eater, one who goes on alms round from house to house without omission, of few wishes, and content—many esteem you; this is the meaning. 'Bound for heaven': for those going to heaven and also for those who have gone. The ninth.

10. Sajjhāyasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Explanation of the Sajjhāya Sutta

230. Dasame yaṃ sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Sajjhāyabahuloti nissaraṇapariyattivasena sajjhāyanato bahutaraṃ kālaṃ sajjhāyanto. So kira ācariyassa divāṭṭhānaṃ sammajjitvā ācariyaṃ udikkhanto tiṭṭhati. Atha naṃ āgacchantaṃ disvāva paccuggantvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭiggahetvā paññattāsane nisinnassa tālavaṇṭavātaṃ datvā pānīyaṃ āpucchitvā pāde dhovitvā telaṃ makkhetvā vanditvā ṭhito uddesaṃ gahetvā yāva sūriyatthaṅgamā sajjhāyaṃ karoti. So nhānakoṭṭhake udakaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā aṅgārakapalle aggiṃ karoti. Ācariyassa nhatvā āgatassa pādesu udakaṃ puñchitvā piṭṭhiparikammaṃ katvā vanditvā uddesaṃ gahetvā paṭhamayāme sajjhāyaṃ katvā majjhimayāme sarīraṃ samassāsetvā pacchimayāme uddesaṃ gahetvā yāva aruṇuggamanā sajjhāyaṃ katvā niruddhasaddaṃ khayato sammasati. Tato sesaṃ upādāyarūpaṃ bhūtarūpaṃ nāmarūpanti pañcasu khandhesu vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Appossukkoti uddesaggahaṇe ca sajjhāyakaraṇīye ca nirussukko. Saṅkasāyatīti yassa dāni atthāya ahaṃ sajjhāyaṃ kareyyaṃ, so me attho matthakaṃ [M 1.0271] patto. Kiṃ me idāni sajjhāyenāti phalasamāpattisukhena kālaṃ ativatteti. Ajjhabhāsīti, “kiṃ nu kho assa therassa aphāsukaṃ jātaṃ, udāhussa ācariyassa? Kena nu kho kāraṇena pubbe viya madhurassarena na sajjhāyatī”ti? Āgantvā santike ṭhitā abhāsi.

230. In the tenth, 'yaṃ sudaṃ' is merely a particle. “Devoted to recitation” means one who, by way of the study for the sake of escape, spends a great deal of time reciting. It is said that he would sweep the teacher's daytime resting place and stand watching for the teacher. Then, upon seeing him approach, he would go forth to meet him, receive his bowl and robe, and when the teacher was seated on the prepared seat, he would fan him with a palm-leaf fan, ask about drinking water, wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and pay homage. Then, while standing, he would take the lesson and recite until sunset. He would place water in the bathing chamber and make a fire in the charcoal brazier. When the teacher had bathed and returned, he would wipe the water from his feet, massage his back, pay homage, and take the lesson. Having recited during the first watch and rested his body during the middle watch, he would take the lesson during the last watch and recite until dawn. Having recited, he contemplates the cessation of sound by way of its perishing. After that, he developed insight into the five aggregates—namely, the remaining derived materiality, primary materiality, and name-and-form—and attained Arahantship. “Unconcerned” means unconcerned with taking the lesson and with the duty of reciting. “He hesitates”: thinking, “For what purpose should I recite now? That purpose of mine has reached its consummation. What is the use of recitation to me now?” He passes the time with the bliss of the attainment of fruition. “She addressed”: thinking, “I wonder, has some discomfort arisen for this elder, or for his teacher? For what reason, I wonder, does he not recite with a sweet voice as before?” Having approached and stood nearby, she spoke.

Dhammapadānīti idha sabbampi buddhavacanaṃ adhippetaṃ[P 1.0297]. Nādhīyasīti na sajjhāyasi. Nādiyasīti vā pāṭho, na gaṇhāsīti attho. Pasaṃsanti dhammabhāṇako pasaṃsaṃ labhati, ābhidhammiko [V 1.0261] suttantiko vinayadharotissa pasaṃsitā bhavanti. Virāgenāti ariyamaggena. Aññāyāti jānitvā. Nikkhepananti tassa diṭṭhasutādino vissajjanaṃ santo vadantīti dīpeti, na buddhavacanassa. Ettāvatā “thero buddhavacanaṃ na vissajjāpetī”ti na niccakālaṃ sajjhāyanteneva bhavitabbaṃ, sajjhāyitvā pana – “ettakassāhaṃ atthassa vā dhammassa vā ādhāro bhavituṃ samattho”ti ñatvā vaṭṭadukkhassa antakiriyāya paṭipajjitabbaṃ. Dasamaṃ.

Herein, by 'Dhammapadāni' all the Buddha's speech is intended. 'Nādhīyasī' means 'you do not recite'. Or, there is the reading 'nādiyasī', which means 'you do not take up the text'. 'They praise': a speaker of the Dhamma obtains praise; an expert in the Abhidhamma, an expert in the Suttanta, and an expert in the Vinaya are praised. 'Virāgena' means 'by the noble path'. 'Aññāya' means 'having known'. 'Nikkhepanaṃ' shows that the good speak of abandoning what is seen, heard, etc., not of abandoning the Buddha's speech. By this much, it is shown that the elder does not abandon the Buddha's speech. Therefore, one should not always just be reciting. But having recited, and having known thus, 'I am capable of being a repository for this much of the meaning or of the text,' one should practice for the sake of making an end of the suffering of the round of rebirth. This meaning is shown. The tenth.

11. Akusalavitakkasuttavaṇṇanā

11. Explanation of the Akusalavitakka Sutta

231. Ekādasame akusale vitakketi kāmavitakkādayo tayo mahāvitakke. Ayoniso manasikārāti anupāyamanasikārena. Soti so tvaṃ. Ayoniso paṭinissajjāti etaṃ anupāyamanasikāraṃ vajjehi. Satthāranti imāya gāthāya pāsādikakammaṭṭhānaṃ katheti. Pītisukhamasaṃsayanti ekaṃseneva balavapītiñca sukhañca adhigamissasi. Ekādasamaṃ.

231. In the eleventh, ‘unwholesome thoughts’ (akusale vitakke) refers to the three great wrong thoughts beginning with sensual thought. ‘Unwise attention’ (ayoniso manasikārā) means by attention that is not the means. ‘So’ (so) means ‘that you’. ‘Abandoning the unwise’ (ayoniso paṭinissajjā) means ‘avoid this attention that is not the means’. Regarding ‘the Teacher’ (satthāraṃ): with this verse, the forest-dwelling deity speaks of an inspiring meditation subject. ‘Joy and happiness without a doubt’ (pītisukhamasaṃsayaṃ) means ‘you will certainly attain strong joy associated with access concentration, and happiness’. The eleventh.

12. Majjhanhikasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Explanation of the Majjhanhika Sutta

232. Dvādasame yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ devatāsaṃyutte nandanavagge vuttameva. Dvādasamaṃ.

232. What is to be said concerning the twelfth discourse has already been stated in the Nandana Chapter of the Devatāsaṃyutta. The twelfth.

13. Pākatindriyasuttavaṇṇanā

13. Explanation of the Pākatindriya Sutta

233. Terasamaṃ devaputtasaṃyutte jantudevaputtasutte vitthāritameva. Terasamaṃ.

233. The thirteenth discourse is elaborated in the Jantu Devaputta Sutta of the Devaputta Saṃyutta. The thirteenth.

14. Gandhatthenasuttavaṇṇanā

14. Explanation of the Discourse on the Scent Thief

234. Cuddasame [M 1.0272] ajjhabhāsīti taṃ bhikkhuṃ nāḷe gahetvā padumaṃ siṅghamānaṃ disvāva – “ayaṃ bhikkhu satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā samaṇadhammaṃ kātuṃ araññaṃ [P 1.0298] paviṭṭho gandhārammaṇaṃ upanijjhāyati, svāyaṃ ajja upasiṅghaṃ svepi punadivasepi upasiṅghissati, evamassa sā gandhataṇhā vaḍḍhitvā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaṃ atthaṃ nāsessati, mā mayi passantiyā nassatu, codessāmi na”nti upasaṅkamitvā abhāsi.

234. In the fourteenth discourse, `ajjhabhāsi` means: having seen that monk taking hold of a stalk and sniffing a lotus, she thought: “This monk, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, has entered the forest in order to practice the ascetic’s duty. He is contemplating a scent object. That monk sniffs today; tomorrow and the day after tomorrow also, he will sniff. Thus, that craving for scent in him, having grown, will destroy his welfare in this life and the next. Let it not be destroyed while I am watching. I will admonish him.” Having approached, she spoke.

Ekaṅgametaṃ [V 1.0262] theyyānanti thenitabbānaṃ rūpārammaṇādīnaṃ pañcakoṭṭhāsānaṃ idaṃ ekaṅgaṃ, ekakoṭṭhāsoti attho. Na harāmīti na gahetvā gacchāmi. Ārāti dūre nāḷe gahetvā nāmetvā dūre ṭhito upasiṅghāmīti vadati. Vaṇṇenāti kāraṇena.

‘This is one factor of thefts’ (`ekaṅgametaṃ theyyānaṃ`) means: this is one factor, one category, among the five divisions of things to be stolen, such as form-objects. This is the meaning. `Na harāmi` means: I do not take it and go away. `Ārā` means: from afar. Holding the stalk, bending it, and standing at a distance, he says, “I only sniff.” `Vaṇṇena` means: by reason of.

Yvāyanti yo ayaṃ. Tasmiṃ kira devatāya saddhiṃ kathenteyeva eko tāpaso otaritvā bhisakhananādīni kātuṃ āraddho, taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Ākiṇṇakammantoti evaṃ aparisuddhakammanto. Akhīṇakammantotipi pāṭho, kakkhaḷakammantoti attho. Na vuccatīti gandhacoroti vā pupphacoroti vā kasmā na vuccati.

For the word `yvāyaṃ`, the division `yo ayaṃ` should be made. It is said that while that monk was conversing with the devatā, a certain ascetic, having descended into the water, began to do things such as digging for lotus roots. Referring to that ascetic, the monk spoke thus. `Ākiṇṇakammanto` means: thus, one whose action is impure. There is also the reading `akhīṇakammanto`, meaning: one whose action is rough. `Na vuccati` means: why is he not called a scent-thief or a flower-thief?

Ākiṇṇaluddoti bahupāpo gāḷhapāpo vā, tasmā na vuccati. Dhāticelaṃva makkhitoti yathā dhātiyā nivatthakiliṭṭhavatthaṃ uccārapassāvapaṃsumasikaddamādīhi makkhitaṃ, evamevaṃ rāgadosādīhi makkhito. Arahāmi vattaveti arahāmi vattuṃ. Devatāya codanā kira sugatānusiṭṭhisadisā, na taṃ lāmakā hīnādhimuttikā micchāpaṭipannakapuggalā labhanti. Tasmiṃ pana attabhāve maggaphalānaṃ bhabbarūpā puggalā taṃ labhanti, tasmā evamāha.

‘One who is crowded with evil’ (`ākiṇṇaluddo`) means one of much evil or one of firm evil; therefore, he is not called so. ‘Stained like a nurse’s garment’ (`dhāticelaṃva makkhito`) means: just as a nurse’s worn, soiled garment is smeared by feces, urine, dust, soot, mud, and the like, so too is he smeared by lust, hatred, and so forth. `Arahāmi vattaveti` means: I am worthy to speak. It is said that the admonition of a devatā is like the instruction of the Fortunate One. That instruction, base persons—persons of inferior aspiration who are wrongly practicing—do not obtain. But indeed, in that very existence, persons who are capable of the paths and fruits do obtain it. Therefore, she spoke thus.

Sucigavesinoti sucīni sīlasamādhiñāṇāni gavesantassa. Abbhāmattaṃ vāti valāhakakūṭamattaṃ viya. Jānāsīti suddho ayanti jānāsi. Vajjāsīti vadeyyāsi. Neva taṃ upajīvāmāti devatā kira cintesi – “ayaṃ bhikkhu atthi me hitakāmā devatā, sā maṃ codessati sāressatīti [M 1.0273] pamādampi anuyuñjeyya, nāssa [P 1.0299] vacanaṃ sampaṭicchissāmī”ti. Tasmā evamāha. Tvamevāti tvaṃyeva. Jāneyyāti jāneyyāsi. Yenāti yena kammena sugatiṃ gaccheyyāsi, taṃ kammaṃ tvaṃyeva jāneyyāsīti. Cuddasamaṃ.

‘One who seeks purity’ (`sucigavesino`) means for one who seeks the pure qualities of virtue, concentration, and wisdom. ‘Like a cloud’ (`abbhāmattaṃ vā`) means like the size of a cloud-peak. ‘You know’ (`jānāsi`) means: you know that this one is pure. ‘You would say’ (`vajjāsi`) means ‘you should speak.’ ‘We do not depend on that’ (`neva taṃ upajīvāma`) means the devatā, it is said, thought: “This monk, thinking, ‘There is a devatā who wishes me well; she will admonish and remind me,’ might indulge in negligence. I will not accept his word.” Therefore, she spoke thus. ‘You yourself’ (`tvameva`) means ‘you alone.’ ‘You should know’ (`jāneyya`) means ‘you should know.’ By which (`yena`) means: you yourself should know that action by which you would go to a good destination. The fourteenth.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary to the Saṃyutta Nikāya.

Vanasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Vana Saṃyutta is concluded.

10. Yakkhasaṃyuttaṃ

10. The Yakkha Saṃyutta

1. Indakasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Indaka Sutta

235. Yakkhasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0263][M 1.0274] paṭhame [P 1.0300] indakassāti indakūṭanivāsino yakkhassa. Yakkhato hi kūṭena, kūṭato ca yakkhena nāmaṃ laddhaṃ. Rūpaṃ na jīvanti vadantīti yadi buddhā rūpaṃ jīvanti na vadanti, yadi rūpaṃ satto puggaloti evaṃ na vadantīti attho. Kathaṃ nvayanti kathaṃ nu ayaṃ? Kutassa aṭṭhīyakapiṇḍametīti assa sattassa aṭṭhiyakapiṇḍañca kuto āgacchati? Ettha ca aṭṭhiggahaṇena tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni, yakapiṇḍaggahaṇena nava maṃsapesisatāni gahitāni. Yadi rūpaṃ na jīvo, athassa imāni ca aṭṭhīni imā ca maṃsapesiyo kuto āgacchantīti pucchati. Kathaṃ nvayaṃ sajjati gabbharasminti kena nu kāraṇena ayaṃ satto mātukucchismiṃ sajjati laggati, tiṭṭhatīti? Puggalavādī kiresa yakkho, “ekappahāreneva satto mātukucchismiṃ nibbattatī”ti gahetvā gabbhaseyyakasattassa mātā macchamaṃsādīni khādati, sabbāni ekarattivāsena pacitvā pheṇaṃ viya vilīyanti. Yadi rūpaṃ satto na bhaveyya, evameva vilīyeyyāti laddhiyā evamāha. Athassa bhagavā – “na mātukucchismiṃ ekappahāreneva nibbattati, anupubbena pana vaḍḍhatī”ti dassento paṭhamaṃ kalalaṃ hotītiādimāha. Tattha paṭhamanti paṭhamena paṭisandhiviññāṇena saddhiṃ tissoti vā phussoti vā nāmaṃ natthi, atha kho tīhi jātiuṇṇaṃsūhi katasuttagge saṇṭhitatelabinduppamāṇaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

235. In the first sutta of the Yakkha Saṃyutta, `indakassa` refers to the yakkha dwelling on Indakūṭa. For from the yakkha, the peak obtained its name, and from the peak, the yakkha obtained his name. `Rūpaṃ na jīvanti vadantīti` means: if the Buddhas do not say that form is a living being, that is, if they do not say that form is a being or a person. This is the meaning. `Kathaṃ nvayanti` is to be parsed as `kathaṃ nu ayaṃ`. `Kutassa aṭṭhīyakapiṇḍametīti` means: from where do the bones and the lump of liver come for this being? And here, by the taking up of ‘bones,’ the three hundred bones are taken; by the taking up of ‘lump of liver,’ the nine hundred pieces of flesh are taken. He asks: ‘If form is not a living being, then from where do these bones and these pieces of flesh come for this being?’ `Kathaṃ nvayaṃ sajjati gabbharasminti` means: for what reason does this being become attached, cling, and remain in the mother's womb? This yakkha, it seems, is a personalist. Holding the view, ‘A being arises in the mother's womb all at once,’ he speaks thus due to his view: the mother of a being lying in the womb eats fish, meat, and so on; all of it, having been digested overnight, dissolves like foam. If form were not a being, it would dissolve in just the same way. Then, to him, the Blessed One, wishing to show that ‘a being does not arise in the mother's womb all at once, but rather grows gradually,’ said the passage beginning, ‘First, there is the kalala.’ Therein, `paṭhamaṃ` means: together with the first rebirth-linking consciousness, there is no name such as ‘Tissa’ or ‘Phussa.’ Rather, there is the kalala, the size of a drop of oil standing on the tip of a thread made from three strands of fine wool. It is with reference to this that it was said:

“Tilatelassa yathā bindu, sappimaṇḍo anāvilo;

Evaṃ vaṇṇappaṭibhāgaṃ, kalalaṃ sampavuccatī”ti.

“Like a drop of sesame oil, like the clear, untroubled cream of ghee; having such an appearance, it is called the kalala.”

Kalalā [V 1.0264][P 1.0301] hoti abbudanti tasmā kalalā sattāhaccayena maṃsadhovanaudakavaṇṇaṃ abbudaṃ nāma hoti, kalalanti nāmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

`Kalalā hoti abbudanti`: from that kalala, after the passing of seven days, there comes to be what is called the abbuda, which has the color of water in which flesh has been washed. The name ‘kalala’ disappears. And this has been said:

“Sattāhaṃ kalalaṃ hoti, paripakkaṃ samūhataṃ;

Vivaṭṭamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, abbudaṃ nāma jāyatī”ti.

“For seven days it is a kalala, ripened and compact; transforming from that state, what is called an abbuda is born.”

Abbudā [M 1.0275] jāyate pesīti tasmāpi abbudā sattāhaccayena vilīnatipusadisā pesi nāma sañjāyati. Sā maricaphāṇitena dīpetabbā. Gāmadārikā hi supakkāni maricāni gahetvā sāṭakante bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā pīḷetvā maṇḍaṃ ādāya kapāle pakkhipitvā ātape ṭhapenti, taṃ sukkhamānaṃ sabbabhāgehi muccati. Evarūpā pesi hoti, abbudanti nāmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

`Abbudā jāyate pesīti`: from that abbuda, after the passing of seven days, what is called a pesi, resembling molten tin, is produced. That should be illustrated with the clear juice of ripe peppers. For village girls, having taken well-ripened peppers, having made a bundle in the corner of a garment, having squeezed it, and having taken the clear essence, place it in an earthen dish in the sun. As it dries, it is released from all sides. Of such a nature is the pesi. The name ‘abbuda’ disappears. And this was also said:

“Sattāhaṃ abbudaṃ hoti, paripakkaṃ samūhataṃ;

Vivaṭṭamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, pesi nāma pajāyatī”ti.

For seven days it is an abbuda, ripened and compact; transforming from that state, what is called a pesi is generated.

Pesi nibbattatī ghanoti tato pesito sattāhaccayena kukkuṭaṇḍasaṇṭhāno ghano nāma maṃsapiṇḍo nibbattati, pesīti nāmaṃ antaradhāyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

From the pesi, the ghana is produced. From that pesi, after the passing of seven days, a lump of flesh called a ghana, having the shape of a chicken's egg, is produced. The name ‘pesi’ disappears. And this was also said:

“Sattāhaṃ pesi bhavati, paripakkaṃ samūhataṃ;

Vivaṭṭamānaṃ tabbhāvaṃ, ghanoti nāma jāyati.

For seven days it is a pesi, ripened and compact; transforming from that state, what is called a ghana is born.

“Yathā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍaṃ, samantā parimaṇḍalaṃ;

Evaṃ ghanassa saṇṭhānaṃ, nibbattaṃ kammapaccayā”ti.

Just as a hen's egg is perfectly round all around, so is the form of the ghana, produced due to kamma as a condition.

Ghanā pasākhā jāyantīti pañcame sattāhe dvinnaṃ hatthapādānaṃ sīsassa catthāya pañca pīḷakā jāyanti, yaṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ “pañcame, bhikkhave, sattāhe pañca pīḷakā saṇṭhahanti kammato”ti.

From the ghana, shoots arise. In the fifth week, for the sake of the two hands, two feet, and the head, five protuberances arise. With reference to this, it was said: “Monks, in the fifth week, five protuberances are established from kamma.”

Ito [V 1.0265] paraṃ chaṭṭhasattamādīni sattāhāni atikkamma desanaṃ saṅkhipitvā dvācattālīse sattāhe pariṇatakālaṃ gahetvā dassento kesātiādimāha. Tattha kesā lomā nakhāpi cāti dvācattālīse sattāhe etāni jāyanti.

After this, having passed over the sixth, seventh, and subsequent weeks and having summarized the teaching, wishing to show the time of maturity in the forty-second week, he spoke the words beginning with ‘hair of the head,’ etc. Therein, as for ‘hair of the head, body hair, and also nails,’ these arise in the forty-second week.

Tena so tattha yāpetīti tassa hi nābhito uṭṭhito nāḷo mātu udarapaṭalena ekābaddho hoti, so uppaladaṇḍako viya chiddo, tena āhāraraso saṃsaritvā āhārasamuṭṭhānarūpaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ so dasa māse yāpeti. Mātukucchigato naroti mātuyā tirokucchigato, kucchiyā abbhantaragatoti attho. Iti bhagavā [M 1.0276] “evaṃ kho, yakkha, ayaṃ satto anupubbena mātukucchiyaṃ vaḍḍhati, na ekappahāreneva nibbattatī”ti dasseti. Paṭhamaṃ.

Thus it maintains itself there. For the umbilical cord, rising from its navel, is bound to the mother’s abdominal wall; it is hollow like a lotus stalk. Through that, nutrient essence flows and generates nutriment-produced matter. Thus it maintains itself for ten months. ‘A man in the mother’s womb’ (Mātukucchigato naro) means: gone into the mother’s womb, gone inside the womb. Thus, the Blessed One shows, “In this way, O yakkha, this being gradually grows in the mother’s womb; it does not come into being all at once.” The first sutta.

2. Sakkanāmasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta

236. Dutiye [P 1.0302] sakkanāmakoti evaṃ nāmako eko yakkho, so kira mārapakkhikayakkho. Vippamuttassāti tīhi bhavehi vippamuttassa. Yadaññanti yaṃ aññaṃ. Vaṇṇenāti kāraṇena. Saṃvāsoti ekato vāso, sakkhidhammo mittadhammoti attho. Sappaññoti supañño sambuddho. Dutiyaṃ.

236. In the second sutta: ‘Sakka by name’ (sakkanāmako) refers to a certain yakkha so named, who was indeed a yakkha of Māra's faction. ‘Of one freed’ (vippamuttassa) means of one freed from the three existences. The word ‘yadaññaṃ’ is analyzed as ‘yaṃ aññaṃ’ (whatever other). ‘By reason’ (vaṇṇena) means by cause. ‘Living together’ (saṃvāso) means living together; the meaning is that the quality of companionship is the quality of a friend. ‘Wise’ (sappañño) refers to the one of good wisdom, the Perfectly Enlightened One. The second sutta.

3. Sūcilomasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sūciloma Sutta

237. Tatiye gayāyanti gayāgāme, gayāya avidūre niviṭṭhagāmaṃ upanissāyāti attho. Ṭaṅkitamañceti dīghamañce pādamajjhe vijjhitvā aṭaniyo pavesetvā katamañce. Tassa “idaṃ upari, idaṃ heṭṭhā”ti natthi, parivattetvā atthatopi tādisova hoti, taṃ devaṭṭhāne ṭhapenti. Catunnaṃ pāsāṇānaṃ upari pāsāṇaṃ attharitvā katagehampi “ṭaṅkitamañco”ti vuccati. Sūcilomassāti kathinasūcisadisalomassa. So kira kassapassa bhagavato sāsane pabbajitvā dūraṭṭhānato āgato sedamalaggahitena gattena supaññattaṃ saṅghikamañcaṃ anādarena apaccattharitvā nipajji, tassa parisuddhasīlassa taṃ kammaṃ suddhavatthe kāḷakaṃ viya ahosi. So tasmiṃ attabhāve visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ asakkonto kālaṃkatvā gayāgāmadvāre saṅkāraṭṭhāne yakkho hutvā nibbatti. Nibbattamattasseva cassa sakalasarīraṃ kathinasūcīhi gavicchivijjhitaṃ viya jātaṃ.

237. In the third sutta, 'gayāyaṃ' (at Gayā) means in the village of Gayā; the meaning is: relying for alms-round on a village situated not far from the Gayā forest. 'Ṭaṅkitamañce' (on a 'ṭaṅkita' bench) refers to a long bench made by piercing the middle of its legs and inserting the crossbars. For that bench, there is no such mark as 'this is the top, this is the bottom'; even when spread out having been turned over, it is just the same. They place it in a shrine for deities. A house made by spreading a stone slab on top of four stones is also called a 'ṭaṅkitamañca'. 'Sūcilomassa' (of Sūciloma) means 'of one having hair similar to a hard needle'. It is said that he, having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, came from a distant place. With a body covered in sweat and dirt, he disrespectfully lay down on a well-prepared communal bench without spreading a groundsheet. For that one of purified virtue, that kamma was like a black spot on a clean cloth. He, being unable to bring about a special attainment in that existence, passed away and was reborn as a yakkha in a refuse heap at the gate of Gayā village. And just upon being reborn, his entire body became as if pierced by hard needles in a criss-cross pattern.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0266] bhagavā paccūsasamaye lokaṃ olokento taṃ yakkhaṃ paṭhamāvajjanasseva āpāthaṃ āgataṃ disvā – “ayaṃ ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ mahādukkhaṃ anubhavi. Kiṃ nu khvāssa maṃ āgamma sotthikāraṇaṃ bhaveyyā”ti? Āvajjento [M 1.0277] paṭhamamaggassa upanissayaṃ addasa. Athassa saṅgahaṃ kātukāmo surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā sugatamahācīvaraṃ pārupitvā devavimānakappaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pahāya hatthigavāssamanussakukkurādikuṇapaduggandhaṃ saṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tattha mahāgandhakuṭiyaṃ viya nisīdi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “sūcilomassa yakkhassa bhavane”ti.

Then one day, the Blessed One, while surveying the world of trainable beings at dawn, saw that yakkha come into the range of his knowledge at the very first reflection. 'This one has experienced great suffering for an entire Buddha-interval. Relying on me, could there be a cause of welfare for him?' Reflecting thus, he saw the strong supporting condition for the first path. Then, desiring to give him aid, he put on his bright red under-robe and donned the Sugata's great outer robe. Leaving the fragrant hut, which was like a divine mansion, he went to the refuse heap, which reeked of the stench of the carcasses of elephants, cattle, horses, humans, dogs, and so on. There he sat as if in the great fragrant hut. Referring to that, it was said: 'in the dwelling of the yakkha Sūciloma'.

Kharoti [P 1.0303] suṃsumārapiṭṭhi viya chadaniṭṭhakāhi visamacchadanapiṭṭhi viya ca kharasarīro. So kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle sīlasampanno upāsako ekadivase vihāre cittattharaṇādīhi atthatāya bhūmiyā saṅghike attharaṇe attano uttarāsaṅgaṃ apaccattharitvā nipajji. Saṅghikaṃ telaṃ abhājetvā attano uttarāsaṅgaṃ apaccattharitvā nipajji. Saṅghikaṃ telaṃ abhājetvā attano hatthehi sarīraṃ makkhesītipi vadanti. So tena kammena sagge nibbattituṃ asakkonto tasseva gāmassa dvāre saṅkāraṭṭhāne yakkho hutvā nibbatti. Nibbattamattassa cassa sakalasarīraṃ vuttappakāraṃ ahosi. Te ubhopi sahāyā jātā. Iti kharassa kharabhāvo veditabbo.

'Khara' means having a rough body, like the back of a crocodile, and like the surface of a roof unevenly covered with roofing tiles. It is said that during the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Kassapa, he was a lay follower endowed with virtue. One day, in the monastery, on the ground that was spread with various decorative coverings, he lay down on a spreading belonging to the Sangha without spreading his own upper robe underneath. They also say that he anointed his body with his own hands using oil belonging to the Sangha without distributing it. On account of that deed, being unable to be reborn in heaven, he was reborn as a yakkha at the refuse heap at the gate of that very village. And for him, just as he was reborn, his entire body became as described. Those two both became friends. Thus, the state of Khara's roughness should be understood.

Avidūre atikkamantīti gocaraṃ pariyesantā samāgamaṭṭhānaṃ vā gacchantā āsanne ṭhāne gacchanti. Tesu sūcilomo satthāraṃ na passati, kharalomo paṭhamataraṃ disvā sūcilomaṃ yakkhaṃ etadavoca – “eso samaṇo”ti, samma, esa tava bhavanaṃ pavisitvā nisinno eko samaṇoti. Neso samaṇo, samaṇako esoti so kira yo maṃ passitvā bhīto palāyati, taṃ samaṇakoti vadati. Yo na bhāyati, taṃ samaṇoti. Tasmā “ayaṃ maṃ disvā bhīto palāyissatī”ti maññamāno evamāha.

'Passing not far away' means that, searching for food or going to their meeting place, they go to a nearby place. Among them, Sūciloma did not see the Teacher. Kharaloma, seeing him first, said this to the yakkha Sūciloma: 'Friend, that is a contemplative. This one contemplative, having entered your dwelling, is sitting.' 'He is not a contemplative; he is a mere contemplative.' It is said that he calls one who sees him and flees in fear a 'mere contemplative', and one who does not fear, a 'contemplative'. Therefore, thinking, 'This one, having seen me, will flee in fear,' he spoke thus.

Kāyaṃ upanāmesīti bheravarūpaṃ nimminitvā mahāmukhaṃ vivaritvā sakalasarīre lomāni uṭṭhāpetvā kāyaṃ upanāmesi. Apanāmesīti ratanasatikaṃ suvaṇṇagghanikaṃ viya thokaṃ apanāmesi. Pāpakoti lāmako amanuñño. So gūthaṃ viya aggi viya kaṇhasappo viya ca parivajjetabbo, na iminā suvaṇṇavaṇṇena sarīrena sampaṭicchitabbo. Evaṃ vutte pana sūcilomo “pāpako kira me samphasso”ti kuddho pañhaṃ taṃ, samaṇātiādimāha. Cittaṃ vā te khipissāmīti yesañhi amanussā cittaṃ [M 1.0278] khipitukāmā honti, tesaṃ setamukhaṃ nīlodaraṃ surattahatthapādaṃ [V 1.0267] mahāsīsaṃ pajjalitanettaṃ bheravaṃ vā attabhāvaṃ nimminitvā dassenti, bheravaṃ vā saddaṃ sāventi, kathentānaṃyeva vā mukhe hatthaṃ pakkhipitvā hadayaṃ maddanti, tena te sattā ummattakā honti khittacittā. Taṃ sandhāyevamāha. Pāragaṅgāyāti dvīsu pādesu gahetvā [P 1.0304] taṃ āviñchetvā yathā na punāgacchasi, evaṃ pāraṃ vā gaṅgāya khipissāmīti vadati. Sadevaketiādi vuttatthameva. Puccha yadākaṅkhasīti yaṃkiñci ākaṅkhasi, taṃ sabbaṃ puccha, asesaṃ te byākarissāmīti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāreti.

'Kāyaṃ upanāmesi' (he presented his body) means: having created a terrifying form, opened a huge mouth, and made the hairs on his entire body stand on end, he presented his body. 'Apanāmesi' (he withdrew it) means: he placed it slightly away, like a lump of gold a hundred cubits in size. 'Pāpako' (evil) means: base, disagreeable. That touch should be avoided like excrement, like fire, and like a black snake; it should not be received by this golden-hued body. When this was said, Sūciloma, becoming angry, [thinking] 'My touch is indeed evil, it seems!', spoke the words beginning with, 'That question, O ascetic...'. 'Cittaṃ vā te khipissāmi' (or I will hurl your mind) means: when non-human beings wish to make the mind distraught, they create and show a terrifying form with a white face, a blue belly, very red hands and feet, a huge head, and blazing eyes; or they make a terrifying sound; or, while one is speaking, they thrust a hand into the mouth and crush the heart. By this, those beings become insane and with minds distraught. Referring to this, he spoke thus. 'Pāragaṅgāya' (beyond the Ganges) means: he says, 'Having seized you by both feet and swung you around, I will hurl you to the far shore of the Ganges in such a way that you cannot return.' 'Sadevake' and so on has the meaning already stated. 'Puccha yadākaṅkhasi' (ask what you desire) means: he offers the invitation of an Omniscient One, [implying] 'Whatever you desire, ask all of it; I will explain it to you without remainder.'

Kutonidānāti kiṃnidānā, kiṃpaccayāti attho? Kumārakā dhaṅkamivossajantīti yathā kumārakā kākaṃ gahetvā ossajanti khipanti, evaṃ pāpavitakkā kuto samuṭṭhāya cittaṃ ossajantīti pucchati?

'Kutonidānā' (from what source?) means: 'what is their origin, what is their condition?' This is the meaning. 'Kumārakā dhaṅkamivossajanti' (like boys letting go of a crow) means: just as boys, having seized a crow, let it go or throw it; so he asks, 'From what source arising do evil thoughts release the wholesome mind?'

Itonidānāti ayaṃ attabhāvo nidānaṃ etesanti ito nidānā. Itojāti ito attabhāvato jātā. Ito samuṭṭhāya manovitakkāti yathā dīghasuttakena pāde baddhaṃ kākaṃ kumārakā tassa suttapariyantaṃ aṅguliyaṃ veṭhetvā ossajanti, so dūraṃ gantvāpi puna tesaṃ pādamūleyeva patati, evameva ito attabhāvato samuṭṭhāya pāpavitakkā cittaṃ ossajanti.

'Itonidānā' means: this existence is the source of these (defilements); therefore, it is called 'itonidānā' (having this as its source). 'Itojā' means: born from this existence. 'Ito samuṭṭhāya manovitakkā' means: just as boys tie a crow's foot with a long thread, wrap the end of the thread around their finger, and release it; though it goes far, it falls back right at their feet. In the same way, evil thoughts, arising from this existence, release the wholesome mind.

Snehajāti taṇhāsinehato jātā. Attasambhūtāti attani sambhūtā. Nigrodhasseva khandhajāti nigrodhakhandhe jātā pārohā viya. Puthūti bahū anekappakārā pāpavitakkā taṃsampayuttakilesā ca. Visattāti laggā laggitā. Kāmesūti vatthukāmesu. Māluvāva vitatā vaneti yathā vane māluvā latā yaṃ rukkhaṃ nissāya jāyati, taṃ mūlato yāva aggā, aggato yāva mūlā punappunaṃ saṃsibbitvā ajjhottharitvā otatavitatā tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ vatthukāmesu puthū kilesakāmā visattā, puthū vā sattā tehi kilesakāmehi vatthukāmesu visattā. Ye naṃ pajānantīti ye “attasambhūtā”ti ettha vuttaṃ attabhāvaṃ jānanti.

'Snehajā' means: born from the adhesive of craving. 'Attasambhūtā' means: produced in the self. 'Nigrodhasseva khandhajā' means: like the aerial roots born from a banyan's trunk. 'Puthū' means: many and various evil thoughts and the defilements associated with them. 'Visattā' means: clinging, stuck. 'Kāmesu' means: to objects of sensual pleasure. 'Māluvāva vitatā vane' means: just as in a forest a māluvā creeper, relying on whichever tree it grows, stands entwining and covering it again and again from root to tip and from tip to root, spread out and enveloping it. Similarly, numerous defilements of sensual pleasure cling to objects of sensual pleasure; or, numerous beings, by means of those defilements of sensual pleasure, cling to objects of sensual pleasure. 'Ye naṃ pajānanti' means: those who know the existence mentioned here in the phrase 'attasambhūtā' (produced in the self).

Yatonidānanti [M 1.0279] yaṃ nidānamassa attabhāvassa tañca jānanti. Te naṃ vinodentīti te evaṃ attabhāvasaṅkhātassa dukkhasaccassa nidānabhūtaṃ samudayasaccaṃ maggasaccena vinodenti. Te duttaranti te samudayasaccaṃ nīharantā idaṃ duttaraṃ kilesoghaṃ taranti. Atiṇṇapubbanti anamatagge saṃsāre supinantepi na tiṇṇapubbaṃ. Apunabbhavāyāti apunabbhavasaṅkhātassa nirodhasaccassatthāya. Iti [V 1.0268] imāya gāthāya cattāri saccāni pakāsento arahattanikūṭena [P 1.0305] desanaṃ niṭṭhapesi. Desanāvasāne sūcilomo tasmiṃyeva padese ṭhito desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito. Sotāpannā ca nāma na kiliṭṭhattabhāve tiṭṭhantīti saha phalapaṭilābhenassa sarīre setakaṇḍupīḷakasūciyo sabbā patitā. So dibbavatthanivattho dibbavaradukūluttarāsaṅgo dibbaveṭhanaveṭhito dibbābharaṇagandhamāladharo suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hutvā bhummadevatāparihāraṃ paṭilabhīti. Tatiyaṃ.

'Yatonidānaṃ' means: they know both the cause of this individual existence and that individual existence itself. 'Te naṃ vinodenti' means: they thus dispel the truth of the origin, which is the cause of the truth of suffering known as individual existence, by means of the truth of the path. 'Te duttaraṃ taranti' means: by removing the truth of the origin, they cross this flood of defilements, which is hard to cross. 'Atiṇṇapubbaṃ' means: in beginningless saṃsāra, it has never been crossed before, not even in a dream. 'Apunabbhavāya' means: for the sake of the truth of cessation, which is known as no new existence. Thus, by revealing the four truths with this verse, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, Sūciloma, standing right there, having directed his knowledge according to the teaching, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. And those called stream-enterers do not remain in a defiled individual existence; thus, simultaneously with the attainment of the fruit, all the white, itchy, boil-like needles on his body fell away. Clad in a divine lower garment, with a divine upper robe of excellent fine cloth, wrapped in a divine turban, adorned with divine ornaments, perfumes, and garlands, he became golden in color and received the attendance of the earth-deities. Third.

4. Maṇibhaddasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Maṇibhadda Sutta

238. Catutthe sukhamedhatīti, sukhaṃ paṭilabhati. Suve seyyoti suve suve seyyo, niccameva seyyoti attho. Verā na parimuccatīti ahaṃ satimāti ettakena verato na muccati. Yassāti yassa arahato. Ahiṃsāyāti karuṇāya ceva karuṇāpubbabhāge ca. Mettaṃsoti so mettañceva mettāpubbabhāgañca bhāveti. Atha vā aṃsoti koṭṭhāso vuccati. Mettā aṃso etassāti mettaṃso. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yassa arahato sabbakālaṃ ahiṃsāya rato mano, yassa ca sabbabhūtesu mettākoṭṭhāso atthi, tassa kenaci puggalena saddhiṃ veraṃ nāma natthi yakkhāti. Catutthaṃ.

238. In the fourth, 'sukhamedhati' means: he obtains happiness. 'Suve seyyo' means: better day by day, always better—this is the meaning. 'Verā na parimuccati' means: just by this much, 'I am mindful,' one is not freed from enmity. 'Yassa' means: of that Arahant. 'Ahiṃsāya' means: both by compassion and by that which precedes compassion. 'Mettaṃso' means: he develops both loving-kindness and that which precedes loving-kindness. Alternatively, 'aṃso' is called a portion. 'Mettaṃso' is so called because he has a portion of loving-kindness. This is what is said: O yakkha, for that Arahant whose mind is always delighted in non-harming, and who has a portion of loving-kindness toward all beings, for him there is no such thing as enmity with any person. Fourth.

5. Sānusuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Sānu Sutta

239. Pañcame yakkhena gahito hotīti so kira tassā upāsikāya ekaputtako. Atha naṃ sā daharakāleyeva pabbājesi. So pabbajitakālato paṭṭhāya sīlavā ahosi vattasampanno, ācariyupajjhāyaāgantukādīnaṃ [M 1.0280] vattaṃ katameva hoti, māsassa aṭṭhamīdivase pāto vuṭṭhāya udakamāḷake udakaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā dhammassavanaggaṃ sammajjitvā dīpaṃ jāletvā madhurassarena dhammassavanaṃ ghoseti. Bhikkhū tassa thāmaṃ ñatvā “sarabhāṇaṃ bhaṇa, sāmaṇerā”ti ajjhesanti. So “mayhaṃ hadayavāto rujati, kāso vā bādhatī”ti kiñci paccāhāraṃ akatvā dhammāsanaṃ [P 1.0306] abhiruhitvā ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento viya sarabhāṇaṃ vatvā otaranto – “mayhaṃ mātāpitūnampi imasmiṃ sarabhaññe pattī”ti vadati. Tassa manussā mātāpitaro pattiyā dinnabhāvaṃ na jānanti. Anantarattabhāve panassa mātā yakkhinī jātā. Sā devatāhi saddhiṃ āgatā[V 1.0269], dhammaṃ sutvā – “sāmaṇerena dinnapattiṃ anumodāmi, tātā”ti vadati. Sīlasampannā ca nāma bhikkhū sadevakassa lokassa piyā hontīti tasmiṃ sāmaṇere devatā salajjā sagāravā mahābrahmaṃ viya aggikkhandhaṃ viya ca naṃ maññanti. Sāmaṇere gāravena taṃ yakkhiniṃ garuṃ katvā passanti. Dhammassavanayakkhasamāgamādīsu “sānumātā sānumātā”ti yakkhiniyā aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ denti. Mahesakkhāpi yakkhā taṃ disvā maggā okkamanti, āsanā vuṭṭhahanti.

239. In the fifth Sutta, regarding the words 'he is seized by a yakkha': Reportedly, he was the only son of that female lay follower. Then she had him go forth when he was still young. From the time of his going forth, he was virtuous and accomplished in his duties, performing the services that were due to teachers, preceptors, and visiting bhikkhus. On the eighth day of the month, he would rise early, set up water at the water-pot stand, sweep the hall for listening to the Dhamma, light a lamp, and announce the listening to the Dhamma in a sweet voice. The bhikkhus, knowing his ability, would request him, saying, 'Recite the Sarabhañña, novice.' Without making any excuse such as, 'I have a pain from heart-wind,' or 'A cough afflicts me,' he would ascend the Dhamma-seat and, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges, recite the Sarabhañña. While descending, he would say, 'May my parents also have a share in the merit of this Sarabhañña.' His human parents did not know that a share of the merit had been given. However, in the immediately following existence, his mother was born a yakkhinī. She came together with devas, listened to the Dhamma, and said, 'I rejoice in the share of merit given by the novice, dear one.' Indeed, bhikkhus accomplished in virtue are dear to the world with its devas. The devas, with modesty and respect, regarded that novice like a Mahābrahmā or a mass of fire. Out of respect for the novice, they regarded the yakkhinī highly. At gatherings of yakkhas for listening to the Dhamma and so on, saying, 'Sānu's mother, Sānu's mother,' they would give the yakkhinī the chief seat, the first water, and the first portion of almsfood. Even powerful yakkhas, seeing her, would step aside from the path and rise from their seats.
