Atha kho sāmaṇero vuḍḍhimanvāya paripakkindriyo anabhiratipīḷito anabhiratiṃ vinodetuṃ asakkonto parūḷhakesanakho kiliṭṭhanivāsanapārupano kassaci anārocetvā pattacīvaramādāya ekakova mātu gharaṃ gato. Upāsikā puttaṃ disvā, vanditvā āha – “tāta, tvaṃ pubbe ācariyupajjhāyehi vā daharasāmaṇerehi vā saddhiṃ idhāgacchasi. Kasmā ekakova ajja āgato”ti? So ukkaṇṭhitabhāvaṃ ārocesi. Saddhā upāsikā nānappakārena gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ dassetvā puttaṃ ovadamānāpi taṃ saññāpetuṃ asakkontī, “appeva nāma attano dhammatāyapi sallakkhessatī”ti anuyojetvāva – “tiṭṭha, tāta, yāva te yāgubhattaṃ sampādemi, yāguṃ pivitvā katabhattakiccassa te manāpāni vatthāni nīharitvā dassāmī”ti vatvā āsanaṃ paññāpetvā adāsi. Nisīdi sāmaṇero. Upāsikā muhutteneva yāgukhajjakaṃ sampādetvā adāsi. Tato “bhattaṃ sampādessāmī”ti avidūre nisinnā taṇḍule dhovati. Tasmiṃ samaye sā yakkhinī “kahaṃ nu kho sāmaṇero? Kiñci bhikkhāhāraṃ labhati[M 1.0281], udāhu no”ti? Āvajjamānā tassa vibbhamitukāmatāya nisinnabhāvaṃ ñatvā, “mā heva kho me devatānaṃ antare lajjaṃ uppādeyya, gacchāmissa [P 1.0307] vibbhamane antarāyaṃ karomī”ti āgantvā sarīre adhimuccitvā gīvaṃ parivattetvā bhūmiyaṃ pātesi. So akkhīhi viparivattehi kheḷena paggharantena bhūmiyaṃ vipphandati. Tena vuttaṃ “yakkhena gahito hotī”ti.

Then, the novice, having reached maturity and with his faculties ripened, was oppressed by discontent. Unable to dispel his discontent, with overgrown hair and nails, wearing soiled robes, and without informing anyone, he took his bowl and robe and went alone to his mother’s house. The female lay follower, seeing her son, paid respects and said, 'Dear son, previously you used to come here with your teachers and preceptors, or with young novices. Why have you come alone today?' He informed her of his state of discontent. Though the devout female lay follower, in various ways, showed him the drawbacks of household life and admonished him, she was unable to make him understand. Thinking, 'Perhaps he will come to realize it on his own,' and giving up on persuading him, she said, 'Wait, dear son, while I prepare gruel and a meal for you. After you have drunk the gruel and finished your meal, I will bring out some pleasant clothes for you.' Having said this, she prepared a seat and gave it to him. The novice sat down. In just a moment, the female lay follower prepared gruel and snacks and gave them to him. Then, thinking, 'I will prepare the meal,' she sat nearby and washed the rice. At that time, that yakkhinī, reflecting, 'Where could the novice be? Is he receiving any alms-food, or not?' became aware that he was sitting with the desire to disrobe. Thinking, 'May he not cause shame for me in the midst of the devas! I shall go and create an obstacle to his disrobing,' she came, took possession of his body, twisted his neck, and threw him to the ground. He writhed on the ground with his eyes rolling and saliva dribbling. Therefore it is said, 'He was seized by a yakkha.'

Abhāsīti upāsikā puttassa taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā vegena gantvā puttaṃ āliṅgetvā ūrūsu nipajjāpesi. Sakalagāmavāsino āgantvā balikammādīni karonti. Upāsikā paridevamānā imā gāthāyo abhāsi.

Regarding 'She spoke': The female lay follower, seeing her son's deranged condition, went quickly, embraced him, and laid him on her lap. All the villagers came and performed offering rituals and the like. The lamenting female lay follower spoke these verses.

Pāṭihāriyapakkhañcāti manussā “aṭṭhamīuposathassa paccuggamanañca anuggamanañca karissāmā”ti [V 1.0270] sattamiyāpi navamiyāpi uposathaṅgāni samādiyanti, cātuddasīpannarasīnaṃ paccuggamanānuggamanaṃ karontā terasiyāpi pāṭipadepi samādiyanti, “vassāvāsassa anuggamanaṃ karissāmā”ti dvinnaṃ pavāraṇānaṃ antare aḍḍhamāsaṃ nibaddhuposathikā bhavanti. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “pāṭihāriyapakkhañcā”ti. Aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgatanti aṭṭhaṅgehi suṭṭhu samāgataṃ, sampayuttanti attho. Brahmacariyanti seṭṭhacariyaṃ. Na te hi yakkhā kīḷantīti na te gahetvā yakkhā kilamenti.

Regarding 'And the special fortnight': People, thinking, 'We will observe the preceding and succeeding observances for the eighth-day uposatha,' undertake the uposatha precepts on the seventh and ninth days. Those who perform the preceding and succeeding observances for the fourteenth and fifteenth days undertake them on the thirteenth and the first day of the following fortnight. Thinking, 'We will perform the succeeding observance for the rains-residence,' they become ones who observe the uposatha uninterruptedly for half a month between the two pavāraṇā ceremonies. With reference to this, it is said, 'and the special fortnight.' Regarding 'well-endowed with the eight factors': this means well-endowed with the eight factors; the meaning is 'associated.' Regarding 'the holy life': this means the excellent conduct. Regarding 'For yakkhas do not play with them': this means yakkhas do not seize and torment them.

Puna cātuddasinti imāya gāthāya sāmaṇerassa kāye adhimuttā yakkhinī āha. Āvi vā yadi vā rahoti kassaci sammukhe vā parammukhe vā. Pamutyatthīti pamutti atthi. Uppaccāpīti uppatitvāpi. Sacepi sakuṇo viya uppatitvā palāyasi, tathāpi te mokkho natthīti vadati. Evañca pana vatvā sāmaṇeraṃ muñci. Sāmaṇero akkhīni ummīlesi, mātā kese pakiriya assasantī passasantī rodati. So “amanussena gahitomhī”ti na jānāti. Olokento pana “ahaṃ pubbe pīṭhe nisinno. Mātā me avidūre nisīditvā taṇḍule dhovati. Idāni panamhi bhūmiyaṃ [P 1.0308] nisinno, mātāpi me assasantī passasantī rodati, sakalagāmavāsinopi sannipatitā. Kiṃ nu kho eta”nti? Nipannakova mataṃ vā ammāti gāthamāha.

Again, with the verse beginning 'On the fourteenth,' the yakkhinī who had possessed the novice’s body spoke. Regarding 'Openly or in secret': this means in someone's presence or absence. Regarding 'there is release': this means there is no release. Regarding 'Even having flown up': this means even having flown up. 'Even if you fly up like a bird and flee, still there is no escape for you,' she says. And having said this, she released the novice. The novice opened his eyes. His mother, with hair disheveled, breathing out and breathing in, was weeping. He did not know, 'I have been seized by a non-human.' But looking around, he thought, 'Before, I was sitting on a bench. My mother was sitting not far away, washing rice. But now I am sitting on the ground, and my mother is breathing out and breathing in, weeping, and all the villagers have gathered. What can this be?' Still lying down, he spoke the verse beginning, 'Mother, am I dead...?'

Kāme [M 1.0282] cajitvānāti duvidhepi kāme pahāya. Punarāgacchateti vibbhamanavasena āgacchati. Puna jīvaṃ mato hi soti uppabbajitvā puna jīvantopi so matakova, tasmā tampi rodantīti vadati.

“Having abandoned sensual pleasures” means having abandoned both kinds of sensual pleasures. “He returns” means he returns by way of disrobing. “For though living again, he is dead” means that having disrobed and living again, he is as one who is dead; therefore, she says that they weep for him too.

Idānissa gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ dassentī kukkuḷātiādimāha. Tattha kukkuḷāti gharāvāso kira uṇhaṭṭhena kukkuḷā nāma hoti. Kassa ujjhāpayāmaseti – “abhidhāvatha, bhaddaṃ te hotū”ti evaṃ vatvā – “yaṃ tvaṃ vibbhamitukāmo yakkhena pāpito, imaṃ vippakāraṃ kassa mayaṃ ujjhāpayāma nijjhāpayāma ārocayāmā”ti vadati. Puna ḍayhitumicchasītiādittagharato nīhaṭabhaṇḍaṃ viya gharā nīharitvā buddhasāsane pabbajito puna mahāḍāhasadise gharāvāse ḍayhituṃ icchasīti attho. So mātari kathentiyā kathentiyā sallakkhetvā hirottappaṃ paṭilabhitvā, “natthi mayhaṃ gihibhāvena attho”ti āha. Athassa mātā “sādhu, tātā”ti tuṭṭhā [V 1.0271] paṇītabhojanaṃ bhojetvā, “kati vassosi, tātā”ti pucchi. Paripuṇṇavassomhi upāsiketi. “Tena hi, tāta, upasampadaṃ karohī”ti cīvarasāṭake adāsi. So ticīvaraṃ kārāpetvā upasampanno buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhanto tepiṭako hutvā sīlādīnaṃ āgataṭṭhāne taṃ taṃ pūrento nacirasseva arahattaṃ patvā mahādhammakathiko hutvā vīsavassasataṃ ṭhatvā sakalajambudīpaṃ khobhetvā parinibbāyi. Pañcamaṃ.

Now, showing him the danger in household life, she spoke the verse beginning with ‘kukkuḷā’. Therein, ‘kukkuḷā’ means that household life is called ‘kukkuḷā’ (hot embers) because of its oppressive heat. As for the phrase ‘To whom should we complain?’: Having said, ‘You are rushing towards this; may you be well!’, she says, ‘You who desire to disrobe have been made wicked by a yakkha; to whom should we complain, explain, or report this perverse action?’ As for ‘Do you wish to burn again?’: the meaning is that just as goods are removed from a burning house, having gone forth from the home into the Buddha’s Dispensation, do you wish to burn again in the household life, which is like a great conflagration? As his mother spoke repeatedly, he reflected and regained his sense of shame and moral dread, saying, ‘There is no purpose for me in the household state.’ Then his mother, pleased, said, ‘Good, dear son,’ and served him excellent food. She asked, ‘How old are you, dear son?’ He replied, ‘I am of full age, lay follower.’ ‘Then, dear son, take the higher ordination,’ she said, giving him cloth for the robes. He had the three robes made, took the higher ordination, and while learning the Buddha’s word, he became a master of the Three Baskets. Fulfilling each aspect of virtue and other qualities as they arose, he soon attained arahantship. Becoming a great expounder of the Dhamma, he lived for one hundred and twenty years, stirring up all of Jambudīpa, and then attained final Nibbāna. The fifth.

6. Piyaṅkarasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Piyaṅkara Sutta

240. Chaṭṭhe jetavaneti jetavanassa paccante kosambakakuṭi nāma atthi, tattha viharati. Dhammapadānīti idha pāṭiyekkaṃ saṅgahaṃ āruḷhā chabbīsativaggā tanti adhippetā[P 1.0309]. Tatra thero tasmiṃ samaye antovihāre nisinno madhurassarena sarabhaññaṃ katvā appamādavaggaṃ bhāsati. Evaṃ tosesīti sā kira puttaṃ piyaṅkaraṃ aṅkenādāya jetavanassa pacchimabhāgato paṭṭhāya gocaraṃ pariyesantī anupubbena nagarābhimukhī hutvā uccārapassāvakheḷasiṅghāṇikadubbhojanāni pariyesamānā therassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ patvā madhurassaraṃ assosi. Tassā so saddo chaviādīni chetvā [M 1.0283] aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca hadayaṅgamanīyo hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Athassā gocarapariyesane cittampi na uppajji, ohitasotā dhammameva suṇantī ṭhitā. Yakkhadārakassa pana daharatāya dhammassavane cittaṃ natthi. So jighacchāya pīḷitattā, “kasmā ammā gatagataṭṭhāne khāṇuko viya tiṭṭhasi? Na mayhaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā pariyesasī”ti punappunaṃ mātaraṃ codeti. Sā “dhammassavanassa me antarāyaṃ karotī”ti puttakaṃ “mā saddaṃ kari, piyaṅkarā”ti evaṃ tosesi. Tattha mā saddaṃ karīti saddaṃ mā kari.

240. In the sixth, ‘at Jetavana’ means that there is a hut called Kosambakakuṭi at the edge of Jetavana, where he was dwelling. ‘Dhammapada verses’ here refers to the text of twenty-six sections which was individually brought into the compilation. There, at that time, the elder, seated inside the monastery, recited the Appamādavagga with a sweet voice and melodious intonation. ‘Thus she appeased him’—it is said that that ogress, carrying her child Piyaṅkara on her hip, had set out from the western part of Jetavana in search of food. Gradually heading towards the city, she was searching for disgusting food such as excrement, urine, spittle, and mucus when she reached the elder's dwelling and heard his sweet voice. That sound, cutting through her skin and so forth and striking the marrow of her bones, became heart-entering and established itself. Then, not even the thought of searching for food arose in her; with attentive ears, she stood listening only to the Dhamma. The yakkha-child, however, due to his youth, had no interest in listening to the Dhamma. Being afflicted by hunger, he repeatedly urged his mother, saying, ‘Mother, why do you stand like a tree stump wherever we go? Are you not searching for food for me to eat or consume?’ She, thinking, ‘He is creating an obstacle to my listening to the Dhamma,’ appeased her child, saying, ‘Do not make a sound, Piyaṅkara.’ Therein, ‘mā saddaṃ kari’ means ‘do not make a sound’.

Pāṇesu cāti gāthāya sā attano dhammatāya samādiṇṇaṃ pañcasīlaṃ dasseti. Tattha saṃyamāmaseti saṃyamāma saṃyatā homa. Iminā pāṇātipātā virati gahitā, dutiyapadena musāvādā virati, tatiyapadena sesā tisso viratiyo. Api muccema pisācayoniyāti api nāma yakkhaloke uppannāni pañca verāni pahāya, yoniso paṭipajjitvā imāya chātakadubbhikkhāya pisācayakkhayoniyā muccema, tātāti vadati. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

By the verse beginning ‘Pāṇesu ca,’ she shows the five precepts she had undertaken according to her own nature. Therein, ‘saṃyamāmase’ means ‘let us restrain, let us be restrained.’ By this first phrase, abstention from taking life is taken; by the second phrase, abstention from false speech is taken; and by the third phrase, the remaining three abstentions are taken. ‘Api muccema pisācayoniyā’ means she says: ‘Dear son, perhaps, by abandoning these five enmities that arise in the yakkha world and by practicing appropriately, we may be freed from this pisāca-yakkha birth which is characterized by hunger and famine.’ The sixth.

7. Punabbasusuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Punabbasu Sutta

241. Sattame [V 1.0272] tena kho pana samayenāti katarasamayena? Sūriyassa atthaṅgamanasamayena. Tadā kira bhagavā pacchābhatte mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā mahājanaṃ uyyojetvā nhānakoṭṭhake nhatvā gandhakuṭipariveṇe paññattavarabuddhāsane puratthimalokadhātuṃ olokayamāno nisīdi. Athekacārikadvicārikādayo paṃsukūlikapiṇḍapātikabhikkhū attano [P 1.0310] attano vasanaṭṭhānehi nikkhamitvā āgamma dasabalaṃ vanditvā rattasāṇiyā parikkhipamānā viya nisīdiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā satthā nibbānapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathesi.

241. In the seventh sutta, ‘But at that time’—at what time was that? At the time of sunset. It is said that at that time the Blessed One, having taught the Dhamma to the great assembly after the meal and dismissed them, bathed in the bathing hall and sat on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the precinct of the Perfumed Chamber, looking towards the eastern world-system. Then monks who were solitary wanderers, wanderers in pairs, and the like, wearers of rag-robes and eaters of alms-food, having left their respective dwellings, approached the Ten-Powered One, paid homage, and sat down surrounding him as if with a red curtain. Then, knowing their inclination, the Teacher gave a Dhamma talk connected with Nibbāna.

Evaṃ tosesīti sā kira dhītaraṃ aṅkenādāya puttaṃ aṅguliyā gahetvā jetavanapiṭṭhiyaṃ pākāraparikkhepasamīpe uccārapassāvakheḷasiṅghāṇikaṃ pariyesamānā anupubbena jetavanadvārakoṭṭhakaṃ sampattā. Bhagavato ca, “ānanda, pattaṃ āhara, cīvaraṃ āhara, vighāsādānaṃ dānaṃ dehī”ti kathentassa saddo samantā dvādasahatthamattameva gaṇhāti. Dhammaṃ desentassa [M 1.0284] sacepi cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā parisā nisīdati, yathā parisaṃ gacchati, bahiparisāya ekaṅgulimattampi na niggacchati, “mā akāraṇā madhurasaddo nassī”ti. Tatrāyaṃ yakkhinī bahiparisāya ṭhitā saddaṃ na suṇāti, dvārakoṭṭhake ṭhitāya panassā mahatiyā buddhavīthiyā abhimukhe ṭhitā gandhakuṭi paññāyi. Sā nivāte dīpasikhā viya buddhagāravena hatthakukkuccādirahitaṃ niccalaṃ parisaṃ disvā – “nūna mettha kiñci bhājanīyabhaṇḍaṃ bhavissati, yato ahaṃ sappitelamadhuphāṇitādīsu kiñcideva pattato vā hatthato vā paggharantaṃ bhūmiyaṃ vā pana patitaṃ labhissāmī”ti antovihāraṃ pāvisi. Dvārakoṭṭhake avaruddhakānaṃ nivāraṇatthāya ṭhitā ārakkhadevatā yakkhiniyā upanissayaṃ disvā na nivāresi. Tassā saha parisāya ekībhāvagamanena madhurassaro chaviādīni chinditvā aṭṭhimiñjaṃ āhacca aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ dhammassavanatthāya niccalaṃ ṭhitaṃ purimanayeneva puttakā codayiṃsu. Sā “dhammassavanassa me antarāyaṃ karontī”ti puttake tuṇhī uttarike hohīti evaṃ tosesi.

‘Thus she pacified them’—it is said that she, carrying her daughter on her hip and holding her son by the finger, searching for excrement, urine, spittle, and snot near the wall enclosure at the back of Jetavana, gradually arrived at the Jetavana gatehouse. And the sound of the Blessed One speaking—‘Ānanda, bring the bowl, bring the robe, give a gift to the eaters of leftovers’—is perceived only up to twelve cubits around. When he teaches the Dhamma, even if an assembly sits filling the entire world-system, the sound travels according to the assembly; it does not go outside the assembly by even a finger’s breadth, lest the sweet sound be lost without cause. There, this ogress, standing outside the assembly, did not hear the sound. But when she stood at the gatehouse, the Perfumed Chamber, situated opposite on the great Buddha-path, appeared to her. Seeing the assembly motionless and free from fidgeting with hands and so on out of reverence for the Buddha, like a lamp flame in a windless place, she thought, ‘Surely there must be some goods to be distributed here, from which I might obtain something of ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so on, dripping from a bowl or a hand, or fallen on the ground,’ and so she entered the monastery. The guardian deity stationed at the gatehouse to prevent those who are to be kept out, seeing the ogress’s supporting condition, did not stop her. As she became one with the assembly, the sweet sound, having pierced her skin and so on, struck her bone marrow and remained there. Her children, in the same way as before, urged her on as she stood motionless to hear the Dhamma. Thinking, ‘They are creating an obstacle to my hearing of the Dhamma,’ she pacified them, saying, ‘O son, O Uttarā, be silent!’

Tattha yāvāti yāva dhammaṃ suṇāmi, tāva tuṇhī hohīti attho. Sabbaganthappamocananti nibbānaṃ āgamma sabbe ganthā pamuccanti, tasmā taṃ sabbaganthappamocananti vuccati. Ativelāti velātikkantā pamāṇātikkantā. Piyāyanāti magganā patthanā. Tato piyataranti yā [V 1.0273] ayaṃ assa dhammassa magganā patthanā, idaṃ mayhaṃ tato piyataranti attho. Piyatarāti vā pāṭho. Pāṇinanti yathā [P 1.0311] pāṇīnaṃ dukkhā moceti. Ke mocetīti? Pāṇineti āharitvā vattabbaṃ. Yaṃ dhammaṃ abhisambuddhanti, yaṃ dhammaṃ bhagavā abhisambuddho. Tuṇhībhūtāyamuttarāti na kevalaṃ ahameva, ayaṃ me bhaginī uttarāpi tuṇhībhūtāti vadati. Saddhammassa anaññāyāti, amma, mayaṃ pubbepi imaṃ saddhammameva ajānitvā idāni idaṃ khuppipāsādidukkhaṃ anubhavantā dukkhaṃ carāma viharāma.

Herein, `yāvā` means: 'For as long as I hear the Dhamma, for that long, be silent.' This is the meaning. `Sabbaganthappamocana` means: On account of Nibbāna, all bonds are released; therefore, it is called `sabbaganthappamocana` (the release from all bonds). `Ativelā` means: beyond the limit, exceeding the measure. `Piyāyanā` means: seeking, aspiring. `Tato piyataraṃ` means: 'This seeking and aspiring for this Dhamma is dearer to me than that.' This is the meaning. Or, `piyatarā` is the reading. `Pāṇinaṃ` means: as it liberates beings from suffering. If it is asked, 'Whom does it liberate?' it should be stated by supplying `pāṇine` (beings). `Yaṃ dhammaṃ abhisambuddhaṃ` means: the Dhamma to which the Blessed One has fully awakened. `Tuṇhībhūtāyamuttarā` means she says: 'Not only have I become silent, but this sister of mine, Uttarā, has also become silent.' `Saddhammassa anaññāya` means: 'Mother, because we did not know this very True Dhamma even before, we now, experiencing this suffering of hunger, thirst, and so on, fare and dwell in misery.'

Cakkhumāti pañcahi cakkhūhi cakkhumā. Dhammaṃ desentoyeva bhagavā parisaṃ sallakkhayamāno tassā yakkhiniyā ceva yakkhadārakassa ca sotāpattiphalassa upanissayaṃ disvā desanaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā catusaccakathaṃ dīpeti, taṃ sutvā tasmiṃyeva dese ṭhitā yakkhinī saddhiṃ puttena [M 1.0285] sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā. Dhītuyāpi panassā upanissayo atthi, atidaharattā pana desanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ nāsakkhi.

`Cakkhumā` means: possessed of the five eyes. While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma, observing the assembly and seeing the supporting condition for the fruit of stream-entry in that ogress and her young son, he turned back the discourse and expounded the talk on the Four Truths. Having heard it, the ogress, standing in that very place, was established in the fruit of stream-entry together with her son. Her daughter also had the supporting condition, but due to being very young, she was unable to accept the teaching.

Idāni sā yakkhinī puttassa anumodanaṃ karontī sādhu kho paṇḍito nāmātiādimāha. Ajjāhamhi samuggatāti ahamhi ajja vaṭṭato uggatā samuggatā sāsane vā uggatā samuggatā, tvampi sukhī hohīti. Diṭṭhānīti mayā ca tayā ca diṭṭhāni. Uttarāpi suṇātu meti, “amhākaṃ catusaccapaṭivedhabhāvaṃ, dhītā me uttarāpi, suṇātū”ti vadati. Saha saccapaṭivedheneva sāpi sūcilomo viya sabbaṃ setakaṇḍukacchuādibhāvaṃ pahāya dibbasampattiṃ paṭilabhati saddhiṃ puttena. Dhītā panassā yathā nāma loke mātāpitūhi issariye laddhe puttānampi taṃ hoti, evaṃ mātu-ānubhāveneva sampattiṃ labhi. Tato paṭṭhāya ca sā saddhiṃ puttakehi gandhakuṭisamīparukkheyeva nivāsarukkhaṃ labhitvā sāyaṃ pātaṃ buddhadassanaṃ labhamānā dhammaṃ suṇamānā dīgharattaṃ tattheva vasi. Sattamaṃ.

Now, that ogress, rejoicing in her son, spoke the words beginning with, 'Excellent indeed is one who is called wise.' Regarding 'Ajjāhamhi samuggatā': 'Today I have emerged from the round of suffering, I have well emerged; or, in the Dispensation, I have become renowned, well renowned. May you too be happy.' Regarding 'Diṭṭhāni': 'They have been seen by me and by you.' Regarding 'Uttarāpi suṇātu me,' she says, 'Let my daughter Uttarā also hear of our attainment of the penetration of the Four Truths.' Together with the penetration of the Truths, she too, like the yakkha Sūciloma, having completely abandoned the state of having white itch, scabies, and so on, attained divine bliss together with her son. As for her daughter, just as in the world, when dominion is gained by parents, it also belongs to their children, in the same way, she attained prosperity solely through her mother's power. And from that time onwards, she, together with her young children, having obtained a dwelling tree right near the Perfumed Chamber, lived right there for a long time, gaining sight of the Buddha in the evening and morning and listening to the Dhamma. The seventh.

8. Sudattasuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Sudatta Sutta

242. Aṭṭhame kenacideva karaṇīyenāti vāṇijjakammaṃ adhippetaṃ. Anāthapiṇḍiko ca rājagahaseṭṭhi ca aññamaññaṃ bhaginipatikā honti. Yadā rājagahe uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍakaṃ mahagghaṃ hoti, tadā rājagahaseṭṭhi taṃ gahetvā [P 1.0312] pañcasakaṭasatehi sāvatthiṃ gantvā yojanamatte ṭhito attano [V 1.0274] āgatabhāvaṃ jānāpeti. Anāthapiṇḍiko paccuggantvā tassa mahāsakkāraṃ katvā ekayānaṃ āropetvā sāvatthiṃ pavisati. So sace bhaṇḍaṃ lahukaṃ vikkīyati, vikkiṇāti. No ce, bhaginighare ṭhapetvā pakkamati. Anāthapiṇḍikopi tatheva karoti. Svāyaṃ tadāpi teneva karaṇīyena agamāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

242. In the eighth, regarding 'kenacideva karaṇīyena,' the act of trade is intended. Anāthapiṇḍika and the seṭṭhi of Rājagaha are husbands of sisters. When merchandise produced in Rājagaha is of great value, the seṭṭhi of Rājagaha takes it with five hundred carts and goes to Sāvatthī. Stopping at a place about a yojana away, he makes his arrival known. Anāthapiṇḍika goes out to meet him, pays him great honor, and having him mount a single vehicle, brings him into Sāvatthī. If the merchandise sells quickly, he sells it. If not, having left it at his sister's house, he departs. Anāthapiṇḍika also does likewise. This Anāthapiṇḍika, on that occasion too, went for that very business. In reference to that, this was said.

Taṃ divasaṃ pana rājagahaseṭṭhi yojanamatte ṭhitena anāthapiṇḍikena āgatabhāvajānanatthaṃ pesitaṃ paṇṇaṃ na suṇi, dhammassavanatthāya vihāraṃ agamāsi. So dhammakathaṃ sutvā svātanāya buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā attano ghare uddhanakhaṇāpanadāruphālanādīni kāresi. Anāthapiṇḍikopi “idāni mayhaṃ paccuggamanaṃ karissati, idāni karissatī”ti gharadvārepi paccuggamanaṃ alabhitvā [M 1.0286] antogharaṃ paviṭṭho paṭisanthārampi na bahuṃ alattha. “Kiṃ, mahāseṭṭhi, kusalaṃ dārakarūpānaṃ? Nasi magge kilanto”ti? Ettakova paṭisanthāro ahosi. So tassa mahābyāpāraṃ disvā, “kiṃ nu te, gahapati, āvāho vā bhavissatī”ti? Khandhake (cūḷava. 304) āgatanayeneva kathaṃ pavattetvā tassa mukhato buddhasaddaṃ sutvā pañcavaṇṇaṃ pītiṃ paṭilabhi. Sā tassa sīsena uṭṭhāya yāva pādapiṭṭhiyā, pādapiṭṭhiyā uṭṭhāya yāva sīsā gacchati, ubhato uṭṭhāya majjhe osarati, majjhe uṭṭhāya ubhato gacchati. So pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭṭho, “buddhoti tvaṃ, gahapati, vadesi? Buddho tāhaṃ, gahapati, vadāmī”ti evaṃ tikkhattuṃ pucchitvā, “ghosopi kho eso dullabho lokasmiṃ yadidaṃ buddho”ti āha. Idaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “assosi kho anāthapiṇḍiko, gahapati, buddho kira loke uppanno”ti.

On that day, however, the chief merchant of Rājagaha did not hear the letter sent by Anāthapiṇḍika, who was staying a yojana away, to inform him of his arrival; he went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma talk, he invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha for the next day and had the digging of ovens, splitting of firewood, and so forth done in his own house. Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, “Now he will come out to greet me, now he will,” did not receive a greeting even at the house door. Having entered inside the house, he received little hospitality. “How are the children, great merchant? Are you not tired from the journey?” Such was the extent of the welcome. Seeing his great preoccupation, he asked, “What is it, householder, is there to be a wedding?” Following the method related in the Khandhaka, he started a conversation and, hearing the word “Buddha” from his mouth, obtained five kinds of joy. That joy, arising from his head, went down to the tops of his feet; arising from the tops of his feet, it went up to his head; arising from both ends, it converged in the middle; arising in the middle, it went to both ends. Pervaded by uninterrupted joy, he asked three times, “Householder, do you say ‘Buddha’?” When the other replied, “Householder, I do say ‘Buddha’,” he then said, “Indeed, this sound, namely ‘Buddha,’ is rare in the world.” With reference to this, it was said: “Anāthapiṇḍika the householder heard, ‘A Buddha, it seems, has arisen in the world.’”

Etadahosi akālo kho ajjāti so kira taṃ seṭṭhiṃ pucchi, “kuhiṃ gahapati satthā viharatī”ti? Athassa so – “buddhā [P 1.0313] nāma durāsadā āsīvisasadisā honti, satthā sivathikāya vasati, na sakkā tattha tumhādisehi imāya velāya gantu”nti ācikkhi. Athassa etadahosi. Buddhagatāya satiyā nipajjīti taṃdivasaṃ kirassa bhaṇḍasakaṭesu vā upaṭṭhākesu vā cittampi na uppajji, sāyamāsampi na akāsi, sattabhūmikaṃ pana pāsādaṃ āruyha supaññattālaṅkatavarasayane “buddho buddho”ti sajjhāyaṃ karontova nipajjitvā niddaṃ okkami. Tena vuttaṃ “buddhagatāya satiyā nipajjī”ti.

It occurred to him: “Indeed, today is not the right time.” So, it is said, he asked that merchant: “Where, householder, does the Teacher reside?” Then he told him: “Buddhas are indeed hard to approach, like venomous snakes. The Teacher is dwelling near the charnel ground; it is not possible for people like you to go there at this time.” Then it occurred to him. “He lay down with mindfulness directed to the Buddha.” That very day, it is said, his mind did not arise even for his goods carts or attendants. He did not even take his evening meal. Instead, having ascended to his seven-storied mansion, he lay down on a well-prepared, adorned, and excellent couch, reciting “Buddho, Buddho,” and fell asleep. Therefore, it was said, “He lay down with mindfulness directed to the Buddha.”

Rattiyā sudaṃ tikkhattuṃ uṭṭhāsi pabhātanti maññamānoti paṭhamayāme tāva vītivatte uṭṭhāya buddhaṃ [V 1.0275] anussari, athassa balavappasādo udapādi, pītiāloko ahosi, sabbatamaṃ vigacchi, dīpasahassujjalaṃ viya canduṭṭhānaṃ sūriyuṭṭhānaṃ viya ca jātaṃ. So “papādaṃ āpanno vatamhi, sūriyo uggato”ti uṭṭhāya ākāsatale ṭhitaṃ candaṃ ulloketvā “ekova yāmo gato, aññe dve atthī”ti puna pavisitvā nipajji. Etenupāyena majjhimayāmāvasānepi pacchimayāmāvasānepīti tikkhattuṃ uṭṭhāsi. Pacchimayāmāvasāne pana balavapaccūseyeva uṭṭhāya ākāsatalaṃ āgantvā [M 1.0287] mahādvārābhimukhova ahosi, sattabhūmikadvāraṃ sayameva vivaṭaṃ ahosi. So pāsādā oruyha antaravīthiṃ paṭipajji.

Indeed, during the night, he rose three times thinking, “It is dawn.” First, in the first watch, after it had passed, he rose and recollected the Buddha, and then strong faith arose in him. A light of joy appeared, all darkness vanished, and it became as if a thousand lamps were lit, like the rising of the moon and the rising of the sun. He thought, “Alas, I have fallen into negligence, the sun has risen,” and stood up. Looking up at the moon in the sky, he reflected, “Only one watch has passed, two more remain,” and then went back inside and lay down again. In this way, he rose three times: at the end of the middle watch and at the end of the last watch. At the end of the last watch, however, he rose in the strong pre-dawn, went to the open space, and found himself facing the great gate. The gate of the seven-storied mansion was open by itself. Descending from the palace, he proceeded along the inner street.

Vivariṃsūti “ayaṃ mahāseṭṭhi ‘buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ gamissāmī’ti nikkhanto, paṭhamadassaneneva sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ aggupaṭṭhāko hutvā asadisaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ katvā cātuddisassa ariyagaṇassa anāvaṭadvāro bhavissati, na yuttamassa dvāraṃ pidahitu”nti cintetvā vivariṃsu. Antaradhāyīti rājagahaṃ kira ākiṇṇamanussaṃ antonagare nava koṭiyo, bahinagare navāti taṃ upanissāya aṭṭhārasa manussakoṭiyo vasanti. Avelāya matamanusse bahi nīharituṃ asakkontā aṭṭālake ṭhatvā bahidvāre khipanti. Mahāseṭṭhi nagarato bahinikkhantamattova allasarīraṃ pādena akkami, aparampi piṭṭhipādena pahari. Makkhikā uppatitvā parikiriṃsu. Duggandho nāsapuṭaṃ abhihani. Buddhappasādo tanuttaṃ gato. Tenassa [P 1.0314] āloko antaradhāyi, andhakāro pāturahosi. Saddamanussāvesīti “seṭṭhissa ussāhaṃ janessāmī”ti suvaṇṇakiṅkiṇikaṃ ghaṭṭento viya madhurassarena saddaṃ anussāvesi.

Thinking, “This great merchant, having set out with the thought, ‘I will go to attend upon the Buddha,’ will, by the very first sight, become established in the fruit of stream-entry. Having become the chief attendant of the Three Jewels and having built an incomparable monastery for the Saṅgha, he will become one with an unclosed door for the assembly of noble ones of the four quarters. It is not proper to close the door for him,” they opened it. It is said that Rājagaha was crowded with people: nine crores inside the city and nine crores outside the city; thus, eighteen crores of people dwelt depending on it. Being unable to carry the dead outside at an unseasonable time, they would stand on the ramparts and throw them outside the gates. The great merchant, just as he had gone out of the city, stepped on a fresh corpse with his foot and also struck another with the back of his foot. Flies flew up and swarmed around. A foul odor struck his nostrils. His faith in the Buddha diminished. Therefore, his light disappeared, and darkness appeared. Thinking, “I will generate enthusiasm in the merchant,” he made a sound to be heard with a sweet voice, as if striking a golden small bell.

Sataṃ kaññāsahassānīti purimapadānipi imināva sahassapadena saddhiṃ sambandhanīyāni. Yatheva hi sataṃ kaññāsahassāni, sataṃ sahassāni hatthī, sataṃ sahassāni assā, sataṃ sahassāni rathāti ayamettha attho. Iti ekekasatasahassameva dīpitaṃ. Padavītihārassāti padavītihāro nāma samagamane dvinnaṃ padānaṃ antare muṭṭhiratanamattaṃ. Kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasinti taṃ ekaṃ padavītihāraṃ soḷasabhāge katvā tato eko koṭṭhāso puna soḷasadhā, tato eko soḷasadhāti evaṃ soḷasa vāre soḷasadhā bhinnassa eko koṭṭhāso soḷasikalā nāma, taṃ soḷasikalaṃ etāni cattāri satasahassāni na agghanti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sataṃ hatthisahassāni sataṃ assasahassāni sataṃ rathasahassāni sataṃ kaññāsahassāni, tā ca kho āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā sakalajambudīparājadhītaro vāti imasmā ettakā lābhā vihāraṃ gacchantassa [V 1.0276] tasmiṃ soḷasikalasaṅkhāte padese pavattacetanāva uttaritarāti. Idaṃ pana vihāragamanaṃ kassa vasena gahitanti? Vihāraṃ gantvā anantarāyena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahantassa. “Gandhamālādīhi pūjaṃ karissāmi[M 1.0288], cetiyaṃ vandissāmi, dhammaṃ sossāmi, dīpapūjaṃ karissāmi, saṅghaṃ nimantetvā dānaṃ dassāmi, sikkhāpadesu vā saraṇesu vā patiṭṭhahissāmī”ti gacchatopi vasena vaṭṭatiyeva.

As for Sataṃ kaññāsahassāni (a hundred thousand maidens), the preceding terms should also be connected with this very word 'thousand'. Indeed, just as one obtains a hundred thousand maidens, so too one obtains a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, and a hundred thousand chariots—this is the meaning here. Thus, each single hundred thousand is indicated. As for padavītihārassa, what is called a padavītihāra is the space, the measure of a fist-cubit, between two feet in even walking. As for Kalaṃ nāgghanti soḷasiṃ (They are not worth a sixteenth part): having divided that one padavītihāra into sixteen parts, and from that one portion again into sixteen, and from that one portion again into sixteen—thus, one portion of that which has been divided into sixteen, sixteen times, is called a soḷasikalā. These four hundred thousand are not worth that soḷasikalā. This is what is said: a hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses, a hundred thousand chariots, and a hundred thousand maidens—and indeed, those maidens wearing ruby earrings are the daughters of kings of all Jambudīpa. More excellent than such a great gain is the very volition that arises in that space designated as a soḷasikalā for one who is going to the monastery. Furthermore, with reference to whom is this going to the monastery taken? With reference to one who, having gone to the monastery, becomes established in the fruit of stream-entry without obstacle. It is indeed also applicable with reference to one who goes thinking, 'I will make an offering with perfumes, garlands, and so on; I will listen to the Dhamma; I will make an offering of lamps; having invited the Saṅgha, I will give a gift; or I will become established in the training rules or in the refuges.'

Andhakāro antaradhāyīti so kira cintesi – “ahaṃ ekakoti saññaṃ karomi, anuyuttāpi me atthi, kasmā bhāyāmī”ti sūro ahosi. Athassa balavā buddhappasādo udapādi. Tasmā andhakāro antaradhāyīti. Sesavāresupi eseva nayo. Apica purato purato gacchanto bhiṃsanake susānamagge aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikasamaṃsalohitantiādīni anekavidhāni kuṇapāni addasa[P 1.0315]. Soṇasiṅgālādīnaṃ saddaṃ assosi. Taṃ sabbaṃ parissayaṃ punappunaṃ buddhagataṃ pasādaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maddanto agamāsiyeva.

The darkness disappeared—so, it is said, he thought: “I am making the perception that I am alone, but I also have attendants following me; why should I fear?” Thus he became courageous. Then a strong faith in the Buddha arose in him. Therefore, the darkness disappeared. The same principle applies to the remaining instances. Moreover, as he went further and further, on the terrifying charnel ground path he saw many kinds of corpses, such as skeletons with flesh and blood. He heard the sounds of dogs, jackals, and the like. Crushing all that danger by repeatedly increasing his faith directed towards the Buddha, he went on indeed.

Ehi sudattāti so kira seṭṭhi gacchamānova cintesi – “imasmiṃ loke bahū pūraṇakassapādayo titthiyā ‘mayaṃ buddhā mayaṃ buddhā’ti vadanti, kathaṃ nu kho ahaṃ satthu buddhabhāvaṃ jāneyya”nti? Athassa etadahosi – “mayhaṃ guṇavasena uppannaṃ nāmaṃ mahājano jānāti, kuladattiyaṃ pana me nāmaṃ aññatra mayā na koci jānāti. Sace buddho bhavissati, kuladattikanāmena maṃ ālapissatī”ti. Satthā tassa cittaṃ ñatvā evamāha.

“Come, Sudatta.” It is said that the householder, while going along, thought: “In this world, many sectarians, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others, say, ‘We are Buddhas, we are Buddhas.’ How indeed shall I know the Teacher's state of being a Buddha?” Then this occurred to him: “The great populace knows the name that has arisen for me through the power of my virtues, but my family-given name, no one knows it except for me. If he is a Buddha, he will address me by my family-given name.” The Teacher, knowing his thought, spoke thus.

Parinibbutoti kilesaparinibbānena parinibbuto. Āsattiyoti taṇhāyo. Santinti kilesavūpasamaṃ. Pappuyyāti patvā. Idañca pana vatvā satthā tassa anupubbikathaṃ kathetvā matthake cattāri saccāni pakāsesi. Seṭṭhi dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā punadivasato paṭṭhāya mahādānaṃ dātuṃ ārabhi. Bimbisārādayo seṭṭhissa sāsanaṃ pesenti – “tvaṃ āgantuko, yaṃ nappahoti, taṃ ito āharāpehī”ti. So “alaṃ tumhe bahukiccā”ti sabbe paṭikkhipitvā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi ānītavibhavena sattāhaṃ mahādānaṃ adāsi. Dānapariyosāne ca bhagavantaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ vassāvāsaṃ paṭijānāpetvā rājagahassa ca sāvatthiyā [M 1.0289] ca antare yojane yojane satasahassaṃ datvā pañcacattālīsa [V 1.0277] vihāre kārento sāvatthiṃ gantvā jetavanamahāvihāraṃ kāretvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa niyyādesīti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Parinibbuto” means: fully extinguished by the final extinguishment of the defilements. “Āsattiyo” means: cravings. “Santin” means: the pacification of the defilements. “Pappuyya” means: having attained. And having said this, the Teacher gave him a progressive discourse and at its conclusion revealed the Four Truths. The merchant, having heard the Dhamma discourse, became established in the fruit of stream-entry. He then invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, and from the next day onward, began giving a great alms-giving. King Bimbisāra and others sent a message to the merchant: “You are a visitor; whatever is insufficient, have it brought from here.” But he refused them all, saying, “Enough, you have many duties.” With wealth brought by five hundred carts, he gave a great alms-giving for seven days. At the conclusion of the alms-giving, he had the Blessed One accept the rains-residence in Sāvatthī. Between Rājagaha and Sāvatthī, at every yojana, having given a hundred thousand while causing forty-five monasteries to be built, he went to Sāvatthī, had the Jetavana Great Monastery built, and dedicated it to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. The eighth.

9. Paṭhamasukkāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. In the ninth.

243. Navame rathikāya rathikanti ekaṃ rathikaṃ gahetvā tato aparaṃ gacchanto rathikāya rathikaṃ upasaṅkamanto nāma hoti. Siṅghāṭakepi eseva nayo. Ettha ca rathikāti racchā. Siṅghāṭakanti catukkaṃ. Kiṃ me katāti kiṃ ime katā? Kiṃ karontīti attho. Madhupītāva [P 1.0316] seyareti gandhamadhupānaṃ pītā viya sayanti. Gandhamadhupānaṃ pīto kira sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na sakkoti, asaññī hutvā sayateva. Tasmā evamāha.

243. In the ninth, “from street to street” means: having taken one street and then going to another, one is said to be approaching from street to street. This same method also applies to a crossroads. And here, “rathikā” means a street. “Siṅghāṭakaṃ” means a four-way junction. “Kiṃ me katā” means “What have these people done?” The meaning is, “What are they doing?” “They lie as if drunk on honey-drink” means: they lie as if they have drunk fragrant honey-drink. For it is said that one who has drunk fragrant honey-drink cannot lift their head; becoming unconscious, they just lie down. Therefore, he spoke thus.

Tañca pana appaṭivānīyanti tañca pana dhammaṃ appaṭivānīyaṃ deseti. Bāhirakañhi sumadhurampi bhojanaṃ punappunaṃ bhuñjantassa na ruccati, “apanetha, kiṃ iminā”ti? Paṭivānetabbaṃ apanetabbaṃ hoti, na evamayaṃ dhammo. Imaṃ hi dhammaṃ paṇḍitā vassasatampi vassasahassampi suṇantā tittiṃ na gacchanti. Tenāha “appaṭivānīya”nti. Asecanakamojavanti anāsittakaṃ ojavantaṃ. Yathā hi bāhirāni asambhinnapāyāsādīnipi sappimadhusakkharāhi āsittāni yojitāneva madhurāni ojavantāni honti, na evamayaṃ dhammo. Ayaṃ hi attano dhammatāya madhuro ceva ojavā ca, na aññena upasitto. Tenāha “asecanakamojava”nti. Pivanti maññe sappaññāti paṇḍitapurisā pivanti viya. Valāhakameva panthagūti valāhakantarato nikkhantaudakaṃ ghammābhitattā pathikā viya. Navamaṃ.

As for 'Tañca pana appaṭivānīyan'ti': He teaches that Dhamma which is not to be rejected. Indeed, an external food, even if very sweet, is not pleasing to one who eats it again and again: 'Take it away! What is the use of this?' It is to be refused, to be removed. This Dhamma is not so. Indeed, the wise, listening to this Dhamma for even a hundred years or a thousand years, do not reach satiety. Therefore, He said, 'appaṭivānīyaṃ.' As for 'Asecanakamojavan'ti': unsprinkled, possessing savor. Indeed, external foods, even such as rice-porridge not mixed with water, become sweet and savory only when sprinkled and combined with ghee, honey, and sugar. This Dhamma is not so. Indeed, this Dhamma, by its own nature, is both sweet and savory; it is not sprinkled with anything else. Therefore, He said, 'asecanakam ojavaṃ.' As for 'Pivanti maññe sappaññā'ti': wise persons drink, as it were. As for 'Valāhakam iva panthagū'ti': like travelers, afflicted by heat, drinking water that has come out from within a cloud. Ninth.

10-11. Dutiyasukkāsuttādivaṇṇanā

10-11. Commentary on the Second Sukkā Sutta and the Like

244. Dasame puññaṃ vata pasavi bahunti bahuṃ vata puññaṃ pasavatīti. Dasamaṃ.

244. In the tenth, as for 'puññaṃ vata pasavi bahun'ti', this means: 'Indeed, much merit is produced.' Tenth.

245. Ekādasamaṃ uttānameva. Ekādasamaṃ.

245. The eleventh is simply clear. Eleventh.

12. Āḷavakasuttavaṇṇanā

12. Commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta

246. Dvādasame [V 1.0278] āḷaviyanti āḷavīti taṃ raṭṭhampi nagarampi. Tañca bhavanaṃ nagarassa avidūre gāvutamatte ṭhitaṃ. Bhagavā tattha viharanto taṃ nagaraṃ upanissāya [M 1.0290] āḷaviyaṃ viharatīti [P 1.0317] vutto. Āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavaneti ettha pana ayamanupubbikathā – āḷavako kira rājā vividhanāṭakūpabhogaṃ chaḍḍetvā corapaṭibāhanatthaṃ paṭirājanisedhanatthaṃ byāyāmakaraṇatthañca sattame sattame divase migavaṃ gacchanto ekadivasaṃ balakāyena saddhiṃ katikaṃ akāsi – “yassa passena migo palāyati, tasseva so bhāro”ti. Atha tasseva passena migo palāyi, javasampanno rājā dhanuṃ gahetvā pattikova tiyojanaṃ taṃ migaṃ anubandhi. Eṇimigā ca tiyojanavegā eva honti. Atha parikkhīṇajavaṃ taṃ udakaṃ viya pavisitvā ṭhitaṃ vadhitvā dvidhā chetvā anatthikopi maṃsena “nāsakkhi migaṃ gahetu”nti apavādamocanatthaṃ kājenādāya āgacchanto nagarassāvidūre bahalapattapalāsaṃ mahānigrodhaṃ disvā parissamavinodanatthaṃ tassa mūlamupagato. Tasmiñca nigrodhe āḷavako yakkho mahārājasantikā bhavanaṃ labhitvā majjhanhikasamaye tassa rukkhassa chāyāya phuṭṭhokāsaṃ paviṭṭhe pāṇino khādanto paṭivasati. So taṃ disvā khādituṃ upagato. Rājā tena saddhiṃ katikaṃ akāsi – “muñca maṃ, ahaṃ te divase divase manussañca thālipākañca pesessāmī”ti. Yakkho – “tvaṃ rājūpabhogena pamatto na sarissasi, ahaṃ pana bhavanaṃ anupagatañca ananuññātañca khādituṃ na labhāmi, svāhaṃ bhavantampi jīyeyya”nti na muñci. Rājā “yaṃ divasaṃ na pesemi, taṃ divasaṃ maṃ gahetvā khādā”ti attānaṃ anujānitvā tena mutto nagarābhimukho agamāsi.

246. In the twelfth, in the word 'Āḷaviyaṃ', 'Āḷavī' is said to refer to both the country and the city. And that abode was situated not far from the city, at a distance of about a gāvuta. The Blessed One, while dwelling there, relying on that city, is said to dwell in Āḷavī. Regarding 'in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka', this is the sequential account: It is said that the king of Āḷavī, having abandoned various theatrical enjoyments, went hunting every seventh day for the purpose of warding off thieves, for the purpose of deterring rival kings, and for the purpose of making an exertion. One day, he made a pact with his army: 'The one by whose side a deer escapes shall bear the burden.' Then, a deer escaped by his very side. The king, endowed with swiftness, took his bow and, on foot, pursued that deer for three yojanas. And eṇi deer can run for a distance of three yojanas. When its speed was exhausted, it entered the water and stood still. The king killed it, cut it in two, and although he had no need for the meat, to avoid the reproach of 'He was not able to catch the deer,' he took it with a carrying pole and was returning. Not far from the city, seeing a great banyan tree with thick leaves and foliage, for the purpose of dispelling his fatigue, he approached its root. And in that banyan tree, the yakkha named Āḷavaka, having received an abode from the Great Kings, dwelt, devouring at midday any living beings who entered the space touched by the shade of that tree. Seeing the king, he approached in order to devour him. The king made a pact with him: 'Release me. I will send you a person and a pot of cooked rice every day.' The yakkha said: 'You, being heedless due to royal enjoyments, will not remember. As for me, I am not able to devour one who has not approached my abode and who has not been permitted. Thus, I could be overcome even by you,' and he did not release him. The king said, 'On whatever day I do not send someone, on that day, you may seize and devour me.' Having thus given his consent regarding himself, he was released by the yakkha and went towards the city.

Balakāyo magge khandhāvāraṃ bandhitvā ṭhito rājānaṃ disvā, “kiṃ, mahārāja, ayasamattabhayā evaṃ kilantosī”ti? Vadanto paccuggantvā paṭiggahesi. Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ anārocetvā nagaraṃ gantvā katapātarāso nagaraguttikaṃ āmantetvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Nagaraguttiko – “kiṃ, deva[P 1.0318], kālaparicchedo kato”ti āha? Na kato bhaṇeti. Duṭṭhu kataṃ, deva, amanussā hi paricchinnamattameva labhanti, aparicchinne pana janapadassābādho bhavissati, hotu deva, kiñcāpi evamakāsi, appossukko tvaṃ rajjasukhamanubhohi, ahamettha kātabbaṃ karissāmīti. So kālasseva vuṭṭhāya bandhanāgāradvāre ṭhatvā ye ye vajjhā honti, te te sandhāya “yo jīvitatthiko, so nikkhamatū”ti [M 1.0291] bhaṇati. Yo paṭhamaṃ nikkhamati, taṃ gehaṃ [V 1.0279] netvā nhāpetvā bhojetvā ca “imaṃ thālipākaṃ yakkhassa dehī”ti peseti. Taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ paviṭṭhamattaṃyeva yakkho bheravaṃ attabhāvaṃ nimminitvā mūlakandaṃ viya khādi. Yakkhānubhāvena kira manussānaṃ kesādīni upādāya sakalasarīraṃ navanītapiṇḍaṃ viya hoti, yakkhassa bhattaṃ gāhāpetuṃ gatapurisā taṃ disvā bhītā yathāmittaṃ ārocesuṃ. Tato pabhuti “rājā core gahetvā yakkhassa detī”ti manussā corakammato paṭiviratā. Tato aparena samayena navacorānaṃ abhāvena purāṇacorānañca parikkhayena bandhanāgārāni suññāni ahesuṃ.

The army, having set up a camp on the road, stood there. Upon seeing the king, they went forward to welcome and receive him, saying, 'Why, great king, are you so weary from the mere fear of disgrace?' The king, without informing anyone of the matter, went to the city. After having his morning meal, he summoned the city guardian and informed him of this matter. The city guardian asked, 'What, lord, was a time limit set?' 'It was not set, minister,' replied the king. 'It was wrongly done, lord. For non-humans only obtain what has been allotted to them. If it is unallotted, an affliction will befall the countryside. Let it be, lord. Even if you have acted thus, be without anxiety and enjoy the happiness of kingship. I will do what needs to be done in this matter.' Then, rising very early, he stood at the prison gate and, with reference to those who were to be executed, said, 'Whoever wishes to live, let him come out.' The first one to come out, he had taken to a house, bathed, and fed, and then sent him with the words, 'Give this pot of cooked rice to the yakkha.' As soon as that man entered the foot of the tree, the yakkha, having manifested a terrifying form, devoured him like a root-bulb. By the yakkha's power, it is said, the entire body of a human, beginning with the hair, becomes like a lump of fresh butter. The men who had gone to have the yakkha's meal delivered, seeing this, were terrified and reported it to their associates. From then on, thinking, 'The king captures thieves and gives them to the yakkha,' people refrained from the act of thievery. Therefore, at a later time, due to the absence of new thieves and the dwindling of old thieves, the prisons became empty.

Atha nagaraguttiko rañño ārocesi. Rājā attano dhanaṃ nagararacchāsu chaḍḍāpesi “appeva nāma koci lobhena gaṇheyyā”ti. Taṃ pādenapi koci nacchupi. So core alabhanto amaccānaṃ ārocesi. Amaccā “kulapaṭipāṭiyā ekamekaṃ jiṇṇakaṃ pesema, so pakatiyāpi maccupathe vattatī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā “amhākaṃ pitaraṃ amhākaṃ pitāmahaṃ pesetīti manussā khobhaṃ karissanti, mā vo etaṃ ruccī”ti vāresi. “Tena hi, deva, dārakaṃ pesema uttānaseyyakaṃ, tathāvidhassa hi ‘mātā me’ti ‘pitā me’ti sineho natthī”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā anujāni. Te tathā akaṃsu. Nagare dārakamātaro ca dārake gahetvā gabbhiniyo ca palāyitvā parajanapade dārake saṃvaḍḍhetvā ānenti. Evaṃ dvādasa vassāni gatāni.

Then the city guard reported to the king. The king had his wealth scattered in the city streets, thinking, 'Perhaps someone might take it out of greed.' But no one even touched it with his foot. Not finding any thieves, he informed his ministers. The ministers said, 'Let us send one old man from each family in turn, for he is naturally on the path to death anyway.' The king forbade it, saying, 'People will be disturbed, thinking, "He is sending our fathers, our grandfathers." Do not let this be agreeable to you.' 'Then, Your Majesty, let us send an infant who is still lying on its back, for such a one has no affection, thinking "This is my mother" or "This is my father,"' they said. The king consented. They did so. In the city, mothers of children took their children and fled, and pregnant women also fled. They raised the children in a foreign land and brought them back. Thus, twelve years passed.

Tato ekadivasaṃ sakalanagaraṃ vicinitvā [P 1.0319] ekampi dārakaṃ alabhitvā amaccā rañño ārocesuṃ – “natthi, deva, nagare dārako ṭhapetvā antepure tava puttaṃ āḷavakakumāra”nti. Rājā “yathā mama putto piyo, evaṃ sabbalokassa, attanā pana piyataraṃ natthi, gacchatha tampi datvā mama jīvitaṃ rakkhathā”ti. Tena ca samayena āḷavakassa mātā puttaṃ nhāpetvā maṇḍetvā dukūlacumbaṭake katvā aṅke sayāpetvā nisinnā hoti. Rājapurisā rañño āṇāya tattha gantvā vippalapantiyā tassā soḷasannañca devisahassānaṃ saddhiṃ dhātiyā taṃ ādāya pakkamiṃsu, “sve yakkhabhakkho bhavissatī”ti. Taṃdivasañca bhagavā paccūsasamayaṃ paccuṭṭhāya [M 1.0292] jetavanavihāre gandhakuṭiyaṃ mahākaruṇāsamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ olokento addasa āḷavakassa kumārassa anāgāmiphaluppattiyā upanissayaṃ yakkhassa ca sotāpattiphaluppattiyā, desanāpariyosāne ca caturāsītipāṇasahassānaṃ dhammacakkhupaṭilābhassāti. So vibhātāya rattiyā purimabhattakiccaṃ katvā suniṭṭhitapacchābhattakicco kāḷapakkhūposathadivase vattamāne oggate sūriye eko adutiyo pattacīvaramādāya pādamaggeneva sāvatthito tiṃsa yojanāni [V 1.0280] gantvā tassa yakkhassa bhavanaṃ pāvisi. Tena vuttaṃ “āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavane”ti.

Then one day, after searching the entire city and not finding even a single child, the ministers reported to the king: 'Your Majesty, there is no child in the city, except for your son, Prince Āḷavaka, in the palace.' The king said: 'Just as my son is dear to me, so it is for all the world. However, there is nothing dearer than oneself. Go, give him also and protect my life.' And at that time, Āḷavaka’s mother, having bathed and adorned her son and made a bundle of fine cloth, was sitting with him lying on her lap. The king’s men, by the king’s command, went there and, while she and the sixteen thousand queens were wailing, took the prince together with his nurse and departed, saying, 'Tomorrow he will be the yakkha’s food.' And on that day, at dawn, the Blessed One, having arisen in the Perfumed Chamber in the Jetavana monastery and entered the attainment of great compassion, while surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw the supporting condition for Prince Āḷavaka's attainment of the fruit of non-returning, for the yakkha's attainment of the fruit of stream-entry, and for the gaining of the Dhamma-eye by eighty-four thousand beings at the conclusion of the discourse. When the night had become light, he, having performed his pre-meal duties and with his post-meal duties well-completed, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, when the sun had set, alone and without a companion, took his bowl and robe, and having traveled thirty yojanas from Sāvatthī on foot, entered the dwelling of that yakkha. Therefore it was said: 'in the dwelling of the yakkha Āḷavaka.'

Kiṃ pana bhagavā yasmiṃ nigrodhe āḷavakassa bhavanaṃ, tassa mūle vihāsi, udāhu bhavaneyevāti? Bhavaneyeva. Yatheva hi yakkhā attano bhavanaṃ passanti, tathā bhagavāpi. So tattha gantvā bhavanadvāre aṭṭhāsi. Tadā āḷavako himavante yakkhasamāgamaṃ gato hoti. Tato āḷavakassa dvārapālo gadrabho nāma yakkho bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā, “kiṃ, bhante, bhagavā vikāle āgato”ti āha. Āma, gadrabha, āgatomhi, sace te agaru, vihareyyāmekarattaṃ āḷavakassa bhavaneti[P 1.0320]. Na me, bhante, garu, apica kho so yakkho kakkhaḷo pharuso, mātāpitūnampi abhivādanādīni na karoti, mā rucci bhagavato idha vāsoti. Jānāmi, gadrabha, tassa sabhāvaṃ, na koci mamantarāyo bhavissati. Sace te agaru, vihareyyāmekarattanti.

But did the Blessed One dwell at the root of that banyan tree where the mansion of Āḷavaka was, or did he dwell in the mansion itself? He dwelt in the mansion itself. For just as the yakkhas see their own mansion, so too does the Blessed One. He went there and stood at the door of the mansion. At that time, Āḷavaka had gone to an assembly of yakkhas in the Himālaya. Then Āḷavaka's gatekeeper, a yakkha named Gadrabha, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said, “Venerable Sir, has the Blessed One come at an untimely hour?” “Yes, Gadrabha, I have come. If it is not a burden to you, I would dwell for one night in Āḷavaka's mansion.” “It is no burden to me, Venerable Sir, but that yakkha is harsh and rough—he does not even pay homage to his own parents. May it not be agreeable to the Blessed One to dwell here.” “I know his nature, Gadrabha. No harm will come to me. If it is not a burden to you, I would dwell for one night.”

Dutiyampi gadrabho yakkho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “aggitattakapālasadiso, bhante, āḷavako, mātāpitaroti vā samaṇabrāhmaṇāti vā dhammoti vā na jānāti, idhāgatānaṃ pana cittakkhepampi karoti, hadayampi phāleti, pādepi gahetvā parasamuddaṃ vā paracakkavāḷaṃ vā khipatī”ti. Dutiyampi bhagavā āha – “jānāmi, gadrabha, sacepi te agaru, vihareyyāmekaratta”nti. Na me, bhante, garu, apica kho so yakkho attano anārocetvā anujānantaṃ maṃ jīvitāpi voropeyya, ārocemi, bhante, tassāti. Yathāsukhaṃ[M 1.0293], gadrabha, ārocehīti. “Tena hi, bhante, tvameva jānāhī”ti bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā himavantābhimukho pakkāmi. Bhavanadvārampi sayameva bhagavato vivaramadāsi. Bhagavā antobhavanaṃ pavisitvā yattha abhilakkhitesu maṅgaladivasādīsu nisīditvā āḷavako siriṃ anubhoti, tasmiṃyeva dibbaratanamaye pallaṅke nisīditvā suvaṇṇābhaṃ muñci. Taṃ disvā yakkhassa itthiyo āgantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā samparivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Bhagavā “pubbe tumhe dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ samādiyitvā pūjaneyyaṃ pūjetvā imaṃ sampattiṃ pattā, idānipi tatheva karotha, mā aññamaññaṃ issāmacchariyābhibhūtā viharathā”tiādinā nayena tāsaṃ pakiṇṇakadhammakathaṃ kathesi. Tā bhagavato madhuranigghosaṃ sutvā sādhukārasahassāni datvā bhagavantaṃ samparivāretvā nisīdiṃsuyeva. Gadrabhopi himavantaṃ gantvā āḷavakassārocesi – “yagghe[V 1.0281], mārisa, jāneyyāsi vimāne te bhagavā nisinno”ti. So gadrabhassa saññaṃ akāsi “tuṇhī hohi, gantvā kattabbaṃ karissāmī”ti. Purisamānena kira lajjito ahosi, tasmā “mā koci parisamajjhe suṇeyyā”ti evamakāsi.

For the second time, Gadrabha the yakkha addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, Āḷavaka is like a fire-heated potsherd. He does not recognize mother or father, or ascetics or brahmins, or the Dhamma. For those who come here, he causes madness of the mind, splits their hearts, and seizing them by the feet, hurls them to the other side of the ocean or to the other side of the world-system." For the second time, the Blessed One said: "I know, Gadrabha. If it is not burdensome to you, I will stay for one night." "Venerable sir, it is not burdensome to me. However, that yakkha might deprive me of life for giving permission without having informed him. Venerable sir, I will inform him." "Inform him as you please, Gadrabha." "Well then, venerable sir, you yourself should know." Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he set off toward the Himavanta. The door of the mansion also opened by itself for the Blessed One. The Blessed One entered the mansion and sat on the very same divine jeweled couch where Āḷavaka would sit on auspicious days and other such occasions to enjoy his glory. He released a golden radiance. Seeing this, the yakkha's women approached, paid homage to the Blessed One, surrounded him, and sat down. The Blessed One gave them a miscellaneous Dhamma talk, saying: "In the past, you gave gifts, undertook virtuous precepts, and honored those worthy of honor, thereby attaining this prosperity. Now, continue in the same way. Do not dwell overcome by jealousy and stinginess toward one another." Hearing the sweet, resounding voice of the Blessed One, they gave thousands of joyful acclamations, surrounded the Blessed One, and remained seated. Gadrabha also went to the Himavanta and informed Āḷavaka: "Good sir, may you know—the Blessed One is seated in your mansion." He made a sign to Gadrabha: "Be silent. I will go and do what must be done." It is said that he was ashamed with the pride of a man; therefore, he acted thus so that no one in the midst of the assembly would hear.

Tadā sātāgirahemavatā bhagavantaṃ jetavaneyeva vanditvā “yakkhasamāgamaṃ gamissāmā”ti saparivārā nānāyānehi [P 1.0321] ākāsena gacchanti. Ākāse ca yakkhānaṃ sabbattha maggo natthi, ākāsaṭṭhāni vimānāni pariharitvā maggaṭṭhāneneva maggo hoti. Āḷavakassa pana vimānaṃ bhūmaṭṭhaṃ suguttaṃ pākāraparikkhittaṃ susaṃvihitadvāraaṭṭālakagopuraṃ upari kaṃsajālasañchannaṃ mañjūsasadisaṃ tiyojanaṃ ubbedhena, tassa upari maggo hoti. Te taṃ padesamāgamma gantuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Buddhānaṃ hi nisinnokāsassa uparibhāgena yāva bhavaggā koci gantuṃ na sakkoti. Te “kimida”nti? Āvajjetvā bhagavantaṃ disvā ākāse khittaleḍḍu viya oruyha vanditvā dhammaṃ sutvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, “yakkhasamāgamaṃ gacchāma bhagavā”ti tīṇi vatthūni pasaṃsantā yakkhasamāgamaṃ agamaṃsu. Āḷavako te disvā, “idha nisīdathā”ti paṭikkamma okāsamadāsi. Te āḷavakassa nivedesuṃ – “lābhā te, āḷavaka, yassa te bhavane bhagavā viharati, gacchāvuso, bhagavantaṃ payirupāsassū”ti. Evaṃ bhagavā bhavaneyeva vihāsi, na yasmiṃ nigrodhe [M 1.0294] āḷavakassa bhavanaṃ, tassa mūleti. Tena vuttaṃ – “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā āḷaviyaṃ viharati āḷavakassa yakkhassa bhavane”ti.

Then Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One at Jetavana, set out with their retinue in various vehicles through the sky, saying, 'We will go to the gathering of yakkhas.' Now in the sky, there is no path everywhere for yakkhas; a path exists only by avoiding the celestial mansions stationed there. But Āḷavaka’s mansion was on the ground, well-guarded, surrounded by walls, with well-arranged gates, watchtowers, and turrets, covered above with a bronze net, resembling a casket, three leagues in height. Above it was the path. When they reached that place, they could not proceed further. For no one can pass above the space where a Buddha has sat, even up to the peak of existence. Wondering, 'What is this?' they reflected and saw the Blessed One. Descending like a thrown clod through the sky, they paid homage, listened to the Dhamma, and circumambulated him. Then, saying, 'We are going to the gathering of yakkhas, Blessed One,' and praising the Three Jewels, they went to the gathering of yakkhas. Āḷavaka, seeing them, said, 'Sit here,' stepped back and offered them a seat. They informed Āḷavaka, 'You are fortunate, Āḷavaka, that the Blessed One dwells in your mansion. Go, friend, and attend upon the Blessed One.' Thus, the Blessed One remained in the mansion, not at the root of the banyan tree where Āḷavaka’s dwelling was. Therefore, it is said: 'Once the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī in the mansion of the yakkha Āḷavaka.'

Atha kho āḷavako…pe… etadavoca – “nikkhama, samaṇā”ti kasmā panāyaṃ etadavoca? Rosetukāmatāya. Tatrevaṃ ādito pabhuti sambandho veditabbo – ayaṃ hi yasmā assaddhassa saddhākathā dukkathā hoti dussīlādīnaṃ sīlādikathā viya, tasmā tesaṃ yakkhānaṃ santikā bhagavato pasaṃsaṃ sutvāyeva aggimhi pakkhittaloṇasakkharā viya abbhantare kopena taṭataṭāyamānahadayo hutvā “ko so bhagavā nāma, yo mama bhavanaṃ paviṭṭho”ti āha. Te ahaṃsu – “na tvaṃ, āvuso, jānāsi bhagavantaṃ amhākaṃ satthāraṃ, yo tusitabhavane ṭhito pañcamahāvilokitaṃ viloketvā”tiādinā nayena yāva dhammacakkapavattanā kathentā paṭisandhiādīsu dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni vatvā, “imānipi tvaṃ, āvuso, acchariyāni nāddasā”ti? Codesuṃ. So disvāpi kodhavasena “nāddasa”nti āha. Āvuso āḷavaka, passeyyāsi vā tvaṃ, na vā, ko tayā attho passatā vā apassatā [P 1.0322] vā? Kiṃ tvaṃ karissasi [V 1.0282] amhākaṃ satthuno, yo tvaṃ taṃ upanidhāya calakkakudha-mahāusabhasamīpe tadahujātavacchako viya, tidhā pabhinnamattavāraṇasamīpe bhiṅkapotako viya, bhāsuravilambitakesarasobhitakkhandhassa migarañño samīpe jarasiṅgālo viya, diyaḍḍhayojanasatapavaḍḍhakāyasupaṇṇarājasamīpe chinnapakkhakākapotako viya khāyasi, gaccha yaṃ te karaṇīyaṃ, taṃ karohīti. Evaṃ vutte duṭṭho āḷavako uṭṭhahitvā manosilātale vāmapādena ṭhatvā – “passatha dāni tumhākaṃ vā satthā mahānubhāvo, ahaṃ vā”ti dakkhiṇapādena saṭṭhiyojanamattaṃ kelāsapabbatakūṭaṃ akkami. Taṃ ayokūṭapahaṭo viya niddhantaayopiṇḍo papaṭikāyo muñci, so tatra ṭhatvā, “ahaṃ āḷavako”ti ugghosesi. Sakalajambudīpaṃ saddo phari.

Then Āḷavaka… and so on… said, “Depart, ascetic!” But why did he say this? Out of a desire to anger him. In this regard, the connection should be understood thus from the beginning: for just as talk of virtue is unpleasant talk to the virtueless, so too is talk of faith unpleasant talk to the faithless. Therefore, upon hearing the praise of the Blessed One from those yakkhas, his heart crackled with anger within him, like a salt crystal thrown into a fire, and he said, “Who is this Blessed One who has entered my dwelling?” They replied, “Friend, do you not know the Blessed One, our Teacher, who, standing in the Tusita realm, surveyed the five great surveyings,” and so on, up to the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, relating the thirty-two premonitory signs at the time of conception and so forth. They urged him, “Friend, have you not seen these wonders too?” Although he had seen them, out of anger, he said, “I have not seen.” “Friend Āḷavaka, you may see or you may not; what use is it whether you see or not? What can you do to our Teacher? Compared to him, you are like a calf born that very day beside a great bull with a large, moving hump; like a young elephant beside a rutting elephant with musth flowing in three streams; like an old jackal beside the king of beasts, the lion, whose shoulders are adorned with a radiant, flowing mane; like a young crow with broken wings beside the Supaṇṇa king whose body is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. Go, do what you must.” When this was said, the enraged Āḷavaka rose up, stood on the Manosilā plateau with his left foot, and said, “Now see whether your Teacher is of great power, or I am,” and with his right foot, he stepped on the sixty-yojana peak of Mount Kelāsa. That peak shed layers, like a red-hot iron ball struck by an iron hammer. Standing there, he roared, “I am Āḷavaka!” The sound spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa.

Cattāro kira saddā sakalajambudīpe sūyiṃsu – yañca puṇṇako yakkhasenāpati dhanañjayakorabyarājānaṃ jūtaṃ jinitvā apphoṭetvā “ahaṃ jini”nti ugghosesi; yañca sakko devānamindo kassapabhagavato sāsane osakkante vissakammadevaputtaṃ sunakhaṃ karitvā – “ahaṃ pāpabhikkhū ca [M 1.0295] pāpabhikkhuniyo ca upāsake ca upāsikāyo ca sabbeva ca adhammavādino khādāmī”ti ugghosāpesi; yañca kusajātake pabhāvatihetu sattahi rājūhi nagare uparuddhe pabhāvatiṃ attanā saha hatthikkhandhe āropetvā nagarā nikkhamma – “ahaṃ sīhassaramahākusarājā”ti mahāpuriso ugghosesi; yañca kelāsamuddhani ṭhatvā āḷavakoti. Tadā hi sakalajambudīpe dvāre ṭhatvā ugghositasadisaṃ ahosi. Tiyojanasahassavitthato ca himavāpi saṅkampi yakkhassānubhāvena.

It is said that four sounds were heard throughout all of Jambudīpa: the sound of the yakkha commander Puṇṇaka who, having defeated King Dhanañjayakorabya in a game of dice, clapped his hands and shouted, “I have won!”; and the sound when Sakka, lord of the devas, during the decline of the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa, had the devaputta Vissakamma take the form of a great black dog and proclaim, “I will devour the evil monks, evil nuns, evil male lay followers, evil female lay followers, and all who speak what is not the Dhamma!”; and the sound in the Kusa Jātaka, when, on account of Pabhāvatī, seven kings besieged the city, and the great being, placing Pabhāvatī with himself on an elephant’s back, departed from the city and shouted, “I am the great King Kusa of the lion’s roar!”; and the sound of Āḷavaka shouting from the summit of Mount Kelāsa. At that time, indeed, it was as if a proclamation had been shouted from the doorways throughout all of Jambudīpa. And by the power of the yakkha, even the Himavanta, three thousand yojanas in breadth, trembled.

So vātamaṇḍalaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi – “eteneva samaṇaṃ palāpessāmī”ti[P 1.0323]. Te puratthimādibhedā vātā samuṭṭhahitvā aḍḍhayojanayojanadviyojanatiyojanappamāṇāni pabbatakūṭāni padāletvā vanagaccharukkhādīni ummūlaṃ katvā, āḷavinagaraṃ pakkhantā jiṇṇahatthisālādīni cuṇṇentā chadaniṭṭhakā ākāse vidhamentā. Bhagavā “mā kassaci uparodho hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Te vātā dasabalaṃ patvā cīvarakaṇṇamattampi cāletuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tato mahāvassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. “Udakena ajjhottharitvā samaṇaṃ māressāmī”ti. Tassānubhāvena uparūpari satapaṭalasahassapaṭalādibhedā valāhakā uṭṭhahitvā pavassiṃsu. Vuṭṭhidhārāvegena pathavī chiddā ahosi. Vanarukkhādīnaṃ upari mahogho āgantvā dasabalassa cīvare ussāvabindumattampi temetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tato pāsāṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Mahantāni mahantāni pabbatakūṭāni dhūmāyantāni [V 1.0283] pajjalantāni ākāsenāgantvā dasabalaṃ patvā dibbamālāguḷāni sampajjiṃsu. Tato paharaṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Ekatodhārāubhatodhārāasisattikhurappādayo dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalaṃ patvā dibbapupphāni ahesuṃ. Tato aṅgāravassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Kiṃsuka vaṇṇā aṅgārā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā vikīrayiṃsu. Tato kukkulavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Accuṇhā kukkulā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle candanacuṇṇaṃ hutvā nipatiṃsu. Tato vālikavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Atisukhumavālikā dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā nipatiṃsu. Tato kalalavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ kalalavassaṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbagandhaṃ hutvā nipati. Tato [M 1.0296] andhakāraṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “bhiṃsetvā samaṇaṃ palāpessāmī”ti. Taṃ caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ andhakārasadisaṃ hutvā dasabalaṃ patvā sūriyappabhāvihatamiva andhakāraṃ antaradhāyi.

He stirred up a windstorm, thinking, “With this, I will drive away the ascetic.” Winds arose from the east and other directions, shattering mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas, uprooting forest trees and groves. They swept toward Āḷavī, crushing old elephant sheds and scattering roof tiles into the sky. The Blessed One resolved, “May no harm come to anyone.” Those winds, upon reaching the Ten-Powered One, could not even stir the edge of his robe. Then he conjured a great rainstorm, thinking, “I will overwhelm the ascetic with water and kill him.” By his power, clouds arose layer upon layer—hundreds and thousands of layers—and poured down rain. The force of the downpour perforated the earth. A great flood came over the forest trees and such, but it could not moisten even a dewdrop on the Ten-Powered One’s robe. Next, he conjured a shower of stones. Massive mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came hurtling through the sky toward the Ten-Powered One but turned into divine flower garlands upon reaching him. Then he conjured a shower of weapons. Single-edged and double-edged swords, spears, razors, and other weapons, smoking and blazing, came through the sky toward the Ten-Powered One but became divine flowers. Next, he conjured a shower of embers. Embers the color of the kiṃsuka flower rained from the sky, but upon reaching the Ten-Powered One’s feet, they scattered as divine flowers. Then he conjured a shower of hot ashes. Extremely hot ashes fell from the sky but turned into sandalwood powder at the Ten-Powered One’s feet. Next, he conjured a shower of sand. Extremely fine, smoking, blazing sand poured from the sky but became divine flowers at the Ten-Powered One’s feet. Then he conjured a shower of mud. That smoking, blazing mud fell from the sky but turned into divine fragrance at the Ten-Powered One’s feet. Finally, he conjured darkness, thinking, “I will terrify the ascetic and drive him away.” That darkness, like a four-factored darkness, upon reaching the Ten-Powered One, vanished as if dispelled by the sun’s radiance.

Evaṃ yakkho imāhi navahi vātavassapāsāṇapaharaṇaṅgārakukkulavālikakalalandhakāravuṭṭhīhi [P 1.0324] bhagavantaṃ palāpetuṃ asakkonto nānāvidhapaharaṇahatthāya anekappakārarūpabhūtagaṇasamākulāya caturaṅginiyā senāya sayameva bhagavantaṃ abhigato. Te bhūtagaṇā anekappakāre vikāre katvā “gaṇhatha hanathā”ti bhagavato upari āgacchantā viya honti. Apica kho niddhantalohapiṇḍaṃ viya makkhikā, bhagavantaṃ allīyituṃ asamatthāva ahesuṃ. Evaṃ santepi yathā bodhimaṇḍe māro āgatavelāyameva nivatto, tathā anivattetvā upaḍḍharattimattaṃ byākulamakaṃsu. Evaṃ upaḍḍharattimattaṃ anekappakāravibhiṃsanakadassanenapi bhagavantaṃ cāletuṃ asakkonto āḷavako cintesi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ kenaci ajeyyaṃ dussāvudhaṃ muñceyya”nti.

Thus, the yakkha, unable to make the Blessed One flee with these nine rains of wind, rain, rocks, weapons, embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness, approached the Blessed One himself with a fourfold army teeming with hordes of spirits of various forms, armed with many kinds of weapons. Those hordes of spirits, creating various terrifying transformations, acted as if they were coming upon the Blessed One to seize and strike him. Yet, like flies on a red-hot iron ball, they were utterly incapable of clinging to the Blessed One. Even so, unlike Māra who retreated at the very moment of his arrival at the Bodhi terrace, they, without retreating, created a disturbance for about half the night. Thus, being unable to shake the Blessed One for about half the night even by showing many kinds of terrifying sights, Āḷavaka thought: 'What if I were to unleash the cloth-weapon, which is invincible by anyone?'

Cattāri kira āvudhāni loke seṭṭhāni – sakkassa vajirāvudhaṃ, vessavaṇassa gadāvudhaṃ, yamassa nayanāvudhaṃ, āḷavakassa dussāvudhanti. Yadi hi sakko duṭṭho vajirāvudhaṃ sinerumatthake pahareyya, aṭṭhasaṭṭhisahassādhikayojanasatasahassaṃ vinivijjhitvā heṭṭhato gaccheyya. Vessavaṇena kujjhanakāle vissajjitaṃ gadāvudhaṃ bahūnaṃ yakkhasahassānaṃ sīsaṃ pātetvā puna hatthapāsaṃ āgantvā tiṭṭhati. Yamena duṭṭhena nayanāvudhena olokitamatte anekāni kumbhaṇḍasahassāni tattakapāle tilā viya pharantāni vinassanti. Āḷavako duṭṭho sace ākāse dussāvudhaṃ muñceyya, dvādasa vassāni devo na vasseyya. Sace pathaviyaṃ muñceyya. Sabbarukkhatiṇādīni sussitvā [V 1.0284] dvādasavassantare na puna viruheyyuṃ. Sace samudde muñceyya, tattakapāle udakabindu viya sabbamudakaṃ susseyya. Sace sinerusadisepi pabbate muñceyya, khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ hutvā vikireyya. So evaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ dussāvudhaṃ uttarisāṭakaṃ muñcitvā aggahesi. Yebhuyyena dasasahassīlokadhātudevatā vegena sannipatiṃsu “ajja [M 1.0297][P 1.0325] bhagavā āḷavakaṃ damessati, tattha dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti yuddhadassanakāmāpi devatā sannipatiṃsu. Evaṃ sakalampi ākāsaṃ devatāhi paripuṇṇamahosi.

It is said that there are four supreme weapons in the world: Sakka’s thunderbolt weapon, Vessavaṇa’s club weapon, Yama’s gaze weapon, and Āḷavaka’s cloth weapon. For if Sakka, in anger, were to strike the peak of Mount Sineru with his thunderbolt weapon, it would pierce through one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas and pass beneath. When Vessavaṇa releases his club weapon in anger, it knocks off the heads of many thousands of yakkhas and then returns to his hand. When Yama looks with his angry gaze weapon, many thousands of kumbhaṇḍas perish, sputtering like sesame seeds on a hot pan. If Āḷavaka, in anger, were to release his cloth weapon into the sky, no rain would fall for twelve years. If he were to release it upon the earth, all trees and grass would wither and would not sprout again for twelve years. If he were to release it into the ocean, all the water would dry up like a drop of water on a hot pan. If he were to release it upon a mountain like Sineru, it would shatter into fragments. He, unfurling his upper robe, which was such a mighty cloth weapon, grasped it. For the most part, the deities from the ten-thousandfold world-system swiftly gathered, thinking, 'Today the Blessed One will tame Āḷavaka; there we shall hear the Dhamma,' and deities eager to witness the battle also assembled. Thus, the entire sky became completely filled with deities.

Atha āḷavako bhagavato samīpe uparūpari vicaritvā vatthāvudhaṃ muñci. Taṃ asanivicakkaṃ viya ākāse bheravasaddaṃ karontaṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ bhagavantaṃ patvā yakkhamānamaddanatthaṃ pādapuñchanacoḷaṃ hutvā pādamūle nipati. Āḷavako taṃ disvā chinnavisāṇo viya usabho uddhatadāṭho viya sappo nittejo nimmado nipatitamānaddhajo hutvā cintesi – “dussāvudhampi me samaṇaṃ nābhibhosi. Kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? “Idaṃ kāraṇaṃ, mettāvihārayutto samaṇo, handa naṃ rosetvā mettāya viyojemī”ti iminā sambandhenetaṃ vuttaṃ – atha kho āḷavako yakkho yena bhagavā…pe… nikkhama samaṇāti. Tatthāyamadhippāyo – kasmā mayā ananuññāto mama bhavanaṃ pavisitvā gharasāmiko viya itthāgārassa majjhe nisinnosi? Ananuyuttametaṃ samaṇassa yadidaṃ adinnaparibhogo itthisaṃsaggo ca? Tasmā yadi tvaṃ samaṇadhamme ṭhito, nikkhama samaṇāti. Eke pana – “etāni aññāni ca pharusavacanāni vatvā evāyaṃ etadavocā”ti bhaṇanti.

Then Āḷavaka, having moved about above near the Blessed One, released his cloth-weapon. That cloth-weapon, like a thunderbolt-wheel in the sky, making a terrifying sound as it smoked and blazed, reached the Blessed One and, for the purpose of crushing the yakkha's pride, became a foot-wiping cloth and fell at his feet. Seeing this, Āḷavaka, like a bull with broken horns, like a snake with fangs extracted, became powerless, without pride, with the banner of his conceit fallen, and he thought: 'Even my cloth-weapon could not overpower the ascetic. What could be the reason?' 'This is the reason: the ascetic is endowed with the dwelling in loving-kindness. Come now, let me provoke him and separate him from his loving-kindness.' It is in this connection that it was said: 'Then the yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One…and said, "Leave, ascetic!"' Therein, this is the intended meaning: 'Why have you entered my dwelling without my permission and are sitting in the midst of my women's quarters like the master of the house? This is improper for an ascetic, namely, this use of what is not given and this association with women. Therefore, if you are established in the ascetic's duty, leave, ascetic!' Some, however, say: 'It was only after speaking these and other harsh words that he said this.'

Atha bhagavā – “yasmā thaddho paṭithaddhabhāvena vinetuṃ na sakkā, so hi paṭithaddhabhāve kayiramāne, seyyathāpi caṇḍassa kukkurassa nāsāya pittaṃ bhindeyya, so bhiyyosomattāya caṇḍataro assa, evaṃ thaddhataro hoti, mudunā pana so sakkā vinetu”nti ñatvā, sādhāvusoti piyavacanena tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā nikkhami. Tena vuttaṃ sādhāvusoti bhagavā nikkhamīti.

Then the Blessed One, knowing: 'Since a harsh person cannot be trained by means of harshness—for if harshness is applied, just as if one were to apply bile to the nose of a fierce dog, it would become even more fierce, so too, he would become even harsher; but with gentleness, he can be trained'—accepted his words with the affectionate address, 'Good, friend,' and departed. Therefore, it is said: 'The Blessed One departed, saying, "Good, friend."

Tato āḷavako – “subbaco vatāyaṃ samaṇo ekavacaneneva nikkhanto, evaṃ nāma nikkhametuṃ sukhaṃ samaṇaṃ akāraṇenevāhaṃ sakalarattiṃ yuddhena abbhuyyāsi”nti muducitto hutvā puna cintesi – “idānipi na sakkā jānituṃ, kiṃ nu kho subbacatāya nikkhanto udāhu kodhano[V 1.0285]. Handāhaṃ [P 1.0326] vīmaṃsāmī”ti. Tato pavisa, samaṇāti āha. Atha subbacoti mudubhūtacittavavatthānakaraṇatthaṃ puna piyavacanaṃ vadanto sādhāvusoti bhagavā [M 1.0298] pāvisi. Āḷavako punappunaṃ tameva subbacabhāvaṃ vīmaṃsanto dutiyampi tatiyampi nikkhama pavisāti āha. Bhagavāpi tathā akāsi. Yadi na kareyya, pakatiyāpi thaddhayakkhassa cittaṃ thaddhataraṃ hutvā dhammakathāya bhājanaṃ na bhaveyya. Tasmā yathā nāma mātā rodantaṃ puttakaṃ yaṃ so icchati, taṃ datvā vā katvā vā saññāpesi tathā bhagavā kilesarodanena rodantaṃ yakkhaṃ saññāpetuṃ yaṃ so bhaṇati, taṃ akāsi. Yathā ca dhātī thaññaṃ apivantaṃ dārakaṃ kiñci datvā upalāḷetvā pāyeti, tathā bhagavā yakkhaṃ lokuttaradhammakhīraṃ pāyetuṃ tassa patthitavacanakaraṇena upalāḷento evamakāsi. Yathā ca puriso lābumhi catumadhuraṃ pūretukāmo tassabbhantaraṃ sodheti, evaṃ bhagavā yakkhassa citte lokuttaracatumadhuraṃ pūretukāmo tassabbhantare kodhamalaṃ sodhetuṃ yāva tatiyaṃ nikkhamanapavisanaṃ akāsi.

Then Āḷavaka thought: 'Indeed, this ascetic is easy to speak to; he departed with just a single word. An ascetic so easy to make depart, and yet for no reason I engaged him in battle all night long.' With a softened heart, he thought again: 'Even now, it is not possible to know—did he depart because he is easy to speak to, or because he is angry? Come now, I shall investigate.' Then he said, 'Enter, ascetic!' And the Blessed One, in order to establish in Āḷavaka's softened mind the conclusion that he was indeed easy to speak to, re-entered while speaking endearing words: 'Very well, friend.' Āḷavaka, wishing to investigate that very state of being easy to speak to again and again, said for a second time and a third time, 'Depart! Enter!' The Blessed One also did so. Had he not done so, the mind of the naturally stubborn yakkha would have become even more stubborn and would not have become a vessel for the Dhamma talk. Therefore, just as a mother pacifies her crying child by giving or doing what it desires, so too the Blessed One, to pacify the yakkha who was crying with the crying of defilements, did what he said. And just as a wet-nurse, by giving something and cajoling a child who does not want to drink milk, makes it drink, so too the Blessed One, to make the yakkha drink the milk of the supramundane Dhamma, acted thus, cajoling him by doing as he requested. And just as a man who wishes to fill a gourd with the fourfold sweet cleans its interior, so too the Blessed One, wishing to fill the yakkha’s mind with the supramundane fourfold sweet, performed the departing and entering up to the third time in order to cleanse the stain of anger from within him.

Atha āḷavako “subbaco ayaṃ samaṇo ‘nikkhamā’ti vutto nikkhamati, ‘pavisā’ti vutto pavisati. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ samaṇaṃ evameva sakalarattiṃ kilametvā pāde gahetvā pāragaṅgāya khipeyya”nti? Pāpakaṃ cittaṃ uppādetvā catutthavāraṃ āha nikkhama, samaṇāti. Taṃ ñatvā bhagavā na khvāhaṃ tanti āha. Evaṃ vā vutte taduttarikaraṇīyaṃ pariyesamāno pañhaṃ pucchitabbaṃ maññissati. Taṃ dhammakathāya mukhaṃ bhavissatīti ñatvā, na khvāhaṃ tanti āha. Tattha na-iti paṭikkhepe. Khoti avadhāraṇe. Ahanti attanidassanaṃ. Tanti hetuvacanaṃ. Tenevettha “yasmā tvaṃ evaṃ cintesi, tasmā ahaṃ, āvuso, neva nikkhamissāmi, yaṃ te karaṇīyaṃ, taṃ karohī”ti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.
