Then the yakkha Āḷavaka thought, 'This ascetic is compliant; when told, "Go out," he goes out; when told, "Enter," he enters. What if I were to weary this ascetic for the entire night in this very way, then, grasping him by the feet, throw him to the far side of the Ganges?' Having given rise to this evil thought, for the fourth time he said, 'Go out, ascetic!' Knowing that, the Blessed One said, 'Indeed, I will not, for that reason.' Or, knowing that when this was said, Āḷavaka, seeking something further to do, would consider that a question should be asked, and that this would be an opening for a Dhamma talk, he said, 'Indeed, I will not, for that reason.' Therein, 'na' is a particle of rejection. 'Kho' is for determination. 'Ahaṃ' is a reference to oneself. 'Taṃ' is a word indicating reason. For that very reason, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'Friend, because you think in this way, therefore I will not go out. Do what you must do.'

Tato āḷavako yasmā pubbepi ākāsena gamanavelāya – “kiṃ nu kho etaṃ suvaṇṇavimānaṃ, udāhu rajatamaṇivimānānaṃ aññataraṃ, handa naṃ passāmā”ti evaṃ attano vimānaṃ āgate iddhimante tāpasaparibbājake pañhaṃ pucchitvā vissajjetuṃ [P 1.0327] asakkonte cittakkhepādīhi viheṭheti, tasmā bhagavantampi tathā viheṭhessāmīti maññamāno pañhaṃ tantiādimāha.

Then, because previously Āḷavaka would harass powerful ascetics and wanderers who, at the time of traveling through the sky, would see his mansion and think, 'What is this? Is it a golden mansion, or is it one of the silver or jewel mansions? Come now, let us see it,' and would thus come to his mansion; having asked them a question, when they were unable to answer, he would harass them by causing mental distraction and so forth. Therefore, thinking, 'I will harass the Blessed One in the same way,' he spoke, beginning with the words, 'A question for you...'

Kuto panassa pañhāti[M 1.0299]? Tassa kira mātāpitaro kassapaṃ bhagavantaṃ payirupāsitvā aṭṭha [V 1.0286] pañhe saha vissajjanena uggahesuṃ. Te daharakāle āḷavakaṃ pariyāpuṇāpesuṃ; so kālaccayena vissajjanaṃ sammussi. Tato “ime pañhāpi mā vinassantū”ti suvaṇṇapaṭṭhe jātihiṅgulakena lekhāpetvā vimāne nikkhipi. Evamete puṭṭhapañhā buddhavisayāva honti. Bhagavā taṃ sutvā yasmā buddhānaṃ pariccattalābhantarāyo vā jīvitantarāyo vā sabbaññutaññāṇabyāmappabhādipaṭighāto vā na sakkā kenaci kātuṃ, tasmā naṃ loke asādhāraṇaṃ buddhānubhāvaṃ dassento na khvāhaṃ taṃ, āvuso, passāmi sadevake loketiādimāha.

From where, then, did his questions come? It is said that his parents, having attended upon the Blessed One Kassapa, learned eight questions along with their answers. While he was still young, they had Āḷavaka learn them; but in the course of time, he forgot the answers. Then, thinking, 'Let these questions not be lost,' they had them inscribed on a golden plate with native vermilion and placed it in the celestial mansion. Thus, these questions that were asked are indeed within the domain of the Buddhas. Hearing this, the Blessed One, showing the unshared power of the Buddhas in the world—since no one can cause an obstruction to the gains relinquished by the Buddhas, a danger to their lives, or an obstruction to the fathom-wide radiance of their omniscient knowledge—said, 'Indeed, friend, I do not see anyone in this world with its gods...' and so on.

Evaṃ bhagavā tassa bādhanacittaṃ paṭisedhetvā pañhāpucchane ussāhaṃ janento āha apica tvaṃ, āvuso, puccha, yadākaṅkhasīti. Tassattho – puccha, yadi ākāṅkhasi, na me pañhāvissajjane bhāro atthi. Atha vā puccha, yaṃ ākaṅkhasi. Sabbaṃ te vissajjessāmīti sabbaññupavāraṇaṃ pavāresi asādhāraṇaṃ paccekabuddhaaggasāvakamahāsāvakehi. Evaṃ bhagavato sabbaññupavāraṇāya pavāritāya atha kho āḷavako yakkho bhagavantaṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi.

Thus, the Blessed One, having prevented his mind bent on harassment and arousing in him an eagerness to ask questions, said: 'Furthermore, friend, ask what you wish.' The meaning of this is: 'Ask, if you wish; for me there is no burden in answering questions.' Or alternatively: 'Ask what you wish. I will answer it all for you.' In this way, he made the omniscient one's invitation, which is unshared with Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, and great disciples. When the Blessed One had thus made the omniscient one's invitation, then the yakkha Āḷavaka addressed the Blessed One in verse.

Tattha kiṃ sūdha vittanti, kiṃ su idha vittaṃ. Vittanti dhanaṃ. Taṃ hi pītisaṅkhātaṃ vittiṃ karoti, tasmā “vitta”nti vuccati. Suciṇṇanti sukataṃ. Sukhanti kāyikacetasikaṃ sātaṃ. Āvahātīti āvahati āneti deti appeti. Have-iti daḷhatthe nipāto. Sādutaranti atisayena sādu. “Sādhutara”ntipi pāṭho. Rasānanti rasasaññitānaṃ dhammānaṃ. Kathanti kena pakārena. Kathaṃjīvino jīvitaṃ kathaṃjīviṃjīvitaṃ. Gāthābandhasukhatthaṃ pana sānunāsikaṃ [P 1.0328] vuccati. Kathaṃjīviṃ jīvatanti vā pāṭho, tassa “jīvantānaṃ kathaṃjīvi”nti attho. Evaṃ imāya gāthāya “kiṃ su idha loke purisassa vittaṃ seṭṭhaṃ? Kiṃ su suciṇṇaṃ sukhamāvahāti? Kiṃ rasānaṃ sādutaraṃ? Kathaṃjīviṃ jīvitaṃ seṭṭhamāhū”ti? Ime cattāro pañhe pucchi.

Herein, `kiṃ sūdha vittaṃ` is to be parsed as `kiṃ su idha vittaṃ` (What indeed is wealth here?). `Vittaṃ` (wealth) means riches. For it creates delight (`vitti`), which is known as joy (`pīti`), therefore it is called 'wealth' (`vitta`). `Suciṇṇaṃ` (well-practiced) means well-done. `Sukhaṃ` (happiness) means physical and mental pleasure. `Āvahāti` (brings) means it brings, fetches, gives, or delivers. The word `have` is a particle in the sense of emphasis. `Sādutaraṃ` (sweeter) means exceedingly pleasant. There is also the reading `sādhutaraṃ`. `Rasānaṃ` (of flavors) means of things known as flavors. `Kathaṃ` (how) means in what manner. The phrase `kathaṃjīviṃ jīvitaṃ` means 'the living of one who lives in what manner'. However, for the sake of ease in reciting the verse, it is spoken with a nasal. There is also the reading `kathaṃjīviṃ jīvataṃ`, the meaning of which is: 'how is the living of those who are living'. Thus, by this verse, these four questions were asked: 'What indeed is a man's best wealth in this world? What, being well-practiced, brings happiness? What is the sweetest of flavors? What manner of living do they call the best?'

Athassa bhagavā kassapadasabalena vissajjitanayeneva vissajjento imaṃ gāthamāha saddhīdha vittanti. Tattha yathā hiraññasuvaṇṇādi vittaṃ upabhogasukhaṃ [M 1.0300] āvahati, khuppipāsādidukkhaṃ paṭibāhati, dāliddiyaṃ vūpasameti, muttādiratanapaṭilābhahetu hoti, lokasantatiñca āvahati, evaṃ lokiyalokuttarā saddhāpi yathāsambhavaṃ lokiyalokuttaraṃ vipākaṃ sukhamāvahati, saddhādhurena paṭipannānaṃ jātijarādidukkhaṃ paṭibāhati, guṇadāliddiyaṃ vūpasameti, satisambojjhaṅgādiratanapaṭilābhahetu hoti.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer him in the very same way that it was answered by Kassapa of the Ten Powers, spoke this verse beginning: 'Faith is wealth here.' Therein, just as wealth such as gold and silver brings the happiness of use and enjoyment, wards off the suffering of hunger and thirst, pacifies poverty, becomes a cause for obtaining jewels such as pearls, and brings about the continuity of the world; so too does mundane and supramundane faith, according to circumstance, bring resultant happiness, both mundane and supramundane. For those who practice with faith as their guide, it wards off the suffering of birth, aging, and so on, pacifies the poverty of virtues, and becomes a cause for obtaining jewels such as the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.

“Saddho [V 1.0287] sīlena sampanno, yaso bhogasamappito;

Yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ bhajati, tattha tattheva pūjito”ti. (dha. pa. 303) –

One who is faithful, endowed with virtue, possessed of fame and wealth; whatever region he resorts to, in that very place he is revered.

Vacanato lokasantatiñca āvahatīti katvā “vitta”nti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pana tesaṃ saddhāvittaṃ anugāmikaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ sabbasampattihetu, lokiyassa hiraññasuvaṇṇādivittassāpi nidānaṃ. Saddhoyeva hi dānādīni puññāni katvā vittaṃ adhigacchati, assaddhassa pana vittaṃ yāvadeva anatthāya hoti, tasmā seṭṭhanti vuttaṃ. Purisassāti ukkaṭṭhaparicchedadesanā. Tasmā na kevalaṃ purisassa, itthiādīnampi saddhāvittameva seṭṭhanti veditabbaṃ.

Because of the saying that it brings forth the continuity of the world, it is called 'wealth'. Furthermore, because for them the wealth of faith is that which accompanies one, is unshared by others, is the cause of all prosperity, and is also the foundation for worldly wealth such as gold and silver. Indeed, it is only one endowed with faith who, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, obtains wealth. For one without faith, however, wealth is only for one's detriment. Therefore, it is said to be the best. The phrase 'for a man' is a teaching that specifies pre-eminence. Therefore, it should be understood that not only for a man, but also for women and others, the wealth of faith is indeed the best.

Dhammoti dasakusaladhammo, dānasīlabhāvanādhammo vā. Suciṇṇoti sukato sucarito. Sukhamāvahatīti soṇaseṭṭhiputtaraṭṭhapālādīnaṃ viya manussasukhaṃ, sakkādīnaṃ viya dibbasukhaṃ, pariyosāne mahāpadumādīnaṃ viya nibbānasukhañca āvahati.

'Dhamma' is the ten wholesome dhammas, or the Dhamma of generosity, virtue, and mental cultivation. 'Well-practiced' means well-done, well-conducted. 'It brings happiness' means it brings forth human happiness, as for Soṇa the merchant's son, Raṭṭhapāla, and others; it brings forth divine happiness, as for Sakka and others; and in the end, it brings forth the happiness of Nibbāna, as for Prince Mahāpaduma and others.

Saccanti ayaṃ saccasaddo anekesu atthesu dissati. Seyyathidaṃ – “saccaṃ bhaṇe na kujjheyyā [P 1.0329]” tiādīsu (dha. pa. 224) vācāsacce. “Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā cā”tiādīsu (jā. 2.21.433) viratisacce. “Kasmā nu saccāni vadanti nānā, pavādiyāse kusalā vadānā”tiādīsu (su. ni. 891) diṭṭhisacce. “Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, brāhmaṇasaccānī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.185) brāhmaṇasacce. “Ekaṃ hi saccaṃ na dutiyamatthī”tiādīsu (su. ni. 890; mahāni. 119) paramatthasacce. “Catunnaṃ saccānaṃ kati kusalā”tiādīsu (vibha. 216) ariyasacce. Idha pana paramatthasaccaṃ nibbānaṃ viratisaccañca abbhantaraṃ katvā [M 1.0301] vācāsaccaṃ adhippetaṃ, yassānubhāvena udakādīni vase vattenti, jātijarāmaraṇapāraṃ taranti. Yathāha –

'Truth'—this word 'truth' is seen in many senses. As follows: in passages such as, 'One should speak the truth, not get angry,' it is in the sense of verbal truth. In passages such as, 'Ascetics and brahmins established in truth,' it is in the sense of the truth of abstinence. In passages such as, 'Why do the disputants, skilled in speaking, proclaim various truths?' it is in the sense of the truth of view. In passages such as, 'Monks, these are the four brahmin-truths,' it is in the sense of the brahmin-truths. In passages such as, 'Indeed, there is one truth, there is not a second,' it is in the sense of the ultimate truth. In passages such as, 'Of the four truths, how many are wholesome?' it is in the sense of the Noble Truths. Here, however, having included the ultimate truth, which is Nibbāna, and the truth of abstinence, verbal truth is intended. By its power, they bring even water and so forth under their control and cross to the far shore of birth, aging, and death. As it was said:

“Saccena vācenudakamhi dhāvati,

Visampi saccena hananti paṇḍitā;

Saccena devo thanayaṃ pavassati,

Sace ṭhitā nibbutiṃ patthayanti.

By a word of truth, one can run upon the water; by truth, the wise overcome even poison; by truth, the deva, thundering, sends down rain; established in truth, they aspire to Nibbāna.

“Ye [V 1.0288] kecime atthi rasā pathabyā,

Saccaṃ tesaṃ sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ;

Sacce ṭhitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca,

Taranti jātimaraṇassa pāra”nti. (jā. 2.21.433);

Whatever flavors exist on the earth, truth is the sweetest of those flavors. Ascetics and brahmins who are established in truth cross to the further shore of birth and death.

Sādutaranti madhurataraṃ paṇītataraṃ. Rasānanti ye ime “mūlaraso khandharaso”tiādinā (dha. sa. 628-630) nayena sāyanīyadhammā, yecime “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ phalarasaṃ (mahāva. 300), arasarūpo bhavaṃ gotamo, ye te, brāhmaṇa, rūparasā saddarasā (pārā. 3; a. ni. 8.11), anāpatti rasarase (pāci. 605-611), ayaṃ dhammavinayo ekaraso vimuttiraso (cūḷava. 385; a. ni. 8.19), bhāgī vā bhagavā attharasassa dhammarasassā”tiādinā (mahāni. 149) nayena rūpācārarasupavajjā avasesā byañjanādayo “dhammarasā”ti vuccanti[P 1.0330]. Tesaṃ rasānaṃ saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ saccameva sādutaraṃ. Sādhutaraṃ vā, seṭṭhataraṃ, uttamataraṃ. Mūlarasādayo hi sarīramupabrūhenti, saṃkilesikañca sukhamāvahanti. Saccarase viratisaccavācāsaccarasā samathavipassanādīhi cittaṃ upabrūheti, asaṃkilesikañca sukhamāvahati. Vimuttiraso paramatthasaccarasaparibhāvitattā sādu, attharasadhammarasā ca tadadhigamūpāyabhūtaṃ atthañca dhammañca nissāya pavattitoti.

Sādutaraṃ means more sweet, more exquisite. By 'flavors' are meant those things that are enjoyable, such as 'the flavor of roots, the flavor of stems,' and so on. And also those which, by the method of such passages as: 'I allow, bhikkhus, all fruit-flavor'; 'The venerable Gotama is without the flavor of form'; 'O brahmin, those flavors of form, flavors of sound'; 'There is no offense in the flavor of a flavor'; 'This Dhamma-Vinaya has a single flavor, the flavor of liberation'; 'The Blessed One partakes of the flavor of meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma,' and so on—excepting the flavors of form and conduct, the remaining things such as letters, words, and sentences are called 'flavors of Dhamma.' Among these flavors, truth is indeed sweeter; truth alone is sweeter. Or, sādutaraṃ means more excellent, more praiseworthy, more supreme. For the flavors of roots and such nourish the body and bring about pleasure tainted by defilements. In the flavor of truth, the flavors of the truth of abstinence and the truth of speech nourish the mind by means of serenity and insight, and bring about undefiled happiness. The flavor of liberation is sweet because it is pervaded by the flavor of ultimate truth. And the flavors of meaning and Dhamma are also sweet because they proceed in dependence on the meaning and the Dhamma which have become the means for its attainment.

Paññājīviṃjīvitanti ettha pana yvāyaṃ andhekacakkhudvicakkhukesu dvicakkhupuggalo gahaṭṭho vā kammantānuṭṭhāna-saraṇagamanadāna-saṃvibhāga-sīlasamādānuposathakammādi gahaṭṭhapaṭipadaṃ, pabbajito vā avippaṭisārakarasīlasaṅkhātaṃ taduttaricittavisuddhiādibhedampi pabbajitapaṭipadaṃ paññāya ārādhetvā jīvati, tassa [M 1.0302] paññāya jīvino jīvitaṃ, taṃ vā paññājīvitaṃ seṭṭhamāhūti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

Here, regarding 'a life lived by wisdom': Among the blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed, there is the person with two eyes who lives by accomplishing with wisdom either the householder's practice—such as undertaking work, going for refuge, giving and sharing, undertaking precepts, and observing the Uposatha—or the renunciant's practice, which is called virtue that causes non-remorse and has further distinctions such as purity of mind. The life of such a one who lives by wisdom, or that life of wisdom, they call the best. Thus the meaning should be understood.

Evaṃ bhagavatā vissajjite cattāropi pañhe sutvā attamano yakkho avasesepi cattāro pañhe pucchanto kathaṃsu tarati oghanti gāthamāha. Athassa bhagavā purimanayeneva vissajjento saddhāya taratīti gāthamāha. Tattha kiñcāpi yo catubbidhamoghaṃ tarati, so saṃsāraṇṇavampi tarati, vaṭṭadukkhampi acceti, kilesamalāpi parisujjhati, evaṃ santepi pana yasmā assaddho oghataraṇaṃ asaddahanto na pakkhandati, pañcasu kāmaguṇesu cittavossaggena pamatto [V 1.0289] tattheva visattattā saṃsāraṇṇavaṃ na tarati, kusīto dukkhaṃ viharati vokiṇṇo akusalehi dhammehi, appañño suddhimaggaṃ ajānanto na parisujjhati, tasmā tappaṭipakkhaṃ dassentena bhagavatā ayaṃ gāthā vuttā.

When the Blessed One had thus answered the four questions, the delighted yakkha, having heard them, wishing to ask the remaining four questions, spoke the verse: "How does one cross the flood?" Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer him in the very same manner as before, spoke the verse: "One crosses by faith." Herein, although one who crosses the fourfold flood also crosses the ocean of saṃsāra, overcomes the suffering of the round of existence, and is purified from the stains of defilements, this being so, however, because the faithless one, not having faith in the crossing of the flood, does not plunge in; being heedless by abandoning the mind to the five strands of sensual pleasure, and because of being stuck right there, does not cross the ocean of saṃsāra; the lazy one, being entangled with unwholesome states, dwells in suffering; and the one without wisdom, not knowing the path to purity, is not purified—therefore, this verse was spoken by the Blessed One to show the opposite of that.

Evaṃ vuttāya cetāya yasmā sotāpattiyaṅgapadaṭṭhānaṃ saddhindriyaṃ, tasmā saddhāya tarati oghanti iminā padena diṭṭhoghataraṇaṃ sotāpattimaggaṃ sotāpannañca pakāseti. Yasmā pana sotāpanno kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanāya sātaccakiriyasaṅkhatena appamādena samannāgato dutiyamaggaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhapetvā sakidevimaṃ [P 1.0331] lokaṃ āgamanamaggaṃ avasesaṃ sotāpattimaggena atiṇṇaṃ bhavoghavatthuṃ saṃsāraṇṇavaṃ tarati, tasmā appamādena aṇṇavanti iminā padena bhavoghataraṇaṃ sakadāgāmimaggaṃ sakadāgāmiñca pakāseti. Yasmā ca sakadāgāmī vīriyena tatiyamaggaṃ ārādhetvā sakadāgāmimaggena anatītaṃ kāmoghavatthuṃ kāmoghasaññitañca kāmadukkhamacceti, tasmā vīriyena dukkhamaccetīti iminā padena kāmoghataraṇaṃ anāgāmimaggaṃ anāgāmiñca pakāseti. Yasmā pana anāgāmī vigatakāmasaññāya parisuddhāya paññāya ekantaparisuddhaṃ catutthamaggapaññaṃ ārādhetvā anāgāmimaggena appahīnaṃ avijjāsaṅkhātaṃ paramamalaṃ pajahati, tasmā paññāya parisujjhatīti, iminā padena avijjoghataraṇaṃ arahattamaggañca arahattañca pakāseti. Imāya ca arahattanikūṭena kathitāya gāthāya pariyosāne yakkho sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi.

When this verse was spoken thus, because the faculty of faith is the proximate cause for the factor of attaining the stream-entry path, therefore, by the phrase 'with faith one crosses the flood,' the Blessed One reveals the stream-entry path, which is the means for crossing the flood of views, and the stream-enterer. Furthermore, because a stream-enterer, endowed with diligence—called persistent effort—for the development of wholesome states, having accomplished the second path, crosses the remaining ocean of saṃsāra, the basis of the flood of existence, which was not yet crossed by the stream-entry path; therefore, by the phrase 'by diligence one crosses the ocean,' the Blessed One reveals the once-returner path, which is the means for crossing the flood of existence, and the once-returner. And because the once-returner, by means of energy, having accomplished the third path, overcomes the basis of the flood of sensual desire—the five strands of sensual pleasure along with the entire sensual realm—and the suffering called sensual passion, reckoned as the flood of sensual desire, which was not yet gone beyond by the once-returner path; therefore, by the phrase 'by energy one overcomes suffering,' the Blessed One reveals the non-returner path, which is the means for crossing the flood of sensual desire, and the non-returner. Furthermore, because the non-returner, with wisdom that is thoroughly purified and has sensual perception departed, having accomplished the completely pure wisdom of the fourth path, abandons the supreme stain called ignorance, which was not yet abandoned by the non-returner path; therefore, by the phrase 'by wisdom one is purified,' the Blessed One reveals the Arahant path, which is the means for crossing the flood of ignorance, and Arahantship. And at the conclusion of this verse, spoken with Arahantship as its pinnacle, the yakkha became established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Idāni [M 1.0303] tameva “paññāya parisujjhatī”ti ettha vuttaṃ paññāpadaṃ gahetvā attano paṭibhānena lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ pañhaṃ pucchanto kathaṃsu labhate paññanti imaṃ chappadaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha kathaṃsūti sabbattheva atthayuttipucchā honti. Ayaṃ hi paññādiatthaṃ ñatvā tassa yuttiṃ pucchati – “kathaṃ, kāya yuttiyā, kena kāraṇena paññaṃ labhatī”ti? Esa nayo dhanādīsu.

Now, taking up that same word 'wisdom' (paññā), mentioned in 'one is purified by wisdom,' and asking a question based on his own insight about a matter mixing the mundane and the supramundane, he uttered this six-footed verse: 'How does one attain wisdom?' Here, 'how' (kathaṃsu) is always a question seeking the rationale for a meaning. For knowing the meaning of wisdom and the like, he asks about its rationale: 'How, by what rationale, for what reason is wisdom attained?' This is the method regarding wealth and so on.

Athassa bhagavā catūhi kāraṇehi paññālābhaṃ dassento saddahānotiādimāha. Tassattho – yena pubbabhāge kāyasucaritādibhedena aparabhāge ca sattatiṃsabodhipakkhiyabhedena dhammena arahanto buddhapaccekabuddhasāvakā nibbānaṃ pattā, taṃ saddahāno arahataṃ dhammaṃ nibbānapattiyā lokiyalokuttarapaññaṃ labhati, tañca kho na saddhāmattakeneva. Yasmā pana saddhājāto upasaṅkamati[V 1.0290], upasaṅkamanto payirupāsati, payirupāsanto sotaṃ odahati, ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇāti, tasmā upasaṅkamanato pabhuti yāva dhammassavanena sussūsaṃ labhati. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – taṃ dhammaṃ saddahitvāpi ācariyupajjhāye kālena upasaṅkamitvā [P 1.0332] vattakaraṇena payirupāsitvā yadā payirupāsanāya ārādhitacittā kiñci vattukāmā honti. Atha adhigatāya sotukāmatāya sotaṃ odahitvā suṇanto labhatīti. Evaṃ sussūsampi ca satiavippavāsena appamatto subhāsitadubbhāsitaññutāya vicakkhaṇo eva labhati, na itaro. Tenāha “appamatto vicakkhaṇo”ti.

Then, wishing to show the yakkha Āḷavaka the gaining of wisdom for four reasons, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'saddahāno'. The meaning of that Pāli is to be understood thus: By which Dhamma, distinguished in the preliminary stage as good bodily conduct and so forth, and in the later stage as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the Arahants—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, and great disciples—have attained Nibbāna; a person who has faith in that practice-Dhamma of the Arahants for the attainment of Nibbāna obtains mundane and supramundane wisdom. But indeed, one does not yet obtain that mundane and supramundane wisdom by mere faith alone. However, although one does not obtain it thus, because a good person in whom faith has arisen approaches teachers and preceptors; the good person who approaches attends upon them; the good person who attends listens well; the good person who listens well hears the practice-Dhamma. Therefore, from approaching onwards up to the hearing of the Dhamma, one obtains the desire to listen well. What is the meaning that is spoken? It is this: Even having faith in that practice-Dhamma, having approached teachers and preceptors from time to time and attended upon them by performing major and minor duties, when the teachers and preceptors, their minds pleased by this attendance, wish to speak something—some Dhamma concerning the aggregates, elements, sense bases, truths, and dependent origination—then a person who listens, having lent an ear with the desire to hear the Dhamma-talk that is obtained, obtains mundane and supramundane wisdom. This is the meaning that is spoken. Furthermore, even when listening well in this way, only a good person who is discerning—being endowed with diligence, not being devoid of mindfulness, and possessing the skill of knowing what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken—obtains mundane and supramundane wisdom; another person does not. Therefore, the Buddha said, 'diligent and discerning'.

Evaṃ yasmā saddhāya paññalābhasaṃvattanikaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipajjati, sussūsāya sakkaccaṃ paññādhigamūpāyaṃ suṇāti, appamādena gahitaṃ na pamussati. Vicakkhaṇatāya anūnādhikaṃ aviparītañca gahetvā vitthārikaṃ karoti. Sussūsāya vā ohitasoto paññāpaṭilābhahetuṃ dhammaṃ suṇāti, appamādena sutadhammaṃ dhāreti, vicakkhaṇatāya dhatānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthamupaparikkhati, athānupubbena paramatthasaccaṃ sacchikaroti, tasmāssa bhagavā “kathaṃsu labhate pañña”nti puṭṭho imāni cattāri kāraṇāni dassento imaṃ gāthamāha.

Thus, in the manner already stated, because through faith one practises the path that leads to the arising of the gaining of mundane and supramundane wisdom; with the desire to hear well, one respectfully hears the means for attaining the Dhamma of the scriptures; through diligence, the Dhamma that has been grasped is not forgotten; and through being a wise person who investigates and reflects, having grasped the meaning that is neither deficient nor excessive and is undistorted, one makes it extensive. Alternatively, a good person with an attentive ear, through the desire to hear well, hears the Dhamma which is the cause for obtaining mundane and supramundane wisdom; through the quality of diligence, one retains the Dhamma that has been heard; through being a wise person who investigates and reflects, one is able to investigate the undistorted meaning of the Dhammas known by means of hearing and retaining, by way of the general characteristics such as impermanence, the minor general characteristics such as the inclining of mind-and-matter, and the specific characteristics such as hardness and contact; thereafter, by way of the path-sequence, one is able to realize the ultimate truth, which is Nibbāna. Therefore, the Blessed One, being asked by that Āḷavaka yakkha, 'How does one obtain wisdom?', and showing these four causes beginning with faith to their final conclusion, spoke this verse beginning with 'Saddahāno arahaṃ dhammaṃ'.

Idāni [M 1.0304] tato pare tayo pañhe vissajjento patirūpakārīti imaṃ gāthamāha. Tattha desakālādīni ahāpetvā lokiyassa lokuttarassa vā dhanassa patirūpaṃ adhigamūpāyaṃ karotīti patirūpakārī. Dhuravāti cetasikavīriyavasena anikkhittadhuro. Uṭṭhātāti, “yo ca sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññatī”tiādinā (theragā. 232) nayena kāyikavīrīyavasena uṭṭhānasampanno asithilaparakkamo. Vindate dhananti ekamūsikāya nacirasseva catusatasahassasaṅkhaṃ cūḷantevāsī viya lokiyadhanañca, mahallakamahātissatthero viya lokuttaradhanañca labhati. So “tīhiyeva iriyāpathehi viharissāmī”ti vattaṃ katvā thinamiddhāgamanavelāya palālacumbaṭakaṃ temetvā sīse katvā galappamāṇaṃ udakaṃ pavisitvā thinamiddhaṃ paṭibāhanto dasahi vassehi arahattaṃ [P 1.0333] pāpuṇi. Saccenāti vacīsaccenāpi “saccavādī bhūtavādī”ti, paramatthasaccenāpi “buddho paccekabuddho ariyasāvako”ti evaṃ kittiṃ pappoti. Dadanti yaṃkiñci icchitapatthitaṃ dadanto mittāni ganthati, sampādeti karotīti attho. Duddadaṃ vā dadaṃ taṃ ganthati. Dānamukhena vā cattāripi saṅgahavatthūni gahitānīti veditabbāni, tehi mittāni karotīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Now, wishing to answer the three subsequent questions, He spoke this verse beginning with patirūpakārī. Herein, one who, without neglecting suitable place, time, and so forth, undertakes the appropriate means for attaining worldly wealth or supramundane wealth, is called a patirūpakārī (one who acts fittingly). Dhuravā (bearing the yoke) means one who has not laid down the burden, by the power of mental energy. Uṭṭhātā (energetic) means one who is endowed with exertion by the power of bodily energy, of unslackened effort, according to the method of the verse beginning, 'He who regards cold and heat as no more than grass...' As for vindate dhanaṃ (he finds wealth): he obtains worldly wealth, just as Cūḷantevāsika gained wealth numbering four hundred thousand in no long time from just one dead mouse; and he obtains supramundane wealth, just as the Elder Mahallaka Mahātissa did. That Elder, having made the resolution, 'I will dwell in only three postures,' at the time when sloth and torpor arose, would wet a straw head-pad, place it on his head, enter water up to his neck, and warding off sloth and torpor, attained Arahantship in ten years. As for saccena (by truth): by verbal truth one attains the fame of being 'a speaker of truth, a speaker of what is real'; and by ultimate truth, one attains the fame of being 'a Buddha, a Paccekabuddha, or a noble disciple'. As for dadaṃ (giving): by giving whatever is wished for and desired, one binds friends; the meaning is, he accomplishes, he makes. Or, by giving what is difficult to give, one binds that friendship. Alternatively, it should be understood that with giving as the foremost, the four bases of sympathy are also included; by means of these, it is said, one makes friends.

Evaṃ [V 1.0291] gahaṭṭhapabbajitānaṃ sādhāraṇena lokiyalokuttaramissakena nayena cattāro pañhe vissajjetvā idāni “kathaṃ pecca na socatī”ti imaṃ pañcamaṃ pañhaṃ gahaṭṭhavasena vissajjento yassetetiādīmāha. Tassattho – yassa “saddahāno arahata”nti ettha vuttāya sabbakalyāṇadhammuppādikāya saddhāya samannāgatattā saddhassa, gharamesinoti gharāvāsaṃ pañca vā kāmaguṇe esantassa gavesantassa kāmabhogino gahaṭṭhassa “saccena kittiṃ pappotī”ti ettha vuttappakāraṃ saccaṃ. “Sussūsaṃ labhate pañña”nti ettha sussūsapaññānāmena vuttova damo. “Dhuravā uṭṭhātā”ti ettha dhuranāmena uṭṭhānanāmena ca vuttā dhiti. “Dadaṃ mittāni ganthatī”ti ettha vuttappakāro cāgo cāti ete caturo dhammā santi. Sa ve pecca na socatīti idhalokā paralokaṃ gantvā sa ve na socatīti.

Having thus answered the four questions common to both householders and renunciants by a method combining the worldly and the supramundane, now, wishing to answer this fifth question, 'How does one not grieve after death?' from a householder’s perspective, He spoke the words beginning with 'yassa ete.' The meaning of this is as follows: Of the faithful one, who is endowed with faith—which is spoken of in the passage 'saddahāno arahataṃ' and is the producer of all wholesome qualities—and of the householder who seeks a home, or seeks the five strands of sensual pleasure, and enjoys sensual pleasures; there is truth of the kind spoken of in the passage 'saccena kittiṃ pappoti.' Restraint is that which is spoken of by the name of wisdom-from-listening in the passage 'sussūsaṃ labhate paññaṃ.' Fortitude is that which is spoken of by the name 'dhura' (yoke) and by the name 'uṭṭhāna' (striving) in the passage 'dhuravā uṭṭhātā.' And generosity is of the kind spoken of in the passage 'dadaṃ mittāni ganthati.' These four qualities exist. 'Sa ve pecca na socati' means that having gone from this world to the next world, that one indeed does not grieve.

Evaṃ [M 1.0305] bhagavā pañcamampi pañhaṃ vissajjetvā taṃ yakkhaṃ codento iṅgha aññepītiādimāha. Tattha iṅghāti codanatthe nipāto. Aññepīti aññepi dhamme puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchassu. Aññepi vā pūraṇādayo sabbaññupaṭiññe puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe pucchassu. Yadi amhehi “saccena kittiṃ pappotī”ti ettha vuttappakārā saccā bhiyyo kittippattikāraṇaṃ vā, “sussūsaṃ labhate pañña”nti ettha sussūsāti paññāpadesena vuttā dammā bhiyyo [P 1.0334] lokiyalokuttarapaññāpaṭilābhakāraṇaṃ vā, “dadaṃ mittāni ganthatī”ti ettha vuttappakārā cāgā bhiyyo mittaganthanakāraṇaṃ vā, “dhuravā uṭṭhātā”ti ettha taṃ taṃ atthavasaṃ paṭicca dhuranāmena uṭṭhānanāmena ca vuttāya mahābhārasahanatthena ussoḷhibhāvappattāya vīriyasaṅkhātāya khantyā bhiyyo lokiyalokuttaradhanavindanakāraṇaṃ vā, “saccaṃ dammo dhiti cāgo”ti evaṃ vuttehi imeheva catūhi dhammehi bhiyyo asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ pecca asocanakāraṇaṃ vā idha vijjatīti ayamettha saddhiṃ saṅkhepayojanāya atthavaṇṇanā. Vitthārato pana ekamekaṃ padaṃ atthuddhārapaduddhārapadavaṇṇanānayehi vibhajitvā veditabbā.

Thus the Blessed One, having answered the fifth question, wishing to urge that yakkha, spoke the words beginning with, 'Come, others as well...'. Therein, 'iṅgha' (Come) is a particle in the sense of urging. 'Others as well' means: you should ask numerous ascetics and brahmins about other dhammas. Or, you should ask other numerous ascetics and brahmins—such as Pūraṇa and others who claim to be omniscient—if there exists here a cause for attaining fame greater than the truth of the kind spoken of in 'Through truth, one attains fame'; or a cause for attaining mundane and supramundane wisdom greater than the qualities spoken of by way of indicating wisdom as 'listening' in 'Through listening, one obtains wisdom'; or a cause for binding friends greater than the generosity of the kind spoken of in 'Giving, one binds friends'; or a cause for finding mundane and supramundane wealth greater than patience—which is called energy, has attained a state of extreme exertion by means of enduring a great burden, and is spoken of by the names 'responsibility' and 'striving' with reference to various purposes, as in 'The responsible one, the striver'; or a cause for not grieving after passing away from this world to the next greater than these very four dhammas spoken of thus: 'truth, self-control, fortitude, and generosity'. This here is the explanation of the meaning, together with the concise application. But in detail, each single word should be understood by analyzing it through the methods of extracting the meaning, extracting the term, and explaining the term.

Evaṃ vutte yakkho yena saṃsayena aññe puccheyya, tassa pahīnattā kathaṃ nu dāni puccheyyaṃ, puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇeti vatvā yepissa apucchanakāraṇaṃ na jānanti, tepi jānāpento yohaṃ ajjapajānāmi, yo attho samparāyikoti āha. Tattha ajjāti ajjādiṃ katvāti adhippāyo. Pajānāmīti yathāvuttena pakārena jānāmi. Yo atthoti ettāvatā “sussūsaṃ labhate pañña”ntiādinā nayena vuttaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ dasseti. Samparāyikoti iminā “yassete caturo [V 1.0292] dhammā”ti vuttaṃ pecca sokābhāvakāraṇaṃ samparāyikaṃ. Atthoti ca kāraṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayaṃ hi atthasaddo “sātthaṃ sabyañjana”nti evamādīsu (pārā. 1; dī. ni. 1.255) pāṭhatthe vattati. “Attho me, gahapati, hiraññasuvaṇṇenā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.250; ma. ni. 3.258) vicakkhaṇe. “Hoti sīlavataṃ attho”tiādīsu (jā. 1.1.11) vuḍḍhimhi. “Bahujano bhajate atthahetū”tiādīsu dhane. “Ubhinnamatthaṃ caratī”tiādīsu (jā. 1.7.66; saṃ. ni. 1.250; theragā. 443) hite[M 1.0306]. “Atthe jāte ca paṇḍita”ntiādīsu (jā. 1.1.92) kāraṇe. Idha pana kāraṇe. Tasmā yaṃ paññādilābhādīnaṃ kāraṇaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ, yañca pecca sokābhāvassa kāraṇaṃ samparāyikaṃ, taṃ yohaṃ ajja bhagavatā vuttanayena [P 1.0335] sāmaṃyeva pajānāmi, so kathaṃ nu dāni puccheyyaṃ puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇeti evamettha saṅkhepato attho veditabbo.

When this was said, the yakkha, since the doubt by which he would ask others had been abandoned, said, 'How indeed should I now ask various ascetics and brahmins?' And making even those who did not know the reason for his not asking understand, he declared, 'I who now understand that which is the cause for the future life.' Herein, 'now' means 'from this day onwards'—this is the intention. 'I understand' means 'I know in the manner described.' 'That which is the cause'—by this much, it indicates the cause pertaining to this present life, as stated by the method in 'One gains wisdom through listening,' etc. 'For the future life'—by this, it indicates the cause pertaining to the future life, which is the cause for the absence of sorrow after death, as stated in 'For whom these four qualities.' And the word 'attha' is a designation for 'cause.' Indeed, this word 'attha' is used in the sense of the meaning of the text in passages such as 'meaningful and well-phrased'; in the sense of need in passages such as 'I have need, householder, of gold and silver'; in the sense of growth in passages such as 'there is growth for the virtuous'; in the sense of wealth in passages such as 'many people associate for the sake of gain'; in the sense of welfare in passages such as 'he acts for the good of both'; and in the sense of cause in passages such as 'when a matter has arisen, the wise.' Here, however, it is used in the sense of cause. Therefore, that cause for gaining wisdom and so forth, pertaining to this present life, and that cause pertaining to the future life, which is the cause for the absence of sorrow after death—that I myself now understand today through the method taught by the Blessed One. So how indeed should I now ask various ascetics and brahmins? Thus, the meaning here should be understood briefly in this way.

Evaṃ yakkho “pajānāmi yo attho samparāyiko”ti vatvā tassa ñāṇassa bhagavaṃmūlakattaṃ dassento atthāya vata me buddhoti āha. Tattha atthāyāti hitāya vuḍḍhiyā ca. Yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalanti “yassete caturo dhammā”ti ettha vuttacāgena yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, taṃ aggadakkhiṇeyyaṃ buddhaṃ pajānāmīti attho. Keci pana “saṅghaṃ sandhāya evamāhā”ti bhaṇanti.

Thus the yakkha, having said, 'I understand that which is the cause for the future life,' and demonstrating that this knowledge of his was rooted in the Blessed One, spoke the verse, 'Truly, the Buddha is for my benefit.' Therein, 'for my benefit' means for welfare and for growth. As for 'where a gift given is of great fruit,' the meaning is: 'I understand that Buddha to be the foremost recipient of offerings, where a gift given is of great fruit by means of the generosity spoken of in the passage, "For whom these four qualities..."' Some teachers, however, say that he spoke thus with reference to the Saṅgha.

Evaṃ imāya gāthāya attano hitādhigamaṃ dassetvā idāni sahitapaṭipattiṃ dīpento so ahaṃ vicarissāmītiādimāha. Tattha gāmā gāmanti devagāmā devagāmaṃ. Purā puranti devanagarato devanagaraṃ. Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammatanti “sammāsambuddho vata bhagavā, svākkhāto vata bhagavato dhammo”tiādinā nayena buddhasubodhitañca dhammasudhammatañca ca-saddena “suppaṭipanno vata bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho”tiādinā saṅghasuppaṭipattiñca abhitthavitvā namassamāno dhammaghosako hutvā vicarissāmīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Thus, having shown his attainment of benefit through this verse, and now revealing his well-undertaken practice, he speaks the verse beginning, 'I shall wander.' Therein, 'from village to village' means from a deity-village to a deity-village. 'From town to town' means from a deity-city to a deity-city. As for 'Paying homage to the Fully Awakened One and to the well-proclaimed nature of the Dhamma,' this is what is meant: having praised both the Buddha's perfect awakening and the Dhamma's well-proclaimed nature by way of 'Indeed, the Blessed One is a Fully Awakened One; indeed, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One,' etc., and, by means of the word 'ca' (and), also the Saṅgha's good practice by way of 'Indeed, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples practices well,' etc., and paying homage, 'I shall wander as a proclaimer of the Dhamma.'

Evamimāya gāthāya pariyosānañca rattivibhāvanañca sādhukārasadduṭṭhānañca āḷavakakumārassa yakkhabhavanaṃ ānayanañca ekakkhaṇeyeva ahosi. Rājapurisā sādhukārasaddaṃ sutvā – “evarūpo sādhukārasaddo ṭhapetvā buddhe na aññesaṃ abbhuggacchati, āgato nu kho bhagavā”ti āvajjentā bhagavato sarīrappabhaṃ disvā pubbe viya bahi aṭṭhatvā nibbisaṅkā antoyeva pavisitvā addasaṃsu bhagavantaṃ yakkhassa bhavane nisinnaṃ, yakkhañca añjaliṃ paggahetvā [V 1.0293] ṭhitaṃ. Disvāna yakkhaṃ āhaṃsu – “ayaṃ te, mahāyakkha, rājakumāro balikammāya ānīto, handa naṃ khāda vā bhuñja vā, yathāpaccayaṃ vā karohī”ti. So sotāpannattā lajjito visesena [M 1.0307] ca bhagavato purato evaṃ vuccamāno atha taṃ kumāraṃ ubhohi hatthehi paṭiggahetvā bhagavato [P 1.0336] upanāmesi “ayaṃ, bhante, kumāro mayhaṃ pesito, imāhaṃ bhagavato dammi, hitānukampakā buddhā, paṭiggaṇhātu, bhante, bhagavā imaṃ dārakaṃ imassa hitatthāya sukhatthāyā”ti imañca gāthamāha –

Thus, the conclusion of this verse, the breaking of dawn, the arising of the sound of acclamation, and the bringing of Prince Āḷavaka to the yakkha’s dwelling—all occurred in a single moment. The royal men, hearing the sound of acclamation and reflecting, “Such a sound of acclamation does not arise for others, except for the Buddha. Has the Blessed One perhaps come?”, saw the radiance of the Blessed One’s body. Unlike before, they did not stand outside but, being fearless, entered right in. They saw the Blessed One seated in the yakkha’s dwelling, and the yakkha standing with his palms joined in reverence. Having seen him, they said to the yakkha, “Great yakkha, this prince has been brought to you as an offering. Come now, either devour him or eat him, or do with him as you please.” But he, being a stream-enterer and being addressed thus in the very presence of the Blessed One, was especially ashamed. Then, taking the prince with both hands, he presented him to the Blessed One, saying, “Venerable Sir, this prince was sent to me. I give him to the Blessed One. Buddhas are compassionate for the welfare of beings. May the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, accept this child for his welfare and for his happiness.” And he spoke this verse:

“Imaṃ kumāraṃ satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ,

Sabbaṅgupetaṃ paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ;

Udaggacitto sumano dadāmi te,

Paṭiggaha lokahitāya cakkhumā”ti.

“This prince, marked with a hundred meritorious signs, endowed with all limbs, complete in all features, with an uplifted heart and joyful mind, I give to you. O One with Vision, please accept him for the welfare of the world.”

Paṭiggahesi bhagavā kumāraṃ. Paṭiggaṇhanto ca yakkhassa ca kumārassa ca maṅgalakaraṇatthaṃ pādūnagāthaṃ abhāsi. Taṃ yakkho kumāraṃ saraṇaṃ gamento tikkhattuṃ catutthapādena pūresi. Seyyathidaṃ –

The Blessed One accepted the prince. And while accepting him, for the purpose of giving a blessing to both the yakkha and the prince, he spoke a verse that was lacking a line. The yakkha, in order to guide the prince to the refuges, completed it three times with a fourth line. As follows:

“Dīghāyuko hotu ayaṃ kumāro,

Tuvañca yakkha sukhito bhavāhi;

Abyādhitā lokahitāya tiṭṭhatha,

Ayaṃ kumāro saraṇamupeti buddhaṃ;

Ayaṃ kumāro saraṇamupeti dhammaṃ;

Ayaṃ kumāro saraṇamupeti saṅgha”nti.

“May this prince be long-lived, and may you, O yakkha, be happy. May you both remain, free from affliction, for the welfare of the world. This prince goes for refuge to the Buddha. This prince goes for refuge to the Dhamma. This prince goes for refuge to the Saṅgha.”

Atha bhagavā kumāraṃ rājapurisānaṃ adāsi – “imaṃ vaḍḍhetvā puna mameva dethā”ti. Evaṃ so kumāro rājapurisānaṃ hatthato yakkhassa hatthaṃ, yakkhassa hatthato bhagavato hatthaṃ, bhagavato hatthato puna rājapurisānaṃ hatthaṃ gatattā nāmato “hatthako āḷavako”ti jāto. Taṃ ādāya paṭinivatte rājapurise disvā kassakavanakammikādayo “kiṃ yakkho kumāraṃ atidaharattā na icchī”ti? Bhītā pucchiṃsu. Rājapurisā “mā bhāyatha. Khemaṃ kataṃ bhagavatā”ti sabbamārocesuṃ[V 1.0294]. Tato “sādhu sādhū”ti sakalaṃ āḷavinagaraṃ ekakolāhalena yakkhābhimukhaṃ ahosi. Yakkhopi bhagavato bhikkhācārakāle anuppatte pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā upaḍḍhamaggaṃ anugantvā nivatti.

Then the Blessed One gave the prince to the king’s men, saying, “Raise him and then give him back to me.” Thus, the prince, having gone from the hands of the king’s men to the hands of the yakkha, from the hands of the yakkha to the hands of the Blessed One, and from the hands of the Blessed One back to the hands of the king’s men, became known by the name “Hatthaka Āḷavaka.” Seeing the king’s men returning with him, the farmers, forest workers, and others, frightened, asked, “What, did the yakkha not want the prince because he is too young?” The king’s men said, “Do not fear. The Blessed One has made it safe,” and they reported everything. Then the entire city of Āḷavī, with a single uproar directed toward the yakkha, exclaimed, “Excellent! Excellent!” The yakkha, too, when the time for the Blessed One's alms round arrived, took the Blessed One's bowl and robe, followed him for half the journey, and then returned.

Atha bhagavā nagare piṇḍāya caritvā katabhattakicco nagaradvāre aññatarasmiṃ vivitte rukkhamūle paññattabuddhāsane nisīdi. Tato mahājanakāyena saddhiṃ rājā ca nāgarā ca ekato sampiṇḍitvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma [M 1.0308] vanditvā parivāretvā [P 1.0337] nisinnā – “kathaṃ, bhante, evaṃ dāruṇaṃ yakkhaṃ damayitthā”ti pucchiṃsu. Tesaṃ bhagavā yuddhamādiṃ katvā “evaṃ navavidhaṃ vassaṃ vassetvā evaṃ vibhiṃsanakaṃ akāsi, evaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Tassāhaṃ evaṃ vissajjesi”nti tamevāḷavakasuttaṃ kathesi. Kathāpariyosāne caturāsītipāṇasahassānaṃ dhammābhisamayo ahosi. Tato rājā ceva nāgarā ca vessavaṇamahārājassa bhavanasamīpe yakkhassa bhavanaṃ katvā pupphagandhādisakkārupetaṃ niccabaliṃ pavattesuṃ. Tañca kumāraṃ viññutaṃ pattaṃ “tvaṃ bhagavantaṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ labhi, gaccha bhagavantaṃyeva payirupāsassu bhikkhusaṅghañcā”ti vissajjesuṃ. So bhagavantañca bhikkhusaṅghañca payirupāsamāno nacirasseva anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāya sabbaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggahetvā pañcasataupāsakaparivāro ahosi. Bhagavā ca naṃ etadagge niddisi – “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ upāsakānaṃ catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi parisaṃ saṅgaṇhantānaṃ yadidaṃ hatthako āḷavako”ti (a. ni. 1.251). Dvādasamaṃ.

Then the Blessed One, having walked for alms in the city and completed his meal, sat down on the prepared Buddha-seat at the foot of a secluded tree near the city gate. Then the king and the citizens, together with a great crowd, having gathered together, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat surrounding him. They asked, “Venerable sir, how did you tame such a fierce yakkha?” The Blessed One, beginning with the battle, related to them: “Thus he caused a ninefold rain to fall, thus he performed terrifying acts, thus he asked a question, and thus I answered him.” He then recited that very Āḷavaka Sutta. At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand living beings attained the penetration of the Dhamma. Thereafter, the king and the citizens built an abode for the yakkha near the abode of the great king Vessavaṇa, furnished it with flowers, perfumes, and other tributes, and established a perpetual offering. When the prince reached maturity, they sent him away, saying, “You obtained your life by depending on the Blessed One. Go and attend upon the Blessed One himself and the community of monks.” He, attending upon the Blessed One and the Sangha, before long, established himself in the fruit of non-returning, learned all the Buddha's word, and came to have a retinue of five hundred lay followers. The Blessed One designated him as foremost in this: “Monks, of my lay disciples who gather an assembly with the four bases of sympathy, Hatthaka of Āḷavī is the foremost.” (A. Ni. 1.251). The twelfth.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī,

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

the Commentary to the Connected Discourses,

Yakkhasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Yakkha Saṃyutta is concluded.

11. Sakkasaṃyuttaṃ

11. The Connected Discourses with Sakka

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Suvīrasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Suvīra Sutta

247. Sakkasaṃyuttassa [V 1.0295][P 1.0338][M 1.0309] paṭhame abhiyaṃsūti kadā abhiyaṃsu? Yadā balavanto ahesuṃ, tadā. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – sakko kira magadharaṭṭhe macalagāmake magho nāma māṇavo hutvā tettiṃsa purise gahetvā kalyāṇakammaṃ karonto satta vatapadāni pūretvā tattha kālaṅkato devaloke nibbatti. Taṃ balavakammānubhāvena saparisaṃ sesadevatā dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhantaṃ disvā “āgantukadevaputtā āgatā”ti nevāsikā gandhapānaṃ sajjayiṃsu. Sakko sakaparisāya saññaṃ adāsi – “mārisā mā gandhapānaṃ pivittha, pivanākāramattameva dassethā”ti. Te tattha akaṃsu. Nevāsikadevatā suvaṇṇasarakehi upanītaṃ gandhapānaṃ yāvadatthaṃ pivitvā mattā tattha tattha suvaṇṇapathaviyaṃ patitvā sayiṃsu. Sakko “gaṇhatha puttahatāya putte”ti te pādesu gahetvā sinerupāde khipāpesi. Sakkassa puññatejena tadanuvattakāpi sabbe tattheva patiṃsu. Te sineruvemajjhakāle saññaṃ labhitvā, “tātā na suraṃ pivimha, na suraṃ pivimhā”ti āhaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya asurā nāma jātā. Atha nesaṃ kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhānaṃ sinerussa heṭṭhimatale dasayojanasahassaṃ asurabhavanaṃ nibbatti. Sakko tesaṃ nivattetvā [P 1.0339] anāgamanatthāya ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

247. In the first [sutta] of the Sakka Saṃyutta, regarding ‘they attacked’: when did they attack? When they were powerful, then they attacked. Herein is the sequential account: It is said that Sakka, having been a young man named Magha in the village of Macala in the country of Magadha, took thirty-three men and, while performing meritorious deeds, fulfilled the seven sets of vows. After passing away there, he was reborn in the deva world. Seeing him, who, by the power of his strong kamma, together with his retinue, was surpassing the other deities in ten respects, the resident deities thought, ‘Newly arrived devaputtas have come,’ and prepared the gandhapāna drink. Sakka gave a sign to his own retinue: ‘Sirs, do not drink the gandhapāna; merely show the appearance of drinking.’ They acted accordingly. The resident deities, having drunk the gandhapāna brought in golden cups to their satisfaction, became intoxicated and, falling down here and there on the golden ground, they slept. Sakka said, ‘Seize, my dears, those delighting in sleep!’ and had them seized by the feet and thrown to the foot of Mount Sineru. Due to Sakka’s power of merit, all their followers also fell right there. Regaining consciousness in the mid-region of Sineru, they cried, ‘Dears, we did not drink sura, we did not drink sura!’ From that time onwards, they came to be called Asuras. Then, for them, an Asura realm of ten thousand yojanas arose on the lower surface of Mount Sineru, produced by kamma and the season. Sakka, having driven them back, established a guard to prevent their return, in reference to which it was said:

“Antarā dvinnaṃ ayujjhapurānaṃ,

Pañcavidhā ṭhapitā abhirakkhā;

Udakaṃ karoṭi-payassa ca hārī,

Madanayutā caturo ca mahatthā”ti.

“Between the two unconquerable cities, five kinds of protection were established: the Water-dwellers, the Bowl-bearers, the Carriers of Drink, those Endowed with Intoxication, and the Four of Great Power.”

Dve [V 1.0296][M 1.0310] nagarāni hi yuddhena gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ayujjhapurāni nāma jātāni devanagarañca asuranagarañca. Yadā hi asurā balavanto honti, atha devehi palāyitvā devanagaraṃ pavisitvā dvāre pidahite asurānaṃ satasahassampi kiñci kātuṃ na sakkoti. Yadā devā balavanto honti, athāsurehi palāyitvā asuranagarassa dvāre pidahite sakkānaṃ satasahassampi kiñci kātuṃ na sakkoti. Iti imāni dve nagarāni ayujjhapurāni nāma. Nesaṃ antarā etesu udakādīsu pañcasu ṭhānesu sakkena ārakkhā ṭhapitā. Tattha udakasaddena nāgā gahitā. Te hi udake balavanto honti. Tasmā sinerussa paṭhamālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Karoṭisaddena supaṇṇā gahitā. Tesaṃ kira karoṭi nāma pānabhojanaṃ, tena taṃ nāmaṃ labhiṃsu. Dutiyālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Payassahārīsaddena kumbhaṇḍā gahitā. Dānavarakkhasā kira te. Tatiyālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Madanayutasaddena yakkhā gahitā. Visamacārino kirate yujjhasoṇḍā. Catutthālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Caturo ca mahantāti cattāro mahārājāno vuttā. Pañcamālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Tasmā yadi asurā kupitāvilacittā devapuraṃ upayanti yuddhesū, yaṃ girino paṭhamaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ, taṃ uragā paṭibāhanti evaṃ sesesu sesā.

Two cities, the city of the devas and the city of the asuras, were named Ayujjhapurāni (Impregnable Cities) because they could not be captured by means of war. For when the asuras are powerful, the devas flee, enter the city of the devas, and when the gate is closed, not even a hundred thousand asuras can do any harm. When the devas are powerful, the asuras flee, and when the gate of the city of the asuras is closed, not even a hundred thousand Sakkas can do any harm. Thus, these two cities are called Ayujjhapurāni. Between them, in these five locations, guards were established by Sakka. Therein, by the word 'uraga' (serpent), the nāgas are meant. For they are powerful in the water; therefore, their guard post is on the first terrace of Sineru. By the word 'karoṭi', the supaṇṇas are meant. It is said their drink and food was named karoṭi, and for that reason they received that name. Their guard post is on the second terrace. By the word 'payassahārī', the kumbhaṇḍas are meant. They are said to be dānava-rakkhasas. Their guard post is on the third terrace. By the word 'madanayuta', the yakkhas are meant. It is said they are unruly and fond of battle. Their guard post is on the fourth terrace. By 'the four great ones', the Four Great Kings are meant. Their guard post is on the fifth terrace. Therefore, if the asuras, with minds agitated by anger, approach the city of the devas for battle, the uragas repel them at the first rampart of the mountain, and likewise the others at the remaining ramparts.

Te pana asurā āyuvaṇṇarasaissariyasampattīhi tāvatiṃsasadisāva. Tasmā antarā attānaṃ ajānitvā pāṭaliyā pupphitāya, “na idaṃ devanagaraṃ, tattha pāricchattako pupphati, idha pana cittapāṭalī, jarasakkenāmhākaṃ [P 1.0340] suraṃ pāyetvā vañcitā, devanagarañca no gahitaṃ, gacchāma tena saddhiṃ yujjhissāmā”ti hatthiassarathe āruyha suvaṇṇarajatamaṇiphalakāni gahetvā, yuddhasajjā hutvā, asurabheriyo vādentā mahāsamudde udakaṃ dvidhā bhetvā uṭṭhahanti. Te deve vuṭṭhe vammikamakkhikā vammikaṃ viya sineruṃ abhiruhitu ārabhanti. Atha nesaṃ paṭhamaṃ nāgehi saddhiṃ yuddhaṃ hoti. Tasmiṃ kho pana yuddhe na kassaci chavi vā cammaṃ vā chijjati, na lohitaṃ uppajjati, kevalaṃ kumārakānaṃ dārumeṇḍakayuddhaṃ viya aññamaññaṃ santāsanamattameva [M 1.0311] hoti. Koṭisatāpi koṭisahassāpi nāgā tehi saddhiṃ yujjhitvā te asurapuraṃyeva pavesetvā nivattanti.

But those asuras are just like the Tāvatiṃsa devas in terms of longevity, beauty, retinue, and sovereignty. Therefore, not realizing the situation, when the Pāṭali tree blossomed, they thought, 'This is not the city of the devas; there the Pāricchattaka tree blossoms, but here the Cittapāṭalī blossoms. The old Sakka, having made us drink liquor, has deceived us, and our city of the devas has been taken. Let us go! We will fight with him!' Mounting elephants, horses, and chariots, taking shields of gold, silver, and jewels, having prepared for battle, and sounding the asura war drums, they rise up, splitting the water of the great ocean in two. Just as termites begin to climb an anthill when it has rained, they begin to ascend Mount Sineru. Then, their first battle is with the nāgas. In that battle, however, no one's outer skin or inner hide is cut, nor does blood flow; it is merely a matter of mutual intimidation, like the mock battle of wooden rams of young boys. Even hundreds or thousands of koṭis of nāgas, having fought with them, drive them back into the asura city itself and then return.

Yadā pana asurā balavanto honti, atha nāgā osakkitvā dutiye ālinde supaṇṇehi saddhiṃ ekatova hutvā yujjhanti. Esa nayo supaṇṇādīsūpi. Yadā pana tāni pañcapi [V 1.0297] ṭhānāni asurā maddanti, tadā ekato sampiṇḍitānipi pañca balāni osakkanti. Atha cattāro mahārājāno gantvā sakkassa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocenti. Sakko tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā diyaḍḍhayojanasatikaṃ vejayantarathaṃ āruyha sayaṃ vā nikkhamati, ekaṃ vā puttaṃ peseti. Imasmiṃ pana kāle puttaṃ pesetukāmo, tāta suvīrātiādimāha.

But when the asuras are powerful, the nāgas retreat and, having united with the supaṇṇas on the second terrace, they fight. This same method applies to the supaṇṇas and others as well. But when the asuras crush all five of these strongholds, then the five forces retreat, even though they are massed together. Then the Four Great Kings go and report the matter to Sakka. Sakka, hearing their words, mounts the Vejayanta chariot, which is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size, and either goes forth himself or sends a son. On this occasion, however, wishing to send a son, he says, 'Dear Suvīra,' and so on.

Evaṃ bhaddantavāti khoti evaṃ hotu bhaddaṃ tava iti kho. Pamādaṃ āpādesīti pamādaṃ akāsi. Accharāsaṅghaparivuto saṭṭhiyojanaṃ vitthārena suvaṇṇamahāvīthiṃ otaritvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷanto nandanavanādīsu vicaratīti attho.

Thus, `Evaṃ bhaddantavāti kho` means: May it be well for you thus. `Pamādaṃ āpādesīti` means: He committed negligence. Surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs, having descended onto the great golden street sixty yojanas in width, while celebrating the festival, he wanders in the Nandana Grove and so on. This is the meaning.

Anuṭṭhahanti anuṭṭhahanto. Avāyāmanti avāyamanto. Alasvassāti alaso assa. Na ca kiccāni kārayeti kiñci kiccaṃ nāma na kareyya. Sabbakāmasamiddhassāti sabbakāmehi samiddho assa. Taṃ me, sakka, varaṃ disāti, sakka devaseṭṭha, taṃ me varaṃ uttamaṃ ṭhānaṃ okāsaṃ disaṃ ācikkha kathehīti vadati. Nibbānassa hi so maggoti kammaṃ akatvā jīvitaṭṭhānaṃ nāma nibbānassa maggo. Paṭhamaṃ.

`Anuṭṭhahanti` means not making effort. `Avāyāmanti` means not striving. `Alasvassāti` is to be parsed as `alaso assa`: he would be lazy. `Na ca kiccāni kārayeti` means he should not do any duty whatsoever. `Sabbakāmasamiddhassāti` means `sabbakāmehi samiddho assa`: he would be endowed with all desires. `Taṃ me, sakka, varaṃ disāti` means: O Sakka, chief of devas, point out, declare, and tell me of that supreme boon, that state and opportunity. Thus he speaks. `Nibbānassa hi so maggoti` means: For that means of livelihood without doing work is the path to Nibbāna. The first.

2. Susīmasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Susīma Sutta

248. Dutiye [P 1.0341] susīmanti attano puttasahassassa antare evaṃnāmakaṃ ekaṃ puttameva. Dutiyaṃ.

248. In the second (sutta), `Susīma` refers to just one son of that name among his thousand sons. The second.

3. Dhajaggasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Dhajagga Sutta

249. Tatiye samupabyūḷhoti sampiṇḍito rāsibhūto. Dhajaggaṃ ullokeyyathāti sakkassa kira diyaḍḍhayojanasatāyāmo ratho[M 1.0312]. Tassa hi pacchimanto paṇṇāsayojano, majjhe rathapañjaro paṇṇāsayojano, rathasandhito yāva rathasīsā paṇṇāsayojanāni. Tadeva pamāṇaṃ diguṇaṃ katvā tiyojanasatāyāmotipi vadantiyeva. Tasmiṃ yojanikapallaṅko atthato, tiyojanikaṃ setacchattaṃ matthake ṭhapitaṃ, ekasmiṃyeva yuge sahassaājaññā yuttā, sesālaṅkārassa pamāṇaṃ natthi. Dhajo panassa aḍḍhatiyāni yojanasatāni uggato, yassa vātāhatassa pañcaṅgikatūriyasseva [V 1.0298] saddo niccharati, taṃ ullokeyyāthāti vadati. Kasmā? Taṃ passantānañhi rājā no āgantvā parisapariyante nikhātathambho viya ṭhito, kassa mayaṃ bhāyāmāti bhayaṃ na hoti. Pajāpatissāti so kira sakkena samānavaṇṇo samānāyuko dutiyaṃ āsanaṃ labhati. Tathā varuṇo īsāno ca. Varuṇo pana tatiyaṃ āsanaṃ labhati, īsāno catutthaṃ. Palāyīti asurehi parājito tasmiṃ rathe ṭhito appamattakampi rajadhajaṃ disvā palāyanadhammo.

249. In the third sutta, 'samupabyūḷha' means gathered together, formed into a mass. 'One should look up at the banner-top' refers to Sakka’s chariot, which is said to be one hundred and fifty yojanas in length. Its rear part is fifty yojanas, the middle chariot-chamber is fifty yojanas, and from the chariot’s joint to the chariot’s head is fifty yojanas. Some also say that by doubling that measure, it is three hundred yojanas long. In it, a couch one yojana in size is spread, a white parasol three yojanas wide is placed atop, and a thousand thoroughbred horses are yoked to a single yoke; of the remaining ornaments, there is no measure. His banner, however, rises two hundred and fifty yojanas high, and when struck by the wind, it produces a sound like that of a five-part musical ensemble. It is said, 'You should look up at it.' Why? Because for those who see it, our king, having come, stands like a firmly planted pillar at the edge of the assembly, and thinking, 'Whom should we fear?' there is no fear. 'Pajāpati' refers to one who, it is said, is of equal appearance and equal lifespan with Sakka and obtains the second seat. Likewise are Varuṇa and Īsāna. Varuṇa, however, obtains the third seat, and Īsāna the fourth. 'He fled' means that when defeated by the Asuras, while standing in that chariot, upon seeing even a tiny silver banner, he was of a nature to flee.

Itipi so bhagavātiādīni visuddhimagge vitthāritāneva. Idamavocāti idaṃ dhajaggaparittaṃ nāma bhagavā avoca, yassa āṇākhette koṭisatasahassacakkavāḷe ānubhāvo vattati. Idaṃ āvajjetvā hi yakkhabhayacorabhayādīhi dukkhehi muttānaṃ anto natthi. Tiṭṭhatu aññadukkhavūpasamo, idaṃ āvajjamāno hi pasannacitto ākāsepi patiṭṭhaṃ labhati.

'Thus indeed, the Blessed One,' etc., are fully explained in the Visuddhimagga. 'This he spoke' means the Blessed One spoke this, known as the Dhajagga Paritta, whose power prevails in a hundred thousand koṭis of world-systems within the sphere of his command. Indeed, by reflecting on this, there is no end to those freed from sufferings such as fear of yakkhas, fear of thieves, and so on. Let alone the stilling of other suffering; indeed, by reflecting on this, one with a serene mind gains a footing even in the sky.

Tatridaṃ vatthu – dīghavāpicetiyamhi kira sudhākamme [P 1.0342] kayiramāne eko daharo muddhavedikāpādato patitvā cetiyakucchiyā bhassati. Heṭṭhā ṭhito bhikkhusaṅgho “dhajaggaparittaṃ, āvuso, āvajjāhī”ti āha. So maraṇabhayena tajjito “dhajaggaparittaṃ maṃ rakkhatū”ti āha. Tāvadevassa cetiyakucchito dve iṭṭhakā nikkhamitvā sopānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu, upariṭṭhito vallinisseṇiṃ otāresuṃ. Tasmiṃ nisseṇiyaṃ ṭhite iṭṭhakā yathāṭṭhāneyeva aṭṭhaṃsu. Tatiyaṃ.

Herein, this is the story: At the Dīghavāpi Cetiya, it is said that while plastering work was being done, a young monk fell from the base of the top railing and slipped down from the belly of the cetiya. The community of monks standing below said, “Friend, reflect upon the Dhajagga Paritta!” Terrified by the fear of death, he said, “May the Dhajagga Paritta protect me!” At that very moment, two bricks came out from the belly of the cetiya, and having become like a staircase, they stood firm. Those standing above lowered a vine ladder. When he stood on the ladder, the bricks returned to their original place. The third.

4. Vepacittisuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Vepacitti Sutta

250. Catutthe [M 1.0313] vepacittīti so kira asurānaṃ sabbajeṭṭhako. Yenāti nipātamattaṃ nanti ca. Kaṇṭhapañcamehīti dvīsu hatthesu pādesu kaṇṭhe cāti evaṃ pañcahi bandhanehi. Tāni pana naḷinasuttaṃ viya makkaṭakasuttaṃ viya ca cakkhussāpāthaṃ āgacchanti, iriyāpathaṃ rujjhanti. Tehi pana citteneva bajjhati, citteneva muccati. Akkosatīti corosi bālosi mūḷhosi thenosi oṭṭhosi goṇosi gadrabhosi nerayikosi tiracchānagatosi, natthi tuyhaṃ sugati, duggatiyeva tuyhaṃ pāṭikaṅkhāti imehi dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosati. Paribhāsatīti, jarasakka, na tvaṃ sabbakālaṃ jinissasi, yadā asurānaṃ jayo bhavissati, tadā tampi evaṃ bandhitvā asurabhavanassa dvāre nipajjāpetvā pothāpessāmīti ādīni vatvā tajjeti. Sakko vijitavijayo na taṃ manasi karoti, mahāpaṭiggahaṇaṃ panassa matthake vidhunanto sudhammadevasabhaṃ pavisati [V 1.0299] ceva nikkhamati ca. Ajjhabhāsīti “kiṃ nu kho esa sakko imāni pharusavacanāni bhayena titikkhati, udāhu adhivāsanakhantiyā samannāgatattā”ti? Vīmaṃsanto abhāsi.

250. In the fourth sutta, as for ‘Vepacitti,’ it is said that he was the foremost among the asuras. ‘Yena’ is merely a particle. ‘With five bonds including the neck’ means by five bonds: on the two hands, the two feet, and the neck. These bonds, however, come into the range of vision like a lotus fiber or a spider's thread, and they obstruct movement. Yet, one is bound by mind alone and freed by mind alone. ‘He abuses’ means he abuses with these ten grounds for abuse: ‘You are a thief, you are a fool, you are a deluded one, you are a rogue, you are a camel, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are one of hell, you are an animal; there is no good destination for you, only a bad destination is to be expected for you.’ ‘He threatens’ means he threatens by saying such things as: ‘Old Sakka, you will not always be victorious. When the victory of the asuras comes to be, at that time, having bound you also in this way and made you lie down at the gate of the asura abode, I will have you beaten.’ Sakka, having won the victory, does not take it to heart; rather, shaking a great shawl over Vepacitti's head, he both enters and leaves the Sudhammā divine assembly. ‘He addressed’ means that, wishing to investigate, ‘For what reason does this Sakka endure these harsh words? Is it out of fear, or else does he endure because he is endowed with patient endurance?’ he spoke.

Dubbalyā noti dubbalabhāvena nu. Paṭisaṃyujeti paṭisaṃyujeyya paṭipphareyya. Pabhijjeyyunti virajjeyyuṃ. Pakujjheyyuntipi pāṭho. Paranti paccatthikaṃ. Yo sato upasammatīti yo satimā hutvā upasammati, tassa upasamaṃyevāhaṃ [P 1.0343] bālassa paṭisedhanaṃ maññeti attho. Yadā naṃ maññatīti yasmā taṃ maññati. Ajjhāruhatīti ajjhottharati. Gova bhiyyo palāyinanti yathā goyuddhe tāvadeva dve gāvo yujjhante gogaṇo olokento tiṭṭhati, yadā pana eko palāyati, atha naṃ palāyantaṃ sabbo gogaṇo bhiyyo ajjhottharati. Evaṃ dummedho khamantaṃ bhiyyo ajjhottharatīti attho.

'Dubbalyā no' means: does he endure out of weakness? 'Paṭisaṃyujeti' means: would he contend with, would he retaliate by overpowering? 'Pabhijjeyyunti' means 'they would be ruined.' 'Pakujjheyyuṃ' is also a reading. 'Paraṃ' means the opponent. 'Yo sato upasammatīti' means 'one who, being mindful, is calm'; I consider his very calmness to be the restraint of the fool—this is the meaning. 'Yadā naṃ maññatīti' means 'because one considers that...'. 'Ajjhāruhati' means 'overwhelms'. 'Gova bhiyyo palāyinanti' means: just as in a cow-fight, while two cows are fighting, the herd stands watching, but when one flees, the entire herd then overwhelms the fleeing one even more. Similarly, the fool overwhelms the patient one even more—this is the meaning.

Sadatthaparamāti sakatthaparamā. Khantyā bhiyyo na vijjatīti tesu sakaatthaparamesu atthesu khantito uttaritaro añño attho na vijjati. Tamāhu paramaṃ khantinti yo balavā titikkhati, tassa taṃ khantiṃ paramaṃ āhu. Bālabalaṃ nāma aññāṇabalaṃ. Taṃ yassa balaṃ, abalameva [M 1.0314] taṃ balanti āhu kathentīti dīpeti. Dhammaguttassāti dhammena rakkhitassa, dhammaṃ vā rakkhantassa. Paṭivattāti paṭippharitvā vattā, paṭippharitvā vā bālabalanti vadeyyāpi, dhammaṭṭhaṃ pana cāletuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Tasseva tena pāpiyoti tena kodhena tasseva puggalassa pāpaṃ. Katarassa? Yo kuddhaṃ paṭikujjhati. Tikicchantānanti ekavacane bahuvacanaṃ, tikicchantanti attho. Janā maññantīti evarūpaṃ attano ca parassa cāti ubhinnaṃ atthaṃ tikicchantaṃ nipphādentaṃ puggalaṃ “andhabālo aya”nti andhabālaputhujjanāva evaṃ maññanti. Dhammassa akovidāti catusaccadhamme achekā. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Khoti nipātamattaṃ. Catutthaṃ.

'Sadatthaparamāti' means 'one's own welfare is supreme'. 'Khantyā bhiyyo na vijjatīti' means: among these supreme benefits for oneself, there exists no other benefit higher than patience. 'Tamāhu paramaṃ khantinti' means: when a strong person endures, they call that patience of his the supreme strength. 'Bālabalaṃ' is the strength of ignorance. For whom that is a strength, it is in fact no strength at all; yet they call it 'strength'—thus it is explained. 'Dhammaguttassāti' means 'of one protected by the Dhamma', or 'of one protecting the Dhamma'. 'Paṭivattāti' means one who, having retaliated by overpowering, might call another a 'fool'; but there is no one who is able to shake a person established in the Dhamma. 'Tasseva tena pāpiyoti' means by that anger, it is worse for that very person. For which one? The one who gets angry back at an angry person. 'Tikicchantānanti' is a plural form used for the singular; the meaning is 'one who is treating'. 'Janā maññantīti' means only blind, foolish worldlings think of such a person—one who is accomplishing the welfare of both oneself and others—as 'this is a blind fool'. 'Dhammassa akovidāti' means unskilled in the Dhamma of the Four Truths. 'Idhāti' means in this Dispensation. 'Kho' is merely a particle. The fourth.

5. Subhāsitajayasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Subhāsitajaya Sutta.

251. Pañcame asurindaṃ etadavocāti chekatāya etaṃ avoca. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “parassa nāma gāhaṃ mocetvā paṭhamaṃ vattuṃ garu. Parassa vacanaṃ anugantvā pana pacchā sukhaṃ [P 1.0344] vattu”nti. Pubbadevāti devaloke ciranivāsino pubbasāmikā, tumhākaṃ tāva paveṇiāgataṃ bhaṇathāti[V 1.0300]. Adaṇḍāvacarāti daṇḍāvacaraṇarahitā, daṇḍaṃ vā satthaṃ vā gahetabbanti evamettha natthīti attho. Pañcamaṃ.

251. In the fifth, regarding 'asurindaṃ etadavoca', it means: he spoke this due to his skillfulness. It is said that it occurred to him thus: 'It is weighty to speak first, having set aside the taking of another's name. But having followed another’s speech, it is easy to speak afterward.' As for 'pubbadevā', it means: those who have long dwelt in the deva world, your former masters; you should first recite what has come down in your tradition. As for 'adaṇḍāvacarā', it means: devoid of the application of punishment; the meaning is that in this matter, there is no taking up of punishment or a weapon. The fifth.

6. Kulāvakasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Kulāvaka Sutta.

252. Chaṭṭhe ajjhabhāsīti tassa kira simbalivanābhimukhassa jātassa rathasaddo ca ājānīyasaddo dhajasaddo ca samantā asanipātasaddo viya ahosi. Taṃ sutvā simbalivane balavasupaṇṇā palāyiṃsu, jarājiṇṇā ceva rogadubbalā ca asañjātapakkhapotakā ca palāyituṃ asakkontā, maraṇabhayena tajjitā ekappahāreneva mahāviravaṃ viraviṃsu. Sakko taṃ sutvā “kassa saddo, tātā”ti? Mātaliṃ pucchi. Rathasaddaṃ, te deva, sutvā supaṇṇā palāyituṃ asakkontā viravantīti. Taṃ sutvā karuṇāsamāvajjitahadayo abhāsi. Īsāmukhenāti rathassa īsāmukhena. Yathā kulāvake īsāmukhaṃ na sañcuṇṇeti, evaṃ iminā īsāmukhena te parivajjaya. So hi ratho puññapaccayanibbatto cakkavāḷapabbatepi [M 1.0315] sinerumhipi sammukhībhūte vinivijjhitvāva gacchati na sajjati, ākāsagatasadiseneva gacchati. Sace tena simbalivanena gato bhaveyya, yathā mahāsakaṭe kadalivanamajjhena vā eraṇḍavanamajjhena vā gacchante sabbavanaṃ vibhaggaṃ nimmathitaṃ hoti, evaṃ tampi simbalivanaṃ bhaveyya. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

252. In the sixth, regarding 'ajjhabhāsi', it is said that for him, who had appeared facing the silk-cotton tree forest, the sound of the chariot, the sound of the thoroughbreds, and the sound of the banner arose from all around like the sound of a thunderbolt falling. Hearing that, the powerful garuḍas in the silk-cotton tree forest fled. But the old and decrepit, the sick and weak, and the young fledglings whose wings had not yet grown, being unable to fly away and terrified by the fear of death, cried out a great cry all at once. Hearing this, Sakka asked Mātali, 'Whose sound is that, my dear?' 'Lord, hearing the sound of your chariot, the garuḍas who are unable to flee are crying out.' Hearing that, with a heart well-inclined with compassion, he spoke. As for 'īsāmukhena', it means with the front of the chariot's pole. Just as the front of the pole should not crush the nests, so with this pole-front you should avoid them. For that chariot, arisen from the cause of merit, goes right through even the Cakkavāḷa mountain range or Mount Sineru when they are in front of it; it does not get stuck, but travels just as if through the sky. If it were to go through that silk-cotton tree forest, then just as when a great cart goes through the middle of a banana grove or a castor-oil plant grove, the entire forest is broken and crushed, so too would that silk-cotton tree forest be. The sixth.

7. Nadubbhiyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Nadubbhiya Sutta.

253. Sattame upasaṅkamīti “ayaṃ sakko ‘yopi me assa supaccatthiko, tassa pāhaṃ na dubbheyya’nti cinteti, mayā tassa paccatthikataro nāma natthi, vīmaṃsissāmi tāva naṃ, kiṃ nu kho maṃ passitvā dubbhati, na dubbhatī”ti cintetvā upasaṅkami. Tiṭṭha vepacitti gahitosīti vepacitti, ettheva tiṭṭha, gahito tvaṃ mayāti vadati. Saha vacanenevassa [P 1.0345] so kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi baddhova ahosi. Sapassu ca meti mayi adubbhatthāya sapathaṃ karohīti vadati. Yaṃ musābhaṇato pāpanti imasmiṃ kappe paṭhamakappikesu cetiyarañño pāpaṃ sandhāyāha. Ariyūpavādinoti kokalikassa viya pāpaṃ. Mittadduno ca yaṃ pāpanti mahākapijātake mahāsatte duṭṭhacittassa [V 1.0301] pāpaṃ. Akataññunoti devadattasadisassa akataññuno pāpaṃ. Imāni kira imasmiṃ kappe cattāri mahāpāpāni. Sattamaṃ.

253. In the seventh, 'he approached' means: he approached thinking, “This Sakka thinks, ‘Whoever may be my extreme enemy, I would not harm even him.’ For him, there is no enemy more hostile than me. I will test him first. I wonder, will he harm me upon seeing me, or will he not harm me?” 'Stop, Vepacitti, you are seized!' means: he says, “Vepacitti, stay right there; you are seized by me.” Simultaneously with his utterance, Vepacitti was bound by the fivefold bonds with the neck as the fifth. 'And make a vow to me' means: he says, “Make an oath to me for the purpose of not doing harm.” 'The evil that comes from speaking falsely' refers to the evil of King Cetiya among those of the first age of this eon. 'Of one who reviles the noble ones' refers to an evil like that of Kokālika. 'And the evil of one who betrays a friend' refers to the evil of the one with a wicked mind towards the Great Being in the Mahākapi Jātaka. 'Of the ungrateful' refers to the evil of an ungrateful one like Devadatta. Indeed, these are the four great evils in this eon. The seventh.

8. Verocanaasurindasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Verocana Asurinda Sutta.

254. Aṭṭhame aṭṭhaṃsūti dvārapālarūpakāni viya ṭhitā. Nipphadāti nipphatti, yāva attho nipphajjati, tāva vāyamethevāti vadati. Dutiyagāthā sakkassa. Tattha khantyā bhiyyoti nipphannasobhanesu atthesu khantito uttaritaro attho nāma natthi. Atthajātāti kiccajātā. Soṇasiṅgālādayopi hi upādāya akiccajāto satto nāma natthi. Ito etto gamanamattampi kiccameva hoti. Saṃyogaparamā tveva, sambhogā sabbapāṇinanti pārivāsikaodanādīni hi asambhogārahāni honti, tāni puna uṇhāpetvā bhajjitvā sappimadhuphāṇitādīhi saṃyojitāni sambhogārahāni honti. Tenāha “saṃyogaparamā tveva, sambhogā sabbapāṇina”nti[M 1.0316]. Nipphannasobhano atthoti ime atthā nāma nipphannāva sobhanti. Puna catutthagāthā sakkassa. Tatthāpi vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

254. In the eighth, 'aṭṭhaṃsu' means they stood like figures of gatekeepers. 'Nipphadā' means completion; Verocana says, 'One should indeed strive for as long as the goal is not achieved.' The second verse is Sakka's. Therein, 'khantyā bhiyyo' means that among beautifully accomplished tasks, there is no task so-called that is more excellent than patience. 'Atthajātā' means having tasks that have arisen. Indeed, taking into account even domestic dogs, wild dogs, and so on, there is no being so-called that is free from tasks. Even the mere act of going from here to there is itself a task. 'Saṃyogaparamā tveva, sambhogā sabbapāṇinanti' means: for things like leftover rice are not fit for consumption; but when those things are again heated, roasted, and combined with ghee, honey, molasses, and so on, they become fit for consumption. Therefore, he said, 'Consumptions for all beings are indeed dependent on combination.' 'Nipphannasobhano attho' means these tasks so-called are beautiful only when they are accomplished. Again, the fourth verse is Sakka's. Therein also, the meaning should be understood in the way that has been stated. The eighth.

9. Araññāyatanaisisuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Sutta about the Seers of the Forest Dwelling.

255. Navame paṇṇakuṭīsu sammantīti himavantapadese ramaṇīye araññāyatane rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānacaṅkamanādīhi sampannāsu paṇṇasālāsu vasanti. Sakko ca devānamindo vepacitti cāti ime dve janā jāmātikasasurā kālena kalahaṃ karonti, kālena ekato caranti, imasmiṃ pana kāle ekato [P 1.0346] caranti. Paṭaliyoti gaṇaṅgaṇūpāhanā. Khaggaṃ olaggetvāti khaggaṃ aṃse olaggetvā. Chattenāti dibbasetacchattena matthake dhārayamānena. Apabyāmato karitvāti byāmato akatvā. Ciradikkhitānanti cirasamādiṇṇavatānaṃ. Ito paṭikkammāti “ito pakkama parivajjaya, mā uparivāte tiṭṭhā”ti vadanti. Na hettha devāti etasmiṃ sīlavantānaṃ gandhe devā na paṭikkūlasaññino, iṭṭhakantamanāpasaññinoyevāti dīpeti. Navamaṃ.

255. In the ninth sutta, 'they dwell in leaf huts' (paṇṇakuṭīsu sammanti) means: they dwell in leaf-halls in a delightful forest dwelling in the Himalayan region, endowed with places for the night, places for the day, walking paths, and so on. 'Sakka, the lord of the devas, and Vepacitti' (Sakko ca devānamindo vepacitti ca) means: these two persons, being son-in-law and father-in-law, at times create a quarrel, and at times go about together; but at this time, they go about together. 'With layered sandals' (āṭaliyo) means with sandals of multiple layers. 'Having slung the sword' (khaggaṃ olaggetvā) means having slung the sword on the shoulder. 'With the parasol' (chattena) means with a divine white parasol being held over the head. 'Having held it straight' (apabyāmato karitvā) means having made it unbent. 'Of the long-ordained' (ciradikkhitānaṃ) means of those who have long undertaken the ascetic practices. 'Go away from here!' (ito paṭikkama) means they say: 'Go away from this place! Avoid it! Do not stand upwind!' 'There are no devas here' (na hettha devā) shows that in this bodily odor of the virtuous ones, the devas do not have a perception of it as repulsive; they indeed have a perception of it as sought after, wished for, and pleasing. The ninth.

10. Samuddakasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Samuddaka Sutta

256. Dasame [V 1.0302] samuddatīre paṇṇakuṭīsūti cakkavāḷamahāsamuddapiṭṭhiyaṃ rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇe vālukapuḷine vuttappakārāsu paṇṇasālāsu vasanti. Siyāpi noti siyāpi amhākaṃ. Abhayadakkhiṇaṃ yāceyyāmāti abhayadānaṃ yāceyyāma. Yebhuyyena kira devāsurasaṅgāmo mahāsamuddapiṭṭhe hoti. Asurānaṃ na sabbakālaṃ jayo hoti, bahuvāre parājayova hoti. Te devehi parājitā palāyantā isīnaṃ assamapadena gacchantā “sakko imehi saddhiṃ mantetvā amhe nāseti, gaṇhatha puttahatāya putte”ti kupitā assamapade pānīyaghaṭacaṅkamanasālādīni viddhaṃsenti. Isayo araññato phalāphalaṃ ādāya āgatā naṃ disvā puna dukkhena paṭipākatikaṃ [M 1.0317] karonti. Tepi punappunaṃ tatheva vināsenti. Tasmā “idāni tesaṃ saṅgāmo paccupaṭṭhito”ti sutvā evaṃ cintayiṃsu.

256. In the tenth sutta, regarding the phrase 'in leaf huts on the seashore': they live in leaf huts of the kind already mentioned, on a sand-heap resembling a silver plate, on the shore of the great ocean at the foot of the Cakkavāḷa mountain range. 'Siyāpi no' means: 'Perhaps for us there might be.' 'We would ask for the bestowal of safety' (abhayadakkhiṇaṃ yāceyyāma) means 'we would ask for the gift of safety.' For the most part, it is said that the battle between the devas and asuras occurs on the surface of the great ocean. The asuras do not always have victory; many times, there is only defeat. When defeated by the devas, they flee, and passing through the hermitage of the sages, they become angry, thinking, 'Sakka, having conspired with these sages, is destroying us. Seize the sleeping ones!' and they destroy the water pots, walkways, halls, and so on in the hermitage. The sages, having returned from the forest bringing fruits, see this and again, with difficulty, restore it. They too, again and again, destroy it in the same way. Therefore, hearing, 'Now their battle is imminent,' they thought thus.

Kāmaṃkaroti [P 1.0347] icchitakaro. Bhayassa abhayassa vāti bhayaṃ vā abhayaṃ vā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – sace tvaṃ abhayaṃ dātukāmo, abhayaṃ dātuṃ pahosi. Sace bhayaṃ dātukāmo. Bhayaṃ dātuṃ pahosi. Amhākaṃ pana abhayadānaṃ dehīti. Duṭṭhānanti viruddhānaṃ. Pavuttanti khette patiṭṭhāpitaṃ.

'Kāmaṃkaro' means: one who does as he wishes. 'Of fear or of safety' means: either fear or safety. This is what is said: 'If you wish to give safety, you are able to give safety. If you wish to give fear, you are able to give fear. But to us, give the gift of safety.' 'Duṭṭhānaṃ' means: of the hostile. 'Pavuttaṃ' means: established in a field.

Tikkhattuṃ ubbijjīti sāyamāsabhattaṃ bhuñjitvā sayanaṃ abhiruyha nipanno niddāya okkantamattāya samantā ṭhatvā sattisatena pahaṭo viya viravanto uṭṭhahati, dasayojanasahassaṃ asurabhavanaṃ “kimida”nti saṅkhobhaṃ āpajjati. Atha naṃ āgantvā “kimida”nti pucchanti. So “na kiñcī”ti vadati. Dutiyayāmādīsupi eseva nayo. Iti asurānaṃ “mā bhāyi, mahārājā”ti taṃ assāsentānaṃyeva aruṇaṃ uggacchati.
