Evamassa tato paṭṭhāya gelaññajātaṃ cittaṃ vepati. Teneva cassa “vepacittī”ti aparaṃ nāmaṃ udapādīti. Dasamaṃ.

'Three times he was startled' means: After eating his evening meal and ascending his bed, as soon as he has lain down and fallen asleep, he rises up, screaming as if surrounded and struck by a hundred spears. The ten-thousand-yojana asura abode falls into turmoil, wondering, 'What is this?' Then they come to him and ask, 'What is this?' He replies, 'It is nothing.' The same occurs during the second watch and so on. Thus, even as the asuras are reassuring him, saying, 'Do not be afraid, great king,' the dawn breaks. In this way, from that time onwards, an illness arose for him and his mind trembled. And for that very reason, another name arose for him: 'Vepacitti.' The tenth.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Section.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Section

1. Vatapadasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Vatapada Sutta

257. Dutiyavaggassa [V 1.0303] paṭhame vatapadānīti vatakoṭṭhāsāni. Samattānīti paripuṇṇāni. Samādinnānīti gahitāni. Kule jeṭṭhāpacāyīti kulajeṭṭhakānaṃ mahāpitā mahāmātā cūḷapitā cūḷamātā mātulo mātulānītiādīnaṃ apacitikārako. Saṇhavācoti piyamudumadhuravāco. Muttacāgoti vissaṭṭhacāgo. Payatapāṇīti deyyadhammadānatthāya sadā dhotahattho. Vossaggaratoti vossajjane rato. Yācayogoti parehi yācitabbāraho, yācayogoti vā yācayogeneva yutto. Dānasaṃvibhāgaratoti dāne ca saṃvibhāge ca rato. Paṭhamaṃ.

257. In the first sutta of the second section, 'vows' (vatapadāni) means the constituents of the vows. 'Completed' (samattāni) means completely fulfilled. 'Well undertaken' (samādinnāni) means taken up. 'One who honors the elders in the family' (kule jeṭṭhāpacāyī) means one who pays respect to the elders in the family: the father's elder brother, mother's elder sister, father's younger brother, mother's younger sister, maternal uncle, maternal uncle's wife, and so on. 'One with gentle speech' (saṇhavāco) means one has endearing, gentle, and sweet speech. 'One with unrestrained generosity' (muttacāgo) means one has relinquished generosity. 'One with a ready hand' (payatapāṇī) means one's hand is always washed for the purpose of giving gifts. 'One who delights in relinquishing' (vossaggarato) means one delights in giving up. 'One fit to be asked' (yācayogo) means one is worthy of being asked by others; or alternatively, 'yācayogo' means one is suited for the practice of being asked. 'One who delights in giving and sharing' (dānasaṃvibhāgarato) means one delights in giving and in sharing. The first.

2. Sakkanāmasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Sakkanāma Sutta

258. Dutiye [M 1.0318][P 1.0348] manussabhūtoti magadharaṭṭhe macalagāme manussabhūto. Āvasathaṃ adāsīti catumahāpathe mahājanassa āvasathaṃ kāretvā adāsi. Sahassampi atthānanti sahassampi kāraṇānaṃ, janasahassena vā vacanasahassena vā osārite “ayaṃ imassa attho, ayaṃ imassa attho”ti ekapade ṭhitova vinicchinati. Dutiyaṃ.

258. In the second sutta, 'having become human' (manussabhūto) means when he was a human being in the village of Macala in the country of Magadha. 'He gave a rest house' (āvasathaṃ adāsi) means having had a rest house built for the great populace at a crossroads of four great roads, he gave it. 'Even a thousand matters' (sahassampi atthānaṃ) means even when a thousand reasons are presented by a thousand people with a thousand words, while standing on a single point he is able to decide, 'This is the meaning of this; this is the meaning of this.' The second.

3. Mahālisuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Mahāli Sutta

259. Tatiye upasaṅkamīti “sakko devarājāti kathenti, atthi nu kho so sakko, yena so diṭṭhapubboti imamatthaṃ dasabalaṃ pucchissāmī”ti upasaṅkami. Tañca pajānāmīti bahuvacane ekavacanaṃ, te ca dhamme pajānāmīti attho. Sakko kira anantare attabhāve magadharaṭṭhe macalagāme magho nāma māṇavo ahosi paṇḍito byatto, bodhisattacariyā viya ca tassa cariyā ahosi. So tettiṃsa purise gahetvā kalyāṇamakāsi. Ekadivasaṃ attanova paññāya upaparikkhitvā gāmamajjhe mahājanassa sannipatitaṭṭhāne kacavaraṃ ubhatopassesu apabyūhitvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ akāsi. Puna tattheva maṇḍapaṃ kāresi. Puna gacchante kāle sālaṃ [V 1.0304] kāresi. Gāmato ca nikkhamitvā gāvutampi aḍḍhayojanampi tigāvutampi yojanampi vicaritvā tehi sahāyehi saddhiṃ visamaṃ samaṃ akāsi. Te sabbeva ekacchandā tattha tattha setuyuttaṭṭhāne setuṃ, maṇḍapasālāpokkharaṇimālāvaccharopanapadīnaṃ yuttaṭṭhānesu maṇḍapasālāpokkharaṇimālāvaccharopanādīni karontā bahuṃ puññamakaṃsu. Magho satta vatapadāni pūretvā kāyassa bhedā saddhiṃ sahāyehi tāvatiṃsabhavane nibbatti. Taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavā jānāti. Tenāha – yesaṃ dhammānaṃ samādinnattā sakko sakkattaṃ ajjhagā, tañca pajānāmīti. Ayaṃ sakkassa sakkattādhigame saṅkhepakathā, vitthāro pana sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya sakkapaṇhavaṇṇanāyaṃ vutto. Tatiyaṃ.

259. In the third [sutta], 'upasaṅkami' means he approached, thinking: 'They speak of Sakka, the king of devas. Does that Sakka truly exist? Has anyone seen him before? I will ask the Ten-Powered One about this matter.' And 'Tañca pajānāmi' is a singular form used in a plural sense, meaning, 'And I know those principles.' It is said that Sakka, in his immediately preceding existence, was a wise and skilled young man named Magha in the village of Macala in the country of Magadha. His conduct was like that of a Bodhisatta. Taking thirty-three men with him, he performed good deeds. One day, after reflecting with his own wisdom, he cleared the rubbish from both sides of the public gathering place in the middle of the village and made the place beautiful. Again, he had a pavilion built there. Later, he had a rest hall constructed. And leaving the village, he and his companions traveled for a gāvuta, half a yojana, three gāvutas, and even a yojana, leveling the uneven ground. All of them, united in purpose, built bridges where bridges were needed; and in places suitable for pavilions, halls, ponds, and the planting of flowering plants, they constructed such things and so on, accumulating much merit. Magha, having fulfilled the seven vows, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with his companions upon the breakup of his body. The Blessed One knows all this. Therefore, he said: 'And I know those principles, by the undertaking of which Sakka attained the state of being Sakka.' This is a brief account of how Sakka attained the state of being Sakka. The detailed explanation, however, is given in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary on the Dīghanikāya, in the explanation of the Sakkapañha Sutta. The third.

4. Daliddasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Explanation of the Dalidda Sutta

260. Catutthe [M 1.0319][P 1.0349] manussadaliddoti manussaadhano. Manussakapaṇoti manussakāruññataṃ patto. Manussavarākoti manussalāmako. Tatrāti tasmiṃ ṭhāne, tasmiṃ vā atirocane. Ujjhāyantīti avajjhāyanti lāmakato cintenti. Khiyantīti kathenti pakāsenti. Vipācentīti tattha tattha kathenti vitthārenti. Eso kho mārisāti ettha ayamanupubbikathā – so kira anuppanne buddhe kāsiraṭṭhe bārāṇasirājā hutvā samussitaddhajapaṭākanānālaṅkārena suṭṭhu alaṅkataṃ nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi attano sirisampattiyā samākaḍḍhitanettena janakāyena samullokiyamāno. Tasmiñca samaye eko paccekabuddho gandhamādanapabbatā āgamma tasmiṃ nagare piṇḍāya carati, santindriyo santamānaso uttamadamathasamannāgato. Mahājanopi rājagataṃ cittīkāraṃ pahāya paccekabuddhameva olokesi. Rājā – “idāni imasmiṃ janakāye ekopi maṃ na oloketi. Kiṃ nu kho eta”nti? Olokento paccekabuddhaṃ addasa. Sopi paccekabuddho mahallako hoti pacchimavaye ṭhito. Cīvarānipissa jiṇṇāni, tato tato suttāni gaḷanti. Rañño satasahassādhikāni dve asaṅkhyeyyāni pūritapāramiṃ paccekabuddhaṃ disvā cittapasādamattaṃ vā hatthaṃ pasāretvā vandanamattaṃ vā nāhosi. So rājā “pabbajito maññe esa usūyāya maṃ na oloketī”ti kujjhitvā “kvāyaṃ kuṭṭhicīvarāni pāruto”ti niṭṭhubhitvā pakkāmi. Tassa kammassa vipākena mahāniraye nibbattitvā vipākāvasesena manussalokaṃ āgacchanto rājagahe paramakapaṇāya itthiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Gahitakālato paṭṭhāya sā itthī kañjikamattampi [V 1.0305] udarapūraṃ nālattha. Tassa kucchigatasseva kaṇṇanāsā vilīnā, saṅkhapalitakuṭṭhī hutvā mātukucchito nikkhanto. Mātāpitaro [P 1.0350] nāma dukkarakārikā honti, tenassa mātā yāva kapālaṃ gahetvā carituṃ na sakkoti, tāvassa kañjikampi udakampi āharitvā adāsi. Bhikkhāya carituṃ samatthakāle panassa kapālaṃ hatthe datvā “paññāyissasi sakena kammenā”ti pakkāmi.

260. In the fourth [sutta], `manussadaliddo` means a destitute person; `manussakapaṇo` means one who has reached a state worthy of compassion; `manussavarāko` means a base person among humans. `Tatrā` means in that place, or in that outshining. `Ujjhāyanti` means they look upon him contemptuously, thinking of him as base. `Khiyanti` means they speak ill of him, making his baseness known. `Vipācenti` means they speak of it here and there, spreading it about. Regarding 'Eso kho mārisa,' this is the sequential narrative: It is said that at a time when no Buddha had arisen, he, having become the king of Bārāṇasī in the Kāsī country, circumambulated the city, which was well-adorned with raised banners, flags, and various ornaments, while being gazed upon by the populace whose eyes were drawn by his own majestic splendor. And at that time, a certain Paccekabuddha, having come from Mount Gandhamādana, was wandering for alms in that city, with tranquil faculties, a peaceful mind, and endowed with supreme taming and calm. The great populace, too, abandoning their respect for the king, looked only at the Paccekabuddha. The king thought, 'Now, in this crowd, not even one person looks at me. What could this be?' Looking about, he saw the Paccekabuddha. That Paccekabuddha was elderly, in the last stage of life. His robes were worn out, and threads were hanging down from here and there. For the king, upon seeing the Paccekabuddha who had fulfilled the perfections for two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons more, there did not arise even a mere mental confidence, nor even a mere paying of homage by extending his hand. That king, becoming angry, thought, 'I suppose this is a royal ascetic; it is out of envy that he does not look at me.' Then, saying, 'Who is this, clad in disgusting robes?', he spat and departed. By the result of that kamma, having been reborn in the great hell, by the remainder of the result, while coming to the human world, he took conception in the womb of an extremely wretched woman in Rājagaha. From the time of conception onwards, that woman did not get even enough rice-gruel to fill her stomach. While he was still in the womb, his ears and nose dissolved. Having become a leper with white, conch-like skin, he came forth from his mother's womb. Parents, indeed, are doers of what is difficult. Therefore, for as long as he was unable to go about holding a bowl, his mother brought and gave him gruel. But when he was able to wander for alms, having placed a bowl in his hand, she departed, saying, 'You will be known by your own kamma.'

Athassa [M 1.0320] tato paṭṭhāya sakalasarīrato maṃsāni chijjitvā chijjitvā patanti, yūsaṃ paggharati, mahāvedanā vattanti. Yaṃ yaṃ racchaṃ nissāya sayati, sabbarattiṃ mahāravena ravati. Tassa kāruññaparidevitasaddena sakalavīthiyaṃ manussā sabbarattiṃ niddaṃ na labhanti. Tassa tato paṭṭhāya sukhasayite pabodhetīti suppabuddhotveva nāmaṃ udapādi. Athāparena samayena bhagavati rājagahaṃ sampatte nāgarā satthāraṃ nimantetvā nagaramajjhe mahāmaṇḍapaṃ katvā dānaṃ adaṃsu. Suppabuddhopi kuṭṭhī gantvā dānaggamaṇḍapassa avidūre nisīdi. Nāgarā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisantā tassāpi yāgubhattaṃ adaṃsu. Tassa paṇītabhojanaṃ bhuttassa cittaṃ ekaggaṃ ahosi. Satthā bhattakiccāvasāne anumodanaṃ katvā saccāni dīpesi, suppabuddho nisinnaṭṭhāne nisinnova desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesetvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito. Satthā uṭṭhāya vihāraṃ gato. Sopi cumbaṭaṃ āruyha kapālamādāya daṇḍamolubbha attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto vibbhantāya gāviyā jīvitā voropito mattikapātiṃ bhinditvā suvaṇṇapātiṃ paṭilabhanto viya dutiyacittavāre devaloke nibbatto attano puññaṃ nissāya aññe deve atikkamma virocittha. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ dassento sakko devānamindo eso kho mārisātiādimāha.

From that time on, flesh kept falling off his entire body in pieces, exudate flowed forth, and great pains arose. On whatever street he lay, he wailed loudly throughout the night. Because of his pitiful cries and lamentations, people throughout the entire street could not get any sleep all night. From that time on, the name Suppabuddha arose for him because he awakens those who are sleeping comfortably. Later, when the Blessed One arrived at Rājagaha, the citizens invited the Teacher and, having made a great pavilion in the middle of the city, gave alms. Suppabuddha the leper also went and sat not far from the alms pavilion. The citizens, serving the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with choice hard and soft food, also gave him rice porridge. When he had eaten the choice food, his mind became unified. When the Teacher had concluded the meal and given the blessing, he revealed the truths. Suppabuddha, remaining seated right where he was, directed his knowledge in accordance with the discourse and became established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher rose and went to the monastery. He too, having taken up his bundle of rags and his bowl, and leaning on a stick, was going to his dwelling when he was deprived of life by a crazed cow. Just as one might break a clay pot and obtain a golden pot, so in the second moment of consciousness, he was reborn in the deva world and, by virtue of his merit, outshone the other devas. To show that reason, Sakka, king of devas, said, 'This, good sir,' and so on.

Saddhāti maggenāgatasaddhā. Sīlañca yassa kalyāṇanti kalyāṇasīlaṃ nāma ariyasāvakassa ariyakantasīlaṃ vuccati. Tattha kiñcāpi ariyasāvakassa ekasīlampi akantaṃ nāma natthi, imasmiṃ panatthe bhavantarepi appahīnaṃ pañcasīlaṃ adhippetaṃ. Catutthaṃ.

Faith means faith that has come by the path. 'And whose virtue is beautiful' means the beautiful virtue of a noble disciple, which is called virtue beloved by the noble ones. Here, although there is no single virtue of a noble disciple that is not beloved, in this context, the five precepts that are unabandoned even in other existences are intended. The fourth.

5. Rāmaṇeyyakasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Rāmaṇeyyaka Sutta

261. Pañcame [P 1.0351] ārāmacetyāti ārāmacetiyāni. Vanacetyāti vanacetiyāni. Ubhayatthāpi [V 1.0306] cittīkataṭṭhena cetyaṃ veditabbaṃ. Manussarāmaṇeyyassāti manussaramaṇīyabhāvassa. Idāni manussaramaṇīyakavasena bhūmiramaṇīyakaṃ dassento gāme vātiādimāha. Pañcamaṃ.

261. In the fifth sutta, 'venerable parks' means parks that are venerated. 'Venerable forests' means forests that are venerated. In both cases, the word 'cetya' should be understood in the sense of that which is venerated. 'Of the state of being delightful to humans' means of the state of being delightful for humans. Now, wishing to show the delightfulness of the land by way of its being delightful to humans, he spoke the words beginning with 'in a village or'. The fifth.

6. Yajamānasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Yajamāna Sutta

262. Chaṭṭhe [M 1.0321] yajamānānanti yajantānaṃ. Tadā kira aṅgamagadhavāsikā manussā anusaṃvaccharaṃ sappimadhuphāṇitādīsu aggaṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne dārūnaṃ saṭṭhimatte sakaṭabhāre rāsiṃ katvā aggiṃ datvā pajjalitakāle “mahābrahmuno yajāmā”ti taṃ sabbaṃ pakkhipanti. “Ekavāraṃ pakkhittaṃ sahassaguṇaphalaṃ detī”ti nesaṃ laddhi. Sakko devarājā “sabbepime sabbaaggāni gahetvā ‘mahābrahmuno yajāmā’ti aggimhi jhāpenti. Aphalaṃ karonti, mayi passante mā nassantu, yathā buddhassa ceva saṅghassa ca datvā bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavanti, evaṃ karissāmī”ti dārurāsiṃ jalāpetvā olokentesu manussesu puṇṇamadivase brahmattabhāvaṃ māpetvā mahājanassa passantasseva candamaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā nikkhanto viya ahosi. Mahājano disvā “imaṃ yaññaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ mahābrahmā āgacchatī”ti jaṇṇukehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāya, añjaliṃ paggayha namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. Brāhmaṇā āhaṃsu “tumhe ‘mayaṃ takkena kathemā’ti maññatha, idāni passatha, ayaṃ vo brahmā sahatthā yaññaṃ paṭiggahetuṃ āgacchatī”ti. Sakko āgantvā dārucitakamatthake ākāse ṭhatvā “kassāyaṃ sakkāro”ti pucchi? Tumhākaṃ, bhante, paṭiggaṇhatha no yaññanti. Tena hi āgacchatha, mā tulaṃ chaḍḍetvā hatthena tulayittha, ayaṃ satthā dhuravihāre vasati, taṃ pucchissāma “kassa dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ hotī”ti[P 1.0352]? Ubhayaraṭṭhavāsino gahetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā pucchanto evamāha.

262. In the sixth sutta, the word 'yajamānānaṃ' means 'of those who make offerings.' It is said that at that time, the people dwelling in the countries of Aṅga and Magadha, every year, would take the best of things such as ghee, honey, and molasses, and in one place, having made a pile of sixty cartloads of firewood and having set it on fire, when it was ablaze, thinking, 'Let us make a sacrifice to the Great Brahmā,' they would put all of it in. Their belief was, 'What is put in once gives a result a thousandfold.' Sakka, the king of the devas, thought: 'All these people, taking all the first-fruits, burn them in the fire, thinking, "Let us make an offering to the Great Brahmā." They are doing something fruitless. While I am watching, let them not be destroyed. I shall act in such a way that, by giving to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, they may generate much merit.' Having caused the pile of wood to burn, while the people were looking on, on the full-moon day, he created the form of a Brahmā and appeared as if emerging from the moon-disc after splitting it, right while the great crowd was watching. The great crowd, seeing this, thought, 'The Great Brahmā is coming to accept this sacrifice.' Placing their knees on the ground and raising their joined palms, they stood paying homage. The brahmins said, 'You think that we speak merely from our own reasoning. Now see! This Brahmā of yours is coming to accept the sacrifice with his own hands.' Sakka, having come and standing in the sky above the pyre of wood, asked, 'For whom is this offering?' 'Venerable sir, it is for you. Please accept our sacrifice,' they said. 'If that is so, come. Do not, having cast aside the scales, weigh by hand. This Teacher dwells in the chief monastery. I will ask him, "A gift given to whom has great fruit?"' Taking the inhabitants of both countries and having gone to the Teacher's presence, he asked, speaking thus.

Tattha puññapekkhānanti puññaṃ icchantānaṃ puññatthikānaṃ. Opadhikaṃ puññanti upadhivipākaṃ puññaṃ. Saṅghe dinnaṃ mahapphalanti ariyasaṅghe dinnaṃ vipphāravantaṃ hoti. Desanāvasāne caturāsītipāṇasahassāni amatapānaṃ piviṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya manussā sabbāni aggadānāni bhikkhusaṅghassa adaṃsu. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

Here, 'for those who seek merit' means: for those who desire merit, for those who have need of merit. 'Merit connected with the aggregates' means: merit that has the aggregates as its result. 'Given to the Saṅgha is of great fruit' means: a gift given to the Noble Saṅgha has an expansive result. At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings drank the deathless nectar. From that time onward, people gave all the foremost gifts to the community of bhikkhus. The sixth.

7. Buddhavandanāsuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Buddhavandanā Sutta

263. Sattame [V 1.0307] uṭṭhehīti uṭṭhaha, ghaṭa, vāyama. Vijitasaṅgāmāti rāgādīnañceva dvādasayojanikassa ca mārabalassa jitattā bhagavantaṃ evaṃ ālapati[M 1.0322]. Pannabhārāti oropitakhandhakilesābhisaṅkhārabhāra. Pannarasāya rattinti pannarasāya puṇṇamāya rattiṃ. Sattamaṃ.

263. In the seventh, 'arise!' means: arise, strive, exert yourself. 'Victorious in battle' means: the Blessed One is addressed thus because he has conquered both the defilements such as lust, and the army of Māra which is twelve yojanas in height. 'The burden laid down' means: one who has laid down the burden of the aggregates, defilements, and volitional formations. 'On the fifteenth night' means: on the night of the fifteenth full moon day. The seventh.

8. Gahaṭṭhavandanāsuttavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Gahaṭṭhavandanā Sutta

264. Aṭṭhame puthuddisāti catasso disā catasso anudisā ca. Bhummāti bhūmivāsino. Cirarattasamāhiteti upacārappanāhi cirarattasamāhitacitte. Vandeti vandāmi. Brahmacariyaparāyaṇeti dasapi vassāni vīsatipi vassāni…pe… saṭṭhipi vassāni āpāṇakoṭikaṃ ekaseyyaṃ ekabhattantiādikaṃ seṭṭhacariyaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caramāneti attho. Puññakarāti catupaccayadānaṃ kusumbhasumanapūjā dīpasahassajālanti evamādipuññakārakā. Sīlavantoti upāsakatte patiṭṭhāya pañcahipi dasahipi sīlehi samannāgatā. Dhammena dāraṃ posentīti umaṅgabhindanādīni akatvā dhammikehi kasigorakkhavaṇijjādīhi puttadāraṃ posenti. Pamukho rathamāruhīti devānaṃ pamukho seṭṭho rathaṃ āruhi. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

264. In the eighth, 'in various directions' means the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions. 'Earth-dwelling' means earth-dwelling devas. 'Long concentrated' means with minds long concentrated through access and absorption concentration. 'He pays homage' means I pay homage. 'Devoted to the holy life' means this is the meaning—practicing the noble conduct, the holy life, such as sleeping alone, eating a single meal, and so on, for ten years, twenty years... up to sixty years, for as long as life lasts. 'Merit-makers' means those who perform meritorious deeds such as giving the four requisites, offering kusumbha and sumana flowers, and lighting a thousand lamps. 'Virtuous' means established in the state of a lay follower, endowed with the five or the ten precepts. 'They support their family righteously' means they support their children and wife through righteous means such as farming, cattle-rearing, and trade, without committing acts such as tunneling. 'The foremost ascended the chariot' means the foremost, the best of the devas, ascended the chariot. The eighth.

9. Satthāravandanāsuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Paying Homage to the Teacher

265. Navame [P 1.0353] bhagavantaṃ namassatīti ekaṃsaṃ uttariyaṃ dukulaṃ katvā, brahmajāṇuko hutvā sirasi añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā namassati. So yakkhoti so sakko. Anomanāmanti sabbaguṇehi omakabhāvassa natthitāya sabbaguṇanemittakehi nāmehi anomanāmaṃ. Avijjāsamatikkamāti catusaccapaṭicchādikāya vaṭṭamūlakaavijjāya samatikkamena. Sekkhāti satta sekkhā. Apacayārāmāti vaṭṭaviddhaṃsane ratā. Sikkhareti sikkhanti. Navamaṃ.

265. In the ninth sutta, 'he pays homage to the Blessed One' means having placed the upper garment, a white muslin robe, over one shoulder, and having become like one who prostrates with both elbows on the ground, he places his joined hands on his head and pays homage. 'That yakkha' means that is Sakka. 'Of unblemished name' means due to the absence of an inferior state with respect to all qualities, he has a name of perfect qualities, with names that arise on account of all qualities. 'Transcending ignorance' means by transcending the ignorance which is the root of the cycle of existence and which conceals the Four Truths. 'Trainees' means the seven trainees. 'Delighting in dismantling' means they delight in the destruction of the cycle of existence. 'They train' means they are training. The ninth sutta.

10. Saṅghavandanāsuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on Paying Homage to the Saṅgha

266. Dasame ajjhabhāsīti kasmā esa punappunaṃ evaṃ bhāsatīti? Sakkassa kira devarañño [V 1.0308] saddo madhuro, suphasitaṃ dantāvaraṇaṃ, kathanakāle suvaṇṇakiṅkiṇikasaddo viya niccharati. Taṃ punappunaṃ sotuṃ labhissāmīti bhāsati. Pūtidehasayāti pūtimhi mātusarīre vā, attanoyeva vā sarīraṃ avattharitvā sayanato pūtidehasayā. Nimuggā [M 1.0323] kuṇapamheteti dasamāse mātukucchisaṅkhāte kuṇapasmiṃ ete nimuggā. Etaṃ tesaṃ pihayāmīti etesaṃ etaṃ pihayāmi patthayāmi. Na te saṃ koṭṭhe opentīti na te saṃ santakaṃ dhaññaṃ koṭṭhe pakkhipanti. Na hi etesaṃ dhaññaṃ atthi. Na kumbhīti na kumbhiyaṃ. Na kaḷopiyanti na pacchiyaṃ. Paraniṭṭhitamesānāti paresaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ paraghare pakkaṃ bhikkhācāravattena esamānā gavesamānā. Tenāti evaṃ pariyiṭṭhena. Subbatāti dasapi…pe… saṭṭhipi vassāni susamādinnasundaravatā.

266. In the tenth sutta, 'he addressed' means: Why does this deity Mātali ask thus again and again? It is said that the voice of Sakka, king of the gods, is sweet, his lips are well-articulated, and when he speaks, the sound that comes out is like the tinkling of a golden bell. Thinking, 'I shall get to hear that again and again,' he asks repeatedly. 'Lying in a putrid body' means because they lie in the putrid body of the mother, or in their own body, they are 'those who lie in a putrid body'. 'Submerged in a corpse' means these beings are submerged for ten months in the corpse, that is, the mother's womb. 'This of them I long for' means I cherish and long for this noble practice of right conduct of theirs. 'They do not put it in their barn' means they do not put the grain that is their property into a barn, for indeed, they have no grain. 'Not in a pot' means not in a pot. 'Not in a basket' means not in a basket. 'Seeking what is prepared by others' means seeking and searching, by means of the alms-round practice, for food cooked in others' homes that has been prepared by others. 'By that' means by this seeking from house to house. 'Of good vows' means for ten... up to sixty years, they are of beautiful conduct, having well undertaken and established it.

Sumantamantinoti dhammaṃ sajjhāyissāma, dhutaṅgaṃ samādiyissāma, amataṃ paribhuñjissāma, samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmāti evaṃ subhāsitabhāsino. Tuṇhībhūtā samañcarāti tiyāmarattiṃ asanighosena [P 1.0354] ghositā viya dhammaṃ kathentāpi tuṇhībhūtā samaṃ carantiyeva nāma. Kasmā? Niratthakavacanassābhāvā. Puthumaccā cāti bahusattā ca aññamaññaṃ viruddhā. Attadaṇḍesu nibbutāti paraviheṭhanatthaṃ gahitadaṇḍesu sattesu nibbutā vissaṭṭhadaṇḍā. Sādānesu anādānāti sagahaṇesu sattesu ca bhavayoniādīnaṃ ekakoṭṭhāsassāpi agahitattā agahaṇā. Dasamaṃ.

'Of excellent counsel' means they say, 'We will recite the Dhamma, we will undertake the ascetic practices, we will partake of the Deathless, we will perform the duties of a recluse'—thus they are speakers of well-spoken words. 'Silent, they wander together' means that even after teaching the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night with a sound like an incessant thunderclap, they become silent and wander together in equanimity. Why? Because of the absence of useless speech. 'And many mortals' means that many beings are in conflict with one another. 'Peaceful among those who have taken up the rod' means that among beings who have taken up the rod for the purpose of harming others, they are quenched, having relinquished the rod. 'Among those who grasp, not grasping' means that among beings who grasp, they are non-grasping because they have not grasped even a single portion of existence, birth, and so on. The tenth.

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter

1. Chetvāsuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Chetvā Sutta

267. Tatiyavaggassa paṭhamaṃ vuttatthameva. Paṭhamaṃ.

267. The meaning of the first (sutta) of the third chapter is just as has been stated. The first.

2. Dubbaṇṇiyasuttavaṇṇanā

2. Commentary on the Dubbaṇṇiya Sutta

268. Dutiye [V 1.0309] dubbaṇṇoti jhāmakhāṇuvaṇṇo. Okoṭimakoti lakuṇḍako mahodaro. Āsaneti paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ. Kodhabhakkhoti sakkena gahitanāmamevetaṃ. So pana eko rūpāvacarabrahmā, “sakko kira khantibalena samannāgato”ti sutvā vīmaṃsanatthaṃ āgato[M 1.0324]. Avaruddhakayakkhā pana evarūpaṃ saṃvihitārakkhaṃ ṭhānaṃ pavisituṃ na sakkonti. Upasaṅkamīti devānaṃ sutvā “na sakkā esa pharusena cāletuṃ, nīcavuttinā pana khantiyaṃ ṭhitena sakkā palāpetu”nti tathā palāpetukāmo upasaṅkami. Antaradhāyīti khantiyaṃ ṭhatvā balavacittīkāraṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā nīcavuttiyā dassiyamānāya sakkāsane ṭhātuṃ asakkonto antaradhāyi. Na sūpahatacittomhīti ettha sūti nipātamattaṃ, upahatacittomhīti āha. Nāvattena suvānayoti na kodhāvattena suānayo, kodhavase vattetuṃ na sukaromhīti vadati. Na vo cirāhanti voti nipātamattaṃ, ahaṃ ciraṃ na kujjhāmīti vadati. Dutiyaṃ.

268. In the second (sutta), 'of bad complexion' means one whose complexion is like a burnt tree stump. 'Hunched' means a dwarf with a large belly. 'On the seat' refers to the Paṇḍukambala stone slab. 'Anger-Eater' is merely a name taken by Sakka. But he was a certain Brahmā of the form realm who, having heard, 'Sakka, it is said, is endowed with the power of patience,' came for the purpose of testing him. Obstructive yakkhas, however, are not able to enter such a well-guarded place. 'He approached' means that having heard from the devas, 'This one cannot be shaken with harshness, but by one adopting humble conduct and standing firm in patience, he can be made to flee,' he approached, desiring to make him flee in that way. 'He disappeared' means that as Sakka stood firm in patience and established strong respect, and humble conduct was being shown, the yakkha, being unable to remain on Sakka’s seat, disappeared. In 'I am not one with a much-afflicted mind,' 'sū' is merely a particle; he says, 'I am not one with an afflicted mind.' 'Not easily led by the cycle' means not easily led by the cycle of anger; he says, 'I am not easy to make act under the power of anger.' In 'I am not angry for long,' 'vo' is merely a particle; he says, 'I do not stay angry for long.' The second.

3. Sambarimāyāsuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Sambarimāyā Sutta

269. Tatiye [P 1.0355] ābādhikoti isigaṇena abhisapakāle uppannābādhena ābādhiko. Vācehi manti sace maṃ sambarimāyaṃ vācesi, evamahaṃ tampi tikicchissāmīti vadati. Mā kho tvaṃ, mārisa, vācesīti vināpi tāva sambarimāyaṃ sakko amhe bādhati, yadi pana taṃ jānissati, naṭṭhā mayaṃ, mā attano ekassa atthāya amhe nāsehīti vatvā nivārayiṃsu. Sambarova sataṃ samanti yathā sambaro asurindo māyāvī māyaṃ payojetvā vassasataṃ niraye pakko, evaṃ paccati. Tumhe dhammikāva, alaṃ vo māyāyāti vadati. Kiṃ pana sakko tassa kodhaṃ tikicchituṃ sakkuṇeyyāti? Āma sakkuṇeyya. Kathaṃ? Tadā kira so isigaṇo dharatiyeva, tasmā naṃ isīnaṃ santikaṃ netvā khamāpeyya, evamassa phāsu bhaveyya. Tena pana vañcitattā tathā akatvā pakkantova. Tatiyaṃ.

269. In the third (sutta), 'afflicted' means: he was afflicted by an illness that arose at the time of the seers' curse. 'Teach me' means: 'If you teach me the Sambari trickery, I will cure you,' thus he speaks. 'Do not, good sir, teach' means: 'Even without the Sambari trickery, Sakka still oppresses us. If he were to learn it, we would be ruined. Do not destroy us for the sake of your own self,' and having said this, they prevented him. 'Like Sambara for a hundred years' means: just as Sambara, the lord of asuras, skilled in trickery, having employed his trickery, was cooked in hell for a hundred years, so too is one cooked. 'You are righteous; enough of trickery for you,' thus he speaks. But could Sakka have cured his anger? Yes, he could have. How? At that time, it is said, that group of seers was still living. Therefore, he could have taken him to the seers and had him ask for forgiveness; thus, it would have brought him relief. However, because he was deceived, he did not do so and just departed. Third.

4. Accayasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Accaya Sutta

270. Catutthe sampayojesunti kalahaṃ akaṃsu. Accasarāti atikkami, eko bhikkhu ekaṃ [V 1.0310] bhikkhuṃ atikkamma vacanaṃ avocāti attho. Yathādhammaṃ [M 1.0325] nappaṭiggaṇhātīti na khamati. Kodho vo vasamāyātūti kodho tumhākaṃ vasaṃ āgacchatu, mā tumhe kodhavasaṃ gamitthāti dīpeti. Mā ca mitte hi vo jarāti ettha hīti nipātamattaṃ, tumhākaṃ mittadhamme jarā nāma mā nibbatti. Bhummatthe vā karaṇavacanaṃ, mittesu vo jarā mā nibbatti, mittabhāvato aññathābhāvo mā hotūti attho. Agarahiyaṃ mā garahitthāti agārayhaṃ khīṇāsavapuggalaṃ mā garahittha. Catutthaṃ.

270. In the fourth (sutta), 'they engaged' means: they made a quarrel. 'He transgressed' means: he transgressed. The meaning is that one monk spoke a word transgressing against another monk. 'He does not accept according to the Dhamma' means: he does not forbear. 'Let anger come under your control' means: 'Let anger come under your control; do not you come under the control of anger,' thus he explains. In 'And may there be no decay in friendships for you,' here 'hi' is a mere particle. May what is called 'alteration' not arise for you in the nature of friendship. Alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative: may enmity not arise for you in regard to friends. The meaning is: may there be no alteration from the state of friendship. 'Do not blame the unblameworthy' means: do not blame the unblameworthy one, a person whose cankers are destroyed. Fourth.

5. Akkodhasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Akkodha Sutta

271. Pañcame mā vo kodho ajjhabhavīti kodho tumhe mā abhibhavi, tumheva kodhaṃ abhibhavatha. Mā ca kujjhittha kujjhitanti kujjhantānaṃ mā paṭikujjhittha. Akkodhoti mettā [P 1.0356] ca mettāpubbabhāgo ca. Avihiṃsāti karuṇā ca karuṇāpubbabhāgo ca. Atha pāpajanaṃ kodho, pabbatovābhimaddatīti lāmakajanaṃ pabbato viya kodho abhimaddatīti. Pañcamaṃ.

271. In the fifth (sutta): 'May anger not overwhelm you' means: may anger not overpower you; you yourselves should overpower anger. 'And do not get angry at the angry' means: do not become angry towards those who are angry. 'Non-anger' means: both loving-kindness and the preliminary part of loving-kindness. 'Non-harming' means: both compassion and the preliminary part of compassion. 'Then anger crushes a wicked person like a mountain' means: anger crushes a base person just as a mountain crushes. Fifth.

Tatiyo vaggo.

The Third Chapter.

Sakkasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Sakka Saṃyutta is concluded.

Iti sāratthappakāsiniyā saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus, in the Sāratthappakāsinī, the commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,

Sagāthāvaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sagāthā Vagga is concluded.

Saṃyuttanikāya-aṭṭhakathāya paṭhamo bhāgo.

The First Part of the Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary.
